1810. TO THE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">KING</a>. In requesting permission to inscribe to your Majesty the present Edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica, the Proprietor hopes, that this humble testimony of his loyalty and duty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be graciously received. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> he is the more encouraged, when he considers the zeal which your Majesty has uniformly shown for the improvement of Arts and Sciences, and the known benevolence of your Majesty's disposition, which has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> made you revered as the Father of your People, and which has always secured a favourable reception to the requests of your subjects. That, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of your Councils, and the vigour of your Fleets and Armies, your Majesty may be enabled soon to restore peace to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; that you may again have leisure to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> direct your undivided <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the improvement of Arts, and the advancement of Knowledge; that you may long reign over a free, a happy, and a loyal people; and that the Sceptre of the British Empire may be swayed by your Majesty's descend- ants to the latest posterity, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> of Your MAJESTY's Most dutiful Subject, And devoted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">Servant</a>,

MOSCOPE

Pages 411-411
WIND-Hatch, in mining, a term used to express the place at which the ore is taken out of the mines. WIND-Shock, a name given by our farmers to a dis- temper to which fruit trees, and sometimes timber trees, are subject. It is a sort of bruise and shiver throughout the whole substance of the tree; but the bark being of- ten not affected by it, it is not seen on the outside, while the inside is twisted round, and greatly injured. It is by some supposed to be occasioned by high winds; but others attribute it to lightning. Those trees are most usually affected by it whose boughs grow more out on one side than on the other. The best way of preventing this in valuable trees, is to take care in the plantation that they are sheltered well, and to cut them frequently in a regular manner while young. WIND-Taught, in sea language, denotes the same as fluff in the wind. Too much rigging, high masts, or any thing catching or holding wind aloft, is said to hold a ship wind-taught; by which they mean, that she stoops too much in her falling in a stiff gale of wind. Again, when a ship rides in a main stream of wind and weather, they strike down her top-masts, and bring her yards down, which else would hold too much wind, or be too much disturbed and wind-taught. WIND-Sails, a sort of wide tube or funnel of canvas, employed to convey a stream of fresh air downward into the lower apartments of a ship. This machine is usually extended by large hoops situated in different parts of its height. It is let down per- pendicularly through the hatches, being expanded at the lower end like the base of a cone; and having its upper side open on the side which is placed to windward, so as to receive the full current of wind; which entering the cavity, fills the tube, and rushes downwards into the lower regions of the ship. There are generally three or four of these in our capital ships of war, which, together with the ventilators, contribute greatly to preserve the health of the crew. WINDAGE of a GUN, is the difference between the diameter of the bore and the diameter of the ball.

NATURE AND CONSTRUCTION OF TRIGONOMETRICAL TABLES

Pages 89-89

It has been demonstrated in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a> (Theor. 31, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. IV.) that any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> at the centre of a circle have to one another the same proportion as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> intercepted between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> which contain the angles. Hence it is easy to infer, that an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> at the centre of a circle has the same ratio to four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> angles, that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> intercepted between the lines which contain the angle has to the whole circumference. It also follows that we may employ arches of a circle as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of angles, and thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of angles is reduced to the comparison of arches of a circle. From this principle we infer the consistency of the first of the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of definitions.

ST THOMAS OF CANTERBURY'S DAY

Pages 14-15

a festival of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, observed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 29, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Thomas Becket archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, who was murdered, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as the Romanists say, martyred, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry II. THOMAS the Reynour, called also Thomas Lermont, and Thomas of Erceldon, was born at Erceldon, a village near <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELROSE">Melrose</a> in Tweedale, in what year is uncertain; but he was an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> when Edward I. was carrying on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in Scotland. The character of Lermont as a prophet, and which was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to him with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, and other early poets in many countries, arose, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may believe Mackenyie in his Lives of Scottich Writers, from his having conferences with Eliza, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a> and prophetess at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADDINGTON">Haddington</a>. Lermont put her predictions into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and thus came in for his share of the prophetic spirit. None of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> prophecies now remain; but the following, which pretends to be one of them, is given Account of from a manuscript of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Edward I., or II. The Scottich countess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNBAR">Dunbar</a> is the lady famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of her castle against the English. Her proper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was Countess of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; but it was common in these times to style a nobleman from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> residence. Thus Gilbert Strongbow, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>, is called Earl of Strigil, from his residence at Strigil-castle, near Chepflow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, &c. La Countesse de Donbar demande a Thomas de Effedoune, quant la guere d'Effocce prendreit syn. E yl la repoundy, et dyt. When man as mad a kyng of a capped mon, When mon is levere other mons thyng than is owen. When londe thouys foreft, and foreft ys felde. When hares kendles othe herilton. When Wyt and Wille werres togedere. When mon makes stables of kyrkes; and fleles castles wyth fytes. When Rokesbours nys no burgh; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a> market is at Forwyleye. When the alde is gan, and the newe is come that doue noht. When Bamhoure ys danged with dede men. When men ledes men in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> to buyen ant to fellen. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of whaty whete is chaunged for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLT">colt</a> of ten marke. When prude prikes, ant pees is leyd in prisoun. When a Scot ne may hym hude afe hare in forme, that the Englysh ne shal hym fynde. When When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ant wrong affente the togedere, When laddes weddeth lovedies, When Scottes fleo fo faute, that for faute of ship, by drouneth hemelfve, When shal this be? Nouther in thynne tyme, ne in myne. Ah comen, ant gone, Withinne twenty wynter ant on. In fact, the prophecies of Lermont appear to have been merely traditional; nay, it seems doubtful if he ever pretended to such folly, notwithstanding MacKenzie's story of Eliza. The reverence of the people for a learned and respectable character seems to have been the sole foundation of Thomas's claim to prophecy. But, in the 16th century, prophecies were made, and ascribed to him, as well as others given to Bede, Merlin, &c. (A). They were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, 1615; reprinted 1682, and 1742. THOMISM. See Aquinas.

ST THOMAS'S DAY

Pages 14-14

a festival of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, observed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 21, in commemoration of St Thomas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>.

STILLING WAVES BY

Pages 370-371

g WAVES by means of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">Oil</a>.** See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. **WAVED,** in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is said of a bordure, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any ordinary or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, in a coat of arms, having its outlines indented in manner of the rising and falling of waves: it is used to denote, that the first of the family in whose arms it stands, acquired its honours by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. **WAVING,** in the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is the making signs to a vessel to come near or keep off. **WAX,** or Bees WAX, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a firm and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substance, moderately heavy, and of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, formed by the bees from the pollen of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a>. The best sort is that of a lively yellow colour, and an agreeable smell, somewhat like that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>: when new, it is toughish, yet easy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>; but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> it becomes harder and more brittle, loses its fine colour, and in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> its smell. It appears that wax and the pollen have for their basis a fat oil, which passes to the state of resin by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the nitric or muriatic acid be digested upon fixed oil for several months, it passes to a state resembling wax. Wax, by repeated distillations, affords an oil which possesses all the properties of volatile oils. It is reduced into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and carbonic acid by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a>. The colouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of wax is insoluble in water and in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>. Fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a> dissolve wax, and render it soluble in water. It is this faponaceous solution which forms the punic wax. It may be used as the basis of several colours; and may be made into an excellent paste for washing the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Ammoniac likewise dissolves it; and as this solvent is evaporable, it ought to be preferred when it is proposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the wax as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> yellow wax, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>, is formed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-wax, sometimes called, very improperly, virgin-wax. The greater the surface is in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, the sooner and more perfectly this operation is performed. The usual way is to melt the wax in hot water; when melted, they press it through a strainer of tolerable fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and pour it into round and very shallow <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>. When hardened by cooling, it is taken out and exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, sprinkling it now and then with water, and often <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it: by this means it soon becomes white. The best sort is of a clear and almost transparent whiteness, dry, hard, brittle, and of an agreeable smell, like that of the yellow wax, but much weaker. The common yellow wax is of very great use both in medicine and in many of the arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. It has been sometimes given internally in dysenteries and erotions of the intestines; but its greatest use is in the making ointments and plasters, and the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of those of the shops owe their confidence to it. The white wax is also an ingredient in some of the cerates and ointments of the shops; and is used in making candles, and in many of the nicer arts and manufactures where wax is required. Sealing-Wax, or Spanish-Wax, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> lac, melted and prepared with resins, and coloured with some suitable pigment. There are two kinds of sealing-wax in use; the one hard, intended for sealing letters, and other such purposes; the other soft, designed for receiving the impressions of seals of office to charters, patents, and such written instruments. The best hard <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> sealing-wax is made by mixing two parts of shell lac, well powdered, and resin and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>, powdered, of each one part, and melting this combined powder over a gentle fire; and when the ingredients seem thoroughly incorporated, working the wax into sticks. Seed-lac may be substituted for the shell-lac; and instead of resin, boiled <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> turpentine may be used. A coarser, hard, red sealing-wax, may be made, by mixing two parts of resin, and of shell-lac, or vermilion and red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, mixed in the proportion of one part of the vermilion to two of the red lead, of each one part; and proceeding as in the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>. For a cheaper kind, the vermilion may be omitted, and the shell-lac also, for very coarse uses. Wax of other colours is made by substituting other colouring matters for vermilion, as verditer for blue, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> for black wax. For uncoloured, soft sealing-wax, take of bees wax, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>; of turpentine, three ounces; and of olive oil, one ounce; <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> them in a proper vessel over the fire, and let them boil for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the wax <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be then fit to be formed into rolls or cakes for use. For red, black, green, blue, yellow, and purple soft sealing-wax, add to the preceding composition an ounce or more of any ingredients directed above for colouring the hard sealing-wax, and stir the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> till the colouring ingredients be incorporated with the wax. WAX-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">Work</a>, the representation of the faces, &c. of persons living or dead; made by applying <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in a kind of paste, and thus forming a mould containing the exact representation of the features. Into this mould melted wax is poured, and thus a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a> are formed; which being painted and set with glass eyes, and the figures dressed in their proper habits, they bear such a resemblance that it is difficult to distinguish between the copy and the original.

SUFFOCATING THESE VERMIN BY

Pages 175-181

g these <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> by means of the fumes of sulphur, as on board of ships, in granaries and other buildings which can be shut up, is sometimes also successfully Vermin. Successfully practised. Rats and other vermin have also been effectually destroyed and eradicated by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> wood in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> apartments, thus producing fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> carbonic acid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, by which they are also suffocated. Moles.—Various methods have been proposed for the destruction of these animals. But the following observations on this subject, which we shall give in the words of the author, seem to be more satisfactory than anything we have met with. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> damage (says he) which moles occasion in cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and particularly gardens, is well known; and the best means of remedying this evil is by destroying all those that make their appearance, as far as possible. The secrets which quacks sell for exterminating these destructive animals are of very little avail; and even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> produces no effect, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> does not drink, and lives only on roots and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. In regard to gins and traps, the moles must be enticed to them by some kind of bait, which does not always produce the intended effect. Buffon advises a trench to be dug around the hills under which they conceal themselves, and thus to cut them off from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the neighbouring ground. This method requires three or four people to dig trenches; and though it may prove effectual, it is attended with too much trouble. The other methods proposed by different naturalists are neither easier nor more certain. "It is well known that this animal lives under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it comes forth from its holes, it is only when compelled to do so, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> accumulated after the heavy rains which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, or when the earth is so much parched and dried by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> drought, that it can no longer continue its labour; but it again creeps back into the earth when it finds a spot convenient for its purpose. "This animal, as already remarked, feeds upon roots and worms, and for this reason is generally found in rich fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; but never in that which is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLY">marly</a> or stony. In the winter time it retires to elevated places, because it is there best secured from inundations. In summer, however, it descends to the low hillocks and flat land, and above all makes choice of meadows for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of its residence; because it finds the earth there freer and softer for it to dig through. If the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> continues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> dry, it repairs to the borders of ditches, the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and streams, and to places contiguous to hedges. "The mole breeds generally at the beginning of winter, and the months when they are found big with young are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> and February. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April a great many of their young may be seen. Among 122 caught in the month of May by my method, there were only four big with young. This animal cannot live without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a>; it is obliged to find its nourishment in the bowels of the earth; and on that account is under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of making those long subterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> which are found between one mole-hill and another. In general it begins to dig five or six inches under the surface; it scrapes the earth before it on one side till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> becomes too great for it to labour with ease; it then works towards the surface; and by pushing with its head, and the assistance of its nervous paws, gradually raises up the earth which inconveniences it, and which produces those small hills so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in fields. After getting rid of the earth in this manner, it proceeds forwards, and continues its labour as before. The farther it goes the more hills are produced. At each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of its labour it throws up four or five. "In places overgrown with grass and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, the mole is often contented with only forcing a passage through between the roots; and when the earth in gardens has been newly watered, it keeps itself at the depth of scarcely half an inch under the surface. This animal shews an equal aversion to great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and in order to avoid both, it forces its way, when either prevail, to the greatest depth in the earth. "It continues its labour at all times, because it is necessary for it to procure nourishment. It is absolutely false that it sleeps throughout the winter, as some naturalists have asserted; for it throws up the earth in the coldest season, as well as during the summer. It is most busily employed towards the end of winter, and at that period forms the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hills. To this it is impelled by more than one reason. In the first place, it must provide nourishment for its young; secondly, it finds it easiest at that time to dig its way through the earth; and lastly, as the air begins to be milder, the animal then recovers that strength which it had lost during the intense cold. At this season, therefore, it is most proper to pursue means for exterminating this animal, as it can be destroyed with greater ease while employed at its labour. "The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> is much stronger than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, and the hills thrown up by the former are much larger as well as more numerous. The periods when the mole is most busily employed in digging are in the morning, at sunrise, at noon, and at sunset. In dry weather moles are observed to throw up the earth for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> only at sunrise, and in winter when the earth has been somewhat heated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays. "A person may easily discover how many moles are contained in a certain space of ground, by counting the fresh raised mole-hills which have no communication with each other. I must remark also, that this animal has very bad sight, being almost totally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>; but its hearing, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is so much the more acute. "I shall now proceed to the method of destroying them. Immediately at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be necessary to make a tour round the garden or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, from which it is wished to exterminate the moles; for at that time they will be all found at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as may be seen by the hills newly thrown up. If the person is then close to the hill, he must proceed as the gardeners do, and turn up with a spade the hill together with the digger. The passage is then cut through before the animal is aware of the attack, and therefore it has not power to escape. If the mole-hill be fresh, even though the animal may not be throwing up earth, the person ought not to lose his time in waiting, but should immediately proceed to the operation above mentioned. "If you find a fresh hill standing by itself, which seems to shew by its situation that it has no communication with any other, which is always the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> when the mole has worked from the surface downwards in endeavouring to procure a more convenient habitation, after the hill has been turned up with the spade, a bucket of water should be poured over the mouth of the passage. By these means the animal, which is at no great distance, will be obliged to come forth, and may be easily caught with the hand. "You "You may discover also whether a hill has any communication with another, if you apply your <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> to it, and then cough or make a loud noise. If it has no communication with the neighbouring hills, you will hear the terrified animal make a noise by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. It will then be impossible for it to escape; and you may either pour water into the hole, or turn up the hill with a spade until the mole is found; for in general it never goes deeper into the earth than from fifteen to eighteen inches. "When any of the beds in a garden have been newly watered, the mole, attracted by the coolness and moisture, readily repairs thither, and takes up its residence in them, making a passage at the depth of scarcely an inch below the surface. In that case it may be easily caught. When you see it at work, you need only <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> behind the animal with your feet on the passage to prevent its retreat, and then turn up the hill with a spade; by which means you will be sure to catch it. "When you dig after it with a spade, the animal forces its way downwards into the earth in a perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, in order that it may better escape the threatened danger. In that case it will not be necessary to dig long, but to pour water over the place, which will soon make the animal return upwards. "People in general are not aware of the great mischief occasioned in fields and gardens by these animals. We are, however, informed by Buffon, that in the year 1740 he planted 15 or 16 acres of land with acorns, and that the greater part of them were in a little time carried away by the moles to their subterranean retreats. In many of these there were found half a bushel, and in others a bushel. Buffon, after this circumstance, caused a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> traps to be constructed, by which in less than three weeks he caught 1350. To this instance of the devastation occasioned by these animals, we may add the following: In the year 1742 they were so numerous in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, that one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> alone caught between five and six thousand of them. The destruction occasioned by these animals is, however, no new phenomenon. We are informed by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENEDOS">Tenedos</a>, the Trojans, and the Æolians, were infested by them in the earliest ages. For this reason a temple was erected to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> Smythius, the destroyer of moles. "Insects.—Many insects, in the different states of existence through which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, are exceedingly troublesome and destructive. Sometimes they spread their devastations in the state of larva or grub, and sometimes in that of perfect insect. "Of the coleopterous insects, the grub of the cockchafer, which is a brownish or chestnut-coloured beetle, commits the greatest ravages. This beetle appears during great part of the summer, the most plentiful in May or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and hence called the May bug. It flies only in the evening, and lodges during the day under the leaves of trees, which it devours, and is sometimes in such numbers, as to defoliate whole woods. The beetle deposits its eggs in the earth, and from these are hatched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or bluish grubs, that feed on the roots of grass, corn, and other vegetables, during the whole summer. In the winter they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> deep in the earth; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, as vegetation advances, they rise to the surface, and renew their work of destruction. In this state they continue for four, five, or six years, before they change to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a> state, in which they remain till the month of May, when the perfect insect appears. As these insects require so many years to assume the perfect form, they only appear occasionally sufficiently numerous to be extensively destructive to the crops of grain, or vegetables in general. Their numbers, however, have often produced great alarm, and even excited the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of governments to offer rewards for an effectual method of destroying them. "In the spring season, if the weather prove warm, when the land is ploughed up, these grubs are generally near the surface as to be turned up with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>; and being thus exposed, they are picked up and devoured by various birds, which, it is suspected, should not be disturbed or driven away in this salutary labour. When these grubs infest meadow land, it has been proposed to drown them in their holes by overflowing it. But it is supposed that this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> would not be successful, even where it is practicable, unless there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of clay immediately under the soil, to retain the water for a sufficient length of time. A more efficacious way is recommended to prevent the increase of the grubs, by destroying the flies in May or June, before they have deposited their eggs. This may be done by shaking and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the trees and hedges in the middle of the day; and, as this is a work which may be performed by children, it is a less difficult task than would at first sight be imagined. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">Domestic</a> fowls are remarkably fond of these beetles, so that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> object is thus gained, the destruction of the beetles and the procuring of food for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>. "Some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the dermestes, and also of the genus pinus, are exceedingly destructive in the cabinets of naturalists, and also to furniture. Various methods have been recommended to stop their ravages. We believe the most effectual is spirit of turpentine, when it can be properly applied. A solution of corrosive sublimate is sometimes employed, but it should be recollected that it seldom fails in time to produce some chemical change on animal and vegetable matters. Objects of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history as birds, animals, &c., are sometimes exposed to the moderate heat of an oven, or before a fire, for several hours; but this method will also be attended with injurious effects, unless practised with great care. Insects which infect furniture have been destroyed by the application of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and allowing it to remain for a day or two, before the furniture is rubbed up. Japanned or varnished furniture may be secured from the effects of these insects, by re-coating it, when they are in the larva state, by which they are deprived of air. Railing, and other works out of doors, which are exposed to the weather, are sometimes eaten with insects, and particularly by some of the larvae of the genus curculio. The wood thus attacked may be prevented from farther ravages, by a fresh coat of paint. "The earwig is a destructive insect in the flower, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, and fruit garden. To prevent their depredations, it has been recommended to take them by the hand, when they come out during the night in search of food. They may be taken also by rolling up a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and hanging it up on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which they infest; for in these places they take shelter through the day. Another method of destroying them has been mentioned, and that is to watch them towards morning with the view of discovering the haunts to which they... they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> during the day; and this discovery being made, which may perhaps be a melon frame, dunghill, or heap of rubbish, the removing of which will destroy the greater number of these troublesome insects. The small insect which commits such depredations among turnips, by eating the feeding leaves as soon as they appear, as frequently to destroy whole crops, is supposed to be a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> polished beetle, belonging to the genus *Chrysomela*. It does not seem to be well ascertained whether this small beetle, which is better known by the name of turnip fly, commits its ravages in the larva or in the beetle state. It is said that it prefers the leaves of the common radish to those of the turnip, and it is therefore recommended to sow radishes along with the turnips, to prevent the destruction of the latter. Of the insects belonging to the order hemiptera, there are some which are exceedingly destructive. The cockroach, a native of the warmer parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> and the West Indies, is a very troublesome, and a very voracious insect. It has been introduced into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and particularly into the seaport <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, in consequence of commercial intercourse. It comes out to feed in the night-time, and eats almost of every thing that comes in its way. Cock-roaches are easily taken by the following method. Cover the outside of a deep glass or basin with paper; introduce some bits of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> into the basin or glass, and set it in a place frequented by the cock-roaches. They creep up by means of the paper on the outside, and drop into the vessel; but in consequence of its smooth polished surface, they cannot effect their escape. In the same way crickets and beetles may be taken and destroyed. It is quite unnecessary to speak of the means of destroying the myriads of locusts which not unfrequently infest eastern countries, and particularly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; for no means are likely to be devised, which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to resist the effects of such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> of foes, by whose ravages every green thing is consumed; but the insect itself becomes, among the poorer inhabitants of those countries, a partial substitute for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the earth which it has destroyed. The insects are taken, reduced to powder, and converted into a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. The common or the bed-bug is a very troublesome, and a very common inmate in the crowded houses of many large towns in this country. Its usual haunts are the crevices of wood, and particularly those pieces of furniture which are usually kept in the warmest corners of the apartment. Cleanliness will perhaps be found the best preservative against the introduction and increase of these insects; but sometimes even the greatest care and attention are ineffectual in keeping houses entirely free from them. When it can be conveniently done, they are completely destroyed by immersing the furniture in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, or by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a> it in an oven; and by filling up the crevices or holes which were their haunts, with glaziers putty, their return and increase will thus be prevented. But a very effectual method of destroying bugs, is to wash the places which they frequent with spirit of turpentine, and then filling up the holes as already mentioned. It is a curious circumstance in the history of these insects, that some persons entirely escape from their attacks, while to others they are exceedingly troublesome and distressing. It is said that lavender-water, sprinkled over the bed-clothes, often prevents their approach. How far this is the vermin, we have had no opportunity of ascertaining. The small moth, which in the caterpillar state commits such ravages on woollen cloths, furs, and other animal substances, which remain for any length of time in dark undisturbed places, may be destroyed with the greatest certainty and facility, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the substances on which they are suspected to make their depredations, to the vapour of spirit of turpentine, or brushing them with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> dipped into the same fluid. This should be done about the months of September or October; but their effects may be prevented by placing the cloths, furs, &c., which are likely to become their residence, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> situation, about the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August. The different kinds of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a> are very numerous. Every animal has its peculiar species, and even mankind are not free from this pest. It is often the consequence of indolence and naughtiness, and it is observed that the lice which infest any animal increase prodigiously when that animal becomes languid and sickly. We believe that the application of spirits of turpentine, already so often recommended, would also be effectual in this case; but mercurial preparations afford a certain remedy against these insects. For this purpose a very small quantity of what is called mercurial ointment may be employed. At the same time it ought to be recollected, that cleanliness is the best preservative. A singular notion prevails in this country, and even among persons who are by no means in the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, that it is a good sign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> when children's heads are infested with these animals; and on this account they are not very anxious in having them entirely eradicated. A moment's reflection may show the absurdity of such an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, so that it would be a waste of time to adduce serious arguments against it. It is perhaps more difficult for mankind to secure themselves and their habitations from the visits of the common flea. Cleanliness, however, may do much even in effecting this; and in particular it appears to us, that it would be extremely useful, frequently to rub up with a piece of cloth the more inaccessible parts of furniture or apartments, or perhaps it would answer better to employ a small hard brush. By the less accessible places we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the corners and crevices of rooms and furniture where dust is apt to collect, and especially the canvas part of a bed. We are persuaded that spirits of turpentine might also be found useful for the destruction of these very troublesome insects. The Scotch myrtle (*Myrica <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">gale</a>*, Lim.) a plant very common in low and moist moorish places in this country, is said to be an excellent remedy, in consequence of its powerful aromatic odour, against the attacks of these animals. For this purpose, the plant is strewn about the apartment or bed which is infested with fleas. The following method of destroying or driving away all kinds of noxious vermin from fields and gardens, it is said, has been proved by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to be effectual. It is recommended by M. Scoloff, and the account of it is taken from the *Philosophical Transactions*. As the destructive power of quicklime (says the author), heightened by a fixed alkali, which corrodes, dissolves and destroys all the tender parts of animals, has been long known, I thought this mixture would be the best means for accomplishing the object I had in view. I took three three parts, therefore, of quicklime, newly made, and two parts of a saturated solution of fixed alkali in water, and thence obtained a somewhat milky liquor sufficiently caustic, highly noxious and poisonous to earthworms and other small animals; for, as soon as it touched any part of their bodies, it occasioned in them violent symptoms of great uneasiness. If this liquor be poured into those holes in which the earthworms reside underground, they immediately throw themselves out as if driven by some force; and, after various contortions, either languish or die. If the leaves of plants or fruit-trees, frequented by the voracious caterpillars, which are so destructive to them, be sprinkled over with this liquor, these insects suddenly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> their bodies and drop to the ground. For, though <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has defended them tolerably well by their hairy skins from anything that might injure their delicate bodies, yet, as soon as they touch with their feet or mouths leaves which have been moistened by this liquor, they become as it were stupified, instantly contract themselves, and fall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. "I had not an opportunity of trying a like experiment on locusts; yet we may conclude, and not without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, from their nature and the general destructive qualities of the above liquor, that they, in like manner, may be driven from corn-fields, if it be possible to sprinkle the corn with the liquor by means of a machine. "With regard to plants or corn, these sustain no injury from the liquor, because it has no power over the productions of the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, as I have fully learned from experience; or, if any hurt be suspected, all the danger will be removed by the first shower that falls. This liquor may be procured in abundance in every place where lime is burnt. If the lime be fresh, one part of it infused in about seventy parts of common water will produce real lime-water. The want of the fixed alkali may be supplied by boiling wood ashes in water, and thickening the ley by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>. "The liquor might be employed also to kill bugs and other domestic insects which are noxious and troublesome; but on account of its strong, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACHRYMATORY">lachrymatory</a> smell, which offends the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body to putridity, I dare not recommend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it in houses that are inhabited. Besides, bugs may be easily got rid of, as I have repeatedly found from experience, by the oily pickle that remains in casks in which salted herrings have been packed. To this liquor they have a strong aversion; and, if they are moistened with it, they die in a very short time." For deflouring insects and caterpillars, which infest fruit trees, the following method is recommended as having been successfully practised. The author observes that "The present year, for instance, (1805), offers a singularity which I have not before perceived. In some districts the cherry-tree has experienced, at the time of its blossoming, colds and winds which have prevented it from setting; but another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, not less disastrous, has attacked the cherry-trees and plum-trees over several districts in France. Great swarms of little animals resembling vine-frettters, but which are not so in reality, established their habitations at the extremity of the branches of the cherry-trees. As soon as a branch was attacked, the leaves curled, and the juice was dried up. On opening the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, a considerable number of ants was discovered, which, jointly with the insect which began the ravages, fucked the branch, and made it wither. What I have remarked is, that usually, when the vine-fretters attack any tree, the neighbouring tree very soon experiences the same fate; but the attack of this year is only partial. In an alley of cherry-trees which I polled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> trees have been attacked, but not those which are next each other. One tree was placed between two which were very much damaged by these insects, and yet this one was not hurt. "On these vermin the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> had no effect at all: this convinces me that they are different from the ordinary kind. "Plum-trees, when attacked by the same insect, do not lose their fruit like the cherry-trees; but the little animals cover them with more rapidity, so as to extinguish even the appearance of fruit. "Having effectually watered a plum-tree, I covered it with ashes, in the manner we treat beans and cabbages, and the vermin were destroyed; but this is only practicable with a tree of low height. "I made one remark, which I think is essential to communicate: it is, that plum-trees planted in ground which is not necessarily watered, are less attacked by these insects than those which have experienced a humidity communicated by the plants in their neighbourhood, to which watering is absolutely necessary. I had one planted in a bed of artichokes: we know very well that this plant requires plenty of water; and the tree was entirely covered with insects. Its leaves withered, and the fruit fell off; while two other plum-trees, in ground not watered at all, were much less attacked. This convinces me that these were not the ordinary vermin abundant in dry seasons. "I was only able to protect my cherries a little, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the extremities of the damaged branches. "Several people had recourse to sulphur; but I did not follow that method. The smoke of sulphur destroys the insect, I admit, but it is at least equally dangerous to the tree; I always prefer an asperion of the tree with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>-suds. This very year I experienced the good effects of it. I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> my plum-trees look green again, and the insects abandon them. The asperion is very easily managed, by means of watering-pots or small garden-engines. I have also employed a ley of wood-ashes with the same success as soap and water. "An observation equally important which I have made is, the great damage done this season in all orchards by the caterpillar. As soon as they devoured the young leaves, they attacked the fruit. In spite of the great care taken in spring to get rid of them, the number of these insects is incredible. I have seen them unite on the large branches, fix their nests to them, and protect them by means of the downy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which covers the buds of the ensuing season. Whatever precaution is taken, it is almost impossible not to destroy these buds. It is only necessary to take off these nests and burn them; and this is the only way of getting rid of the coves. I employed the same asperion for my apple-trees, and by that means got rid of their enemies also. "The following methods are practised in Germany for freeing granaries from mites or weevils: "I. Cover completely the walls and rafters, above and below, of the granaries which are infested by weevils." Vermi. vils, with quicklime flaked in water in which trefoil, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a>, and hyssop have been boiled. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> ought to be applied as hot as possible. 2. A very sagacious farmer has succeeded in destroying weevils by a very easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. In the month of June, when his granaries were all empty, he collected great quantities of the largest-sized ants in sacks, and then scattered them about the places infested with the weevils. The ants immediately fell upon and devoured every one of them; nor have any weevils since that time been seen on his premises. 3. Another method, not less efficacious, but which requires a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of care and attention in the application of it, is the following:—Place in your granaries a number of chafing-dishes filled with lighted pieces of wood. Every aperture must then be carefully closed, in order to prevent any fresh air from entering. The carbonic acid gas, produced from the burning wood, proves fatal to the insects. Rats and mice, also, are so strongly affected by it, that they are seen running out of their holes, and dying in all directions. The persons employed to manage this process must take great care of their own safety, by keeping a current of air around them until the burning wood is properly placed. Another danger may arise from the premises taking fire; but this also may be avoided by proper caution, particularly if they are paved with brick or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>.* 4. Grain, it is said, has been preserved from weevils and other destructive insects, by covering the heaps with pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> cloth dipped in water and wrung out. At the end of two hours the weevils are found adhering to the cloths, which are to be removed carefully and plunged in water for some time to drown. A plant of henbane placed in the middle of a heap of grain is said also to drive away the insects. They must then be watched and destroyed as they attempt to escape. Sulphur or flower of brimstone is recommended as being an excellent remedy against the effects of insects on plants. It may be applied by dusting the leaves affected, either by tying it up in muslin cloth, or with a puff for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> powder, or with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DREDGING">dredging</a> box. But the sulphur not only destroys the worms and insects which infest trees; it seems also to render the trees more healthy and vigorous. This was particularly the case with some peach trees on which it was sprinkled. The following method, discovered by M. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a>, is proposed for destroying earth-flies, bugs, ants, &c. Take black soap, of the best kind, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, the same quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a> two pounds, and sixty <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of river or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-water. Divide the water into two parts, one of which must be poured into a vessel destined for that purpose: suffer the soap to dissolve in it, and add the mushrooms after they have been a little pounded. Boil the other half of the water in a kettle, and tie up the sulphur in a bit of rag or piece of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and suspend from it a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in order that it may sink in the water. During the time the water is kept boiling, which must be at least twenty minutes, stir it continually with a stick, and press the bag containing the sulphur, that the latter may be forced out into the water, and communicate to it the necessary fire, girth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. When the liquor is taken from the fire, pour it directly into the cask, and stir it round for a considerable time: the process of stirring must be repeated daily till it acquire a fetid smell. Experience has shown that the more fetid the mixture is, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> is the greater. Each time that the mixture is stirred, the cask must be stopped immediately after. When you wish to use the liquid, nothing is necessary but to sprinkle a little of it on the plants which you are desirous of preserving, or to dip their branches in it. It will be better, however, to make use of a syringe, having at the end a head, an inch or an inch and a half in diameter, pierced with small holes. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> may be used for tender plants; when you apply the liquid to trees, a syringe with larger holes must be employed. Caterpillars, beetles, earth-fleas, bugs, and the tree-lice which infest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees, will be destroyed by the first application of the liquid. Insects which reside below the earth, such as wasps, hornets, ants, &c., require that the liquid should be squirted out gently, and without intermission, that it may better penetrate to their nests. Ants nests, according to their size, require from two to three measures of liquid, and in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it must be applied for twenty-four hours. When the ants assemble in another place, the process must be repeated. Two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUX_VOMICA">nux vomica</a> may be added to the mixture, and boiled along with the sulphur. This sublimate, particularly when you wish to destroy ants, will be of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. When the whole of the liquid in the cask has been used, the residue must be buried in the earth to prevent domestic animals from eating it.* The use of elder as a preservative to vegetables against the depredations of insects is detailed in the following observations. Common elder has appeared to me useful, 1st, For preventing cabbage plants from being devoured or damaged by caterpillars; 2d, To prevent blights, and their effects on fruit and other trees; 3d, To preserve corn from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flies and other insects; 4th, To secure turnips from the ravage of flies, &c. 1st, The strong and fetid odour of a bunch of elder leaves induced me to think that different kinds of butterflies might be inconvenienced by it in proportion to their delicacy. I therefore took some young twigs of elder, at the period when butterflies began to appear, and whipped well with them some cabbage plants, but in such a manner as not to damage them. Since that time, during two summers, though the butterflies hovered round the plants, I never saw one of them <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> on them; and I do not think that a single butterfly was hatched on the cabbages treated in this manner, though a neighbouring board was dirtied by them in the usual manner. 2d, After a short reflection on the effects here mentioned, and on blights, which, in my opinion, are chiefly occasioned by small flies and small insects, whose organs are still more delicate than those of the former, I was induced to whip in the same manner with elder twigs, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as I could reach, the branches of a plum-tree which grew in an espalier. The whipped leaves remained green and in a good condition, while from at least six inches above to the top of the tree the rest of the leaves were blighted, wrinkled, and full of worms. It is here to be observed that the tree was in full flower when I whipped it, therefore much too late for this operation, which ought to have been performed once or twice before flowering. But I am of opinion, that if trees were besprinkled with a strong infusion of elder every every eight or 15 days, the success would be certain, and that there would be no danger of injuring either the flowers or the fruit. 3rd. What the farmers call the yellows in corn, and which they consider as a kind of blight, is the effect, as every one knows, of a small yellow fly with blue wings, nearly of the size of a gnat. It lays its eggs in the ear of wheat, and produces a worm almost invisible to the naked eye, but which, when seen by a magnifying glass, is a large yellow larva, having the shining colour of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>. This fly is so productive, that I have counted upwards of forty worms in the chaff of one ear of wheat, which was a number sufficient to destroy it entirely. I therefore proposed to make my experiment as soon as possible; but the heat and drought of the season having advanced the wheat more than usual, it was in flower before I could attempt it. Next morning, however, at break of day, two servants having drawn bundles of elder over the ears of wheat on each side of the furrow, backwards and forwards, in places where the wheat was not so far advanced, I hoped that the fetid effluvia of the elder would prevent the flies from remaining on the ears that were covered with them: and, indeed, I was not entirely disappointed; for, on examining my wheat some time after, I found that the part which had been beaten with elder was much less damaged than that which had not been treated in the same manner. I have no doubt, that, had I employed this precaution sooner, the corn would have been completely preserved. Should this be the case, the process is simple; and I flatter myself that fine crops of corn may be saved by these means from this small insect, which is so destructive to them. One of these yellow flies laid on my thumb at least eight or ten eggs, of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form, in the small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of time which I employed in walking over two or three furrows, holding it by the wings, and which I could not observe without the assistance of a magnifying glass. 4th. It often happens that whole crops of turnips are destroyed while young, in consequence of being pricked by certain insects. I have great reason to think that this evil may be prevented in an effectual manner, by causing a person to draw a bunch of elder, sufficiently large to cover about the breadth of a foot, over the young turnips, going backwards and forwards. What confirms me in this idea is, that, having drawn a bunch of elder over a bed of young cauliflowers which had begun to be pricked, they afterwards remained untouched by these insects. Another fact which tends to support this idea is, that when my neighbourhood, about eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years ago, was so infested with caterpillars that they devoured all the vegetables, leaving scarcely a green leaf untouched, they spared the elder trees amidst this general devastation, and never molested them. In reflecting on these circumstances, I am of opinion that the elder might be introduced with advantage into our gardens, as the means of preserving fruit-trees and various plants from the rapacity of insects. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> elder appears to me to exhale a much more fetid smell than the common elder, and therefore ought to be preferred in making experiments on this subject.*

THESEA

Pages 13-13

in antiquity, feasts celebrated by the Athenians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, consisting of sports and games, with mirth and banquets. Such as were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and unable to contribute to them were entertained at the public expense.

THESEUS

Pages 13-13

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of antiquity, ranked among the demigods, whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is fabulous. He was the reputed son of Ægeus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He threw Sciron, a cruel robber, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a precipice; fastened Procrustes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> pine, which being let loose tore him asunder; killed the Minotaur kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a> by King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>; and by the affluence of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, Ariadne, who gave him a clue, escaped out of that labyrinth, and sailed with his deliverer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAXOS">Naxos</a>, where he had the ingratitude to leave her. Theseus afterwards overcame the Centaurs, subdued the Thebans, and defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a>. He assisted his friend Pirithous in his expedition to the infernal regions to carry off Proserpine; but was imprisoned by Pluto, till he was released by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. He is also said to have established the Ithmean games, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>; to have united the twelve cities of Attica; and to have founded a republic there, 1236 B.C. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, taking a voyage into Epirus, he was seized by Aidonius king of the Molossians; meanwhile Melanthus rendered himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Athens. But at length Theseus being released from prison, retired to Scyros, where King Lycomedes caused him to be thrown from the top of a rock. Theseus had several wives; the first of whom was Helena the daughter of Tyndarus; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, Hypolita <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the Amazons; and the last, Phedra filleter to Ariadne, who punished him for his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> to her sister, by her incestuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for his son Hippolitus.

THESIS

Pages 13-13

a general position which a person advances, and offers to maintain. In taking degrees in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, the candidates are generally obliged to write a thesis, which they must afterwards defend.

THESIUM

Pages 13-13

Base Fluellin; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of pentandria, and order of monogynia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THESPIS

Pages 13-13

a famous Greek tragic poet, and the first representor of tragedy at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He carried his troop from village to village in a waggon, from which they performed their pieces. Alcætis was the first tragedy they performed at Athens, 536 B.C. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">THEATRE</a>.

THESSALIAN CHAIR

Pages 13-13

so called from Thessaly, where chairs of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> were most in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; it is recommended by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a machine for reducing a recent luxation of the shoulder bone. The back of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> is perpendicular to the seat, as Galen tells us; by which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> it is distinguished and accommodated to the operation.

THESSALY

Pages 13-13

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, whose boundaries have been different at different periods. Properly speaking, Thessaly was bounded on the south by the southern parts of Greece, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Graecia Propria; east, by the Ægean; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> and Mygdonia; and west, by Illyricum and Epirus. It was generally divided into four separate provinces, Thessaliotes, Pelagiotis, Iliotissi, and Phthiotis, to which some add <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a>. It has been severally called Æmonia, Peliæicum, Argot, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELLAS">Hellas</a>, Argeia, Dryopis, Pelopidia, Pyrrhœa, &c. The name of Thessaly is derived from Lempris-Thessalus, one of its monarchs. Thessaly is famous for its deluge which happened there in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and cities are also celebrated, such as Olympus, Pelion, Ossa, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARISSA">Larissa</a>, &c. The Argonauts were partly natives of Thessaly. The inhabitants of the country passed for a treacherous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, so that false <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was called Thessalian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, and a perfidious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> a Thessalian deceit. Thessaly was originally governed by kings, till it became subject to the Macedonian monarchs. The cavalry was universally esteemed, and the people were superstitious and addicted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> and incantations. See Lucan, lib. vi. ver. 438, &c.; Dionys. i. 219; Curt. lib. iii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 2; Aelian, Var. Hist. lib. iii. cap. 1; Paul. lib. iv. cap. 36; lib. x. cap. 1; Mela, lib. ii. cap. 3; Justin, lib. vii. cap. 6; Diod. iv. Thessaly is now called Janina, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of European <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, bounded by Macedonia on the north, by the Archipelago on the east, by Achaia or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVADIA">Livadia</a> on the south, and by Epirus on the west.

THETIS

Pages 13-13

in Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the wife of Oceanus, and the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a> and Doris, who were married to each other; and from this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> sprung the nymphs of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Among the sea nymphs there was one named Thetis the Younger, who excelled all the rest in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and for whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> conceived such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, that he resolved to espouse her; but being informed by the Delphines that she would bring forth a son who would rise above his father, he married her to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a>. To their nuptials all the gods and goddesses were invited except <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">Discord</a>, who, to be revenged for this contempt, threw a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> apple into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, on which was engraven, For the fairest. Juno, Pallas, and Venus, disputed for this apple; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> being chosen to decide the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, adjudged it to Venus. From this marriage of Thetis and Peleus sprung <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>.

THEURGY

Pages 13-14

ἱεραγονια, a name which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> gave to that sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> which we sometimes call <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> magic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the white art. The word is formed from ἱερος, "God," and γονια, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>;" q.d. the art of doing divine things, or things which God alone can do: or the power of working extraordinary and supernatural things, by invoking the names. Theurgy names of God, saints, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, &c. Accordingly, those who have written of magic in general, divide it into three parts: the first whereof is called theurgy, as operating by divine or celestial means; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> magic, performed by the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and the third, comprehending <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECROMANCY">necromancy</a>, sorcery, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a> or magic, performed by the affluence of demons or departed men. See MAGIC. THIBET. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIBET">TIBET</a>. THIGH. See ANATOMY, No. 58.

a general name for any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> operation of the mind. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>. THIRLAGE. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">LAW</a>, No. clxx. 12—18.

THIRIPS

a genus of insects belonging to the order of hemiptera. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THIRST

Pages 14-14

an uneasy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> arising from a deficiency of the saliva to moisten the inward parts of the mouth. Hence arises a strong desire for drink; and thirst is a symptom generally attending fevers of all kinds.—Thirst is best allayed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> kept a while in the mouth, then spit out, and repeated as required; a bit of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> chewed with a little water, which latter may be gradually swallowed; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the person is very hot, brandy is the best for holding in the mouth, but should be spit out again: except in fevers, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> draughts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water are hurtful. Preservation against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">Hunger</a> and Thirst. See HUNGER.

THISTLE

Pages 14-14

a name applied to different genera and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging chiefly to the syngenesia class. See CARDUIUS, ONOPORDUM, SERRATULA, SONCHUS, and alfo DIPSACUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Order of the THISTLE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of St Andrew, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> in Scotland, the rise and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of which is variously related by different authors. Lefley bishop of Rois reports, that the night before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between Athelstan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> and Hungus king of the Picts, a bright <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, in form of that whereon St Andrew (the tutelar saint of Scotland) suffered martyrdom, appeared to Hungus; who having gained the victory, ever after bore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of that cross on his banners. Others assert, that Achaius king of Scotland first instituted this order, after having made the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> offensive and defensive with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> king of France. But although the thistle had been acknowledged as the symbol of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Scotland from the reign of Achaius, yet some refer the beginning of this order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VII. of France. Others <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the foundation of it as low as the year 1500. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ensign is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> collar composed of thistles and sprigs of rue interlaced with annulets of gold, having pendent thereto the image of St Andrew with his cross, and the motto, NEMO ME IMPUNE LACESSET. "No body shall provoke me with impunity."
