The ordinary or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ensign worn by the knights is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of four silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and over them a green circle, bordered and lettered with gold, containing the said motto, and in the centre is a thistle; all which is embroidered on their left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and worn with the collar, with a green ribbon over the left shoulder, and brought under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> arm; pendent thereto is the image of St Andrew, with his cross, in a purple robe, within an oval of gold enamelled vert, with the former motto; but sometimes they wear, encircled in the same manner, a thistle crowned. About the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Reformation, this order was dropped, till James II. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> resumed it, by creating eight knights. The Revolution unfettered it again; and it lay neglected, till <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, in 1703, restored it to the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, of twelve knights of St Andrew.

THLAPSI

Pages 14-14
BASTARD-CRESS, or mithridate-mustard; a genus of plants belonging to the clas of tetradynamia. See BOTANY Index. THOLOUSE. See TOULOUSE. THOMÆANS, THOMISTS. See CHRISTIANS of ST THOMAS. THOMAS AQUINAS. See AQUINAS.

THOINIA

Pages 17-17

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of diandria, and order of monogynia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THOITH

Pages 17-17
or THEUT, (called by the Phoenicians Taanit, by the Greeks Hermes, and by the Romans Mercury), was a Phoenician of very superior talents, and one of the civilizers of mankind. He was prime minister to Osiris, whom, after his death, he deified; and he was himself deified by his countrymen the Egyptians, for the benefits that he had rendered to the human race. See Mercury, Mythology, No 34, and Polytheism, No 18.

THOMSON

Pages 15-16

James, an excellent British poet, the son of a Scotch divine, was born in the shire of Roxburgh in 1700, and was educated in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> with a view to the ministry. But his genius inclining him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, which he soon found would be incompatible with that of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least might prevent his being provided for in that way in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he relinquished his views of engaging in the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, and repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of some encouragement which he had received from a lady of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> there, a friend of his mother. The reception he met with wherever he was introduced, emboldened him to risk the publication of his excellent poem on Winter.—This piece was published in 1726; and from the universal applause it met with, Mr Thomson's acquaintance was courted by people of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and fashion. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> advantage which it procured him was the acquaintance of Dr Rundle, afterward bishop of Derry, who introduced him to the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Talbot; and some years after, when the eldest son of that nobleman was to make his tour on the continent, Mr Thomson was chosen as a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> for him. The expectations which his Winter had raised, were fully satisfied by the successive publications of the other seasons; of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">Summer</a>, in the year 1727; of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">Spring</a>, in the following year; and of Autumn, in a quarto edition of his works, in 1730. Beside the Seasons, and his tragedy of Sophonisba, written and acted with applause in the year 1729, he had, in 1727, published his poem to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, with an account of his chief discoveries; in which he was assisted by his friend Mr Gray, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> well versed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. That same year the resentment of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, for the interruption of their trade by the Spaniards in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, running very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, Mr Thomson zealously took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in it, and wrote his Battainia, to rouse the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. With the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Talbot, our author visited most of the courts in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and returned with his views greatly enlarged; not only of exterior <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and the works of art, but of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and manners, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and policy of the several states, their connections, and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> institutions. How particular and judicious his observations were, we see in his poem on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a>, begun soon after his return to England. We see at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to what a high pitch his care of his country was raised, by the comparisons he had all along been making of our happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> with those of other nations. To inspire his fellow-subjects with the like sentiments, and show them by what means the precious freedom we enjoy may be preserved, and how it may be abused or lost, he employed two years in composing that noble <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, upon which he valued himself more than upon all his other writings. On his return to England with Mr Talbot (who soon after died), the chancellor made him his secretary of briefs; a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of little attendance, suiting his retired indolent way of life, and equal to all his wants. From this office he was removed, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, deprived him of his noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>. He then found himself reduced to a state of a precarious dependence. In this situation, having created some few debts, and his creditors finding that he had no longer any certain support, became inexorable; and imagined by confinement to force that from his friends, which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> would not permit him to ask. One of these occasions furnished Quin, the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, with an opportunity of displaying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> goodness of his heart, and the disinterestedness of his friendship. Hearing that Thomson was confined in a spunging <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for a debt of about 70l. he repaired to the place; and, having inquired for him, was introduced to the bard. Thomson was a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> disconcerted at seeing Quin, as he had always taken pains to conceal his wants; and the more so, as Quin told him he was come to sup with him. His anxiety upon this head was however removed, upon Quin's informing him, that, as he supposed it would have been inconvenient to have had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> dressed in the place they were in, he had ordered it from an adjacent tavern; and, as a prelude, half a dozen of claret was introduced. Supper being over, and the bottle circulating pretty briskly, Quin said, "It is time now we should <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> accounts." This astonished Thomson, who imagined he had some demand upon him; but Quin perceiving it, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, "Mr Thomson, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> I have had in perusing your works I cannot estimate at less than a hundred pounds, and I insist upon now acquitting the debt." On saying this, he put <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of that value, and took his leave, without waiting for a reply. The profits arising from his works were not inconsiderable; his tragedy of Agamemnon, acted in 1738, yielded a good sum. But his chief dependence was upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, who settled on him a handsome allowance, and honoured him with many marks of particular favour. Notwithstanding, this, however, he was (A) Sibylla and Banister Anglicus are mentioned in the time of Edward IV. (MSS. Cot. Dom. A. IX.) Among Latin prophecy of Bridlington is there given. Waldhave and Eltraine seem also English prophets. In the whole collection, therefore, Thomas is the only Scottish one. Mr Thomson's poem, entitled the Castle of Indolence, was his last work published by himself; his tragedy of Coriolanus being only prepared for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, when a fatal accident robbed the world of one of the best of men and best of poets. He would <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> walk the distance between London and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a> (where he lived) with any acquaintance that offered, with whom he might chat and rest himself, or perhaps dine by the way. One summer evening being alone in his walk from town to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMMERSMITH">Hammersmith</a>, he had over-heated himself, and in that condition imprudently took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> to carry him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEW">Kew</a>; apprehending no bad consequence from the chill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> on the river, which his walk to his house, towards the upper end of Kew-lane, had always hitherto prevented. But now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> had so feasted him, that the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he was in a high fever. This, however, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of proper medicines, was removed, so that he was thought out of danger; till the fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> having tempted him to expose himself once more to the evening dews, his fever returned with violence, and with such symptoms as left no hopes of a cure. His death happened on the 27th of August 1748. Mr Thomson had improved his taste upon the finest originals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. The autumn was his favourite season for poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and the deep silence of the night he commonly chose for his studies. The amusement of his leisure hours were civil and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, voyages, and the best relations of travellers. Though he performed on no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, he was passionately fond of music, and would sometimes listen a full <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> at his window to the nightingales in Richmond gardens; nor was his taste less exquisite in the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. As for the more distinguishing qualities of his mind and heart, they best appear in his writings. There his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to the Supreme Being, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of mankind, of his country, and friends, shine cut in every page; his tenderness of heart was so unbounded, that it took in even the brute <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. It is not known, that through his whole life he ever gave any person a moment's pain, either by his writings or otherwise. He took no part in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> squabbles of his time, and was therefore respected and left undisturbed by both sides. These amiable virtues did not fail of their due reward; the applause of the public attended all his productions, and his friends loved him with an enthusiastic ardour. "As a writer (says Dr Johnson), he is entitled to one praise of the highest kind; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of thinking, and of expressing his thoughts, is original. His blank <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> is no more the blank verse of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, or of any other poet, than the rhymes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> are the rhymes of Cowley. His numbers, his pauses, his diction, are of his own growth, without transcription, without <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. He thinks in a peculiar train, and thinks always as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius; he looks round on Nature and on life with the eye which Nature bestows only on a poet; the eye that distinguishes, in every thing represented to his view, whatever there is on which imagination can delight to be detained, and with a mind that at once comprehends the vast, and attends to the minute. The reader of the Seasons wonders that he never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> before what Thomson fawns him, and that he never yet has felt what Thomson impregnes." His testamentary executors were the lord Lyttelton, whose care of our poet's fortune and fame ceased not with his life; and Mr Mitchell, a gentleman equally noted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of his private friendship, and for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and spirit as a public minister. By their united interests, the orphan play of Coriolanus was brought on the stage to the best advantage; from the profits of which, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> and other effects, a handsome sum was remitted to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>. His remains were deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Richmond, under a plain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, without any inscription. A handsome monument was erected to him in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> in the year 1762, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of which was defrayed by the profits arising from a splendid edition of all his works in 1749; Mr Millar the bookseller, who had purchased all Mr Thomson's copies, giving up his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> on this grateful occasion. A monument has also been erected to him at the place of his birth. THORAX. See Anatomy. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">WHITE</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">LAW</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">THORN</a>. See Crataegus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THORN

Pages 16-16

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in Regal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULM">Culm</a>. It was formerly a Hanseatic town, and still enjoys <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> privileges; is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well fortified; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fortifications, and a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of houses, were ruined by the Swedes, in 1703. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>, and contains 10,000 inhabitants. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 42. N. Lat. 53. 6. THORNBACK. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-RAIA">RAIA</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THORNHILL

Pages 16-17

Sir James, an eminent English painter, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> in 1676, of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family; but was constrained to apply to some profession by the distresses of his father, who had been reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of selling his family estate. His inclination directed him to the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>; and on his arrival at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> he applied to his uncle, the famous Dr Sydenham, who enabled him to proceed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the art under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a painter who was not very eminent. However, the genius of Thornhill made ample amends for the insufficiency of his instructor, and by a happy application of his talents he made so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a progress, that he gradually rose to the highest reputation. His genius was well adapted to historical and allegorical compositions; he possessed a fertile and fine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; and he sketched his thoughts with great ease, freedom, and spirit. He excelled also equally in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>, trait, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; showed an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and had a free and firm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>. Had he been so fortunate as to have studied at Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, to acquire greater correctness at the one, and a more exact knowledge of the perfection of colouring at the other, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> among the moderns might perhaps have been his superior. Nevertheless, he was so eminent in many parts of his profession, that he must forever be ranked among the best painters of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and his performances in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> of St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at London, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, are such public proofs of his merit as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> convey his name to posterity with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. This painter lived in general esteem; he enriched himself by the excellence of his works; was appointed state-painter to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, from whom he received the honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>; had the singular satisfaction to repurchase his family estate; and was so much distinguished as to be elected one of the members of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. He died in 1732.

THOUGHT

Pages 17-17

a general name for all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> consequent on the operations of the mind, and even on the operations themselves. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>.

THRACE

Pages 17-17

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> very frequently mentioned by the Greek and Latin writers, deriving its name, according to Josephus, from Tiras one of the sons of Japhet. It was bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Mount <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HAEMUS">Haemus</a>; on the south, by the Aegean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the west, by Macedon and the river Strymon; and on the east, by the Euxine sea, the Hellespont, and the Propontis.—The Thracian Chersonesus is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> inclosed on the south by the Aegean sea, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Melas, and on the east by the Hellespont; being joined on the north to the continent by a neck of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> about 37 furlongs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The inland parts of Thrace are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and barren, the snow lying on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the year; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> provinces are productive of all sorts of grain and necessaries for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and withal so pleasant, that Mela compares them to the most fruitful and agreeable countries of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Thracians were deemed a brave and warlike <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, but of a cruel and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> temper; being, according to the Greek writers, strangers to all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. It was to the Thracians, however, that the Greeks were chiefly indebted for the polite arts that flourished among them; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, Musaeus, Thamyris, and Eumolpus, all Thracians, were the first, as Euclathius informs us, who charmed the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> with their eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, and persuaded them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> their Thracian fierceness for a sociable life and peaceful manners; nay, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of Greece was anciently peopled by Thracians. Tereus, a Thracian, governed at Daulis in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, where the tragic story of Philomela and Procne was acted. From thence a body of Thracians passed over to Euboea, and possessed themselves of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Of the same nation were the Aones, Tembices, and Hyanthians, who made themselves masters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>; and great part of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> itself was inhabited by Thracians, under the command of the celebrated Eumolpus. It is not therefore without the utmost ingratitude and injustice that the Greeks style them Barbarians, since to them chiefly they were indebted both for the peopling and polishing of their country. Thrace was anciently divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of petty states, which were first subdued by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon. On the decline of the Macedonian empire, the country fell under the power of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under subjection to them till the irruption of the Turks, in whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> it still remains.

THRASHING

Pages 17-22

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, the operation by which corn is separated from the straw. This operation is performed in a variety of ways, sometimes by the feet of animals, sometimes by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAIL">flail</a>, and sometimes by a machine. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> method of separating the corn from the straw was by the hoofs of cattle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> horses. This was practised by the Ishmaelites, as we find from the books of Moses; it was also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>*. Flails and thrashing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> were also plentiful, so not uncommon among these nations†. The flail xviii. 30, which was used by the Romans, called baculatus, fulgus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, iii. or perica, was probably nothing more than a cudgel or club. Pole. The thrashing machine, which was called tribula or tribulum, and sometimes traha, was a kind of sledge made of boards joined together, and loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Horses were yoked to this machine, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was seated upon it to drive them over the sheaves of corn. Different methods are employed in different countries for separating the corn from the stalk. In the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of France the flail is used; but in the southern districts it is generally performed by the feet of animals. Animals are also used for the same purpose in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Morea, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and in the vicinity of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a>, where the flail is also sometimes used. It appears that in hot climates the grains do not adhere so firmly to the stalk as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> countries, and therefore may be more easily separated. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> explain the reason why animals are so frequently employed in hot countries for treading out the corn; whereas in cold climates we know they are seldom tried, and have no reason to suppose that they would answer the purpose. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and wheat are thrashed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and maize with sticks; for it has not been possible to teach the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the flail. The animals used for treading out corn are, oxen, cows, horses, mules, and even asses when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. The operation is performed in this manner: The sheaves, after being opened, are spread in such a manner that the ears of the corn are laid as much uppermost as possible, and a man, standing in the centre, holds the halters of the cattle, which are made to trot round as in a manege; whilst other men with forks... Thrashing-forks shake the straw up from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and the cattle are trotted over it again and again till they have beaten out all the grain. This method is expeditious enough; but besides bruising a considerable quantity of corn, it requires a great many cattle, and injures the legs of the horses and mules, which are preferred before cows and oxen for this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The flail is undoubtedly a much better <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for thrashing corn than the feet of animals, for it separates the grain from the straw and husks both more effectually and more expeditiously; yet it is liable to many objections. It is a very laborious employment, too severe indeed even for a strong man; and as it is usually the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the thrasher rather to thrash much than to thrash clean, a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of corn will generally be left upon the straw. It is therefore an object of great importance in husbandry to procure a proper machine for separating the corn from the straw. The first thrashing machine attempted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, of which we have received any account, was invented in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> by Mr Michael Menzies about the year 1732. It consisted of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of instruments like flails, fixed in a moveable beam, and inclined to it at an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of ten degrees. On each side of the beam in which the flails were fixed, floors or benches were placed for spreading the sheaves on. The flails were moved backwards and forwards upon the benches by means of a crank fixed on the end of an axle, which made about 30 revolutions in a minute. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> thrashing machine was invented by Mr Michael Stirling, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Dunblane, <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-PERTHSHIRE">Perthshire</a>. Of this discovery we have received a very accurate and authentic account from his son, the reverend Mr Robert Stirling minister of Crieff. It is an old proverb, that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> is the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. This was verified on the present occasion. Besides his ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> servants, Mr M. Stirling had occasion sometimes to hire an additional number to thrash out his grain, and frequently found it difficult to procure so many as he needed. This naturally led him to reflect whether the operation of thrashing could not easily be performed by machinery. Accordingly, so early as the year 1753, under the pretence of joining in the amusements of his children, he formed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mill, in which two iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, made to rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> alternately, represented the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of two flails, by which a few stalks of corn put under them might be speedily thrashed. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> he executed on a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> sufficiently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> within two years after, making the springs about ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, each of which had one end firmly screwed into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> plank, and the other terminated in a round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a> of solid iron, two feet long and above an inch in diameter. Under these the sheaves were conveyed gradually forward in a narrow channel or trough, by passing between two indented <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> cylinders, similar to those now used in the most of the thrashing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> in that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and called feeders. In this manner the thrashing was executed completely, and with considerable rapidity; but as the operation was performed on a low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, and no method contrived for carrying off the straw, the accumulation of it produced such confusion, and the removal of it was attended with such danger, that this scheme was very soon entirely abandoned. The mortification arising from disappointment, and especially the scoffs of his neighbours, for what was universally accounted an absurd and ridiculous attempt, served only to stimulate the exertions of the inventor to accomplish his designs on another plan. Laying aside therefore the iron springs with the feeders, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> adapted to them, he retained only an outer or water wheel, with an inner or cog wheel moving on the same axle: to this inner wheel, which had 48 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> or cogs, he applied a vertical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNDLE">trundle</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> notches, the axle of which passed through a floor above the wheel, and having its upper pivot secured in a beam fix feet above that floor. At the distance of three feet three inches above the floor two straight pieces of squared wood, each four feet long, passed through the axle of the trundle at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, forming four arms, to be moved round horizontally. To the extremities of these arms were fixed four iron plates, each 20 inches long, and eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> at the end next the arms, but tapering towards a point at the other end. This large horizontal fly, constituting four thrashers, was inclosed within a wooden cylindrical box three feet and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and eight in diameter. On the top of the box was an opening or port (two or three ports were made at first, but one was found sufficient) eight inches wide, and extending from the circumference a foot and a half towards its centre, through which the corn sheaves descended, being first opened and laid one by one on a board with two ledges gently declining towards the port; on which board they were moderately pressed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a boy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, to prevent them from being too hastily drawn in by the repeated strokes of the thrashers. Within the box was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, along which the straw and grain fell down into a wide wire riddle two feet <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, placed immediately under a hole of nearly the same size. The riddle received a jerk at every revolution of the spindle from a knob placed on the side of it, and was instantly thrust backward by a small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> pressing it in the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The short straw, with the grain and chaff which passed through the wide riddle, fell immediately into an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> strait riddle, which hung with one end raised and the other depressed, and was moved by a contrivance equally simple as the other; and having no ledge at the lower end, the long chaff which could not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the riddle dropped from thence to the ground; while the grain and most of the chaff falling through the riddle into a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of common barn-fanners that stood under it on the ground floor, the strong grain, the weak, and the chaff, were all separated with great exactness. The fanners were moved by a rope or band running circuitously in a shallow niche cut on the circumference of the cog-wheel. The straw collected gradually in the bottom of the box over the wide riddle, and through an opening, two and a half feet wide, and as much in height, left in that side of the box nearest the brink of the upper floor, was drawn down to the ground with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> by the person or persons employed to form it into sheaves or rolls. Such was the thrashing mill invented by Mr Michael Stirling, which, after various alterations and improvements he completed in the form now described, A.D. 1758. By experiment it was found that four bolls of oats, Linlithgow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, could be thrashed by it in 25 minutes. From that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he never used a common flail in thrashing, except for humbling or bearding barley. Thrashing. In every other kind of grain he performed the whole operation of thrashing with the mill; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> always to use it till 1772, when he retired from business, and his thrashing mill became the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of his second son, who continues to use it with equal advantage and satisfaction. Several machines were constructed on the same plan, particularly one near Stirling, under Mr Stirling's direction, for Mr Moir of Leckie, in 1765, which, we understand, has been used ever since, and gives complete satisfaction to the proprietor. There was another erected in 1778 by Mr Thomas Keir (in the parish of Muthil and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>), who has contrived a method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> barley with it: and by the addition of a small spindle with short arms contiguous to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the box, and moved by a band common to it and the great spindle to which it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>, the straw is shaken and whirled out of the box to the ground. That this machine did not come immediately into general use, was owing partly to the smallness of the farms in that part of the country, whose crops could easily be thrashed by the few <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> necessarily retained on them for other purposes; and chiefly to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> that the machine could only be moved by water; an apprehension which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> proves to be entirely groundless. The machine however, was ingenious, and did great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the worthy inventor, and certainly deserved a better fate than it was destined to undergo. A third thrashing mill was invented in 1772, by two persons nearly about the same time, and upon the same principles. The inventors were, Mr Alderton who lived near <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALNWICK">Alnwick</a>, and Mr Smart at Wark in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>. The operation was performed by rubbing. The sheaves were carried round between an indented drum of about six feet diameter, and a number of indented rollers arranged round the circumference of the drum, and attached to it by means of springs; so that while the drum revolved, the fluted rollers rubbed the corn off from the straw by rubbing against the flutings of the drum. But as a considerable quantity of the grain was bruised in passing between the rollers, the machine was soon laid aside. In 1776 an attempt was made by Mr Andrew Meikle, an ingenious millwright in the parish of Tyningham, East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>, to construct a new machine upon the principles which had been adopted by Mr Menzies already mentioned. This consisted in making <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> in the flails, which Mr Menzies had formed without any. But this machine, after much labour and expense, was soon laid aside, on account of the difficulty of keeping it in repair, and the small quantity of work performed, which did not exceed one boll or six <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a> bushels of barley per <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. Some time after this, Mr Francis Kinloch, then junior of Gilmerton, having visited the machine invented in Northumberland, attempted an improvement upon it. He inclosed the drum in a fluted cover; and instead of making the drum itself fluted, he fixed upon the outside of it four fluted pieces of wood, which by means of springs could be raised a little above the circumference of the drum, so as to press against the fluted covering, and thus rub off the ears of corn as the sheaves passed round between the drum and the fluted covering. But not finding this machine to answer his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> (for it bruised the grain in the same manner as the Northumberland machine did), he sent it to Mr Meikle, that he might, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, rectify its errors. Mr Meikle, who had long directed his thoughts to this subject, applied himself with much ardour and perseverance to the improvement and correction of this machine; and after spending a good deal of time upon it, found it was constructed upon principles so erroneous, that to improve it was impracticable. At length, however, Mr Meikle's own genius invented a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, different in principle from the machines which had already been constructed. This model was made in the year 1785; and in the following year the first thrashing machine on the same principles was erected in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLOA">Alloa</a>, in the county of Stirling, by Mr George Meikle the son of the inventor. This machine answered completely the wishes of Mr Stein, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> for whom it was erected, who gave the most ample testimony of his satisfaction both to the inventor and to the public. The fame of this discovery soon spread over the whole country, and a great many farmers immediately applied to Mr Meikle, desiring to have thrashing mills erected on their farms. The discovery, it appeared, would be profitable, and it was reasonable that the inventor should enjoy the profits of his invention. He accordingly applied for a patent; which, after considerable expense, arising from the opposition of some persons, who claimed a share in the discovery, was granted.—These machines are now becoming very common in many parts of Scotland, and are increasing very considerably in number every year over all the united <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. We will now endeavour to describe this machine in its most improved state; which is so simple that with the affluence of a plate, exhibiting the plan of elevation, fig. 1, the ground plan, fig. 2, and the 3d showing its essential parts in a distinct manner, we hope it will be easily understood by all our readers who have not had an opportunity of seeing it. The power employed for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> that part of the machine which separates the corn from the straw is produced by four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> (when moved by horses), the teeth of which move in one another and turn the drum, on which four scutchers are fixed. The sheaves are introduced between two fluted rollers, which hold them firm, and draw them in gradually, while the scutchers strike off the grain from the straw as it passes through. This will suffice for a general idea of this machine. We will now be more particular. The large spur-wheel A, fig. 1, and 2, which has Fig. 1. and 276 cogs, is horizontal, and moves the pinion B, which has 14 teeth. The pinion B moves the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-wheel C, which has 84 teeth; the wheel C moves a second pinion D, which has 16 teeth; and the pinion D moves the drum HIKL. The drum is a hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> three feet and a half diameter, and placed horizontally; on the outside of which the scutchers are fixed by strong screw bolts. The scutchers consist of four pieces of wood, faced on one side with a thin plate of iron, placed at an equal distance from each other, and at right angles to the axis of the drum. The sheaves are spread on an inclined board F, fig. 3, from which they are introduced between two fluted rollers GG made of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> iron, about three inches and a half in diameter, and making about 35 revolutions in a minute. As these rollers are only about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of Thrashing of an inch distant from the scutchers or leaves of the drum HIKL, they serve to hold the sheaves fast, while the scutchers \(a, b, c, d\) moving with prodigious velocity, separate the grain completely from the straw, and at the same time throw out both grain and straw upon the concave <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> M, lying horizontally with slender parallel ribs, so that the corn passes through them into a hopper N placed below. From the hopper it passes through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> or riddle O into a pair of fans P, from which, in the most improved machines, it comes out clean and fit for the market. The straw, after being thrown by the scutchers \(a, b, c, d\) into the rack, is removed from it by a rake QRS into a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> contiguous V. The rake consists of four thin pieces of wood or leaves; on the end of each of these leaves is ranged a row of teeth e, f, g, h, five inches long. The rake moves in a circular manner in the concave rack, while the teeth catch hold of the straw, and throw it out of the rack. These are all the essential parts of the machine; the rest may be easily understood by the references to the Plate. W is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-course, No. 1, which is 27 feet diameter. X is the pillar for supporting the beams on which the axle of the spur-wheel is fixed. YYY are three spindles for moving the two fluted rollers, the rake, and fans. To the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> now given we have only to add, that the drum has a covering of wood Z at a small distance above it, for the purpose of keeping the sheaves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the scutchers. The advantages of this machine are many. As the drum makes 300 revolutions in a minute, the four scutchers together make 200 strokes in the same space of time. From such power and velocity, it is evident that much work must be performed. When the horses go at the rate of two and one-third miles per hour, from three to six bolls will be thrashed; but as the quantity thrashed will be less when the straw is long than when it is short, we shall take the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> at four bolls. One gentleman, whose veracity and accuracy we can depend on, assures us, that his mill thrashed 63 bolls in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; by which, we suppose, he meant 10 hours. To prove the superior advantage of this machine to the common method of thrashing with flails, a gentleman ordered two equal quantities of oats to be thrashed by the mill and by flails. When the corn was cleaned and measured, he obtained one-sixteenth more from the sheaves thrashed by the mill than from those thrashed by the flail. We are also informed by another gentleman who has studied this machine with much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and calculated its advantages with care, that, independently of having the corn much cleaner separated from the straw than is usually done by flails, there is a saving of 30 or 40 per cent. in the expense of thrashing. The number of persons requisite for attending the mill when working is six: One person drives the horses; a second hands the sheaves to a third, who unties them, while a fourth spreads them on the inclined boards and presses them gently between the rollers; a fifth person is necessary to riddle the corn as it falls from the fans, Thrashing and a sixth to remove the straw (A). This machine can be moved equally well by water, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, or horses. Mr Meikle has made such improvements on the wind-mill as to render it much more manageable and convenient than formerly; and we are informed many wind-mills are now erecting in different parts of the country. As to the comparative expense of these different machines, the erection of the horse machine is least; but then the expense of employing horses must be taken into consideration. One of this kind may be erected for 70l. A water mill will cost 10l. more on account of the expense of the water-wheel. A wind-mill will cost from 200l. to 300l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>.

THRASYBULUS

Pages 22-22

a renowned Athenian general and patriot, the deliverer of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from the yoke of the 30 tyrants, lived about 294 B.C.

THRASYMENUS TACUS

Pages 22-22

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, No. 3, a lake of Etruria, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a>, and not far from the Tiber, fatal to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Now *Lago de Perugia* in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> State.

THRAVE OF CORN

Pages 22-22

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> denoting 24 sheaves <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four shocks of five sheaves to the shock; though in some countries they only reckon 12 sheaves to the thrave.

THREAD

Pages 22-22

a small line made up of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fine fibres of any vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> animal substance, such as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, cotton, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; from which it takes its name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cotton, or silk thread. **THREATENING LETTERS.** Knowingly to send any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> without a name, or with a fictitious name, demanding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, or any other valuable thing, or threatening (without any demand) to kill or fire the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of any person, is made felony without benefit of clergy. And sending letters, threatening to accuse any person of a crime punishable with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, transportation, pillory, or other infamous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, with a view to extort from him any money or other valuable chattels, is punishable by statute 30 Geo. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 24, at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, with fine, imprisonment, pillory, whipping, or transportation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THRESHING">THRESHING</a>.** See **Thrashing**. **THRIFT.** See **Statice**, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THRINAX

Pages 22-22

Small Jamaica Fan-palm, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas of palmæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THROAT

Pages 22-22

the anterior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an animal, between the head and the shoulders. **THROAT-WORT.** See Campanula, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THRONE

Pages 22-23

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> seat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of state, enriched with ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, raised on one or more steps, and covered with a kind of canopy. Such are the thrones in the rooms of audience of kings and other sovereigns. **THROSTLE.** --- (A) We add, on the authority of an experienced <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, that of the six persons necessary to attend the thrashing machine, only two can in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> to the account of the machine; namely, the person who manages the horses, and the one who feeds the machine: For in the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of thrashing by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAIL">flail</a>, it requires the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons as the thrashing machine does to clear an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of corn from the chaff in the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. THRUSSH. See Turdus.

THUANUS

Pages 23-23

Jacobus Augustus, youngest son of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> de Thou, was famous for his erudition. He was born in 1533; and having finished his studies and travels, was made president a-mortier, and took possession thereof in 1595. He was employed in several important offices of state, and in reforming the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in Latin, from the year 1543 to 1658, in 138 books; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, both for subject and style, worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. He also left <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, besides poems; and died at Paris, 1617.

THUCYDIDES

Pages 23-23

a celebrated Greek historian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> 471 B.C. He was the son of Olorus, and grandson of Militiades, who is thought to have been descended from Militiades the famous Athenian general, and to have married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thrace's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. He was educated in a manner suitable to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, that is, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and eloquence. His <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in the former was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a>, in the latter Antipho; one, by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> in the eighth book of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, for power of speech almost a miracle, and feared by the people on that account. Suidas and Pho-tius relate, that when <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> recited his history in public, a fashion in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> then and many ages after, Thucydides felt so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a sting of emulation, that it drew tears from him; inasmuch that Herodotus himself took notice of it, and congratulated his father on having a son who showed so wonderful an affection to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>. Herodotus was then 29 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Thucydides about 16. When the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out, Thucydides conjectured truly, that it would prove a subject worthy of his labour; and it no sooner commenced than he began to keep a journal. This explains the reason why he has attended more to chronological order than to unity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. During the same war he was commissioned by his countrymen to relieve Amphipolis; but the quick <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of Brasidas the Lacedaemonian general defeated his operations; and Thucydides, unsuccessful in his expedition, was banished from Athens. This happened in the eighth year of this celebrated war; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his banishment the general began to write an impartial history of the important events which had happened during his administration, and which still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to agitate the several states of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. This famous history is continued only to the 21st year of the war, and the remaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> till the demolition of the walls of Athens was described by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of Theopompus and Xenophon. Thucydides wrote in the Attic dialect, as being possessed of most vigour, purity, elegance, and energy. He spared neither time nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to procure authentic materials; and the Athenians, as well as their enemies, furnished him with many valuable communications, which contributed to throw great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on the different transactions of the war. His history has been divided into eight books; the last of which is imperfect, and supposed to have been written by his daughter. The historian of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a> has often been compared with the son of Olorus, but each has his peculiar excellence. Sweetness of style, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, may be called the characteristics of the former; while Thucydides stands unequalled for the fire of his descriptions, the conciseness, and at the same time the strong and energetic manner of his narratives. His relations are authentic, as he himself was interested in the events he mentions; his impartiality is indubitable, as he nowhere betrays the least resentment against his countrymen, and the factious partizans of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEON">Cleon</a>, who had banished him from Athens. The history of Thucydides was so admired by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, that he transcribed it eight different times, and read it with such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, that he could almost repeat it by heart. Thucydides died at Athens, where he had been recalled from his exile about 411 years B.C. The best edition of Thucydides is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, published in 1696, folio, and that of Duker, published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1731, folio.

THUIA

Pages 23-23

the Arbor Vitæ; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a>, and order of monocæ; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 31st order, Coniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THULE

Pages 23-23
or Thyle, in Ancient Geography, an island in the most northern parts of the German ocean. Its situation was never accurately ascertained by the ancients, hence its present name is unknown by modern historians. Some suppose that it is the island now called Iceland, or part of Greenland, and others that it was Foula. See Foula.

THUMB

Pages 23-23

in Anatomy, one of the extremities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. THUMB-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">Cap</a>, an uninhabited <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lies about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Lagoon island; it is low, woody, of a circular form, and not much above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in compass. THUMMIM. See Urim.

THUNBERGIA

Pages 23-23

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas of didynamia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THUNDER

Pages 23-23

the noise occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> of a flash of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> echoed back from the inequalities on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in like manner as the noise of a cannon is echoed, and in particular circumstances forms a rolling lengthened <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>. THUNDERBOLT. When lightning acts with extraordinary violence, and breaks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shatters any thing, it is called a thunderbolt; which the vulgar, to fit it for such effects, suppose to be a hard body, and even a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. But that we need not have recourse to a hard <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body to account for the effects <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> attributed to the thunderbolt, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be evident to any one who considers those of the pulvis fulminans and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>; and more especially the astonishing powers of electricity. It has been supposed that meteoric <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> may have given rise to the notion of a thunderbolt. THUNDER-Houle. See Electricity.

THURINGIA

Pages 23-24

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> in Germany. It is a fruitful tract, abounding in corn, especially wheat; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, sheep, and horses. It is about 73 miles in length, and as much in breadth. It contains 47 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 14 boroughs, between 700 and 800 villages, 300 noble estates, 7 superintendencies, and 5 under-confestories. Thuringia, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Thuringi, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Catti, a branch of the Vandals, Thuringia Vandals, mentioned by Tacitus, was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, afterwards a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, then a landgraviate, and was governed by its own princes for many ages, till 1124, when it devolved to the marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, and, with that country, afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Saxony. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Thuringia is only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ancient, nay, but a part of the ancient South Thuringia, which comprehends besides, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share of the modern Franconia, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, &c. On the extinction of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> line of the ancient landgraves in 1247, it came to the margraves of Meissen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> to the present electoral family. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the diet, on account of his share in the landgraviate or circle of Thuringia. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERFURT">Erfurt</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

THURSDAY

Pages 24-24

the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, but the sixth of that of the Jews.

THUS

Pages 24-24

FRANKINCENSE, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> brittle resin, brought to us in little globes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> masses, of a brownish or yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on the outside, internally whitish or variegated with whitish specks. It is supposed to be the produce of the pine that yields the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> turpentine, and to concrete upon the surface of the terebinthinate juice soon after it has issued from the tree. See INCENSE. THUYA. See Thuja.

THYALLIS

Pages 23-23

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas dendria, and order of monogynia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 38th order, Tricoccæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

THYMS

Pages 24-24

THYME; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of didynamia, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 42d order, Vericilliate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. THYMS. See ANATOMY Index.

THYRSUS

Pages 24-24

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of flowering resembling the cone of a pine. It is, says Linnaeus, a panicle contracted into an oval <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>-shaped form. The lower footstalks, which are longer, extend horizontally, whilst the upper ones are shorter and mount vertically. Lilac and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>-bur furnish examples.

TIARA

Pages 24-24

an ornament <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> wherewith the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Persians covered their head; and with which the Armenians and kings of Pontus are represented on medals; these last, because they were defended from the Persians. Latin authors call it indifferently tiara and cedaris. Strabo says, the tiara was in form of a tower; and the scholiast on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, Acharnæ, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> i. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> 2, affirms, that it was adorned with peacocks feathers. Tiara is also the name of the pope's triple <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. The tiara and keys are the badges of the papal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; the tiara of his civil <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and the keys of his jurisdiction: for as soon as the pope is dead, his arms are represented with the tiara alone, without the keys. The ancient tiara was a round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. John XXIII. first encompassed it with a crown, Boniface VIII. added a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> crown; and Benedict XII. a third.

TIARELLA

Pages 24-24

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of decandra; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 13th order, Succulentae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TIBER

Pages 24-24

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which runs through the pope's territories, passing by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORVIETO">Orvieto</a>; and having visited Rome, falls into the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSTIA">Ostia</a>, 15 miles below that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>.

TIBET

Pages 24-26

called by the Tartars Baramota, Bootan, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tangoot, and by the Chinese T'ang, is situated between 27° and 35° <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude; and is reckoned to be 1350 miles from east to west, and 480 from north to south. It is bounded on the north by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Mongols and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Kobi; on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; on the west by Hindoostan, and on the south by the same country and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVA">Ava</a>. In the valleys lying between the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are many tribes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> people; and a dispute happening between the heirs of one of the rajahs or petty princes, one party called to their assistance the Boutaners, and the other the British. The latter prevailed; and the fame of British valour being carried to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Tibet, the Teeshoo <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMA">Lama</a>, who ruled the state under the Delai-Lama, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in his minority, sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, desiring peace for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who had been engaged in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the British. This was readily granted by the governor; and Mr Bogle was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the court of Tibet, where he resided several months; and after an absence of a year and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, returned to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>. The account of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s expedition hath not been published by himself; but from Mr Stewart's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Sir John Pringle, published in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. lxvii. we learn the following particulars, collected from his papers. "Mr Bogle divides the territories of the Delai-Lama into two different parts. That which lies immediately contiguous to Bengal, and which is called by the inhabitants Doopo, he distinguishes by the name of Bootan; and the other, which extends to the northward as far as the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, called by the natives Pu, he styles Tibet. Bootan is ruled by the Dah Terriah, or Deb Rajah. It is a country of steep and inaccessible mountains, whose summits are crowned with eternal snow; they are intersected with deep valleys, through which pour numberless torrents that increase in their course, and at last, gaining the plains, lose themselves in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Bengal. These mountains are covered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their sides with forests of stately trees of various sorts; some (such as pines, &c.) which are known in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; others, such as are peculiar to the country and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The valleys and sides of the hills which admit of cultivation are not unfruitful, but produce crops of wheat, barley, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>. The inhabitants are a stout and warlike people, of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, in size rather above the middle European stature, hasty and quarrelsome in their temper, and addicted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of spirituous liquors; but honest in their dealings, robbery by violence being almost unknown among them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is Talley Seddein, situated on the Patchoo. Tibet begins properly from the top of the great ridge of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, and extends from thence in breadth to the confines of Great Tartary, and perhaps to some of the dominions of the Russian empire. The woods, which everywhere cover the mountains in Bootan, are here totally unknown; and, except a few straggling trees near the villages, nothing of the sort is to be seen. The climate is extremely severe and rude. At Chamnaning, where he wintered, although it be in latitude 31° 39', only 80° to the northward of Calcutta, he often found the thermometer in his room at 29° by Fahrenheit's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>; and in the middle of April the standing waters were all frozen, and heavy showers of snow perpetually fell. This, no doubt, must be owing to the great elevation of the country, and to the vast..." The Tibetans are of a smaller size than their southern neighbours, and of a less robust make.
