Their complexions are also fairer, and many of them have even a ruddiness in their countenances unknown to the other climates of the east. Those whom Mr Bogle <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> at Calcutta appeared to have quite the Tartar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. They are of a mild and cheerful temper; the higher ranks are polite and entertaining in conversation, in which they never mix either strained compliments or flattery. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, both in Bootan and Tibet, are clothed in coarse woollen stuffs of their own manufacture, lined with such skins as they can procure: but the better orders of men are dressed in European cloth, or China <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, lined with the finest Siberian furs. The use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> is totally unknown among them. The chief food of the inhabitants is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of their cattle, prepared into cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, or mixed with the flour of a coarse barley or of peas, the only grain which their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> produces; but they are furnished with rice and wheat from Bengal and other countries in their neighbourhood. They also are supplied with fish from the rivers in their own and the neighbouring provinces, salted and sent into the interior parts. They have no want of animal food from the cattle, sheep, and hogs, which are raised on their hills; and are not destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>. They have a singular method of preparing their mutton, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the carcass entire, after the bowels are taken out, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and bleak northern winds which blow in the months of August and September, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, so dry up the juices and parch the skin, that the meat <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> keep uncorrupted for the year round. This they generally eat raw, without any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of this country, which are intimately blended together, would make a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. It suffices to say, that at present, and ever since the expulsion of the Eluth Tartars, the kingdom of Tibet is regarded as depending on the empire of China, which they call Cathay; and there actually reside two mandarins, with a garrison of a thousand Chinese, at Lahafia the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, to support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; but their power does not extend far: and in fact the Lama, whose empire is founded on the surest grounds, personal affection and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> reverence, governs every thing internally with unbounded authority. Every body knows that the Delai Lama is the great object of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> for the various tribes of heathen Tartars, who roam through the vast tract of continent which stretches from the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a> to Correa on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, the most extensive religious dominion, perhaps, on the face of the globe. See LAMA. It is an old notion, that the religion of Tibet is a corrupted Christianity: and even Father Diderot, a Jesuit (but not of the Chinese mission) who visited the country about the beginning of this century, thinks he can resolve all their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> into ours; and affirms, with a truly mystical penetration, that they have certainly a good notion of the Trinity, since in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a>- dresses to the Deity, they say as often konciok-gik in the plural as konciok in the singular, and with their rofaries pronounce these words om, ha, hum. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, that the religion of Tibet, from whatever source it sprung, is pure and simple in its source, conveying very exalted notions of the Deity, with no contemptible system of morality: but in its progress it has been greatly altered and corrupted by the inventions of worldly men; a fate we can hardly regret in a system of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, since we know that that of truth has been subject to the same. Polygamy, at least in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> receive the word, is not in practice among them; but it exists in a manner still more repugnant to European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; for there is a plurality of husbands, which is firmly established and highly respected there. In a country where the means of subsisting a family are not easily found, it seems not impolitic to allow a set of brothers to agree in raising one, which is to be maintained by their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> efforts. In short, it is usual in Tibet for the brothers in the family to have a wife in common, and they generally live in great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and comfort with her; but not sometimes little dissensions will arise (as may happen in families constituted upon different principles), an instance of which Mr Bogle mentions in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a modest and virtuous lady, the wife of half a dozen of the Teehoo Lama's nephews, who complained to the uncle that the two youngest of her husbands did not furnish that share of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and benevolence to the common stock which duty and religion required of them. In short, however strange this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> may appear to us, it is an undoubted fact that it prevails in Tibet. The dead are exposed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINNACLE">pinnacle</a> of some neighbouring mountain, to be devoured by wild beasts and birds of prey, or waited away by time and the vicissitudes of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> in which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a>. The mangled carcases and bleached <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> lie scattered about; and amidst this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of horror, some miserable old wretch, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or woman, loit to all feelings but those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, generally sets up an abode, to perform the dismal office of receiving the bodies, affixing each a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and gathering up the remains when too widely dispersed. To the account of Tibet which we have given from the communications of Mr Bogle, we may add the information which we have obtained from a later traveller, Mr Saunders* surgeon at Boglepoor in Bengal, who made a journey into Tibet in the year 1783. His observations chiefly respect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions and districts of the country. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which Mr Saunders found were almost all European plants, a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them being natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. From the appearance of the hills he concludes that they must contain many ores of metal and pyrites. There are inexhaustible quantities of tincal or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, and rock-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is plentiful; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-dust is found in great quantities in the beds of rivers, and sometimes in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses, lumps, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> veins; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, cinabar containing a large proportion of quicksilver, copper, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, he thinks, might easily be procured. But the inhabitants of Tibet have no better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> than the dung of animals. A coal mine would be a valuable discovery. We are told, that in some parts of China bordering on Tibet coal is found and used as fuel. It is remarkable that the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> prevails at the foot. foot of the mountains of Tibet as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, a glandular swelling in the throat commonly called goitre. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> spoken in Tibet is different from that of the Tartars. The astronomers are acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the heavenly bodies, and able to calculate eclipses; but the lamas are generally ignorant; few of them can read, much less understand their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> books.

TIBULLUS

Pages 26-26

AULUS ALBIUS, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, and a celebrated Latin poet, was born at Rome 43 B.C. He was the friend of Horace, Ovid, Macer, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men in the reign of Augustus. He accompanied Messala Corvinus in his expedition against the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORCYRA">Corcyra</a>: but falling sick, and being unable to support the fatigues of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on account of the weakness of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he quitted the profession of arms, and returned to Rome, where he died before the year 17; when Ovid showed his grief for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a fine elegy upon him. Tibullus wrote four books of elegies, which are still extant: they are written in a tender and agreeable style, and in very elegant Latin. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURAT">Murat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger have written learned and curious commentaries on the works of this poet. The best edition of Tibullus is that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> Bronckhufus, published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1798, in one volume quarto. We have an English poetical version by Mr Grainger.

TIBUR

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Latium, pleasantly situated on the Anio. Here Horace had his villa and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and here he wished to end his days. Here Adrian built an extraordinary villa called Tiburina, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with the names of the provinces and of the most considerable places, (Spartan); near which Zenobia had a house called Zenobia, (Trebellius, Pollio). Hither Augustus often retreated on account of its salubrity, (Suetonius): for which it is greatly recommended, (Martial). Anciently, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had far extended their territory, it was the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of banishment, (Ovid). It had a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; and therefore called Herculeum. In the temple was a library, (A. Gellius). Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma, on the Tevere.

TICINUS

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a river in Insubria, rising in Mount Adula, traversing the Lacus Verbanus southwards, and falling into the Po near Ticinum. Between this river and the Po <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> gained his first victory over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> under P. Scipio. The general himself escaped with the utmost difficulty, and that by the bravery of his son the first S-pio Africanus. Now the Tegno, rising in Mount Godard, running south through the Lago Maggiore and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, into the Po. TICK. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACARUS">ACARUS</a>, ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TICKELL

Pages 26-26

THOMAS, an excellent English poet, was the son of the Reverend Richard Tickell, and was born in 1686, at Bridekirk in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, of which he was made fellow; and while he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at that university, he addressed to Mr Addison a complimentary copy of verses on his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROSAMOND">Rosamond</a>, which introduced him to an acquaintance with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, who discovering his merit, became his sincere friend. On Mr Addison being made secretary of state, he appointed Mr Tickell his under-secretary; and on his being obliged to resign that office on account of his ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he recommended him so effectually to Mr Cragg's successor, that he was continued in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> till that gentleman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In 1724, Mr Tickell was appointed secretary to the lords justices in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and enjoyed that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived. He wrote some poems, which, when separately published, met with a favourable reception, and passed through several editions: they are now printed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> Poets. After Mr Addison's death Mr Tickell had the care of the edition of his works printed in 4 vols. 4to; to which he prefixed an account of Mr Addison's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and a poem on his death. Mr Tickell died in the year 1740.

TICKERA

Pages 26-26

a considerable article of merchandise in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZZAN">Fezzan</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; it is valued by travellers as a portable and highly salubrious food. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of pounded dates, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, formed into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATE">pate</a>, and highly dried in an oven.

TIDE

Pages 26-49

is a word which expresses that rising and falling of the waters which are observed on all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> coasts. There is a certain depth of the waters of the ocean which would obtain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> all were at rest: but observation shows that they are continually varying from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, and that some of these variations are regular and periodical. 1st. It is observed, that on the shores of the ocean, and in bays, creeks, and harbours, which communicate freely with the ocean, the waters rise up above this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> height twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and as often sink below it, forming what is called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">FLOOD</a> and an EBB, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">HIGH</a> and LOW <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">WATER</a>. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between high and low water is called a TIDE; the water is said to FLOW and to EBB; and the rising is called the FLOOD-TIDE, and the falling is called the EBB TIDE. 2nd. It is observed, that this rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the waters is variable in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, for instance, it is sometimes 21 feet between the greatest and least depth of the water in one day, and sometimes only 12 feet. These different heights of tide are observed to succeed each other in a regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, diminishing from the greatest to the least, and then increasing from the least to the greatest. The greatest is called a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">SPRING</a> TIDE, and the least is called a NEAP TIDE. 3rd. This series is completed in about 15 days. More careful observation shows that two series are completed in the exact <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of a lunation. For the spring tide in any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is observed to happen precisely at a certain interval of time (generally between two and three days) after new <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; and the neap tide at a certain interval after half moon: or, more accurately speaking, it is observed that the spring tide always happens when the moon has got a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of degrees eastward of the line of conjunction and opposition, and the neap tide happens when she is a certain number of degrees from her first or last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a>. Thus the whole series of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> appears to be regulated by the moon. 4th. It is observed that high water happens at new and full moon, when the moon has a certain determined position with respect to the meridian of the place of observation, preceding or following the moon's southing. Tide. fouthing a certain interval of time; which is constant with respect to that place, but very different in different places. 5th. The time of high water in any place appears to be regulated by the moon; for the interval between the time of high water and the moon's fouthing never changes above three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, whereas the interval between the time of high water and noon changes six hours in the course of a fortnight. 6th. The interval between two succeeding high waters is variable. It is least of all about new and full moon, and greatest when the moon is in her quadratures. As two high waters happen every day, we may call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of their interval a tide day, as we call the diurnal revolution of the moon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> day. The tide is shortest about new and full moon, being then about 24° 37' ; about the time of the moon's quadratures it is 25° 27'. These values are taken from a mean of many observations made at Barbadoes by Dr Mafkelyne. 7th. The tides in similar circumstances are greatest when the moon is at her smallest distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or in her perigee, and, gradually diminishing, are smallest when she is in her apogee. 8th. The same remark is made with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s distance, and the greatest tides are observed during the winter months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. 9th. The tides in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ocean increase as the moon, by changing her declination, approaches the zenith of that place. 10th. The tides which happen while the moon is above the horizon are greater than the tides of the same day when the moon is below the horizon. Such are the regular phenomena of the tides. They are important to all commercial nations, and have therefore been much attended to. It is of the tides, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> speaks, when God is said to set bounds to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and to say, "thus far shall it go, and no farther." <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> is the earliest profane author who speaks of the tides. Indeed it is not very clear that it is of them that he speaks (in the 12th book of the Odyssey) when he speaks of Charybdis, which rises and retires thrice in every day. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> and Diodorus Siculus speak more distinctly of the tides in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> sea. Pytheas of Marseille is the first who says anything of their cause. According to Strabo he had been in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, where he must have observed the tides of the ocean. Plutarch says expressly that Pytheas ascribed them to the moon. It is somewhat wonderful that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> says so little about the tides. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Alexander, his pupil, were startled at their first appearance to them near the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>; and we should have thought that Aristotle would be well informed of all that had been observed there. But there are only three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> concerning them in all Aristotle's writings, and they are very trivial. In one place he speaks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tides observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Europe; in another, he mentions their having been ascribed by some to the moon; and in a third, he says, that the tide in a great sea exceeds that in a small one. The Greeks had little opportunity of observing the tides. The conquests and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gave them more acquaintance with them. Caesar speaks of them in the 4th book of his Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>. Strabo, after Poseidonius, classes the phenomena into daily, monthly, and annual. He observes, that the sea rises as the moon gets near the meridian, whether above or below the horizon, and falls again as the rises or falls; also, that the tides increase at the time of new and full moon, and are greatest at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice. Pliny explains the phenomena at some length; and says, that both the sun and moon are their cause, dragging the waters along with them (B. II. c. 97). Seneca (Nat. Quæst. III. 28.) speaks of the tide with correctness; and Macrobius (Sonn. Scip. I. 6.) gives a very accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of their motions. It is impossible that such phenomena should not excite <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> curiosity as to their cause. Plutarch (Plaut. Phil. III. 17.), Galileo (Synt. Mund. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">Dial</a>. 4.), Riccioli in his Almagest, ii. p. 374., and Gaffendi, i. p. 27., have collected most of the notions of their predecessors on the subject; but they are of so little importance, that they do not deserve our notice. Kepler speaks more like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> (De Stella Maris, and Epit. Astron. p. 355.). He says that all bodies attract each other, and that the waters of the ocean would all go to the moon were they not retained by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of the earth; and then goes on to explain their elevation under the moon and on the opposite side, because the earth is less attracted by the moon than the nearer waters, but more than the waters which are more remote. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a complete explanation of the tides was reserved for Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton. He laid hold of this class of phenomena as the most incontestable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, and has given a most beautiful and synoptical view of the whole subject; contenting himself, however, with merely exhibiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> consequences of the general principle, and applying it to the phenomena with singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. But the wide steps taken by this great philosopher in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> leave ordinary readers frequently at fault: many of his assumptions require the greatest mathematical knowledge to satisfy us of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> therefore proposed to illustrate this among other parts of the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and published the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the tides as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> problem. This produced three excellent dissertations by M. Laurin, Dan. Bernoulli, and Euler. Aided by these, and chiefly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, we shall here give a physical theory, and accommodate it to the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> by giving the rules of calculation. We have demonstrated in our dissertations on the physical principles of the celestial motions, that it is an unexpected fact, that every particle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in the solar system is actually deflected toward every other particle; and that the deflection of a particle of matter toward any distant sphere is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the quantity of matter in that sphere directly, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the distance of the particle from the centre of that sphere inversely: and having found that the heaviness of a piece of terrestrial matter is nothing but the supposed opponent to the force which we exert in carrying this piece of matter, we conceive it as possessing a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, that is, distinguishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, manifested by its being gravity or heavy. This is heaviness, gravitas, gravity; and the manifestation of this quality, or the event in which it is seen, whether it be directly falling, or deflecting in a parabolic curve, or stretching a coiled spring, or breaking a rope, or simply prelging on its support, is gravitatio, gravitation; and the body is said to gravitate. When all obstacles are removed from the body, body, as when we cut the string by which a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> is hung, it moves directly downwards, tendit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> terram. Si discedatur funis tenderet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> ad terram. Dum vero funis integer perfest, lapis terram versus nisi cenfatur. By some metaphysical processes, which it is needless at present to trace, this nus ad motum has been called a tendency in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Indeed the word has now come to signify the energy of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> quality in those <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where its simplest and most immediate manifestation is prevented by some obstacle. The stone is now said to tend towards the earth, though it does not actually approach it, being withheld by the string. The stretching of the string in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> perpendicular to the horizon is conceived as a full manifestation of this tendency. This tendency, this energy of its heaviness, is therefore named by the word which distinguishes the quality; and it is called gravitation, and it is said to gravitate. But Sir Isaac Newton discovered that this deflection of a heavy body differs in no respect from that general deflection observed in all the bodies of the solar system. For 16 feet, which is the deflection of a stone in one second, has the very same proportion to \( \frac{1}{3} \) th of an inch, which is the simultaneous deflection of the moon, that the square of the moon's distance from the centre of the earth has to the square of the stone's distance from it, namely, that of 3600 to 1. Thus we are enabled to compare all the effects of the mutual tendencies of the heavenly bodies with the tendency of gravity, whose effects and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> are familiar to us. If the earth were a sphere covered to a great depth with water, the water would form a concentric spherical shell; for the gravitation of every particle of its surface would then be directed to the centre, and would be equal. The curvature of its surface therefore would be everywhere the same, that is, it would be the uniform curvature of a sphere. It has been demonstrated in former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, after Sir Isaac Newton, that the gravitation of a particle C (fig. 1.) to the centre O, is to that of a particle E at the surface as CO to EO. In like manner the gravitation of o is to that of p as o to p O. If therefore EO and OP are two communicating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, of equal lengths, the water in both would be in equilibrium, because each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> would exert the same total pressure at O. But if the gravitation of each particle in PO be diminished by a certain proportion, such as \( \frac{1}{3} \) th of its whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, it is plain that the total pressure of the column PO <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be \( \frac{1}{3} \) th part less than that of the column EO. Therefore they will no longer be in equilibrium. The weight of the column EO will prevail; and if a hollow tower PP be built at the mouth of the pit PO, the water will sink in EO and rise in OP, till both are again in equilibrium, exerting equal total pressures at O. Or we may prevent the sinking at E by pouring in more water into the tower PP. The same thing must happen in the canal FC perpendicular to EO, if the gravitation of every particle be diminished by a force acting in the direction CF, and proportional to the distance of the particle from C, and such, that when eC is equal to oO, the force acting on e is equal to the force acting on o. In order that the former equilibrium may be restored after this diminution of the gravitation of the column FC, it is plain that more water must be poured into the oblique tower FF. All this is evident when we consider the matter hydrostatically. The gravitation of the particle e may be represented by oO; but the diminution of the pressure occasioned by this at O is represented by Cc. Hence we can collect this much, that the whole diminution of pressure at C is to the whole diminution of pressure at O as the sum of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> CC to the sum of all the lines OO, that is, as \( fC^2 \) to \( PO^2 \). But the weight of the small quantity of water added in each tower is diminished in the same proportion; therefore the quantity added at FF must be to the quantity added at PP as \( fC \) to \( PO \). Therefore we must have \( Ff : PP = fC : PO \), and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> E, F, P, must be in the circumference of an ellipse, of which PO and EO are the transverse and conjugate semi-axes. What we have here supposed concerning the diminution of gravity in these canals is a thing which really obtains in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. It was demonstrated, when treating of the Precession of the Equinoxes, that if the sun or moon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the direction OP, at a very great distance, there results from the unequal gravitation of the different particles of the earth a diminution of the gravity of each particle; which diminution is in a direction <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to OP, and proportional to the distance of the particle from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> passing through the centre of the earth at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to the line OP. Thus it happens that the waters of the ocean have their equilibrium disturbed by the unequal gravitation of their different particles to the sun or to the moon; and this equilibrium cannot be restored till the waters come in from all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and rise up around the line joining the centres of the earth and of the luminaries. The spherical ocean must acquire the form of a prolate spheroid <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the revolution of an ellipse round its transverse axis. The waters will be highest in that place which has the luminary in its zenith, and in the antipodes to that place; and they will be most depressed in all those places which have the luminary in their horizon. P and P' will be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and EOQ will be the equator of this prolate spheroid. Mr Ferguson, in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, affirms another cause of this arrangement, viz., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the centrifugal forces of the different particles of water, while the earth is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre of gravity of the earth and moon. This, however, is a mistake. It would be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> if the earth and moon were attached to the ends of a rod, and the earth kept always the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> toward the moon. It is evident that the accumulation at P and P', and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> at the equator, must augment and diminish in the same proportion with the disturbing force. It is also evident that its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> quantity may be discovered by our knowledge of the proportion of the disturbing force to the force of gravity.—Now this proportion is known; for the proportion of the gravitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> centre to the sun or moon, to the force of gravity at the earth's surface, is known; and the proportion of the gravitation of the earth's centre to the luminaries, to the difference of the gravitations of the centre and of the surface, is also known, being very nearly the proportion of the distance of the luminaries to twice the radius of the earth. Although this reasoning, by which we have ascertained the elliptical form of the watery spheroid, be sufficiently ciently convincing, it is very imperfect, being accommodated to one condition only of equilibrium, viz. the equilibrium of the canals \( f \) and \( c \). There are several other conditions equally necessary to which this lax reasoning will not apply, such as the direction of the whole remaining gravitation in any point \( F \). This must be perpendicular to the surface, &c. &c. Nor will this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of investigation ascertain the eccentricity of the spheroid without a most intricate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. We must therefore take the subject more generally, and show the proportion and directions of gravity in every point of the spheroid. We need not, however, again demonstrate that the gravitation of a particle placed anywhere without a perfect spherical shell, or a sphere consisting of concentric spherical shells, either of uniform density, or of densities varying according to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of the radius, is the same as if the whole matter of the shell or sphere were collected in the centre. This has been demonstrated in the article Astronomy. We need only remind the reader of some consequences of this theorem which are of continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the present investigation. 1. The gravitation to a sphere is proportional to its quantity of matter directly, and to the square of the distance of its centre from the gravitating particle inversely. 2. If the spheres be homogeneous and of the same density, the gravitations of particles placed on their surfaces, or at distances which are proportional to their diameters, are as the radii; for the quantities of matter are as the cubes of the radii, and the attractions are inversely as the squares of the radii; and therefore the whole gravitations are as \( \frac{r^3}{r^2} \), or as \( r \). 3. A particle placed within a sphere has no tendency to the matter of the shell which lies without it, because its tendency to any part is balanced by an opposite tendency to the opposite part. Therefore, 4. A particle placed anywhere within a homogeneous sphere gravitates to its centre with a force proportional to its distance from it. It is a much more difficult problem to determine the gravitation of particles to a spheroid. To do this in general terms, and for every situation of the particle, would require a train of proportions which our limits will by no means admit; we must content ourselves with as much as is necessary for merely ascertaining the ratio of the axes. This will be obtained by knowing the ratio of the gravitation at the pole to that at the equator. Therefore, Let \( NmSgN \) (fig. 2.) be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a> through the axis of an oblate homogeneous spheroid, which differs very little from a sphere. \( NS \) is the axis, \( mg \) is the equatorial diameter, \( O \) is the centre, and \( NMSQ \) is the section of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> sphere. Let \( P \) be a particle situated at any distance without the sphere in its axis produced; it is required to determine the gravitation of this particle to the whole matter of the spheroid? Draw two lines \( PAC, PBD \), very near to each other, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off two small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> \( <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, CD \); draw \( GAa, HBb, ICc, KDd \), perpendicular to the axis; also draw \( OE \) and \( AL \) perpendicular to \( PAC \), and \( OF \) perpendicular to \( PD \), cutting \( PC \) in \( f \). Join \( OA \). Let \( OA \), the radius of the inscribed sphere be \( r \), and \( OP \) the distance of the gravitating particle be \( d \), and \( Mm \), the elevation of the equator of the spheroid, Tide, or the ellipticity, be \( e \). Also make \( AE = x \), and \( OE = y = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2} \). Then \( AE - BF = x \) and \( Ff = y \), \[ \frac{x}{\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}} \] Suppose the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> to turn round the axis \( OP \). The little space \( ABba \) will <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of the redundant matter; so will \( CDdc \). This ring may be considered as consisting of a number of thin rings generated by the revolution of \( <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a> \). The ring generated by \( Aa \) is equal to a parallelogram whose base is the circumference described by \( A \) and whose height is \( Aa \). Therefore let \( c \) be the circumference of a circle whose radius is \( 1 \). The ring will be \( Aa \times c \times AG \). But because \( <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">maN</a> \) is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of an ellipse, we have \( MM : Aa = MO : AG = r : AG \), and \( Aa = MM \times \frac{AG}{r} = \frac{e}{r} \times AG \). Therefore the surface of this ring is \( = \frac{e}{r} \times AG^2 \). We have supposed the spheroid to be very nearly spherical, that is, \( e \) exceedingly small in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of \( r \). This being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, all the particles in \( Aa \), and consequently all the particles in the ring generated by the revolution of \( Aa \), will attract the remote particle \( P \) with the same force that \( A \) does very nearly. We may say the same thing of the whole matter of the ring generated by the revolution of \( ABba \). This attraction is exerted in the direction \( PA \) by each individual particle. But every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of a particle \( A \) is accompanied by the action of a particle \( A' \) in the direction \( PA' \). These two compose an attraction in the direction \( PO \). The whole attraction in the directions similar to \( PA \) is \( = \frac{e}{r} \times AG^2 \times GH \), for \( GH \) measures the number of parallel plates of which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> ring is composed. This being decomposed in the direction \( PG \) is \( = \frac{e}{r} \times AG^2 \times PG \times GH \). But \( \frac{AG^2}{PA^2} \times \frac{OE^2}{PO^2} \times GH \). Therefore the attraction of the ring, estimated in the direction \( PO \), is \( = \frac{e}{r} \times \frac{AG^2}{PA^2} \times \frac{OE^2}{PO^2} \times GH \). Further, by the nature of the circle, we have \( HG : AB = AG : AO \); also \( AB : BL = AO : OE \). But \( PA : AG = PO : OE \), and \( OE = \frac{AG \times PO}{PA} \). Therefore \[ AB : BL = AO : \frac{AG \times PO}{PA}, = AO \cdot PA : PO \cdot AG \] Also \( BL : LA = EO : EA \), And \( LA : Ff = PA : Pf = ultimately PA : PE \). Therefore, by equality, \( HG : Ff = AG \cdot AO \cdot PA \cdot EO \cdot PA : AO \cdot PO \cdot AG \cdot EA \cdot PE \). Or \( HG : Ff = EO \cdot PA^2 : PO \cdot EA \cdot PE \). And \( HG = Ff \times \frac{EO \cdot PA^2}{PO \cdot PE \cdot EA} \). Now substitute this value of \( HG \) in the formula expressing the attraction of the ring. This changes it to \[ \frac{e}{r} \times \frac{OE^2 \cdot PE}{PO^2} \times \frac{OE \cdot PA^2}{PO \cdot PE \cdot EA} \times Ff, \text{ or } \frac{e}{r} \times \frac{OE^2 \cdot PA^2}{PO^4 \cdot EA} \times Ff. \] In like manner, the attraction of the the ring generated by the revolution of CD \( \frac{c}{r} \times OE^3 \cdot PC^3 \cdot PO^4 \cdot EA \times Ff \). Therefore the attraction of both is \[ = c \frac{e}{r} \times Ff \times OE^3 \cdot PA^3 + PC^3 = c \frac{e}{r} \times Ff \times \frac{y^2}{x^2} \times PA^3 + PC^3. \] But \( PA^3 + PC^3 = 2PE^3 + 2EA^3 = 2PE^3 + 2x^3 \). Therefore the attraction is \[ 2c \frac{e}{r} \times Ff \times \frac{y^2}{x^2} \times PE^3 + x^3. \] But \( Ff = y = \frac{x}{z} \). Therefore \( Ff \frac{y^2}{x} = \frac{x}{y} \times \frac{y^2}{x} = y^2 \times \frac{x}{y} = r^2 - x^2 \times \frac{x}{y} \). Therefore the attraction of the two rings is \[ 2c \frac{e}{r} \times \frac{y^2}{x^2} \times PE^3 + x^3. \] But \( PE^3 = PO^3 - OE^3 = d^3 - (r^3 - x^3) = d^3 - r^3 + x^3 \). Therefore the attraction of the two rings is \[ 2c \frac{e}{r} \times \frac{y^2}{x^2} \times d^3 - r^3 + x^3. \] The attraction of the whole shell of redundant matter will be had by taking the fluent of this formula, which is \[ 2c \frac{e}{r} \times \left( r^3 d^3 + \frac{3}{3} r^2 x^3 - r^4 x - \frac{d^3 x^3}{3} - \frac{2x^5}{5} \right), \] and then make \( x = r \). This gives \( 2c \frac{e}{r} \times \left( d^3 r^3 + r^5 - r^5 - \frac{1}{3} d^3 r^3 - \frac{1}{3} r^5 \right) \), which is \( 2c \frac{e}{r} \times \left( \frac{4}{3} r^5 - \frac{4}{5} r^5 \right) \), \[ = \frac{4}{3} c e r^3 - \frac{4}{5} r^5. \] To this add the attraction of the inscribed sphere, which is \( \frac{4}{3} c e r^3 \), and we have the attraction of the whole spheroid \[ = \frac{4}{3} c e r^3 + \frac{4}{3} c e r^3 - \frac{4}{5} c e r^5. \] Cor. 1. If the particle P is situated precisely in N, the pole of the spheroid, the attraction of the spheroid is \( \frac{4}{3} c e r + \frac{8}{3} c e \). If the spheroid is not oblate, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and if the greater semi-axis be \( r \), and the depression at the equator be \( e \), the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> is the same, taking \( e \) negatively. Therefore the attraction for a particle in the pole, or the gravitation of a particle in the pole, is \( \frac{4}{3} c e r - \frac{8}{3} c e \). But if the polar semi-axis be \( r + e \), and the equatorial radius be \( r \), so that this oblong spheroid has the same axis with the former oblate one, the gravitation of a particle in the pole is \( \frac{4}{3} c e r + \frac{8}{3} c e \). Cor. 2. If a number of parallel planes are drawn perpendicular to the equator of an oblong spheroid, whose longer semi-axis is \( r + e \), and equatorial radius \( r \), they will divide the spheroid into a number of similar ellipses; and since the ellipse through the axis has \( r + e \) and \( r \) for its two semi-axes, and the radius of a circle of equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> with this ellipse is a mean proportional between \( r \) and \( r + e \), and therefore very nearly \( r + \frac{1}{2} e \), when \( e \) is very small in comparison of \( r \), a particle on the equator of the oblong spheroid will be as much attracted by these circles of equal areas, with their corresponding ellipses, as by the ellipses. Now the attraction at the pole of an oblate spheroid was \( \frac{4}{3} c e r + \frac{8}{3} c e \). Therefore putting \( \frac{1}{2} e \) in place of \( e \), the attraction on the equator of the oblong spheroid will be equal to \( \frac{4}{3} c r + \frac{8}{3} c e \). Thus we have ascertained the gravitations of a particle situated in the pole, and of one situated in the equator, of a homogeneous oblong spheroid. This will enable us to solve the following problem: If the particles of a homogeneous oblong fluid spheroid attract each other with a force inversely as the squares of their distances, and if they are attracted by a very distant body by the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and if the ratio of the equatorial gravity to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force be given; to find what must be the proportion of the semi-axis, so that all may be in equilibrium, and the spheroid preserve its form? Let \( r \) be the equatorial radius, and \( r + e \) be the polar semi-axis. Then the gravitation at the pole \( m \) is \( \frac{4}{3} c e r + \frac{8}{3} c e \), and the gravitation at the equator is \( \frac{4}{3} c r + \frac{8}{3} c e \). Now by the gravitation towards the distant body placed in the direction of the polar axis, the polar gravitation is diminished, and the equatorial gravitation is increased; and the increase of the equatorial gravitation is to the diminution of the polar gravitation as NO to \( 2mO \). Therefore if the whole attraction of the oblong spheroid for a particle on its equator be to the force which the distant body exerts there, as G to P, and if the spheroid is very nearly spherical, the absolute weight at the equator will be \( \frac{4}{3} c e r + \frac{8}{3} c e + \frac{4}{3} c e r \cdot \frac{P}{G} \). And the absolute weight at the pole will be \( \frac{4}{3} c e r + \frac{8}{3} c e - \frac{4}{3} c e r \cdot \frac{P}{G} \). Their difference is \( \frac{4}{3} c e r + 2c e r \cdot \frac{P}{G} \). Now if we suppose this spheroid to be composed of similar concentric shells, all the forces will decrease in the same ratio. Therefore the weight of a particle in a column reaching from the equator to the centre will be to the weight of a similarly situated particle of a column reaching from the pole to the centre, as the weight of a particle at the equator to the weight of a particle at the pole. But the whole weights of the two columns must be equal, that they may <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> each other at the centre. Their lengths must therefore be reciprocally as the weights of similarly situated particles; that is, the polar semi-axis must be to the equatorial radius, as the weight of a particle at the equator to the weight of a particle at the pole. Therefore we must have \( \frac{4}{3} c e + 2c e r \cdot \frac{P}{G} : \frac{4}{3} c e + \frac{8}{3} c e - \frac{4}{3} c e r \cdot \frac{P}{G} = e : r \). Hence we derive \( 2c e r \cdot \frac{P}{G} = \frac{8}{3} c e \), or \( 4G : 15P = r : e \). This determines the form of the fluid spheroid when the ratio of G to P is given. It is well known that the gravitation of the moon to the earth is to the disturbing force of the sun as 178,725 to 1 very nearly. The lunar gravitation is increased as the approaches the earth in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> duplicate ratio of the distances. The disturbing force of the sun diminishes in the simple ratio of the distances; therefore the weight of a body on the surface of the earth is to the disturbing... disturbing force of the sun on the same body, in a ratio compounded of the ratio of \(178,725\) to \(1\), the ratio of \(3600\) to \(1\), and the ratio of \(62\) to \(1\); that is, in the ratio of \(38604600\) to \(1\). If the mean radius of the earth be \(29934500\) feet, the difference of the axis, or the elevation of the pole of the watery spheroid produced by the gravitation to the sun, will be \(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{178,725} \times \frac{1}{3600} \times \frac{1}{62}\) feet, or very nearly \(2\frac{1}{2}\) inches. This is the tide produced by the sun on a homogeneous fluid sphere. It is plain, that if the earth consists of a solid nucleus of the same density with the water, the form of the solar tide will be the same. But if the density of the nucleus be different, the form of the tide will be different, and will depend both on the density and on the figure of the nucleus. If the nucleus be of the same form as the surrounding fluid, the whole will still maintain its form with the same proportion of the axis. If the nucleus be spherical, its action on the surrounding fluid will be the same as if all the matter of the nucleus by which it exceeds an equal bulk of the fluid were collected at the centre. In this case, the ocean cannot maintain the same form; for the action of this central body being proportional to the square of the distance inversely, will augment the gravity of the equatorial fluid more than it augments that of the circumpolar fluid; and the ocean, which was in equilibrium (by supposition), must now become more protuberant at the poles. It may, however, be again balanced in an elliptical form, when it has acquired a just proportion of the axes. The process for determining this is tedious, but precisely similar to the preceding. If the density of the nucleus exceed that of the fluid about \(\frac{1}{52}\), we shall have \(r : e = G : 3P\), which is nearly the form which has been determined for the earth, by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> of degrees of the meridian, and by the vibration of pendulums. The curious reader will do well to consult the excellent dissertations by Clairaut and Boscovich on the Figure of the Earth, where this curious problem is treated in the most complete manner. Mr Bernoulli, in his dissertation on the Tides, has committed a great mistake in this particular. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, if the nucleus be less dense than the waters, or if there be a great central hollow, the elevation produced by the sun will exceed \(2\frac{1}{2}\) inches. It is needless to examine this any farther. We have collected enough for explaining the chief affections of the tides. It is known that the earth is not a sphere, but swelled out at the equator by the diurnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>. But the change of form is so very small in proportion to the whole bulk, that it cannot sensibly affect the change of form afterwards induced by the sun on the waters of the ocean. For the disturbing force of the sun would produce a certain protuberance on a fluid sphere; and this protuberance depends on the ratio of the disturbing force to the force of gravity at the surface of this sphere. If the gravity be changed in any proportion, the protuberance will change in the same proportion. Therefore if the body be a spheroid, the protuberance produced at any point by the sun will increase or diminish in the same proportion that the gravity at this point has been changed by the change of form. Now the change of gravity, even at the pole of the terrestrial spheroid, is extremely small in comparison with the whole gravity. Therefore the change produced on the spheroid will not sensibly differ from that produced on the sphere; and the elevations of the waters above the surface, which they would have assumed independent of the sun's action, will be the same on the spheroid as on the sphere. For the same reason, the moon will change the surface already changed by the sun, in the same manner as she would have changed the surface of the undisturbed ocean. Therefore the change produced by both these luminaries in any place will be the same when acting together as when acting separately; and it will be equal to the sum, or the difference of their separate changes, according as these would have been in the same or opposite directions. Let us now consider the most interesting circumstance of the form of an elliptical tide, which differs very little from a sphere. Let \(TR, TW\) be perpendicular to the equatorial diameter and to the axis, so that they are the cosine and the sine of \(TOQ\) to the radius \(TO\) or \(OQ\). Therefore \(OT : TR = TV : TZ\). But in the ellipse \(OQ\), or \(OT : TR = Q_{q} : TV\). Therefore \(OT^{2} : TR^{2} = Q_{q} : TZ\), and \(TZ = \frac{Q_{q} \cdot TR^{2}}{OT^{2}}\). And in the very same manner it may be shown, that \(TZ = Q_{q} \times \text{fin}^{2} Z\). 3. The elevation of the point \(T\) above another point \(T'\), whose angular distance \(TOT'\) from the point \(T\) is \(90^{\circ}\), is \(= Q_{q} \times \text{cof}^{2} Z - \text{fin}^{2} Z\). Then \(I'Z' = Q_{q} \times \text{cof}^{2} Z'\), and \(TZ - T'Z', Z' = Q_{q} \times \text{cof}^{2} Z - \text{fin}^{2} Z'\). But the arch \(QT'\) is the complement of \(Q'T\), and therefore \(\text{cof}^{2} Z' = \text{fin}^{2} Z\). Therefore \(TZ - T'Z' = Q_{q} \times \text{cof}^{2} Z - \text{fin}^{2} Z\). 4. \(Q_{q} = \frac{1}{2} Q_{q}\). For the inscribed sphere is to the spheroid as \(OQ\) to \(O_{q}\). But the inscribed sphere is to the sphere \(s_{o}n\) as \(OQ^{3}\) to \(O_{q}^{3}\). Therefore because the sphere \(s_{o}n\) is equal to the spheroid \(S_{q}N_{q}\), we have \(OQ : O_{q} = OQ^{3} : O_{q}^{3}\), and \(O_{q}\) is the first of two mean proportions between \(OQ\) and \(O_{q}\). But \(Q_{q}\) is very small in comparison with \(OQ\). Therefore \(Q_{q}\) is very nearly \(\frac{1}{2}\) of \(Q_{q}\). Since \(s_{o}n\) is the sphere of equal capacity, it is the form of the undisturbed ocean. The best way therefore of conceiving the changes of form produced by the sun or moon, or by both together, is to consider the elevations or depressions which they produce above or below this surface. Therefore, . The elevation \( rZ \) of the point \( Z \) above the equi- capacious sphere is evidently \( = Q \times \cos^2 Z - \frac{1}{4} Q \times q \). Also the depression \( r'Z' \) of the point \( Z' \) is \( = Q \times \sin^2 Z' - \frac{3}{4} Q \times q \). N.B. Either of these formulae will answer for either the elevation above, or the depression below, the natural ocean: For if \( \cos^2 Z \) is less than \( \frac{1}{4} \), the elevation given by the formula will be <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>; that is, the point is below the natural surface. In like manner, when \( \sin^2 Z' \) is less than \( \frac{3}{4} \), the depression is negative, and the point is above the surface. But if \( \cos^2 Z \) be \( = \frac{1}{4} \), or \( \sin^2 Z' \) be \( = \frac{3}{4} \), the point is in the natural surface. This marks the place where the spheroid and the equal sphere intersect each other, viz. in \( P' \); the arch \( P'o \) being \( 54^\circ 44' \) very nearly, and \( PS = 35^\circ 16' \). Let \( S \) represent the whole elevation of the pole of the solar tide above its equator, or the difference between high and low water produced by the sun; and let \( M \) represent the whole elevation produced by the moon. Let \( x \) and \( y \) represent the zenith distances of the sun and moon with respect to any point whatever on the ocean. Then \( x \) and \( y \) will be the arches intercepted between that point and the summits of the solar and lunar tides. Then the elevation produced by both lu- minaries in that plane is \( S \cdot \cos^2 x + M \cdot \cos^2 y - \frac{1}{4} M \); or, more concisely, \( S \cdot \cos^2 x + M \cdot \cos^2 y - \frac{1}{4} S + M \), and the depression is \( S \cdot \sin^2 x + M \cdot \sin^2 y - \frac{3}{4} S + M \). Let the sun and moon be in the same point of the heavens. The solar and lunar tides will have the same axis; the cosines of \( x \) and \( y \) will each be \( 1 \), and the elevation at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> pole will be \( S + M - \frac{1}{4} S + M = \frac{3}{4} S + M \). The depression at any point \( 90^\circ \) from this pole will be \( \frac{1}{4} S + M \), and the whole tide is \( S + M \). Let the moon be in quadrature, as in \( a \) (fig. 3.). The appearance at \( s \) will be known, by considering that in this place the cosine of \( x \) is \( 1 \), and the cosine of \( y \) is \( 0 \). Therefore the elevation at \( s = S - \frac{1}{4} S + M = \frac{3}{4} S - \frac{1}{4} M \). The depression at \( a = S - \frac{3}{4} S + M = \frac{1}{4} S - \frac{3}{4} M \). The difference or whole tide \( = S - M \). In like manner, the whole elevation at \( a \) above the in- scribed sphere is \( M - S \). Hence we see that the whole tide, when the moon is in quadrature, is the difference of \( S \) and \( M \). We also see, that if \( M \) exceeds \( S \), the water will be higher at \( a \) than at \( s \). Now it is a matter of observation, that in the quadratures it is high water under the moon, and low water under the sun. It is also a matter of observation, that in the free ocean, the ebb tide, or the water at \( s \), immediately under the sun, is below the natural surface of the ocean. Hence we must conclude, that \( \frac{3}{4} S \) is less than \( \frac{1}{4} M \), or that \( M \) is more than double of \( S \). This agrees with the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUTATION">nutation</a> and precession, which seem to make \( S = \frac{3}{4} M \). In all other positions of the sun and moon, the place of high water will be different. It is high water where the sum of the elevations produced by both luminaries above the natural ocean is greatest; and the place of low water is where the depression below the natural ocean is greatest. Therefore, in order that it may be high water, we must have \( S \cdot \cos^2 x + M \cdot \cos^2 y - \frac{1}{4} S + M \) a maximum; or, neglecting the constant quan- tity \( \frac{S + M}{3} \), we must have \( S \cdot \cos^2 x + M \cdot \cos^2 y \) a maximum. In like manner, to have low water in a place where the zenith distances of the sun and moon are \( v \) and \( w \), we must have \( S \cdot \sin^2 v + M \cdot \sin^2 w \) a maximum. Lemma 1. By the first Lemma we see, that in order that there may be high water at any place, when the zenith <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- tances of the sun and moon are \( x \) and \( y \), we must have \( S \cdot \cos^2 x + M \cdot \cos^2 y \) a maximum. Therefore we must have \( S \cdot \sin^2 2x + M \cdot \sin^2 2y = 0 \), or \( S \cdot \sin^2 2x = M \cdot \sin^2 2y \), which gives us \( \sin^2 2x: \sin^2 2y = M : S \). In like manner, the place of low water requires \( \sin^2 2v : \sin^2 2w = M : S \). From this last circumstance we learn, that the place of low water is \( o \), removed \( 90^\circ \) from the place of high water; whereas we might have expected, that the spheroid would have been most protuberant on that side on which the moon is: For the fines of \( 2v \) and of \( 2w \) have the same proportion with the fines of \( 2x \) and of \( 2y \). Now we know that the fine of the double of any arch is the same with the fine of the double of its complement. Therefore if low water be really distant \( 90^\circ \) from high water, we shall have \( \sin^2 2x : \sin^2 2y = \sin^2 2v : \sin^2 2w \). But if it is at any other place, the fines cannot have this proportion. Now let \( s \) be the point of the earth's surface which has the sun in the zenith, and \( m \) the point which has the moon in the zenith. Let \( h \) be any other point.
