We have not met with any accounts of a tide being observed in this sea. It should be much greater, though still very small, in the Mediterranean sea. Accordingly, tides are observed there, but still more remarkably in the Adriatic, for a reason which will be given by and by. We do not know that tides have been observed in the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of North America. These tides, though small, should be very regular. Should there be another great basin in the neighbourhood of \(z x\), lying east or west of it, we should observe a curious phenomenon. It would be low water on one side of the shore \(z\) when it is high water on the other side of this partition. If the tides in the Euxine and Caspian seas, or in the American lakes which are near each other, could be observed, this phenomenon should appear, and would be one of the prettiest examples of universal gravitation that can be conceived. Something like it is to be seen at Gibraltar. It is high water on the east side of the rock about 10 o'clock at full and change, and it is high water on the west side, not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> distant, at 12. This difference is perhaps the chief cause of the singular current which is observed in the Straits mouth. There are three currents observed at the same time, which change their directions every 12 hours. The small tide of the Mediterranean proceeds along the Barbary shore, which is very uniform all the way from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, with tolerable regularity. But along the northern side, where it is greatly obstructed by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the islands, and the east coast of Spain, it flows very irregularly; and the perceptible high water on the Spanish coast differs four hours from that of the southern coast. Thus it happens, that one tide ranges round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a> point, and another along the shore near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEUTA">Ceuta</a>, and there is a third current in the middle different from both. Its general direction is from the Atlantic. Atlantic ocean into the Mediterranean sea, but it sometimes comes out when the ebb tide in the Atlantic is considerable. Suppose the moon over the middle of the Mediterranean. The surface of the sea will be level, and it will be half tide at both ends, and therefore within the Straits of Gibraltar. But without the Straits it is within half an hour of high water. Therefore there will be a current setting in from the Atlantic. About three and a half hours after, it is high water within and half ebb without. The current now sets out from the Mediterranean. Three hours later, it is low water without the Straits and half ebb within; therefore the current has been setting out all this while. Three hours later, it is half flood without the Straits and low water within, and the current is again setting in, &c. Were the earth fluid to the centre, the only sensible motion of the waters would be up and down, like the waves on the open ocean, which are not brushed along by strong gales. But the shallowness of the channel makes a horizontal motion necessary, that water may be supplied to form the accumulation of the tide. When this is formed on a flat shelving coast, the water must flow in and out, on the flats and sands, while it rises and falls. These horizontal motions must be greatly modified by the channel or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> along which they move. When the channel contracts along the line of flowing water, the wave, as it moves up the channel, and is checked by the narrowing shores, must be reflected back, and keep a-top of the waters still flowing in underneath. Thus it may rise higher in these narrow seas than in the open ocean. This may serve to explain a little the great tides which happen on some coasts, such as the coast of Normandy. At St Malo the flood frequently rises 50 feet. But we cannot give any thing like a full or satisfactory account of these singularities. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Fundy, and particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNAPOLIS">Annapolis</a> Royal, the water sometimes rises above 100 feet. This seems quite inexplicable by any force of the sun and moon, which cannot raise the waters of the free ocean more than eight feet. These great floods are unquestionably owing to the proper timing of certain oscillations or currents adjoining, by which they unite, and form one of great force. Such violent motions of water are frequently seen on a small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> in the motions of brooks and rivers; but we are too little acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRAULICS">hydraulics</a> to explain them with any precision. We have seen that there is an oscillation of waters formed under the sun and moon; and that in consequence of the rotation of the earth, the inertia and the want of perfect fluidity of the waters, and obstructions in the channel, this accumulation never reaches the place where it would finally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> if the earth did not turn round its axis. The consequence of this must be a general current of the waters from east to west. This may be seen in another way. The moon in her orbit round the earth has her gravity to the earth diminished by the sun's disturbing force, and therefore moves in an orbit less incurvated than she would describe independent of the sun's action. She therefore employs a longer time. If the moon were so near the earth as almost to touch it, the same thing would happen. Therefore suppose the moon turning round the earth, almost in contact with the equator, with her natural undisturbed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIODIC">periodic</a> time, and that the earth is revolving round its axis in the same time, the moon would remain continually above the same spot of the earth's surface (suppose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Quito), and a spectator in another planet would see the moon always covering the same spot. Now let the sun act. This will not affect the rotation of the earth, because the action on one part is exactly balanced by the action on another. But it will affect the moon. It will move more slowly round the earth's centre, and at a greater distance. It will be left behind by the city of Quito, which it formerly covered. And as the earth moves round from west to east, the moon, moving more slowly, will have a motion to the west with respect to Quito. In like manner, every particle of water has its gravity diminished, and its diurnal motion retarded; and hence arises a general motion or current from east to west. This is very distinctly perceived in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It comes round the Cape of Good Hope, ranges along the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and then sets directly over to America, where it meets a similar stream which comes in by the north of Europe. Meeting the shores of America, it is deflected both to the south along the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, and to the north along the North American shores, where it forms what is called the Gulf Stream, because it comes from the gulf of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>. This motion is indeed very slow, this being sufficient for the accumulation of seven or eight feet on the deep ocean; but it is not altogether inefﬁcient. We may expect differences in the appearances on the western shores of Europe and Africa, and on the western shores of America, from the appearances on the eastern coasts of America and of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, for the general current obstructs the waters from the western shores, and sends them to the eastern shores. Also when we compare the wide opening of the northern extremity of the Atlantic ocean with the narrow opening between Kamtchatka and America, we should expect differences between the appearances on the west coasts of Europe and of America. The observations made during the circumnavigation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook and others show a remarkable difference. All along the west coast of North America the inferior tide is very trifling, and frequently is not perceived. In the very same manner, the disturbing forces of the sun and moon form a tide in the fluid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> which surrounds this globe, consisting of an elevation and depression, which move gradually from east to west. Neither does this tide ever attain that position with respect to the disturbing planets which it would do were the earth at rest on its axis. Hence arises a motion of the whole air from east to west; and this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of the trade-winds. They are a little accelerated by being heated, and therefore expanding. They expand more to the westward than in the opposite direction, because the air expands on that side into air which is now cooling and contracting. These winds very evidently follow the sun's motion, tending more to the south or north as he goes south or north. Were this motion considerably affected by the expansion of heated air, we should find the air rather coming northward and southward from the torrid zone, in consequence of its expansion in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. We repeat it, it is almost solely produced by the aerial tide, and is necessary for the very formation of this tide. We cannot perceive the accumulation. It cannot affect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>, as many many think, because, though the air becomes deeper, it becomes deeper only because it is made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> by the gravitation to the sun. Instead of pressing more on the cistern of the barometer, we imagine that it presses less; because, like the ocean, it never attains the height to which it tends. It remains always too low for equilibrium, and therefore it should press with less force on the cistern of a barometer. There is an appearance precisely similar to this in the planet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. He is surrounded by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> which is arranged in zones or belts, probably owing to climate differences of the different latitudes, by which each seems to have a different kind of sky. Something like this will appear to a spectator in the moon looking at this earth. The general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and appearance of the sky is considerably different in the torrid and temperate zones. Jupiter's belts are not of a constant shape and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; but there often appear large spots or tracts of cloud, which retain their shape during several revolutions of Jupiter round his axis. To judge of his rotation by one of these, we should say that he turns round in 9.55. There is also a brighter spot which is frequently seen, occupying one certain situation on the body of Jupiter. This is surely adherent to his body, and is either a bright coloured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or perhaps a tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> hovering over some volcano. This spot turns round in 9.51. And thus there is a general current in his atmosphere from east to west. Both the motion of the air and of the water tend to diminish the rotation of the earth round its axis; for they move slower than the earth, because they are retarded by the luminaries. They must communicate this retardation to the earth, and must take from it a quantity of motion precisely equal to what they want, in order to make up the equilibrated tide. In all probability this retardation is compensated by other causes; for no retardation can be observed. This would have altered the length of the year since the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPARCHUS">Hipparchus</a>, giving it a smaller number of days. We see causes of compensation. The continual washing down of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> from the elevated parts of the earth must produce this effect, by communicating to the valley on which it is brought to reflect the excess of diurnal velocity which it had on the mountain top. While we were employed on this article, a book was put into our hands called Studies of Nature, by Mr Saint Pierre. This author attacks the Newtonian theory of the tides, as erroneous in principle, and as quite insufficient for explaining the phenomena; and he attributes all phenomena of the tides to the liquefaction of the ices and snows of the circumpolar regions, and the greater length of the polar than of the equatorial axis of the earth. He is a man of whom we wish to speak with respect, for his constant attention to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> causes, and the proof thence resulting of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and goodness of God. For this he is entitled to the greater praise, that it required no small degree of fortitude to reflect the influence of national example, and to retain his piety in the midst of a people who have drunk the very dregs of the atheism of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. This is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of merit rarely to be met with in a Frenchman of the present day; but as a philosopher, M. de St Pierre can lay claim to no other merit except that of having collected many important facts. The argument which he employs to prove that the earth is a prolate spheroid, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> demonstration of the truth of the contrary opinion; and the melting of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> and snows at the poles cannot produce the smallest motion in the waters. Were there even ten times more ice and snow floating on the northern sea than there is, and were it all to melt in one minute, there would be no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> from it; for it would only fill up the space which it formerly occupied in the water. Of this any person will be convinced, who shall put a handful of snow squeezed hard into a jar of water, and note the exact height of the water. Let the snow melt, and he will find the water of the same height as before. TIDE-Waiters, or Tide-men, are inferior officers belonging to the customhouse, whose employment is to watch or attend upon ships until the customs be paid: they get this name from their going on board ships on their arrival in the mouth of the Thames or other ports, and so come up with the tide.

TIERCE

Pages 49-49
or TIERCE, a measure of liquid things, as wine, oil, &c containing the third part of a pipe, or 42 gallons.

TIERCED

Pages 49-49

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes the shield to be divided by any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the partition-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, as party, coupy, tranchy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tailly, into three equal parts of different colours or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. TIGER. See FELIS, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TIGER-WOLF

Pages 49-49

the name of the hyena at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">CANIS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TIGRIS

Pages 49-49

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which has its source near that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> in the mountain Tchirdir in Turcomania: afterwards it separates <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIARBEKIR">Diarbekir</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERZERUM">Erzerum</a>, and Khufifan from Irac-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; and uniting with the Euphrates at Gorno, it falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Bafforah, under the name of Schar el-Arab. This river passes by Diarbekir, Gezira, Mouful, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, Gorno, and Bafforah.

TILIA

Pages 49-49

LIME <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> LINDEN-TREE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of polyandria; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the Columniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TILLEMONT

Pages 49-49

SEBASTIAN LE NAIN DE. See NAIN. TILLER of a SHIP, a strong piece of wood fastened in the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>, and in small ships and boats called the helm.

TILLOEA

Pages 49-49

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of tetrandria; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 13th order, Succulentae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TILLOTSON

Pages 49-50

JOHN, a celebrated archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was the son of Robert Tillotson of Sowerby, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, clothier; and was born there in the year 1630. He studied in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; and in 1656 left this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, in order to become <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the son of Edmund Prideaux, Esq., of Ford <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. He was afterwards curate to Dr Hacket <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Cheshunt, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>. In 1663, he was presented by Sir Thomas Barnardiston to the rectory of Ketton <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Kedington in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>; but was the next year chosen preacher to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn, when he procured Ketton to be bestowed on his curate. He was greatly admired in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> for his sermons; and in the same year was chosen Tuesday-lecturer at St Lawrence's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, London, where his lectures were frequented by all the divines of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and by many persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and distinction. In 1666, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a> at Cambridge; in 1669, was made prebendary of Canterbury; in 1672, was admitted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>; and three years after, was made a prebendary of St Paul's cathedral, London. In 1679, he became acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Shrewsbury, whom he converted from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>; and the next year refused to sign the clergy of London's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of thanks to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Charles II. for not agreeing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. In 1683, he visited the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Ruffell when under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>; and attended him in his last moments on the scaffold. In 1689, he was installed dean of St Paul's; made clerk of the closet to King William and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; and appointed one of the commissioners to prepare matters to be laid before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, in order to a comprehension of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, as well dissenters as churchmen; but this attempt was frustrated by the zeal of those members of that body, who refused to admit of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in things confessedly indifferent. In 1691, Dr Tillotson was, notwithstanding the warmest remonstrances and intrigues on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, consecrated archbishop of Canterbury, and four days after was sworn one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; their majesties always repaying an entire confidence in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, moderation, and integrity. In 1694, he was seized with a palsy, of which he died in the 65th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was interred in the church of St Lawrence Jewry, London, where a handsome monument is erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. This learned and pious divine, while living, was greatly inveighed against by the enemies of the revolution. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> there was found a bundle of bitter libels which had been published against him, on which he had written with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, "I forgive the authors of these books, and pray God that he may also forgive them." It is remarkable, that while this truly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was in a private station, he always laid aside two-tenths of his income for charitable uses. One volume in folio of Dr Tillotson's sermons was published in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and corrected by his own hand; they were translated into French by Barbeyrac. Those which came abroad after his death, from his chaplain Dr Barker, made two volumes in folio, the copy of which was sold for £500. This was the only legacy he left to his family, his extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> having consumed his yearly revenues as constantly as they came to his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. King William, however, gave two grants to his widow; the first of which was an annuity of £400, during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> life, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of £200, as an addition to the former annuity. Dr Tillotson wrote some other works besides his Sermons; and also published Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>'s works, and Dr Wilkins's Treatise of the Principles and Duties of Natural <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, and a volume of that divine's Sermons.

TIMBER

Pages 50-50

wood fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c. See **TREE**, and **<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRENGTH_OF_MATERIALS">STRENGTH of Materials</a>**.

TIMBERS

Pages 50-50

the ribs of a ship, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the incurved pieces of wood, branching outward from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> in a vertical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, so as to give strength, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and solidity, to the whole fabric. See **SHIP-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">BUILDING</a>**, book i., chap. ii.

TIME

Pages 50-50

a succession of phenomena in the universe, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> marked by certain periods or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, chiefly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and revolution of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The general idea which time gives in every thing to which it is applied, is that of limited duration. Thus we cannot say of the Deity, that he exists in time; because eternity, which he inhabits, is absolutely uniform, neither admitting limitation nor succession. See **<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>**, No. 299. **Time**, in **Music**, is an affection of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, by which it is said to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> or short, with regard to its continuance in the same tone or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tune. Musical time is distinguished into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> or duple time, and triple time. **Duple**, **duplet**, or **common time**, is when the notes are in a duple duration of each other, viz. a semibreve equal to two minims, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIM">minim</a> to two crotchets, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROTCHET">crotchet</a> to two quavers, &c. Common or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> time is of two kinds. The first when every <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> is equal to a semibreve, or its value in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of notes of a less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is where every bar is equal to a minim, or its value in less notes. The movements of this kind of measure are various, but there are three common distinctions; the first **slow**, denoted at the beginning of the line by the mark C; the second **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>**, marked thus ; and the third **very brief**, thus marked . Triple time is when the durations of the notes are triple of each other, that is, when the semibreve is equal to three minims, the minim to three crotchets, &c., and it is marked T.

TIME-KEEPERS

Pages 50-50
or **Instruments for measuring Time**. See **CLOCK**, **DIAL**, **WATCH**, &c. **Harrison's TIME-KEEPER**. See **HARRISON** and **LONGITUDE**.

TIMOLEON

Pages 50-50

a celebrated Corinthian general, who restored the Syracusans to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and drove the Carthaginians out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. See **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">SYRACUSE</a>**, No. 50—54.

TIMON

Pages 50-51

the Sceptic, who is not to be confounded with Timon the Misanthrope, was a Philiasian, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Pyrrho, and lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a>. He took no little pains to invite disciples to his school, that it has been said of him, that as the Scythians <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, Timon gained pupils by running from them. He was fond of rural retirement; and was so much addicted to wine, that he held a successful contest with several celebrated champions in drinking. Like Lucian, he wrote with sarcastic humour against the whole body of philosophers. The fragments of his satirical poem *Silli*, often quoted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, have been carefully collected by Henry Stephens in his *Poetica Philosophica*. Timon lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 90 years. **Timon**, surnamed **Misanthropos**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>-hater, a famous Athenian, who lived about 420 B.C. He was one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> asked, why he loved the young <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCIBIADES">Alcibiades</a> while he detested all the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>? on which he replied, "It is because I foresee that he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the ruin of the Athenians." He carefully avoided all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; yet went one day to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the people, and cried with a loud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, "That he had a fig-tree on which several persons had hanged themselves;" Timon, themselves; but as he intended to cut it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, in order to build a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it stood, he gave them notice of it, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any of them had a mind to hang themselves, they must make haste and do it speedily." He had an epitaph engraved on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, filled with imprecations against those who read it. Shakespeare has formed a tragedy on his story.

TIMOR

Pages 51-51

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to the south of the Moluccas, and to the east of the island of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, being 150 miles in length, and 37 in breadth. It abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a>-wood, wax and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; and the Dutch have a fort here. The inhabitants are Pagans, and are little better than savages; and some pretend they had not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of fire many years ago.

TIMOTHEUS

Pages 51-51

one of the most celebrated poet-musicians of antiquity, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>, an Ionian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, 446 years B.C. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>; and not only excelled in lyric and dithyrambic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, but in his performance upon the cithara. According to Pausanias, he perfected that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> by the addition of four new strings to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> which it had before; though Suidas says it had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> before, and that Timotheus only added two, the 10th and 11th, to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. See Lyre. With respect to the number of strings upon the lyre of Timotheus: The account of Pausanias and Suidas is confirmed in the famous senatus-consultum against him, still extant, preserved at full length in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>. Mr Stillingfleet has given an extract from it, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the simplicity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Spartan music. The fact is mentioned in Athenaeus; and Cæsabon, in his notes upon that author, has inserted the whole original text from Boethius, with corrections. The following is a faithful translation of this extraordinary Spartan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. "Whereas Timotheus the Milesian, coming to our city, has dishonoured our ancient music, and, defiling the lyre of seven strings, has, by the introduction of a greater variety of notes, corrupted the ears of our youth; and by the number of his strings, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, has given to our music an effeminate and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> dress, instead of the plain and orderly one in which it has hitherto appeared; rendering melody infamous, by composing in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHROMATIC">chromatic</a> instead of the enharmonic:—The kings and the ephori have therefore resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon Timotheus for these things: and, farther, to oblige him to cut all the superfluous strings of his eleven, leaving only the seven tones; and to banish him from our city; that men may be warned for the future not to introduce into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> any unbecoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>." The same story, as related in Athenæus, has this additional circumstance. That when the public executioner was on the point of fulfilling the sentence, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the new strings, Timotheus, perceiving a little statue in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with a lyre in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of as many strings as that which had given the offence, and showing it to the judges, was acquitted. It appears from Suidas, that the poetical and musical compositions of Timotheus were very numerous, and of various kinds. He attributes to him 19 nomes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> canticles, in hexameters; 36 poems, or preludes; 18 dithyrambs; 21 hymns; the poem in praise of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>; one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>; three tragedies, the Persians, Phœnissas, and Laertes; to which must be added a fourth, mentioned Timotheus by several ancient authors, called Niobe, without forgetting the poem on the birth of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. Stephen of Byzantium makes him author of 18 books of nomes, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, for the cithara, to 8000 verses; and of 1000 Hymnus, or preludes, for the nomes of the flutes. Timotheus died in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, according to Suidas, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 97; though the Martyrs, much better authority, lay at 92; and Stephen of Byzantium fixes his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in the fourth year of the 105th Olympiad, two years before the birth of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>; whence it appears, that this Timotheus was not the famous player on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> so much esteemed by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who was animated to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> by his performance as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> his arms; and who employed him, as Athenæus informs us, together with the other great musicians of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, at his nuptials. However, by an inattention to dates, and by forgetting that of these two musicians of the same name the one was a Milesian and the other a Theban, they have been hitherto often confounded. TIMUR-BEG. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>.

TINCAL

Pages 51-51

the name by which crude <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> impure <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a> is sometimes known. See Borax, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TINDAL

Pages 51-51

Dr Matthew, a famous English writer, was the son of the reverend Mr John Tindal of Beer-Ferres in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and was born about the year 1657. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, whence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and was afterwards elected fellow of All-Souls. In 1685 he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and in the reign of James II. declared himself a Roman Catholic; but soon renounced that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. After the revolution he published several pamphlets in favour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the press, &c., His "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">Rights</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> asserted," occasioned him having a violent contest with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-church clergy; and his treatise "Christianity as old as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">Creation</a>," published in 1733, made much noise, and was answered by several writers, particularly by Dr Conybeare, Mr Forster, and Dr Leland. Dr Tindal died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in August 1733. He left in manuscript a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of his "Christianity as old as the Creation;" the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to which has been published. Mr Pope has satirized Dr Tindal in his Dunciad.

TINNING

Pages 51-51

the covering <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lining anything with melted tin, or tin reduced to a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>. Looking-glasses are foliated or tinned with plates of beaten tin, the whole bigness of the glass, applied or fastened thereto by means of quicksilver. See Foliating of Looking Glasses.

TINNITUS AURUM

Pages 51-51

a noise in the ears like the continual <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of bells, very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in many disorders, particularly in nervous fevers.

TIPPERARY

Pages 51-52

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, bounded on the west by those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>, on the east by the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILKENNY">Kilkenny</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN_S_COUNTY"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s county, on the south by the county of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>, ford, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s-county and the territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> O'Carols. It extends about 42 miles in length, 27 in breadth, containing 599,500 acres, divided into 12 baronies, in which are several market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and boroughs. It sends eight members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. two for the county, two for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Cathel, and two for each of the boroughs of Clonmel, Fethard, and Thurles. The north <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is mountainous and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; but in the south the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is milder, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> much more fertile, producing plenty of corn, and good pasture for the numerous herds of cattle and flocks of sheep with which it abounds. The north part is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, and for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> gave the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, and afterwards of marquis and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, to the noble family of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a>, descended from a sister of Thomas à Becket archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, till, at the accession of George I., the last duke was attainted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, and died abroad. In that part of the county, the family had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> prerogatives and privileges granted them by Edward III. Another district in this county was anciently called the County of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a> of Tipperary, from a famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> in it styled Holy Cross, on account of a piece of Christ's cross that was said to be preserved there. This abbey and district enjoyed also special privileges in former times. The remains of the abbey, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather the spot where it stood, are still held in great veneration, and much resorted to by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>.

TIPSTAFF

Pages 52-52

an officer who attends the judges with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> tipped with silver, and takes into his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> all prisoners who are committed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> turned over at a judge's chambers.

TIPULA

Pages 52-52

the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">Crane</a>-fly; a genus of insects belonging to the order of diptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TIROL

Pages 52-52
or Tyrol, a county of Germany in the circle of Austria, under which may be included the territories belonging to the bishops of Brixen, Trent, and Chur, the Teutonic Order, and the prince of Dietrichstein, the Austrian seigniories before the Allerberg, and the Austrian districts in Swabia. It is 150 miles in length, and 120 in breadth, and contains 28 large towns. The face of the country is very mountainous. Of these mountains, some have their tops always buried in snow; others are covered with woods, abounding with a variety of game; and others are rich in metals, and marble of all colours. Of the lower, some yield plenty of corn, others wine, and woods of chestnut trees. The valleys are exceeding fertile also, and pleasant. In some places considerable quantities of flax are raised, in others there is a good breed of horses and horned cattle; and, among the mountains, abundance of chamois and wild goats. In this country are also found precious stones of several sorts; as garnets, rubies, amethysts, emeralds, and a species of diamonds, agates, carnelians, calcadoes, malachites, &c.; nor is it without hot baths, acid waters, salt pits, mines of silver, copper, and lead, mineral colours, alum, and vitriol. The principal river of Tirol is the Inn, which, after traversing the country, and receiving a number of lesser streams into it, enters Bavaria, in which, at Passau, it falls into the Danube. The men here are very tall, robust, and vigorous; the women also are stout, and generally fair; and both sexes have a mixture of the Italian and German in their tempers and characters. As there is little trade or manufacture in the country, except what is occasioned by the mines and salt works, many of the common people are obliged to seek a subsistence elsewhere. A particular kind of salutation is used all over Tirol. When a person comes into a house, he says, "Hail! Jesus Christ;" the answer is, "May Christ be praised, and the Holy Virgin his mother." Then the master of the house takes the visitor by the hand. This salutation is fixed up in print at all the doors, with an advertisement tacked to it, importing, that Pope Clement XI. granted 100 days indulgence, and a plenary abolution, to those who should pronounce the salutation and answer, as often as they did it. The emperor has forts and citadels so advantageously situated on rocks and mountains all over the country, that they command all the valleys, avenues, and passes that lead unto it. The inhabitants, however, to keep them in good humour, are more gently treated, and not so highly taxed as those of the other hereditary countries. As to the states, they are much the same in this country as in the other Austrian territories, except that the peasants here send deputies to the diets. Tirol came to the house of Austria in the year 1363, when Margaret, countess thereof, bequeathed it to her uncles the dukes of Austria. The arms of Tirol are an eagle gules, in a field argent. The counts of Trap are hereditary stewards; the lords of Glotz, chamberlains; the princes of Trautson, marshals; the counts of Wolfenstein, masters of the horse and carvers; the house of Spaur, cup-bearers; the counts of Kungl., sewers and rangers; the counts of Brandis, keepers of the jewels; the house of Welsberg, purveyors and staff-bearers; and the counts of Coalto, falconers. Besides the governor, there are three sovereign colleges, subordinate to the court at Vienna, which sit at Innspruck, and have their different departments. Towards the expenses of the military establishment of this country, the proportion is 100,000 florins yearly; but no more than one regiment of foot is generally quartered in it. Tirol is divided into six quarters, as they are called; namely, those of the Lower and Upper Innthal, Vintfogow, Etch, Eifack, and Pufferthal.

TITAN

Pages 52-53

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the son of Coelus and Terra, and the elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, suffered the latter to enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, on condition that he should bring up none of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue, by which means the crown should at length revert to him; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> being spared by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of Rhea, Saturn's wife, Titan and his children were so enraged at seeing their hopes frustrated, that they took up arms to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the injury; and not only defeated Saturn, but kept him and his wife prisoners till he was delivered by Jupiter, who defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a>; when from the blood of these Titans slain in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, proceeded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, scorpions, and all venomous reptiles. See SATURN. Such is the account given by the poets of this family of Grecian and Roman gods. From the fragments of Sanchoniathon, however, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, many learned men have inferred that the Titans were an early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of ambitious heroes, who laid the foundation of that idolatry which quickly overspread the world, and that by assuming the names of the luminaries of heaven they contrived to get themselves everywhere adored as the Dii majorum gentium. That the word Titan signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, there can indeed be very little doubt. Every one knows that such was its signification in the Æolic dialect; and as it is evidently compounded of Ti, which, in some oriental tongues, signifies bright <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clear, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">Tan</a>, which signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, it may be fairly concluded that Titan was the name of the sun before the word was imported into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> question among antiquarians is, of what country was that race which, assuming to themselves the names of the heavenly bodies, introduced into the world that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of idolatry which is known by the appellation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">Hero</a>-worship? M. Pezron, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> published many years ago, and entitled The Antiquities of Nations, maintains that the Titans were a family of Sace or Scythians, who made their first appearance beyond Media and Mount Imaus, in the upper regions of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; that they were the descendants of Gomer the son of Japheth and grandson of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>; and that after conquering a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world, upon entering Upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, they quitted their ancient name of Gomerians or Cimmerians, and assumed that of Titans. All this, he says, happened before the birth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> and the foundation of the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>; and he makes Uranus, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in the order of succession, to have conquered Thrace, Greece, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, and a great part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Uranus was succeeded by Saturn, and Saturn by Jupiter, who flourished, he says, 300 years before Moses, and divided his vast empire between himself, his brother Pluto, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>-german <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, who was called Telamon. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this genealogy of the Titans M. Pezron appeals to the most approved Greek historians; but unluckily for his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, these writers have not a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> by which it can be fairly supported. It supposes not only the great antiquity of the Scythians, but likewise their early progress in arts and sciences, contrary to what we have proved in other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of this work. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, no 4 and 5. Others, taking the fragment of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANCHONIATHO">Sanchoniatho</a>'s Phoenician history for their guide, have supposed the Titans to have been the descendants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>. Of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was Bishop <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>; and our learned friend Dr Deig, to whom we have been indebted for greater favours, indulged us with the perusal of a manuscript, in which, with erudition and ingenuity struggling for the pre-eminence, he traces that impious family from the profane son of Noah, and shows by what means they spread the idolatrous worship of themselves over the greater part of the ancient world. Cronus, of whose exploits some account has been given elsewhere (see Sanchoniatho), he holds to be Ham; and tracing the progress of the family from Phoenicia to Cyprus, from Cyprus to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, thence to Crete, and from Crete to Samothrace, he finds reason to conclude that the branch called Titans or Titanides flourished about the era of Abraham, with whom, or with his son <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, he thinks the Cretan Jupiter must have been <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a>. As they proceeded from countries which were the original seat of civilization to others in which mankind had sunk into the grossest barbarism, it was easy for them to persuade the ignorant inhabitants that they derived the arts of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> the sun, and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their relation to him to assume to themselves divine honours. To ask how they came to think of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> impiety, is a question as foolish as it would be to ask how Ham their ancestor became so wicked as to entail the curse of God upon himself and his posterity. The origin of evil is involved in difficulties; but leaving all inquiries into it to be prosecuted by the metaphysician and moralist, it is surely more probable that the worship of dead men originated among the descendants of Ham than among those of Shem and Japheth; and that the fragment of Sanchoniatho, when giving an account of the origin of the Titans, the undoubted authors of that worship, is more deserving of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> than the fabulous and comparatively late writers of Greece and Rome.

TITHES

Pages 53-55

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, are defined to be the tenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the increase, yearly arising and renewing from the profits of lands, the stock upon lands, and the personal industry of the inhabitants: the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> being usually called predial, as of corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, hops, and wood; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> mixed, as of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, pigs, &c., consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> products, but nurtured and preserved in part by the care of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and of these the tenth must be paid in goods; the third personal, as of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> occupations, trades, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, and the like; and of these only the tenth-part of the clear gains and profits is due. We shall, in this article, consider, 1. The original of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of tithes. 2. In whom that right at present subsists. 3. Who may be discharged, either totally <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in part, from paying them. 1. As to their original, we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not put the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the clergy to tithes upon any divine right; though such a right certainly commenced, and we believe as certainly ceased, with the Jewish theocracy. Yet an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and competent maintenance for the ministers of the gospel is undoubtedly jure divino, whatever the particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of that maintenance may be. For, besides the positive precepts of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, natural reason will tell us, that an order of men who are separated from the world, and excluded from other lucrative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> for the sake of the rest of mankind, have a right to be furnished with the necessaries, conveniences, and moderate enjoyments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, at their expense; for whose benefit they forego the usual means of providing them. Accordingly all municipal laws have provided a liberal and decent maintenance for their national priests or clergy; ours, in particular, have established this of tithes, probably in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Jewish law: and perhaps, considering the degenerate state of the world in general, it may be more beneficial to the English clergy to found their title on the law of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, than upon any divine right whatsoever, unacknowledged and unsupported by temporal sanctions. We cannot precisely ascertain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when tithes were first introduced into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Possibly they were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> of Christianity among the Saxons by Augustin the monk, about the end of the fifth century. But the first mention of them which we have met with in any written English law, is a constitutional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, made in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> held A.D. 786, wherein the payment of tithes in general is strongly enjoined. This canon or decree, which at first bound not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>, was effectually confirmed by two kingdoms. kingdoms of the heptarchy, in their parliamentary conventions of estates, respectively consisting of the kings of Mercia and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, dukes, senators, and people. Which was a few years later than the time that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> established the payment of them in France, and made that famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of them into four parts; one to maintain the edifice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the second to support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, the third the bishop, and the fourth the parochial clergy. The next authentic mention of them is in the fædus Edwardi et Guthrunis or the laws agreed upon between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Guthrun the Dane, and Alfred his son Edward the Elder, successive kings of England, about the year 920. This was a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> between those monarchs, which may be found at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in the Anglo-Saxon laws: wherein it was necessary, as Guthrun was a Pagan, to provide for the subsistence of the Christian clergy under his dominion; and accordingly, we find the payment of tithes not only enjoined, but a penalty added upon non-obscurrence: which law is seconded by the laws of Athelstan, about the year 930. And this is as much as can certainly be traced out with regard to their legal original. 2. We are next to consider the persons to whom tithes are due. Upon their first introduction, though every man was obliged to pay tithes in general, yet he might give them to what priests he pleased; which were called arbitrary consecrations of tithes; or he might pay them into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the bishop, who distributed among his diocesan clergy the revenues of the church, which were then in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. But when dioceses were divided into parishes, the tithes of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> were allotted to its own particular minister; first by common consent or the appointments of lords of manors, and afterwards by the written law of the land. Arbitrary consecrations of tithes took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> again afterwards, and were in general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> till the time of King John. This was probably owing to the intrigues of the regular clergy, or monks of the Benedictine and other orders, under Archbishop Dunstan and his successors; who endeavoured to wean the people from paying their dues to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> or parochial clergy (a much more valuable set of men than themselves), and were then in hopes to have drawn, by sanctimonious pretences to extraordinary purity of life, all ecclesiastical profits to the coffers of their own <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>. And this will naturally enough account for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the monasteries and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses which were founded in those days, and which were frequently endowed with tithes. For a layman, who was obliged to pay his tithes somewhere, might think it good policy to erect an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, and there pay them to his own monks, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them to some abbey already erected: since for this donation, which really cost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> little or nothing, he might, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the times, have masses for ever sung for his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. But in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of years, the income of the poor laborious parish-priests being scandalously reduced by these arbitrary consecrations of tithes, it was remedied by Pope Innocent III. about the year 1200, in a decretal epistle sent to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, and dated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Lateran: which has occasioned Sir Henry Hobart and others to mistake it for a decree of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Lateran, held A.D. 1179, which only prohibited what was called the infodation of tithes; or their being granted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> laymen; whereas this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of Pope Innocent to the archbishop enjoined the payment of tithes to the parsons of the respective parishes where every man inhabited, agreeable to what was afterwards directed by the same pope in other countries. This epistle, says Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, bound not the lay subjects of this realm; but being reasonable and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, it was allowed of, and so became lex terræ. This put an effectual stop to all the arbitrary consecrations of tithes; except some footsteps which still continue in those portions of tithes which the parson of one parish hath, though rarely, a right to claim in another: for it is now universally held, that tithes are due, of common right, to the parson of the parish, unless there be a special exemption. This parson of the parish may be either the actual incumbent, or else the appropriator of the benefice; appropriations being a method of endowing monasteries, which seems to have been devised by the regular clergy, by way of substitution to arbitrary consecrations of tithes. 3. We observed that tithes are due of common right to the parson, unless by special exemption; let us therefore see, thirdly, who may be exempted from the payment of tithes, and how lands and their occupiers may be exempted or discharged from the payment of tithes, either in part or totally; first, by a real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>; or, secondly, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>. First. A real composition is when an agreement is made between the owner of the lands and the parson or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, with the consent of the ordinary and the patron; that such lands shall for the future be discharged from payment of tithes, by reason of some land or other real recompense given to the parson in lieu and satisfaction thereof. This was permitted by law, because it was supposed that the clergy would be no losers by such composition; since the consent of the ordinary, whose duty it is to take care of the church in general, and of the patron, whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> it is to protect that particular church, were both made necessary to render the composition effectual: and hence have arisen all such compositions as exist at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> by force of the common law. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> showing that even this caution was ineffectual, and the petitions of the church being by this and other means every day diminished, the disabling statute 13 Eliz. c. 10. was made; which prevents, among other spiritual persons, all parsons and vicars from making any conveyances of the estates of their churches, other than for three lives of 21 years. So that now, by virtue of this statute, no real composition made since the 13 Eliz. is good for any longer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> than three lives or 21 years, though made by consent of the patron and ordinary: which has indeed effectually demolished this kind of traffic; such compositions being now rarely heard of, unless by authority of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Secondly, a discharge by custom or prescription, is where time out of mind such persons or such lands have been either partially or totally discharged from the payment of tithes. And this immemorial usage is binding upon all parties; as it is in its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of universal consent and acquiescence, and with reason supposes a real composition to have been formerly made. This custom or prescription is either de modo decimandi, or de non decimando. A modus decimandi, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called by the simple name of a modus only, is where there is by custom a particular particular manner of tithing allowed, different from the general law of taking tithe in kind, which are the actual tenth-part of the annual increase. This is sometimes a pecuniary compensation, as twopence an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> for the tithe of land; sometimes it is a compensation in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> and labour, as that the parson shall have only the twelfth cock of hay, and not the tenth, in consideration of the owner's making it for him; sometimes, in lieu of a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of crude or imperfect tithe, the parson shall have a less quantity when arrived at greater maturity, as a couple of fowls in lieu of tithe-eggs, and the like. Any means, in short, whereby the general law of tithing is altered, and a new method of taking them is introduced, is called a modus decimandi, or special manner of tithing. A prescription de non decimando is a claim to be entirely discharged of tithes, and to pay no compensation in lieu of them. Thus the king by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> is discharged from all tithes. So a vicar shall pay no tithes to the rector, nor the rector to the vicar, for ecclesia decimas non facit ecclesia. But these personal privileges (not arising from or being annexed to the land) are personally confined to both the king and the clergy; for their tenant or lesee shall pay tithes, though in their own occupation their lands are not generally tithable. And, generally speaking, it is an established rule, that in lay hands, modus de non decimando non <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALET">valet</a>. But spiritual persons or corporations, as monasteries, abbeys, bishops, and the like, were always capable of having their lands totally discharged of tithes by various ways: as, 1. By real composition. 2. By the pope's bull of exemption. 3. By unity of possession; as when the rectory of a parish, and lands in the same parish, both belonged to a religious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, those lands were discharged of tithes by this unity of possession. 4. By prescription; having never been liable to tithes, by being always in spiritual hands. 5. By virtue of their order; as the Knights <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPLARS">Templars</a>, Cistercians, and others, whose lands were privileged by the pope with a discharge of tithes. Though, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of abbeys by Henry VIII., most of these exemptions from tithes would have fallen with them, and the lands become tithable again, had they not been supported and upheld by the statute 31 Henry VIII. c. 13, which enacts, that all persons who should come to the possession of the lands of any abbey then dissolved, should hold them free and discharged of tithes, in as large and ample a manner as the abbeys themselves formerly held them. And from this original have sprung all the lands which being in lay hands, do at present claim to be tithe-free; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a man can show his lands to have been such abbey-lands, and also immemorially discharged of tithes by any of the means before mentioned, this is now a good prescription de non decimando. But he must show both these requisites: for abbey-lands, without a special ground of discharge, are not discharged of course; neither will any prescription de non decimando avail in total discharge of tithes, unless it relates to such abbey-lands. It is universally acknowledged that the payment of tithes in kind is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> discouragement to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. They are inconvenient and vexatious to the husbandman, and operate as an impolitic tax upon industry. The clergyman, too, frequently finds them troublesome and precarious; his expenses in collecting are a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWBACK">drawback</a> from their value, and his just <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> are with difficulty secured: he is too often obliged to submit to imposition, or is embroiled with his parishioners in disputes and litigations, no less irksome to his feelings than prejudicial to his interest, and tending to prevent those good effects which his precepts should produce. It is therefore of the utmost importance to parochial tranquillity, and even to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, that some just and reasonable standard of composition could be fixed. Land has been proposed, but in the present state of the division of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> this is impossible: and as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is continually changing in its value, it would also be a very improper standard, unless some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> could be formed by which the composition could be increased as the value of money diminishes. A plan of this kind has been published in the Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> instituted at Bath, vol. iv. which those who are interested in this subject may consult for farther information.

TITHING

Pages 55-55

(Tithinga, from the Sax. Theothunga, i.e. Decuriam), a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of ten men, with their families, knit together in a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and all bound to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, for the peaceable behaviour of each other. Anciently no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was suffered to abide in England above forty days, unless he were enrolled in some tithing.—One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants of the tithing was annually appointed to preside over the rest, being called the tithing-man, the head-borough, and in some countries the borstholder, or borough's elder, being supposed the discreetest man in the borough, town, or tithing. The distribution of England into tithings and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> is owing to King Alfred. See BORSTHOLDER.

TITIANO VECELLI

Pages 55-56
or TITIAN, the most universal genius for painting of all the Lombard-school, the best colourist of all the moderns, and the most eminent Pilkington's Dictionary for histories, portraits, and landscapes, was born at Ca. Diccionary dore, in the province of Friuli, in the state of Venice, of Painters in 1477, or in 1480 according to Vafari and Sandrart. His parents sent him at ten years of age to one of his uncles at Venice, who finding that he had an inclination to painting, put him to the school of Giovanni Bellino. But as soon as Titian had seen the works of Giorgione, whose manner appeared to him abundantly more elegant, and less constrained than that of Bellino, he determined to quite the style to which he had so long been accustomed, and to pursue the other that recommended itself to him, by having more force, more relief, more nature, and more truth. Some authors affirm, that he placed himself as a disciple with Giorgione; yet others only say, that he cultivated an intimacy with him; but it is undoubtedly certain that he studied with that great master; that he learned his method of blending and uniting the colours; and practised his manner so effectually, that several of the paintings of Titian were taken for the performances of Giorgione; and then his success inspired that artist with an invincible jealousy of Titian, which broke off their connection for ever after. The reputation of Titian rose continually; every new work contributed to extend his fame through all Europe; and he was considered as the principal ornament of the age in which he flourished. And yet, Sandrart observes that amidst all his applause, and constant employment at Venice, his income and fortune were inconsiderable; and he was more remarkable for the extensiveness of his talents, than for the affluence of his circumstances. But when his merit was made known to the emperor Charles V., that monarch knew how to set a just value on his superior abilities; he enriched him by repeated bounties, allowed him a considerable pension, conferred on him the honour of knighthood, and what was still more, honoured him with his friendship.
