He painted the portrait of that benefactor several times; and it is recorded by Sandrart, that one day, while the emperor was sitting for his picture, a pencil happening to drop from the painter, he stooped, took it up, and returned it; obligingly answering to the modest apology of the artist (who blushed at the condescension of so great a monarch), that the merit of a Titian was worthy of the attendance of an emperor. The excellence of Titian was not so remarkably apparent in the historical compositions which he painted as in his portraits and landscapes, which seem to be superior to all competition; and even to this day, many of them preserve their original beauty, being as much the admiration of the present age as they have deservedly been of the ages past.—It is observed of Titian by most writers, that in the different periods of his life, he had four different manners; one resembling his first instructor Bellino, which was somewhat stiff; another, in imitation of Giorgione, more bold, and full of force; his third manner was the result of experience, knowledge, and judgement, beautifully natural, and finished with exquisite care, which manner was peculiarly his own; and in those pictures which he painted between the years of approaching old age and his death may be noticed his fourth manner. His portraits were very differently finished in his early, and in his latter time, according to the testimony of Sandrart. At first he laboured his pictures highly, and gave them a polished beauty and lustre, so as produce their effect full as well when they were examined closely as when viewed at a distance; but afterwards, he so managed his penciling, that their greatest force and beauty appeared at a more remote view, and they pleased less when they were beheld more nearly. So that many of those artists who studied to imitate him, being misled by appearances which they did not sufficiently consider, have imagined that Titian executed his work with readiness and a masterly rapidity; and concluded that they should imitate his manner most effectually by a freedom of hand and a bold pencil: Whereas in reality, Titian took abundance of pains to work up his pictures to so high a degree of perfection; and the freedom that appears in the handling was entirely effected by a skilful combination of labour and judgement. It cannot be truly affirmed, that Titian equalled the great masters of the Roman school in design; but he always took care to dispose his figures in such attitudes as showed the most beautiful parts of the body. His taste in designing men was not generally to correct or elegant as it appeared in his boys and female figures; but his colouring had all the look of real flesh, his figures breathe. He was not so bold as Giorgione, but in tenderness and delicacy he proved himself much superior to him and all other artists. The expression of the passions was not his excellence, though even in that respect many of his figures merited the justest commendation; but he always gave his figures an air of ease and dignity. His landscapes are universally allowed to be unequalled, whether we consider the forms of his trees, the grand ideas of nature which appear in his scenery, or his distances which agreeably delude and delight the eye of every observer; and they are executed with a light, tender, and mellow pencil. He learned from nature the harmony of colours, and his tints seem astonishing, not only for their force, but their sweetness; and in that respect his colouring is accounted the standard of excellence to all professors of the art. It would prove almost an endless task to enumerate the variety of works executed by this illustrious artist, at Rome, Venice, Bologna, and Florence, as well as those which are to be seen in other cities of Italy, in England, Spain, Germany, and France; but there are two, which are mentioned as being truly admirable. One is, a Last Supper, preserved in the refectory at the Escorial in Spain, which is infinitely fine; the other is at Milan, representing Christ crowned with thorns. The principal figure in the latter has an attitude full of grace and dignity more than mortal, and the countenance shows a benevolence and humility, combined with dignity and pain, which no pencil but that of Titian could so feelingly have described. It is admirably coloured, and tenderly and delicately penciled; the heads are wonderfully beautiful, the composition excellent, and the whole has a charming effect by the chiaroscuro. He was of so happy a constitution, that he was never ill till the year 1576, when he died of the plague, at 99 years of age. His disciples were Paulo Veronese, Giacomo Tintoret, Giacomo de Porte Bassano, and his sons. TITLARK. See ALAUDA, ORNITHOLOGY Index.

TITLE

Pages 56-58

an appellation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> given to princes and persons of distinction. Titles were not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> as they are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. Till the reign of Constantine the title of Illustrious was never given except to those who were distinguished in arms or letters: But at length it became <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in the families of princes, and every son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was illustrious. The title of Highness was formerly given only to kings. The kings of England before the reign of Henry VIII. were addressed by the title of your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>. That monarch first assumed the title of Highness, and afterwards that of Majesty. The title of majesty was first given him by Francis I. in their interview in 1520. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. was the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> who assumed the same title. Princes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, and clergy, generally have one title derived from their territories and estates, and another derived from their rank or from some other remarkable circumstance. The pope is called the Bishop of Rome, and has the title of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">Holiness</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> has his name generally from some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and is saluted by the name of Eminence, or most Eminence. An archbishop, besides being named from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, is called his Grace and most Reverend; a bishop is also distinguished by the name of his diocese, and has the title of his Lordship and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> Reverend. Inferior clergymen are denominated Reverend. The titles of crowned heads derived from their dominions it is unnecessary to mention. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to mention those by which they are addressed. To an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> emperor is given the title of Imperial Majesty; to kings, that of Majesty; to the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Highnesses; to those of Spain, Infant; to electors, Electoral Highnesses; to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, Most Serene Highness; to the other princes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and Germany, Highness; to the doge of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, Most Serene Prince; to the grand-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, Eminence; to nuncios and ambassadors of crowned heads, Excellency; to dukes, Grace; to marquises, earls, and barons, Lordship. The emperor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, among his titles, takes that of Tien Su, "Son of Heaven." The Orientals, it is observed, are exceedingly fond of titles: the simple governor of Schiras, for instance, after a pompous enumeration of qualities, lordships, &c., adds the titles of Flower of Courtesy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUTMEG">Nutmeg</a> of Consolation, and Rose of Delight. Title, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes any right which a person has to the possession of a thing, or an authentic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> whereby he can prove his right. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Right, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">Property</a>, &c. Title to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a> in the British <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">Constitution</a>. See Succession. Titmouse. See Parus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITULAR">Titular</a>, denotes a person invested with a title, in virtue of which he holds an office or benefice, whether he perform the functions thereof or not. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITUS_VESPASIANUS">Titus Vespasianus</a>, the Roman emperor, the son of Vespasian; of whom it is related, that not being able to recollect any remarkable good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> he had done on a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he exclaimed, "I have lost a day!" He might truly be called the father of his people; and though Rome laboured under various public calamities during his reign, such was his equitable and mild administration, that he constantly preserved its popularity. He was a great lover of learning, and composed several poems. He reigned but two years; and it is thought Domitian his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> poisoned him, A.D. 81, aged 41. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Rome. Tiviot Hills. See Cheviot. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a>, the modern name of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIBUR">Tibur</a>. Toad. See Rana, Herpetology Index. Toad Fish. See Lophius, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. Toad-Fish. See Antirrhinum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Toad <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, an argillaceous stone. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICOTIANA">Nicotiana</a>, Botany Index, and Snuff. Tobacco-Pipe-Fish. See Fistularia, Ichthyology Index. Tobacco <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">Pipes</a>, Manufacture of. The art of making tobacco-pipes, or, as it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called, pipe-making, though one of the simplest <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a>, is sufficiently curious to merit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of arts and sciences. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of pipe-making may be divided into six stages; viz. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">Beating</a> or preparing the clay; 2. Rolling; 3. Moulding; 4. Trimming; 5. Drying; and 6. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">Preparation</a> of the Clay.—The fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> clay employed by the pipe-makers, is dug from the quarries in masses of about a cubic foot each. Before it can be used in the manufacture of tobacco-pipes, it must be reduced to the consistence of a tough paste. To effect this, after its outer surface has been cleared from dirt or dust, it is broken into small pieces about as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as a goose's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, and thrown into a tub with such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of soft <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has shown to be sufficient to bring it to the proper consistence. After lying till it has soaked up all the water, which usually requires from 12 to 24 hours, it is taken from the tub and laid on a thick strong wooden <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>. Here it is beaten by a heavy four-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> instrument, in such a manner as to cut it from one end to the other into very thin slices. It requires considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to perform this operation and it is surprising how thin the workmen will sometimes cut the slices, and how equally they will thus divide the clay. This beating is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, alternately folding up the clay and slicing it, till the whole is perfectly smooth. It is then ready for rolling. Rolling.—The operation of rolling reduces the clay into pieces of a proper size and length for making pipes, and almost to the proper form. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a> sits at a bench with a smooth board before him, and holds in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> another smooth board about 18 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and about half an inch thick, having one end rounded off on one side, so as to produce a corresponding hollow in the clay. He now takes a piece of the beaten clay, and rolls it out, first with his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and then with the board, till it acquire the form of a long slender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, with one end considerably larger than the rest. This large end is to form the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a>, and the cylinder the shank of the future pipe. The pieces of clay thus formed are laid beside each other on a flat board, and are now ready for moulding. Moulding.—This is the most complex operation, and requires the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of instruments. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these is the mould, which is composed of two long pieces of iron, formed so as to join together, and having their corresponding sides cut into the shape of half a tobacco pipe, each piece being hollowed so as to form half a slender cylinder, with a larger cavity at the upper end, and at such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> as it is intended the bole of the pipe shall make with the shank. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a> above that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of each side of the mould which stands beyond what is intended to form the bole, there is a notch for admitting a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> to cut off the superfluous clay. To receive the united mould there is a vice, having at one end two upright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, between which moves a long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, and to this lever, near the points, there is loosely attached a piece of iron ending below in a smooth conical head, capable of entering the large opening of the mould, but rather smaller than that opening, so as that when forced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into it, a sufficient thickness of clay may be left between the cone and the sides of the mould, to form the bole of the pipe. One side of this vice is fixed, and the other moveable, towards the former. The moveable side has attached to it an iron screw with a very long lever as its handle, so that by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the screw one way or the other, the moveable side of the vice may be forced nearer the fixed side, or suffered to return to its original position. Besides these principal instruments, the moulder requires a slender <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wire, fixed in a handle at one end, and having its other extremity formed into a very small head; a saucer containing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> well impregnated with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and a small woollen or cotton <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. When about to mould his pipes, he lays hold of the shank of one of the rolled pieces, and with great dexterity, which practice alone can teach, he passes up the oiled... oiled wire through its whole length, till he finds it arrived at the commencement of the larger extremity of the clay. This extremity he then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> to the proper angle, and having oiled the inside of each part of his mould, he lays the piece of clay with the wire in it, into one part of the mould, and covers it with the other. He now puts the mould containing the clay into the vice, and with the left hand turning round the handle of the screw, so as to fix the mould firmly within the vice, he, with the right hand, presses down the lever with its conical head, and thus forms the cavity of the bole. He now withdraws the mould, cuts off with his knife the superfluous clay from the bole, opens the mould, takes out the pipe, and now only withdraws the wire. He then lays the moulded pipe on a flat board, in the same manner as the rolled pieces before described. The pipes thus moulded require to be trimmed, that is, to have the prominences arising from the joining of the mould, and other superfluous pieces of clay taken off, so as to render the surface smooth and round. Trimming.—The operation of trimming is generally performed by boys and girls, as it requires very little skill. The trimmer has before him a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood, about the length of the pipe, and of considerable thickness, elevated a little at the remote end. He has also a thick piece of smooth iron, one edge of which has across it two or more semicylindrical grooves, capable of receiving half the shank of a pipe. Taking one of the rough moulded pipes, the trimmer carefully passes up the hollow of the shank, a wire similar to that employed in moulding, and holding the pipe by the bole, while the shank lies before him on the wooden block, he pares off with a blunt knife all the excrescences of clay, both from the shank and bole, and rubs the former, while lying on the block, with the grooved part of his iron, so as to render it as smooth as possible. He now cuts off the ragged piece at the extremity of the shank, withdraws the wire, and lays the pipe on the drying frame. One great object of the trimmer is, to see that the pipe is completely perforated, which he discovers by blowing through it; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he finds the hole choked up, he must open it by pushing the wire as far as possible. If this does not succeed, he breaks the pipe as useless. Drying.—The pipe has now received all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> that can be bestowed on it by the maker, previous to its being burned; but as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> of it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, while soft and pliable, would make it crack, it is necessary that it be properly dried. For this purpose, a frame is prepared, composed of three or four long pieces of wood, fastened to two end pieces in such a manner, as that the middle of the frame shall be the lowest, to give the shanks of the pipes that curve which they generally possess. After being trimmed, the pipes are laid beside each other in this concave frame, with their boles hanging down over the edges of the frame, and their shanks <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> within its hollow. In this position they are exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> till they are dry and firm. They are then ready for burning or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>. Burning.—For burning or baking the pipes, there is to be prepared a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a> of a simple but peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. It is built in the form of a cylinder, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> at the bottom and on the sides, and open at the top. Below the bottom is a grate for receiving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and round the sides are constructed vertical or spiral flues, opening at the top, and communicating below with the grate. The sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> on its interior are pretty thin, and are formed of a cement composed of clay mixed with fresh cow dung. In the middle of the cavity is placed a pedestal composed of the same materials, for the pipes to lean against. When the pipes are sufficiently dried, they are arranged round this pedestal, resting against it, and against each other, with their boles next the bottom of the furnace. They are thus placed in successive layers, till the furnace be sufficiently full, when the open space at top is filled up with bricks placed over each other, so as to leave interstices for the free circulation of the air, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> which issue through the flues. In these interstices are laid several pieces of broken dried pipes, to serve as pyrometers for ascertaining the state of the included pipes during the burning. The fire is now lighted, and kept up, till, on examining the pieces of clay laid in the interstices of the bricks, it is concluded that the pipes within the furnace are sufficiently baked. The fire is then suffered to go out, and the whole to cool till the next day, when the bricks are taken down, the pipes removed, and packed in barrels for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. After being burnt, the pipes are sometimes glazed, which is done by rubbing them, while warm, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> and a little white wax. In some places the extremities of the shanks are rendered smooth by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> them before burning in the ordinary potters glazing, which prevents that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> to the lips so unpleasant in new unglazed pipes.

TOBAGO

Pages 58-59

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, ceded to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1763, taken by the French in 1781, and retaken by the British in 1793. It lies in the latitude of 11 degrees 10 minutes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and 59 degrees 40 minutes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> west from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, about 40 leagues south-west from Barbados, 35 south-east from St Vincent's, 20 south-east from Grenada, 12 north-east from the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Trinidad, and between 30 and 40 north-east from the Spanish main. According to the latest accounts, it is somewhat more than 30 miles in length from north-east to south-west, between 8 and 9 in breadth, and from 23 to 25 leagues in circumference. The English visited this island very early, Sir Robert <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a> being there in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. In that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., William <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> procured a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of this, with two other small islands; but died before he was able to carry into execution his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of settling them. In A.D. 1632 some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> sent over a small colony thither, and gave it the name of New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALCHEREN">Walcheren</a>; but before they were able thoroughly to establish themselves, they were destroyed by the Indians assisted by the Spaniards. Ten years after, James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a> sent a colony thither, who settled themselves upon Great Courland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and made considerable progress in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a>. A.D. 1654, Messieurs Adrian and Cornelius Lampius, two opulent merchants of Flushing, sent a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people thither, who settled on the other side of the island, and lived in amity with the Courlanders, until they learned that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> had seized the person of their duke and dispossessed him of his dominions, when they attacked and forced his subjects to submit. The duke being afterwards restored, he obtained from Charles II. a grant of this island, dated the 17th of November 1664. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> d'Estrees, by order of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, totally ruined it at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 1677; and from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> waste till Britain took possession of it after the treaty of Paris. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, notwithstanding its vicinity to the line, is so tempered by the breezes from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, as to be very supportable even to Europeans; and hath the same advantages with that of Grenada, in having regular seasons, and also in being exempt from the hurricanes. There are throughout the island many rising grounds, though except at the north-east extremity, there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it that can be styled mountainous; and even there the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is far from being rugged <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> impassable. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> either Dutch or French writers, is as fertile and luxuriant as any of the islands, and very finely diversified. Ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of all sorts have been raised in great plenty, a vast variety of vegetables, excellent in their kind, some for food, some for physic. Almost every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of useful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> is to be found here, and some of an enormous size; amongst others, the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a> tree, as the Dutch confess, and of which none could be better judges; whole groves of salamans, and of trees that bear the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPAL">copal</a>, with other odoriferous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> that render the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> wholesome and pleasant. It is as well watered as can be wished, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the sea on both sides, many smaller streams, and fine fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> in almost every part of the island. The seascape is indented by 10 or 12 fair and spacious bays, and there are amongst these one or two ports capable of receiving as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships as ever visited those seas. There are wild hogs in great plenty, abundance of fowls of different kinds, and a vast variety of sea and river fish. At the north-east extremity lies Little Tobago, which is two miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, very capable of improvement.

TOBOLSKI

Pages 59-59

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, is situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Tobol and Irtil, in N. Lat. 58° 12', E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 68° 18'. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> stands upon the ascent of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill, the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is inhabited by Mahometan Tartars, who carry on a considerable traffic upon the river Irtil, and convey their merchandise quite across <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. The river Irtil is reckoned as rapid as the Danube; runs from the south, and empties itself into the Ob; the Tobol washes the other side of the town, and a little below it falls into the Irtil. By means of these two rivers, there is a constant flow of merchandise into the city during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season. Toboliski is therefore a great mart for the commodities of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, Tartary, and other countries: and here is a great concourse of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. All sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are plentiful and cheap. An hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> is sold for 16 copecks, equal to about eightpence <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; a sturgeon weighing 40 pounds, for half that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; an ox for two six-dollars, and every other article in proportion: the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> in great variety. The supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of judicature for all Siberia is held in this city, which is also the seat of a metropolitan, sent hither from Moscow to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> spiritual jurisdiction over the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Toboliski is well fortified, and defended by a strong garrison, under the command of the waiwode, who resides in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and takes <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the fur tribute, which is here depoited in proper magazines. This governor enjoys a very extensive command, and can occasionally bring into the field 9000 men, besides a strong body of Tartars on horseback, to make head against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALMUCKS">Kalmucks</a> and Cossacks, in their repeated incursions. A sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Russians, called Jenishkars, are kept in continual pay by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, on the banks of the Irtil, to supply travellers on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">czar</a>'s account with men, boats, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, to convey them as far as Surgut on the Ob, a voyage of 200 leagues by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method of travelling in the summer; but in winter the journey by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is not half so long, being performed in sleds over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> and snow, with which the country is covered. These sleds are moved by a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of dogs, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> draw a load of 300 pounds with surprising expedition. They are hired at easy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>, and during one half of the year may be seen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> over the snow in great numbers. The city is supposed to contain 15,000 inhabitants. It is 800 miles east from Moscow, and 1000 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>. TODDA PANKA. See Cycas, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TODDY

Pages 59-59

a name given to the juice of the cocoanut tree. See Arack.—Toddy is also a name given to a mixture of spirits, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. TODDY-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>. See Loxia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TODUS

Pages 59-59

the Tody; a genus of birds belonging to the order of picae. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TOGA

Pages 59-59

in Roman antiquity, a wide woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mantle, which seems to have been of a semicircular form, without sleeves; differing both in richness and largeness, according to the circumstances of the wearer, and used only upon occasion of appearing in public. Every body knows that the toga was the distinguishing mark of a Roman; hence, the jus togae, or privilege of a Roman citizen; i.e. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of wearing a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and of taking, as they explain it, fire and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> through the Roman empire.

TOISE

Pages 60-60

a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> containing six of their feet, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a fathom.

TOKAY WINE

Pages 59-60

derives its name from a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, where it is produced. There are four sorts of wine made from the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, distinguished at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOKAY">Tokay</a> by the names of essence, aufpruch, maflach, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wine. The essence is made by picking out the half-dried and shrivelled grapes, and putting them into a perforated vessel, where they remain as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as any juice runs off by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> pressure of their own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. This is put into small casks. The aufpruch is made by pouring the expressed juice of the grapes from which the former had been picked on those that yielded the essence, and treading them with the feet. The liquor thus obtained stands for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two to ferment, and then is poured into small casks, which are kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> for about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and afterwards put into casks. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is again repeated by the addition of more juice to the grapes which have already undergone the two former pressures, and they are now wrung with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and thus is had the maflach. The fourth kind is made by taking all the grapes together at first, and submitting them to the greatest pressure: this is chiefly prepared by the peasants. The essence is thick, and very sweet and delicious; it is chiefly used to mix with the other kinds. The aufpruch is the wine <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> exported, and which is known in foreign countries by the name of Tokay. The goodness of it is determined by the following rules. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> should neither be reddish nor very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> silver: in trying it, the palate and tip Tokay Wine of the tongue should be wetted without swallowing it, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it manifest any acrimony to the tongue it is not good; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> ought to be soft and mild: when poured out, it should form globules in the glass, and have an oily appearance: when genuine, the strongest is always of the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>: when swallowed, it should have an earthy astringent taste in the mouth, which is called the taste of the root. All tokay wine has an aromatic taste, which distinguishes it from every other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of wine. It keeps to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and improves by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: but is never good till about three years old. It is the best way to transport it in casks; for when it is on the seas, it ferments three times every season, and thus refines itself. When in bottles, there must be an empty space left between the wine and the cork, otherwise it would burst the bottle. A little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is put upon the surface, and a piece of bladder tied over the cork. The bottles are always laid on their sides in sand. Phil. Trans. vol. xxii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> ii. p. 292, &c. TOKENS. See TRADESMEN'S Tokens.

TOLAND

Pages 60-60

JOHN, a famous writer, was born near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in 1670, and educated in the Popish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; but at 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> embraced the principles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. He studied three years at the university of Glasgow; was created <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; and afterwards completed his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, where he resided two years. He then went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where, having the advantage of the public library, he collected materials upon various subjects, and composed some pieces; among which was, A Dissertation to prove the received <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the tragical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Attilus Regulus, the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>. He began likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of greater <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, in which he undertook to show that there are no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> in the Christian religion. He published it in 1696 at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Christianity not mysterious. This book gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence, and was attacked by several writers. He afterward wrote in favour of the Hanoverian succession, and many other pieces. In 1707 he went into Germany, where he visited several courts; and in 1710 he was introduced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Eugene, who gave him several marks of his generosity. Upon his return to England he was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> supported by the liberality of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Oxford <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, and kept a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Epsom; but soon losing his lordship's favour, he published several pamphlets against that minister's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. In the last four years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he lived at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUTNEY">Putney</a>, but used to spend most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the winter in London. Mr Toland died at London in 1722. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of uncommon abilities, published a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of curious tracts, and was perhaps the most learned of all the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a> writers; but his private character was far from being an amiable one; for he was extremely vain, and wanted those social virtues which are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ornaments as well as duties of life. His posthumous works, two volumes octavo, were published in 1726, with an account of his life and writings, by Mr Des Maizeaux.

TOLEDO

Pages 60-60

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and trading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in New Castile, of which it was formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. About two centuries ago it is said to have contained more than 200,000 inhabitants; but they are now diminished to 20,000, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at most to 30,000. It is advantageously seated on the river Tajo, which surrounds it on two sides; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> side, it has an ancient wall built by a Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and flanked with 100 towers. It is seated on a mountain, which renders the streets uneven, and which are narrow; but the houses are fine, and there are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of superb structures, besides 17 public squares, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are kept. The finest buildings are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> castle and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; which last is the richest and most considerable in Spain. It is seated in the middle of the city, joining to a handsome street, with a fine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> before it. Several of the gates are very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>. There is also a superb temple, extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, from whence there is a very distant prospect. The Sagrario, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> chapel, is a real <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, in which are 15 large cabinets let into the wall, full of prodigious quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver vessels, and other works. There are two mitres of silver gilt, set all over with pearls and precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, with three collars of maffy gold, enriched in like manner. There are two bracelets and an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, consisting of large diamonds and other jewels. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the gold in the crown is 15 pounds. The vessel which contains the consecrated wafer is of silver gilt, as high as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and so heavy, that it requires 30 men to carry it; within it is another of pure gold enriched with jewels. Here are 38 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, most of which are worthy a traveller's notice, with many other sacred buildings, a great number of churches belonging to 27 parishes, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. Without the town are the remains of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, and other antiquities. Toledo is an archbishop's see, and the seat of the primacy of Spain. His revenue is said to be worth 400,000 ducats, but there are large deductions to be made from it. It pays 15,000 ducats to the monks of the Escorial, besides several other pensions. Toledo has also a university. It was formerly celebrated for the exquisite temper of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> blades made there. It is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 15'. N. Lat. 39° 50', and is 37 miles south from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>.

TOLERATION

Pages 60-61

in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, is either civil <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>. Civil toleration is an impunity and safety granted by the state to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> that does not maintain doctrines inconsistent with the public peace: and ecclesiastical toleration is the allowance which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> grants to its members to differ in certain opinions, not reputed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a>. As the gods of Paganism were almost all local and tutelary, and as it was a maxim universally received that it was the duty of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to worship, together with his own deities, the tutelary gods of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in which he might chance to reside, there was no room for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> in the Heathen world, on account of different sentiments in religion, or of the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> with which the various deities were worshipped. Had the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> joined their fellow-citizens in the worship of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, Juno, and the rest of the rabble of Roman divinities, they would have been suffered to worship, without molestation, the Creator of the world and the Redeemer of mankind; for in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the God of the Christians would have been looked upon as a Being of the same kind with the gods of the empire; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> principle of intercommunity would have remained unviolated. But the true God had expressly prohibited Toleration prohibited both Jews and Christians from worshipping any other god besides Himself; and it was their refusal to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> that precept of their religion which made their Heathen masters look upon them as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHEISTS">Atheists</a>, and persecute them as a people inimical to the state. Utility, and not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, was the object for which the Heathen legislatures supported the national religion. They well knew that the stories told by their poets of their different divinities, of the rewards of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a>, and of the punishments of Tartarus, were a collection of fables; but they had nothing better to propose to the vulgar, and they were not such strangers to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart, as to suppose that mankind could live together in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> without being influenced in their conduct by some religion. Widely different from the genius of Paganism was the spirit of the Jewish dispensation. Truth, which is in fact always coincident with general utility, was the great object of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic <a </a>class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The children of Israel were separated from the rest of the world, to preserve the knowledge and worship of the true God, at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when all the other nations on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, forgetting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> that made them, were falling prostrate to flocks and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and worshipping devils and impure spirits. Such was the contagion of idolatry, and so strong the propensity of the Israelites to the customs and manners of the Egyptians, and other polytheistic nations around them, that the purpose of their separation could not have been served, had not <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEHOVAH">Jehovah</a> condescended to become not only their tutelary God, but even their supreme civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">Magistrate</a> (see <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, No. 151.) so that under the Mosaic economy, idolatry was the crime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, and as such justly punished by the laws of the state. Among the Jews, the church and state were not indeed different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>. They were so thoroughly incorporated, that what was a sin in the one was a crime in the other; and the forfeiture of ecclesiastical privileges was the forfeiture of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of citizens. In many respects the Christian religion is directly opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> law of Moses. It is calculated for all nations, and intended to be propagated among all. Instead of separating one people from another, one of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects is to disseminate universal benevolence, and to inculcate upon the whole human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, that mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> which naturally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> from the knowledge that all men are brethren. Its ultimate end being to train its votaries for heaven, it concerns itself no farther with the affairs of earth than to enforce by eternal sanctions the laws of morality; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of its Founder not being of this world, it leaves every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to fabricate its own municipal laws, so as best to serve its own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the various circumstances in which it may be placed; and denounces a curse upon all who pay not to those laws the fullest obedience, when they are not obviously inconsistent with the laws of piety and virtue, which are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> obligation. The Christian church therefore must always remain a distinct society from the state; and though, till the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of hazardous innovations, it has been deemed expedient in every country, where the truth of the gospel is admitted, to give to the religion of Christ a legal establishment, and to confer immunities on its ministers, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> has been adopted, not to secure the purity of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, which appeals to the private judgment of each individual, but merely to preserve the peace of society, and to put a restraint upon those Toleration actions of which human laws cannot take cognizance. With religion, Christian governments have no further concern than as it tends to promote the practice of virtue. The early Christians, however, not understanding the principle upon which penal laws were employed to preserve the purity of the Jewish religion; and, as our blessed Lord observed to two of his apostles, not knowing what spirit they were of—hastily concluded that they had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to enforce the doctrines and worship of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, by the same means which had been used to preserve the Israelites steady to the doctrines and worship of the Old. Hence, though they had suffered the cruellest persecutions themselves (see Persecution), they no sooner got the power of the state in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, than they persecuted the Pagans for their idolatry; and afterwards, when heresies arose in the church, persecuted one another for expressing in different phrases metaphysical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as no human mind can fully comprehend. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> had forewarned them that there must be heresies in the church, that they who are approved may be made manifest; but it did not occur to them that perfection for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is the worst of all heresies, as it violates at once truth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>.

TOLIFERA

Pages 62-62

the Balsam-of-Tolu tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas of decandria. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, p. 182. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No 2483. TOMATOES. See Solanum, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TOLU

Pages 62-62

a town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in Terra Firma, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>; famous for the fine balsam of Tolu, brought into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> from thence, and produced from a tree like a pine. It is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, 60 miles south of Carthagena. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72° 55'. N. Lat. 9° 40'.

TOMB

Pages 62-63

includes both the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sepulchre wherein a defunct is interred, and the monument erected to preserve his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. The word is formed from the Greek τύμβος, tumulus, "sepulchre;" or, according to Menage, from the Latin tumba, which signifies the same. In many nations it has been customary to burn the bodies of the dead, and to collect the ashes with pious care into an urn, which was deposited in a tomb or sepulchre. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a>. Among many nations it has also been the practice to lay the dead body in a tomb, without confining it, after having wrapped it up decently, and sometimes placing it in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>. See Coffin. The tombs of the Jews were generally hollow places hewn out of a rock. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> buried Sarah in a cave. Such was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> too in which the kings of Judah and Israel were interred; and such was the place in which the body of our Saviour was deposited by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> of Arimathea. But it is probable that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people buried their dead in graves; for our Saviour compares the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a> to "graves which appear not, and the men that walk over them are not aware of them." Over the tombs, perhaps only of people of distinction, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or monument was erected, to intimate to passersby that they were burying places, that they might not pollute themselves by touching them. With the same intention, as Lightfoot informs us, they whitened them every year on the 15th of February. The Egyptians also buried their dead in caves, called catacombs. See Catacomb. The pyramids, as some think, were also employed for the same purpose. Sometimes also, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> their dead, they placed them in niches in some magnificent apartment in their houses. The Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> burned their dead, and deposited their ashes in a tomb. The Greeks interred the ashes without the cities, by the sides of their highways. Sometimes indeed, by way of particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, they were buried in an elevated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town; and the Macedonians were allowed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and round their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>: But this was forbidden among the Romans by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the twelve tables, In urbe ne sepelio, neve urio; yet Valerius Publicola, Posthumus Tubertius, and the family of the Claudii, were buried in the Capitol. To bury by the sides of public public <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> was common among the Romans also; hence their epitaphs frequently began with *filius viator*. Highways were made choice of probably for two reasons: 1. That the dead might not be offensive or injure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the living, which they certainly would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> buried in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> or populous places; and, 2dly, That they might hold out to travellers a lesson of mortality, and teach the rustic morals to die. As it would swell this article to too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a size to describe all the different kinds of tombs which have been used by different nations and ages, we must content ourselves with shortly describing the tombs of a few nations, and adding a few concomitant circumstances. The tombs of the Parsees are singular. The deceased, after lying a proper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>, is carried, followed by his relations and friends, the females chanting a requiem, and deposited in a tomb of the following <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. It is a circular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, open at top, about 55 feet diameter, and 25 feet in height, filled to within 5 feet of the top, excepting a well of 15 feet diameter in the centre. The part so filled is terraced, with a slight declivity toward the well. Two circular grooves three inches deep are raised round the well; the first at the distance of four, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> at ten, feet from the well. Grooves of the like depth or height, and four feet distant from each other at the outer part of the outer circle, are carried straight from the wall to the well, communicating with the circular ones, for the purpose of carrying off the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, &c. The tomb, by this means, is divided into three circles of partitions: the outer, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet by four; the middle six by three; the inner, four by two: the outer for the men, the middle for the women, the inner for the children; in which the bodies are respectively placed, wrapped loosely in a piece of cloth, and left to be devoured by the vultures; which is very soon done, as numbers of those animals are always seen hovering and watching about these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARNEL">charnel</a> houses, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of their prey. The friends of the deceased, or the persons who have <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the tomb, come at the proper time, and throw the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> into their receptacle, the well in the centre; for which purpose, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rakes and tongs are deposited in the tomb. The entrance is closed by an iron door, four feet <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, on the eastern side, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> up as the terrace, to which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is raised. Upon the wall, above the door, an additional wall is raised, to prevent people from looking into the tomb, which the Parsees are particularly careful to prevent. A Persian inscription is on a stone inserted over the door, which we once copied, but have forgotten its tenor. From the bottom of the wall subterraneous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to receive the bones, &c. and prevent the well from filling. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sepulchres found in Russia and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, some are perfect tumuli, raised to an enormous height, while others are almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the ground. Some of them are encompassed with a square wall of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> placed in an erect position; others are covered only with a small heap of stones, or they are tumuli adorned with stones at top. Some are walled with brick within, and vaulted over; others are no more than pits or common graves. In some the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is excavated several fathoms deep; others, and especially those which are topped by a lofty tumulus, are only dug of a sufficient depth for covering the carcase. In many of these sepulchres the bones of men, and frequently of horses, are found, and in a condition that renders it probable the bodies were not burnt before they were inhumed. Other bones show clearly that they have been previously burnt; because a part of them is unconsumed, and because they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a disordered manner, and some of them are wanting. Urns, in which other nations of antiquity have deposited the ashes of their dead, are never met with here. But sometimes what remained of their bodies after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a>, and even whole carcases, are found wrapped up in thin plates of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. Many dead bodies are frequently been deposited together in one tomb; a certain indication that either a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> had been fought in the neighbourhood of the place, or that some families buried their relations in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> tomb. The Moors, like all other Mahometans, hold it a thing irreverent, and contrary to the spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, to bury their dead in mosques, and to profane the temple of the Most High by the profanation of dead bodies. In the infancy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> had the like piety, and gave example of the respect in which they held temples dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship; but ill-guided <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, mingled with superstitious vanities, and that contagious spirit of self-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> which pervades all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs, without respecting the altar of God, have, together, infensibly perverted men's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> grounds of the Mahometans are most of them without the city; the emperors have their sepulchres distinct and distant from the mosque, in sanctuaries, built by themselves, or in places which they have indicated: their tombs are exceedingly simple; the Moors do not imitate the ostentation of Europeans, where superb monuments are raised rather to gratify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of the living than the merit of the dead. All Mahometans inter the dead at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> set apart for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. The defunct is not kept in the house, except he expires after sunset; but the body is transported to the mosque, whither it is carried by those who are going to prayer. Each, from a spirit of devotion, is desirous to carry in his turn. The Moors sing at their burial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; which usage perhaps they have imitated after the Christians of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, for the oriental Mahometans do not sing. They have no particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> appropriated to mourning; their grief for the loss of relations is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of the heart they do not attempt to express by outward symbols. Women regularly go on the Friday to weep over and pray at the sepulchres of the dead, whose memory they hold dear. Among the northern nations it was customary to bury their dead under heaps of stones called cairns, or under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a>: (See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> CAIRNS and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">BARROW</a>). The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIBET">Tibet</a>, it is said, neither bury nor burn their dead, but expose them on the tops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. See TIBET. TOMPION; a sort of bung or cork used to stop the mouth of a cannon. At <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> this is carefully encircled with tallow or putty, to prevent the penetration of the water into the bore, whereby the powder contained in the chamber might be damaged or rendered incapable of service.

TONE

Pages 63-64
or Tune, in Music, a property of sound, whereby it comes under the relation of grave and acute; or the degree of elevation any sound has, from the degree of twittness of the vibrations of the parts of the sonorous body. The variety of tones in human voices arises partly from the dimensions of the windpipe, which, like a flute, the longer and narrower it is, the flatter the tone it gives; but principally from the head of the larynx or knot of the throat: the tone of the voice being more or less grave as the rima or cleft thereof is more or less open. The word tone is taken in four different senses among the ancients: 1. For any sound; 2. For a certain interval, as when it is said the difference between the diapente and diatessaron is a tone; 3. For a certain locus or compass of the voice, in which sense they used the Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian tones; 4. For tension, as when they speak of an acute, grave, or a middle tone. Tone is more particularly used, in music, for a certain degree or interval of tune, whereby a sound may be either raised or lowered from one extreme of a concord to the other, so as still to produce true melody. TONGUE. See ANATOMY, No. 102.

TONIC

Pages 64-64

in Music, signifies a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tension, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> produced by a vocal string in a given degree of tension, or by any sonorous body when put in vibration. Tonic, says Rousseau, is likewise the name given by Aristoxenus to one of the three kinds of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHROMATIC">chromatic</a> music, whose divisions he explains, and which was the ordinary chromatic of the Greeks, proceeding by two semitones in succession, and afterwards a third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>. TONIC <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINANT">Dominant</a>. See DOMINANT. TONNAGE and Poundage, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> duty on wine and other goods, the origin of which seems to have been this: About the 21st of Edward III., complaint was made that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> were robbed and murdered on the seas. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> thereupon, with the consent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, levied a duty of 2s. on every ton of wine, and 1½d. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> on all goods imported; which was treated as illegal by the commons. About 25 years after, the king, when the knights of shire were returned home, obtained a like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> from the citizens and burgesses, and the year after it was regularly granted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. These duties were diminished sometimes, and sometimes increased; at length they seem to have been fixed at 3s. tonnage and 1s. poundage. They were at first usually granted only for a stated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years, as, for two years in Ric. II.; but in Henry VI.'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they were granted him for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by a statute in the 31st year of his reign; and again to Edward IV. for the term of his life also: since which time they were regularly granted to all his successors for life, sometimes at the first, sometimes at other subsequent parliaments, till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.; when, as the noble historian expresses it, his ministers were not sufficiently solicitous for a renewal of his legal grant. And yet these imposts were imprudently and unconstitutionally levied and taken, without consent of parliament, for 15 years together; which was one of the causes of those unhappy discontented, justifiable at first in too many instances, but which degenerated at last into causeless rebellion and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. For, as in every other, so in this particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the king (previous to the commencement of hostilities) gave the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> ample satisfaction for the errors of his former conduct, by passing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, whereby he renounced all power in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Tonnage, levying the duty of tonnage and poundage, without the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TONQUIN">Tonquin</a>'s express consent of parliament; and also all power of imposition upon any merchandises whatever. Upon the restoration this duty was granted to King Charles II. for life, and so it was to his two immediate successors; but now, by three several statutes, 9 Ann. c. 6. 1 Geo. I. c. 12. and 3 Geo. I. c. 7. it is made perpetual, and mortgaged for the debt of the public.

TONQUIN

Pages 64-65

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, beyond the Ganges; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Yunnan in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, on the east by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Tonquin, on the south by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COCHIN_CHINA">Cochin China</a>, and on the west by the kingdom of Laos. It is about 1200 miles in length and 500 in breadth; and is one of the finest and most considerable kingdoms of the East, as well on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> it contains and the trade it carries on. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is thick set with villages; and the natives in general are of a middle stature and clean limbed, with a tawny <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. Their faces are oval and flat, and their noses and lips well proportioned. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, lank, and coarse; and they let it hang <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their shoulders. They are generally dexterous, nimble, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and ingenious in mechanic arts. They weave a multitude of fine silks, and make curious lacquer-works, which are transported to other countries. There is such a number of people, that many want employment; for they seldom go to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> but when foreign ships arrive.
