The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and goods brought hither by the English and Dutch put them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; for they have not money of their own sufficient to employ themselves; and therefore one-third at least must be advanced beforehand by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and the ships must stay here till the goods are finished, which is generally five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six months. They are so addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, that when everything else is lost, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> stake their wives and children. The garments of the Tonquinese are made either of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> or cotton; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> wear only cotton of a dark tawny <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Their houses are small and low; and the walls either of mud, or hurdles daubed over with clay. They have only a ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, with two or three partitions; and each room has a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole to let in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. The villages consist of 30 or 40 houses, surrounded with trees; and in some places there are banks to keep the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from overflowing their gardens, where they have oranges, betels, melons, and salad-herbs. In the rainy season they cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to another without wading through the water; they sometimes have boats. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> called Caicho there are about 20,000 houses with mud-walls, and covered with thatch; a few are built with brick, and roofed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>-tiles. In each yard is a small arched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> like an oven, about six feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, made of brick, which serves to secure their goods in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of fire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets are very wide, and paved with small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Tonquin has three palaces in it, such as they are; and near them are stables for his horses and elephants. The house of the English <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> is seated at the north end of the city, fronting the river, and is the best in the city. The people in general are courteous, and civil to strangers; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men are proud, haughty, and ambitious; the soldiers insolent, and the poor thieves. They buy all their their wives, of which the great men have several; but the poor are flinted for want of money. In hard times the men will sell both their wives and children to buy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> to maintain themselves. The women offer themselves to strangers as wives while they stay, and agree with them for a certain price. Even the great men will offer their daughters to the merchants and officers who are likely to stay six months in the country. They are not afraid of being with child; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are girls they can sell them well when they are young, because they are fairer than the other inhabitants. These women are said to be very faithful; and are treated with money and goods by the Europeans during their absence, and will make great advantage with them. The first new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> in the year that happens after the middle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, is a great festival; when they rejoice for 10 or 12 days together, and spend their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in all manner of sports. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> drink is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, but they make themselves merry with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARRACK">arrack</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is spoken very much in the throat; and some of the words are pronounced through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and has a great resemblance to the Chinese. They have several mechanic arts or trades; such as smiths, carpenters, joiners, turners, weavers, tailors, potters, painters, money-changers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-makers, workers in lacquer, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-founders.—Their commodities are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, mukl, silks, calicoes, drugs of many sorts, woods for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, lacquered wares, earthen wares, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, aniseeds, and worm-seeds. The lacquered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> is not inferior to that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, which is accounted the best in the world. With all these merchandises, one would expect the people to be very rich, but they are in general very poor; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trade being carried on by the Chinese, English, and Dutch. The goods imported, besides silver, are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, sulphur, English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, spices, and great guns. TONSILS. See ANATOMY, No 102.

TONSURE

Pages 65-65

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a particular manner of shaving <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clipping the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> or monks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tonsure of the clergy was nothing more than polling the head, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the hair to a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, for the sake of decency and gravity: and the same observation is true with respect to the tonsure of the ancient monks. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> have carried the affair of tonsure much farther; the candidate for it kneeling before the bishop, who cuts the hair in five different parts of the head, viz. before, behind, on each side, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>.

TONTINE

Pages 65-65

a loan given for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> with benefit of survivorship; so called from the inventor Laurence Tonti, a Neapolitan. He proposed his scheme in 1653 to reconcile the people to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarine's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, by amusing them with the hope of becoming suddenly rich. He obtained the consent of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> would not <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> the edict. He made attempts afterwards, but without success. It was not till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. was distressed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of Augsburg, and by his own immense expenses, that he had recourse to the plans of Tonti, which, though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> laid aside, were not forgotten. By an edict in 1689 he created a Tontine royale of 1,400,000 livres annual rent, divided into 14 clafs. The actions were 300 livres a piece, and the proprietors were to receive 10 per cent. with benefit of survivorship in every claf. This scheme was executed but very imperfectly; for none of the clafs rose to above 25,000 livres, instead of 100,000, according to the original <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>; though the annuities were very regularly paid. A few years after, the people seeming in better humour for projects of this kind, another tontine was erected upon nearly the same terms, but this was never above half full. They both subsided in the year 1726, when the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> united the 13th claf of the first tontine with the 14th of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; all the actions of which were polled by Charlotte Bonnemay, widow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Barbiere, a surgeon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, who died at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 96. This gentlewoman had ventured 300 livres in each tontine; and in the last year of her life she had for her annuity 73,500 livres, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> about 3600l. a-year, for about 30l. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the tontine is this; there is an annuity, after a certain rate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, granted to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people; divided into clafs, according to their respective ages; so that annually the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of each claf is divided among the survivors of that claf; till at last it falls to one, and upon the extinction of that life, reverts to the power by which the tontine was erected, and which becomes thereby security for the due payment of the annuities.

TOP

Pages 65-66

a fort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a>, surrounding the lower masthead, from which it projects on all sides like a scaffold. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> intention of the top is to extend the topmast throats, so as to form a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the mast, and thereby give additional support to the latter. It is sustained by certain timbers fixed across the hounds <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shoulders of the mast, and called the treble-trees and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-trees. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> above-mentioned, the top is otherwise extremely convenient to contain the materials necessary for extending the small sails, and for fixing or repairing the rigging and machinery with more facility and expedition. In ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> it is used as a kind of redoubt, and is accordingly fortified for attack or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; being furnished with livvets, musketry, and other fire-arms, and guarded by a thick <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of corded hammocks. Finally, it is employed as a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for looking out, either in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or night. Top-Mast, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a mast, or that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which stands between the upper and lower pieces. See the article MAST. Top-Sails, certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sails extended across the top-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> by the topsail-yard above, and by the yard attached to the lower mast beneath; being fastened to the former by robands, and to the latter by means of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> blocks fixed on its extremities, through which the topsail-sheet is inserted, passing from thence to two other blocks fixed on the inner part of the yard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> close by the mast; and from these latter the sheets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> downwards to the deck, where they may be slackened or extended at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. See the article SAIL.

TOPHUS

Pages 66-66

in Medicine, denotes a chalky <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stony concretion in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body; as the bladder, kidney, &c., but especially in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>.

TOPICS

Pages 66-66
or Topical Medicines, are the same with external remedies, or those applied outwardly to some diseased and painful part: such are plasters, cataplasms, ungents, &c.

TOPOGRAPHY

Pages 66-66

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> draught of some particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, or small tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, as that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> or town, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, or tenement, field, garden, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, castle, or the like; such as surveyors set out in their plots, or make draughts of, for the information and satisfaction of the proprietors.

TOPSHAM

Pages 66-66

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, in England, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXMOUTH">Exmouth</a>, five miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, to which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the river was formerly navigable; but in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> was choked up deignedly, so that ships are now obliged to load and unload at Topsham. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 26. N. Lat. 50. 39.

TORBAY

Pages 66-66

a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the English channel, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, a little to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a>, formed by two capes, called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">Bury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">Points</a>, and Bob's Nose.

TORDYLIUM

Pages 66-66
HART-WORT, a genus of plants belonging to the clas of pentandria, and in the natural system arranged under the 45th order, Umbellatae. See Botany Index.

TORIES

Pages 66-66

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, opposed to the Whigs. The name of Tories was given to a sort of banditti in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and was thence transferred to the adherents of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. by his enemies, under the pretence that he favoured the rebels in Ireland. His partisans, to be even with the republicans, gave them the name of Whigs, from a word which signifies why, in derision of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> fare. The Tories, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cavaliers, as they were also called, had then principally in view the political <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England; and the round-heads, or Whigs, proposed chiefly the maintaining of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and interests of the people, and of Protestantism. This is the most popular account; and yet it is certain the names Whig and Tory were but little known till about the middle of the reign of King Charles II. M. de Cize relates, that it was in the year 1678 that the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> was first observed to be divided into Whigs and Tories; and that on occasion of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of Titus Oates, who accused the Catholics of having conspired against the king and the state, the appellation of Whig was given to such as believed the plot real; and Tory to those who held it fictitious. These parties may be considered either with regard to the state or to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The state Tories are either violent or moderate: the first would have the king to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, and therefore plead for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> obedience, non-resistance, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Stuart. The moderate Tories would not suffer the king to lose any of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>; but then they would not sacrifice those of the people. The state Whigs are either strong republicans or moderate ones. The first (says Rapin) are the remains of the party of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, who attempted to change <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> to a commonwealth: but these make to slender a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, that they only served to strengthen the party of other Whigs. The Tories would persuade the world, that all the Whigs are of this kind; as the Whigs would make us believe that all the Tories are violent. The moderate state Whigs are much in the same sentiments with the moderate Tories, and desire that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> may be maintained on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> foundation: all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is, that the first bear a little more to the parliament and people, and the latter to that of the king. In short, the old Whigs were always jealous of the encroachments of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> prerogative, and watchful over the preservation of the liberties and properties of the people.

TORMENTILLA

Pages 66-66

Tormentil, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas of icelandica, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 35th order, Senticoceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TORNADO

Pages 66-66

a sudden and vehement gust of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass, frequent on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>.

TORPOR

Pages 66-66

a numbness, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> defect of feeling and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Galen says it is a sort of intermediate disorder between palsy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>.

TORREFACTION

Pages 66-66

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, is the roasting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scorching of a body by the fire, in order to discharge a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> either unnecessary or hurtful in another operation. Sulphur is thus discharged from an ore before it can be wrought to advantage.

TORRENT

Pages 66-66

denotes a temporary stream of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> falling suddenly from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, whereon there have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rains, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an extraordinary thaw of snow.

TORRICELLI

Pages 66-66

Evangelista, an illustrious Italian mathematician and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAENZA">Faenza</a> in 1608. He was trained in Latin literature by his uncle a monk; and after cultivating mathematical knowledge for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> without a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he studied it under Father Benedict Castelli, professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at Rome. Having read Galileo's dialogues, he composed a treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, on his principles, which brought him acquainted with Galileo, who took him home as an assistant; but Galileo died in three months after. He became professor of mathematics at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and greatly improved the art of making telescopes and microscopes; but he is best known for finding out a method of ascertaining the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> by quicksilver; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a> being called, from him, the Torricellian tube. He published <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a> Geometrica, 4to, 1644; and died in 1647.

TORRICELLIAN EXPERIMENT

Pages 66-67

a famous experiment made by Torricelli, by which he demonstrated the pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> in opposition to the doctrines of suction, &c., finding that pressure able to support only a certain length of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other fluid, in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> glass tube. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">Barometer</a>.

TORSK

Pages 67-67
or TUSK. See Gadus, Ichthyology Index. TORTOISE. See Testudo, Epetetology Index. Tortoise-shell, the shell, or rather scales, of the testaceous animal called a tortoise; used in inlaying, and in various other works, as for snuff-boxes, combs, &c. Mr Cateby observes, that the hard strong covering which includes all sorts of tortoises, is very improperly called a shell; being of a perfect bony contexture; but covered on the outside with scales, or rather plates, of a horny substance; which are what the workmen call tortoise-shell. There are two general kinds of tortoises, viz. the land and sea tortoise, testudo terraeiris and marina. The sea-tortoise, again, is of several kinds; but it is the caret, or testudo imbricata of Linnaeus, alone which furnishes that beautiful shell so much admired in Europe. The shell of the caretta, or hawksbill tortoise, is thick; and consists of two parts, the upper, which covers the back, and the lower the belly: the two are joined together at the sides by strong ligaments, which yet allow of a little motion. In the front-part is an aperture for the head and fore-legs, and behind for the hind-legs and tail. It is the under shell alone that is used: to separate it, they make a little fire beneath it, and as soon as ever it is warm, the under shell becomes easily separable with a point of a knife, and is taken off in laminae or leaves. The whole spoils of the caret consist in 13 leaves or scales, eight of them flat, and five a little bent. Of the flat ones, there are four large ones, sometimes a foot long, and seven inches broad. The best tortoise-shell is thick, clear, transparent, of the colour of antimony, sprinkled with brown and white. When used in marquetry, &c. the workmen give it what colour they please by means of coloured leaves, which they put underneath it. Working and joining of Tortoise-shell.—Tortoise-shell and horn become soft in a moderate heat, as that of boiling water, so as to be pressed, in a mould, into any form, the shell or horn being previously cut into plates of a proper size. Plumer informs us, in his Art de Tourner, that two plates are likewise united into one by heating and pressing them; the edges being thoroughly cleaned, and made to fit close to one another. The tortoise-shell is conveniently heated for this purpose by applying a hot iron above and beneath the juncture, with the interposition of a wet cloth to prevent the shell from being scorched by the irons: these irons should be pretty thick, that they may not lose their heat before the union is effected. Both tortoise-shell and horns may be stained of a variety of colours, by means of the colouring drugs commonly used in dying, and by certain metallic solutions.

TORTURE

Pages 67-67

a violent pain inflicted on persons to force them to confess the crimes laid to their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for crimes committed. Torture was never permitted among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> except in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of slaves: it would therefore appear, that it was a general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> among them, that a slave had such a tendency to falsehood, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> could only be extorted from him. To the disgrace of the professors of Christianity, torture was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> practised. Torture by those who called themselves Catholics, against those whom they termed heretics; that is, those who differed in opinion from themselves. Finding that they could not bring over others to adopt their sentiments by the force of argument, they judged it proper to compel them by the force of punishment. This practice was very general among orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, but especially among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a>. By the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of England, torture was at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> employed to compel those criminals who stood obstinately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a> when brought to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, and refused either to plead guilty or not guilty; but it is now abolished (see Arraignment, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">Rack</a>). A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> which have been invented to torture men, and an account of the instances in which they have been employed, would exhibit a dismal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> character.

TORUS

Pages 67-67

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> round moulding used in the bases of columns. See Architecture. TOUCAN. See Rhamphastos, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TOUCH-NEEDLE

Pages 67-68

among assayers, refiners, &c. little bars of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, combined together, in all the different proportions and degrees of mixture; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of which is to discover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity of any piece of gold <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver, by comparing the mark it leaves on the touch-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> with those of the bars. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> usually tried by the touch-stone are gold, silver, and copper, either pure, or mixed with one another in different degrees and proportions, by fusion. In order to find out the purity or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of base metal in these various admixtures, when they are to be examined they are compared with these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, which are mixed in a known proportion, and prepared for this use. The metals of these needles, both pure and mixed, are all made into laminae or plates, one-twelfth of an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and of a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their breadth in thickness, and an inch and half-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; these being thus prepared, you are to engrave on each a mark indicating its purity, or the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and quantity of the admixture in it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> rough marbles, the basaltes, or the softer kinds of black pebbles, are the most proper for touch-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. The method of using the needles and stone is thus: The piece of metal to be tried ought first to be wiped well with a clean towel or piece of soft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, that you may the better see its true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; for from this alone an experienced person, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in some degree, judge beforehand what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> metal is, and how and with what debased. Then choose a convenient, not over <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, part of the surface of the metal, and rub it several times very hardly and strongly against the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOUCHSTONE">touchstone</a>, that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a deceitful coat or crust should have been laid upon it, it may be worn off by that friction: this, however, is more readily done by a grindstone or small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>. Then wipe a flat and very clear part of the touchstone, and rub against it, over and over, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned part of the surface of the piece of metal, till you have, on the flat surface of the stone, a thin metallic crust, an inch long, and about an eighth of an inch broad: this done, look out the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> that seems most like to the metal under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, wipe the lower part of this needle: very clean, and then rub it against the touchstone, as you did the metal, by the side of the other line, and in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to it. When this is done, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you find no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the colours of the two marks made by your needle and the metal under trial, you may with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> pronounce that metal and your needle to be of the same alloy, which is immediately known by the mark engraved on your needle. But if you find a difference between the colour of the mark given by the metal, and that by the needle you have tried, choose another needle, either of a darker or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> colour than the former, as the difference of the tinge on the touchstone directs; and by one or more trials of this kind you will be able to determine which of your needles the metal answers, and thence what alloy it is of, by the mark of the needle; or else you will find that the alloy is extraordinary, and not to be determined by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of your needles.

TOUCHSTONE

Pages 68-69

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, smooth, glossy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, used to examine the purity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called it *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> Lydus*, the Lydian stone, from the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> whence it was originally brought. Any piece of pebble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> black flint <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> answer the purposes of the best lapis lydus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Even a piece of glass made rough with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERY">emery</a> is used with success, to distinguish true <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> from such as is counterfeit; both by the metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and the test of aquafortis. The true touchstone is of a black colour, and is not uncommon in many parts of the world. **TOUCHWOOD.** See BOLETUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOULON">TOULON</a>,** a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and seaport of France, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Provence which is now denominated the department of the Var. It is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, having been founded, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, by a Roman general. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of the department, and before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> revolution in 1789 was an episcopal see. The inhabitants are computed at 80,000. It is divided into the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">Quarter</a> and the New Quarter. The first, which is very ill built, has nothing remarkable in it but the Rue aux Arbres, the Tree-Street, which is a kind of course or mall, and the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; the gate of this is surrounded by a balcony, which is supported by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERMINI">termini</a>, the masterpieces of the famous Puget. The New Quarter, which forms as it were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> city, contains beside the magnificent works constructed in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV., many fine houses (among which that of the late seminary merits beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> the preference) and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, lined with trees, and serving as a parade. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">Merchants</a> Haven, along which extends a noble quay, on which stands the town-house, is protected by two moles, begun by Henry IV. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_HAVEN">New Haven</a> was constructed by Louis XIV., as were the fortifications of the city. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of this haven is an arsenal, containing all the places necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and fitting out of vessels: the first object that appears is a rope-walk, entirely arched, extending as far as the eye can reach, and built after the designs of Vauban: here <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> are made, and above is a place for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. Here likewise is the armory for muskets, pistols, halberds, &c. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> are cannon placed in piles, bombs, grenades, mortars, and balls of various kinds, ranged in wonderful order. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> sail-room, the foundry for cannon, the dockyards, the bafons, &c. are all worthy of observation. Both the Old and New Port have an outlet into the spacious outer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> or harbour, which is surrounded by hills, and formed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> almost circular. Its circuit is of very great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and the entrance is defended on both sides by a fort with strong batteries. In a word, the bafons, docks, and arsenal, at Toulon, warranted the remark of a foreigner that visited them in the late reign, that "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France was greater there than at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>." Toulon is the only mart in the Mediterranean for the re-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of the products of the East Indies. This place was destroyed toward the end of the tenth century, and pillaged by the African pirates almost as soon as rebuilt. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>, at the head of the Imperial troops, obtained possession of it in 1524, as did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. in 1536; but in the next century Charles Emanuel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy could not enter it, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Eugene in 1707 ineffectually laid siege to it. This city was surrendered by the inhabitants in September 1793 to the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Hood, as a condition and means of enabling them to effect the re-establishment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> in France, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of 1789. Lord Hood accordingly, in conjunction with the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and naval forces, took possession of the harbour and forts in trust for Louis XVII. It was garrisoned for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by the British troops, and their allies the Spaniards, Neapolitans, and Sardinians; but the French having laid siege to it, the garrison was obliged to evacuate the place in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following, after having destroyed the grand arsenal, two ships of 84 guns, eight of 74, and two frigates; and carried off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, a ship of 120 guns, with an 80 and 74 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> ship. This exploit was most gallantly performed, after it was found impossible to defend the town, or to carry off the ships. Lord Hood entrusted the management of the affair to Sir <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYDNEY">Sydney</a> Smith, so distinguished for his intrepidity. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Hare commanded the fireship which was towed into the grand arsenal; and so eager was he to execute his orders, that instead of setting fire to the train in the usual cautious manner, he fired a pistol loaded with powder into the bowl of the train, composed of 36 pounds of powder, and other combustibles. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, he was blown into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> with such violence, as to knock a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of the Victory's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> overboard, and narrowly escaped with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. A Spanish captain was appointed to set fire to the small arsenal, but cowardice prevented him from executing his orders; and this is the reason why the whole French ships were not destroyed. We have been favoured with this account by an officer of the British fleet. Toulon is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the Mediterranean, 17 leagues south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>, 15 south-east of Marseilles, and 217 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. Long. 5° 56' N. Lat. 43° 7'. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">TOULOUSE</a>,** a very ancient city of France, in the department of Upper Garonne, and late province of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, with an archbishop's see. It is the most considerable city in France next to Paris and Lyons, although its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> bears no proportion to its extent. According to Mr Neckar's calculation, it contains 56,000 inhabitants. The streets are very handsome, Toulouse, some, and the walls of the city, as well as the houses, are built with bricks. The town-house, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> structure, forms a perfect square, 324 feet long and 66 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> front occupies an entire side of the grand square, lately called the Place Royale. In the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, called the Hall of Illustrious Men, is the statue of the Chevalier d'Aucre, and the busts of all the great men to whom Toulouse has given birth. Communicating with the ocean on one side by the river Garonne, and with the Mediterranean on the other by the canal of Languedoc, Toulouse might have been a great commercial city; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the inhabitants has been directed to the sciences and belles-lettres. Of course, there are two colleges, two public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>. The little commerce of Toulouse consists in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, drapery, blankets, mignionets, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, mercery, hardware, and books. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Garonne is at least equal to those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>; it forms the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the suburb of St Cyprian and the city. The quays extend along the banks of the Garonne; and it has been in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> to line them with new and uniform houses. Toulouse is 37 miles east of Auch, 125 south-east of Bordeaux, and 350 south-west of Paris. E. Long. 1° 27', N. Lat. 43° 36'.

TOUR

Pages 69-69

Henry de la, Viscount Turenne, a celebrated French general, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Henry de la Tour <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bouillon, and was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a> in 1611. He made his first campaigns in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, under Maurice and Frederic Henry princes of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>; who were his uncles by the mother's side; and even then distinguished himself by his bravery. In 1634 he marched with his regiment into Lorraine; and having contributed to the taking of La Mothe, was, though very young, made marshal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. In 1636 he took Saarwerne, and the year following the castles of Hirtz and Sole; on which occasion he performed an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> like that of Scipio's, with respect to a very beautiful woman whom he sent back to her husband. The viscount Turenne <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to distinguish himself in several sieges and battles, and in 1644 was made marshal of France; but had the misfortune to be defeated at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Mariendal in 1645. However, he gained the battle of Nortlingen three months after; restored the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a> to his dominions; and the following year made the famous junction of the French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> with that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> commanded by General Wrangel, which obliged the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> to demand a peace. Afterwards that duke breaking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> he had concluded with France, he was defeated by the viscount Turenne at the battle of Zumarflaufen, and in 1648 driven entirely out of his dominions. During the civil wars in France he sided with the princes, and was defeated at the battle of Rhetel in 1650; but soon after was restored to the favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, who in 1652 gave him the command of his army. He acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> at the battles of Jergeau, Gren, and the suburbs of St Anthony, and by the retreat he made before the army commanded by the princes at Ville Neuve St George. In 1654 he made the Spaniards raise the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAS">Arras</a>; the next year he took Conde, St Guilian, and several other places; gained the famous battle of Dunes; and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>, Oudenarde, and almost all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>: this obliged the Spaniards to conclude the peace of the Pyrenees in 1660. These important services occasioned his being made marshal-general of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a> and armies. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> being renewed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in 1667, Turenne commanded in Flanders; and took so many places, that in 1668 the Spaniards were obliged to sue for peace. He commanded the French army in the war against the Dutch in 1672; took 40 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in 22 days; pursued the elector of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> even to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>; gained the battles of Slintheim, Ladenburg, Enheim, Muthhausen, and Turkeim; and obliged the Imperial army, which consisted of 70,000 men, to repass the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. By this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> the viscount Turenne acquired immortal honour. He passed the Rhine to give battle to General Montecucculi, whom he followed as far as Safpach; but mounting upon an eminence to discover the enemy's camp, he was killed by a cannon-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> in 1675. All France regretted the loss of this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> exploits had raised the admiration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

TOURAINE

Pages 69-69

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, on the east by Orleanois, on the south by Berris, and on the west by Anjou and Poitou. It is about 58 miles in length, and 55 in breadth where it is broadest. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is watered by 17 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, besides many brooks, which not only render it delightful, but keep up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the neighbouring provinces. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is so fruitful that it is called the garden of France. It now forms the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDRE">Indre</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

TOURMALINE

Pages 69-69

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mineral belonging to the siliceous genus. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TOURNAMENT

Pages 69-70

a martial sport <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> cavaliers used to perform, to show their bravery and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. It is derived from the French word tourner, i.e., "to turn round," because to be expert in these exercises, much agility both of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was requisite, they riding round a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the ancient Circe. The first tournaments were only courses on horseback, wherein the cavaliers tilted at each other with canes in manner of lances; and were distinguished from jousts, which were courses or careers, accompanied with attacks and combats, with blunted lances and swords. See Joust. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who published the tournament, used to lend a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> at arms, with a safe-conduct, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, to all the princes, knights, &c. signifying that he intended a tournament and clashing of swords, in the presence of ladies and damels; which was the usual formula of invitation. They first engaged man against man, and then troop against troop; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, the judges allotted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> to the best cavalier, and the best striker of swords; who was accordingly conducted in pomp to the lady of the tournament; where, after thanking her very reverently, he saluted her and likewise her two attendants. These tournaments made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> diversion of the 13th and 14th centuries. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> says, it was Henry the Fowler, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, who died in 936, that first introduced them; but it appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, that the true inventor of this famous sport, at least in France, was one Geoffrey, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Preuilly, about the year 1066. Instances of them occur among the English in the reign reign of King Stephen, about the year 1140; but they were not much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> till Richard's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, towards the year 1149. After which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> these diversions were performed with extraordinary magnificence in the Tilt-yard near St James's, Smithfield, and other places. The following is the account of a tournament, from Mailand. King Richard II. desiring to hold a tournament at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> after Michaelmas, sent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> heralds to make proclamations of it in all the principal courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and accordingly not a few princes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of the prime <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, reported hither from France, Germany, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, &c. This solemnity began on Sunday afternoon, from the Tower of London, with a pompous cavalcade of 60 ladies, each leading an armed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> by a silver chain, being attended by their "quires of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>," and, passing through Cheapside, rode to Smithfield, where the jousts and tournaments <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several days with magnificent variety of entertainments; on which occasion the king kept open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at the bishop of London's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> for all persons of distinction, and every night concluded with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. At last, however, they were found to be productive of bad effects, and the occasions of several fatal misfortunes—as in the instance of Henry II. of France, and of the tilt exhibited at Chalons, which, from the numbers killed on both sides, was called the little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of Chalons. These and other inconveniences, resulting from those dangerous pastimes, gave the popes occasion to forbid them, and the princes of Europe gradually concurred in discouraging and suppressing them.

TOURNAY

Pages 70-70

a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a district called Tourneaisis, with a bishop's see. It is divided into two parts by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>; and is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, well built, and carries on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in woollen stuffs and stockings. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a very handsome structure, and contains a great many chapels, with rich ornaments, and several magnificent tombs of marble and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. The town was taken by the allies in 1709; but was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, though the Dutch had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to put in a garrison. "It was taken by the French in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1745, who demolished the fortifications. In 1781 the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> II. obliged the Dutch to withdraw their garrison. It was taken by the French in 1791, abandoned by them in 1793, and again conquered by them in 1794. It is 14 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LILLE">Lille</a>, 30 south-west of Ghent, and 135 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by east from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 28'. N. Lat. 50° 33'.

TOURNEFORT

Pages 70-70
JOSEPH PITTON DE, a famous French botanist, was born at Aix in Provence in 1656. He had a passion for plants from his childhood, which overcame his father's views in putting him to study philosophy and divinity; therefore on his death he quitted theology, and gave himself up entirely to physic, href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, and botany. He wandered over the mountains of Dauphiny, Savoy, Catalonia, the Pyrenees, and the Alps, in search of new species of plants, which he acquired with much fatigue and danger. His fame in 1683 procured him the employment of botanic professor, in the king's garden; and by the king's order, he travelled into Spain, Portugal, Holland, and England, where he made prodigious collections of plants. In 1700, Mr Tournefort, in obedience to another order, simplified over all the isles of the Archipelago, upon the Tournefort coasts of the "xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black Sea, in Bithynia, Pontus, Cappadocia, Armenia, and Georgia; making observations on natural history at large, ancient and modern geography, religion, manners, and commerce. He spent three years in this learned voyage; and then returning his profession, was made professor of physic in the college royal. He died in consequence of an accidental crush of his breast by a cart-wheel, which brought on a spitting of blood and hydrothorax, that carried him off in 1703. He wrote Elements of Botany, both in French and Latin; A Relation of his Voyage into the Levant; with other pieces of less consideration.

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> formed with screws, for compressing any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with rollers, &c., for the stopping of hemorrhages. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

Towers are built for fortresses, &c., as the Tower of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. See London, No. 46.

TRACHINUS

the Weever, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of jugulares. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TRACT

Pages 70-70

in matters of literature, denotes a small treatise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> written discourse upon any subject.

TRADE

in general, denotes the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, consisting in buying, selling, and exchanging of commodities, bills, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, &c. See Commerce, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">Coin</a>, Money, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, &c. TRADE-Winds denote certain regular winds at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, blowing either constantly the same way, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> alternately this way and that; thus called from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> commerce. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a>.

TRADES MEN'S TOKENS

Pages 70-70

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> among medalists with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> coins. This is a subject curious enough to deserve <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, though we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not go so far as Mr Pinkerton does, who says that it is a subject in which the perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is interested. Since the year 1789 provincial halfpence have been made and circulated in considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> medals and coins have been frequently of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to historians, it is to be regretted that many of these provincial halfpence are rendered useless in this respect by unmeaning figures and puerile devices. Utility and elegance ought to be studied; for this view it has been proposed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> on this subject, that all coins should be distinguished by one of the following five characteristics. 1. Fac similes of magnificent beautiful buildings. 2. Representations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and useful undertakings. 3. Emblems of the industry and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. 4. The illustrious men, &c., to whom the nation has given birth. 5. Important historical events.

TRADITION

Pages 70-72

something handed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to another without being written. Thus the Jews Tradition Jews pretended, that besides their written <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> contained in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, Moses had delivered an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> law which had been conveyed down from father to son; and thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> are said to value particular doctrines supposed to have descended from the apostolic times by tradition. **TRAGACANTH.** See **ASTRAGALUS**, *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*. **TRAGEDY,** a dramatic poem, representing some signal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> performed by illustrious persons, and which has frequently a fatal issue <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> end. See **<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">POETRY</a>**, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. I. **TRAGI-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">COMEDY</a>,** a dramatic piece, partaking both of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of tragedy and comedy; in which a mixture of merry and serious events is admitted. **TRAGOPOGON,** Goat's-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of Syngenesia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 49th order, Compositae. See **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Index**. **TRAJAN,** Marcus Ulpius, a celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, who gained many victories over the Parthians and Germans, pushing the empire to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> on the east and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> sides. He died at Siliunte, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, which from him was called Trajanopolis, in the year 117. **TRAJAN'S <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">Column</a>,** a famous historical column erected in Rome, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the emperor Trajan. It is of the Tuscan order, though somewhat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>: its height is eight diameters, and its pedestal Corinthian: it was built in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> called Forum Romanum. Its base consists of 12 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of an enormous size, and is raised on a socle, or foot, of eight steps: withinside is a staircase illuminated with 44 windows. It is 140 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which is 35 feet short of the Antonine column, but the workmanship of the former is much more valued. It is adorned from top to bottom with bas-reliefs, representing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> actions of the emperor against the Dacians. **TRAIN,** a line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> laid to give fire to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> thereof, in order to do execution by blowing up <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, works, buildings, &c. **TRAIN of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a>,** includes the great guns and other pieces of ordnance belonging to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the field. **TRAIN-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">Oil</a>,** the oil procured from the blubber of a whale by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>. **TRALLIAN,** Alexander, a Greek writer on physic, a native of Tralles in Lydia, who lived about the middle of the fifth century. His works are divided into 12 books; in which he treats of distempers as they occur, from head to foot. He was the first who opened the jugular vein, and that used <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTHARIDES">cantharides</a> as a blister for the gout. Dr Freind, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Physic, styles him one of the most valuable authors since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>. Though he appears on the whole to have been a rational physician, yet there are things in his writings that favour of enthusiasm and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. **TRA-LOS-MONTES,** a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, called in Latin *Tranmontana*, because situated on the east side of a chain of hills that separate it from Entre Duero-e-Minho. It is bounded on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>; on the south by the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEIRA">Beira</a> and Leon; by the last of which it is bounded also to the east. Its length from north to south is upwards of 120 miles, and its breadth about 80. It is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and produces little corn, but plenty of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of several sorts, and abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>. **TRANSACTIONS,** a name generally given to a collection of the papers read before literary or philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>. The name of Philosophical Transactions was first adopted by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The Philosophical Transactions to the end of the year 1700 were abridged in three volumes by Mr John Lowthorp: those from the year 1700 to 1720 were abridged in two volumes by Mr Henry Jones: those from 1719 to 1733 were abridged in two volumes by Mr John Eames and Mr John Martyn; Mr Martyn <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the abridgement of those from 1732 to 1744 in two volumes, and of those from 1743 to 1750 in two volumes. They were for many years published in numbers, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of them was always, from time to time, the single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the respective secretaries, till the year 1752, when the society thought fit that a committee should be appointed to reconsider the papers read before them, and to select out of them such as they should judge most proper for publication in the future Transactions. They are published annually in two parts at the expense of the society, and each fellow is entitled to receive one copy gratis of every volume published after his admission into the society. They were first set on foot in 1665, by Mr Oldenburg, secretary of the society, and were continued by him till the year 1677. Upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, they were discontinued till <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1678, when Dr Grew resumed the publication of them, and continued it for the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1678, and January and February 1679, after which they were intermitted till January 1683. During this last <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> they were supplied in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> by Dr Hooke's Philosophical Collections. They were also interrupted for three years, from December 1687 to January 1691, beside other smaller interruptions amounting to near one year and a half more, before October 1695, since which time the Transactions have been regularly carried on. **TRANSCENDENTAL,** or **TRANSCENDENT,** something elevated, or raised above other things; which passes and transcends the nature of other inferior things. **TRANSCRIPT,** a copy of any original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, particularly that of an act or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> inserted in the body of another. **TRANSFER,** in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, an act whereby a person surrenders his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, in anything moveable or immoveable to another. **TRANSFORMATION,** in general, denotes a change of form, or the assuming a new form different from a former one. **TRANSFUSION,** the act of pouring a liquor out of one vessel into another. **TRANSFUSION of Blood,** an operation by which it was some time ago imagined that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of animals would be renewed, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>, or the next thing to it, conferred on those who had undergone it. The method of transfusing Dr Lower gives us to the following effect: take up the carotid artery of the dog, or other animal, whose blood is to be transfused into another of the same, or a different kind; separate it from the nerve of the eighth <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>, and lay it bare above... Transfusion—an inch. Make a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a> on the upper part of the artery; and an inch nearer the heart another ligature with a running knot, to be loosened and fastened as occasion requires. Draw two threads between the two ligatures, open the artery, put in a quill, and tie up the artery again upon the quill by the two threads, and stop the quill by a stick. Then make bare the jugular vein of the other animal for about an inch and a half in length, and at each end make a ligature with a running knot; and in the space between the two knots draw under the veins two threads, as in the other. Open the vein, and put into it two quills, one into the defending part of the vein, to receive the blood from the other dog, and carry it to the heart; the other quill put into the other part of the jugular, towards the head, through which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> animal's own blood is to run into ditches. The quills thus tied fast, stop them up with sticks till there be occasion to open them. Things thus disposed, fasten the dogs on their sides towards one another, in such manner as that the quills may go into each other; then unstop the quill that goes down into the second dog's jugular vein, as also that coming out of the other dog's artery; and by the help of two or three other quills put into each other, as there shall be occasion, insert them into one another. Then slip the running knots, and immediately the blood runs through the quills as through an artery, very impetuously. As the blood runs into the dog, unstop the quill in the upper part of his jugular, for his own blood to run out at, though not constantly, but as you perceive him able to bear it, till the other dog begins to cry and faint, and at last die. Lastly, Take both quills out of the jugular, tie the running knot fast, and cut the vein afraiden, and sew up the skin: the dog, thus dismiffed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> run away as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> nothing ailed him. In the Philosophical Transactions we have accounts of the success of various transfusions practised at London, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, &c. Sir Edmund <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> transfused forty-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> ounces of blood out of a calf into a sheep; the sheep, after the operation, appearing as well and as strong as before. M. Denis transfused the blood of three calves into three dogs, which all continued brisk, and ate as well as before. The same person transfused the blood of four wethers into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> twenty-five years old, which thence received much strength, and a more than ordinary appetite. Soon after this operation was introduced at Paris, viz. in 1667 and 1668, M. Denis performed it on five <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> subjects, two of whom recovered of disorders under which they laboured, one being in perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> suffered no inconvenience from it; and two persons who were ill, and submitted to the operation, died; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the magistrates issued a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, prohibiting the transfusion on human bodies under pain of imprisonment. Mr John Hunter, we are told, made many ingenious experiments to determine the effects of transfusing blood, some of which are sufficient to attract <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. But whether such experiments can ever be made with safety on the human body, is a point not easily determined. They might be allowed in desperate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> proceeding from a corruption of the blood, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, &c. as in hydrophobia.

TRANSITIVE

Pages 72-72

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, an epithet applied to such verbs as signify an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> which passes from the subject that does it, to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> upon another subject which receives it.
