Under the head of verbs transitive come what we usually call verbs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>; other verbs, whose action does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> out of themselves, are called neuters.

TRANSLATION

Pages 72-72

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of transferring <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> removing a thing from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another; as we say, the translation of a bishop's see, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, a seat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, &c. TRANSLATION is also used for the version of a book or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> out of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> into another. The principles of translation have been clearly and accurately laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Dr Campbell of Aberdeen in his invaluable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">Preliminary</a> Dissertations to his excellent translations of the gospels. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> rules which he establishes are three: 1. That the translation should give a complete transcript of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the original. 2. That the style and manner of the original should be preserved in the translation. 3. That the translation should have all the ease of original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The rules deducible from these general laws are explained and illustrated with much judgment and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Principles of Translation, by Mr Tytler, judge-advocate of Scotland.

TRANSMARINE

Pages 72-72

something that comes from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> belongs to the parts beyond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

TRANSMIGRATION

Pages 72-72

the removal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> translation of a whole people into another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, by the power of a conqueror. TRANSMIGRATION is particularly used for the passage of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> out of one body into another. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">METEMPSYCHOSIS</a>.

TRANSMUTATION

Pages 72-75

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALCHEMY">alchemy</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of changing imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver. This is also called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> operation; and, they say, it is to be effected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE"><a class="xref" hre</a>f="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The trick of transmuting cinnabar into silver is thus: the cinnabar, being bruised grossly, is stratified in a crucible with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANULATED">granulated</a> silver, and the crucible placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fire; and, after due <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for calcination, taken off; then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, being poured out, is found to be cinnabar. Transmuta-cinnabar turned into real silver, though the silver grains appear in the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and form as when they were put into the crucible; but the mischief is, coming to handle the grains of silver, you find them nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> friable bladders, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> crumble to pieces between the fingers. The transmutability of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> seems to have been believed by Mr Boyle; and Bishop Watson thinks that it has not yet been disproved. See his Chemical Essays. Transmutation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">Acids</a>, or of Metals, is the change of one acid or of one metal into another. Transom, among builders, denotes the piece that is framed across a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>-light window. Transoms, in a ship, certain beams or timbers extended across the sternpost of a ship, to fortify her afterpart, and give it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> most suitable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> for which she is calculated. Transparency, in Physics, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in certain bodies, whereby they give passage to the rays of light: in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to opacity, or that quality of bodies which renders them impervious to the rays of light. It has been generally supposed by philosophers, that transparent bodies have their pores disposed in straight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, by which means the rays of light have an opportunity of penetrating them in all directions; but some experiments in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> have made it apparent, that by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of this fluid the most opaque bodies, such as sulphur, pitch, and sealing-wax, may be rendered transparent as glass, while yet we cannot suppose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of their pores to be any way altered from what it originally was (see Electricity). There is a curious instance of an increase of transparency in rubbing a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> over one that has been written upon or printed: while the white paper is at rest, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> or print will perhaps scarcely appear through it; but when in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, will be very easily legible, and continue so till the motion is discontinued. Transposition, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a disturbing or dislocating the words of a discourse, or a changing their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, to please the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> by rendering the contexture more smooth, easy, and harmonious. Transubstantiation, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, the conversion or change of the substance of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and wine in the eucharist, into the body and blood of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; which the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> suppose to be wrought by the consecration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, No. 5. Transversalis, in Anatomy, a name given to several muscles. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. Transverse, something that goes across another from corner to corner: thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> and bars in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a> are transverse pieces or bearings; the diagonals of a parallelogram or a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> are transverse lines. Transylvania, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, annexed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Upper Hungary and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a> and Wallachia, on the south by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a>, and on the west by Upper and Lower Hungary. It is surrounded on all parts by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which, however, are not barren. The inhabitants have as much corn and wine as they want themselves; and there are rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of gold, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, quicksilver, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>. It has undergone various revolutions; but it now belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. The inhabitants are of several sorts of religions; as Papists, Lutherans, Calvinists, Socinians, Photinians, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, Greeks, and Mahometans. It is about 162 miles in length, and 150 in breadth. The administration of affairs is conducted by 12 persons; namely, three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, three Lutherans, three Calvinists, and three Socinians. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> is commanded by the governor, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> is the more important, as Transylvania is the bulwark of Christendom. It is divided into several small districts, called palatinates and counties; and is inhabited by three different nations, Saxons, Silesians, and Hungarians. Hermannstadt is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town. Trapezium, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> figure contained under four unequal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> lines. Trapezius, a muscle. See Anatomy, Part II. Trapp, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> rock. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a>. Travellers Joy. See Clematis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">Traverse</a>, or Transverse, in general, denotes something that goes athwart another; that is, crosses and cuts it obliquely. Traverse, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, implies a compound course, or an assemblage of various courses, lying at different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the meridian. See Navigation. Traverse Board, a thin circular piece of board, marked with all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass, and having eight holes bored in each, and eight small pegs hanging from the centre of the board. It is used to determine the different courses run by a ship during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the watch, and to ascertain the distance of each course. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVESTY">Travesty</a>, a name given to an humorous translation of any author. The word is derived from the French travestir "to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>." Treacle, or Mlasses. See <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>. Treacle Beer. See Spruce. Treacle Mustard. See Clypeola, Botany Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">Treason</a>, a general appellation, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, to denote not only offences against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, but also that accumulation of guilt which arises whenever a superior reposes a confidence in a subject or inferior, between whom and himself there subsists a natural, a civil, or even a spiritual relation; and the inferior so abuses that confidence, so forgets the obligations of duty, subjection, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, as to destroy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of any such superior or lord. Hence treason is of two kinds, high and petty. High Treason, or Treason Paramount (which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the crimen laesae maiestatis of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, as Glanvil denominates it also in our English law), is an offence committed against the security of the king or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, whether by imagination, word, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>. In order to prevent the inconveniences which arose in England from a multitude of constructive treasons, the statute 25 Edw. III, c. 2, was made; which defines what offences only for the future should be held to be treason; and this statute comprehends all kinds of high-treason under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> distinct branches. "1. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> doth compass or imagine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of our lord the king, of our lady his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, or of their eldest son and heir." Under this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> it is held that a queen-regnant (such as Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>) Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>) is within the words of the act, being invested with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> power, and intitled to the allegiance of her subjects: but the husband of such a queen is not comprised within these words; and therefore no treason can be committed against him. Let us next see what is a compassing or imagining the death of the king, &c. These are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms: the word compass signifying the purpose or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the mind or will; and not, as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> speech, the carrying such design to effect. And therefore an accidental stroke, which may mortally wound the sovereign, per infortunium, without any traitorous intent, is no treason: as was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of Sir Walter Tyrell, who, by the command of King William Rufus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HART">hart</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> glanced against a tree, and killed the king upon the spot. But as this compassing or imagination is an act of the mind, it cannot possibly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under any judicial cognizance, unless it be demonstrated by some open or overt act. The statute expressly requires, that the accused "be thereof upon sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> attainted of some open act by men of his own condition." Thus, to provide weapons or ammunition for the purpose of killing the king, is held to be a palpable overt act of treason in imagining his death. To conspire to imprison the king by force, and move towards it by assembling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, is an overt act of compassing the king's death; for all force used to the person of the king, in its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> may tend to his death, and is a strong presumption of something worse intended than the present force, by such as have so far thrown off their bounden duty to their sovereign: it being an old observation, that there is generally but a short <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> and the graves of princes. It seems clearly to be agreed, that by the common law and the statute of Edw. III., words spoken amount only to a high misdemeanor, and no treason. For they may be spoken in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, without any intention; or be mistaken, perverted, or misremembered by the hearers; their meaning depends always on their connection with other words and things; they may signify differently even according to the tone of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> with which they are delivered; and sometimes silence itself is more expressive than any discourse. As therefore there can be nothing more equivocal and ambiguous than words, it would indeed be unreasonable to make them amount to high treason. And accordingly, in 4 Car. I. on a reference to all the judges, concerning some very atrocious words spoken by one Pyne, they certified to the king, "that though the words were as wicked as might be, yet they were no treason; for unless it be by some particular statute, no words will be treason." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the words be set <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in writing, it argues more deliberate intention; and it has been held, that writing is an overt act of treason; for scribere est agere. But even in this case the bare words are not the treason, but the deliberate act of writing them. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of treason is, "if a man do violate the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, or the king's eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> unmarried, or the wife of the king's eldest son and heir." By the king's companion is meant his wife; and by violation is understood carnal knowledge, as well without force as with it: and this is high treason in both parties if both be consenting; as some of the wives of Henry VIII. by fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> evinced. 3. The third species of treason is, "if a man do levy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against our lord the king in his realm." And this may be done by taking arms, not only to dethrone the king, but under pretence to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, or the laws, or to remove evil counsellors, or other grievances whether real or pretended. For the law does not, neither can it, permit any private man, or set of men, to interfere forcibly in matters of such high importance; especially as it has established a sufficient power for these purposes in the high <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>: neither does the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> justify any private, or particular resistance for private or particular grievances; though, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of national oppression, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> has very justifiably risen as one man, to vindicate the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> subsisting between the king and his people. 4. "If a man be adherent to the king's enemies in his realm, giving to them aid and comfort in the realm or elsewhere," he is also declared guilty of high treason. This must likewise be proved by some overt act; as by giving them intelligence, by feeding them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, by selling them arms, by treacherously surrendering a fortress, or the like. 5. "If a man counterfeit the king's great or privy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>," this is also high treason. But if a man takes wax <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the great seal off from one patent, and fixes it to another, this is held to be only an abuse of the seal, and not a counterfeiting of it: as was the case of a certain chaplain, who in such a manner framed a dispensation for non-residence. But the knavish artifice of a lawyer much exceeded this of the divine. One of the clerks in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> glued together two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>; on the uppermost of which he wrote a patent, to which he regularly obtained the great seal, the label going through both the skins. He then dissolved the cement, and taking off the written patent, on the blank skin, wrote a fresh patent of a different import from the former, and published it as true. This was held no counterfeiting of the great seal, but only a great misprision; and Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> mentions it with some indignation that the party was living at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. 6. The sixth species of treason under this statute is, "if a man counterfeit the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; and if a man bring false money into the realm counterfeit to the money of England, knowing the money to be false, to merchandise and make payment withal." As to the first branch, counterfeiting the king's money; this is treason, whether the false money be uttered in payment or not. Also if the king's own minters alter the standard or alloy established by law, it is treason. But gold and silver money only are held to be within this statute. With regard likewise to the second branch, importing foreign counterfeit money in order to utter it here; it is held that uttering it, without importing it, is not within the statute. 7. The last species of treason ascertained by this statute is, "if a man slay the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, or the king's justices of the one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> or the other, justices in eyre, or justices of assize, and all other justices assigned to hear and determine, being in their places doing their offices." These high magistrates, as they represent the king's majesty during the execution of their offices, are therefore for the time equally regarded by the law. But this statute extends only to the actual killing of them; and not to wounding, or a bare attempt to kill them. It extends also only to the officers therein specified; and therefore the barons of the exchequer, as such, are not within Treaon within the protection of this act; but the lord keeper or commissioners of the great seal now seem to be within it, by virtue of the statutes 5 Eliz. c. 18. and 1 W. and M. c. 21. The new treasons, created since the statute 1 M. c. 1, and not comprehended under the description of statute 25 Edw. III., may be comprised under three heads. The first species relates to Papists; the second to falsifying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> or other royal signatures, as falsely forging the sign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a>, privy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a>, or privy seal, which shall be deemed high treason (1 M. stat. ii. c. 6.). The third new species of high treason is such as was created for the security of the Protestant succession in the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>. For this purpose, after the act of settlement was made, it was enacted by statute 13 and 14 W. III. c. 3, that the pretended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, assuming the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of King James III. should be attainted of high treason; and it was made high-treason for any of the king's subjects to hold correspondence with him or any person employed by him, or to remit money for his use. And by 17 Geo. II. c. 39, it is enacted, that if any of the sons of the pretender shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or attempt to land in this kingdom, or be found in the kingdom or any of its dominions, he shall be adjudged attainted of high treason; and corresponding with them or remitting money to their use is made high-treason. By 1 Ann. stat. 2, c. 17, the offence of hindering the next in succession from succeeding to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> is high-treason; and by 6 Ann. c. 7, if any person shall maliciously, advisedly, and directly, by writing or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, maintain, that any other person hath any right to the crown of this realm, otherwise than according to the act of settlement, or that the kings of this realm with the authority of parliament are not able to make laws to bind the crown and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>; such person shall be guilty of high treason. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of high treason in general is very solemn and terrible. 1. That the offender be drawn to the gallows, and not be carried or walk; though usually (by connivance, at length ripened by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> into law) a pledge or hurdle is allowed, to preserve the offender from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> torment of being dragged on the ground or pavement. 2. That he be hanged by the neck, and then cut down alive. 3. That his entrails be taken out, and burned while he is yet alive. 4. That his head be cut off. 5. That his body be divided into four parts. 6. That his head and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> be at the king's disposal. The king may, and often doth, discharge all the punishment except beheading, especially where any of noble blood are attainted. For beheading being part of the judgement, that may be executed, though all the rest be omitted by the king's command. But where beheading is no part of the judgement, as in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> or other felonies, it hath been said that the king cannot change the judgement, although at the request of the party, from one species of death to another. In the case of coining, which is a treason of a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> from the rest, the punishment is milder for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> offenders; being only to be drawn and hanged by the neck till dead. But in treasons of every kind the punishment of women is the same, and different from that of men. For as the natural modelly of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> forbids the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> and publicly mangling their bodies, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> (which is to the full as terrible to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> as the other) is to be drawn to the gallows, and there to be burned alive. For the consequences of this judgement, see Attainder, Forfeiture, and Corruption of Blood. Petty or Petit Treaon, according to the statute 25 Edward III. c. 2, may happen three ways: by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> killing his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, a wife her husband, or an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> person (either <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> or regular) his superior, to whom he owes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and obedience. A servant who kills his master whom he has left, upon a grudge conceived against him during his service, is guilty of petty treason: for the traitorous intention was hatched while the relation subsisted between them, and this is only an execution of that intention. So if a wife be divorced a mensa et thoro, till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINCULUM">vinculum</a> matrimoniis subsists; and if she kills such divorced husband, she is a traitress. And a clergyman is understood to owe canonical obedience to the bishop who ordained him, to him in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> he is beneficed, and also to the metropolitan of such suffragan or diocesan bishop; and therefore to kill any of these is petit treason. As to the rest, whatever has been said with respect to wilful Murder, is also applicable to the crime of petit treason, which is no other than murder in its most odious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; except that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> shall be as in cases of high treason, before the improvements therein made by the statutes of William III. But a person indicted of petit treason may be acquitted thereof, and found guilty of manslaughter or murder: and in such case it should seem that two witnesses are not necessary, as in cases of petit treason they are. Which crime is also distinguished from murder in its punishment. The punishment of petit treason in a man, is to be drawn and hanged, and in a woman to be drawn and burned: the idea of which latter punishment seems to have been handed down to us from the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>, which condemned a woman to be burned for murdering her husband; and it is now the usual punishment for all sorts of treasons committed by those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> sex. Persons guilty of petit treason were first debarred the benefit of clergy by statute 12 Henry VII. c. 7, which has since been extended to their aiders, abettors, and counsellors, by statutes 23 Henry VIII. c. 1, 4, and 5 P. and M. c. 4.

TRANSPORT

Pages 72-72

from transit, "it passes over," signifies the passage of any planet over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stars.

TREASURE

Pages 81-81

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLE">orle</a>, usually held to be half the breadth thereof.

TREE

Pages 76-80

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vegetable rising with one woody stem to a considerable height. Trees may be divided into two classes, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and fruit-trees; the first including all those trees which are used in machinery, ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, in general, for purposes of utility; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> comprehending those trees valued only, or chiefly, for their fruit. It is not necessary to form a third class to include trees used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, as timber is used for this purpose where it is abundant; and where it is not abundant the branches of the timber trees, or such of them as are dwarfish, unhealthy, or too small for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> purposes, are used as fuel. The anatomy and physiology of trees have already been given under the generic name Plant and Sap. Certain trees, it is well known, are natives of particular districts; but many of them have been transplanted from their native <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and now flourish luxuriantly in distant countries, so that it becomes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of very considerable difficulty to ascertain their original soil. The following rules are given for this purpose by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> Daines Barrington. 1. They must grow in large masses, and cover considerable tracts of ground, the woods not ending abruptly, by a change to other trees, except the situation and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> become totally different. 2. They must grow kindly in copses, and shoot from the stool, so as to continue for ever, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not very carefully grubbed up. 3. The seed must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> kindly; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> but where a succession in the greatest profusion <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> continue. Lastly, trees that give names to many places are probably indigenous. The growth of trees is a curious and interesting subject; yet few experiments have been made to determine what the additions are which a tree receives annually in different periods of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The only observations which we have seen on this subject worth repeating were made by the ingenious Mr Barker, to whom the Philosophical Transactions are much indebted for papers containing an accurate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, which he has kept for many years. He has drawn up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> to point out the growth of three kinds of trees, oaks, ashes, and elms; which may be seen in the Philosophical Transactions for 1788. We shall give his conclusions. "I find (says he) the growth of oak and ash to be nearly the same. I have some of both sorts planted at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and in the same hedges, of which the oaks are the largest; but there is no certain rule as to that. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> growth of an oak or an ash is about an inch in girth in a year; some thriving ones will grow an inch and a half; the unthriving ones not so much. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> trees grow more timber in a year than small ones; for if the annual growth be an inch, a coat of one-sixth of an inch is laid on all round, and the timber added to the body every year is its length multiplied into the thickness of the coat and into the girth, and therefore the thicker the tree is, the more timber is added." We will present our readers with a table, showing the growth of 17 kinds of trees for two years. The trees grew at Cavenham in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>. See Husbandry, No 165, where the growth of 11 kinds of trees in 21 years is given. Trees sometimes attain a very great size; this must depend in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> on the richness of soil, but no less on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Indeed heat is so essential to the growth of trees, that as we go from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> within the polar circles where vegetation begins, and advance to the equator, we find the trees increase in size. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, and other places in the same latitude, yield no trees at all; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> which they produce are dwarfish; whereas, in warm climates, they often grow to an immense size. Mr Martham <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> spruce and silver firs in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>-yard in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> above 40 yards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and one of 39 yards was 18 inches diameter at the small end. He was informed that they came from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. The largest tree in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, mentioned by travellers, is the chestnut tree on Mount Etna, already described under the article Etna, No 18. It is a certain fact that trees acquire a very great size in volcanic countries. Beside the multitude of fine groves in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, there are many detached oaks 20 feet in circumference, and many elms of the same size, especially in the romantic way to Eufello, called the Galleria. In travelling by the side of the lake of Bolsena, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> leads through an immense <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of oaks, spread upon beautiful hills. Where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> has been sufficiently softened, they are clean and straight, and of a considerable size; but where the lava has not been converted into a soil proper for strong vegetation, they are round-headed, and of less size; however, taken all together, they make a magnificent appearance; and the spot itself ought to be ranked among the fine parts of Italy. The same may be observed of the small lake of Vico, encompassed with gentle risings, that are all clothed with forest-trees. Some yews have been found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> 60 feet round. Palms in Jamaica attain the height of 200 feet; and some of the pines in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> are 280 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Of all the different kinds known in Europe, oak is best for building; and even when it lies exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, there is none equal to it. Fir-timber is the next in degree of goodness for building, especially in England, where they build upon leaves. It differs from oak in this, that it requires not much seasoning, and therefore no great stock is required beforehand. Fir is used for flooring, wainscoting, and the ornamental parts of building within doors. Elm is the next in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, especially in England and France: it is very tough and pliable, and therefore easily worked: it does not readily split; and it bears driving of bolts and nails better than any other wood; for which reason it is chiefly used by wheelwrights and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a>-makers, for shafts, naves, &c. Beech is also used for many purposes: it is very tough and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> when young, and of great strength; but liable to warp very much when exposed to the weather, and to be worm eaten when used within doors; its greatest use is for planks, bedsteads, chairs, and other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods. Ash is likewise a very useful wood, but very scarce in most parts of Europe; it serves in buildings, or for any other use, when screened from the weather; handpikes and oars are chiefly made of it. Wild chestnut timber is by many esteemed to be as good as oak, and seems to have been much used in old buildings; but whether these trees are more scarce at present than formerly, or have been found not to answer so well as was imagined, it is certain that this timber is now but little used. Walnut-tree is excellent for the joiner's use, it being of a more curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> than beech, and not so subject to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. The poplar, alder, and alpen trees, which are very little different from each other, are much used instead of fir; they look well, and are tougher and harder. The goodness of timber not only depends on the soil and situation in which it stands, but likewise on the season wherein it is felled. In this people disagree very much; some are for having it felled as soon as its fruit is ripe, others in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and many in the autumn. But as the sap and moisture of timber is certainly the cause that it perishes much sooner than it otherwise would do, it seems evident, that timber should be felled where there is the least sap in it, viz. from the time that the leaves begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> till the trees begin to bud. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> usually commences about the end of April in England, because the bark then rises most freely; for where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of timber is to be felled, the statute requires it to be done then, for the advantage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> chiefly regarded the age of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> in felling their timber; their rule was to fell it in the wane, or four days after the new moon, or sometimes in the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. Pliny advises it to be in the very instant of the change; which happening to be in the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the winter solstice, the timber, says he, will be incorruptible. Timber should likewise be cut when of a proper age; for when it is either too young or too old, it will not be so durable as when cut at a proper age. It is said that oak should not be cut under 60 years old, nor above 200. Timber, however, should be cut in its prime, when almost fully grown, and before it begins to decay; and this will be sooner or later according to the dryness and moistness of the soil where the timber grows, as also according to the bigness of the trees; for there are no fixed rules in felling of timber, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> and judgment must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> here as in most other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is necessary in the seasoning of timber. Some advise the planks of timber to be laid for a few days in some pool or running stream, in order to extract the sap, and afterwards to dry them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or air. By this means, it is said, they will be prevented from either chopping, calting, or cleaving; but against shrinking there is no remedy. Some again are for burying them in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, others in a heat; and some for scorching and sealing them in fire, especially piles, pots, &c., which are to stand in water or earth. The Venetians first found out the method of seasoning by fire; which is done after this manner: They put the piece to be seasoned into a strong and violent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>; in this they continually turn it round by means of an engine, and take it out when it is everywhere covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> coaly crust; the internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the wood is thereby so hardened, that neither earth nor water can damage it for a long time afterwards. Dr Plott says, it is found by long experience, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> or body of the trees, when barked in the spring, and left standing naked all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> exposed to the sun and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, are so dried and hardened, that the fappy part in a manner becomes as firm and durable as the heart itself. This is confirmed by M. Buffon, who, in 1738, presented to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy of sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> a memoir entitled, "An easy method of increasing the solidity, strength, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of timber;" for which purpose he observes, "nothing more is necessary than to strip the tree entirely of its bark during the season of the rising of the sap, and to leave it to dry completely before it be cut <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>." By many experiments, particularly described in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a>, it appears, that the tree should not be felled till the third year after it has been stripped of the bark; that it is then perfectly dry, and the sap become almost as strong as the rest of the timber, and stronger than the heart of any other oak tree which has not been so stripped; and the whole of the timber stronger, heavier, and harder; from which he thinks it fair to conclude, that it is also more durable. "It would no longer (he adds) be necessary, if this method were practised, to cut off the sap; the whole of the tree might be used as timber; one of 40 years growth would serve all the purposes for which one of 60 years is now required; and this practice would have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> advantage of increasing the quantity, as well as the strength and solidity, of the timber." The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> board, in answer to the inquiries of the commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> revenue, in May 1789, informed them, that they had then standing some trees stripped of their bark two years before, in order to try the experiment of building one half of a floop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with that timber, and the other half with timber felled and stripped in the common way. This very judicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of making the experiment, if it be properly executed, will undoubtedly go far to ascertain the effects of this practice. We are sorry that we are not able to inform our readers what was the result of the experiment. After the planks of timber have been well seasoned and fixed in their places, care is to be taken to defend or preserve them; to which the smearing them with linseed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, tar, or the like oleaginous matter, contributes much. The ancients, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, advise the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>-drying of all instruments made of wood, by hanging them up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> where wood fires are used. The Dutch preserve their gates, portcullises, drawbridges, sluices, &c., by coating them over with a mixture of pitch and tar, wherein they strew small pieces of cockle and other shells, beaten almost to powder, and mixed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-sand, which incrusts and arms them wonderfully against all assaults of wind and weather. When timber is felled before the sap is perfectly at rest, it is very subject to worms; but to prevent and cure this, Mr Evelyn recommends the following remedy as the most approved: Put common sulphur into a cucubit, with as much aquafortis as will cover it three fingers deep; distil it to dryness, which is performed by two or three rectifications. Lay the sulphur that remains at bottom, being of a blackish or land-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, on a marble, or put it in a glaas, and it will dissolve into an oil; with this oil anoint the timber which is infected with worms. This, he says, will not only prevent worms, but preserve all kinds of woods, and many other things, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, nets, and mats, from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, either in water, air, or snow. An experiment to determine the comparative durability of different kinds of timber, when exposed to the weather, was made by a nobleman in Norfolk; of which account is given by Sir Thomas Beevor. This nobleman, in the year 1774, ordered three posts, forming two sides of a quadrangle, to be fixed in the earth on rising ground in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>. Into these posts were mortised planks, an inch and a half thick, cut out of trees from 30 to 45 years growth. These, after standing 10 years, were examined, and found in the following state and condition: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> was perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; larch, the heart sound, but the sap quite decayed; spruce fir, sound; silver fir, in decay; Scotch fir, much decayed; pine, after, quite rotten; chestnut, perfectly sound; abele, sound; beech, sound; walnut, in decay; sycamore, much decayed; birch, quite rotten. Sir Thomas Beevor justly remarks, that the trees ought to have been of the same age; and Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> Young adds, they ought to have been cut out of the same plantation. The immense quantity of timber consumed of late years in ship-building and other purposes has diminished in a very great degree the quantity produced in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. On this account, many gentlemen who well know their country, alarmed with the fear of a scarcity, have strongly recommended it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to pay some attention to the cultivation and preservation of timber. We find, on the best authority, that of Mr Irving inspector general of imports and exports, that the shipping of England in 1760 amounted to 6107 in number, the tonnage being 433,922; and the shipping in Scotland amounted to 976 in number, the tonnage being 52,818. In 1788 the whole shipping of Britain and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> and their colonies amounted to 13,800, being 1,359,732 tons burden, and employing 107,925 men. The tonnage of the royal navy in the same year was 413,667. We are informed also, on what we consider as the best authority (the report of the commissioners of the land revenue), that the quantity of oak timber, of English growth, delivered into the dockyards from 1760 to 1788 was no less than 768,676 loads, and that the quantity used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> yards in the same time was 516,630 loads; in all 1,285,306 loads. The foreign oak used in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> was only 137,766 loads. loads. So that, after deducting the quantity remaining in the dock-yards in 1760 and 1788, and the foreign oak, there will remain about 1,054,284 loads of English oak, consumed in 28 years, which is at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> 37,653 loads per annum, besides from 8,300 to 10,000 loads expended annually by the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> within the same period (a). The price of wood has risen in proportion to the demand and to its diminution. At the conquest, woods were valued, not by the quantity of timber which they contained, but the number of swine which the acorns could support. In 1608, oak in the forests was sold at 10s. per load, and firewood for 2s. per load. In 1663 or 1665, in navy contracts from 2l. to 2l. 1s. 6d. per load was given. In 1776 it rose to 4l. 5s. per load, and 3s. in addition, because no tops are received. Plank four inch fold in 1769 for 7l. a load, three inch 6l.; which prices were the same in 1792. So great an expenditure of valuable timber within so short a period, gives reason to fear that the forests of this country will soon be entirely dismantled, unless something is done to raise fresh supplies. The building of a 70 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> ship, it is said, would take 40 acres of timber. This calculation is indeed too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, that it is scarcely credible. This, however, is no exaggeration. According to the prevailing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of experienced surveyors, it will require a good soil and good management to produce 40 trees on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, which, in a hundred years, may, at an average, be computed at two loads each. Reckoning, therefore, two loads at 8l. 16s., one acre will be worth 350l. and consequently 40 acres will only be worth 14,000l. Now a 70 gun ship is generally supposed to cost 70,000l.; and as ships do not last a great many years, the navy continually requires new ships, so that the forests must be stripped in a century or two, unless young trees are planted to supply their place. Many plans have been proposed for recruiting the forests. Premiums have been held forth to individuals; and it has been proposed that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-lands should be set apart for the special purpose of raising timber. With respect to individuals, as they must generally be disposed to sow or plant their lands with those vegetables which will best reward their labours, it is not to be expected that they will set apart their fields for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> trees unless they have a greater return from them than other crops. But bad must that land be which will not yield much more than 350l. produce in 100 years. But though it be evident that good land will produce crops much more lucrative to the proprietor than timber, yet still there are lands or pieces of land which might be applied with very great advantage to the production of wood. Uneven ground, or the sides of fields where corn cannot be cultivated, might very properly be set apart for this purpose; barren lands, or such as cannot be cultivated without great labour and expense, might also be planted. Hedge-rows and clumps of trees, and little woods scattered up and down, would shelter and defend the fields from destructive winds, would beautify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country, render the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> warmer, improve barren lands, and furnish wood for the arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. But to cultivate forest timber has also been thought of such national importance, that it has been deemed worthy of the attention of government. It has been proposed to appropriate such part of the crown-lands as are fit for the purpose solely of producing timber for the navy. This appears a very proper scheme in speculation; but it has been objected, that for government to attempt the farming of forests would be really to establish groups of officers to pocket salaries for doing what, it is well known, will never be done at all. But to this objection we reply, that such an agreement might be made with the inspectors of forests, as to make it their own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to cultivate trees with as much care as possible. Their salary might be fixed very low, and raised in proportion to the number of trees which they could furnish of such a size in a certain number of years. After all, we must acknowledge that we must depend greatly on Russia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, for supplying us with timber; and while these countries take our manufactures in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, we have no reason to complain. Still, however, we ought surely not to neglect the cultivation of what is of so much importance to our existence as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, for it may often be impossible in time of war to obtain timber from foreign countries. In the beginning of this article we mentioned the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of trees into timber or forest-trees and fruit trees. We have already said all that our limits will permit respecting the former: we will now, therefore, say something of the latter. Our observations shall be confined to the methods of preserving fruit trees in blossom from the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, and from other diseases to which they are liable. The Chevalier de Dienenberg of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, we are told in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, has discovered a method of effectually preserving trees in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> blossom from the fatal effects of those frosts which sometimes in the spring destroy the most promising hopes of a plentiful crop of fruit. His method is extremely simple. He surrounds the trunk of the tree in blossom with a wisp of straw or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. The end of this he sinks, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> tied to it, in a vessel of spring water, at a little distance from the tree. One vessel will conveniently serve two trees: or the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> may be lengthened so as to surround several, before its end is plunged into the water. It is necessary that the vessel be placed in an open situation, and by no means shaded by the branches of the neighbouring trees, that the frost may produce all its effect on the water, by means of the cord communicating with it.—This precaution is particularly necessary for those trees the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of which appear nearly at the same time as the leaves; which trees are peculiarly exposed to the ravages of the frost. The proofs of its efficacy, which he had an opportunity of observing in the (a) A writer in the Bath Transactions says, that the aggregate of oaks felled in England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> for 30 years past has amounted to 320,000 loads a-year; and affirms that he has documents in his possession founded on indisputable facts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between this account, and that which we have given in the text from the report of the commissioners, we leave to be reconciled by those who have proper opportunities. We give the facts merely on the authority of others. spring of 1787, were remarkably striking. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> apricot espaliers in his garden began to blossom in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of March. Fearing that they would suffer from the late frosts, he surrounded them with cords as above directed. In effect, pretty sharp frosts took place six or eight nights; the apricot-trees in the neighbouring gardens were all frozen, and none of them produced any fruit, whilst each of the chevalier's produced fruit in abundance, which came to the greatest perfection. The following is the method proposed by Mr William Forsyth for curing injuries and defects in trees; for which a reward was given to him by his Majesty, on condition that he should make it public. It is equally applicable to forest as to fruit trees (B). Take one bushel of fresh cow-dung, half a bushel of lime rubbish of old buildings (that from the ceilings of rooms is preferable); half a bushel of wood ashes; and a sixteenth part of a bushel of pit or river sand. The three last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> are to be sifted fine before they are mixed; then work them well together with a spade, and afterwards with a wooden beater, until the stuff is very smooth, like fine <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> used for the ceilings of rooms. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> being thus made, care must be taken to prepare the tree properly for its application by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> away all the dead, decayed, and injured parts, till you come to the fresh found wood, leaving the surface of the wood very smooth, and rounding off the edges of the bark with a draw-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, or other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, perfectly smooth, which must be particularly attended to. Then lay on the plaster about one-eighth of an inch thick all over the part where the wood or bark has been so cut away, finishing off the edges as thin as possible. Then take a quantity of dry powder of wood-ashes, mixed with a sixth part of the same quantity of the ashes of burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; put it into a tin box, with holes in the top, and shake the powder on the surface of the plaster, till the whole is covered over with it, letting it remain for half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to absorb the moisture; then apply more powder, rubbing it on gently with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and repeating the application of the powder, till the whole plaster becomes a dry smooth surface. All trees cut down near the ground should have the surface made quite smooth, rounding it off in a small degree, as before mentioned; and the dry powder directed to be used afterwards should have an equal quantity of powder of alabaster mixed with it, in order the better to resist the dripping of trees and heavy rains. If any of the composition be left for a future occasion, it should be kept in a tub or other vessel, and urine of any kind poured on it, so as to cover the surface; otherwise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> will greatly hurt the efficacy of the application. Where lime rubbish of old buildings cannot be easily got, take powdered chalk, or common lime, after having been flaked a month at least. As the growth of the tree will gradually affect the plaster, by raising up its edges next the bark, care should be taken, where that happens, to rub it over with the finger when occasion may require (which is best done when moistened by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>), that the plaster may be kept whole, to prevent the air and wet from penetrating into the wound. By this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, some old worn-out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a> trees, that Forsyth bore only a few small, hard fruit, of a kernelly texture, were made to produce pears of the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and finest flavour the second summer after the operation; and in four or five years they bore such plenteous crops, as a young healthy tree would not have produced in four times that period. By this process, too, some large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> elms, in a most decayed state, having all their upper parts broken, and a small portion only of the bark remaining, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out stems from their tops, above thirty feet in height, in six or seven years from the first application of the composition. Thus may valuable trees be renovated; and forest trees, which are useful or ornamental from their particular situation, be preserved in a flourishing state. But what is far more interesting, a perfect cure has been made, and sound timber produced, in oak trees, which had received very considerable damage from blows, bruises, cutting of deep letters, the rubbing off the bark by the ends of rollers, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of carts, or from the breaking of branches by storms. TREFOIL. See Trifolium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TREMELLA

Pages 80-80

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of cryptogamia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TREMOR

Pages 80-80

an involuntary shaking, chiefly of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and head, sometimes of the feet, and sometimes of the tongue and heart.—Tremors arising from a too free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of spirituous liquors require the same treatment as palpitations.

TRENCHES

Pages 80-80

in fortification, are ditches cut by the besiegers, that they may approach the more securely to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> attacked, whence they are also called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of approach.

TRENT

Pages 80-81

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the bishopric of that name, is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and stands in a fertile and pleasant plain, in the midst of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. The river Adige washes its walls, and creeping for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> among the hills, runs swiftly into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Trent has three considerable churches, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>; this is a very regular piece of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> is all of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble; and is remarkable for being the place where the famous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Trent... (B) A paste for covering the wounds of trees, and the place where grafts are inserted, was discovered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago. It is recommended in a Treatise on Fruit Trees, published by Thomas Hitt in 1755; a third edition of which, with additions, was published in 1768. It consists of a mixture of clay and cow's dung diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This paste he directs to be laid on the wound with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>; it adheres firmly, he says, without cracking till the wound heals. We are informed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, to whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> we pay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect, that this paste answers every purpose which Mr Forsyth's can serve. Trent was held, whose decisions are now the standing rule of the Romish church. E. Long. 11. 5. N. Lat. Trent, one of the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in England, which rises in the moorland of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, and runs south-west by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>-under-Line; and afterwards dividing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in two parts, runs to Burton, then to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a> and Newark: and so continuing its course due <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to Gainborough on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, it joins several rivers, and falls into the Humber. Trent, Council of, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, denotes the council assembled by Paul III. in 1545, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by 25 sessions till the year 1563, under Julius III. and Pius IV., in order to correct, illustrate, and fix with perspicuity, the doctrine of the church, to restore the vigour of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the lives of its ministers. The decrees of this council, together with the creed of Pope Pius IV., contain a summary of the doctrines of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. These decrees were subscribed by 255 clergy, consisting of four legates, 2 other cardinals, 3 patriarchs, 25 archbishops, 168 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, besides inferior clergy. Of these 150 came from Italy, of course the council was entirely under the influence of the pope. For a more particular account of the council of Trent, see Motheim's Church History, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> Universal History, vol. xxiii., and Father Paul's History of the Council of Trent. TRENTON. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>. TREPANNING. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TRES TABERNAE

Pages 81-81

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Latium, lying on the Via Appia, on the left <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> south side of the river Alturna, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the Paludes Pomptinae. Its ruins are now seen near Cisterna, a village in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma, 21 miles from Rome, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> went out to meet St. Paul.

TRESPASS

Pages 81-81

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies any transgression of the law, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, felony, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> misprision of either: but it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used for any wrong or damage that is done by one private person to another, or to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> in his forest.

TRESSLE TREES

Pages 81-81

in Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>, two strong bars of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> fixed horizontally on the opposite sides of the lower mast-head, to support the frame of the top and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the top-mast.

TREVERI

Pages 81-81
or Treviri, in Ancient Geography, an ancient and a powerful people, both in horse and foot, according to Caesar; extending far and wide between the Meuse and the Rhine. Their chief town was called Treviri. Now Trier or Trèves.

TREVES

Pages 81-81
or Triens (in Latin Treverae, Trevors, Treviris, or Augusta Treviorum), the capital of the German archbishopric of the same name, stands 60 miles west of Mentz, 52 south of Cologne, and 82 north of Strasbourg. This city vies with most in Europe for antiquity, having been a large and noted town before Augustus settled a colony in it. It was free and imperial till the year 1569, when it was surpried and subjected by its archbishop James III. It stands on the Moselle, over which it has a fair stone bridge. The cathedral is a large building; and near it stands the elector's palace, which not long ago was rebuilt. Here are three collegiate and five parish churches, three colleges of Jesuits, thirteen monasteries and nunneries, an university founded in 1472, a house of the Teutonic order, and another of that of Malta, with some remains of the ancient Roman theatre. Roman coins and medals are often found in the ruins of the old city. In the cathedral they pretend to have our Saviour's coat and St. Peter's staff, to which they ascribe miracles. The private houses here are mean; and the city is neither well fortified nor inhabited. E. Long. 6. 41. N. Lat. 49. 45.

TRIAL

Pages 81-88

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of a cause according to the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> before a proper judge; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it is the manner and order observed in the hearing and determining of causes. Trials are either civil or criminal. I. Civil Trials. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of trials in civil <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>: By record; by inspection or examination; by certificate; by witness; by wager of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; by wager of law; and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. The first five are only had in certain special or eccentric cases, where the trial by jury would not be so proper or effectual: (See them explained under their respective titles). The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the last, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> criterion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> in the law of England, shall be explained in this article. As trial by jury is esteemed one of the most important privileges which members of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> can enjoy, and the bulwark of the British <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of reflection must be stimulated by the desire of inquiring into its origin and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, as well as to be acquainted with the forms and advantages by which it is accompanied. We <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> therefore begin with tracing it to its origin. Its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> has been ascribed to our Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> by Sir William Blackstone. "Several authors (says that illustrious lawyer) have endeavoured to trace the original of juries up as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the Commentaries themselves, the first inhabitants of our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; but certain it is that they were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the earliest Saxon colonies, their institution being ascribed by Bishop Nicholson to Woden himself, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. Hence it is, that we may find traces of juries in the laws of all those nations which adopted the feudal system, as in Germany, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; who had all of them a tribunal composed of twelve good men and true, boni homines, usually the vassals or tenants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, being the equals or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of the parties litigant; and, as the lord's vassals judged each other in the lord's courts, so the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s vassals, or the lords themselves, judged each other in the king's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. In England we find actual mention of them so early as the laws of King <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>, and that not as a new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>.
