the WREATH, a genus of shell-fish. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">CONCHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. TURBOT. See PLEURONECTES, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a> Index. TURCÆ <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> TURCI (Mela); supposed to be the Tuisci of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>; whom he places between <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a> and the Montes Ceraunii. The name is said to denote, "to delocate, or lay waste." <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> places them among the wild or barbarous nations of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. There is a very rapid river called Turk, running into the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, from which some suppose the Turks to take their name. They made no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the world till towards the 7th century; about the beginning of which they felled forth from the Portae Caucasiae, laid waste Peria, and joined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> against Chofores <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. In 1042 they subdued the Persians, in whose pay they served, and from whom they derived the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and afterwards pouring forth, overrun <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, Cappadocia, and the other countries of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, under distinct heads or princes, whom Ottoman subduing, united the whole power in himself, which to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> continues in his family, and who fixed his seat of empire at Prusa in Bithynia. His successors subdued all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and at length took Constantinople in 1453; which put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to the Roman empire in the East, under Constantine the last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. It is a standing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> or prophecy among the Turks, that their empire <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> at length be overturned by the Franks or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; which seems now to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> on apace towards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a>. TURCOISE. See TURQUOISE.

TURGOT

Pages 122-122
ANNE ROBERT JAMES, a celebrated French financier, was born at Paris in 1727, of a very ancient Norman family. His father was a long time provost of the corporation of merchants; during which he was the object of general admiration, on account of his prudent administration. M. Turgot was the youngest of three brothers, and was destined for the church. He had scarcely attained the age at which reflection commences, when he resolved to sacrifice all temporal advantages to liberty and conscience, and to pursue his ecclesiastical studies without declaring his repugnance to their proposed object. At the age of 23 years he took his degree, and was elected prior of the Sorbonne. The time when it was necessary for him to declare that he would not be an ecclesiastic was now arrived. He announced this resolution to his father by letter, showing the motives which induced him to decline the clerical order. His father consented, and he was appointed matter of requits. M. Turgot prepared himself for this office by particular application to those parts of science which are most connected with its functions and duties, viz. ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy, agriculture, manufactures, commerce, &c. About this period he wrote some articles for the Encyclopédie, of which the principal are Etymology, Existence, Expandibility, Fair, and Foundation. He had prepared several others, but the persecution against the Encyclopédie induced him to decline farther contributions. In 1761 M. Turgot was appointed intendant of Limoges, when he gave activity to the society of agriculture; opened a mode of public instruction for female professors of midwifery; procured for the people the attendance of able physicians during the raging of epidemic diseases; established houses of industry, supported by charity (the only species of alms-giving which does not encourage idleness); introduced the cultivation of potatoes into his province, &c. &c. While M. Turgot proceeded with unremitting activity and zeal, in promoting the good of the people over whom he was placed, he meditated projects of a more extensive nature, such as an equal distribution of the taxes, the construction of the roads, the regulation of the militia, the prevention of a scarcity of provision, and the protection of commerce. At the death of Louis XV. the public voice called M. Turgot to the first offices of government, as a man who united the experience resulting from habits of business to all the improvement which study can procure. After being at the head of the marine department only a short time, he was, August 24, 1774, appointed comptroller general of the finances. During his discharge of this important office, the operations he carried on are astonishing. He suppressed 23 kinds of duties on necessary occupations, useless contracts, or merited compensations. He abolished the corvée, or the labour required from the public for the highways, saving the nation thirty millions of livres annually.—He set aside another kind of corvée, which respected the carriage of military stores and baggage.—He abated the rigour in the administration of indirect impositions, to the great profit of the contributors, the king, and the financiers; beside many other essential improvements in political economy. At length, however, by the artifices of the courtiers, he was deprived of his offices; and in retirement he devoted himself to the sciences and the belles lettres, which he had cultivated in his youth. Natural philosophy and chemistry were his favourite pursuits; sometimes he indulged in poetry. He composed, it is said, only one Latin verse, intended for a picture of Dr Franklin. Eripuit calo fulmen, mox fecit tyrannis." He died in 1781.

TURIN

Pages 122-123

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, where the sovereign resides, with an archbishop's see, a strong citadel, and an university. It is seated on a vast plain, at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Doria and Po. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is unhealthy in the autumn. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, Turkey.

TURKEY

Pages 123-130

an extensive empire, situated partly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and partly in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the empire of Russia, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and the Mediterranean; on the south by the Mediterranean and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; and on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. In its present state, we may compute it as extending from the river Unna, in east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> about 17°, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which separate it from Persia, in about 50° of east longitude from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> about 33° from west to east; while from the most southerly point, a little above Baflora, in north latitude 31°, to the confines of European Russia, in north latitude 47°, it occupies a range of 16° of latitude. In British miles its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is estimated at 1750 in length, by a medial breadth of about 1000, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> at 652,960 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Turkey is naturally divided into European and Asiatic, separated from each other by the Black sea, the Archipelago, and the straits by which these are connected. European Turkey is subdivided into 11 provinces, viz., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a>, Bessarabia, Wallachia, Bosnia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a> (partially), Bulgaria, Romelia (including <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> and Thrace), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a> (including Epirus), Croatia (partially), and the Morea, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; while Asiatic Turkey is subdivided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> provinces, viz., <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>), Diarbek (Mesopotamia), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> (including Judea), <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IBERIA">Iberia</a>), Turcomania (<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>), Irac-Arabia, and Kurdistan (<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>). See each of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in the general <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> belonging to Turkey are extremely numerous; comprising those of the Archipelago, or the Grecian islands, and several in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. The most important are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEMNOS">Lemnos</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a> or Mytilene, Scio, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, Cos, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, Cyprus, Candia, Paros, Delos, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAXIA">Naxia</a>, Sanctorini, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATMOS">Patmos</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGROPONT">Negropont</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROS">Andros</a>*, Colteri or Salami*, Egina, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZANTE">Zante</a>*, Cephalonia, Leucadia, Corfu, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERIGO">Cerigo</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYTHERA">Cythera</a>, which see under their proper heads. Both European and Asiatic Turkey abound in mountainous tracts, interspersed with numerous plains and valleys, and here and there a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of considerable extent. The plains are watered by numerous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and, in the Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, consist chiefly of pasture grounds. Among the mountains of European Turkey may be noticed the Carpathian chain, which divides it from the Austrian territories; the celebrated mountains of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HAEMUS">Haemus</a>; the Acroceranian mountains; and the classical hills of Pindus, Ossa, Pelios, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOS">Athos</a>. The most important mountains of Asiatic Turkey are, Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, dividing it from Russia; Mount Taurus, now called Thuron; Olympus; Ida; the mountains of Elend, and perhaps Mount Ararat, the resting-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the Ark, dividing it from Persia; and Mount Lebanon, celebrated in scripture for its cedars. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> river of European Turkey is the Danube, with its tributary streams, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">Save</a>, the Morava, the Bofna, and the Pruth; but we may also notice the Marilia or Hebrus, and the Vardan or Axius. In Asiatic Turkey are seen the Kifil-Irmak or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALYS">Halys</a>, the Sacaria, the Sarabat or Hermus, the Minder or Meander, the Araxes, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, the Jordan, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of European Turkey are of little importance, and in the Asiatic part there are only three that merit notice. These are the Dead sea and the sea of Galilee in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, and the Van in Armenia. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in the greater part of the Turkish empire is delightful, and the seasons mild and genial. The heats of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, except in the deserts of Syria, and on the shores of the Black sea, are tempered by the keen winds that blow from the higher regions, and the winter is in general extremely mild. The unhealthiness of the large <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Asiatic Turkey, is owing much more to the indolent and dirty habits of the people, than to any infalibility of the climate. Turkey affords a most ample field to the naturalist, whether his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to explore the animal, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, vegetable, or the mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In the first of these he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find the lion, a variety of the tiger, the hyena, the jackal, the ibex, the goat and cat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGORA">Angora</a>, and many other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Europe. Among the birds, one of the most numerous and most useful is the stork; partridges of a large size, quails, woodcocks, cranes, and several birds of prey, are also very common. The Black sea and the Archipelago abound with excellent fish, and contain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>, and other marine animals. Among the insects, that destructive animal the locust is a frequent visitant's, and Sonnini particularizes the tarantula, and a monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of spider, which he calls galeode araneoides, or the scorpion spider. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals, the Turks abound in excellent horses, asses of a large size, and that most useful beast of burden, the camel. To enumerate the vegetable productions of Turkey, would far exceed our scanty limits. The forests of European Turkey, though far less extensive than in ancient times, furnish abundance of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, especially oak, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, larch, walnut, chestnut, and beech, while the olive, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>, the almond, the peach, the mulberry, the cherry, the lemon, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions of Asiatic Turkey. Many of the most valuable drugs employed in medicine, are also the produce of this empire, especially opium, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, asafoetida and other fetid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, scammony, fennel, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, and coloquintida. Both <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> are found in Turkey, but from the indolence of the natives they are scarcely ever worked. Many of the islands abound in mineral treasures, especially Cyprus, where are found mines of gold, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, vitriol, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and where rock crystal, jasper, and several precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are occasionally procured. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> mineral production of Turkey, however, is its marble, of which it furnishes several of the most rare and beautiful varieties. That from the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Paros, is proverbially excellent. The people whom we now call Turks, and who form the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the Turkish empire, are generally believed to be the descendants of the ancient Scythians. They are supposed to have migrated from the Altai mountains in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, about the middle of the fifth century, and to have gradually diffused themselves towards the west, till they reached the lake Maeotis, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> sea of Azof, near which they settled in Armenia Minor or Turcomania. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Roman empire in the east was sufficiently strong to prevent the invaders from extending beyond the river <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OXUS">Oxus</a>, on the banks of which they established themselves, and soon became a formidable foe to the emperors of Constantinople. There is little certain or interesting in the history of these barbarians till the reign of the caliph Othman, or Ofan, who in the end of the 13th century established what from him has been called the Ottoman empire. He first took the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, and fixed the seat of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> at Prusa, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Bithynia. His successor Orkan was a restless, ambitious, and cruel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who greatly extended the limits of the empire, took possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLIPOLI">Gallipoli</a>, and penetrated into Thrace. Amurath the grandson of Ofan, in 1362, established the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> bands called janissaries, which still form the chief engines and chief moderators of Turkish despotism. These were first composed of young Christian slaves that had been taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and educated in the Mohammedan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. They were inured to obedience by severe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and trained to warlike exercises; and as every sentiment which enthusiasm can inspire, and every mark of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which the favour of the prince could confer, were employed to animate them with martial ardour, and excite in them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of their own importance, these janissaries, (or new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>) soon became the chief strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of the Ottoman arms. On the assassination of Amurath in 1389, he was succeeded by his son Bajazet, furred named Ildirim, or the Thunderbolt, whose reign forms one of the most splendid epochs in the Turkish history. Early in this reign, viz., in 1396, the Hungarians were defeated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a> in Bulgaria, and in 1402, was fought the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between Bajazet and Timur or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>, the chief of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a>, between Cesarea and Aneyra, which ended in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of Bajazet, and the temporary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> of the Turks. See MOGULS, No. 19 and 20. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Bajazet, his son Moufa became sultan, and in 1412 defeated the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Sigismund with great slaughter. Moufa was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Mohammed I., by whom he had been affianced. The reign of Amurath II., successor of Mohammed, contributed greatly to increase the splendour of the Turkish empire. In this reign Constantinople was attacked, but for the present escaped pillage. Amurath was successfully opposed in his hostilities against the Christian princes, by the Albanian chief George Castrion, whom the Turks call <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDERBEG">Scanderbeg</a>. Amurath was succeeded by Mohammed II., and soon after his accession, viz., in 1453, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Constantinople was taken by the Turks, and has ever since remained the capital of their empire. The events of which we have thus drawn the faint outline, are related at some length in the article CONSTANTINOPOLITAN HISTORY, No. 111.—168. Three years after the taking of Constantinople, Mohammed laid siege to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>, from which, after an attempt of obstinate resistance, he was at length repulsed with considerable loss. Abandoning his attempt on Hungary, the sultan made preparations for an expedition into Greece, where the princes Thomas and Demetrius, brothers of the emperor, still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to maintain their authority. Alarmed at the progress of the Turkish arms, these princes resolved on retiring into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, on which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> was seized by the Albanians. This tribe sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> to Mohammed, offering to give up to him the Grecian cities and fortresses, provided they should be allowed to keep the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but this offer was rejected by the sultan, who under the appearance of assailing the Greeks, entered the country with a formidable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, defeated the Albanians, took several cities, and carried off great numbers of the inhabitants. Mohammed was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son Bajazet II., in 1481, preferred by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a> to his elder brother Zizan, who fled for protection to Pope Alexander VI., by whom he is said to have been poisoned, at the instigation of Bajazet, and for the reward of 300,000 ducats. Selim, his youngest son and successor, was a successful prince. He conquered <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, Antioch, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, Damascus, and Gaza, and defeated the Persians. Solyman, furred named the Magnificent, one of the most accomplished, enterprising, and warlike, of the Turkish princes, ascended the Ottoman throne in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the death of Selim. Having quelled some insurrections in Asia, he commenced hostilities against the European princes, and entering Hungary, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Belgrade, then reckoned the chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> of that kingdom against the Turkish power. He next turned his victorious arms against the island of Rhodes, then the seat of the knights of St John of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. After incredible efforts of courage and military conduct, the knights obtained an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, and retired to the small island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, where they fixed their residence. See MALTA. He afterwards annexed Hungary to the Ottoman empire. His dominions extended from Algiers to the river Euphrates, and from the farther end of the Black Sea to the extremity of Greece and Epirus. During the siege of Sigeth, a city of Hungary, before which the Turks lost above 30,000 men, Solyman expired in the 74th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and 41st of his reign. His son and successor, Selim II., besieged and took Selim II., Cyprus; but in the famous sea fight at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>, in 1571, the Turkish fleet was utterly destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> John of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. He afterwards invested and took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a> by storm, putting the garrison to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. On his death, Amurath III., ascended the Ottoman throne, and extended his dominions on both sides by the addition of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAAB">Raab</a> in Hungary, and Tigris in Persia. His son, Mohammed III., has no claim to notice except... Turkey except on account of his barbarity. He began his reign by strangling 19 of his brothers, and ordering 12 of his father's wives, whom he suspected to be pregnant, to be drowned. This monster of cruelty had, however, a successful reign of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. During the government of his son, Achmet I., the affairs of Turkey underwent a material change for the worse*. On his death, the janizaries and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVAN">divan</a> elected his brother Multapha, whom in two months they declared incapable of reigning, and threw him into prison; after this they proclaimed his young nephew, Olman, the son of Achmet, emperor. This prince formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of curbing the power of the janizaries, for which he was deposed and murdered; and Multapha was again called from his prison to the imperial throne, but was soon after strangled. Under Amurat, or Morad IV., surnamed Gasi, the Intrepid, everything again assumed a new appearance. He was successful in his wars, and took <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a> from the Persians. A debauch of wine put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and dishonoured his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. His son Ibrahim, who succeeded him, had every vice; he was a weak prince, and wholly destitute of courage. He was strangled by four mutes. After a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of inactivity, the Turks again became formidable to Europe, under Mohammed IV., who succeeded him. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> vizier Kupuli, who at once directed the councils and conducted the armies of the Porte, took Candia from the Venetians. After carrying on many wars against the Germans, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, the Ruffians, and other European powers, he was compelled to resign the turban to Soliman II. in 1687, a prince happy in his domestic government, but unsuccessful in his wars. His brother, Achmet II., was likewise unfortunate in his wars. In his reign the Turks were driven out of Hungary and Transylvania†. The accession of his nephew, Multapha II., to the Ottoman throne, gave a new turn to the affairs of the Porte. Possessed of more vigour than his predecessor, he resolved to command his troops in person. He accordingly took the field, passed the Danube, stormed Lippa, seized Itul, and falling suddenly on a body of Imperialists, under Veterani, he killed that officer, dispersed his forces, and closed with success the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. He was afterwards defeated by Prince Eugene in an uncommonly bloody battle at Zenta, a small village on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Thuyfe, in the kingdom of Hungary. About 20,000 Turks were left dead on the field, and 10,000 were drowned in the river, endeavouring to avoid the fury of the sword. The magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> of the sultan, and all the stores, fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Prince Eugene, and soon after this misfortune the haughty Multapha was dethroned. His brother and successor, Achmet III., gave an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDER">Bender</a>, a Turkish town in Moldavia, after his defeat at the battle of Pultava. (See Russia, No. 118, and Sweden, No. 140.) Being unsuccessful in his war against Koul Khan and the Persians (see Persia), he was deposed, and succeeded by Mohammed V. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of Achmet III. till the accession of Multapha III. in 1754, nothing of importance occurs in the history of the Turkish empire. During the reign of this latter sultan was begun and terminated that destructive war with Russia, of which the principal events have been enumerated in the article Russia, No. 143 and 144. In this reign an extraordinary alarm was excited in Turkey by the sudden appearance of a new prophet in Upper Asia. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, whose name was Shiek Manjour, pretended that he was predestined by the eternal immutable decrees of heaven to fill up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> to mankind; and that, as he was to be the last, so he was the greatest of the prophets. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his ministry was in the wide and desolate regions on the borders of the Caspian sea; and though the first rumour of his proceedings represented him as at the head of a multitude of armed enthusiasts, ready to overturn the established government, and the religion of Mohammed, it was soon discovered that all the military fury of his zeal was directed against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. About the same time a formidable rebellion broke out in Egypt, which, though it has never properly formed a part of the Turkish empire, may be considered as tributary to the Turks, and as constituting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> of that empire. This rebellion, which has been sufficiently noticed under the article Egypt, No. 125, was suppressed chiefly by the wise conduct and intrepid bravery of Hoffsan Bey, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> pacha, who at the age of 70, fought with all the ardour of youth, and all the skill of the most consummate general. That veteran, however, was recalled before he was able to carry all his patriotic designs into execution, that he might aid the divan with his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, in the critical situation into which the empire was brought by the arrogant claims of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Russia. The result of the deliberations was a precipitate <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of war against that court, contrary to the better judgement of the old pacha. The war commenced in autumn 1787, and the hordes of Tartars which were first brought into the field, headed by the new prophet, were everywhere defeated by the superior discipline of the Russian troops commanded by Prince Potemkin. Some enterprises which were undertaken by the Turks against the island of Tannan and the Crimea were attended with as little success as the attempts of the Tartars; while the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> declared to the Porte, that he would assist his ally the empress of Russia with an army of 80,000 men. Four Austrian armies were accordingly assembled; one at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARLSTADT">Carlstadt</a> in Croatia, under the command of General de Vins; another at Petervaradin in Hungary, commanded by General Langlois; a third on the borders of Lithuania, under General Febris; and the fourth in the Bucovine, under the orders of the prince of Saxe-Cobourg. Two other generals, 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-generals, and 30 <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-generals, were all ordered to prepare for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the frontier armies. The war between the Turks and Austrians was carried on with various success. At first the advantage was evidently on the side of the Ottomans, and the imperial Joseph acquired no warlike renown. His declared purpose was to get possession of Belgrade; from which, however, he was repulsed with disgrace. The prince of Saxe-Cobourg in his department of the war displayed indeed prodigies of valour; but being opposed to a superior force, he was long obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> only on the defensive. At length being joined by a body of Russian forces under General Soltikof, preparations were made for commencing in form the siege of Choczin, which was surrendered to the allied armies on Michaelmas. Turkey. mas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> 1788, after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> which would have done honour to the ablest general in Europe. Still, however, success seemed to lean to the Turks. The grand vizier made a sudden incursion into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANAT">Banat</a>, and spread consternation and dismay to the very gates of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. The Austrian affairs seemed approaching to a very alarming crisis; not only the splendid views of conquest which were beheld in the imagined partition of a tottering empire had totally disappeared, but had left in their place the sad and gloomy reverse of a discontented and impoverished people, an exhausted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and an army thinned by pestilence and desertion. The first campaign of an invasive war had already produced an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the territory of the invader. In this situation of affairs Marshal Laudohn was with some difficulty drawn from his retirement to take the command of the army in Croatia; and under his auspices fortune began to smile on the Austrian arms. He quickly reduced Dubicza and Nevi, though they were both defended by the most obstinate bravery. He then sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before Turkish Gradica; but the autumnal rains coming on with such violence, that the Save overflowed its banks, he was compelled to raise the siege. During this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the war in the Banat raged with the utmost violence; torrents of blood were shed on both sides; much desperate valor displayed on the one side, and many brave actions performed on the other; while a very great part of that fine but unfortunate country suffered all the desolation and ruin that fire and sword, under the dominion of vengeance and animosity, could inflict. The inhabitants were objects of commiseration; but the injustice with which the emperor had commenced the war, made his personal losses be considered as nothing more than the due reward of his conduct. In the midst of these military operations Achmet IV. was deposed, and succeeded by Selim III. the late sultan. The new emperor did not want either courage or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and he continued the war with Russia and Austria, with great spirit and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. Those events of this war in which the Russians were more immediately concerned, have been already noticed under the article RUSSIA, No. 156, 158, 160 and 161; so that we have merely to relate the remaining operations of the Austrians. Marshal Laudohn renewed his attempts upon Gradica as soon as the season would permit, and after a brave defence it fell into his hands. This, with some other successes routed the emperor from his inactivity, and made him seriously determine on the attack which he had long meditated on Belgrade. The enterprise was intrusted to Laudohn, who, with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> which seemed constantly to attend him, made himself master of the place in less than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. The rest of the campaign was little else than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of the most important successes. While one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of General Laudohn's forces took possession of Czernitz in Wallachia, another made itself master of Cladova in Serbia. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCHAREST">Bucharest</a>, the capital of the former of these provinces, fell without opposition into the hands of Prince Cobourg; while Akerman on the Black Sea was reduced by the Russians; and Bender surrendered to Prince Potemkin, not without suspicion of sinister practices, on the 15th of November. Soon after this, the emperor Joseph died, and his successor Leopold shewed a desire for peace. After the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Orsova, therefore, which happened on the 16th of April 1790, the war was carried on with languor on the part of Austria; and in the month of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> a conference was agreed on at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REICHENBACH">Reichenbach</a>, at which the ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, Austria, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and the United Provinces, assisted, and at which also an envoy from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> was occasionally present. After a negotiation, which continued till the 17th of August, it was agreed that a peace should be concluded between the king of Hungary and the Ottoman Porte; that the basis of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> should be a general surrender of all the conquests made by the former, retaining only Choczm as a security till the Porte should accede to the terms of the agreement, when it also was to be restored. In the following year the Porte was compelled to conclude a peace with the empress of Russia, and from that period till the deposition of Selim in 1807, no event of consequence has occurred. The Porte has alternately been at war with Britain and with France, but in neither contest has the acquired either honour or territory. As the very confined limits to which we are now reduced forbid us to dwell on these minor transactions, we shall hasten to conclude this historical outline with an account of the revolution which placed Mahomet IV. on the Ottoman empire. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> 1807, the spirit of insurrection had shown itself among the janizaries belonging to the garrisons of the Dardanelles, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of the grand vizier. In the afternoon of the 25th of May, the garrisons of the castles of the Dardanelles were in a state of tumult, on account of the European uniform, the new and accelerated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a>, &c. Hali Aga, the commandant of Madchidja-fon of Muburna, on the Asiatic shore, was murdered. Indche-fasha IV. Bey, commandant of the entrance of the Black Sea, only escaped the same fate by flight. The reis effendi happening to come to inspect that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the same time, the military immediately rose upon him as one of the introducers of the nizam geded. He endeavoured to save himself in a bark, by passing over to Buyukdere, but 100 pistol shots laid him and his attendants dead. It seems that the rage of the janizaries had been embittered against him by the recollection of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> he made to raise their pay, on condition they would adopt the new discipline, and which promise he never performed. Another circumstance increased the spirit of opposition; the sultan had given notice that the janizaries were no longer to attend him as usual to the mosque, but that this duty was to devolve upon the troops disciplined after the European manner. Thousands of janizaries were now marching to Constantinople, and arrived in the suburb of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERA">Pera</a> on the evening of the 28th. They swore to each other to conduct the revolution with the best order. Any person who should in the least injure any Frank was to suffer death. One individual janizary only met with his fate, for taking <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> from a Greek (a baker), without paying for it. Behind the janizaries <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, in the well-known place called Eimeldan, the janizaries planted their colours, and took with them their camp kettles; an infallible signal of insurrection. For a time, the sultan thought of defending himself; and troops, powder, and cannon, were brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>. Soon after the mufti, the feimen bache, the kaimakan, and the two kazeakars of Romelia and Natolia, joined the janizaries. Turkey. zaries. A council was held in form, and it was pro- posed as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a>, to request the grand seignior to abolish the new discipline by a fetwa from the mufti. The grand seignior, however, thought he should be able to put a stop to the insurrection before the step could be taken, in consequence of his sending the heads of Mahmud, Terfana Emin, Hagai Ibrahim, and the kiaga Mehmed Effendi, to the Eimeldan. This measure completely failed; the janizaries were more enraged than ever; they did not require the heads of the universally esteemed Mahmud Effendi, but that of the Reis Effendi, then in the camp of the grand vizier. The janizaries continued to search every place for those ministers, who had promoted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> of the European discipline, and publicly avowed themselves as its patrons, namely, Fransito, Ibrahim, Jusuf Aga, Hadlchi Ibrahim, and Achmet Bey, captains of the grand seignior's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>; Haffan Aga, Achmet Effendi, and others, 12 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, who were all taken, dragged to the Eimeldan, and there cut to pieces. At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> the grand seignior sent a hatti icherif, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, in which he for ever abolished the nizam geded, and pronounced an execration on it. But the hatti icherif was not now accepted; the deposition of the grand seignior was resolved on. The whole force of the janizaries now proceeded to the feraglio. The mufti and the ullemas alone entered the haram, while the rest of the ministers, the agas, the janizaries, and the people, surrounded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. Multapha IV., born on the 7th of September 1799, the eldest son of the sultan Achmet IV., set aside in 1789, was raised to the Turkish throne. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>- ing to ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, Selim, the former sultan, threw himself at the feet of Multapha, kissed the border of his garment, and immediately repaired to that department of the feraglio occupied by the princes of the Ottoman blood who no longer reign. The solemn invitation to Multapha, to ascend the throne, was made on the 26th of May, and on the 3rd of June the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of invest- ing him with the fabric of the prophet, took place. The population of the whole Turkish empire is usu- ally estimated at 18,000,000. Of these, 10,000,000 have been allotted to Asiatic Turkey, and the remain- ing 8,000,000 to Turkey in Europe. A considerable part of this population consists of Jews and mercantile Christians, from different parts of Europe, who are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- tinguished by the name of Franks. The government of Turkey is despotic, but the power of the sultan is by no means so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> as we are generally led to suppose. Besides, being strictly subject to the laws of the Koran, and thus to the na- tional religion, such obstructions to his absolute will are raised by the power of the mufti, or chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and judge, by the frequent insurrections of the janizaries, and the ambition of the pachas, or governors of provinces, that many Christian sovereigns are much more despotic. The principal title of the sultans is, as we have seen, grand seignior, and the court of Constantinople is usu- ally styled the Porte, or Ottoman Porte, either from the large gate at the entrance of the feraglio, or, what is more probable, from the palace of the vizier, where all the affairs of state are transacted. The principal mini- sters of the Porte are the grand vizier or prime minister, the mufti, the reis effendi or chief secretary of state, the kiflar-aga or chief of the black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>, and the aga of the janizaries. The revenues of the whole Turkish empire are com- puted at about 7,000,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>, while the usual ex- pense does not exceed 5,000,000. This revenue is partly derived from the capitation tax on unbelievers and from the customs, but principally from the tax on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, a- mounting to about 6s. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>. The sultan is also supposed to possess a considerable private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, but of this nothing certain is known. The military strength of Turkey is but inconside ra- ble for so large an empire. The whole of the land forces are supposed never to exceed 150,000 men, and these are ill disciplined, and now dispirited by successive disastrous wars. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> is estimated at 30 sail of the line; but the ships are ill-built, badly manned, and wretch- edly navigated. In short, the military strength of the Ottoman empire is not improperly said to be more de- structive to its own provinces than to any state with which they are at war, and more terrible to its friends than its enemies. The established religion of Turkey is Mahometanism, the tenets of which have been already explained under laws, the articles Mahometanism and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a>. The laws of the empire are entirely founded on the Koran; but in particular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the judges are guided by certain commentaries on that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which have acquired the force of laws. The chief of these are the commentaries of Abou-Hanife. The mufti, or Mohammedan pontiff, resides at Con- stantinople, but his power has seldom interfered with the civil government. Next to him in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> are the moul- lahs, who, though esteemed dignitaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, are in fact rather doctors of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, while the Koran is also a code of civil observance. From the mollahs are selected the inferior muftis or judges throughout the empire, and the cadielquiers, or chief justices. The next class of divines includes the imams, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> priests, who perform the service of the mosques, while the cadis are judges annually appointed to administer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in the towns and villages, and being regard- ed as churchmen, like the mollahs, have directed their chief <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the judicial part of the Ko- ran. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> view it will be observed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> orders of muftis and imams somewhat resemble the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and parochial clergy; while the other distinctions arise from the singularity of both religion and laws being united in the Koran, so that a lawyer or judge must be at the same time a skil- ful divine. The Turks have also their monks, styled dervishes, of four various orders and institutions, dedi- cated by solemn vows to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> offices, public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, and preaching. The Greeks, along with their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, retain their priests, bishops, archbishops, and patriarchs; but their church is in the last state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>, and its dignities openly sold by the Turks; this abomi- <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, however, it must be confessed, partly arises from the miserable ambition and avarice of the Greek ec- clesiastics, who think they can atone by idle ceremo- nies for the neglect of all the invaluable morality of the gospel. The Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is of far inferior reputation Language and litera- ture. Turkey. Literature, however, is not wholly neglected, and it has been repeatedly attempted to establish a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> press at Constantinople; but the design failed from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the copyists, who inferred that this art would deprive them of their bread. A late traveller informs us that there are in this capital several kuttub-chans, or public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, among which are those of St Sophia, and the Soliman Janiay; but none are so elegant as that founded by the grand vizier Raghid, which is wholly built of marble in the midst of a square court, and is filled with books chiefly theological. A librarian constantly attends, and there are convenient seats with carpets and cushions. In the neighbourhood is a school founded by the same vizier, in which about 120 boys are taught to read and write. The market for books is extensive, containing many shops well supplied with oriental <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>. The Turks have their ancient poets, historians, and divines; but of little reputation when compared with those of Persia or Arabia. The state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> among the Turks may be conceived to be very low, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> is indeed a chief part of the national character. The only profession which requires a shadow of learning is that of the law, which is intimately connected with their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. The celebrated doctors have disciples, who are trained up to that department; but there seems nothing that can deserve the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> or university. The Turks cannot be regarded as a commercial people, though they admit of an extensive commercial intercourse with the states of Europe, through the medium of Frank and Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. The chief ports are <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> and Constantinople, the former of which is the great centre of the Levant trade, while the latter is concerned chiefly in the trade with Russia, by the Black Sea. At both these ports, and indeed throughout the Turkish empire, the trade is nominally carried on by factors from the different European states; but it is managed more immediately by Jew or Armenian brokers, who take numerous advantages of the ignorance of the factors, and seldom fail to enrich themselves at the expense of their employers. The commodities exported from Turkey, chiefly to Britain, Germany, Italy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and France, consist for the most part of bees wax, boxwood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, cotton yarn, walnut planks, sponges, opium and other drugs enumerated in No. 9, madder root, and other dye stuffs, and various dried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, such as figs, raisins, and currants. The imports are chiefly tin and tin plates, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, shallows, cotton yarn and cotton goods, muslins, clocks and watches, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a> and glass <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, pistols and military stores, logwood, rum, coffee, and various spices, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, ginger, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>. The exports are principally from Smyrna, where the trade is carried on almost entirely by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, while at Constantinople the imports are generally paid for by cash or bills. The exchange is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> against the Turks. The Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> usually employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is the piastre, which, according to the exchange or agio, is rated at from 13 to 17 in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> sterling, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> value of the piastre is about £6. Each piastre is divided into 40 paras, and each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARA">para</a> into three alpers. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> employed is the kilo, equal to about one cwt. English, divided into 44 oke, and each oke into 400 drahm. From their jealousy with respect to strangers, it is extremely difficult to form a true estimate of the national character of the Turks. An intelligent writer, who seems well qualified to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> our judgement in this respect, has thus delineated the Turkish character. "The Turks are in general a sagacious, thinking people; in the pursuit of their own interest, or fortune, their attention is fixed on one object, and they persevere with great steadfastness until they attain their purpose. They are in common life seemingly obliging and humane, not without appearances of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>; perhaps all or either of these, when extended towards Christians, are practised with a view of some advantage. Interest is their supreme good; where that becomes an object of competition, all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of friendship, all ties of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a>, are dissolved; they become delusive, no barrier can stop their pursuit, or abate their rancour towards their competitors. In their demeanour they are rather hypochondriac, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, sedate, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>; but when agitated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, furious, raging, ungovernable; big with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>; jealous, suspicious, and vindictive beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>; perpetuating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation. In matters of religion, tenacious, supercilious, and morose." The manners and customs of the Turks are distinguished by the peculiarity of their religion from those of other European nations. On the birth of a child, the father himself gives the name, putting at the same time a grain of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> into its mouth. The circumcision is not performed till the age of 12 or 14. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a> is only a civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, which either party may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, and is managed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> mediation, the youth seldom seeing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> till after the ceremony. The dead are perfumed and covered with incense, and buried in a cloth, open at top and bottom, that the deceased may be able to fit up and answer the questions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> of death. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-grounds are near the highways, and stones are often placed at the heads of the graves, with carved turbans denoting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. As they never intrude upon a former grave, the cemeteries are very extensive. In diet the Turks are extremely moderate, and their meals are dispatched with great haste. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">Rice</a> is the favourite food, and is dressed in three ways. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, the meat is cut into small pieces, and in roasting till smaller, a bit of meat and an onion being placed alternately on a very long spit. The fish of the Archipelago are excellent, and the beef tolerable, except that of the buffalo, which is very hard. The hares, partridges, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, are of superior flavour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> is usually spread on a low wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> pronounces a short prayer. The frugal repast is followed by fruits and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which are succeeded by hot coffee and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>. The houses of the Turks are seldom expensive; the chief furniture is the carpet which covers the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, with a low sofa on one side of the room. In regard to dress, Tournefort observes that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the turban is unhealthy. The shirt is of calico, and the loose robe is fastened by a girdle, in which is stuck a dagger, while the tobacco box, pocket-book, &c., are worn in the bosom. The robe is generally of European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cloth, trimmed with various furs. The shoes or slippers are slight, and unfit for much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. The dress of the women differs little from that of the men, the chief distinction being the head-dress; that of the fair sex consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> like... Turkey like an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>, formed of pasteboard covered with cloth of gold, with a veil extending to the eyebrows, while a fine handkerchief conceals the under part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. The personal cleanliness of both sexes is highly laudable; but the European eye is not pleased with the female custom of staining the nails with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> tincture. The amusements of the Turks partake of their indolent apathy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except hunting, and those of a military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. To recline on an elegant carpet, or in a hot seat by the side of a stream, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> the delicate tobacco of Syria, may be regarded as their chief amusement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESS">Chess</a> and draughts are favourite games; but those of chance are considered as incompatible with strict morals. The coffee-houses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> furnish other sources of amusement; and the bairam, or festival which follows their long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a>, is a season of universal dissipation.* It appears to be a mistaken notion, that the practice of eating opium, to procure intoxication, is general among the Turks. We are assured by a late traveller, that this practice is confined to a few individuals, who are regarded by the majority of their countrymen with as much contempt as drunkards are in the more polished <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of Europe. Turkey. See Meleagris, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Turmeric. See Curcuma, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Turnep, a species of Brassica. See Botany Index; and for the culture, see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. Turnep-Bread. See Bread. Turnep-Fly. See Chrysomela, Entomology Index. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">Turning</a>, the art of forming hard bodies, as wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, iron, into a round or oval shape, by means of a machine called a lathe. This art was well known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and seems to have been carried by them to a very great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection; at least, if we believe the testimony of Pliny and several other authors, who tell us, that those precious vases enriched with figures in half-relief, which still adorn our cabinets, were turned on the lathe. The art of turning is of considerable importance, as it contributes essentially to the perfection of many other arts. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> uses it for many ornaments, both within and without highly finished houses. The mathematician, the astronomer, and the natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, have recourse to it, not only to embellish their instruments, but also to give them the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> and precision. In short, it is an art absolutely necessary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a>, the watchmaker, the joiner, the smith. Turning is performed by the lathe, of which there are various kinds, and several instruments, as gouges, chisels, drills, formers, screw tales, used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> what is to be turned into its proper form as the lathe turns round. The following is a simple kind of lathe (fig. 1), in which a is the footstool, b the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, c the frame of the lathe, d d the puppets, e e the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, f the spanging-tree. The lathe should be fixed in a place very well lighted; it should be immovable, and neither too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> nor too low. The puppets should neither be so low as to oblige the workman to stoop in order to see his work properly, nor so high that the little chips, which he is continually driving off, should come into his eyes. The piece to be turned should be rounded (if it be wood) before it be put on the lathe, either with a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a> made for the purpose, or with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, or with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>, fixing it in a vice, and having it down till it is everywhere almost of an equal thickness, and leaving it a little bigger than it is intended to be when finished off. Before putting it on the lathe, it is also necessary to find the centres of its two end surfaces, and that they should be exactly opposite to each other, that when the points of the puppets are applied to them, and the piece is turned round, no side may belly out more than another. To find these two centres, lay the piece of wood to be turned upon a plank; open a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> to almost half the thickness of the piece; fix one of the legs in the plank, and let the point of the other touch one of the ends of the piece, brought into the same plane with the plank on which the compasses is fixed and very near the fixed leg. Describe four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> on that end at equal distances from each other at the circumference of the end, but intersecting one another within; the point of intersection is the centre of the end. In the same manner mark the centre of the other end be found. After finding the two centres, make a small hole at each of them, into which insert the points of the puppets, and fix the piece so firmly as not to be shaken out, and yet loose enough to turn round without difficulty. The piece being thus fixed, it is necessary in the next place to adjust the cord, by making it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> twice round the piece, and in such a manner that the two ends of the cord, both that which is fixed to the spang and to the foot-board, come off on the side on which the turner stands, that the piece may move against the edge of the cutting-tool and be turned. If the lathe be moved by a wheel, the manner of adjusting the cord needs no directions. If the workman does not choose to be at the trouble to find the two centres of the piece in the manner described above, let him lay, as nearly as he can, the centre of one end upon the point of the left hand puppet, and then let him push forward the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand puppet, striking it with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">mallet</a> till its point is as near as he can in the centre of the other end of the piece; and then fixing the right hand puppet by a gentle blow of the mallet on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>, let him turn round the piece to see by the eye if the centres have been properly found. If any part of it bellies out, let him strike that part gently with the mallet till it goes properly; then let him strike one of the puppets pretty smartly to drive the points into the piece, and afterwards fix the puppet by striking the key. If the workman cannot judge by the eye whether the piece be turning properly round its centres or not, he should apply gently the point of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called a triangular graver, leaning it on the ref, and it will mark by a line the place where the piece is out of its centre; and by striking upon this line with a mallet, the piece can easily be placed properly. The ref, of which we have just spoken, ought to be placed upon the two arms of the lathe, and fixed with screws as near the piece as the workman pleases. The piece being fixed between the two points of the puppets (or, as they are called in Scotland, the heads), the cord adjusted, and the ref fixed as near the work as possible without touching it; the workman is now to take a gouge (fig. 2, in which a is the mouth and b the handle) of a proper size in his left hand, and hold it by the handle a little inclined, keeping the back of the hand... hand lowermost. With his right hand, the back of which is to be turned upwards, he is to grasp it as near the end as possible on this side of the reft; then leaning the gouge on the reft, he is to present the edge of it a little higher than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> diameter of the piece, so as to form a kind of tangent to its circumference; then putting the right foot on the foot-board, and turning round the wheel, and holding the gouge firmly on the reft, the piece will be cut neatly. In the same manner are the chisels, formers, and other instruments to be used, taking care that the wood be cut equally, and that the instrument be not pushed improperly, sometimes stronger than at others; and taking care also that the instrument used do not follow the work, but that it be kept firmly in the hand without yielding. The young turner ought to endeavour to acquire the management of the gouge and the chisel, which are the instruments by far the most frequently used, and the most necessary in this art: by them, almost entirely, are the soft woods turned; for as for hard woods and other things, as box, ebony, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, ivory, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, they are hardly ever turned except by shaving off. In that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> gravers are to be used with square, round, or triangular mouths (fig. 3, 4, 5). They should be held horizontally while applied to the wood, and not obliquely as directed for the gouge and the chisel. After the work is completely turned, it is next to be polished; and this cannot be done with the instruments hitherto mentioned. Soft woods, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-tree, hazel, maple, ought to be polished with shark-skin or Dutch rushes. There are different species of sharks; some of which have a grayish, others a reddish skin. Shark-skin is always the better to be a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> used; at first it is too rough for polishing. The Dutch-rush (equisetum hyemale), which grows in moist places among mountains, and is a native of Scotland. The oldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> are the best. Before using them they should be moistened a little, otherwise they break in pieces almost immediately, and render it exceedingly difficult to polish with them. They are particularly proper for smoothing the hard woods, as box, lignum vitae, ebony, &c. After having cleaned up the piece well, it should be rubbed gently either with wax or olive-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, then wiped clean and rubbed with its own rappings or with a cloth a little worn. Ivory, horn, silver, and brads, are polished with pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> finely pounded and put upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth a little moistened: with this the piece is rubbed as it turns round in the lathe; and to prevent any dirt from adhering to any part of it, every now and then it is rubbed gently with a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> dipped in water. To polish very finely, the workmen make use of tripoli, a particular kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and afterwards of putty or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of tin. Iron and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> are polished with very fine powder of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERY">emery</a>; this is mixed with oil, and put between two pieces of very tender wood, and then the iron is rubbed with it. Tin and silver are polished with a burnisher and that kind of red stone called in France sanguiine dune. They may be polished also with putty, putting it dry into thamoy-skim, or with the palm of the hand. To succeed in turning iron, it is necessary to have a lathe exceedingly strong in all its parts, and exceedingly well fixed. The puppets should be short, and the reft well fixed very near the work; the back of the reft should be two or three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> lower than the iron to be turned. The lathe and other instruments being prepared, it is necessary to determine the length and thickness of the iron to be turned according to the design which is to be executed, and to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of it in wood a little thicker than it ought to be: Then one exactly like this is to be forged of the best iron that can be procured; that is to say, it must not be new, but well prepared and well beaten with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a>; it must have no flaws, nor cracks, nor pimples. New iron, which has not been well beaten, often contains round drops of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> iron, called by the workmen grains, which blunt the edges of the gouges, chisels, and other instruments used for cutting, break them, or make them slide. The iron being forged according to the model, it should be annealed, that is, heated red hot and allowed to cool slowly on the coals till the fire go out of itself. Some people, to soften the iron, cover it over with clay and allow it to cool. The iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> being thus made, it is next to be put upon the lathe, finding the centres as formerly directed, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORING">boring</a> a small hole in them that the iron may not escape from the points. The points should be oiled from time to time to prevent their being excessively heated and spoiled while the iron is turning. A crochet is then to be applied to the iron to be turned, a little above its centre, pretty gently, and by this means the inequalities of the cylinder will be taken off. Other instruments are then to be applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLD">mold</a> the iron according to the model; and whenever any of them grow hot, they are to be plunged into a basin of water lying beside the workman. If the iron, after being properly turned, is to be bored like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, one of the puppets is to be removed and another substituted in its place, having a square hole through it, into which the collar of the iron is to be fixed firmly, so as not to shake; then borers are to be applied, like those which locksmiths use to bore keys; and beginning with a small one, and afterwards taking larger ones, the hole is to be made as wide and deep as necessary; great care must be taken to hold the borers firm on the reft, otherwise there is danger of not boring the hole straight. The borer must be withdrawn from time to time to oil it and to clean the hole.
