Since it is difficult to make a hole quite round with borers alone, it is necessary to have also an instrument a good deal smaller than the hole, one of the sides of which is sharp, very well tempered, and a little hollow in the middle. This instrument being fixed in a pretty long handle, is to be applied with steadiness to the inner surface of the hole, and it will entirely remove every inequality that may have been there before its application. To cut a screw upon the cylinder, some persons use an instrument consisting principally of a female screw; but this is rather an improper instrument; for if one presses too violently, or inclines it ever so little to the right or left, he runs the greatest risk of spoiling the screw. To avoid this danger, some use it only to trace out the lines of the screw, and afterwards finish it with a file. But the following is a much better way. Take a tap for making a female screw, the threads of which have been cut very accurately, and exactly of the size of the screw which you want; and having put it in the opening which you have traced in the collar of the axis

TURNING

Pages 130-134

Plate DXL. Fig. 1. Fig. 2. Fig. 3. Fig. 4. Fig. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">VARIATION</a> of the Compafs. Fig. 1. Fig. 3. Fig. 2. W. Trewin Sculpt Turning axis on which the screw is to be cut, folder it with tin, sal-ammoniac, and rosin, as exactly corresponding to the axis as possible. Take then a puppet with a hole cut into a corresponding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> screw, into which the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> screw is to be put. The axis on which the screw is to be cut must be placed exactly horizontally between the two puppets. The reft is then to be brought as near as possible to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the screw is to be cut, and a small hollow should be cut in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it which is exactly opposite to the place where the screw is to be cut, to hold your <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> firmly and prevent it from shaking. The instrument with which the screw is to be cut should be very sharp, and its point should make an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of 60° with the screw to be cut; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you wish the screw to be cut very deep, it should make an angle a little larger. The lathe being now put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, the tap fixed at the end of the axis <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> move gradually through the female screw in the puppet; and your instrument in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> will trace a similar male screw on the axis fixed in the lathe. Many persons, after having in this manner drawn the outlines of the screw, finish it with a screw-tale of three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> corresponding exactly to the size of the screw, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>; but this last method is rather improper. For turning ovals, a lathe of somewhat different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> is used. The axis or spindle, having on it the pulley over which the band-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> passes for turning the lathe, is fixed between the two puppets so as to turn round easily: one end of it passes through one of the puppets, and to it is firmly fixed a circular plate of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, so that it turns round along with the spindle. Upon this plate two brazen segments of circles are fastened, the circumferences of which correspond to the circumference of the plate: their chords are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>, and equally distant from the centre of the plate, so that they leave a distance between them. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> in each of them: in these grooves another plate is placed which exactly fills up the space between the two grooves, but is shorter than the diameter of the larger circular plate on which it is laid. This plate is made to slide in the grooves. To its centre is fixed a short spindle, on which the piece of wood to be turned is fixed. When the lathe is set a going, the circular plate moves round, and carries the piece along with it; the plate of brass on which the piece is fixed being fixed loosely in the grooves already described, slides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a little every time that the grooves become perpendicular to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> (and there are particular contrivances to prevent it from sliding down too far); and by these two motions combined, the circular one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plate, and the straight one of the small, the circumference of the piece of wood to be turned necessarily describes an oval; and gouges or other tools being applied in the usual manner supported on the reft, it is cut into an oval accordingly. The small plate may be made to slide either more or less in the grooves; and by this contrivance the transverse diameter of the oval, or rather ellipse, may be made longer or shorter at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. 1. The method of moulding boxes of shell and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>.—In the first place, form a proper mould, which must consist of two pieces, viz. of a circle about half an inch thick, which should slope a little in order to draw out the moulded shell the more easily; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> fitted to the outside of the circle, so that both together make the shape of a box. These two pieces being adjusted, it is necessary to round the shell to be moulded of such a size that, when moulded, it will be a little higher than the ring of the mould, that there may be no deficiency. The mould is then to be put into a press on a plate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, exactly under the screw of the press; put there the shell upon the circle of the mould, so that its centre also is exactly opposite to the screw of the press; then take a piece of wood formed into a truncated cone, and not so thick as the diameter of the circle of the mould, nor so deep as the ring: then put a plate of iron above the cone, and screw down the press gently and cautiously till the whole is well fixed: then plunge the whole into a cauldron of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> placed above a fire. In 8 or 10 minutes the shell or horn will begin to soften; screw the press a little firmer that the wooden cone may sink into the softened shell: repeat this from time to time till the cone is quite sunk in the mould; then take out the press and plunge it into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water. When it is cold, take the box now formed out of the mould, and put into the inside of it a new mould of tin exactly of the form you wish the inside of the box to be; do the same with the outside, put it again into the press and plunge it into boiling water; screw the press gradually till the box receive the desired form. 2. Method of preparing green wood so that it will not split in the turning.—Cut the wood into pieces of a proper size, put them into a vessel full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a> ley. Boil them about an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; take the cauldron from the fire, allow the ley to cool; and take out the wood and dry it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. 3. Method of giving an ebony-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> to hard and fine woods.—After forming the wood into the defined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, rub it with aquafortis a little diluted. Small threads of wood will rise in the drying, which you will rub off with pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Repeat this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> again, and then rub the wood with the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>: Put into a glazed earthen vessel a pint of strong <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, two ounces of fine iron-filings, and half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of pounded <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, and allow them to infuse for three or four hours on hot cinders. At the end of this time augment the fire, and pour into the vessel four ounces of copperas, and a choping of water having half an ounce of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a> and as much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a> dissolved in it; and make the whole boil till a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> rises. Rub several layers of this upon the wood; and when it is dry, polish it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, on which you have put a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">tripoli</a>. 4. Method of giving to plum-tree the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">brazil</a> wood.—Slake lime with urine, and bedaub the wood over with it while it is hot: allow it to dry; then take off the coat of lime and rub it with shamoy skin well oiled. Or, steep the wood in water, having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> dissolved in it: then, having allowed brazil wood to dissolve in water five or six hours, steep the wood in it, kept lukewarm during a night; and when it is dry, rub it, as before directed, with shamoy skin well oiled. 5. Method of giving a fine black colour to wood—Steep the wood for two or three days in lukewarm water in which a little alum has been dissolved; then put a handful of logwood, cut small, into a pint of water, and boil it down to less than half a pint. If you then add a little indigo, the colour will be more beautiful. Spread a layer of this liquor quite hot on the wood with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, which will give it a violet colour. When it is dry, spread on another layer; dry it again and give it a third: then boil verdigris at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> in its own vinegar, and spread a layer of it on the wood; when it is dry, rub it with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, and then with oiled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> skin. This gives a fine black, and imitates perfectly the colour of ebony. 6. Method of cleaning and whitening <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> before using them.—Having taken off with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the useless ends of the bones, make a strong ley of ashes and quicklime, and into a pailful of this ley put four ounces of alum, and boil the bones in it for an hour; then take the vessel containing the ley off the fire, and let it cool; then take out the bones and dry them in the shade. 7. Method of soldering shells.—Clean the two sides of the shells which you wish to join together; then, having joined them, wrap them up in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> folded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> and well moistened; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> two plates of iron pretty hot that they may keep their heat for some time; and putting the shells rolled up between them under a press, which you must screw very tight, leave them there till the whole is cold, and they will be soldered. If you do not succeed the first time, repeat the process. 8. Method of moulding shells.—Put six pints of water into a kettle; add to it an ounce of olive or other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; make the water boil; then put in your shell, and it will grow soft. Take it out and put it into a mould under a press, and it will take the figure you want. This must be done quickly; for if the shell cool ever so little, the process will fail. It will not require much pressure. 9. Method of tinging bones and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>.—Boil shavings of scarlet in water. When it begins to boil, throw in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a pound of ashes made from the dregs of wine, which will extract the colour: then throw in a little rock alum to clear it, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the water through a linen cloth. Steep the ivory or bone in aquafortis, and put it into the water. If you wish to leave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spots, cover the places destined for them with wax. 10. To tinge ivory black.—Steep the ivory during five or six days in water of galls with ashes made with dried dregs of wine and arsenic; then give it two or three layers of the same black with which plum-tree is blackened, in order to imitate ebony. Or, dissolve silver in aquafortis, and put into it a little rofe-water. Rub the ivory with this, and allow it to dry in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. 11. Method of hardening wood to make pulleys.—After finishing the pulley, boil it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight minutes in olive oil, and it will become as hard as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. 12. To make Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>.—Take of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> lac in grains four ounces; put it into a strong bottle with a pound of good spirit of wine, and add about the bulk of a hazel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> of camphor. Allow them to mix in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> in the sun, or in winter on hot embers for 24 hours, shaking the bottle from time to time. Pass the whole through a fine cloth, and throw away what remains upon it. Then let it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> for 24 hours, and you will find a clear part in the upper part of the bottle, which you must separate gently, and put into another vial, and the remains will serve for the first layers. TURNSTONE. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRINGA">TRINGA</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TURPETH

Pages 134-134

the cortical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the root of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of convolvulus. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">MATERIA MEDICA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TURQUOISE

Pages 134-134

is the tooth of an animal penetrated with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> ore.

TURRITIS

Pages 134-134

Tower-mustard; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class tetradynamia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 39th order, Siliquose. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. TURTLE. See TESTUDO, EREPTOLOGY Index. TURTLE-Dove. See COLUMBA, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> Index. TUSCAN order, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. See ARCHITECTURE, No. 42. TUSCAN <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, a yellowish kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> found in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and particularly about <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, where there is a stratum eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ten feet thick, at the depth of five or six feet from the surface. It is supposed to have an alluring <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>.

TUSCANY

Pages 134-135

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Heturia, and, excepting some detached parts, is encompassed by a part of the Mediterranean, called here the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state; the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>; and the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>; its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south being about 116 English miles, and from east to west about 80. Though some parts of it are mountainous, yet both the hills and dales are covered with vines, olives, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>, lemon, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> yield also <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, &c. and some of the finest marble. Here is also plenty of corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, saffron, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, with mineral waters, rich pasture, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-pits, sulphur, alabaster, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALCEDONY">calcedony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, amethysts, carnelians, jaspers, crystals, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> slate. In some places the elms and ashes yield <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> river in Tuscany is the Arno, which has its source in the Apennine mountains, and falls into the sea below <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>. There are some other smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. This duchy fell under the dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> about 455 years before Christ. The Ostrogoths possessed themselves of it in the fifth century, and after them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, who were expelled by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> anno 800; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which it became subject to the German emperors, who appointed governors over it. At last the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, Pisa, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, and some others, during the contentions between the pope and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and their respective adherents, the Guelphs and Gibbelines, withdrew themselves from the dominion of both, and erected themselves into separate commonwealths. In that of Florence, John de Medici, a popular nobleman, so inflamed himself into the favour of his countrymen, that they invested him with sovereign power. Pope Pius V. conferred the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> on Cosmo de Medici anno 1570, in whose family the duchy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> until the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Gaston de Medici, who died anno 1737. The duchy was then transferred to the duke of Lorrain, afterwards the em- peror Francis I. in lieu of the duchy of Lorrain, which, by the peace of 1736, was given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Stanislaus during his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and then was to be annexed to France. Leopold, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Francis I., and afterwards emperor of Germany, succeeded to this duchy. It is now enjoyed by Leopold's second son, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the present emperor of Germany, Francis II. The grand duke's annual revenues are computed at about 500,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, arising chiefly from the tenths of all estates that are sold <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> alienated, and the ground-rents of the houses in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, and the duties on almost all manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Tuscany now forms part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Italy subject to France.

TUSSILAGO

Pages 135-135
COLT'S-FOOT; a genus of plants belonging to the class of syngenesia; and in the natural system ranging under the 49th order, Compositae. See BOTANY Index.

TUTOR

Pages 135-135

in the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is one chosen to look to the persons and estate of children left by their fathers and mothers in their minority. The different kinds of tutory established among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and the powers and duties of tutors, are described in Inst. Leg. i. tom. xiii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 1. and 2. to which the reader is referred. See also the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">GUARDIAN</a>.—For the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and effects of tutory in the Scotch law, which is founded on that of the Romans, see SCOTS LAW, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. Sect. 7. TUTOR is also used in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> for a member of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, who takes on him the instruction of young students in the arts and faculties.

TWEDELALE

Pages 135-135
or PEEBLES, a county in the south of Scotland. See PEEBLES-SHIRE.

TWEED

Pages 135-135

a river of Scotland, which rises on the confines of Clydeladale, and running eastward through Tweedale, and dividing the shire of Merle from Teviotdale and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, falls into the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at Berwick. It abounds with salmon. See BERWICK.

TWELFTH-DAY

Pages 135-135

the festival of the Epiphany, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the manifestation of Christ to the Gentiles; so called, as being the twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, exclusive, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTMAS_DAY">Christmas-day</a>.

TWILIGHT

Pages 135-135

that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, whether in the morning before sunrise, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the evening after sunset, supposed to begin and end when the least stars that can be seen by the naked eye cease or begin to appear. TWINKLING OF THE STARS. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">OPTICS</a>, No. 21.

TWINS

Pages 135-135

two young ones delivered at a birth, by an animal which ordinarily brings forth but one. TWITE. See FRINGILLA, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TYMPAN

Pages 135-135

among printers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> frame belonging to the press, covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, on which the blank sheets are laid in order to be printed off. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">PRINTING</a>-PRESS.

TYMPANUM

Pages 135-135

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, a kind of wheel placed round an axis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cylindrical beam, on the top of which are two levers or fixed flaves for the more easily <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the axis in order to raise a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> required.

TYMPANY

Pages 135-135
or TYMPANITES, in Medicine. See MEDICINE, No. 337, and SURGERY Index.

TYNDALE

Pages 135-135

WILLIAM, a zealous English reformer, and memorable for having made the first English version of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, was born on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before 1500. He was of Magdalene-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he distinguished himself by imbibing early the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, and by zealously propagating them. Afterwards he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and from thence went to live with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> in the capacity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his children.—While he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there, he showed himself so furious for Luther, and so inveterate to the pope, that he was forced, merely for the security of his person, to leave the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. He next endeavoured to get into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Tonfall bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, but did not succeed. His zeal for Lutheranism made him desirous to translate the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> into English; and as this could not safely be done in England, he went into Germany, where, setting about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he finished it in 1527. He then began with the Old Testament, and finished the five books of Moses, prefixing discourses to each book, as he had done to those of the New Testament. At his first going over into Germany, he went into <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and had much conference with Luther; and then returning to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, made his abode chiefly at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>. During his peregrinations from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to another, he suffered shipwreck upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and lost all his books and papers. His translations of the Scriptures being in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time sent to England, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> noise there; and, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the clergy, did so much mischief, that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was issued, prohibiting the buying <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> them. But the clergy were not satisfied with this, they knew Tyndale capable of doing infinite harm, and therefore thought of nothing less than removing him out of the way. For this purpose one Philips was sent over to Antwerp, who insinuated himself into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of friendship betrayed him into custody. He was sent to the castle of Filford, about 18 miles from Antwerp; and though the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> at Antwerp did what they could to procure his release, and letters were also sent from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cromwell and others out of England, yet Philips betirred himself so heartily, that he was tried and condemned to die. He was first strangled by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hangman, and then burned near Filford castle, in 1536. While he was tying to the stake, he cried with a fervent and loud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, "Lord, open the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of England's eyes."

TYPE

Pages 135-135

an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, image, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> representation of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, which is termed the antitype. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the word occurs often in the writings of divines, who employ it to denote that prefiguration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> events of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> which they have found or fancied in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> transactions recorded in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>.

TYPHA

Pages 136-136

Cat's-tail; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of monocots, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 3rd order, Calamariae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. TYPHON. See Whirlwind.

TYPHON

Pages 136-136

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians. See Polytheism, No. 29.

TYRANT

Pages 136-136

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, denoted simply a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> monarch; but the ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> which several persons invented with that sacred character made of it, has al- tered the import of the word; and tyrant now conveys the idea of an unjust or cruel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who rules in a more despotic manner than the laws allow.

TYRE

Pages 136-136

formerly a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, situated under the 54th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and 32d of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It was built, ac- cording to some writers, 2760 years before the Chris- tian era. There were two cities of that name; the one called Palestynus, situated on the continent; and the other the city of Tyre, built on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the shore. It was about 19 miles in circum- ference, including Palestynus; the town on the island was about four miles round. The buildings of Tyre were very magnificent; the walls were 150 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in proportion. This city was at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the most famous commercial city in the world. Of its commercial transactions, the most particular account that is to be found in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writer has been given by the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, which at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> con- veys a magnificent idea of the extensive power of that state. It resisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> for 13 years; at the end of which, wearied with fruitless efforts, the inhabitants resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> be- tween them and their enemy, and passed accordingly in- to the island. The new city stood out against Alexan- der the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months; and before he could take it, he was obliged to fill up the strait which sepa- rated the island from the continent. It was repaired af- terwards by Adrian, and became the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. It afterwards fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the A- rabs; and after being taken by Baldwin II. king of Je- rusalem, it was destroyed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> in 1289, and abandoned. An excellent account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> state may be found in Volney's Travels, vol. ii. It now consists of a small village, composed of fisher- men's huts, and containing about 50 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> families. TYRIAN DYE. See Murex, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

TYRONE

Pages 136-136

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, 46 miles in length and 37 in breadth; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a> and Lough Neagh, on the south by Fermanagh, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DONEGAL">Donegal</a>. It is a rough and rugged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but tolerably fruitful; contains 12,683 houses, 30 parishes, 4 baronies, 4 boroughs, and formerly sent 16 members to the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNGANNON">Dungannon</a>. U, V. U, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> u, the 20th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> and 5th vowel of our alpha- bet, is formed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> by a round configu- ration of the lips, and a greater extrusion of the under one than in forming the letter o, and the tongue is also more camouflaged. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is short in curf, muf, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUN">tun</a>, tul; but is lengthened by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> e, as in tune, tube, &c. In some words it is rather acute than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; as in brute, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, lute, &c. It is mostly long in polysyllables; as in union, curious, &c.; but in some words it is obscure, as in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, venture, &c. This letter in the form of V or v, is properly a consonant, and as such is placed before all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>; as in vacant, venal, vibrate, &c. Though the letters v and u had always two sounds, they had only the form v till the beginning of the fourth century, when the other form was introduced, the in- convenience of expressing two different sounds by the same letter having been observed long before. In nu- merals V stands for five; and with a dash added at top, thus V, it signifies 5000. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a>, amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, V. A. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> for veterani affigati; V. B. viro bono; V. B. A. viri boni arbitrati; V. B. F. vir bene fidei; V. C. vir con- sularis; V. C. C. F. vale, conjux charissime, feliciter; V. D. D. voto dedicatur; V. G. verbi gratia; Vir. Ve. virgo vestalis; Vl. videlicet; V. N. quinto nonarum.

UBES

Pages 149-149

Sr., a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, 21 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>. It stands on an eminence, with a very strong castle built on a rock. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> around is fertile in corn, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; and it is furnished with good fish from the sea, and a small lake in the neighbourhood. Here <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of fine <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> are made, which is carried to the American plantations. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 54' N. Lat. 38° 22'.

UBIQUITARIANS

Pages 149-149

formed from ubique, "everywhere," in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Lutherans which rose and spread itself in Germany; and whose distinguishing doctrine was, that the body of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ is everywhere, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in every <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Brentius, one of the earliest reformers, is said to have first broached this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, in 1560. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> himself, in his controversy with Zuinglius, had thrown out some unguarded expressions, that seemed to imply a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the omnipresence of the body of Christ; but he became sensible afterwards, that this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was attended with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulties, and particularly, that it ought not to be made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of Christ's corporal presence in the eucharist. However, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Luther, this absurd <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> was renewed, and drest up in a specious and plausible form by Brentius, Chemni- Vol. XX. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. tius, and Andreae, who maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of the properties of Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. It is indeed obvious, that every Lutheran who holds the doctrine of consubstantiation (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>), whatever he may pretend, must be an Ubiquitarian.

UBIQUITY

Pages 149-149

Omnipresence; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> of the Deity, whereby he is always intimately present to all things; gives the effect to all things; knows, preserves, and does all in all things.

UDDER

Pages 149-149

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARATIVE_ANATOMY">comparative anatomy</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> is prepared, answering to the mammae <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> breasts in women. See Anatomy, Comparative.

UKRAINE

Pages 194-194

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, lying on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, Russia, and Little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. Its name properly signifies a frontier. By a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> between Russia and Poland in 1693, the latter remained in possession of all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Ukraine lying on the west side of the river Dnieper, which is but indifferently cultivated; while the country on the east side, inhabited by the Cossacks, is in much better condition. The Russian part is comprised in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Kiof; and the emperors of Russia having obtained the Polish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of Kiof, by the treaty of partition in 1793, the whole of the Ukraine, on both sides of the Dnieper, belongs now to that ambitious and formidable power. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is Kiof.

ULIETEA

Pages 194-194

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is about 21 leagues in circuit. Its productions are plantains, cocoa-nuts, yams, hogs, and fowl; the two latter of which are scarce. The foil on the top of one of the hills was found to be a kind of flone marle; on the sides were found some scattered flints, and a few small pieces of a cavernous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spongy flone <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which seemed to contain fome remains of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, fo that it may possibly be here lodged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. Nothing was feen on this island to diftinguish either its inhabitants, or their manners, from the other neighbouring islands. The first Europeans who landed on this shore were Mr (now Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>) Banks and Dr Solander; they were received by the natives in the most courteous manner, reports concerning them having been their harbingers from Otaheite. Every body feemed to fear and reftect them, placing in them at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the utmost confidence: behaving, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> confiduous that their visitors pofted the power of doing them mischief without a difposition to make ufe of it.

ULIGINOUS

Pages 194-194

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, an appellation given to a moit, moorish, and fenny foil.

ULLAGE

Pages 194-194

in gauging, is fo much of a cask <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other vessel as it wants of being full.

ULM

Pages 194-194

a free and imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, in the circle of Swabia, seated on the river Iller. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, defended by fortifications; and the inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. Here the archives of the circle are depofited, and it carries on a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it in 1702, by a stratagem; but, in 1704, the French being vanquished at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Hochfchet, the Bavarians surrendered it by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> have but two churches, all the rest belonging to the Protestants. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 12. N. Lat. 48. 25.

ULMUS

Pages 194-194

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas of pentandra; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fytem arranged under the 53d order, Scabridae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ULSTER

Pages 194-194

the most northerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. In Latin it is called Ultonia, in Irish Cui Guilly; and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. It is bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> on the west, St George's channel and the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the east, the Deucalondian ocean on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and on the south and south-west the provinces of Leinfler and Connaught. Its greatest length is near 120 miles, its breadth about 100; and its circumference, including the windings and turnings, 460; containing 9 counties, 58 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and boroughs, 1 archbishopric, 6 bishoprics, and 214 parishes. Ulster abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which supply it with variety of fine fish, especially salmon, besides what it has from the sea, with which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is bounded. The southern parts of it are rich, fertile,

ULTERIOR

Pages 195-195

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, is applied to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, which, with regard to the rest of that country, is situated on the farther side of the river, mountain, or other boundary which separates the two countries.

ULTRAMARINE

Pages 195-195

a beautiful blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> used by the painters, prepared from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli by calcination. See LAZULITE, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ULTRAMONTANE

Pages 195-195

something beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is principally applied in relation to France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which are separated by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>.

ULUG BEIG

Pages 195-195

a Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and learned astronomer, was descended from the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>, and reigned at Samarcan about 40 years; after which he was murdered by his own son in 1449. His catalogue of the fixed stars, rectified for the year 1434, was published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> by Mr Hyde, in 1665, with learned notes. Mr Hudson printed in the English <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> Ulug Beig's Tables of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">Longitude</a> and Latitude of Places; and Mr Greaves published, in Latin, his Astronomical Epochs, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in 1650. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ULYSSES

Pages 195-195
king of Ithaca, the son of Laertes, and father of Telemachus, and one of those heroes who contributed most to the taking of Troy. After the destruction of that city, he wandered for 10 years; and at last returned to Ithaca, where, with the assistance of Telemachus, he killed Antinous and other princes who intended to marry his wife Penelope and seize his dominions. He at length resigned the government of the kingdom to his son Telemachus; and was killed by Telegonus, his son by Circe, who did not know him. This hero is the subject of the Odyssey.

UMBELLA

Pages 195-195

an UMBEL, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of receptacle; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of flowering, in which a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of slender footstalks proceed from the same centre, and rise to an equal height, so as to form an even and generally round surface at top. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>. UMBELLATÆ, the name of a class in Ray's and Tournefort's methods, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> grow in umbels, with five petals that are often unequal, and two naked seeds that are joined at top and separated below. The same plants constitute the 4th order of Linnaeus's Fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Method. See BOTANY.

UMBELLIFEROUS PLANTS

Pages 195-195

are such as have their tops branched and spread out like an umbrella.

UMBER

Pages 195-195
or UMBRE, a soft brown or blackish substance, used in painting. See MINERALOGY Index.

UMBRELLA

Pages 195-195

a moveable canopy, made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other cloth spread out upon ribs of whale-bone, and supported by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, to protect a person from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, or the scorching beams of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>.

UMBRELLATE

Pages 194-195

well cultivated, and inclosed; but the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the northern is open and mountainous.—The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> are in general the neatest and best built of any in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-houses; which in most parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> are constructed of no better materials than clay and straw. The inhabitants of Ulster are also more like the English in their manners and dialect than those of the other three provinces; for as it includes within itself the whole, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by far the greater part, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture, the best branch of trade in the kingdom, they have consequently the greatest intercourse with England. An Englishman, in some parts of it, indeed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> imagine himself, from the familiarity of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and manners, in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. This province had anciently petty kings of its own. It was first subjected to the English in the reign of Henry II. by John Courcy, the first who bore the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Ulster; but it afterwards threw off the yoke, and was never entirely reduced till the reign of James I. when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of Scots by his encouragement went and settled in it. Of these, most of the present inhabitants are the descendants. This province was the first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of the bloody massacre in 1641.

in general, a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, denoting the twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of any thing; particularly the twelfth part of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, called in English an ounce; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the twelfth part of a foot, called an inch.

UNCTION

Pages 195-195

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of anointing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rubbing with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> or other fatty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Unction, in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, is used for the character conferred on sacred things by anointing them with oil. Unctions are very frequent among the Hebrews. They anointed both their kings and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priests at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of their inauguration. They also anointed the sacred vessels of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> and temple, to sanctify and consecrate them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of God. The unction of kings is supposed to be a ceremony introduced very late among the Christian princes. It is said that none of the emperors were ever anointed before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> or Justin. The emperors of Germany took the practice from those of the eastern empire: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Pepin of France was the first who received the unction. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, unction always accompanied the ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">Extreme</a> unction, or the anointing persons in the article of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, was also practised by the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, in compliance with the precept of St James, chap v. 14th and 15th verses; and this extreme unction the Roman church has advanced to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a sacrament. It is administered to none but such as are affected with some mortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, or in a decrepit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. It is refused to impotent persons, as also to criminals. The parts to be anointed are the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the mouth, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the feet, and the reins. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> are anointed in the palms of the hands, but priests on the back of it; because the palms of their hands have been already consecrated by ordination. The oil with which the sick person is anointed represents the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of God, which is poured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> used at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of anointing expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> of sins thereby granted to the sick person; for the prayer is this: "By this holy unction, and his own most pious mercy, may the Almighty God forgive thee whatever sins thou hast committed by the sight," when the eyes are anointed; "by the hearing," when the ears are anointed; and so of the other senses.

UNDECEMVIR

Pages 195-197

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> from the Athenians, who had 10 other colleagues <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> associates. joined with him in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. The functions of the undecemviri at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> were much the same with those of the late *prevots de marcé* in France. They took care of apprehending of criminals; secured them in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and when they were condemned, took them again into custody, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> might be executed on them. They were chosen by the tribes, each tribe naming its own; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the tribes after Callisthenes was but 10, which made 10 members, a scribe or notary was added, which made the number 11. **UNDERSTANDING.** See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a> and Logic. **UNDERWALDEN,** a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and the fifth in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the canton of Lucern and by the lake of the Four Cantons, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which separate it from the canton of Bern, and on the west by the canton of Bern. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of this canton is the Roman Catholic. **UNDULATION,** in Physics, a kind of tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or vibration observable in a liquid, by which it alternately rises and falls like the waves of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. **UNGUENT,** or Ointment, in Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a topical remedy or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, chiefly used in the dressing of wounds or blisters. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>. **UNICORN,** an animal famous among the ancients, and thought to be the same with the rhinoceros. Sparrman informs us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the unicorn described by the ancients has been found delineated by the Nefe Hottentots on the plain surface of a rock in Cafraria; and therefore conjectures, that such an animal either does exist at present in the internal parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, or at least once did so. Father Lobo affirms that he has seen it. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a> in his Travels in Southern Africa, affords additional reason to believe in the existence of this curious animal. **UNICORN-Fish.** See Monodon, Cetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **UNIFORM,** denotes a thing to be similar, or consistent either with another thing, or with itself, in respect of figure, structure, proportion, or the like; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to disform. **UNIFORMITY,** regularity, a similitude or resemblance between the parts of a whole. Such is that we meet with in figures of many sides, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> respectively equal, and answerable to each other. A late ingenious author makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to consist in uniformity, joined or combined with variety. Where the uniformity is equal in two objects, the beauty, he contends, is as the variety; and where the variety is equal, the beauty is as the uniformity. **Uniformity,** is particularly used for one and the same form of public prayers, and administration of sacraments, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, &c. of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, prescribed by the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a>, 1 Eliz. and 13 and 14 Car. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 4. called the Act of Uniformity. See Liturgy. **UNION,** a junction, coalition, or assemblage of two or more different things in one. **Union,** or The Union, by way of eminence, is more particularly used to express the act by which the two separate kingdoms of England and Scotland were incorporated into one, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. This union, in vain attempted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. was at length effected in the year 1707, 6 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, when 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> were agreed to by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of both nations; the purport of the most considerable Union being as follows: 1. That on the first of May 1707, and for ever after, the kingdoms of England and Scotland shall be united into one kingdom, by the name of Great Britain. 2. The succession to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> of Great Britain shall be the same as was before settled with regard to that of England. 3. The united kingdom shall be represented by one parliament. 4. There shall be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges between the subjects of both kingdoms, except where it is otherwise agreed. 5. When England raises 2,000,000l. by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-tax, Scotland shall raise 48,000l. 6. The standards of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, of weights, and of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, shall be reduced to those of England throughout the united kingdoms. 7. The laws relating to trade, customs, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>, shall be the same in Scotland as in England. But all the other laws of Scotland shall remain in force; but alterable by the parliament of Great Britain. Yet with this caution, that laws relating to public policy are alterable at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the parliament; laws relating to private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> are not to be altered but for the evident utility of the people of Scotland. 8. Sixteen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> are to be chosen to represent the peerage of Scotland in parliament, and 45 members to fit in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons. 9. The 16 peers of Scotland shall have all privileges of parliament; and all peers of Scotland shall be peers of Great Britain, and rank next after those of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the union, and shall have all privileges of peers, except sitting in the house of lords, and voting on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of a peer. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the 25 articles of union, which are ratified and confirmed by statute 5 Anne, c. 8., in which statute there are also two acts of parliament recited; the one of Scotland, whereby the church of Scotland, and also the four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of that kingdom, are established for ever, and all succeeding sovereigns are to take an oath inviolably to maintain the same; the other of England, 5 Anne, c. 6., whereby the acts of uniformity of 13 Eliz. and 13 Car. II. (except as the same had been altered by parliament at that time), and all other acts then in force for the preservation of the church of England, are declared perpetual; and it is stipulated, that every subsequent king and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> shall take an oath inviolably to maintain the same within England, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and the town of Berwick-upon-Tweed. And it is enacted, that these two acts "shall for ever be observed as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> and essential conditions for the union." Upon these articles and act of union, it is to be observed, 1. That the two kingdoms are to inseparably united, that nothing can ever disunite them; except the mutual consent of both, or the successful resistance of either, upon apprehending an infringement of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which, when they were separate and independent nations, it was mutually stipulated should be "fundamental and essential conditions of the union." 2. That whatever else may be deemed "fundamental and essential conditions," the preservation of the two churches, of England and Scotland, in the same state that they were in at the time of the union, and the maintenance of of the acts of uniformity which established the liturgy, are expressly declared so to be. 3. That therefore any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of either of these churches, or in the liturgy of the church of England (unless with the consent of the respective churches, collectively or representatively given), would be an infringement of those "fundamental and essential conditions," and greatly endanger the union. 4. That the municipal laws of Scotland are ordained to be still observed in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, unless altered by parliament; and as the parliament has not yet thought proper, except in a few instances, to alter them, they still, with regard to the particulars unaltered, continue in full force. For an account of the union of Ireland with Great Britain, thus forming the united kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, see IRELAND, No. 120.

UNITARIANS

Pages 197-197

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given to those who confine the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> to the One only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and supreme God, and Father of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ.

UNITED BRETHREN

Pages 197-197
or Unitas Fratrum; a society of Christians, whose chief residence is at Herrnhut in Saxony. They are commonly called Moravians, from their original country, and Herrnhuters, from their chief place of residence. Some account of this society has already been given under HERRNHIUT; but as that account may, by some, not be deemed sufficiently full, we shall here add a summary of their institutes, derived from a communication by one of their own clergy. Though the church of the United Brethren is episcopal, their bishops possess no elevation of rank or pre-eminence authority, their church being governed by synods or consistories from all the congregations, and by subordinate bodies, called conferences. The synods are generally held once in seven years. In the first sitting a president is chosen; and the elders appointed by the former synod to superintend the unity, lay down their office, though they still form a part of the assembly, as well as the bishops, the lay elders, and those ministers who have the inspection of several congregations in one province. Questions of importance, or of which the consequences cannot be foreseen, are decided by lot, though this is never used till after mature deliberation and fervent prayer. In the synods, the state of the unity, and the concerns of the congregations and missions, are taken into consideration. Towards the conclusion of every synod, a kind of executive board is appointed, called the elders' conference of the unity, consisting of 13 elders, and divided into four committees or departments, one for superintending missions into heathen countries; a second for watching over the conduct of congregations; a third for managing the economical concerns of the unity, and a fourth for maintaining the discipline of the society. These conferences, however, are amenable to a higher committee, called the elders' conference, the powers of which are very extensive. It appoints and removes every servant in the unity, authorizes the bishops to ordain presbyters or deacons, and to consecrate other bishops, and in short, possesses the supreme executive power over the whole society. A bishop of the United Brethren can discharge no office but by the appointment of the synod, or of the elders' conference. Indeed their deacons can perform every office of the bishops, except ordination, and appear to confirm young persons when they first become candidates for the communion. Even female deacons are employed for the purpose of privately admonishing their own sex, and visiting them in cases of sickness. There are also lay elders, whose business it is to watch over the constitution and discipline of the unity; to enforce the observance of the laws of the country in which missions are established, and to guard the privileges conferred on the brethren by the government under which they live. On Sunday, besides the public prayers, one or two sermons are preached in every church, and after the morning service, an exhortation is given to the children. Previous to the holy communion, which is administered on some Sunday once a month, and on Maunday Thursday, each person before he communicates, must converse on the state of his soul with one of the elders. Love feasts are frequent, and on Maunday Thursday the society have a solemn footwashing. Our limits will not permit us to give a systematic view of the doctrinal tenets of the Brethren. Though they acknowledge no other standard of truth than the sacred scriptures, they adhere to the Augsburg confession, and speak respectfully of the 39 articles of the church of England. They profess to believe that the kingdom of Christ is not confined to any particular party, community, or church; and they consider themselves as spiritually joined in the bond of Christian love to all who are taught of God, and belong to the universal church of Christ, however much they may differ in forms, which they deem non-essentials. For a fuller account of this society, see Cranmer's Ancient and Modern History of the Protestant Church of the United Brethren, London 1780, and An Exposition of Christian Doctrine, as taught in the Protestant Church of the United Brethren, London 1784.

UNITED PROVINCES

Pages 197-203

otherwise called the Republic of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Batavian republic, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, occupying that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> which lies between Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> and Brabant, now the French departments of Lys, Escaut, Deux Nether and Dyle on the south, and the district of East Friesland on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east; being bounded on the north and west by the German ocean or North <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Westphalia. They are situated between the parallels of 51° 10', and 53° 35' N. lat. and between 3° 10', and 7° 5' E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. In British miles the length of this country, from north to south, is estimated at 165, its breadth from west to east about 100, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> at 10,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Before the French revolution, this part of the Low Countries was divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> provinces, viz. Guelderland or Gelders, Holland, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, Friesland, Overvessel, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, besides the dependencies of Dutch Brabant and Dutch Flanders. Overysel | Salland | | | | | | Twenthe | | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVENTER">DEVENTER</a>, Zwol, Campen, Coeverden. | | | Wollenhoven | | | | | | Drenthe | | | | | VII. Groningen | Groningen | | | GRONINGEN, Winchoten. | | | Ommeland | | | | | | Drent | | | | | | Dutch Brabant | | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOIS_LE_DUC">Bois-le-duc</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom. | A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of these provinces is composed of islands formed by the mouths of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which here disembogue their waters into the German ocean. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> islands are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALCHEREN">Walcheren</a>, Joodland, South and North Beveland, and Wolfersdyk, composing West Zealand; Schouwen, Duiveland, Fertholm, and St Philipsland, forming East Zealand; Goeree in South Holland, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEXEL">Texel</a>, Vlieland, and Ameland, to the west and north of Frieland.
