The Dutch had formerly considerable colonial territory; but this is now reduced to part of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, and the Molucca islands, with some other settlements in the East Indies; some trading factories on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; St Eustatius and part of Surinam in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country is, in general, extremely uniform, consisting of large tracts of marshy pastures, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> heaths, interspersed with several large rivers, and numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. There are a few hills in the eastern districts, but the coasts are so low, that, but for the dykes or sea walls, they would be inundated by the sea. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> consists almost entirely of alluvial <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLD">mold</a>, and is very productive. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is moist, inclement, and peculiarly inhospitable to strangers; intermittent fevers and similar diseases, the attendants on a marshy and watery soil, being extremely frequent. The winters are colder and the summers hotter than in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The principal rivers of the United Provinces are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, the Maese or Meuse, and the Escaut or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>, which separates them from French Flanders. There are few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, except the sea of Haerlem, near the Zuider Zee. There is little interesting in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Holland; the animals and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> resembling those of the adjacent countries of France and Germany, and its mineral products being extremely few. Its chief <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> products are <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, madder and flower roots, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> and cheese. The state of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> is but little advanced; as almost the whole country is under grass, and the corn produced is not nearly sufficient for home consumption. The changes which the coasts of the Dutch provinces have undergone, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the shifting of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, beds of rivers, the encroachments or retiring of the sea, and tempests from the German ocean, render their progressive geography an interesting object. We find that in the latter periods of the Roman empire, the river Rhine divided itself into two great branches at Burginafium, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Schenk, about five miles north-west of Colonia Trajana, near the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>. The southern branch joined the Meuse at the town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLA">Mola</a> or Muvi, while the northern branch passed by Durstadt, Utrecht, and Leyden, to the ocean. The northern branch of the Rhine was joined to the Yssel by the canal of Druus (see Batavorum Infula), while this latter river flowed into a considerable lake called Flevo, now a southern portion of the Zuider Zee. When the canal of Druus was (a) See each of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in the general <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. was neglected, the waters of the Rhine poured into the Yssel with such violence as to increase the lake of Flevo to a great expanse of waters, so that instead of a river which once ran from that lake to the sea for nearly 50 Roman miles, there was opened the wide <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> which now forms the entrance. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the northern branch of the Rhine became much diminished, and the canal of Druius gradually disappeared. The estuaries of the Meuse and the Scheldt being open to great inroads from the sea, have also materially changed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and position; and the latter in particular, which once formed merely a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, divided into four or five smaller branches, which are now extensive creeks, dividing the islands of Zeeland and South Holland. In the beginning of the 15th century, the estuary of the Meuse suddenly formed a vast lake to the south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>, overwhelming 72 villages, and 100,000 inhabitants. By a subsequent change, the Rhine was again subdivided, the northern branch falling into the Leck, while the southern formed the modern Waal. The early history of these provinces, from their subjection by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, till they fell under the dominion of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, has been already given under the article NETHERLANDS, so that we have here to relate only those transactions which have taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> since the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> (b). At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. the Dutch provinces were in a very flourishing condition. In this small tract were then reckoned not fewer than 350 large walled cities, and 6300 considerable towns or large villages, all become rich by their application to arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The same application had diffused a spirit of independence among the inhabitants, who were jealously alive to every invasion of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges. The reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> had made considerable progress among all ranks, and the doctrines of Calvin had been embraced by a great majority of the people. Hence, nothing could be more impolitic than the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> taken by Philip to advance the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, and to enforce obedience to the tyrannical acts of his deputies. The establishment of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, the increase of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bishoprics, the appointment of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Grandvède to be chief counsellor to the duchess of Parma, the regent of the Netherlands, and the enormous taxes levied to support the Spanish forces, were no trifling grievances, and created such a spirit of disaffection, that when the duchess assumed the reins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, in the year 1560, the murmurs of the people could no longer be suppressed. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> of the malcontents, at the head of whom were William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>, with the counts of Egmont and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, waited on the duchess at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, and insisted either on the dismissal of Cardinal Grandvède, or the calling of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states-general. The duchess thought proper to comply with the former of these requests, but as that minister was succeeded by two of his creatures, who trod exactly in his footsteps, and in particular increased the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> persecutions, and the power of the inquisition, the popular ferment became greater than ever. The patriots sent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Egmont to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, to lay their grievances before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; but that monarch with his accustomed insincerity, returned a favourable answer to their remonstrances, without changing any of the obnoxious measures of the government at Brussels. In the meantime the diabolical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> that had been formed between Charles IX. of France and Isabella of Spain, for the massacre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">protestants</a>, which soon after took place, had been whispered in the Low Countries, and in consequence a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> was formed for the purpose of abolishing the court of inquisition. This association, headed by Henry de Brodenrode, a descendant of the earls of Holland, waited on the regent in such a formidable body, that she was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> the exertion of her utmost influence towards obtaining their demands. It is said, however, that she could obtain no better terms from the bigotted Philip than that heretics should in future be hanged instead of burnt. As the people found that their dutiful remonstrances could obtain no redress, they determined to take into their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the necessary reformation. In several towns in Flanders, the people assembled, destroyed churches, pulled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> images, and committed other acts of violence. The principal inhabitants, however, while they were preparing to resist the oppressive acts of the government, behaved with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and moderation; a new oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> had been exacted, and this the counts of Egmont and Horn, probably with a view to temporise, were induced to take, but the prince of Orange steadily refused, and retired into Germany, whither he was followed by great numbers of all ranks and conditions, so that within a few days 100,000 families had left the Low Countries. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> so much alarmed the duchess of Parma, that she resigned the regency. The duchess was succeeded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alva, Duke of Alva who had been sent into the Netherlands with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 10,000 veteran troops, to intimidate the people, and enforce obedience to the civil power. We have already drawn the character of this bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> (see Alva), and have shown how well he was calculated to execute the orders of a tyrannical and bigotted <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He no sooner entered on his government than the whole country was filled with terror; Counts Egmont and Horn were ignominiously executed, and the estates of the prince of Orange were confiscated. This prince and his brother had been labouring to support the cause of their injured countrymen among the German patriots. (b) There is no part of the history of nations more interesting in itself, or more replete with useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> to rulers and subjects, than that which records the struggles of a brave people to preserve or regain their liberties and independence. Hence the glorious contest which the Dutch provinces maintained against the power of Spain, and by which they finally triumphed over tyranny and oppression, might well deserve a much fuller detail than our confined limits <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> enable us to afford. In the compendious view which we have here given of these transactions, we have endeavoured to catch the more prominent features, and thus in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> preserve the spirit of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>. We may refer our readers for a minute account of these events to The Modern Universal History, vol. xxxi., and Watson's History of the Reigns of Philip II. and Philip III. German princes, and had raised a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of Germans, by which they were enabled to make head against the regent. The prince of Orange, who had been always a favourite with the people, was now rendered more popular in consequence of his sufferings in their cause, and was invited to take the command of the armed bodies which were preparing to resist the duke of Alva. The prince first penetrated into Brabant, and attempted to surprise Ruremond, but was defeated by a detachment of the Spanish army; but his brother soon after overpowered a body of Spaniards, and killed 600. In a subsequent engagement, however, with the main body of Alva's army, Prince Louis was entirely defeated, and all his infantry cut in pieces. The prince of Orange finding that he could not at present keep the field against so formidable an enemy, and that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> deserted in consequence of his ill success and want of pay, was, in 1569, obliged to disband his army, and return to Germany. The duke of Alva did not fail to make the most of his success. All the prisoners taken in the last <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> were put to death, and the tenth part of every man's estate, with a tenth of all merchandise, were exacted as an annual payment from the inhabitants, under the penalty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> execution. The states offered to pay an annual subsidy of 2,000,000 florins, in place of these taxes; but these offers were rejected with disdain. The people thus driven to despair, were resolved to strain every nerve to resist these oppressing acts. The tradesmen in the towns shut their shops, and the peasants refused to bring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. In the meantime a squadron of ships, which is known by the name of gueux, had been fitted out by the prince of Orange, and the command given to Lumey. The willing success of this squadron, which had captured Brielle, in the island of Voon, and repulsed a force sent against it by the duke of Alva, induced the Zeelanders to collect all their ships, and also oppose the enemy at sea. A considerable advantage was gained by this fleet, against a Spanish squadron commanded by the duke of Medina Celi. The duke was entirely defeated, many of his ships were taken, and the Zeelanders carried off a booty of nearly 1,000,000 of livres. To increase his army, the governor had draughted men from the garrisons of most of the fortified towns, and thus exposed them to the attacks of the patriots. Accordingly, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> of Nassau surprized Mons, the count de Bergues gained possession of several towns in Overijssel, Guelderland, and Friesland; while another party of the malcontents made themselves masters of North Holland. The duke of Alva now began to feel that he had gone too far, and attempted when too late, to conciliate the good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the people. He published an edict consenting to remit the most oppressive taxes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the state could suggest any other method of raising the necessary supplies, and he convoked the states-general of the Provinces to assemble at the Hague. His promises and his threats were, however, now disregarded; and the states who, in contempt of his authority had assembled at Dordrecht, openly espoused the cause of their country, declared the prince of Orange commander of the national forces, and raised a considerable sum for the payment of his troops. The prince's forces now amounted to 15,000 foot and 7000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, with which he advanced into Brabant, and took Ruremond by assault. He then possessed himself of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MECHLIN">Mechlin</a>, Oudenarde, and Dendermond, and having levied contributions on those inhabitants who adhered to the government, he marched towards Mons, then besieged by the duke of Alva, with an intention to raise the siege, by bringing the duke to a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. This, however, Alva declined, and Mons was obliged to capitulate. In the midst of these successes, a damp was thrown over the ardour of the patriots, by the news of the horrid massacre of St Bartholomew *, and in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the spirits of the Spaniards revived. The prince of France, Orange found himself obliged to retire to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Holland, leaving the cities which he had taken at the mercy of the army. Mechlin opened its gates, and was pillaged without mercy, while the other towns were evacuated by the garrisons, and loaded with heavy impositions. In a short time nothing remained to the patriots, but the provinces of Holland and Zealand; but these stood firm in the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and soon became the seat of a fanguinary warfare. Frederic de <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a> was detached by the duke of Alva to reduce the insurgents in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. He quickly reduced Waarden, where his soldiers committed the most horrid acts of barbarity. The capture of this place was followed by that of Haarlem after an obstinate resistance. To <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> this ill success by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, however, the Zealander obtained many important advantages by sea. They attacked the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, and carried off several ships; and when the governor equipped a squadron to oppose them, it was thrice encountered by Wertz, the Zealander <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, and totally defeated. In the meantime the Spanish forces, under Frederic of Toledo, consisting of 16,000 veterans, sat down before Alkmaer, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Holland, a town without regular fortifications, and defended only by 300 burghers and 800 soldiers, in great want of provisions, and without any prospect of speedy relief; yet this place, though attacked with great vigour, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of 20 pieces of heavy cannon, which effected a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> in one of the walls, held out against every attempt, and the Spanish soldiers who attempted to storm the place by the breach, were repulsed with great slaughter, and Frederic was at length compelled to raise the siege. Notwithstanding these partial successes, the affairs of the patriots were still in a precarious situation. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Louis de Requenes, who had succeeded the duke of Alva in the government, was directed to carry on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the utmost vigour. The prince of Orange had, after a long siege, made himself master of Middleburgh, but had sustained a great loss by the defeat and death of his brother Louis. The patriotic cause derived some advantage, however, from a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> which took place in the Spanish army, but this advantage was of a transient <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. In the commencement of the year 1575, an attempt at negotiation took place between the contending parties, but they could come to no terms of accommodation, and the war was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with great virulence. Though much distressed in his finances, Philip made extraordinary efforts to crush the patriots, and succeeded so far, that they almost despaired of ultimate success. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILEMMA">dilemma</a> they sent a deputation to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> of England, offering to become her subjects, if she would would afford them her protection; but from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> reasons she declined the offer. The distresses which Philip now experienced, and the death of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> Requesens, did more for the cause of the patriots than all their own exertions. Profiting by these events, in the latter end of this year they attacked and carried the citadel of Ghent; while the inhabitants of Antwerp, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> for having been pillaged by the Spanish garrison that held the citadel, united in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cause, by what was called the pacification of Ghent. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> application to Queen Elizabeth met with more success, and she advanced them the sum of 20,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, on condition that they would not invite the French into their territories, that they would listen to any reasonable terms of accommodation, and repay the loan in the course of the ensuing year. Agreeably to these conditions, a cessation of hostilities was granted to the States by Don John of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, the present governor, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> was entered into with him for disbanding the foreign troops. The weak state of the government required some concessions, and Don John acceded to the pacification of Ghent, by which most of the demands of the patriots were granted. The provinces of Holland and Zealand, however conceiving that by this treaty the other provinces had conceded too much, refused their concurrence, and hostilities soon recommenced. The king of Spain dissatisfied with the concessions of Don John, recalled that governor, and appointed the archduke Matthias in his room, while he made additional preparations for a vigorous prosecution of the war. The States-general in their turn made another application to Queen Elizabeth, and obtained from her, not only a promise of 100,000l. sterling, but of a body of forces consisting of 5000 foot, and 1000 horse; in return for which, the States agreed to put into her possession certain fortified towns, and to transport and pay the forces. These supplies, however, Elizabeth afterwards declined funding, though she professed all possible good will towards the provinces and their cause. A change of measures which about this time took place in the States of Guelderland and Groningen, in favour of the protestant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, contributed not a little to aid the general cause of the patriots, though several of the provinces were still torn by intestine dissensions and jarring interests. At last the prince of Orange, perceiving that little confidence was to be placed in the unanimity of provinces rent by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, different in religion, and divided by ambition, political maxims, and private interest, formed the scheme of more closely uniting the provinces of which he was governor, and cementing them with those more contiguous, in which the protestant interest prevailed. Such an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> was subject to fewer difficulties than attended the more general one of uniting all the provinces; it was in fact the only measure that could be proposed with safety, and it was prosecuted with that alacrity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> for which William was deservedly celebrated. On the 23rd of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1579, deputies from the provinces of Holland, Zealand, Utrecht, Friesland, Groningen, Overijssel, and Guelderland, met at Utrecht, and signed the alliance ever since known by the name of the Union of Utrecht, the basis of that commonwealth so renowned by the appellation of the United Provinces. This treaty of alliance was founded on the infracting of the pacification of Ghent solemnly acceded to by Philip, and the late invasion of certain towns in Guelderland. It was not hereby intended to divide the seven provinces from the other ten, or to renounce the pacification of Ghent; its object was to preserve the liberty stipulated in that pacification, by more vigorous operations, and united councils. The chief articles of this union were the following. That the seven provinces shall unite themselves in interest as one province, never to be separated or divided by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>, donation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, or agreement; referring to each particular province and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> all its privileges, rights, customs, and statutes. In all disputes arising between either of the provinces, the rest shall interpose only as mediators. They shall assist each other with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and fortune against every foreign attempt upon any particular province, whether to establish sovereignty, the Catholic religion, arbitrary measures, or whatever else may appear inconsistent with the liberties of the province, and the intention of the alliance. All frontier towns belonging to the United Provinces shall, if old, be fortified at the expense of the provinces; if new, at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> expense of the union. That the public imposts and duties shall be farmed for three months to the highest bidder, and employed with the king's taxes in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. No province, city, or member of the union, shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> an alliance with any foreign prince or power, without the concurrence of all the other members. That foreign powers shall be admitted into the alliance, only by consent of all the contracting parties. As to religion, the provinces of Holland and Zealand shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in that particular as they think advisable; the rest shall adhere to the purport of the edict published by the archduke Matthias, which prescribed, that no man should be oppressed on account of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. All the inhabitants, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 18 to 60, shall be trained and disciplined to war. That peace and war shall be declared by the unanimous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of all the provinces; other matters that concern the internal policy shall be regulated by a majority. That the States shall be held in the usual constitutional manner, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a> shall be deferred to future determination. Finally, the parties agree, that the interpretation of these articles shall remain in the States-general; but, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of their failing to decide, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a>. Soon after the union of Utrecht, King Philip did all his utmost to disconcert the projects of the prince of Orange, and to reduce the provinces to their obedience. He offered to restore him to all his estates, to indemnify him for all his losses, and give him the first place in his esteem and favour; but William was too wise to rely on the promises of a prince who had already shewn himself perfidious, and too generous to abandon a cause in which he had embarked from no interested motives. He determined to share the fate of the United Provinces, and not to disappoint the hopes which they had conceived of his conduct. In the mean time the duke of Parma was doing his utmost to disconcert the projects of the prince of Orange, and to reduce the provinces to their obedience. He besieged and took the town of Marien; invested Maestricht, and carried it after a siege of four months, and reduced the republican general La Noue to such straits, that he was glad to retreat under the cannon of Antwerp. At length the Provinces, by the advice of the prince of Orange, resolved to solicit the alliance. affiliation and protection of the duke of Anjou, to whom they had formerly applied in vain, and to offer him the sovereignty of their territories. Accordingly, in 1582, they solemnly renounced their allegiance to Philip, and acknowledged as their sovereign, Francis <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> de Valois, duke of Alençon and Anjou; and in the following year they published an edict, entitled the abdication of Philip king of Spain, for ever excluding that monarch from any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or authority over the Netherlands. In the beginning of the year 1582, the duke of Anjou, who had already taken an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> part in favour of his new subjects, and had opposed the duke of Parma with some success, arrived in Holland from England; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of February he was solemnly installed at Antwerp as duke of Brabant. It appears, however, that the prince of Orange, though he had been the great promoter of this measure, and even placed the ducal coronet on the head of the new sovereign, still possessed the greatest influence and authority in the United Provinces. When Philip of Spain found that he could not bribe the prince of Orange to his interests, he resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> every method to rid himself of so dangerous an opponent. Soon after the signing of the union of Utrecht, Philip had proscribed the prince, and offered a reward of 25,000 crowns to any person that should bring him dead or alive to Madrid. The greatness of the reward, and a bigotted regard for the interests of the Catholic religion, prompted several to attempt murdering the prince of Orange. He narrowly escaped assassination in 1582; but, two years after, he met his unmerited fate at Delft, by the hands of one Guion, or, as he is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called, Balthazar Gerrard. About the same time the duke of Anjou died in France; and the provinces of Holland and Zealand appointed Maurice, son of the late prince of Orange, to be their stadtholder and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-general. For an account of the actions of this great man, see the article MAURICE OF <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">NAPOLEON</a>. Philip II. died in 1598, and Philip III. prosecuted the war with the United Provinces with as much rancour as his predecessors, but with much worse success. The great defeat sustained by the archduke Albert in 1600, and many subsequent disasters, induced the court of Madrid at length to listen to terms of accommodation. In 1607 a suspension of hostilities took place, and the year following a treaty on terms favourable to the Provinces was concluded for 12 years. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the truce, both parties prepared for a renewal of hostilities; but now the Spaniards fought with considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a>: From a strange policy, which they have since frequently practised, in their contests with the powers of Europe, the Dutch contrived to advance their commercial interests at the expense of their enemy. A very lucrative trade took place between the principal Dutch ports and those of Spain, by which the Spaniards were supplied by their enemies even with ammunition and warlike stores. At the same time the Dutch enriched themselves by numerous prizes taken from the Spaniards, and, in particular, gave a severe blow to the resources of the court of Madrid, by capturing the flota from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> valued at 15,000,000 of livres. These repeated losses of the Spaniards proved the inability of their continuing the war against a people so determined as the Dutch. Accordingly, in 1648, they agreed to a treaty of peace, by which his Catholic majesty renounced all right and sovereignty over the states-general of the United Provinces; and these provinces were henceforth declared a free and independent republic. It was also agreed between the contending powers, that each should remain in unmolested possession of those places which they severally held at the signing of the treaty. From this time to the year 1670 we meet with nothing very remarkable in the history of the United Provinces. By invariably pursuing the maxims of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, industry, and frugality, the republic had attained the highest pitch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. Amsterdam became the emporium of Europe, and the richest city in the universe. The population of the Provinces, especially of Holland, was much greater than at any former or subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, though it is scarcely credible that, as some authors affirm, Holland alone should then contain 3,000,000 of inhabitants. The states despatched ministers and consuls to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>; to the Great Mogul, the king of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and the khan of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> of Russia, and the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. They were considered as an important <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of Europe; and no treaty was concluded without the concurrence of their ambassadors. It is not surprising that the successes of the Dutch, and dispute the prosperous condition in which they now beheld themselves, should have rendered them rather arrogant towards the neighbouring states. Louis XIV. of France had conceived himself affronted by a foolish boast of one of the Dutch ministers, and he was particularly jealous of the advantage which the new republic had acquired over his subjects in the trade to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The triple alliance formed about this time between England, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and the United Provinces, was an additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> with the French king to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> off all intercourse with the Dutch, and to curb their growing power. He began by prevailing on Charles II. of England to abandon the triple alliance; a request to which that worthless monarch, alive to nothing but his pleasures and his avarice, readily agreed, on condition of being well paid for his treachery. Louis also persuaded several of the German princes to unite their forces with his against the republic, and of all the Germanic body, only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> interested himself for the safety of the states-general. The French king assembled an army of 100,000 men, which he divided into four columns, one commanded by himself in person, with the assistance of Marshal Turenne; another by the prince of Condé; a third by General Croqui, and a fourth under the conduct of the duke of Luxemburg. Such an army <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> towards the frontiers could not but terrify the Dutch, now torn with civil and religious factions. The partisans of the Orange family were for abolishing the perpetual edict, and raising William prince of Orange to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> enjoyed by his predecessors; but the De Witt faction opposed him violently, though they could not prevent the young prince from being chosen captain-general and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-admiral. Many hoped that William's new dignity would incline his uncle Charles II. to return to the triple alliance; but that hope was frustrated by the conduct of his majesty, who, in conjunction with the Most Christian king, declared United Provinces declared war against the states-general on the 7th of April. A month after, the elector of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> and bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> followed the example of the two kings. The Dutch put themselves in the best posture of defense that circumstances would admit. Maastricht was strongly garrisoned; the prince of Orange had assembled an army of 25,000 men, with which he advanced to the banks of the Yssel; and the Dutch fleet cruised off the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, to prevent the junction of the naval forces of England and France, which amounted to 150 ships. All Europe watched the first motions of the two powerful kings, seconded by the best generals of the age. Holland could be attacked only by the Rhine or the Meuse, and the French generals and ministers differed by which of these inlets the first <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> should be made. At length, after much deliberation, it was determined to attack the Dutch on both these sides at the same time, in order the more to disconcert their councils. The campaign began with the siege of Rheninberg, Vefel, Orsoi, and Rurick, four towns well fortified, and deemed the keys of Holland. Nothing could oppose armies so well appointed, led by generals so skilful and so experienced. The four towns were compelled to surrender within a few days of each other; and a severe defeat sustained by a body of Dutch troops, in attempting to defend the passage of the Rhine, by the prince of Condé, served still more to dishearten the troops of the flutes-general. It is almost incredible with what rapidity, towns and fortresses yielded to the fortune of his majesty's arms. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Betau, the most fruitful country of the United Provinces, and the surrender of Tolhusfert, obliged the prince of Orange to abandon the Yssel, lest he should be attacked in the rear, and to retire to the very heart of the country, as far as Rhenen in the province of Utrecht. By this means the town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARNHEM">Arnhem</a>, the forts of Knotsemborough, Voorn, St André, and Shenck, this last the strongest in the Netherlands, with a variety of other forts and towns, surrendered as soon as summoned; and at last Nimeguen, a town strong from the nature of the works and fortifications, and garrisoned by 8000 fighting men, including the inhabitants, was invested. After the citizens had for eight days exhibited signal proofs of courage in defense of their liberties, they were forced to yield to the superior skill of Turenne.

UNITY

Pages 206-206

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. There are three unities to be observed, viz. the unity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and that of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In the epic poem, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and almost the only, unity, is that of the action. Some regard indeed ought to be had to that of time; for that of place there is no room. The unity of character is not reckoned among the unities. See POETRY, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. 3.

UNIVERSAL

Pages 206-206

something that is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to many things; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it is one thing belonging to many or all things.

UNIVERSE

Pages 206-206

a collective name, signifying the whole world; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the assemblage of heaven and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, with all things therein. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">GEOGRAPHY</a>.

UNIVERSITY

Pages 206-207

is the name of a corporation formed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of youth in the liberal arts and sciences, and authorized to admit such as have studied in it, to certain degrees in different faculties, which not only serve as certificates of proficiency in science, but also confer on those who obtain them considerable privileges within the university, as well as some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the state without it. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">Universities</a> generally comprehended within them one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more colleges; but this is not always the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; for the university of St Andrew's was in being before either of its colleges was founded, and it would continue in being, with all its privileges, though both its colleges were levelled with the dust. In every university with which we are acquainted, there are four faculties, viz. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, Physic, and the Arts and Sciences, comprehending <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, &c.; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and some other universities, Music is considered as a fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>. In each of these there are two degrees, those of Bachelor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>; for though in the universities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> we have no such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as Doctor in Arts and Sciences, our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Arts answers to the degree of Doctor in Philosophy, which is conferred by many of the universities on the continent. Universities in their present form, and with their present privileges, are institutions comparatively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. They sprang from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of regular clergy, or from the chapters of cathedrals in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, where young men were educated for holy orders, in that dark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when the clergy possessed all the little erudition which was left in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. These convents were seminaries of learning probably from their first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>; and we know with certainty, that in Old Aberdeen there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in which youth were instructed in theology, the canon law, and the school philosophy, at least 200 years before the university and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> were founded. The same was doubtless the case in Oxford and Cambridge, and probably in every town in Europe, where there is now a university which has any claims to be called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; for it was not till the more eminent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> began to see the importance of literature and science, that universities distinct from convents were founded, with the privilege of admitting to degrees, which conferred some rank in civil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. These universities have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been considered as lay corporations; but as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that they had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> origin which we have assigned to them, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to observe, that the pope arrogated to himself the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of vesting them with all their privileges; and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the Reformation, every university in Europe conferred its degrees in all the faculties by authority derived from a papal bull. It is perhaps no improbable conjecture, that the church of Rome derived her idea of academical honours from the Jews, among whom literary distinctions extremely similar subsisted before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a> of our Saviour. Among them, the young student, with respect to his learning, was called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>; from his minority a junior; and the chosen or elected, on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disciples. When he had made some progress in knowledge, and was deemed worthy of a degree, he was by imposition of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> made רְבוּיָה, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> to a Rabbi, the person who officiates using this form, I afficiate thee, or, Be thou afficiated; and as soon afterwards as he was thought worthy to teach others, the afficiate was raised to the rank of Rabbi. Whether this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> suggested the idea or not, it has certainly some resemblance to that by which a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in our universities passes through the degree of Bachelor to that of Master of Arts or Doctor. The most ancient universities in Europe are those of OXFORD, CAMBRIDGE, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">PARIS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">SALAMANCA</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">BOLOGNA</a>; and in the two English universities, the first colleges are those of University, Balliol, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a>, in the former, and St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s in the latter. Oxford and Cambridge, however, were universities, or, as they were then called, studiers, some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of years before colleges or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> were built in them; for the former flourished as a seminary of learning in the reign of Alfred the Great, and the other, could we believe its partial partizans, at a period still earlier. The universities of Scotland are four, ST ANDREWS, GLASGOW, ABERDEEN, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">EDINBURGH</a>. In Ireland there is but one university, viz. that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">DUBLIN</a>, founded by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and very richly endowed. An idle controversy has been agitated, whether the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the English or of the Scotch universities be best adapted to answer the ends of their institution; and, as might be expected, it has been differently decided, according to the partialities of those who have written on the subject. Were we to hazard our own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, we should say, that each has its advantages and disadvantages; and that while the English universities, aided The account given by a late traveller (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>'s Voyage to Cochin-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>) of the luxurious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of living at Batavia, affords a melancholy, but accurate <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Dutch gluttony. University aided by their great schools, to which we have nothing that can be compared, are unquestionably fitted to carry their young members farthest in the knowledge of the learned languages, the mode of teaching in our own universities is better adapted to the promotion of arts and sciences, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of that knowledge which is of most importance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. **University-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>**, in England. The two universities enjoy the sole jurisdiction, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the king's courts, over all civil actions and suits whatsoever, where a scholar or privileged person is one of the parties; excepting in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the right of freehold is concerned. And then by the university <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> they are at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to try and determine, either according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, or according to their own local customs, at their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>; which has generally led them to carry on their process in a course much conforming to the civil law. This privilege, so far as it relates to civil causes, is exercised at Oxford in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>'s court; the judge of which is the vice-chancellor, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSESSOR">assessor</a>. From his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> lies to delegates appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>; from thence to other delegates of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they all three concur in the same sentence, it is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a>, at least by the statutes of the university, according to the rule of the civil law. But if there be any discordance or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in any of the three sentences, an appeal lies in the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to judges delegates appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, under the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. As to the jurisdiction of the university courts in criminal matters, the chancellor's court at Oxford, and probably also that of Cambridge, hath authority to try all offences or misdemeanors under the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, felony, or mayhem; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of treason, felony, and mayhem, by a particular charter, is committed to the university jurisdiction in another court, namely, the court of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of the university. The process of the trial is this. The high steward issues one precept to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, who thereupon returns a panel of 18 freeholders; and another precept to the bedells of the university, who thereupon return a panel of 18 matriculated laymen, *laicos privilegio universitatis gaudentes*: and by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> formed de mediate, half of freeholders and half matriculated persons, is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> to be tried; and that in the guildhall of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Oxford. And if execution be necessary to be awarded in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of finding the party guilty, the sheriff of the county must execute the university process; to which he is annually bound by an oath. **Vocabulary**, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, denotes the collection of the words of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, with their significations, otherwise called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, lexicon, or nomenclature. See Dictionary. A vocabulary is properly a smaller kind of dictionary, which does not enter so minutely into the origin and different acceptations of words. **Vocal**, something that relates to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> or speech; thus vocal music is that set to words, especially verses, and to be performed by the voice; in contradistinction to instrumental music, composed only for instruments, without singing. **Vocative**, in Grammar, the fifth case or case of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>. See Grammar. **Voetius** or **Voet**, Gisbert, an eminent divine of the 16th century, was professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and the Oriental tongues at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, where he was also minister. He affiliated at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>; and died in 1676, aged 87. He wrote a great number of works; and was the declared enemy of Descartes and his philosophy. His followers are called Voetians. Voetius had two sons, Daniel and Paul, both authors. John Voetius, the son of Paul, was doctor and professor of law at Herborn, and wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the Pandects. **Voice**, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> produced in the throat and mouth of an animal, by peculiar organs. Voices are either articulate or inarticulate. Articulate voices are those whereof several confine together to form some intelligible or little system of sounds: such are the voices expressing the letters of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, numbers of which joined together form words. Inarticulate voices are such as are not organized, or assembled into words; such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARKING">barking</a> of dogs, the braying of asses, the hissing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, the fingering of birds, &c. For a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the organs of the voice, see Anatomy; see also Physiology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Voice**, in Grammar, a circumstance in verbs, whereby they come to be considered as either active or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>, i.e., either expressing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> impressed on another subject, as, I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>; or receiving it from another, as, I am beaten. See Grammar. **Voice**, in matters of election, denotes a vote or suffrage. **Voice**, in Oratory. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLAMATION">Declamation</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, No. 5.; and Oratory, No. 129—131. **Volant**, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, in a coat of arms, is drawn <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, or having its wings spread out. **Volatile**, in Physics, something that is easily dissipated by fire or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. **Volatile Alkali**. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">Ammonia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. **Volatilisation**, the art of rendering fixed bodies volatile, or of resolving them by fire into a vapour. **Volcano**, a name given to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, or to vents for subterranean fires. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a> Index, Aetna, Hecla, &c. **Voley**, a bird-cage, of such a size that the birds have room to fly up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in it. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>**, the largest river in Europe, derives its origin from two small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in the forest of Volkonofski about 80 miles from Tver, a town in Russia. It is navigable a few miles above that town. This noble river waters some of the finest provinces in the Russian empire, and at last falls into the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by several mouths, below <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRACAN">Astracan</a>. The Volga is subject to annual inundation. In the year 1774, the inundations exceeded the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-mark by nearly 40 feet, since which period they have been rather on the decline; for in 1775, they rose only to 39 feet 2 inches above that mark; in 1782, they rose to 26 feet; in 1785, to 25 feet 2 inches; and in the year 1791, their height was the same. Pallas is of opinion that this phenomenon may have originated from the diminished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of snow and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> which had fallen in the higher countries; from the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of the Caspian sea, and the gradual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the different mouths of the river, or perhaps from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> operation of all these causes. **Volition**,

URSULINES

Pages 211-211

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an order of nuns, founded originally by St Angela of Brescia, in the year 1537; and so called from St Ursula, to whom they were dedicated.

URTICA

Pages 211-211

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class of morceae; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system classified under the 53rd order, Scabridae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Urtica Marina. See Animal-Flower.

USANCE

Pages 211-211

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, is a determined <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> fixed for the payment of bills of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, reckoned either from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the bills being accepted, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the day of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>; and thus called because regulated by the usage and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the places whereon they are drawn.

USHANT

Pages 211-211

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of France, 15 miles west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Brittany, at the entrance of the British channel.

USHER

Pages 211-211

an officer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> who has the care and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the door of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, chamber, or the like. USHER of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Rod, the eldest of the gentlemen ushers, daily waiters at court, whose duty is to bear the rod before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> at the feast of St George, and other solemnities.

USQUEBAUGH

Pages 211-211

a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> liquor, chiefly taken by way of dram. There are several different methods of making this liquor; but the following is esteemed one of the best: To two gallons of brandy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other spirits, put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of Spanish liquorice, half a pound of raisins of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, four ounces of currants, and three of sliced dates; the tops of baum, mint, savory, thyme, and the tops of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of rosemary, of each two ounces; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> and mace, well bruised, nutmegs, aniseeds, and coriander seeds, bruised likewise, of each four ounces; of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a> or lemon, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-peel, scraped, of each an ounce: let all these infuse 48 hours in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, often shaking them together; then let them stand in a cool place for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>: after which the clear liquor is to be decanted off, and to it is to be put an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of neat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> port, and a gallon of canary; after which it is to be sweetened with a sufficient quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> refined <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. Vol. XX. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II.

USTION

Pages 211-211

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, the preparing of certain substances by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> them.

USUFUIT

Pages 211-211

in the Civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enjoyment of any lands or tenements; or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of receiving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and profits of an inheritance, or other thing, without a power of alienating or changing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> thereof.

USURER

Pages 211-211

a person <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of usury.

USURIOUS CONTRACT

Pages 211-211

is any bargain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> whereby a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is obliged to pay more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> than the statute allows.

USURPATION

Pages 211-211

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is an injurious using <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enjoying of a thing for continuance of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that belongs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to another.

USURY

Pages 211-211

an unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> upon the loan of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, to receive the same again with exorbitant increase. Under the article <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">Interest</a>, it was observed, that by statute 37 Hen. VIII. c. 9, the rate of interest was fixed at 10l. per cent. per annum: which the statute 13 Eliz. c. 8, confirms, and ordains, that all brokers shall be guilty of a praemunire who transact any contracts for more, and the securities themselves shall be void. The statute 21 Jac. I. c. 17, reduced interest to 8l. per cent.; and it having been lowered in 1650, during the usurpation, to 6 per cent. the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> was re-enacted after the Restoration by statute 12 Car. II. c. 13, and, lastly, the statute 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, st. 2, c. 16, has reduced it to 5 per cent. Wherefore not only all contracts for taking more are in themselves totally void, but also the lender shall forfeit treble the money borrowed. Also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any servicer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROKER">broker</a> take more than 5s. per cent. procurement-money, or more than 12d. for making a bond, he shall forfeit 20l. with costs, and shall suffer imprisonment for half a-year. UTERUS. See Anatomy, No. 108.

UTICA

Pages 211-211

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> Propria, on the Mediterranean: a Tyrian colony, and older than <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, (Sil. Italicus); its name, according to Bochart, denoting old: reckoned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to it; but after the destruction of Carthage, became the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and centre of all the Roman transactions in Africa, according to Strabo; who adds, that it stood on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> with Carthage, at one of the promontories called Apollonium, bounding the bay on the west side, the other to the east called Hermea, being at Carthage. It became famous by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cato, who thence was called Uticensis.

UTRECHT

Pages 211-211

in Latin Ultrajectum, Trajectum vetus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inferius, or Trajectum Rheni, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name, so called from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ferry or palage here over the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; the word being compounded of trecht, which in Dutch signifies "a ferry," and oud

UZ

Pages 212-212
or UTZ, the country and place of residence of Job. In the genealogy of the patriarchs there are three persons called Uz, either of which might give this district its name. The first was the grandson of Sem, by his son Aram (Gen. xxii. 23.), who, according to Josephus, occupied the Trachonitis, and Damascus, to the north of Palestine: but Job was among the sons of the East. Another Uz was the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother (Gen. x. 21.), who appears to have removed, after passing the Euphrates, from Haran of Mesopotamia to Arabia Deserta. The third Uz was a Horite, from Mount Seir (Gen. xxxvi. 28.), and thus not of Eber's posterity. Now the question is, from which of these Job's country, Uz, took its name: Not from the first, as is already shown; nor from the second, because his country is always called Seir, or Edom, never Uz; and then called a south, not an east, country, in Scripture. It therefore remains, that we look for the country and place of residence of Job in Arabia Deserta, for which there was very probable reasons. The plunderers of Job are called Chaldeans and Sabeans, next neighbours to him. These Sabeans came not from Arabia Felix, but from a nearer Sabe in Arabia Deserta (Ptolemy); and his friends, except Eliphaz the Temanite, were of Arabia Deserta. UZBECK TARTARY. See TARTARY. W. W, or w, is the 21st letter of our alphabet; and is composed, as its name implies, of two v's. It was not in use among the Hebrews, Greeks, or Romans; but chiefly peculiar to the northern nations, the Teutones, Saxons, Britons, &c. But still it is not used by the French, Italians, Spaniards, or Portuguese, except in proper names, and other terms borrowed from languages in which it is originally used, and even then it is founded like the single v. This letter is of an ambiguous nature; being a consonant at the beginning of words, and a vowel at the end. It may stand before all the vowels except u; as water, wedge, winter, wonder; it may also follow the vowels a, e, o, and unites with them into a kind of double vowel, or diphthong; as in saw, sew, cow, &c. It also goes before r, and follows f and th; as in wrath, swear, thwart: it goes before h also, though in reality it is founded after it; as in when, what, &c. In some words it is obscure, as in shadow, widow, &c.

VACCINIUM

Pages 136-136

the Whortle-berry, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bilberry, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of angiosperms, and arranged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system under the 18th order, Bicornes. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VACUUM

Pages 136-136

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, denotes a space devoid of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body. It has been greatly disputed whether there be in na- ture a perfect vacuum, or space void of all matter; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> bodies consist of material <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> atoms, it is evident that there must be vacuities, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> would be im- possible (see <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, No. 193.). We can even produce something very near a vacuum in the receiver of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> and in the Torricellian tube (see Pneu- matics, p. 23).

VADIUM

Pages 136-136

a pledge in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is either vivum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mor- tuum. VADIUM Vivum, or Living Pledge, is when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> borrows a sum (suppose 200l.) of another; and grants him an estate, as of 20l. per annum, to hold till the rents and profits shall repay the sum so borrowed. This is an estate conditioned to be void as soon as such sum is raised. And in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or pledge is said to be living: it subsists, and survives the debts; and, immediately on the discharge of that, reverts to the borrower.

VADIUM VAGABOND

Pages 136-137
or Vagrant, one who wanders illegally, without a settled habitation. Such persons are cognizable by the laws. See IDLENESS.

VAGINA

Pages 137-137

properly signifies a sheath <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scabbard; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> vagina is used in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a terminus, because resembling a sheath out of which the statue seems to issue. VAGINA. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VAILLANT

Pages 137-137

John Foy, a physician and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> medalist, to whom, according to Voltaire, France was indebted for the science of medals, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. for one half of his cabinet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a> in 1632. Through the means of the minister Colbert he travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, to collect medals for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> cabinet; and returned with so many as made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s cabinet superior to any in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In one of his voyages the ship was taken by an Algerine corsair. After a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of near five months he was permitted to return to France, and received at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> 25 <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medals which had been taken from him. He embarked in a vessel bound for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, and was carried on with a favourable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> for two days, when another corsair appeared, which, in spite of all the fire they could make, bore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon them within the reach of cannon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. Mr Vaillant, dreading the miseries of a fresh <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, resolved, however, to secure the medals which he had received at Algiers, and therefore swallowed them. But a sudden turn of the wind freed them from this adversary, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> them upon the coasts of Catalonia, where, after expecting to run <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a> every moment, they at length fell among the sands at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>. Mr Vaillant got to shore in a skiff, but felt himself extremely incumbered with the medals he had swallowed, which might weigh altogether five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six ounces, and therefore did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a> waters.
