He had recourse to a couple of physicians; who were a little puzzled with the singularity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; however, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> relieved him from time to time, and he found himself in possession of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> when he got to Lyons. Among his collection was an Otho, valuable for its rarity.—He was much careful on his return; and when Louis XIV. gave a new form to the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> in 1701, Mr Vaillant was first made associate, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENSIONARY">pensionary</a>. He wrote several works relating to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> coins, and died in 1706.

VAIRY

Pages 137-137

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, expresses a coat, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the bearings of a coat, when <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> or chequered with vairs.

VALAIS

Pages 137-137

a valley in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, which extends from the source of the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> to the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. It is near 100 miles in length, but of unequal breadth. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, which separate it from the cantons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> and Uri, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Forche, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and the Val d'Aoste, and on the west by Savoy and the republic of Geneva. The inhabitants profess the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and are subject to the swelling of the throat called bronchocelitis; and idiots are said to abound among them more than in any other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the globe. They are naturally hardy, enterprising, and good-natured. Valais is surrounded on all sides by very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountains, most of which are covered with perpetual snow. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is fertile in corn, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSCAT">muscat</a>-wine, which is produced here is excellent, and well known all over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> comprehends 55 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> parishes, with one bishop. The religion is the Roman Catholic.

VALANTIA

Pages 137-137

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas polygamia, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 4th order, a/perifolies. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VALE

Pages 148-148

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> frequently used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> vessels dug from under ground, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> otherwise found, and preserved in the cabinets of the curious. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, the appellation vale is also given to those ornaments placed on cornices, pediments, or pedestals, representing the vellus of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, particularly those used in sacrifice, as incense-pots, flower-pots, &c. See PORTLAND-Vale.

VALENCIA

Pages 137-137

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name. It contains about 12,000 houses, besides those of the suburbs and the summerhouses round it. It has an university, and an archbishop's see; and was taken from the Moors by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in the 14th century. The town is handsome, and adorned with very fine structures. It is not very strong, though there are some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a> along the sides of the walls. They have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, which bring in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sums to the inhabitants. It is seated on the river Guadalaviar, over which there are five handsome bridges; and it is about three miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, where there is a harbour, 110 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, and 165 east by south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. This city surrendered to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Peterborough in the year 1705; but it was lost again in 1707. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, o. 18. N. Lat. 39. 23.

VALENCIENNES

Pages 137-137

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, strong, and considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> and late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hainault, containing about 20,000 souls. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a> divides it into two parts. It is a very important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: the citadel and fortifications, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Vauban, were constructed by order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV., who took this town from the Spaniards. It was confirmed to him by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Nimuegen, in 1678. In 1793, it surrendered to the allies after a severe siege, but was afterwards abandoned; and is now in possession of the French. Besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, this city is noted for manufactories of woollen stuffs and very fine linens. It is 20 miles west-south-west of Mons, 17 north-east of Cambrai, and 120 north-east by north of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 37. N. Lat. 50. 21.

VALENS

Pages 137-138

Flavius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the East, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>. Killed by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> in the year 379. See CONSTANTINOPLE, No. 76. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">VALENTINIAN</a> I., emperor of the West, a renowned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, but a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> over his subjects. See ROME, No. 523. VALENTINIAN II., emperor of the West, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> celebrated for his virtues, and above all for his moderation; yet a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was formed against him by Ar- Valentini- bogafles, the commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of his armies; and he was strangled in the year 392. See Rome, No. 536.

VALENTINIANIS

Pages 138-138

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Christian heretics, who sprung up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, and were called from their leader Valentinus. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIANS">Valentinians</a> were only a branch of the Gnostics, who realized <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> personified the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> concerning the Deity, whom they called Pleroma or Plenitude. Their system was this: the first principle is Bythos, i.e., Depth, which remained many ages unknown, having with it Ennoe or Thought, and Sige or Silence; from these sprung the Nous or Intelligence, which is the only son, equal to and alone capable of comprehending the Bythos; the sister of Nous they called Aletheia or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a>; and these constituted the first quaternity of aeons, which were the source and original of all the rest: for Nous and Aletheia produced the World and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>; and from these two proceeded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> and the Church. But besides these 8 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> aeons, there were 22 more; the last of which, called Sophia, being desirous to arrive at the knowledge of Bythos, gave herself a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of uneasiness, which created in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">Anger</a> and Fear, of which was born <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">Matter</a>. But the Horos or Bounder stopped her, preferred her in the Pleroma, and restored her to Perfection. Sophia then produced the Christ and the Holy Spirit, which brought the aeons to their last perfection, and made every one of them contribute their utmost to form the Saviour. Her Enthymese, or Thought, dwelling near the Pleroma, perfected by the Christ, produced every thing that is in the world by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> passions. The Christ sent into it the Saviour, accompanied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, who delivered it from its passions, without annihilating it: from thence was formed corporeal matter. And in this manner did they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> concerning God, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

VALERIAN

Pages 138-138
or Valerianus, Publius Licinius, emperor of Rome, remarkable for his captivity and cruel treatment by Sapor I., king of Persia. See Rome, No. 491.

VALERIANA

Pages 138-138

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clasf triandra, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 48th order, aggregate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VALERIUS MAXIMUS

Pages 138-138

a Latin historian, sprung from the families of the Valerii and Fabii, which made him take the name of Valerius Maximus. He studied polite literature, and afterwards followed Sextus Pompey to the wars. At his return he composed an account of the actions and remarkable sayings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men; and dedicated that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Tiberius. Many of the learned think that this is the same that is now extant, and bears the name of Valerius Maximus; but others maintain, that what we have now is only an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of the work written by this celebrated historian, and that this abridgment was made by one Nepotian of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. However, this work is well written, and contains a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of memorable actions performed by the Greeks and Romans that are worthy of being read.

VALET

Pages 138-138

a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, used as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name for all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> men servants employed in the more servile offices, as grooms, footmen, coachmen, &c. But with us it is only used in the phrase valet de chambre, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> whose office is to dress and undress his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, &c.

VALETTA

Pages 138-138

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> (see Malta, No. 26.). It is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 34'. N. Lat. 35° 54'.

VALETUDINARY

Pages 138-138

among medical writers, denotes a person of a weak and sickly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and frequently out of order.

VALID

Pages 138-138

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, an appellation given to acts, deeds, transactions, &c., which are clothed with all the formalities requisite to their being put into execution, and to their being admitted in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>.

VALLADOLID

Pages 138-138

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Old Castile, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a principality of the same name, with a bishop's see and an university. It is surrounded with strong walls, embellished with handsome buildings, large public squares, piazzas, and fountains; containing 11,000 houses, with fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> houses, adorned with balconies. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> in the middle of the city, surrounded with handsome brick houses, having under them piazzas, where people may walk dry in all weathers. Within these piazzas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and tradesmen keep their shops. All the houses are of the same height, being four stories; and there are balconies at every window, of gilt <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. In the whole there are 70 monasteries and nunneries; the finest of which is that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>, remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which is one of the most magnificent in the city. The kings resided a long while at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which still remains, is of very large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, though but two stories high; within are fine paintings of various kinds, and at one of the corners a curious clock, made in the same manner as that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>. The environs of the city are a fine plain, covered with gardens, orchards, vineyards, and meadows. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Esvurga and Peñuega, in W. Long. 4° 25'. N. Lat. 41° 50'.

VALUE

Pages 138-138

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, denotes the price <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> worth of any thing.

VALVE

Pages 138-138

in Anatomy, a thin membrane applied on several cavities and vessels of the body, to afford a passage to certain humours going one way, and prevent their reflux towards the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from whence they came.

VANBRUGH

Pages 138-139

Sir John, a celebrated English dramatic writer and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, was descended of a family in Cheshire which came from France, though by his name he appears to have been originally of Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. He was born about the middle of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and received a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. His first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, called the Relapse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Virtue in Danger, was acted in the year 1697 with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause; which gave him such encouragement, encouragement, that he wrote eleven more comedies. He was the friend of Mr Congreve, whose genius was naturally turned for dramatic performances; and these two gave new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the English stage, and restored its flinking reputation. Sir John was also esteemed an able architect. Under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> was raised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLENHEIM">Blenheim</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. He died in 1726.

VANDELLIA

Pages 139-139

a genus-of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class didynamia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. VAN-DIEMEN'S <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">LAND</a>. See DIEMEN.

VANDYCK

Pages 139-139

SIR ANTHONY, a celebrated painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in the year 1599. After giving early proofs of his genius, he became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of the illustrious Rubens. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Augustines at Antwerp, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> altar, is a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Rubens representing, in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> fitting with the child <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> in her lap, and in another part several saints, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, standing. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of one of these, St Sebastian, is said to have been painted by Vandyck when he was only a disciple of Rubens. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> being engaged one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> abroad, his disciples went into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>-room, where, after having been some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> employed in admiring his works, they began to play <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> romp in such a manner, that the breast of St Sebastian, which was not yet dry, was brushed away by a hat thrown at random. This accident put an end to their play: they were very anxious to restore it, fearing that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Rubens discovered it they should all be discarded. At length it was agreed that Anthony should undertake to mend the faint's breast. In short, taking his master's pallet and brushes, he succeeded so well that his companions imagined Rubens would overlook it. They were mistaken; for Rubens at his return knew immediately that someone had touched upon his performance: calling his disciples, he asked them why any one had dared to meddle with his painting? They were some time doubtful whether they should confess or deny the fact. Threats at length prevailed: they owned that Vandyck had thrown his hat upon it. Upon this, closeting Vandyck, instead of chiding him, he told him, that "it was proper and even necessary for him to travel into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the only school that produced excellent painters." By this advice, and with the affluence of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, he set out for Italy, about the year 1621, being then about 21 or 22 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Having stayed a short time at Rome, he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, where he attained the beautiful colouring of Titian, Paul Veronese, and the Venetian school. After a few years he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, with so noble, so easy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> a manner of painting, that Titian himself was hardly his superior: and no other matter could equal him in portraits. Soon after his return, he accidentally met with D. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENIERS">Teniers</a>, who accosted him with great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, and asked him whether he had much business since he came from Rome? "What business, think you, can I have had time to do (replied Vandyck)? I am only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> arrived here. Would you believe, that I offered to draw that fat brewer's picture who just passed by us for two pistoles, and that the looby laughed in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, saying it was too dear? I assure you, that if the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a> do not turn up better, I shall make no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> stay at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>." Soon after this, he painted those two famous pictures, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a> and a dying Christ; the first in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-church, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Vandyck in that of the Capuchins, at Termond. Vandyck, finding he could not make a fortune in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of going over into England. Accordingly he borrowed some guineas of Teniers, and set out, furnished with letters of recommendation. His superior genius soon brought him into great reputation; and above all, he excelled in portraits, which he drew with an inconceivable facility, and for which he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> a very high price, according to the instructions which had been given him on that head. It is affirmed, that for some of them he received 400 guineas apiece. He soon found himself loaded with honours and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>; and as he had a noble and generous heart, he lived equal to his fortune. He married a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Ruthven, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Gowry; and, though he had but little fortune, maintained her in a style suitable to her birth. He generally kept a magnificent equipage, and a numerous retinue. He died in 1641, at the age of 42, leaving <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, it is said, to the amount of 40,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>.

VANE

Pages 139-139

a thin slip of bunting hung to the mast-head, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other conspicuous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the ship, to show the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> sewed upon a wooden frame called the stock, which contains two holes whereby to slip over the spindle, upon which it turns about as the wind changes.

VAPOUR

Pages 139-139

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, the particles of bodies rarefied by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and thus rendered specifically <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, in which they rise. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">EVAPORATION</a>, and HEAT, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VAPOUR-BATH

Pages 139-139

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to a chemist's bath <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, in which a body is placed so as to receive the fumes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. We also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the term vapour-bath, when a sick person is made to receive the vapours arising from some liquid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> placed over a fire. Many contrivances have been proposed for this purpose; and their expediency and utility are well known to those who are conversant in this business. A late writer has suggested a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of vapour <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> is reduced to a tin-boiler, tin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> wrapped in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> box with a cotton cover, for the reception of the body and circulation of the vapour.

VAPOURS

Pages 139-139

in Medicine, otherwise called hypochondriacs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spleen. See MEDICINE, No 276 and 321.

VARI

Pages 139-145

in Medicine, little, hard, and ruddy tumors, which frequently infect the faces of young persons of a hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a> of body. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">VARIATION</a> of the Compass, is the deviation of the magnetic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mariner's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> from the meridian or true <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south line. On the continent it is called the declination of the magnetic needle; and this is a better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, for reasons which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear by and by. We have given the general facts relating to magnetic variation under the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">MAGNETISM</a>, No 19; and under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> COMPASS, and Azimuth COMPASS, we have noticed the methods of ascertaining the variation at any particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. We shall here only give a short historical account of the progressive discoveries respecting magnetic variation, and notice the the explanations that have been offered to account for this phenomenon. About the time that the polarity of the magnet was first observed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the magnetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, both in Europe and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, was nearly in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the meridian. It was therefore an infallible present to the mariner, giving him a sure direction in his course through the pathless ocean. But by the time that the European navigators had engaged in their adventurous voyages to far distant shores, the deviation of the needle from the meridian was very sensible even in Europe. The son of Columbus positively says, that it was observed by his father in his first voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and made his companions so anxious lest they should not find the way back again to their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, that they mutinied and refused to proceed. It is certain that Gonzales Oviedo and Sebastian Cabot observed it in their voyages. Indeed it could not possibly escape them; for in some parts of their several tracks the needle deviated above $25^\circ$ from the meridian; and the rudest dead reckoning, made on the supposition of the needle pointing due north and south, must have thrown the navigators into the utmost confusion. We know that spherical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a> was at that time abundantly familiar to the mathematicians of Europe, and that no person pretended to take the command of a ship bound to a distant port that was not much more informed in this science than most masters of ships are at present. The deviation of the compass, however, was not generally allowed by mathematicians, who had not yet become sensible of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of quitting the Aristotelian trammels, and investigating <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> by experiments. They chose rather to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> the navigators with inaccuracy in their observations than the schoolmen with errors in principles. Pedro de Medina at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALLADOLID">Valladolid</a>, in his *Arte de Navigar*, published in 1545, denies the variation of the compass. But the concurring reports of the commanders of ships on distant voyages, in a few years, obliged the landmen in their closets to give up the point; and Martin Cortez, in a treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> before 1556, treats it as a thing completely established, and gives rules and instruments for discovering its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. About the year 1580 Norman published his discovery of the dip of the needle, and speaks largely of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> deviation from the plane of the meridian, and attributes it to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of a point, not in the heavens, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and describes methods by which he hoped to find its place. To the third, and all the subsequent editions of Norman's book (called the *New Attractive*), was subjoined a dissertation by Mr Burroughs, comptroller of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, on the variation of the compass, in which are recorded the quantity of this deviation in many places; and he laments the obstacle which it causes to navigation by its total uncertainty previous to observation. The author indeed offers a rule for computing it, *a priori*, founded on some conjecture as to its cause; but, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and candour of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, acknowledges that this is but a guess, and intreates all navigators to be judicious in their observations, and ready in communicating them to the public. Accordingly observations were liberally contributed from time to time, and were published in the subsequent treatises on navigation. But in 1635 the mariners were thrown into a new and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perplexity, by the publication of a *Discourse* Mathematical on the Variation of the Magnetic Needle, Variation by Mr Henry Gillebrand, Greatham professor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. He had compared the variations observed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by Burroughs, Gunter, and himself, and found that the north end of the mariner's needle was gradually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> more to the westward. For Norman and Burroughs had observed it to point about $11\frac{1}{2}$ degrees to the east of north in 1580; Gunter found its deviation only $6^\circ$ in 1622, and he himself had observed only $4^\circ$ in 1634; and it has been found to deviate more and more to the westward ever since, as may be seen from the tables given under MAGNETISM. Mr Bond, teacher of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in London, and employed to edit and improve the impressions of the popular treatises of navigation, about 1650, declared, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> called the "Seaman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDAR">Kalendar</a>," that he had discovered the true progress of the deviation of the compass; and published in another work, called the "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">Longitude</a> Found," a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the variation for 50 years. This was, however, a gratuitous prognostication, not founded on any well-grounded principles; and though it agreed very well with the observations made in London, which showed a gradual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to the westward at the rate of $-12'$ annually, by no means agreed with the observations made in other places. See Phil. Trans. 1668. But this news soon lost its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>: for the inconsistency with observation appeared more and more every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and all were anxious to differ over some general rule, by which a near guess at least might be made as to the direction of the needle in the most frequented seas. Halley recommended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in the most <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> manner to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; and, after much unwearyed solicitation, obtained a ship to be sent on a voyage of discovery for this purpose. He got the command of this ship, in which he repeatedly traversed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, and went as far as the 50th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of southern latitude. See his very curious speculations on this subject in the Phil. Trans. 1683 and 1692. After he had collected a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of observations made by others, and compared them with his own, he published in 1700 a synoptical account of them in a very ingenious form of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> chart, where the ocean was criss-crossed by a number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> passing through those planes where the compass had the same deviation. Thus, in every point of one line there was no variation in 1700; in every point of another line the compass had $20^\circ$ of east variation; and in every point of a third line it had $20^\circ$ of west variation. These lines have since been called *Halleyan lines*, or curves. This chart was received with universal applause, and was undoubtedly one of the most valuable presents that science has made to the arts. The polarity of the magnetic needle, and a general though intricate connection between its positions in all parts of the world, naturally makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> speculate about its cause. We see that Cortez ascribed it to the attraction of an eccentric point, and that Bond thought that this point was placed not in the heavens, but in the earth. This notion made the basis of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of Magnetism of Dr Gilbert of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>. See MAGNETISM, No. 71. Gilbert's theory may be understood from the following general proposition. Let NS (fig. 1.) be a magnet, of which N is the north Fig. 1. Variation. North and S the south pole: Let \( ns \) be any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, poised on a point \( c \) like a compass needle. It will arrange itself in a position \( nc \) precisely the same with that which would be afforded by a compass needle of the same size and shape, having \( n \) for its north and \( s \) its south pole. And while the piece of iron remains in this position, it will be in all respects a magnet similar to the real compass needle. The pole \( n \) will attract the south pole of a small magnetized needle, and repel its north pole. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> be held over \( ns \), and fine iron-filings be strewned on it, they will arrange themselves into curves issuing from one of its ends and terminating at the other, in the same manner as they will do when strewned on a paper held over a real compass needle. But this magnetism is quite temporary; for if the piece of iron \( ns \) be turned the other way, placing \( n \) where \( s \) now is, it will remain there, and will exhibit the same phenomena. We may here add, that if \( ns \) be almost infinitely small in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of NS, the line \( ns \) will be in such a position that if \( sa \), \( sb \), be drawn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to \( nc \), \( sc \), we shall have \( sa \) to \( sb \), as the force of the pole \( N \) to the force of the pole \( S \). And this is the true cause of that curious disposition of iron-filings when strewn round a magnet. Each fragment becomes a momentary magnet, and arranges itself in the true magnetic direction, and when so arranged, attracts the two adjoining fragments, and co-operates with the forces, which also arrange them. We throw this out to the ingenious mechanician as the foundation of a complete theory of the magnetic phenomena. When the filings are infinitely fine, the curves \( nc \) have this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, that, drawing the tangent \( nc \), we always have \( sa \cdot sb = \text{force of } N : \text{force of } S \); and thus we may approximate at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of magnetic attraction and repulsion. The theory, of which an outline is given under Magnetism, is founded on this principle, and applies with success to every phenomenon yet observed. Now, to apply this theory to the point in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>.—Let \( ns \) (fig. 2.) be a small compass needle, of which \( n \) is the north and \( s \) the south pole: let this needle be poised horizontally on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> \( cd \); and let \( ns' \) be the position of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> needle. Take any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> iron, and hold it upright, or nearly so, as represented by \( <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> \). The lower end \( B \) will repel the pole \( n \) and will attract the pole \( s \), thus exhibiting the properties of a north pole of the bar \( AB \). Keeping \( B \) in its place, turn the bar round \( B' \) as a centre, till it come into the position \( A'B' \) nearly parallel to \( ns' \). You will observe the compass needle \( ns \) attract the end \( B' \) with either pole \( n \) or \( s \), when \( B'A' \) is in the position \( B'a \) perpendicular to the direction \( ns' \) of the dipping needle: and when the bar has come into the position \( B'A' \), the upper end \( B' \) will show itself to be a south pole by attracting \( n \) and repelling \( s \). This beautiful experiment was exhibited to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in 1673 by Mrs Hindshaw. From this it appears, that the great magnet in the earth induces a momentary magnetism on soft iron precisely as a common magnet would do. Therefore (says Dr Gilbert) it induces permanent magnetism on magnetizable ores of iron, such as loadstones, in the same manner as a great loadstone would do; and it affects the magnetism already imparted to a piece of tempered <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> precisely as any other great magnet would. Vol. XX. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. Therefore the needle of the mariner's compass in every part of the world arranges itself in the magnetic direction, so that if poised as a dipping needle should be, it will be a tangent to one of the curves \( ncS \) of fig. 1. The horizontal needle being so poised as to be capable of playing only in a horizontal plane, will only arrange itself in the plane of the triangle \( ncS \). That end of it which has the same magnetism with the south pole \( S \) of the great magnet included in the earth will be turned towards its north pole \( N \). Therefore what we call the north pole of a needle or magnet really has the magnetism of the south pole of the great primitive magnet. If the line \( NS \) be called the axis, and \( N \) and \( S \) the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of this great magnet, the plane of any one of these curves \( ncS \) will cut the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface in the circumference of a circle, great or small according as the plane does or does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the centre of the earth. Dr Halley's first thought was, that the north pole of the great magnet or loadstone which was included in the bowels of the earth was not far from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAFFIN_S_BAY">Baffin's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and its south pole in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean south-west from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>. But he could not find any positions of these two poles which would give the needle that particular position which it was observed to assume in different parts of the world; and he concluded that the great terrestrial loadstone had four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> poles (a thing not unfrequent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> loadstones, and easily producible at pleasure), two of which are stronger and two weaker. When the compass is at a great distance from the two north poles, it is affected so as to be directed nearly in a plane passing through the strongest. But if we make it approach much more to the weakest, the greater vicinity will compensate for the smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> force of the weak pole, and occasion considerable irregularities. The appearances are favourable to this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. If this be the real <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the great magnet, it is almost a desperate task to ascertain by computation what will be the position of the needle. Halley seems to have despaired: for he was both an elegant and a most expert mathematician, and it would have cost him little trouble to ascertain the places of two poles only, and the direction which these would have given to the needle. But to say what would be its position when acted on by four poles, it was necessary to know the law by which the magnetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> varied by a variation of distance; and even then, the computation would have been exceedingly difficult. In order to account for the change of variation, Dr Halley supposes this internal magnet not to adhere to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> shell which we inhabit, but to form a nucleus or kernel detached from it on all sides, and to be so poised as to revolve freely round an axis, the position of which he hopes to discover by observation of the compass. Dr Halley imagined that the nucleus revolved from east to west round the same axis with the earth. Thus the poles of the magnet would change their positions relatively to the earth's surface, and this would change the direction of the compass needle. The great Euler, whose delight it was always to engage in the most difficult mathematical researches and computations, undertook to ascertain the position of the needle in every part of the earth. His dissertation on this subject is to be seen in the 13th volume of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Royal Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and is exceedingly Variation, irgly beautiful, abounding in those analytical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">tours</a> d'adrefle in which he surpassed all the world. He has reduced the computation to a wonderful simplicity. He found, however, that four poles would engage him in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> which would be excessively intricate, and has contented himself with computing for two only; observing that this supposition agrees so well with observation, that it is highly probable that this is the real constitution of the terrestrial magnet, and that the coincidence would have been perfect if he had <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> on the due positions of the two poles. He places one of them in lat. 76° north, and long. 96° west from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>. The fourth pole is placed in lat. 38° south, and long. 158° west from Teneriffe. These are their situations for 1757.—Mr Euler has annexed to his dissertation a chart of Halleyan curves suited to these assumptions, and fitted to the year 1757. It must be acknowledged, that the general course of the variations according to this theory greatly resembles the real state of things; and we cannot but own ourselves highly indebted to this great mathematician for having made so fine a first attempt. He has improved it very considerably in another dissertation in the 22d volume of these memoirs. But there are still such great differences, that the theory is of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the navigator, and it only serves as an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> for a farther prosecution of the subject. Since that time another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> variation chart has been published, fitted to a late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; but the public has not sufficient information of the authorities or observations on which it is founded. The great object in all these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> is to facilitate the discovery of a ship's longitude at sea. For the lines of variation being drawn on the chart, and the variation and the latitude being observed at sea, we have only to look on the chart for the intersection of the parallel of observed latitude and the Halleyan curve of observed variation. This intersection must be the place of the ship. This being the purpose, the Halleyan lines are of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; but they do not give us a ready <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the direction of the needle. We have always to imagine a line drawn through the point, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the meridian in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> corresponding to the Halleyan line. We should learn the general magnetic affections of the globe much better if a number of magnetic meridians were drawn. These are the intersections of the earth's surface with planes passing through the magnetic axis, cutting one another in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of 9° or 10°. This would both show us the places of the magnetic poles much more clearly, and would, in every place, show us at once the direction of the needle. In all those places where these magnetic curves touch the meridians, there is no variation; and the variation in every other place is the angle contained between these magnetic meridians and the true ones. The program of a work of this kind has been published by Mr Churchman, who appears to have engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> with great zeal and considerable opportunities. It is pretty certain that the north magnetic pole (or point, as Mr Churchman calls it) is not far removed from the stations given it by Halley and Euler; and there seems no doubt but that in the countries between <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's bay</a> and the western coasts of North America the needle will have every position with respect to the terrestrial meridian, so that the north end of a compass needle will even point due south in several places. Almost everything that can be desired in this inquiry would be obtained by a few well-chosen observations made in those regions. It would be of immense advantage to have the dips ascertained with great precision. These would enable us to judge at what depth under the surface the pole is situated; for the well-informed mechanician, who will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> seriously what we have said about the magnetic curves, will see that a compass needle, when compared with the great terrestrial magnet, is but as a particle of iron-filings compared to a very large <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> magnet. Therefore, from the position of the dipping needle, we may infer the place of the pole, if the law of magnetic action be given; and this law may be found by means of other experiments which we could point out. See MAGNETISM, No 89, &c., &c. Mr Churchman has adopted the opinion of only two poles. According to him, the north pole was (in 1800) in Lat. 58° N. and Long. 134° W. from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, very near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Fairweather; and the south pole lies in Lat. 58° S. and Long. 165° E. from Greenwich. He also imagines that the north pole has moved to the eastward, on a parallel of latitude, about 65 since the beginning of the 19th century (from 1800), and concludes that it makes a revolution in 1096 years. The southern pole has moved less, and completes its revolution in 2280 years. This motion he attributes to some influences which he calls magnetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, and which he seems to consider as celestial. This he infers from the changes of variation. He announces a physical theory on this subject, which, he says, enables him to compute the variation with precision for any time past or to come; and he even gives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of trigonometrical computation illustrated by examples. But as this publication (entitled The Magnetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>), published for the author, by Darton and Harvey, 1794, is only a program, he expresses himself obscurely, and somewhat enigmatically, respecting his theory. He speaks of the influence of one pole being greater than that of the other; and says, that in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the magnetic equator, where the needle will be parallel to the axis, will not be in the middle between the poles. This is true of a common magnet. He must therefore abide by this supposition in its other consequences. The magnetic meridians must be planes passing through this axis, and therefore must be circles on the surface of the earth. This is incompatible with the observations; nay, his charts are so in many places, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, where the variations by his chart are three times greater than what has been observed.—His parallels of dip are still more different from observation, and are incompatible with any phenomena that could be produced by a magnet having but two poles. His rules of computation are exceedingly exceptionable. He has in fact but one example, and that so particular, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of computation will not apply to any other. This circumstance is not taken notice of in the enunciation of his first problem; and the reader is made to imagine that he has got a rule for computing the variation, whereas all the rules of calculation are only running in a circle. The variation computed for the port of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and Paul in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a>, by the rule, is ten times greater than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. For our own part, we have little hopes of this problem ever being subjected to accurate calculation. We believe, Variation, believe, indeed, that there is a cofinical change going on in the earth, which will produce a progressive change in the variation of the needle; and we see none more likely than Dr Halley's motion. There is nothing repugnant to our knowledge of the universe in the supposition of a magnetic nucleus revolving within this earth; and it is very easy to conceive a very simple motion of revolution, which shall produce the very motion of the sensible poles for which Mr Churchman contends. We need only suppose that the magnetical axis of this nucleus is not its axis of revolution. It may not even bifurcate that axis; and this circumstance will cause the two poles to have different degrees of motion in relation to the shell which surrounds it. But this regular progress of the magnet within the earth may produce very irregular motions of the compass needle, by the intervention of a third body susceptible of magnetism. The theory of which we have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> given a hint comes here to our assistance. Suppose NS (fig. 3.) to represent the primitive magnet in the earth, and NS' to be a stratum of iron ore susceptible of magnetism. Also let NS' be another small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of a similar ore; and let their situations and magnitudes be such as is exhibited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The fact will be, that N will be the north pole and S the south pole of the great stratum, and NS' and NS' will be the north and south poles of the small mass or loadstone. Any person may remove all doubts as to this, by making the experiment with a magnet NS, a piece of iron or soft tempered steel NS', and another piece NS'. The well-informed and attentive reader will easily see, that by such interventions every conceivable anomaly may be produced. While the great magnet makes a revolution in any direction, the needle will change its position gradually, and with a certain regularity; but it will depend entirely on the size, shape, and situation, of these intervening masses of magnetizable iron ore, whether the change of variation of the compass shall be such as the primitive magnet alone would have produced, or whether it shall be of a kind wholly different. Now, that such intervening disturbances may exist, is past <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>. We know that even on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a> of earth which we inhabit, and with which only we are acquainted, there are extensive <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> or otherwise disposed masses of iron ores in a state susceptible of magnetism; and experiments made on bars of hard tempered steel, and on bits of such ores, assure us that the magnetism is not induced on such bodies in a moment, but propagated gradually along the mass.—That such disturbances do actually exist, we have many relations. There are many instances on record of very extensive magnetic rocks, which affect the needle to very considerable distances. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBA">Elba</a> in the Mediterranean is a very remarkable instance of this. The island of Canna also, on the west of Scotland, has rocks which affect the needle at a great distance. A similar effect is observed near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAROE_ISLANDS">Faroe <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the North sea; the compass has no determined direction when brought on shore. Journ. de Sciences, 1679, p. 174. In Hudson's straits, in latitude 63°, the needle has hardly any polarity. Elliot's Voyage to Hudson's Bay. Bouguer observed the same thing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. Nay, we believe that almost all rocks, especially of whin or trappe <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, contain iron in a proper state. All this refers only to the thin crust through which Variation, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> eye has occasionally penetrated. Of what may be below we are ignorant; but when we see appearances which tally so remarkably with what would be the effects of great masses of magnetical bodies, modifying the general and regularly progressive action of a primitive magnet, whose existence and motion is inconsistent with nothing that we know of this globe, this manner of accounting for the observed change of variation has all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> that we can desire. Nay, we apprehend that very considerable changes may be produced in the direction of the compass needle, even without the supposition of any internal motion. If the great magnet resembles many loadstones we are acquainted with, having more than two poles, we know that these poles will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> on each other, and gradually change each other's force, and consequently the direction of the compass. This process, to be sure, tends to a state of things which will change no more.—But the period of human <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, or of the history of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, may make but a small part of the history of this globe; and therefore this objection is of little force. There can be no doubt of the operation of the general terrestrial magnetism on everything susceptible of magnetic properties; and we cannot hesitate to explain in this way many changes of magnetic direction which have been observed. Thus, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Father de la Torre observed, that during a great eruption of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a> the variation was 16° in the morning, at noon it was 14°, and in the evening it was 10°, and that it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that state till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> grew so dark as no longer to be visible in the night; after which it slowly increased to 13½°, where it remained. Daniel Bernoulli found the needle changed its position 45' by an earthquake. Professor <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a> at Mainz observed that the declination of the needle in that place was greatly affected by the earthquake in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>. Such streams of lava as flowed from Hecla in the last dreadful eruption must have made a transference of magnetic matter that would considerably affect the needle. But no observations seem to have been made on the occasion; for we know that common ironstone, which has no effect on the needle, will, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> cementation with any inflammable substance, become magnetic. In this way Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a> sometimes made artificial loadstones.—But these are partial things, and not connected with the general change of variation now under consideration. We have said so much on this subject, chiefly with the view of cautioning our readers against too languid expectations from any pretensions to the solution of this great problem. We may certainly gather from these observations, that even although the theory of the variation should be completed, we must expect (by what we already know of magnetism in general) that the disturbances of the needle, by local causes intervening between it and the great influence by which it is chiefly directed, may be so considerable as to affect the position of the compass needle in a very sensible manner; for we know that the metallic substances in the bowels of the earth are in a state of continual change, and this to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> altogether unknown. There is another irregularity of the mariner's needle that we have noticed under Magnetism, p. 365, namely, the daily variation. This was first observed Variation by Mr George Graham in 1722 (Philosophical Transactions, No 383), and reported to the Royal Society of London. It usually moves (at least in Europe) to the westward from 8 morning till 2 P.M. and then gradually returns to its former situation. The diurnal variations are seldom less than 6°, and often much greater. Mr Graham mentions (Philosophical Transactions, No 428.) some observations by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Hume, in a voyage to America, where he found the variation greatest in the afternoon. This being a general phenomenon, has also attracted the attention of philosophers. The most detailed accounts of it to be met with are those of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> (see Magnetism), in Philosophical Transactions, vol. ii., part i., p. 399, and those of Van Swinden, in his Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a> and Magnetism. Mr Canton attempts to account for these changes of position, by observing that the force of a magnet is weakened by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. A small magnet being placed near a compass needle, ENE from it, so as to make it deflect 45° from the natural position, the magnet was covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> vessel, into which hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> was poured. The needle gradually receded from the magnet 45°, and returned gradually to its place as the water cooled. This is confirmed by uniform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. The parts of the earth to the eastward are first heated in the morning, and therefore the force of the earth is weakened, and the needle is made to move to the westward. But as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> warms the western side of the earth in the afternoon, the motion of the needle must take the contrary direction. But this way of explaining by a change in the force of the earth supposes that the changing cause is acting in opposition to some other force. We do not know of any such. The force, whatever it may be, seems simply to produce its own effect, in deranging the needle from the direction of terrestrial magnetism. If Æpinus's theory of magnetic action be admitted, we may suppose that the sun acts on the earth as a magnet acts on a piece of soft iron, and in the morning propels the fluid in the north-west parts. The needle directs itself to this constricted fluid, and therefore it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> to the eastward of the magnetic north in the afternoon. And (to abide by the same theory) this induced magnetism will be somewhat greater when the earth is warmer; and therefore the diurnal variation will be greatest in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. This change of position of the constricted fluid must be supposed to bear a very small ratio to the whole fluid, which is naturally supposed to be constricted in one pole of the great magnet in order to give it magnetism. Thus we shall have the diurnal variation a very small quantity. This is departing, however, from the principle of Mr Canton's explanation; and indeed we cannot see how the weakening the general force of the terrestrial magnet should make any change in the needle in respect to its direction; nor does it appear probable that the change of temperature produced by the sun will penetrate deep enough to produce any sensible effect on the magnetism. And if this be the cause, we think that the derangements of the needle should vary as the thermometer varies, which is not true. The other method of explaining is much better, if Æpinus's theory of magnetic attraction and repulsion be just; and we may suppose that it is only the secondary magnetism (i.e., that of the magnetizable minerals) that is sensibly affected by the heat; this will account very well for the greater mobility of the fluid in summer than in winter. A great objection to either of these explanations is the prodigious diversity of the diurnal variations in different places. This is so very great, that we can scarcely ascribe the diurnal variation to any change in the magnetism of the primitive terrestrial magnet, and must rather look for its cause in local circumstances. This conclusion becomes more probable, when we learn that the deviation from the meridian and the deviation from the horizontal line are not affected at the same time. Van Swinden ascribes them solely to changes produced on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> themselves. If their magnetism be greatly deranged by the sun's position, it may throw the magnetic centre away from the centre of the needle's motion, and thus produce a very small change of position. But if this be the cause, we should expect differences in different needles. Van Swinden says, that there are such, and that they are very great; but as he has not specified them, we cannot draw any conclusion. But, besides this regular diurnal variation, there is another, which is subjected to no rule. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> borealis is observed (in Europe) to disturb the needle exceedingly, sometimes drawing it several degrees from its position. It is always observed to increase its deviation from the meridian, that is, an aurora borealis makes the needle point more westerly. This disturbance sometimes amounts to six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> degrees, and is generally observed to be greatest when the aurora borealis is most remarkable. The observation of the connection of the polarity of the needle with the aurora borealis occurred to the late Professor Robison in 1759, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDSHIPMAN">midshipman</a> on board the Royal William in the river St Lawrence. The point of the heavens to which all the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> converged was precisely that which was opposite to the south end of the dipping needle. This is a very curious phenomenon, and we have not been able to find any connection between this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a> and the position of a magnetic needle. It is to be observed, that a needle of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> or wood, or any substance except iron, is not affected. We long thought it an electric phenomenon, and that the needle was affected as any other body balanced in the same manner would be; but a copper needle would then be affected. We see the needle frequently disturbed both from its general annual position, and from the change made on it by the diurnal variation. This is probably the effect of aurora borealis which are invisible, either on account of thick <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> or daylight. Van Swinden says, he seldom or never failed to observe aurora borealis immediately after any anomalous motion of the needle; and concluded that there had been one at the time, though he could not see it. Since no needle but a magnetic one is affected by the aurora borealis, we may conclude that there is some natural connection between this meteor and magnetism. This should farther incite us to observe the circumstance above mentioned, viz., that the south end of the dipping needle points to that part of the heavens where the rays of the aurora appear to. Variation to converge. We wish that this were diligently observed in places which have very different variation and dip of the mariner's needle. For the diurnal and this irregular variation, consult the Dissertations of Celsius and of Hiotter, in the Memoirs of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>; Wargentin, Philosophical Transactions, vol. xlviii.; Braun (Comment. Petropol. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVI">Novi</a>, tom. v. vii. ix.); Graham and Canton as above.

VARIETY

Pages 145-145

a change, succession, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, in the appearance or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of things; in opposition to uniformity. Variety, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, is a change in some less essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, size, pubescence or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. —Externally; by the plaiting or interweaving of the branches—by bundling or uniting of several stalks into one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> flat one; by the greater breadth, or narrowness, or curling of leaves—by becoming awnless, or smooth, or hirtute. Internally; by becoming mutilated in the corolla; or having one larger than ordinary—by luxuriancy, multiplication, or fulness—by becoming proliferous, or crested—by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> bulbs instead of seeds—or being viviparous. The usual causes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> are, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, exposure, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, winds, culture.

VARIX

Pages 145-145

in Medicine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of a vein, arising from the too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thickness of the blood.

VARNISH

Pages 147-148

which gives them a smoothness and lustre. Melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> is generally used for the first, and flint for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. See GLAZING. Varnish, among medalists, signifies the colours antique medals have acquired in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> alone is able to give to medals, and art has never yet attained to counterfeit, enhances the value of them; that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> which certain foils in which they have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> lain tinges the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> withal: some of which are blue, almost as beautiful as the turquoise; others with a certain shining polished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, vastly finer than Brafii figures. The most usual varnish is a beautiful green, which hangs to the finest strokes without effacing them, more accurately than the finest enamel does on metals. No metal but <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> is susceptible of this; for the green rust that gathers on silver always spoils it, and it must be got off with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lemon juice. Fallifiers of medals have a false or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> varnish, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> on their counterfeits, to give them the appearance or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of being antique. But this may be discovered by its softness; it being softer than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> varnish, which is as hard as the metal itself. Some deposit their spurious metals in the earth for a considerable time, by which means they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> a sort of varnish, which may impose upon the less knowing; others use false <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">ammonia</a>, and others burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>.

VARRO

Pages 148-148

MARCUS TERENTIUS, the most learned of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was born 28 years B.C. He was a senator of the first distinction, both for birth and merit; and bore many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offices. He was an intimate friend of Cicero; and this friendship was confirmed and immortalized by a mutual dedication of their learned works to each other. Thus Cicero dedicated his Academic Questions to Varro; and Varro dedicated his treatise on the Latin tongue to Cicero. In the civil wars he was zealously attached to Pompey; but after his defeat soon submitted to Caesar, who was reconciled to him. Afterwards he applied his whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to letters, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the Greek and Latin <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> at Rome. He was above 70 when Antony proscribed him; however, he found means to escape and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, though he could not save some of his works and his library from being plundered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. After this storm was over, he pursued his studies as usual; and Pliny relates, that he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and to write when he was 88 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was 80 when he wrote his three books De re Rustica, which are still extant. Five of his books De lingua Latina, which he addressed to Cicero, are all extant. There remain, too, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> fragments of his works, particularly of his Menippean Satires, which are medleys of prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; and Scaliger has collected some of his epigrams from among the Catalepta Virgili. His books De lingua Latina, and De re Rustica, were printed with the notes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger, Turnebus, and Victorius, by Henry Stephens at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1573, in 8vo, and have been published separately since among the Autores de lingua Latina, and the Autores de re Rustica. There was another Varro of antiquity, called Atacinus, who was born about 10 years after the first, at a small town near <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>.
