Though infinitely below the Roman in learning, he was at least as good, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not a better, poet; which perhaps has made Lillius Gyraldus and other critics confound them. He composed many works in verse; some fragments of which were collected, and published with those of other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, at Lyons in 1603. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> works were, A poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Sequani, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>; and the Astronomics, that went under the name of Planciades the grammarian. But the Argonautics, in four books, was what gained him the greatest reputation: and though indeed nothing but a translation of Apollonius Rhodius, yet was so well done as to be commended by Quintilian.

VARRONIA

Pages 148-148

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clafs pentandria, and arranged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system under the 4th order, Alperifoliace. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VASSAL

Pages 148-148

in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> customs, signified a tenant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> feudatory; or person who vowed fidelity and homage to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, on account of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, &c., held of him in fee; also a slave or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, and especially a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>.—Vassallus is said to be quasi inferior socius; as the vassal is inferior to his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and must serve him; and yet he is in a manner his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, because each of them is obliged to the other. See FEUDAL System.

VATICAN

Pages 148-148

a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the pope in Rome, which is said to consist of several thousand rooms; but the parts of it most admired are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> staircase, the pope's apartment, and especially the library, which is one of the richest in the world, both in printed books and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>.

VAUBAN

Pages 148-148

SEBASTIAN LE PRESTRE, SEIGNEUR DE, marshal of France, and the greatest engineer that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> ever produced, was born in 1628. He displayed his knowledge of fortification in the course of many sieges, and his services were rewarded with the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> honours. He was made governor of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LILLE">Lille</a> in 1668, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> general of the fortifications of France in 1678, governor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> in 1689, and a marshal of France in 1703. He died in 1707, after having brought the arts of attacking and defending fortified places to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection unknown before. His writings on these subjects are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem.

VAUDOIS

Pages 148-149

Valdenses, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Waldenses, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of reformers, who made their first appearance about the year 1160. The origin of this famous sect, according to Mosheim, was as follows: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, an opulent merchant of Lyons, surnamed Valdensis, or Validifius from Vaux or Waldum, a town in the marquisate of Lyons, being extremely zealous for the advancement of true piety and Christian knowledge, employed a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> called Stephanus de Eoifa, about the year 1160, in translating from Latin into French the four Gospels, with other books of Holy Scripture, and the most remarkable sentences of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> doctors, which were so highly esteemed. Vandots UBI VEE esteemed in this century. But no sooner had he perused these sacred books with a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, than he perceived that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> which was now taught in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, differed totally from that which was originally inculcated by Christ and his apostles. Struck with this glaring <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> between the doctrines of the pontiffs and the truths of the Gospel, and animated with zeal, he abandoned his mercantile vocation, distributed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> (whence the Waldenses were called poor men of Lyons), and forming an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> with other pious men, who had adopted his sentiments and turn of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, he began in the year 1180 to assume the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a public teacher, and to instruct the multitude in the doctrines and precepts of Christianity. Soon after Peter had assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his ministry, the archbishop of Lyons, and the other rulers of the church in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, vigorously opposed him. However, their opposition was unsuccessful; for the purity and simplicity of that religion which these good men taught, the spotless innocence that shone forth in their lives and actions, and the noble contempt of riches and honours which was conspicuous in the whole of their conduct and conversation, appeared so engaging to all such as had any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of true piety, that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their followers daily increased.—They accordingly formed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assemblies, first in France, and afterwards in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, from whence they propagated their sect throughout the other provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> with incredible rapidity, and with such invincible fortitude, that neither fire, nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, nor the most cruel inventions of merciless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, could damp their zeal, or entirely ruin their cause.

VAULT

Pages 149-149

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, an arched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, so contrived that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> which form it sustain each other. Vaults are on many occasions to be preferred to sloping <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flat ceilings, as they give a greater height and elevation, and are besides more firm and durable. VAYER. See Mothe.

VEDAS

Pages 149-149

the sacred books of the Hindoos, believed to be revealed by God, and called immortal. They are considered as the fountain of all knowledge <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> and divine, and are four in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; of which we have the following account in the first volume of the Asiatic Researches: The Rigveda consists of five sections; the Yajurveda of eighty five; the Samaveda of a thousand; and the Atharvaveda of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>; with eleven hundred sāhas, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branches, in various divisions and subdivisions. The Vedas in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> are infinite; but have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> reduced to this number and order: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them is that which explains the duties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in a methodical arrangement; and in the fourth is a system of divine ordinances. From these are reduced the four Upavedas, the first of which was delivered to mankind by Brahma, Indra, Dhanwantari, and five other deities; and comprises the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of disorders and medicines, with the practical methods of curing diseases. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> consists of music, invented for the purpose of raising the mind by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to the felicity of the Divine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; the third treats of the fabrication and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of arms; and the fourth of sixty-four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> arts. Of however little value we may esteem the mechanical arts of the Hindoos, and however desppicable their theological system may really be, the Upaveda, which treats of diseases and the method of curing them, surely deserves to be studied by every European physician practising in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. There are indeed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of medical books in the Sanscrit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; for though the theories of their authors may be groundless and whimsical, they contain the names and descriptions of many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and minerals, with their uses, discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, in the cure of diseases.

VEDETTE

Pages 149-149

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, a centinel on horseback, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s head towards the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where any danger is to be feared, and his carbine advanced, with the butt-end against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> thigh. When the enemy has encamped, there are vedettes posted at all the avenues, and on all the rising grounds, to watch for its security. To VEER and HAUL, to pull a rope tight, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> it in and slackening it alternately, till the body to which it is applied acquires an additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, like the increased vibrations of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a>, so that the rope is tightened to a greater tension with more facility and dispatch. This method is particularly used in hauling the bowlines. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is said to veer and haul when it alters its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and becomes more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less fair. Thus it is said to veer aft and to haul forward.

VEER

Pages 149-150

Ter-Veer, anciently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>-Veer, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> in the United Provinces, standing at the mouth of the East Schelde, about four miles from Middleburgh, and eight from Flushing. Veer, in Dutch, signifies a passage <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ferry over an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or a river; and as there was once a ferry here over the Schelde to the village of Compen, on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Beveland, the town thereby got the name of Veer, Camp-Veer, and Ter-Veer. It is well fortified, and formerly enjoyed a good trade, especially to Scotland; the natives enjoying particular privileges here. The harbour is very good, and the arsenal the best furnished in the world. Hence the Veres, anciently earls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, are said to have derived both their origin and name.

VEERING

Pages 150-150
or WEARING, the operation by which a ship, in changing her course from one board to the other, turns her stern to windward. Hence it is used in opposition to TACKING, wherein the head is turned to the wind and the stern to leeward. See SEAMANSHIP.

VEGA

Pages 150-159

LOPEZ DE, a celebrated Spanish poet. He was the son of Felix de Vega and Francisca Fernandez, who were both descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> families, and lived in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. Our poet was born in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> on the 25th of November 1562. He was, according to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, a poet from his cradle; and beginning to make verses before he had learned to write, he used to bribe his elder school-fellows with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his breakfast, to commit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> he had composed. Having lost his father while he was yet still a child, he engaged in a frolic very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to a lively boy, and wandered with another lad to various parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, till, having spent their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and being conducted before a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> at Segovia for offering to sell a few trinkets, they were sent home again to Madrid. Soon after this adventure, our young poet was taken under the protection of Geronimo Manrique, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVILA">Avila</a>, and began to distinguish himself by his dramatic compositions, which were received with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause by the public, though their author had not yet completed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>: for, after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he became a member of the university of Alcala, where he devoted himself for four years to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He was then engaged as secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alva, and wrote his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> in compliment to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>: who is frequently mentioned in his occasional poems. He quitted that employment on his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Isabel de Urbina, a lady (says his friend and biographer Perez de Montalvan) beautiful without artifice, and virtuous without affectation. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> was soon interrupted by a painful incident:—Having written some lively verses in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of a person who had taken some injurious freedom with his character, he received a challenge in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>; and happening, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUEL">duel</a> which ensued, to give his adversary a dangerous wound, he was obliged to fly from his family, and shelter himself in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>. He resided there a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but connubial affection recalled him to Madrid. His wife died in the year of his return. His affliction at this event led him to relinquish his favourite studies, and embark on board the Armada which was then preparing for the invasion of England. He had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> who served in that fleet as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>; and being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> in an engagement with some Dutch vessels, his virtues were celebrated by our afflicted poet, whose heart was peculiarly alive to every generous affection. After the ill success of the Armada, the disconsolate Lopez de Vega returned to Madrid, and became secretary to the marquis of Malpica, to whom he has addressed a grateful sonnet. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of this patron he passed into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Lemos, whom he celebrates as an inimitable poet. He was once more induced to quit his attendance on the great, for the more inviting comforts of a married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> choice was Juana de Guardio, of noble birth and singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. By this lady he had two children, a son who died in his infancy, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> named Feliciana, who survived her father. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his little boy is said to have hastened that of his wife, whom he had the misfortune to lose in about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years after his marriage. Having now experienced the precariousness of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> enjoyments, he devoted himself to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> life, and fulfilled all the duties of it with the most exemplary piety: still continuing to produce an astonishing variety of poetical compositions. His talents and virtues procured him many unlooked-for honours. Pope Urban VIII. sent him the crosiers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>, and appointed him to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of profit in the Apostolic Chamber; favours for which he expressed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> by dedicating his Corona Tragica (a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> poem on the fate of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Scots) to that liberal pontiff. In his 73rd year he felt the approaches of death, and prepared himself for it with the utmost composure and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. His last hours were attended by many of his intimate friends, and particularly his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> patron the duke of Sessa, whom he had made his executor; leaving him the care of his daughter Feliciana, and of his various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>. The manner in which he took leave of those he loved was most tender and affecting. He said to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> and biographer Montalvan, That true fame consisted in being good: and that he would willingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> all the applause he had received to add a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of virtue to the actions of his life. Having given his dying benediction to his daughter, and performed the last ceremonies of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he expired on the 25th of August 1635. VEGETABLE PHYSIOLOGY.—Under the article <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>, and also under PLANT, we have already delivered some of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> received doctrines on this subject. But as some late investigations seem to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to new views with regard to the structure and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of vegetables, we have thought it necessary to resume the subject, and to give as full a detail of the experiments and observations to which we allude as our limits <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> permit: we shall first treat of the structure, and secondly of the physiology of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. I. STRUCTURE OF PLANTS.—In considering the structure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> anatomy of plants, we shall treat, 1st, of the root; 2d, of the stem and branches; 3d, of the leaves; and 4th, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; in the order in which they are now enumerated. 1. The Root.—The root is that organ belonging to vegetables by which they are supplied with nourishment, and by which they are fixed to a commodious situation. It was formerly supposed to be composed of outer and inner bark, of wood and of pith; but Mrs Ibbetson, who has lately communicated* to the public the results of an elaborate Vegetable elaborate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of experiments on this subject, thinks Phyliology, that it is wholly composed of the rind much thickened, with perhaps a very little of the outer bark, but no inner bark; of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wood, hardly any pith, and no spiral vessels. Mrs Ibbetson searched in vain for the larger vessels of the inner bark, till it occurred to her that the want of this bark accounted for there being no leaves on the root. Mrs Ibbetson had often been as- sured that roots were found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> leaves, but on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of these supposed roots, she found that they were branches which crossed the root. The root consists of the caudex, stock or main body, and of the radicule or fibres which arise from the cau- dex, and are the organs by which the moisture is imme- diately imbibed. In botanical terminology, we generally consider all that part of a plant which is under ground as the root; but Linné comprehends under his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, what we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> the body or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the plant; and he went so far as to call the stems of trees "roots above ground"; but as Dr Smith justly remarks, this seems paradoxical and scarcely correct. Dr Smith adds, that perhaps it would be more accurate to call the caudex a subterra- neous stem; although he is rather inclined to think that it has functions distinct from the stem, analogous to di- gestion; for there is evidently a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> of the root, at least the secre- ted ones, and those of the rest of the plant. In botanical physiology, by the term root, is often un- derstood the parts only which serve to keep the plants firm in the ground; thus the bulbous and fleshy roots as they are called, are strictly speaking, not roots; the radicules or fibres being the real roots. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of roots is various; they are either annual, biennial, or perennial. 2. The Stems and Branches.—Linné long ago divided the stems of trees into four parts; the rind, the bark, the wood, and the pith; and nearly a similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> has been adopted by most vegetable physiologists till the present time. Mrs Ibbetson (aided by a powerful solar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>), however, thinks that nature <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out a more regular division, a division marked not only by the form, but by the difference of the juices, with which the parts are swelled. Mrs Ibbetson divides the stem of trees into six parts: 1. The rind; 2. The bark and inner bark; 3. The wood; 4. The spiral nerves; 5. The nerves or circle of life (corona of Hill); and 6. The pith. 1. Of the rind.—Mrs Ibbetson conceives the rind to be merely an outward covering to the tree, which pre- vents its juices from being evaporated by the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. The rind is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under ground; but it may be as useful there to prevent the entrance of the dust and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, the pressure of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, or the injury of insects. The rind is composed of two rows of cylinders, with a single line to divide them. The cylinders are filled with a gelatinous liquor. There are seldom more than four or five layers of vessels in the rind; but it is in ge- neral so covered with parasitic plants, as powdery li- chens, &c., that its thickness is often more than dou- bled. The rind does not appear to be necessary to plants in general, as there are many in which the bark serves as a covering in its stead; but it seems to form an essen- tial part of trees. 2. Of the bark and inner bark.—These parts, though certainly different as to form, contain the same kind of juice; and being so nearly allied, may be treated of as one. From the bark and inner bark the leaves take their origin, as will be shown when we come to treat of the formation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>-bud. Mrs Ibbetson conceives that the juice of the bark is the blood of the tree. In the bark alone are produced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, the resins, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, &c.; in short all that belongs to the tree; gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> to it; all that makes one plant differ from another, and all its virtues, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the expression may be used. The bark is generally green; the inner bark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, or green. The former consists of vessels crossing each other; the latter of bundles of vessels of two sizes. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels consist of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cylinders, having a bottom with a hole in it, through which the liquid passes, though not with perfect ease. Mrs Ibbetson says that on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> several pieces of the inner bark to the solar microscope, the moment the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> fell on the specimen, the juice, which had before proceeded up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> rather slowly, was sud- denly propelled forward with a force truly astonishing. When the heat and light were increased by causing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of the rays to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the vessels, the side divi- sions of the vessels were broken through, thus inundat- ing the specimen; but when a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of light and heat was kept up, it was curious to observe the liq- uid passing from pipe to pipe, in one regular and easy flow, making only a short stop as it filtered through the straitened apertures at the bottom of the vessels. Mrs Ibbetson has often stood for more than an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> watch- ing the current, (which passes, however, much slower than the sap does), nor could she perceive while the heat and light were on it, that it required any addi- tional expedient to hasten its momentum; but during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and darkness of night, she supposes that the pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> grain mentioned by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a>, may very likely assist its flow, as it is at night that the bastard grain is pressed against the cylinders. The bastard grain is found however only in the wood; but the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> at the bottom of the large vessels of the inner bark, may probably serve the same purpose, the impetus of the current being increased by the lessening of the apertures of the vessels. The vessels of the inner bark are very thick in pro- portion to their size, and there is placed in them a pec- uliar circular body, which resembles a cullender full of holes too small that no liquid could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through. In viewing the thick juice which runs through these pipes, Mrs Ibbetson observed many bubbles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the size of which was increased or diminished according to the tempera- ture; and as their size varied, so was the flow of the liquid accelerated or retarded. To see these vessels well, the specimens may be placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> which is to be fastened in a running stream for some time, or boiled thoroughly, and then thrown into green wax per- fectly melted. Mirel says that "some plants have the same juices in every part of them:" but Mrs Ibbetson does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>- cide with his idea, for she did not find it to be so; though the potent smell of the liquid belonging to the bark often extends to other parts of the plant, yet it gener- ally vanishes if kept separate for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, or becomes so Vegetable faint in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the real liquid of the bark as to prove that it does not form an ingredient of these parts. Mirbel says that the cylinders of the inner bark are merely vacancies of the ordinary vessels; but Mrs Ibbetson states that they are exactly the same as these vessels, and occupy the same place. They have a peculiar shape, being unlike any other vessels of the tree, and they perform a particular office. The vessels of the bark are smaller, and more simple than those of the inner bark, and are divided by a line or two, running longitudinally between them. 3. Of the Wood.—This is a very obvious part. Place the item of any plant in a coloured liquid, and every vessel which conveys the sap from the earth to the top of the tree will be tinged. The sap is a thin watery liquor, probably medicated from the earth, in order to become suitable for the life of vegetables. Mrs Ibbetson supposes that the sap may vary with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, though on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> she has never found that change which might have been suspected. If we make a transverse section of the stem of a tree, two different kinds of layers present themselves in the wood; some running in a circular manner, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> call the silver grain; and others from the circumference to the centre, which they denominate the bastard grain. Linne long ago believed that one of the circular layers was added to the tree each year. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> has often been controverted, and among others by Duhamel and Mirbel; but Mrs Ibbetson has had an opportunity of verifying the accuracy of Linne's opinion. She also observed that the layer was large or small according to the exposure of the tree, and the favourableness of the season: thus in exposed situations, the circles taken as a whole, were much narrower than in trees not exposed. In some trees she noticed only half of a circular layer. Mrs Ibbetson thinks the bastard stripe consists of two lines or strings, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> between them; and they appear from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> susceptibility to be formed of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-like substance as the spiral vessels, which we are immediately to notice. Mr Knight merely calls them scales; but as he mentions their pressing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> (which they certainly do) to the cylinders at night, and during cold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, it is obvious (whichever of the opinions we adopt) that the bastard grains are capable of supplying the place of the sun's rays, by their pressure. The wood-vessels are far more simple in structure than those of the bark; they are very narrow cylinders, and the two rows next to the corona are covered by the spiral vessels. It is indeed difficult to determine the exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the spiral vessels even with the assistance of the solar microscope, for it is by unwinding them alone that they can be known; and their extreme fineness confuses, in consequence of which they have been taken for sap vessels. Neither Mr Knight nor Mirbel was led into this mistake, and Mrs Ibbetson thinks that there can be no doubt that these vessels (formerly so called) are <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> strings which hold no liquid. The vessels of the wood may be best seen in slices of the stems of young trees; and if not very visible when recently cut, they will soon become so if the slices are kept in a dry place. If the wood-vessels are cut longitudinally and observed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> magnifier, as soon as the light is permitted to come on the glass, the flow of sap will be accelerated, and with perfect ease will run up vessels so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> that to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> them is almost impossible. A few of the wood-vessels are separated and run with the spiral vessels to each leaf, in order to nourish it, as will be more particularly noticed when we come to treat of the leaf-bud. But little of the sap, however, passes off in this way from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> current, which flows on; its chief purpose being to form the stamen and the pollen appertaining to it, and afterwards to lend its principal aid to the formation of the fruit and seed. 4. The spiral vessels are a quantity of solid strings coiled up into a spiral form. Mrs Ibbetson supposes them to be formed of a leather-like substance, and, as already mentioned, to be rolled round the wood. In this spiral manner they run up the stems of trees and plants of every kind, (with a few exceptions) and from thence into every leaf and flower. These spiral cords are finly too small to be observed by the naked eye. They run into every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a> of the leaf, and are fastened to its edges, thus croiling among the vessels in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> like a spider's web; by which disposition they can draw the leaves in any way that is necessary for them. The larger of the interior wood-vessels are each supplied with sets of ten or twelve spiral cords, but the smaller of these have only three or four to each. In the cabbage leaf and in the burdock, the spiral cords may be found in bundles almost as thick as a packthread, but in smaller leaves they are properly proportioned. These spiral cords, Mrs Ibbetson thinks, are the cause of the motions of plants. See Plant, p. 601, where these cords are called air-vessels. 5. Of the corona or circle of life.—The next part to be noticed is the small circle of vessels situated between the wood and the pith, the importance of which, in the formation of the seed, will be noticed under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">Impregnation</a> of the Seed; where are also related strong proofs to show that a plant cannot exist a day without the corona, and that if a young plant be deprived of this part, it will not grow again, though it will certainly do so if the plant be somewhat old. It is very curious that almost every botanical anatomist should have figured this part, without giving it a name, or noticing it particularly; and that these anatomists should have attributed all its powers to the pith, which, from the short term of its existence, and its being perpetually impeded in its progress to make way for the flower-bud, can evidently have but little influence. The circle of life, however, has not escaped the notice of Hill, who termed it the corona. The circle of life consists of rows of little cylinders which have their own peculiar juice, generally of an astringent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. From the corona all branches take their rise, and from it all wood threads grow. The cylinders of which it is composed run up into all flower-buds, but never approach the leaf-bud as is represented by fig. 1 and 2.; when these cylinders enter the flower-bud, they make their way distinctly to each separate flower. Vegetable flower, forming the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a>, and after depositing in each physiology, vide the line, which is the first origin of life, they are afterwards impregnated, or acquire the power of giving life by the juice of the stamen, which runs through the same string into the seed. That the principal vitality of the plant resides in the corona, we think is proved by the experiments and observations of Mrs Ibbetson under Impregnation of Seed, and seems to be farther confirmed by the following remarks. When a branch is cut from a tree, or a tree is torn up, the corona or circle of life is the first part that dies; and if, after a sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, we examine the flowers of a fruit tree, we shall find that neither the calyx, the corolla, the filaments, nor the seeds are hurt, but that the pistils are destroyed. And if we now observe the pistils with care, we shall see that it is the line of life which is decayed, and that this is the first part in which mortification commences. The peculiar liquor of the pistil acquires a blood-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and the vessels which run up to the stigma become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, instead of their natural yellow colour. If in wood, this line is injured (either by the decay of the bark or other means) the circle will undulate into a thousand forms, for the purpose of regaining a healthy situation in which it may pursue its course. Mrs Ibbetson, to prove the power of the circle of life, relates the following observations respecting the pod reptans. She had often measured in winter, seven or eight yards of this grass, which appeared perfectly dead; and yet in May or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, she perceived life in it at the most distant end from the stalk. Next <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> she took up two of these creeping branches which were much alike; and on dissecting one of them through its whole length, she found in it a collection of little vessels not thicker than a very fine thread. This collection of vessels had run about half way the length of the branch, which was about three yards. Mrs Ibbetson having merely opened the cover of the grass, laid it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> again, and the little vessels continued increasing till they reached the end of the branch, when they made a stop, and it was perceived that the grass began to thicken; and at the end nearest the roots, the dead part became inflated with juice, lost by degrees its dead appearance, thickened about the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> within, and at last shot forth fresh leaves and fresh roots from every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>. Mrs Ibbetson has since watched with the greatest care, and found that the fine thread which runs through the grass protected by the dead scale, was the circle of life. When this thread is stopped by the covers decaying, it waits till the season permits the rest of the plant to grow. From what has been said, it is evident that the dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> may be inflated with a living juice, and live itself again, provided the life near the stem of the plant be not extinguished. Mrs Ibbetson has observed this to happen in many plants, as in hydrangea, in which the stalks apparently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> down and are inflated again, or at least a part of them. 6. Pith.—Linnaeus considered the pith of plants as of equal importance with the spinal marrow of animals; but Mrs Ibbetson thinks this part of but little consequence, and transfers this importance to the circle of life, which she compares to the brain and spinal marrow. She conceives that the pith forms merely a source of moisture for the plant when required. The pith flops with every flower-bud, and begins again to grow as soon as the bud is past; it decreases as the strength and size of the tree increase; it is the only part of the tree which is devoid of vessels; it is merely a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, not a bundle of cylinders, and is commonly of a remarkably splendid or silver white colour. It has been said that the pith affumes a variety of figures, but Mrs Ibbetson thinks this is a mistake, though she admits a few different sorts. All young trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> are provided with pith; but in the progress of their growth they need it no longer, the wood being a good substitute. On the same account, in general, we find no pith in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> plants, which have a hollow stem, and rarely suffer from drought. Linnaeus thought that the pith was the seat of life and the source of vegetation; or in a word, the primary part of the plant. Duhamel considered it as of but little importance at all. Wildenow and Knight concur with Mrs Ibbetson in regarding it as a reservoir of moisture for the young plants; and Dr Smith holds a medium opinion between that of Linnaeus and the other authors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> named. He says "there is in certain respects an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between the medulla of plants, and the nervous system of animals; it is no less affluently protected than the spinal marrow; it is branched off and diffused through the plant, as nerves through the animal. Hence it is not absurd to presume that it may in like manner give life and vigour to the whole, though by no means, any more than nerves, the organ or source of nourishment." We were somewhat surprised to find that Mrs Ibbetson had not particularly noticed the cellular tissue as a distinct part to be seen in the stems of trees, as it has been long known; we shall therefore subjoin a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it. It is a succulent cellular substance, generally of a green colour, at least in the leaves and branches. Duhamel long ago called it enveloppe cellulaire, and Mirbel more lately, tissu herbeux. Duhamel supposed that the cellular tissue formed the cuticle, or epidermis; but this is not very probable, as his own experiments show that when the cuticle is removed, the cellular integument exfoliates, at least in trees, or is thrown off in consequence of the injury, and a new cuticle, covering a new layer of the cellular tissue, is formed under the old one. This substance is very universal, even in mosses and ferns. Leaves consist almost entirely of a plate of this substance, covered on each side by the cuticle. The stems and branches both of annual and perennial plants are invested with it; but in woody plants it is dried up, and reproduced almost continually, such parts only having that reproductive power. The old layers remain, are pushed outward by the new ones, and form at length the rugged dry dead covering of the old trunks of trees. The cellular integument is a part of plants of the greatest importance; for in it the juices of plants are operated on by light, air, &c. With regard to the branches of trees, it has been already noticed, that they derive their origin from the corona; and they are composed exactly of the same parts as the trunks from which they arise. 3. The Leaves.—Mrs Ibbetson has, with the assistance Vegetable ances of the solar microscope, and by great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to this natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, been enabled to give some new and interesting views on this subject. Her opinion respecting the formation of the leaf-bud is, "That leaves are formed or woven by the vessels or cotton that is generally supposed by botanists (to be) placed there to defend the bud from the severities of winter; that these vessels (or cotton) are a continuation of those of the bark and inner bark in the stem of the plant; that these vessels compose the various interlacing branches of the leaf, which are soon filled up by the concentrated and thickened juices of the inner bark, which form the pabulum of the leaf." Mrs Ibbetson says the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of her assertion may be easily seen by dissecting early buds, in which, except two or three, nothing but the cotton-like vessels will be found. She asks then what could be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these vessels? and answers, that to put them within the bud to keep the outside warm is against nature, for it is contrary to nature. The leaf-bud in its first state consists of two or three scales, including a parcel of vessels, which appear like very moist coarse cotton, but when drawn out and placed in the solar microscope, they show themselves to be merely the vessels of the bark and inner bark elongated and curled up in various forms. These vessels are of three kinds like the bark, &c. First, three or four short thick ones which appear to grow from the larger vessels of the inner bark, and through which the thickened juice flows, but with this difference, that the holes are not there. Then there are two smaller-sized vessels, which exactly resemble the smaller vessels of the bark. Mrs Ibbetson has always found the short thick kind of vessels to form the mid-rib of the leaves, and the smaller-sized vessels to compose the interlacing fibres (or vessels) of the other parts of the leaves; and from often comparing the full grown leaf with the leaf of the bud, she feels the most thorough conviction that the latter takes its origin as above noticed. The pabulum of the leaf which lies between the vessels, is composed of that thick juice which runs in the bark or inner bark of the tree, and which does not exist in any other part of it. The pabulum differs essentially from the sap, and may be called the blood of the tree, as it possesses peculiar properties in different trees; thus it is of a gummy nature in one, of a resinous in a second, and of an oily nature in a third, &c. Mrs Ibbetson is not certain whether the pabulum both flows forwards and in a retrograde direction; but she is convinced that the greatest part of it is taken up in forming the leaves. The pabulum of the leaf, after the vessels are arranged and crooked, grows over in bladders, making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> layers with the smaller pipes (vessels), and with the branches of the leaf. Mrs Ibbetson states, that she does not know any tree which gives a more convincing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the formation of the leaves in the bud, than may be seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of November or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. Several different mid-ribs may be taken out at once from the same leaf-bud, which have an innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of extremely fine filken vessels fastened to or growing up from each side of them. When these vessels have become sufficiently interlaced with each other, the pabulum will begin to grow over them, in form of Vegetable small bladders full of a watery-juice; and then larger vessels will <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> over them, which will soon be followed by another row of bladders, and a similar process will go on until the leaf has attained its proper thicknesses. The leaves thus formed are very small, but when once their shape is completed every part of them continues to increase in size. Fig. 6 represents the leaf-bud of the horse-chestnut, as it was examined by Mrs Ibbetson about the month of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>. Mrs Ibbetson next notices the arrangement of the leaves in the buds of different trees; but we shall consider them by and bye. The rolling, folding, or plaiting, &c., of the leaf-bud, it is observed, does not merely take place at once; but to complete the process of budding, it appears that this arrangement of the leaves is repeated several times. During this arrangement the bud-leaves are immersed in the glutinous liquor which runs in the bark (and forms the pabulum); and the pressure of the leaves is very great. By this pressure and the rolling, &c., the leaves are completed; so if a leaf be taken from the bud before this process commences, it may be compared to a piece of cloth before it is dressed; for its back will be obscured by the ends of vessels, which, had it remained in situ, would have been all rubbed off, except the hairs which remain on many plants. We come now to the formation of the edge of the leaf, a curious and beautiful process. The bud if opened will appear full of the glutinous liquor which forms the pabulum, and the leaves arranged in the manner proper to the particular tree from which the bud is taken. If one of the leaves be taken out, the edges (in whatever manner folded) will exhibit a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> row of bubbles, following the fold of the edge of the leaf; and it will appear as if it were let with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRILLIANTS">brilliants</a>. Things being in this state, all that is wanting for the completion of the leaf is the formation of the pores, now to be mentioned. Mrs Ibbetson states that in many hundred forming leaves which she exposed to the solar microscope, she had never once been able to see the pores; which she has often observed after the leaves have completely quitted the bud; and she is uncertain whether this is owing to the greater thickness of the young leaf, and its being covered with more hairs than it is afterwards, which obscure or conceal the pores; or whether it be caused by the upper net-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the leaf growing last. While the upper and under cuticles of the leaf are growing, the edge of it is completing; for the bubbles generally divide, and partly dry up, leaving horny points in their stead. When the edges of the leaves are completely formed, they burst from the bud and assume a different aspect. The vessels of the leaves (those confined within the mid ribs and side ribs of the leaves) are of two sorts, the spiral, and the nourishing. The spiral vessels are those cork-thread-like wires which surround the two last rows of the sap vessels. The nourishing vessels are the only parts formed of the wood. They convey the sap necessary for the support of the leaves, and run on each side of the spiral vessels. To prove that she has given a fair and accurate account of the formation of the leaf, Mrs Ibbet- Vegetable form adds the following remarks. The colour of leaves, the observer, is not to be found in their substance, but in the liquid with which it is filled. The darkest green leaf that can be procured, has both its upper and under cuticles of a perfect white colour. In the cuticle the pores are to be found. A leaf has rather a thicker net below than it has above; but this does not sufficiently account for the varieties of tints in different leaves. The under net (or cuticle) does not lie so close to the pabulum of the leaf as the upper one; which may account for the colour not piercing so much through. When the two nets (or cuticles) are taken off, then the pabulum of the leaf appears. The pabulum is formed of little bladders, filled with a dark-green liquid, and interlaced with vessels. When the pabulum is removed, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of large vessels presents itself; then a collection of bladders; which is followed by the larger lines (or veins) of the leaf. We next meet with another bed of bladders, which is covered by the under cuticle. Though the bladders differ in size and colour as well as in thickness in different leaves, yet the general arrangement is the same in most plants; but there are exceptions, as the firs, grasses, or those grassy leaves of early spring, which we have in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, crocus, snow-drop, &c., for their leaves are of a different nature. But we shall now refer to the figures, which will serve to illustrate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of formation, &c., of the leaf-bud. Fig. 7. 8. 9. Fig. 7, 8, 9, exhibit the commencement of the formation and growth of leaves; \(a, a, a, a\), the mid rib; \(b, b, b\), the young vessels appearing like cotton; \(c, c\), the spiral nerves; \(d\), the smaller vessels crossing each other. Fig. 10. shews the formation of the pabulum; \(e, e\), the fine vessels growing up each side of the mid rib; \(f\), the pabulum. Fig. 11. bud of the lime-tree (tilia Europaea). 4. Of the Flowers, including the calyx, corolla, stamina, and pistillum.—Linnaeus long ago expressed his opinion that each of these parts was formed from a particular part of the stem; thus the calyx was formed by the bark, the corolla by the inner bark, the stamina by the wood, and the pistillum by the pith. Linnaeus also reckoned the pith of a plant (which he considered to be of equal importance with the spinal marrow of animals), as the sole formative organ of the whole vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Linnaeus's idea respecting the formation of the calyx, corolla, &c., has been often refuted; but Mrs Ibbetson comes forward to defend the opinion of the illustrious author with a little modification. She does not, as already noticed, consider the pith as of great importance; she therefore says, that the corona or circle of life forms the pistil, not the pith; and thinks that each part of the stem has, when it arrives near the flower stalk, its peculiar juice. Mrs Ibbetson, as a strong proof that the circle of life forms the pistil, says that it is to be found in all these leaves that bear the flower either on the middle or on their side; but in no other leaves. She first observed this in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, where this circle leads directly up to the flower; then in scopulopendrums, and afterwards in xylophyllus. The leaves of such plants are more woody than any Vegetable others, as every one may know on breaking them. In Phylogeny, such plants also, the circle of life may be traced as leading from one flower to another. Mrs Ibbetson also thinks that all those parts which concur in forming the flower also join in forming the fruit and seed. Mrs Ibbetson then adverts to the opinion of Wildenow, when he says, "we find in the springing flower, elongations of air-vessels, but we never see the elongations from each particular part, one forming the future calyx, another the corolla, and so forth." For instance, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sunflower (Helianthus annuus), where in an immense large receptacle, numerous small flowers are placed, how should these elongations be able to unfold themselves into florets from the bark, inner bark, &c., through such a receptacle? There would arise a confusion amongst these small parts which is never met with." "How should, besides, the stamina be formed in herbs, which are not ligneous, or the pistil in plants which have no pith? Every one may thus easily conceive that all these opinions are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> hypotheses, which may be refuted, even without the aid of anatomical dissection." Mrs Ibbetson attacks Wildenow's opinion, and says that he adduces the fyngenean clasps to prove the accuracy of it, the clasps which contains the very plants that would have proved the mistake of his argument, had he dissected them. Mrs Ibbetson then proposes the following questions to Wildenow. Why, if the nourishment of each part of the stem be not confined to each different part of the flower, does the whole arrangement of the parts alter, the moment it gets to the flower-stalk. Why are there particular vessels to confine and carry the juice to each peculiar part, if it were not of consequence that this juice should touch no other places? For what purpose is the curious and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> management in the bottom and top of a seed-vessel, which enables the dissector to say, that "there are five divisions of little vessels proceeding from the wood; I know, therefore (though I do not see it), that this must be a pentandrian flower; here is but one middle vessel proceeding from the circle of life (for the pith flows), it is therefore of the order monogynia; here are five divisions of little vessels proceeding from the inner bark, it must therefore have five petals?" Mrs Ibbetson wishes others to be convinced of these facts as well as herself. If a cut be made above or below the seed-vessel of a lily, a violet, or a tulip, the thinker conviction of her accuracy will follow. Why in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> above or below the seed-vessel of a fyngenean flower can you directly tell, whether it belong to the order superflua, aquilis, or segregata? Look at the bottom of the seed-vessel of the Sonchus; every <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>-hole of the vessel of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> is carried up by corresponding vessels in the outward cuticle of the seed till it meets and joins the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a> of the males; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> liquor is protruded through the inside of the seed, and is perhaps one of the strongest proofs of the impregnation of the female. In the fyngenean clasps (see fig. 12.), the delicacy of the vessels, which may be supposed too small for a liquid to flow through them, must not impede the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that it does so, when we con- Vegetable fider the circulation of blood in the diminutive animal Physiology that torments the body of the flea or louse. Mrs Ibbetson says she has seen the liquor run up with the utmost celerity through the upper cuticle of a very small seed of a plant belonging to the fyngeneian clas, till it met the male and continued its course. It is to be understood that the juice from the corolla flows in the rest of the cuticle, and that the largest vessels are those for the Fig. 12. 13. the male liquor. See fig. 12. 13. II. PHYSIOLOGY OF PLANTS.—In treating this part of the subject, we propose to consider, first, the impregnation of seeds, and, second, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a> of vegetables. 1. The impregnation of the seed.—The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of what is included under this title, forms one of the most beautiful and interesting pursuits of the vegetable physiologist. Mrs Ibbetson has communicated some curious observations on this subject. Provided with a powerful solar microscope for opaque objects, she proceeds to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the seed, and the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> of the infant plant, or rather of the germ or vessel which precedes it; and she remarks that it is almost impossible to ascertain the exact time when the seed is first formed in the pericarp; but that she has always found it in the winter buds when they were large enough for dissection. It is curious to observe the vessels, which, she says, may properly be called the life, tracing their way to each flower-bud; for a seed may be said to depend for perfection on two separate moments: the one in which the life first enters the seed, when the whole outward form appears to be perfected; and the second, when the impregnation of the seed takes place, by the ripening of the pollen. But when the life enters, it leaves a little string, and remains for a long time afterwards in a torpid state. This string crosses the corculum, or heart of the seed, so called because it is the cradle of the infant plant. She then states that the seed is attached to the feed-vein by two distinct organs, termed by the first botanists the umbilical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, but as she thinks improperly, since they do not convey nourishment to the infant plant, which is wholly the office of the second set of vessels. We cannot agree with Mrs Ibbetson in her opinion; for although the umbilical cord of an infant contains nourishing vessels, it also contains nerves, and yet we would never think of restricting this term alone to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>. The first of the connecting organs Mrs Ibbetson conceives to be the circle of life, first, because without it the plant dies, and, second, because although every other part be eradicated by degrees and the circle of life be uninjured, the plant will grow again. She has made these experiments many thousand times and with the above results. The circle of life consists of delicate simple vessels, which carry a juice of a particular nature, and may be traced in every part lying between the wood and the pith. These vessels are not to be found in the leaf-bud; for they pass by it to the female flower, where they establish a new life in the feed: a life which will enable it to grow, but not to Vegetable give life without impregnation. These vessels are the Physiology, life, therefore, from which all flower-branches grow and all root-threads proceed. In calling these vessels the circle of life, Mrs Ibbetson says the only expression what its office seems to denote. Mrs Ibbetson goes on to describe the next (or second) organ by which the seed is attached to the feed-vein. It consists of the nourishing vessels, which she is inclined to think proceed from the inner bark; at least they may certainly be traced thence after the infant plant has left the seed. When introduced, they enter not the seed at the same place as the life does; they come not into the corculum, but pass it, and spread themselves over a small spot below it, which is visibly of a different nature from the rest of the feed. In farinaceous plants this spot is yellow and yields a milk-white juice; but in other seeds it is white, and gives a glutinous water of a sweetish taste. Mrs Ibbetson thinks it probable that the nourishing vessels come from the fruit filled with this juice, which medicated with that part of the seed (which very apparently dissolves), they together form a nourishment suited to the infant plant. When the seed is far perfected, it remains in an almost torpid state, or growing very little; while the flower expands daily, and the stamens are hastily advancing to their perfect state. It is now that by an almost imperceptible contraction of the lower part of the pistil, the juice is raised to the stigma (A) on which it may be seen hanging in a large glutinous drop, which never falls off. As soon, however, as the mid-day heat abates, this juice, which is peculiar to the pistil, retires again within the tube, the contraction ceasing with the heat that caused it. The same process goes on daily, till the stamens are ripe and ready to give out their interior powder to the pistil, which is always so placed as to receive the greater part of it; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTHER">anther</a> (B) requires only moisture to burst it, it soon yields that fine and imperceptible dust, which quickly melting and mixing with the before-mentioned liquid, forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of so powerful and stimulating a quality, that it no sooner runs down the interior of the style, and touches the nerve of life in the heart of the feed, than this vessel floats forth in the most surprising degree, forming directly a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of circular hook within the void; which in less than two days is often completely filled, though it had perhaps for many weeks before lain in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> torpor. This circular nerve is soon covered by an excrescence that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> it; but if the corculum be divided with a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCET">lancet</a>, the circular hook is discoverable, until the young plant is near leaving its cradle or feed. At the turn of the hook, the cotyledons grow, and the root shoots from the covered end. The plant may be now said to lie in the feed in a contrary direction from that in which it will at a future time grow, since the root is above, and the stem below: but nature has provided for their change of place, since it is effected as they leave the feed. It has been already noticed that the nourishment of the infant plant (A) In the journal it is said "to the pointal;" but certainly stigma is meant, for pistil and pointal are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>. (B) In the journal it is called pollen, but anther must be meant. Vegetable plant is medicated between the juice brought in the nourishing vessels, and the peculiar spot in the feed, forming a liquid which continues to abound; indeed the infant plant may be said to repose in it, till the root has opened the whole or part of the seed. The root then changes its direction, and runs into the earth, soon forming a number of stringy hairs, which serve as so many suckers to draw the liquid nourishment from the earth, while the plant quickly swells, by the rapid progress it makes, the advantage it receives from its change of diet; for it soon rises itself from its prostrate posture, emerges from the seed, and is now seen in its proper direction. The above account, we think Mrs Ibbetson justly remarks, affords a complete <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of the sexual system. In the syngeneian orders, the pistil being mostly single, runs up from the seed; and the juice of the pistil has no other way of reaching the pointal (stigma must be here meant), but by passing through the seed, which it does without producing any effect, or filling up the vacancy at the top of the corculum. But as soon as the juice of the pistil becomes mixed with the pollen, which diffuses in it, the void of the corculum is filled, the hook is soon afterwards formed, and the plant is raised to life. Mrs Ibbetson relates some experiments which she made to ascertain whether the umbilical cord was, or was not, the life of the plant. She placed a bean in the earth, and when the infant plant was ready to leave the seed she opened it with a fine lancet, and cut off the cotyledons, just where they join the heart and the circular hook which have been before described. She then tied a piece of very fine thread round the bean, and replaced it in the earth. The cotyledons grew again, though higher up, but they appeared very weak and sickly for some time. She cut off the root of another bean which had been placed in the earth, and which was of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> as the above, and found that the root grew again in a few days and appeared quite healthy. In a third experiment she separated and cut off the nourishing vessels from each side of the bean; but a great number of hairs grew from the wounded part, which, by attaining moisture from the earth for nourishment, supplied the place of the vessels cut off; so that it was not ascertained whether or not the bean would live independent of these vessels, which was the object of the experiment. We observe here, however, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> provision of nature for the embryo plant: hairs being formed to supply it with moisture when the nourishing vessels are destroyed. Mrs Ibbetson next took a bean which had been about four days in the earth, and opening it with great care took out with a fine lancet the part which she esteems the cord of life, that is the part which crosses the corculum and shot forth on the first impregnation of the plant. oo figs. 14. and 15. represent the nourishing vessels of a bean; L to n two seminal leaves or cotyledons; // the cord of life, which is more easily seen in the seed of the lily, fig. 15. // crossing the empty part of the corculum. Mrs Ibbetson took a flower of the lilium genus, as having a large vessel easily attained; and being careful not to separate it from the nourishing vessels, she divided the line of life fig. 16. //, cutting each thread between the seeds, and fo cutting off their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>; but did not touch oo, which she thinks is the nourishing vessel. The consequence was, that the seeds of this flower were never impregnated. Mrs Ibbetson next tried the effect of taking the nerve of life from the chestnut, the walnut, acorn, &c.; first opening a seed without touching the nerve, that she might be certain that the opening was not the cause of its death. Fig. 17. represents the Fig. 17. heart taken out of a seed of the chestnut; / is the circular hook already described; oo the nourishing vessels, and // the line of life, which was taken out from some seeds where it crosses the heart at m. Fig. 18. is the Fig. 18. seed of the gooseberry; oo the nourishing vessels, e the line of life, and m the corculum or heart. She found that all those seeds from which she took the nerve of life died; and that the others, which had been merely laid open, lived. She remarks that it is only at the beginning of life, that the plant can be killed by this process; for when older, if the nerves of life decay, they shoot out above the declining part, and run into any part of the stem that is pure, to preserve themselves. Mrs Ibbetson then states that this nerve is the source of life in very decayed trees; and is also the cause of a double pith, or at least the appearance of it, in many trees. To observe this line of life, seeds must be examined in their first formation; for when it has done its office, it detaches itself. When the seed is boiled, the line of life and nourishing vessels mark themselves by becoming of a dark colour. 2. Irritability of vegetables.—In entering upon this subject, we ought to warn our readers, that very opposite opinions have been entertained respecting it; some physiologists of the greatest eminence allowing that we have satisfactory proofs of the irritability of vegetables in a variety of plants, but more particularly in the motions of the mimosa, dionea, &c.; while others of no less respectability ascribe these motions to the influence of light, heat, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. As neither muscles nor nerves have ever been demonstrated in the vegetable structure, of course the proofs of the irritability of vegetables are drawn from the intimate analogy which seems to exist between the motions of some plants and those of animals. Some physiologists, from observing the similarity of motions in the two kingdoms, were naturally led to ascribe them to the same cause; others, from not being able to observe the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> organs, namely, muscles, in both kingdoms, denied that plants could possess irritability; a third set, wavering the idea of irritability in the vegetable kingdom, have laboured to shew that the motions of plants depend on mechanical causes alone. We shall first notice the observations of Mrs Ibbetson, who ascribes the motions of plants to the spiral wires which we have described. Her opinion is founded upon a number of new observations made with the solar microscope, which we shall proceed to relate. 1st. The spiral vessels are not to be found in any plants to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is unnecessary. She could not observe these vessels in any of the firs, in any of the plants which spread their leaves upon the surface of the water, in any of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> weeds (c), of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICHENS">lichens</a>, or of the grasses; and she does not think (c) She afterwards excepts the conservae, which have motion. that they exist in the fcolopendrums or leumas. We would here observe that if these observations were completely true, they would certainly afford a strong proof in confirmation of her opinion; but we suspect that they are not altogether just, especially as we observe a discrepancy in the papers of Mrs Ibbetson. Thus at one part she has given us a very minute description of the spiral vessels in the runners of the poa reptans, and now she says they are not to be found in the grases (d). Mrs Ibbetson's second argument is, that if a plant whose leaves present their faces to the light, be turned so that the backs are to the sun, the leaves in a few hours will regain their former position; but if this be often repeated, although the plant will not suffer, yet the leaves will be longer at every repetition in returning to their former situation, or will cease to move at all. She accounts for this by saying, that the spiral-like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> vessels are relaxed by the operation, and lose their power of coiling into their usual form. Others would account for the above fact by saying that the irritability of the plant was exhausted by these repeated and unnatural actions; in the same manner as the mimosa becomes gradually less sensible to impressions when too often renewed. Mrs Ibbetson's third argument is, that those leaves which have most motion, are provided with most spiral vessels, and have these vessels most twisted; as in the populus tremula. Fourth proof. Mrs Ibbetson divided the spiral vessels of a vine leaf while growing, without touching the nourishing vessels; and from that moment it never contracted, and when placed with its back to the light, it did not alter its position, though it was long before it decayed. Both <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol9.html#article-GALVANISM">galvanism</a> cause these leaves to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, by affecting the spiral wires (not the cuticle), for when the leaf is deprived of these vessels it does not contract at all. We would here remark that we suspect much, in the above experiment, that more than the spiral vessels was divided: at any rate there is very great discordance between Mrs Ibbetson's experiments and that of M. Candelierini, who found that vine leaves turned to the light when they were separated from the stem and suspended by a thread. Fifth argument. Mrs Ibbetson observed, when she placed some of the spiral vessels taken from a cabbage leaf upon one end of a long netting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, and caused a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> to approach, that they were much agitated, and at last flung themselves off the needle. We think no conclusion can be drawn from what is here stated. The fresh water convolvulus and the dodder tribe, are the only plants, without leaves, that Mrs Ibbetson is acquainted with, which have spiral vessels.
