Mrs Ibbetson says that the spiral vessels are so very tough, and so very tightly coiled, in the leaf stem (petiole) of the geranium cordifolium, that she has by means of them been enabled to draw up the leaf; but it is difficult to be done. The sixth proof is drawn from the effect produced by moisture on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Kater's hygrometer, which will be noticed soon. General Observations.—Mrs Ibbetson says the spiral Vegetable wires may be considered as a secondary cause of motion, as they are primarily acted upon by light and moisture. By means of the spiral wire, all the movements of plants are made; by it, flowers open in the morning and shut in the evening; the leaves turn, and the creeping plants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> in their regular order. Mrs Ibbetson lays the opening of the flower at a different time of the day, or its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> in a different manner, does not militate against the above statement; as strong light and dry weather produce a contraction of the wire, while darkness and moisture effect a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of it. It depends wholly upon the position in which the spiral wire is placed, whether by its dilatation the flowers shall be opened or shut, as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> the same spring may be made to turn to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or to the left, to open or to shut a box. Most of the flowers which Mrs Ibbetson has observed to close at noon, have an extremely slender corolla, formed only of a double cuticle without palatum; and hence they are soon overcome by heat, and relaxation directly takes place; as in the convolvulus nil, the evening or tree primrose, &c. We must add, however, that we regard this account of the spiral vessels with some degree of doubt. We suspect that the spiral vessels, if they have the power of opening or shutting a flower, will always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in one uniform manner; i.e., if they are able to open it, they will always do so, and vice versa. The nymphaea also raises itself out of the water, and expands, about seven o'clock in the morning; and closes again, reposeful upon the surface, about four in the evening. Now its petals are much thicker than those of the leontodon taraxacum, which floats up its flowers between eight and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in the evening. We could multiply instances; but we conceive we have said enough to shew, that the flowers with the most slender corolla are not uniformly those which soonest close. Mrs Ibbetson says, contrary to the opinion of Mirbel, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in which the spiral vessels are inclosed is capable of being stretched; indeed it is formed of so thin (or rather so loose) a substance, as plainly to be intended to dilate and contract. The case is composed of a very few thin vessels, interlaced with an extremely fine spiral wire; while the larger spiral vessels fill up the case in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> manner, the nourishing vessels form a regular circle of tubes around it. See fig. 29, and 30. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> grass (andropogon contortum of Linne), of which Captain Kater's hygrometer is formed.—The chief part of it is made with the spiral awn of an Indian grass, which readily untwists in a moist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and vice versa. Now Mrs Ibbetson asks, if the most trifling change of moisture can untwist one foot of vegetable fibre, and by this means manage an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, why should not a quantity of similar formed fibres or spiral vessels produce the same effect on leaves and flowers? She says, Captain Kater's hygrometer moves very sensibly if a finger be placed within half an inch of the fibre (awn). Now, the most sensitive plant we have will not move but with the touch." We are quite aware of the effects of moisture on some vegetables. (d) She found the spiral vessels also in the andropogon contortum. We have strong proofs of it in some of the mosses, as in the *bryum hygrometricum*, which, if the fruitstalk be moistened at the bottom, makes three or four revolutions; if the upper part be moistened it turns the contrary way. We can scarcely compare these motions with those of the mimosa; for it is quite evident that they are produced by moisture: but as we are to speak of the motions of the mimosa in a little, we would only observe, that when Mrs Ibbetton says "the sensitive plant will not move but with the touch," she argues against herself; for this shows that it is acted upon by the same causes as animal muscles, and that it is not governed by moisture alone. The only sensitive part of the Indian grass is the awn, which is formed of a leather-like substance, infinitely thicker and stronger than the usual spiral vessels in plants. The awn is formed of two apparently flat pieces, with a cylindric hollow running through the middle, which is filled with a thick spiral wire. Fig. 21, 22, 23, and 24. Each side of the awn is bristled; but the bristles do not add to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. Of the Nettle.—The awn or fling of the nettle is a long pipe with a bag at the end, divided into two parts; the smaller contains the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, and the larger is situated below it. This bag seems also to be composed of a leather-like substance, and is likewise affected by light and moisture. The moment the upper part of the pipe is touched, the under part of the bag whirls up, breaks the poison bladder, and throws its contents violently up the pipe, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the person who touches it.

in general, denotes any thing that carries <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bears another along; but is more particularly used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a> for any liquid serving to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> some medicine, in order that it may be administered more commodiously to the patient.

VEIL

a piece of stuff, serving to cover <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hide anything. In the Romish churches, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, they have veils or curtains over the altar, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a>, images of saints, &c. A veil of crape is worn on the head by nuns, as a badge of their profession: the novices wear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> veils, but those who have made the vows <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> ones. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">Nun</a>.

VEIN

Pages 162-162

among miners, is a fissure in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> flints which contains ore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, caulk, clay, chert, croil, brownhen, pitcher-chert, cur, which the philosophers call the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of all colours. When it bears ore, it is called a quick vein; when no ore, a dead vein.

VELARIUS

Pages 162-162

in antiquity, an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the Roman emperors, being a kind of usher, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> was behind the curtain in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s apartment, as that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>'s was at the entry of the ballustrade; and that of the officarii at the door. The velarii had a superior of the same denomination, who commanded them.

VELEZ-DE-GOMARA

Pages 162-162

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Eriff. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ACARIA. With a harbour and a handsome castle, where the governor resides. It is seated between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 0. N. Lat. 35. 10.

VELI

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Etruria, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and powerful rival of Rome; distant about 100 stadia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 miles, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west; situated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and steep rock. Taken after a siege of 10 years by Camillus, five years before the taking of Rome by the Gauls; and thither the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of their city, had thoughts of removing; but were dissuaded from it by Camillus (Livy). It remained standing after the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and a colony was there settled, and its territory assigned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. But after that it declined gradually, as not to leave a single trace standing. Famous for the slaughter of the 300 Fabii on the Cremera (Ovid). The spot on which it stood lies near Isola, in St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s patrimony (Holstenus).

VELITES

Pages 162-162

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Velites footmen, who were armed lightly with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>, a cask, cuirass, and shield. VELLEJUS PATERCULUS. See PATERCULUS.

VELLUM

Pages 162-162

is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, that is finer, evener, and more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> parchment. The word is formed from the French velin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Latin vitulinus, "belonging to a calf."

VELOCITY

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, swiftness; that affection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> whereby a moveable is disposed to run over a certain space in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. It is also called celerity, and is always <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the space moved. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">Quantity</a>, No. 11 and 14, &c.

VELVET

Pages 162-162

a rich kind of stuff, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, covered on the outside with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, short, fine, soft flage, the other side being a very strong close tissue. The nap <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flage, called also the velvetting, of this stuff, is formed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the threads of the warp, which the workman puts on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow-channelled ruler or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, which he afterwards cuts, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> tool along the channel of the needle to the ends of the warp. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and best manufactories of velvet are in France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>: there are others in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, set up by the French refugees; whereof that at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a> is the most considerable; but they all come short of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of those in France, and accordingly are sold for 10 or 15 per cent. less. There are even some brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; but they are the worst of all.

VENAL

Pages 162-162
or VENOUS, in Anatomy, something that bears a relation to the veins. This word is also used for something bought with money, or procured by bribes.

VENEERING

Pages 162-169

VANEERING, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fineering, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARQUETRY">marquetry</a>, or inlaying, whereby several thin slices or leaves of fine wood, of different kinds, are applied and fastened on a ground of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wood. There are two kinds of inlaying: the one, which is the more ordinary, goes no farther than the making of compartments of different woods; the other requires much more art, and represents <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, birds, and the like figures. The first kind is what we properly call veneering; the latter we have already described under Marquetry. The wood intended for veneering is first sawed out into slices or leaves, about a line thick: in order to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them, the blocks or planks are placed upright in a kind of vice or sawing press: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of which may be seen under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> referred to. These slices are afterwards cut into slips, and fashioned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> ways, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> proposed; then the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> being carefully adjusted, and the pieces brought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to their proper thickness, with several planes for the purpose, they are glued down on a ground or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of dry wood, with good strong English <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>. The pieces thus joined and glued, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> small, is put in a press; if <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, it is laid on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, covered with a board, and pressed down with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, or pieces of wood, one end whereof reaches to the ceiling of the room, and the other bears on the boards. When the glue is quite dry they take it out of the press and finish it; first with little planes, then with divers scrapers, some whereof resemble rasps, which take off dents, &c., left by the planes. When sufficiently scraped, the work is polished with the skin of which... VEN a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-dog, wax, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> and polisher of shave-grafs: which is the last operation.

VENEREAL

Pages 169-169

something belonging to venery; as the lues venerae, &c. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VENERY

Pages 169-169

is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPULATION">copulation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coition, between the two sexes; it has also been employed by old writers as applicable to hunting or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, as beasts of venery.

VENETIAN BOLE

Pages 169-169

a fine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, and called in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> shops Venetian red.—It is dug up in Carinthia, and sent from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to all parts of the world; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it is much superceded by a bright colochoar of vitriol.

VENICE

Pages 169-172

State of, a celebrated republic, which for nearly ten centuries formed one of the most powerful of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> states of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Its dominions lay chiefly along the coasts at the head of the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, comprehending not only a considerable tract round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Venice, but several districts both to the east and west of that sea, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Corfu, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZANTE">Zante</a>, Cephalonia, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERIGO">Cerigo</a>, and some others of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the Archipelago. It was bounded to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, to the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and to the east by Croatia, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Europe. The republic of Venice is said to have taken its rise from a small Italian colony, who in the middle of the 5th century were driven by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTILA">Attila</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Huns from the cities of Aquileia, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, &c., and took refuge in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of small islands where now stands the city of Venice. Here they established themselves, and formed a small independent state, adopting the consular form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> which had so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> prevailed at Rome. By the end of the 5th century they had become of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, and were able to raise and maintain a fleet and a small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. They engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, and distinguished themselves against the Illyrian pirates, and the inhabitants of the neighbouring port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIESTE">Trieste</a>. They also assisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> in his contest with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, and received from him and his general Narses, many marks of favour and distinction. About the year 697, the tribunitian power, which had prevailed in Venice from the end of the 5th century, was abolished, and the states elected a supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, whom they called doge, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>. He was to represent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and majesty of the state; to assemble and preside at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, where he had a casting vote in all disputed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; to nominate to all offices, places, and preferments, and to enjoy the same authority in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> as in the state. Excepting a short intermission of about five years, the power of the doges <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the republic. Under the doges, the power and wealth of the republic continued to increase. In 765, the Heraclians and Gezulans, subjects of the republic, revolted, and threw themselves on the protection of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. That emperor settled them for the present at Malamoe, in the neighbourhood of the Venetian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; but from this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> they were quickly driven by the forces of the republic. Incensed at this affront committed against his authority, Charlemagne ordered his son Pepin to declare war against the Venetians; but as Astolphus king of the Lombards was then laying waste the territories of the church, the troops of Pepin were, by the intrigues of the pope, dispatched against that powerful monarch; and though, on the defeat of Astolphus they marched against the Venetians, it does not appear that the enterprise was productive of either honour or success. The war with Pepin was renewed in 804, on occasion of Obelerio, the doge of Venice, shewing an inclination to favour the Greek emperor Nicephorus against Pepin. Obelerio was related to the French monarch, having married his sister; and as on this account the Venetians were jealous of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of their doge, he was superseded, and Valentin nominated commander in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Pepin had collected a numerous and well appointed army, and had fitted out a fleet to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> against the Venetians by sea. With this formidable force he advanced directly to Venice, but here he was opposed with all the valour of independent citizens fighting for their liberties. The Venetians, however, notwithstanding the most obstinate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, the most vigorous sallies, and their intrepidity selling every inch of ground at an incredible expense of the Venetian blood, were at length reduced to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city nearest south of the Rialto (see the next article); this stream and An. 804. their own bravery, being now their only defence. While Pepin was preparing to throw a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the canal, they resolved, as a last effort, to attack Pepin's fleet, and to vanquish or die in defence of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Embarking all the troops they could spare, they bore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with the advantage of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and tide, upon the enemy, and began the attack with such fury, as obliged the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> to give way. The lightness of their ships, and the knowledge of the foundings, gave the Venetians every advantage they could wish: the enemy's fleet was run <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>, and the greater part of their troops perished in attempting to escape; the ships were all to a few either taken or destroyed. During this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> at sea, Pepin resolved to assault the city by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, not doubting but the garrison was so weakened by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of forces they had sent on board the fleet, as to be able to make but a slight resistance. Having for this purpose thrown a bridge over the Rialto, he was marching his troops across it, when he found himself attacked on every side by the Venetians from their boats, and others who had posted themselves on the bridge. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was long, bloody, and doubtful, until the Venetians employed all their power to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> down the bridge; which at last yielded to their obstinate endeavours, a prodigious slaughter of the French ensued; they fought, however, like men in despair, seeing no hopes of safety but in victory; but all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> being cut off with the troops on shore, they were to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> either killed or drowned. The number of slain was so great, that the space between the Rialto and Malamoe was covered with dead bodies, and has ever since gone by a name expressive of the prodigious slaughter. Pepin was so struck with the intrepidity of the Venetians, that he raised the siege, abandoned the enterprise, and concluded a peace with the republic. In 839, the Venetians engaged in an offensive and defensive <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> against the Saracens, with the Greek Venetian emperor Michael, to whose alliance they sent a fleet of sixty galleys. In an engagement which took place between the allied fleets and that of the Saracens, the former... mer were completely defeated, and almost all the Venetian galleys were either taken or destroyed. On the news of this defeat, the capital was thrown into the greatest consternation, justly dreading an attack from the victorious Saracens. This alarm, however, soon subsided, on finding that the barbarians had turned off on the side of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>. The city now became a prey to internal dissension. Popular tumults were frequent, and in one of these the doge was murdered. By the prudent and vigorous administration of a succeeding doge, Orso Participato, good order was re-established, and at the commencement of the 10th century, the reputation of the republic for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> prowess was much advanced by a victory gained over the Huns, who had invaded <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and defeated Berengarius. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 11th century, Venice began to make a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> among the states of Europe, having acquired the sovereignty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> and Croatia, with which in 1084 they were formally invested by the Constantinopolitan emperor. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a crusade, or holy war against the Saracens, was preached up by the emissaries of the pope, and the Venetian republic engaged in the undertaking with such ardour, as to equip a fleet of 200 sail, under the command of the doge Vitalis Michael. Before he failed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, however, the doge found it necessary to chastise the Pisans, whom he defeated in a terrible engagement. He then sailed for Asia, at that time besieged by the Christian forces, and it was chiefly by his valour that that city, as well as Caesarea and Tiberias, fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. From these victories he was recalled to repel an invasion of Dalmatia by the Normans, whom he also defeated, carrying off considerable booty. His successor assisted Baldwin in the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a>, but was defeated and killed in attempting to quell a rebellion of the Croatians. Under the government of Domenico Micheli, who succeeded Ordelapho, the pope's nuncio arrived at Venice, and excited such a spirit of enthusiasm among all ranks and degrees of men, that they strove whose names should be first enrolled for the holy war. The doge, having fitted out a fleet of 60 galleys, sailed with it to Joppa, which place the Saracens were at that time besieging. The garrison was reduced to the last extremity when the Venetian fleet arrived, which surprized and defeated that of the enemy with great slaughter; soon after which the Saracens raised the siege with precipitation. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> was next besieged, and soon was obliged to capitulate; on which occasion, as well as on the taking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a>, the Venetians shared two-thirds of the spoils. While the doge was absent on those important affairs, the emperor of Constantinople, jealous of the growing power of the Venetians, resolved to take advantage of their apparent incapacity to resist an attack at home. The Venetians, however, had timely notice of his approach, and instantly recalled the doge, who on his return laid waste and destroyed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round Chios, seized on the islands of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROS">Andros</a>, then belonging to the emperor, and reduced several places in Dalmatia which had revolted. In 1173, the republic ventured to oppose Frederick Barbarossa in his attack on the pope. Frederick, after a haughty reply to an embassy sent him by the Venetians, dispatched against them his son Otho, who soon arrived before the city with 75 galleys. The doge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEBASTIANO">Sebastiano</a> Ziani sailed out with the few vessels he had got equipped, to give the enemy battle. The fleets met off the coast of Itria, and a terrible engagement ensued, in which the imperial fleet was totally defeated, Otho himself taken prisoner, and 48 of his ships destroyed. On the doge's return, the pope went out to meet him, and presented him with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, saying, "Take this, Ziani, and give it to the sea, as a testimony of your dominion over it. Let your successors annually perform the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, that posterity may know that your valour has purchased this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, and subjected this element to you, even as a husband subjects his wife." Otho was treated with the respect due to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and soon conceived a great friendship for Ziani. At last, being permitted to visit the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, on his parole, he not only prevailed on his father to make peace with the Venetians, but even to visit their city, so famed for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and naval power. He was received with all possible respect, and on his departure attended to Ancona by the doge, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and the whole body of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. During this journey he was reconciled to the pope; and both agreed to pay the highest honours to the doge and republic. In the beginning of the 13th century, the Venetians They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> in conjunction with the French, besieged and took Con- possession of Constantinople, as has been related under the article Con-stantinopolitan <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, No. 144—149, which they held till the year 1261. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the Genoese, by their successful War with application to commerce, having raised themselves in the Ge- such a manner as to be capable of rivalling the Vene-noese, tians, a long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of wars took place between the re- publics; in which the Venetians generally had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a>- vantage, though sometimes they met with terrible over- throws. These expensive and bloody quarrels undoubtedly contributed to weaken the republic notwithstanding its successes. In the year 1348, however, the Genoese were obliged to implore the protection of Visconti duke of Milan, in order to support them against their implacable enemies the Venetians. Soon after this, in the year 1352, the latter were utterly defeated with such loss, that it was thought the city itself must have fallen into the hands of the Genoese, had they known how to improve their victory. This was in a short time followed by a peace; but from this time the power of the republic began to decline. Continual war with the states of Italy, with the Hungarians, and their own rebellious subjects, kept the Venetians employed, so that they had no leisure to oppose the Turks, whose rapid advances might have alarmed all Europe. After the destruction of the eastern empire, however, in 1453 the Turks began more immediately to interfere with the republic. Whatever valour might be shewn by the Venetians, or whatever successe they might boast of, it is certain the Turks ultimately prevailed; so that for some time it seemed scarcely possible to resist them. What also contributed greatly to the decline of the republic, was the discovery of a passage to the East Indies by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope in 1497. Till then the greatest part of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> goods imported into Europe passed through the hands of the Venetians; but as soon as the Cape was discovered, the conveyance by the way of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> almost entirely ceased. Still, however, the Venetian power power was strong; and in the beginning of the 16th century they maintained a war against almost the whole force of France, Germany, and Italy, associated against them in what has been called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">League</a> of Cambrai. Soon after, however, we find them entering into an alliance with the king of France against the emperor. After this, nothing of importance occurs in the history of the Venetian republic till the year 1645, when the republic was involved in a new and languishing conflict with the Turks, in defense of the important <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Candia. The transactions to which this war gave rise, and the spirit and bravery displayed by the Venetians, in defending their colonial possessions, are amply detailed under the article CANDIA. At the end of the 17th century, the Venetians obtained an important acquisition of territory by the conquest of the Morea, which at the peace of Carlowitz in 1699, was formally ceded by Turkey to the state of Venice*. During the war of the Succession, the states of Venice observed a strict neutrality. They considered that dispute as unconnected with their interests; taking care, however, to keep on foot an army on their frontiers in Italy, of sufficient force to make them respected by the belligerent powers. But soon after the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, the Venetians were again attacked by their old enemies the Turks, who beholding the great European powers exhausted by their late efforts, and unable to assist the republic, thought this the favorable moment for recovering the Morea, which had been so lately ravished from them. The Turks obtained their object, and at the peace of Passarowitz in 1715, which terminated this unsuccessful war, the Venetian states yielded up the Morea; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> seignior on his part restoring to them the small islands of Cerigo and Cerigetto, with some places which his troops had taken during the course of the war in Dalmatia. From the peace of Passarowitz to the conclusion of the 18th century, the affairs of Venice ceased to form an interesting part of the history of Europe. Ever since the league of Cambrai, the republic, weakened by its continual struggles with Turkey, had declined in power and in consequence, was incapable of opposing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to the encroachments of its more powerful neighbors. During the first war which the French republic maintained against the emperor in Italy, the states of Venice afforded a tempting object to each of the contending parties; and in May 1797, the capital was occupied by a body of French troops, who, under pretence of quelling a tumult that had arisen in the city, took possession of the forts, and subverted the existing authorities. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Campo Formio, concluded between the emperor and the French republic in October of the same year, the French consented that the emperor should take possession of the Venetian territory, with the islands in the Archipelago, which had been subjected to the Venetian republic; and by the subsequent treaty of Lunéville in 1801, this acquisition of territory to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> was confirmed, so that the Venetian republic must now be considered as an Austrian province. It is not necessary for us to be very minute in our account of the late <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and government of Venice. The government was strictly aristocratical, being vested in the great council or senate, in which each of the nobility had a seat. The nobility were extremely numerous, being computed at not fewer than 2000, whereas the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the state did not exceed 250,000. Besides the great council, or il consiglio grande, there were four others; one composed of the doge and six counsellors, called la signoria; another called il consiglio du pregadi, consisting of about 250 of the nobility; a third united to la signoria, consisting of 28 aldermen, or great lages, which gave audience to ambassadors; and a fourth, composed of 10 counsellors, who took cognizance of all criminal matters, and before whom even the doge himself must appear, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> accused. The secret business of the state was often carried on by spies and informers; and there were in the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of lions with open mouths, which formed so many receptacles for secret and anonymous information. The office and privileges of the doge of Venice have been already mentioned under the article DOGE. Of late this office was little more than nominal; and the doge was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> state puppet, without authority and without power. His establishment, however, was splendid, and his revenue not contemptible. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of electing the doge deserves notice, as it was well calculated to prevent bribery, or the exertion of party influence. He was elected by a plurality of voices, and held his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> they made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver balls, which were put into a vessel, and served for balloting. Those who drew <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> balls, first elected 40 counsellors, who drew 12 others, and elected 25 in addition. Of this number nine persons, who had drawn golden balls, chose 40 more; 11 of those, appointed in the same way, chose 41 counsellors, who finally proceeded to the election, till 25 votes or more fell upon the same person, who was then declared doge. After this election they placed the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> upon his head, upon which he took possession of the doge's palace. He never uncovered his head to any person, because he did not wear the cap in his own name, but in that of the republic. The military strength of the Venetians consisted of nearly 30,000 land forces, under the command of a capitano, who was always a foreigner of distinction; besides a considerable fleet, which they boasted could, in time of war, be increased to 60 men of war, and above 100 galleys. The ordinary revenues of the state have been computed at rather more than 1,000,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, a considerable part of which arose from the customs, and the duty on <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> made at Corfu and Chioggia. Venice, the city which was the seat of government of the Venetian republic, is built on 72 small islands at the head of the Adriatic or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice, about five miles from the main land. That part of the gulf which lies between the city and the continent forms a kind of laguna or lake, which, at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is very shallow, and on the opposite side of the islands there are numerous shallows, the channels between which are marked by stakes, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> ships in entering the port. The lagunes that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between the islands form so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> that intersect the city in all directions, and over these the streets communicate by not fewer than 500 bridges. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> or great canal is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and has a serpentine course through the middle of the city, but the others are narrow and crooked. The streets are also narrow and winding, but clean and neat. The houses are built on piles, and have each a door opening to the adjacent adjacent canal, and another to the street. As the narrowness of the streets but ill adapts them for walking in, the only places of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> on land are the Rialto, a noble bridge across the great canal, bordered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> and shops, and the great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of St Mark, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIAZZA">Piazza</a> di San Marco, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> quadrangle, formed of several buildings, some of which are magnificent. Of these, the ducal palace, where the business of the state used to be transacted; the patriarchal church of St Mark; the steeple of St Mark, at a little distance from the church; the church of St Geminiano; and the new and old Procuratie, are most deserving the notice of travellers. The canals form the great medium of communication, as well as the principal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of relaxation and amusement to the inhabitants. Here ply numerous gondolas, (see Gondola, and Macgill's Travels, vol. i.) which are rowed with admirable speed and dexterity by the gondoliers; and here are occasionally held races, or rather rowing matches. As the canals are, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, the receptacles of all the filth of the city, they become, in hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, very offensive; while, in winter, from their free communication with the gulf, they are frequently agitated by the Adriatic storms. The whole city is about six miles in circumference, and the inhabitants are estimated at 160,000. The inhabitants of Venice carried on a flourishing trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of glass, besides military stores and implements of war. At some distance from the city there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and commodious lazaretto, where ships coming from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> unload their goods, and perform <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-QUARANTINE">quarantine</a> from 20 to 40 days. This celebrated city, once the seat of power, opulence and the fine arts, whose carnival revelries have been the subject of so many animated descriptions, has undergone a melancholy change. Her streets and canals no longer resound with the strains of the musician and the serenades of watchful lovers, and her gay gondolas, which were formerly occupied by fashionable groups and parties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, are now become the vehicles of trade, or serve for the accommodation of the folder and the mechanic. The trade of the city, which had long declined, has, since the cession of the Venetian territory to Austria, been almost entirely transferred to Trieste. Venice is 72 miles E. by N. of Mantua; 115 N. E. of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>; 140 E. of Milan; 212 N. of Rome, and 300 N. by W. of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. Long. 12° 33'. N. Lat. 41° 26'.

VENIRE FACIAS

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a judicial writ lying where two parties plead and come to issue, directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, to cause 12 men of the same neighbourhood to meet and try the same, and to say the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> upon the issue taken.

VENTER

Pages 172-172

signifies the belly; but it is also used for the children by a woman of one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>: there is in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> a first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> venter, &c. where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> hath children by several wives; and how they shall take in descents of lands.

VENTILATOR

Pages 172-172

a machine by which the noxious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, as an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, gaol, ship, chamber, &c. may be discharged and changed for fresh. The noxious qualities of bad air have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> known; and no one has taken greater pains to let the mischief arising from foul air in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than Dr Hales; who has also proposed an easy and effectual remedy by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his ventilators; his account of which ventilator was read to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in May 1741. In the November following M. Trievald, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, informed Dr Mortimer secretary to the Royal Society, that he had in the preceding <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> invented a machine for the use of his majesty's men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in order to draw out the bad air from under their decks, the least of which exhausted 36,172 cubic feet in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at the rate of 21,732 tons in 24 hours. In 1742 he sent one of them, formed for a 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> ship to France; which was approved of by the Royal Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and the king of France ordered all the men of war to be furnished with the like ventilators. The ventilators invented by Dr Hales consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> box ABCD (fig. 1) of any size; in the middle of one side of this box a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> partition or midriff is fixed by hinges X, and it moves up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from A to C, by means of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod ZR, fixed at a proper distance from the other end of the midriff, and passing through a small hole in the cover of the box up to R. Two boxes of this kind may be employed at once, and the two iron rods may be fixed to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> FG (fig. 2.) moving on a fixed centre O; so that by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> raising and pressing down of the lever FG, the midriffs are also alternately raised and depressed, whereby these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> bellows are at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> in air, and pouring it out, through apertures with valves made on the same side with, and placed both above and below the hinges of the midriffs. In order to render the midriffs light, they are made of four bars lengthwise, and as many across them breadthwise, the vacant spaces being filled up with thin panels of fir board; and that they may move to and fro with the greatest ease, and without touching the sides of the boxes, there is an iron regulator fixed upright to the middle of the end of the box AC (fig. 1) from N to L, with a notch cut into the middle of the end of the midriff at Z; so that the midriffs, in rising and falling, suffer no other friction than what is made between the regulator and the notch. Moreover, as the midriff ZX moves with its edges only one-twentieth of an inch from the sides of the box ABCDFE, very little air <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> escape by the edges; and, therefore, there will be no need of leathern sides as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> bellows. The end of the box at AC is made a little circular, that it may be better adapted between A and C to the rising and falling midriff; and at the other end X of the midriff a flap of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> may be nailed over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> needful. The eight <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> valves through which the air is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, are placed at the hinge-end of the boxes BK (fig. 2.) as at 1, 2, 3, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALVE">valve</a> 1 opens inward to admit the air to enter, when the midriff is depressed at the other end by means of the lever FG. And at the same time the valve 3 in the lower ventilator is shut by the compressed air which passes out at the valve 4. But when that midriff is raised, the valve 1 shuts, and the air passes out at the valve 2. And it is the same with the valves 5, 6, &c. of the other box; so that the midriffs are alternately rising and falling, and two of the ventilators drawing in air, and two blowing it out; the air entering at the valves 1, 3, 6, 8, and passing out at the valves 2, 4, 5, 7. Before these last valves there is fixed to the ventilators a box QQNM (fig. 3.) as a common receptacle for all the air which comes out of these valves; which

VERA-CRUZ

Pages 173-173

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, with a very secure and commodious harbour, defended by a fort. Here the flotilla annually arrives from Spain to receive the produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>; and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a fair is held here for all manner of rich merchandise brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and the East Indies by way of the South sea, and for the merchandise of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by way of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. This town is not two miles in circumference; and about it there is a wall of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-side. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is unwholesome; and there are very few Spaniards here unless when the flotilla arrives, and then it is crowded with people from all parts of Spanish America. It is 200 miles south-east of Mexico. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 37° 25'. N. Lat. 19° 12'.

VERAGUA

Pages 173-173

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, bounded on the east by that of Costa Rica, on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, and on the south by the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is about 125 miles in length from east to west, and 60 in breadth from north to south. It is a mountainous barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but has plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver. Concepcion is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

VERD

Pages 173-173
CAPE, a promontory on the west coast of Africa, 40 miles north-west of the mouth of the river Gambia. W. Long. 17° 38'. N. Lat. 14° 45'. The islands of Cape de Verd are seated in the Atlantic ocean, about 400 miles west of the Cape. They are between the 13th and 19th degree of latitude; and the principal are 10 in number, lying in a semicircle. Their names are, St Antony, St Vincent, St Lucia, St Nicholas, the isle of Sal, Bona Vista, Mayo, St Jago, Fuego, and Brava.

VERDIGRISE

Pages 173-173

the acetate of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, much used by painters as a green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. See Copper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VERDITER

Pages 173-174
or VERDATE, a preparation of copper, sometimes used by painters, &c., for a blue; but but more usually mixed with a yellow for a green colour. See Copper, Chemistry Index, and Colour-Making, No. 28.

VERGE

Pages 174-174

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the compass of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which bounds the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>; and which is thought to have been 12 miles round. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> verge is also used for a stick <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rod, whereby one is admitted tenant to a copyhold estate, by holding it in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and swearing fealty to the lord of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>.

VERGERS

Pages 174-174

certain officers of the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, whose business it is to carry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wands before the judges. There are also vergers of cathedrals, who carry a rod tipped with silver before the bishop, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, &c.

VERMES

the sixth class of animals in the Linnaean system, comprehending five orders. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

or VERMICHELLY, a composition of flour, cheese, yolks of eggs, sugar, and saffron, reduced to a paste, and formed into long slender pieces like worms, by forcing it with a piston through a number of little holes. It was first brought from Italy; and is chiefly used in soups and pottages.

VERMICULAR
