an epithet given to any thing that bears a relation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resemblance to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>.

VERMIFORMIS

Pages 174-174

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to various parts in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>.

VERMILION

Pages 174-174

a bright and beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, composed of quicksilver and sulphur, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> under the name of minium. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No. 1701, and 1713; but what goes by the name of minium amongst us, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, known also by the name of red-lead. See Chemistry, No. 1832. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">VERMIN</a> is a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, denoting those animals which are either directly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> indirectly injurious to mankind, the inferior animals, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; as fleas, caterpillars, flies, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, &c.

VERMIN

Pages 174-175

Destruction of. As we propose in this article to point out the means of destroying some of those animals that are hurtful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> troublesome to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, we shall employ the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> vermin, in a more extended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, including also under it, mice, rats, moles, &c. We shall endeavour to collect the most useful observations that have been made on the means of diminishing or exterminating such animals as are obviously injurious. We cannot avoid here remarking, that although the seemingly excessive increase of one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of animals is hurtful or inconvenient to another, or to man himself, and their existence is attended with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> loss and damage, by their infesting and destroying grains and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> destined for the food of man or those animals that are subservient to him; we are not of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this excess ought to be considered merely as a useless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a> in the great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of being; nor are we of opinion that their numbers ought not to be reduced, because we are too short-sighted to comprehend the wise purposes for which they are called into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. We have heard such a doctrine held up, although we are inclined to suspect that it is founded on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of singularity or indolence, rather than proceeding from pure motives of benevolence. But we must abstain from such discussions, and occupy the limits allotted to the proper subject of consideration. Rats and Mice.—Various methods have been proposed for the destruction of these vermin. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> has been recommended as very effectual. Take of the seeds of staveacre (delphinium lapathiflorum), or of lousewort (pedicularis palustris), powdered, more or less as the occasion requires, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; of oatmeal, three parts; mix them well, and make them up into a paste with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Lay pieces of this paste in the holes, and on the places where mice and rats frequent; and it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> effectually kill or rid the places of those kind of vermin by their eating of it. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> for encouraging arts proposed a premium of 50l. for a preparation capable of alluring or fascinating rats so that they might be taken alive. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of new traps, &c. were invented, and the following methods of alluring the rats to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were published. One of the methods which is most easily and efficaciously practised, is the trailing of some pieces of their most favourite food, which should be of the kind which has the strongest scent, such as toasted cheese or boiled <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> herrings, from the holes or entrances of the closet to their recesses in every part of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or contiguous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. At the extremities and at different parts of the course of this trailed track, small quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, or any other kind of their food, should be laid to bring the greater number into the tracks, and to encourage them to pursue it to the place where they are intended to be taken; at that place, when time admits of it, a more plentiful repast is laid for them, and the trailing repeated for two or three nights. Besides this trailing and way-baiting, some of the most expert of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RAT">rat</a>-catchers have a shorter, and perhaps more effectual method of bringing them together; which is the calling them, by making such a whistling noise as resembles their own call; and by this means, with the affluence of the way-baits, they call them out of their holes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them to the repast previously prepared for them at the places designed for taking them. But this is much more difficult to be practised than the art of trailing; for the learning of the exact notes or cries of any kind of beasts or birds, so as to deceive them, is a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> which is attained only by few. In practising either of those methods of trailing or calling, great caution must be used by the operator to suppress and prevent the scent of his feet and body from being perceived; which is done by overpowering that scent, by other scents of a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. In order to do this, the feet are to be covered with cloths rubbed over with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, or other strong smelling substances; and even <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of rhodium is sometimes used for this purpose, but sparingly, on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price, though it has a very alluring as well as disgusting effect. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this caution of avoiding the scent of the operators feet, near the track, and in the place where the rats are proposed to be collected, be not properly observed, it will very much obstruct the success of the attempt. tempt to take them; for they are very shy of coming where the scent of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> feet lies very fresh, as it intimates to their sagacious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> the presence of human creatures, whom they naturally dread. To the above-mentioned means of alluring by trailing, way-baiting and calling, is added another of very material efficacy, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of oil of rhodium, which like the marum syriacum and valerian in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of cats, has a very extraordinary fascinating power on these animals. This oil, as it is extremely dear, is therefore sparingly used. It is exalted in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the place, and at the entrance of it, where the rats are intended to be taken, particularly at the time when they are to be last brought together, in order to their destruction; and it is used also by smearing it on the surface of some of the implements used in taking by the method below described; and the effect it has in taking off their caution and dread, by the delight they appear to have in it, is very extraordinary. It is usual, likewise, for the operator to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> as well as scent, which is done by putting a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> or cloak, of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> form, and makes him appear like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, or some such inanimate thing, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> must likewise be scented as above, to overpower the smell of his person; and besides this, he is to avoid all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> till he has secured his point of having all the rats in his power. When the rats are thus enticed and collected, where time is afforded, and the whole in any house and outbuildings are to be cleared away, they are suffered to regale on what they most like, which is ready prepared for them, and then to go away quietly for two or three nights; by which means those that are not allured the first night, are brought afterwards, either by their fellows, or the effects of the trailing, &c. and will not fail to come duly again, if they are not disturbed or molested. But many of the rat-catchers make shorter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and content themselves with what can be brought together in one night; but this is never effectual, unless where the building is small and entire, and the rats but few in number. The means of taking them when brought together are various. Some entice them into a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bag, the mouth of which is sufficiently capacious to cover nearly the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the place where they are collected; which is done by smearing some vessel, placed in the middle of the bag, with oil of rhodium, and laying in the bag baits of food. This bag, which before lay flat on the ground with the mouth spread open, is to be suddenly closed when the rats are all in. Others drive or frighten them, by flight noises or motions into a bag of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> form, the mouth of which, after all the rats are come in, is drawn up to the opening of the place by which they entered, all other ways of retreat being secured. Others, again, intoxicate or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> them, by mixing with the repast prepared for them, the coccus indicus, or the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUX_VOMICA">nux vomica</a>. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> four ounces of coccus indicus, with 12 ounces of oatmeal, and two ounces of treacle or honey, made into a moist paste with strong beer; but if the nux vomica be used, a much less proportion will serve than is here given of the coccus. Any similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of these drugs, with that kind of food the rats are most fond of, and which has a strong flavour to lure that of the drugs, will equally answer the end. If indeed coccus indicus be well powdered, and infused in strong beer for some time, at least half the quantity here directed will serve as well as the quantity before mentioned. When the rats appear to be thoroughly intoxicated with the coccus, or sick with the nux vomica, they may be taken with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and put into a bag or cage, the door of the place being first shut, lest those who have strength and sense remaining should escape. In destroying rats, advantage may be taken of that remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of instinct which they possess of departing on places, where they find themselves disturbed or harassed, and retiring to new haunts. It is well known, that after one or two rats are poisoned, or taken in traps, or wounded or otherwise injured, and afterwards permitted to escape, the whole colony immediately disappears. The practice, however, of destroying rats that frequent dwelling-houses, by poison, should be as much as possible avoided; for they retire to places behind the wainscot, &c. from which, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, their putrid bodies emitting a most offensive smell cannot be removed. But it is far less difficult than is generally imagined to secure the different apartments of a dwelling-house, and even the cellars, from the inroads of rats and mice, and thus to prevent their unwelcome visits, by shutting up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> through which they enter. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a> and lime, when they can be applied, are effectual; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, by introducing pieces of broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> or glass, along with it, will also answer the purpose; and even a piece of cork, with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> or two stuck through it to prevent them from eating it away, is a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to mice entering through a hole in wood, and may even prevent the entrance of rats. We have seen this method of shutting up the holes, as soon as they were opened by the industry of the enemy, readily pursued for some time, attended with the fullest success, even in an old house of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and finished from top to bottom with wood, some of which was much decayed. Often for the sake of food, rats and mice frequent gardens, fields, and woods, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season; but, on the approach of winter, they return to their former haunts in the habitations of man; and, accordingly, it is observed, that houses which are free from those vermin during the summer, swarm with them about the end of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">Attention</a> to this circumstance in the habits of these animals, may be the means of securing us from their visits and depredations; for if, at the time alluded to, every hole and cranny through which rat or mouse can enter, be shut up, and carefully kept <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and secure, the perseverance of the foe is exhausted and overcome by repeated and constant resistance, and thus he is forced to abandon the unequal contest, and to retire to other haunts where his motions are less interrupted. Various other methods have been proposed for the destruction of rats; and although we have thrown out a hint against the use of arsenic for this purpose, in dwelling-houses; yet where it can be employed with perfect safety, and without risk of the nuisance alluded to, as in cellars and outhouses, it is undoubtedly one of the most effectual to which we can have recourse.

VERNACULAR

Pages 181-181

a word applied to something that is peculiar to any one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

VERNIER SCALE

Pages 181-182

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> excellently adapted for the graduation of mathematical instruments, thus called from its inventor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Vernier, a person of distinction in the Franche Comté. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONIUS">NONIUS</a>. Vernier's method is derived from the following principle. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> two equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circular arcs, A, B, are so divided, that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of equal divisions in B is one less than the number of equal divisions of A, then <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> the excess of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of B above one division of A be compounded of the ratios of one of A to A, and of one of B to B. For let A contain 11 parts, then one of A to A is as 1 to 11, or \(\frac{1}{11}\). Let B contain 10 parts, then one of B to B is as 1 to 10, or \(\frac{1}{10}\). Now \(\frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{11} = \frac{11-10}{10 \times 11} = \frac{1}{10 \times 11} = \frac{1}{10} \times \frac{1}{11}\). Or if B contains \(n\) parts, and A contains \(n+1\) parts; then \(\frac{1}{n}\) is one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of B, and \(\frac{1}{n+1}\) is one part of A. And \(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1} = \frac{n+1-n}{n \times n+1} = \frac{1}{n} \times \frac{1}{n+1}\). The most commodious divisions, and their aliquot parts, into which the degrees on the circular limb of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> may be supposed to be divided, depend on the radius of that instrument. Let R be the radius of a circle in inches; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to be divided into \(n\) parts, each being \(\frac{1}{p}\)th part of an inch. Now the circumference of a circle, in parts of its diameter \(2R\) inches, is \(3,1415926 \times 2R : : 10 : \frac{3,1415926}{360} \times 2R\) inches. Or, \(0,01745329 \times R\) is the length of one degree in inches. Or, \(0,01745329 \times R \times p\) is the length of \(1^\circ\), in \(p\)th parts of an inch. But as every degree contains \(n\) times such parts, therefore \(n = 0,01745329 \times R \times p\). The most commodious perceptible division is \(\frac{1}{8}\) or \(\frac{1}{10}\) of an inch. Example. Suppose an instrument of 30 inches radius, into how many convenient parts may each degree be divided? how many of these parts are to go to the breadth of the vernier, and to what parts of a degree may an observation be made by that instrument? Now \(0,01745 \times 1 = 0,5236\) inches, the length of each degree: and if \(p\) be supposed about \(\frac{1}{8}\) of an inch for one division; then \(0,5236 \times p = 4,188\) shows the number of such parts in a degree. But as this number must be an integer, let it be 4, each being \(1^\circ\): and let the breadth of the vernier contain 31 of those parts, or \(7^\circ\), and be divided into 30 parts. Here \(n = \frac{1}{4}; m = \frac{1}{30}\); then \(\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{120}\) of a degree, Vernier degree, or $30'$, which is the least part of a degree that instrument can show. If $n = \frac{1}{5}$ and $m = \frac{1}{36}$; then $\frac{1}{5} \times \frac{1}{36} = \frac{60}{5 \times 36}$ of a minute, or $20''$. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, taken as examples in the instruments <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made from 3 inches to 8 feet radius, shows the divisions of the limb to nearest tenths of inches, so as to be an aliquot of $60'$s, and what parts of a degree may be estimated by the vernier, it being divided into such equal parts, and containing such degrees as their columns show. | Rad. inches | Parts of a degree | Parts in vernier | Breadth of vernier | Parts observed | |------------|------------------|-----------------|-------------------|---------------| | 3 | 1 | 15 | 1 5½ | 4' 0'' | | 6 | 1 | 20 | 20½ | 3' 0'' | | 9 | 2 | 20 | 10½ | 1' 30'' | | 12 | 2 | 24 | 12½ | 1' 15'' | | 15 | 3 | 20 | 6½ | 1' 0'' | | 18 | 3 | 30 | 10½ | 0' 40'' | | 21 | 4 | 30 | 7½ | 0' 30'' | | 24 | 4 | 36 | 9½ | 0' 25'' | | 30 | 5 | 30 | 7½ | 0' 20'' | | 36 | 6 | 30 | 5½ | 0' 20'' | | 42 | 8 | 30 | 3½ | 0' 15'' | | 48 | 9 | 40 | 4½ | 0' 10'' | | 60 | 10 | 36 | 3½ | 0' 10'' | | 72 | 12 | 30 | 2½ | 0' 10'' | | 84 | 15 | 40 | 2½ | 0' 6'' | | 96 | 15 | 60 | 4 | 0' 4'' | By altering the number of divisions, either in the degrees or in the vernier, or in both, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> can be observed to a different degree of accuracy. Thus, to a radius of 30 inches, if a degree be divided into 12 parts, each being five minutes, and the breadth of the vernier be 21 such parts, or $1\frac{1}{2}$, and divided into 20 parts, then $\frac{1}{12} \times \frac{1}{20} = \frac{1}{240} = 15''$: or taking the breadth of the vernier $2\frac{1}{2}$, and divided into 30 parts; then $\frac{1}{12} \times \frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{360}$, or $10''$. Or $\frac{1}{12} \times \frac{1}{50} = \frac{1}{600} = 6''$; where the breadth of the vernier is $4\frac{1}{2}$.

VERONA

Pages 182-182

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Veronese, and in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; situated on the river Adige, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 24'. N. Lat. 45° 26'. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in compass; and is strongly fortified. It contains 57,400 inhabitants.

VERONESE

Pages 182-182

a territory of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Trentino, on the east by the Vicentino and Pidano, on the south by the Mantuan, and on the west by the Bresciano. It is about 35 miles in length, and 27 in breadth; and fertile in corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and cattle. VERONICAE. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAGLIARI">CAGLIARI</a>.

VERONICA

Pages 182-182

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class of diandria; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 40th order, Perforate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VERSAILLES

Pages 182-182

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> and Oise, 10 miles west-south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It contains 60,000 inhabitants, and since the Revolution has been created a bishop's see. In the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII., it was only a small village. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> built here a hunting-hut in 1630, which Baillonpierre calls "the paltry chateau of Versailles." Although the situation was low and very unfavourable, Louis XIV. built a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> here, which was the usual residence of the kings of France till the 6th of October 1789, when the late unfortunate Louis XVI. and his family were removed from it to the Thulleries. The buildings and the gardens are adorned with a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, done by the greatest masters, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER_WORKS"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-works are all worthy of admiration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> gallery is thought to be as curious a piece of workmanship of that kind as any in the world; nor is the chapel less to be admired for its fine <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> and ornaments. The gardens, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>, are five miles in circumference, and surrounded by walls. There are three fine avenues to Versailles; one of which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Paris, the other comes from Seaux, and the third from St Cloud. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 12'. N. Lat. 48° 48'.

VERSE

Pages 182-182

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a line consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short syllables, which run with an agreeable cadence. Verse is also used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a>, &c.

VERSIFICATION

Pages 182-182

the art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> manner of making <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; also the tune and cadence of verse. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">POETRY</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> III.

VERSION

Pages 182-182

a translation of some book <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> out of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> into another. See TRANSLATION.

VERT

Pages 182-182

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for a green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It is called vert in the blazon of the coats of all under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>; but in coats of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> it is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a>; and in those of kings venus. In engraving it is expressed by diagonals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> drawn athwart from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to left, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEXTER">dexter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> corner to the sinister base. VERTEBRÆ. See ANATOMY, No. 30.

VERTEX

Pages 182-182

is also used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> for the point of the heaven directly over our heads, properly called the zenith.

VERTICILLATAE

Pages 182-182

the name of a class in Ray's and Boerhaave's Methods, consisting of herbaceous vegetables. It is also the name of the 42nd order in Linnæus's Fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Method.

VERTICILLUS

Pages 182-182

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of flowering, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are produced in rings at each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of the stem, with very short foot-stalks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is exemplified in mint, horehound, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order described above.

VERTICITY

Pages 182-182

is that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the loadstone whereby it turns <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> directs itself to one particular point.

VERTUMNUS

Pages 182-183

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a god who presided over gardens and orchards, honoured among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETRUSCANS">Etruscans</a>, from whom the worship of this deity was transmitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Vertumnus had a temple near the market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at Rome, being represented as one of the tutelar deities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. The commentators on Ovid say, that he was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Hetruria, who, by his diligent and successful cultivation of fruit and gardens, obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being ranked among the gods.

VERUMONTANUM

Pages 183-183

in *Anatomy*, a small eminence near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> where the semen is discharged into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>. **VERVAINE**. See **Verbena**, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **VERTOT d'AUBERG**, Rene Aubert de, a celebrated historian, was descended from a noble and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in Normandy, and born in 1655. At 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> he became a Franciscan friar; afterwards he entered into the order of the Premonstratenses, in which he had several benefices: and at length was a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> ecclesiastic. He became secretary to the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, member of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>, and historiographer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1735. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Revolutions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. 2. The Revolutions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. 3. The Revolutions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. 4. The History of Malta. These works are written in elegant French, and translated into most of the languages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

VESALIUS

Pages 183-183

Andreas, a celebrated physician and anatomist, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> about the year 1512. He studied physic at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> under James Sylvius; but applied himself chiefly to anatomy, which was then very little known, dispositions being esteemed unlawful and impious: and it appears from his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> *De humani corporis fabrica*, that he perfected himself in this useful knowledge very early. About the year 1537, the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> made him professor in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, where he taught anatomy for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V, called him to be his physician, as he was also to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. Vesalius was now at the height of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, when all of a sudden he formed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of taking a journey to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; concerning which journey we are told the following story. A young Spanish nobleman he attended, being believed to be dead, Vesalius obtained leave to open him to explore the true cause of his illness; but when he opened the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, he perceived symptoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the heart <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>. The parents, not satisfied with prosecuting him for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, accused him of impiety to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, in hopes that tribunal would punish him with greater rigour: but the king interposing, saved him on condition of his making a pilgrimage to the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>. He was shipwrecked on his return, and thrown upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZANTE">Zante</a>, where he perished, in 1564. He was the author of several works, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which is *De humani corporis fabrica*.

VESICATORIUM

Pages 183-183

a Blister; an application of an acrid <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> made to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, in order to draw a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of humours to that part, and thus elevate the scurfskin into a blister.

VESPA

Pages 183-183

the Wasp; a genus of insects belonging to the order of hymenoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VESPASIAN

Pages 183-183

the 10th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Rome; remarkable for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> and other virtues. See Rome, No. 332—339.

VESPER

Pages 183-183

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, denote the afternoon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; answering in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to the evening prayers of the church of England.

VESPERTILIO

Pages 183-183

the Bat; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, belonging to the order of primates. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VESSEL

Pages 183-183

a general name given to the different sorts of ships which are navigated on the ocean, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. It is, however, more particularly applied to those of the smaller kind, furnished with one or two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>. See Ship.

VESTA

Pages 183-183

one of the lately discovered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, of which the elements have been determined by Dr Gauß in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>. ### Elements of Vesta | Epoch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, meridian of Seeberg | 108° 19' VESTALIA

Pages 183-183

in Roman antiquity, a festival celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Vesta, on the 5th of the ides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>: that is, on the ninth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>.

VESTALS

Pages 183-184

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, were priestesses of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Vesta, and had the perpetual fire committed to their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; they were at first only four in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, but afterwards increased to six; and it does not appear that their number ever exceeded six, among whom was one superior to the rest, and called vestalis maxima. The vestals were chosen from six to ten years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and obliged to strict continency for 30 years; the first 10 of which were employed in learning the ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, the next 10 in the performance of them, and the last 10 in teaching them to the younger vestals. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">VESUVIUS</a> The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the vestals consisted of a head-dress called *infula*, which sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the head, and from whence hung certain laces called *vitta*; a kind of surplice made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and over it a purple mantle with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> train to it.

VESTIBLE

Pages 184-184
or **VESTIBULE**, in Architecture, a kind of entrance into a large building; being an open place before the hall, or at the bottom of the staircase.

VESTRY

Pages 184-184

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> adjoining to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, where the vestments of the minister are kept; and also a meeting at such place, consisting of the minister, church-wardens, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men of most parishes, who make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> vestry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> meeting. By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> there are select vestries, being a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons chosen to have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the parish, make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>, and take the accounts of church-wardens, &c.

VESUVIUS

Pages 184-187

a celebrated volcano of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, six miles east from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. This mountain has two tops; one of which only goes by the name of Vesuvius, the other being now called Somma; but Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the latter is what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called Vesuvius. The perpendicular height of Vesuvius is only 3700 feet, though the ascent from the foot to the top is three Italian miles. One side of the mountain is well cultivated and fertile, producing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty of vines; but the south and west sides are entirely covered with cinders and ashes; while a sulphureous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> constantly issues from the top, sometimes attended with the most violent explosions of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, the emission of great streams of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, and all the other attendants of a most formidable volcano. The first of these eruptions recorded in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the year 79; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the two cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum were entirely buried under the stones and ashes thrown out. Incredible mischief was also done to the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and numbers of people lost their lives, among whom was Pliny the Elder. It is the opinion of the best judges, however, that this eruption was by no means the first that had ever happened. The very streets of those cities which were at that time overwhelmed are said to be partly paved with lava. Since that time 30 different eruptions have been recorded, some of which have been extremely violent. In the year 1538, a mountain, three miles in circumference and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in perpendicular height, was thrown up in the course of one night. The first great eruption taken notice of by Sir William Hamilton was that of 1767, which, though very violent, was mild in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with that of 1538. From this time (1767) Vesuvius never ceased for ten years to send forth smoke, nor were there many months in which it did not throw out stones, scoriae, and cinders; which, increasing to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, were usually followed by lava; so that from the year 1767 to 1779 there were <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> eruptions, some of them very considerable. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August that year, however, an eruption took place, which, for its extraordinary and terrible appearance, may be reckoned among the most remarkable of any recorded concerning this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other volcano. During the whole month of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> the mountain <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>. Subterraneous explosions and rumbling noises were heard; quantities of Vesuvian smoke were thrown up with great violence, sometimes with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot stones, scoriae, and ashes; and towards the end of the month these symptoms increased to such a degree as to exhibit, in the night-time, the most beautiful fireworks that can be imagined. On Thursday 5th August the volcano appeared most violently agitated; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and sulphureous smoke issued continually and impetuously from its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATER">crater</a>, one puff seeming to impel another; so that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of them was soon accumulated, to appearance four times the height and size of the volcano itself. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of smoke were exceedingly white, so that the whole resembled an immense accumulation of bales of the whitest cotton. In the midst of this very white smoke, vast quantities of stones, scoriae, and ashes, were thrown up to the height of 2000 feet; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of liquid lava, seemingly very heavy, was lifted up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> enough to clear the rim of the crater, and take its way <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. This lava, having run violently for some hours, suddenly ceased, just before it had reached the cultivated parts of the mountain, near four miles from the spot whence it issued. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, all this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, was intolerable at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Somma and Otaiano; and was sensibly felt at Palma and Lauri, which are much farther off. Reddish ashes fell so thick on the two former, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> was darkened, and that objects could not be distinguished at the distance of ten feet. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> filaments of a vitrified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, like spun glass, were mixed, and fell with these ashes; several birds in cages were suffocated, and the leaves of the trees in the neighbourhood of Somma were covered with white and very corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. About 12 at night, on the 7th, the fermentation of the mountain seemed greatly to increase. Our author, who was watching the motions of the volcano from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>-fion of fire at Naples, which has a full view of it. Several picturesque effects had been observed from the approach of the deep red fire within the crater of Vesuvius-clouds, and which mounted high amongst those huge clouds on the top of it; when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> storm, called in that country a *tropea*, came on suddenly, and blended its heavy watery clouds with the sulphureous and mineral ones, which were already like to many other mountains piled up on the top of the volcano. At this moment a fountain of fire was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> up to an incredible height, casting so bright a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, that the smallest objects were clearly distinguishable at any place within five miles or more of Vesuvius. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> stormy clouds, passing swiftly over, and at times covering the whole or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of fire, at other times clearing away and giving a full view of it, with the various tints produced by its reverberated light on the white clouds above in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> flashes of forked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> that attended the tropea, formed such a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> as no power of art can express. One of his Sicilian majesty's gamekeepers, who was out in the fields near Otaiano whilst this storm was at its height, was surprized to find the drops of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> scald his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; a phenomenon probably occasioned by the clouds having acquired a great degree of heat in passing through the above-mentioned column of fire. On the 8th, the mountain was quiet till towards six o'clock in the evening, when a great smoke began to gather over its crater; and about an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after a rumbling blazing subterraneous noise was heard in the neighborhood of the volcano; the usual throws of red-hot stones and scoriae began and increased every instant. The crater, viewed through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a>, seemed much enlarged by the violence of last night's explosions, and the little mountain on the top was entirely gone. About nine o'clock a most violent report was heard at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTICI">Portici</a> and its neighborhood, which shook the houses to such a degree as made the inhabitants run out into the streets. Many windows were broken, and walls cracked by the concussion of the air on this occasion, though the noise was but faintly heard at Naples. In an instant a fountain of liquid transparent fire began to rise, and gradually increasing, arrived at last at the amazing height of ten thousand feet and upwards. Puffs of smoke, as black as can possibly be imagined, succeeded another hastily, and accompanied the red-hot, transparent, and liquid lava, interrupting its splendid brightness here and there by patches of the darkest hue. Within these puffs of smoke, at the very moment of emission, a bright but pale electrical fire was observed playing briskly about in zig-zag <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> was south-west, and, though gentle, was sufficient to carry these puffs of smoke out of the column of fire; and a collection of them by degrees formed a black and extensive curtain behind it; in other parts, of the sky it was perfectly clear, and the stars bright. The fiery fountain, of such immense magnitude, on the dark ground just mentioned, made the finest contrast imaginable; and the blaze of it reflected from the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which was at that time perfectly smooth, added greatly to this sublime view. The lava, mixed with stones and scoriae, having risen to the amazing height already mentioned, was partly directed by the wind towards Otaiano, and partly falling, still red hot and liquid, upon the top of Vesuvius, covered its whole cone, part of that of the summit of Somma, and the valley between them. The falling matter, being nearly as inflamed and vivid as that which was continually issuing fresh from the crater, formed with it one complete body of fire, which could not be less than two miles and a half in breadth, and of the extraordinary height above mentioned, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> a heat to the distance of at least five miles round. The breathwork on the mountain of Somma was soon in a blaze, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of it being of a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from the deep red of the matter thrown out by the volcano, and from the silvery blue of the electrical fire, still added to the contrast of this most extraordinary scene. The black cloud, increasing greatly, once bent towards Naples, and threatened the city with speedy destruction; for it was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with electrical fire, which kept constantly darting about in bright zig-zag lines. This fire, however, rarely quitted the cloud, but usually returned to the great column of fire whence it proceeded; though once or twice it was seen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the top of Somma, and set fire to some dry grass and bushes. Fortunately the wind carried back the cloud just as it reached the city, and had begun to occasion great alarm. The column of fire, however, still continued, and diffused such a strong light, that the most minute objects could be discerned at the distance of ten miles or more from the mountain. Mr Morris informed our author, that at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORRENTO">Sorrento</a>, which is 12 miles distant from Vesuvius, he read the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>-page of a book by that volume Vesuvius. All this time the miserable inhabitants of Otaiano and Distretti were involved in the utmost distress and danger by the inhabiting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of stones which fell upon them, and which, had they continued for a longer time, would most certainly have reduced their town to the same situation with Herculaneum and Pompeii. The mountain of Somma, at the foot of which the town of Otaiano is situated, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> Vesuvius from the view of its inhabitants; so that till the eruption became considerable it was not visible to them. On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> night, when the noise increased, and the fire began to appear above the mountain of Somma, many of the inhabitants flew to the churches, and others were preparing to quit the town, when a sudden and violent report was heard; soon after which they found themselves involved in a thick cloud of smoke and ashes; a horrid crashing noise was heard in the air, and presently fell a vast shower of stones and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces of scoriae, some of which were of the diameter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight feet, which must have weighed more than 1000 pounds before they were broken, as some of the fragments which Sir William Hamilton found in the streets still weighed upwards of 60 pounds. When these large vitrified masses either struck against one another in the air, or fell on the ground, they broke in many pieces, and covered a large space of ground with vivid sparks of fire, which communicated their heat to every thing that was combustible. These masses were formed of the liquid lava; the exterior parts of which were become black and porous by cooling in their fall through such a vast space; whilst the interior parts, less exposed, retained an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> heat, and were perfectly red. In an instant the town and country about it was on fire in many parts, for there were several straw huts in the vineyards, which had been erected for the watchmen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>; all of which were burnt. A great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of wood in the heart of the town was all in a blaze; and had there been much wind, the flames must have spread universally, and all the inhabitants would have been burnt in their houses; for it was impossible for them to stir out. Some, who attempted it with pillows, tables, chairs, the tops of wine casks, &c., on their heads, were either knocked down or soon driven back to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> and in the cellars of their houses. Many were wounded, but only two persons died of their wounds. To add to the horror of the scene, incessant volcanic lightning was whizzing about the black cloud that surrounded them, and the sulphureous smell and heat would scarcely allow them to draw their breath. In this dreadful situation they remained about 25 minutes, when the volcanic storm ceased all at once, and Vesuvius remained full of silence. Some time after the eruption had ceased, the air continued greatly impregnated with electrical matter. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Cottolengo told our author, that having, about thirty minutes after the great eruption had ceased, held after in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> bottle, armed with a pointed wire, out at his window at Naples, it soon became considerably charged. But whilst the eruption was in force, its appearance was too alarming to allow one to think of such experiments. He was informed also by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Monte Mileto, Vesuvius. that his son, the duke of Popoli, who was at Monte Miletto the 8th of August, had been alarmed by the shower of cinders that fell there; some of which he had sent to Naples weighing two ounces; and that stones of an ounce <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> had fallen upon an estate of his ten miles farther off. Monte Miletto is about 30 miles from the volcano. The abbe Caglioni also related, that his sister, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a> in a convent at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANFREDONIA">Manfredonia</a>, had written to inquire after him, imagining that Naples must have been destroyed, when they, at so great a distance, had been alarmed by a shower of ashes which fell on the city at 11 o'clock at night, so much as to open all the churches, and go to prayers. As the great eruption happened at nine o'clock, these ashes must have traveled 100 miles in the space of two hours. Nothing could be more dismal than the appearance of Ottaiano after this eruption. The houses were unroofed, half buried under the black scoriae and ashes; all the windows towards the mountain were broken, and some of the houses themselves burnt; the streets choked up with ashes, in some narrow places not less than four feet thick; and a few of the inhabitants who had just returned, were employed in clearing them away, and piling them up in hillocks, to get at their ruined houses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the prince of Ottaiano is situated on an eminence above the town, and nearer the mountain. The steps leading up to it were deeply covered with volcanic matter; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> was totally destroyed, and the windows broken, but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> itself, being strongly built, had not suffered much. An incredible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fragments of lava were thrown out during the eruption, some of which were of immense magnitude. The largest measured by Sir William Hamilton was 108 feet in circumference and 17 in height. This was thrown at least a quarter of a mile clear of the mouth of the volcano. Another, 66 feet in circumference and 19 in height, being nearly of a spherical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, was thrown out at the same time, and lay near the former. This last had the marks of being rounded, nay almost polished, by continual rolling in torrents or on the sea-shore. Our author conjectures that it might be a spherical volcanic salt, such as that of 45 feet in circumference mentioned by M. de St Fond, in his Treatise of Extinguished Volcanoes. A third of 16 feet in height and 92 in circumference was thrown much farther, and lay in the valley between Vesuvius and the Hermitage. It appeared also, from the large fragments that surrounded this mass, that it had been much larger while in the air. Vesuvius continued to emit smoke for a considerable time after this great eruption, so that our author was apprehensive that another would soon ensue; but from that time nothing comparable to the above has taken place. From the time of this great eruption to the year 1784 our author kept an exact diary of the operations of Vesuvius, with drawings, showing, by the quantity of smoke, the degree of fermentation within the volcano. The operations of the subterraneous fire, however, appear to be very capricious and uncertain. One day there is the appearance of a violent fermentation, and the next every thing is tranquil; but whenever there has been a considerable ejection of scoriae and cinders, it has been a constant observation, that the lava soon made its appearance, either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> over the crater, or forcing its way through the crevices in the conical part of the mountain. An eruption took place in the month of November 1784, and continued for some time, but without any remarkable circumstance. Vetch. See Vicia. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Veteran, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, an appellation given to a soldier grown old in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, or who had made a certain number of campaigns. Veterinary art. See Farriery. Vexillum, in Botany; the upper petal of a peabloom, or butterfly-shaped flower, which is generally larger than any of the others. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIALES">Viales</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a name given among the Romans to the gods who had the care and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> and highways. Viaticum, in Roman antiquity, an appellation given in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all officers of any of the magistrates; as liators, accensis, scribes, criers. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIBEX">Vibex</a>, is sometimes used by physicians, for a black and blue spot in the skin occasioned by an efflux or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRAVASATION">extravasation</a> of blood. Vibration, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, a regular, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a body, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a>. Viburnum, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class pentandra; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 43d order, Dumenae. See Botany Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">Vicar</a>, a person appointed as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to another, to perform his functions in his absence, and under his authority. Vicar, in the canon-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, the predial <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> whereof are appropriated or appropriated; that is, belong either to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> house, &c. or to a layman who receives them, and only allows the vicar the small tithes, or a convenient salary. See the article Parson and Vicar. Vice, in ethics, is ordinarily defined an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, denoting either an excess or defect from the just medium wherein virtue is placed. Vice, in smithery and other arts converging in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, a machine or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> serving to hold fast any thing they are at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon, whether it is to be beaten, filed, or rivetted. Vice is also used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> words to denote the relation of something that comes instead or in the place of another; as vice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, vice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, &c. are officers who take place in the absence of admirals, &c. Viceroy, a governor of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, who commands in the name and instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, with full and sovereign authority. Vicia, a genus of plants of the class diadelphia; and in the natural system arranged under the 32d order, Papilionaceae. See Botany Index. Vicissitude, the regular succession of one thing after another; as the vicissitude of day and night, of the seasons, &c. Victim, denotes a sacrifice offered to some deity, of a living creature, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or beast, which is slain to appease his wrath, or to obtain some favour. Victor, Sextus Aurelius, a Roman historian, who flourished under the emperors Constantius and Julian; as we learn from many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his own writings, and also from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a>. This historian relates, that Constantius made him <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, and honoured Victory honoured him with a brazen statue, on account of his excellent qualifications; although, as he owns of himself, he was born in an obscure village, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and illiterate parents. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> believed that he was an African: it is certain, that he dwells much upon the praises of that country, which he calls the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; decus terrarum. Two books of his are extant in the historical way: one De viris illustribus urbis Roma; the other, De Cesaribus; to which is prefixed Libellus de origine gentis Romanae. The whole makes an abridged history of Rome, from its foundation down to the reign of Julian inclusive.

VICTORY

Pages 187-187

in Pagan worship, is represented by Hebe as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Styx and Pallas; and Varro calls her the daughter of Heaven and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> erected a temple to her, where they prayed to the gods to give success to their arms. They painted her in the form of a woman, clad in cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. In some medals, she is represented with wings <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, holding a laurel <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a palm in the other; but in other medals, she is seen standing upon a globe, with the same crown and branch of palm.

VIDA

Pages 187-187

MARCUS HIERONYMUS, bishop of Alva, in Montferrat, and one of the most excellent Latin poets that have appeared since the Augustan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a> in 1470. Having distinguished himself by his learning and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature, he was made bishop of Alva in 1552. After continuing two years with Pope Clement VII. at Rome, he went to reside upon his fee; where, for 30 years, he performed all the offices of a good bishop and a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and though he was mild, gentle, and full of goodness, he was far from wanting spirit, that when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Alva was besieged by the French, he used all possible means to prevent its being given up, by strenuously exhorting the people, and, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> were scarce, by supplying them at his own expense. His Poetics, and poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-worm, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for his masterpiece; his poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESS">chess</a> is also greatly admired. He also wrote hymns, eclogues, and a poem entitled Chriftados in six books; all which are in Latin, and have gained him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. His works in prose consist of dialogues, fynodical constitutions, letters, and other pieces. He died in 1566, soon after being made bishop of Cremona.

VIENNA

Pages 187-187

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the circle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, in Germany, and of the whole German empire, is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> resides. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> itself is not of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; nor can it be enlarged, it being limited by a very strong fortification; but it is very populous. The streets, in general, are narrow, and the houses built <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Some of the public buildings are magnificent; but they appear externally to no great advantage, on account of the narrowness of the streets. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of them are the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the library, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>; the palaces of the princes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICHTENSTEIN">Lichtenstein</a>, Eugene, &c. Vienna was twice ineffectually besieged by the Turks; namely, in 1589 and 1683. At the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the siege was raised by John Sobieski, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, who totally defeated the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> before the walls of this place. There is no great danger that Vienna <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ever again be subjected to the inconveniences of a siege. Yet, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> that should happen, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> has been taken, which will prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of destroying the suburbs; namely, no houses without the walls are allowed to be built nearer to the glacis than 600 yards; so that there is a circular field of that breadth all round the town, which, exclusive of the advantage above-mentioned, has a very beautiful and salutary effect. These magnificent suburbs, and the town together, are said to contain above 300,000 inhabitants; yet the former are not near so populous, in proportion to their size, as the town; because many houses in the suburbs have extensive gardens belonging to them, and many families, who live during the winter within the fortifications, spend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> in the suburbs. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is built of free-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, is 114 yards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 48 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and the steeple is 447 feet high. Instead of a weathercock there was a Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the siege in 1589; but, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> siege in 1683, it was changed for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, which three months after was thrown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by a storm. At present there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spread eagle, over which is a gilded cross. Joining to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is the archbishop's palace, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of which is very fine. The university had several thousand students, who, when this city was besieged, mounted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, as they did also in 1741. Beside this, there is the academy of Lower Austria; and the archducal library is much frequented by foreigners, as it contains above 100,000 printed books, and 10,000 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>. The academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> is remarkable for the fine pictures it produces. The archducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and a cabinet of curiosities of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Austria, are great rarities. The inhabitants, in general, live in a splendid manner; and people of distinction have all sorts of wines at their tables, which they are very free with to foreigners. There is a port of harbour on the Danube, where there are magazines of naval stores, and ships have been fitted out to serve on that river against the Turks. Vienna is an archbishop's see. It is seated at the place where the river Vienna <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Wein, falls into the Danube, 30 miles west of Presburgh, 350 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-north-east of Rome, 520 south-east by south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, 565 east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and 680 east-south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. E. Long. 16. 28. N. Lat. 48. 13.

VIGIL

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> before any solemn feast; because then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were wont to watch, fast, and pray, in their churches.

VIGILS OF PLANTS

Pages 187-188

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> under which botanists comprehend the precise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> open, expand, and shut. As all plants do not flower in the same season, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; in like manner, those which flower the same day, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, do not open and shut precisely at the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. Some open in the morning, as the lip flowers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> flowers with flat spreading petals; others at noon, as the mallows; and a third set in the evening, or after sunset, as some geraniums and opuntias: the hour of shutting is equally determined. Of those which open in the morning, some shut soon after, while others remain expanded till night. The hours of opening, like the time of flowering, seem to vary, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the plant, the temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and that of the season. Flowers, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> delicacy would be hurt by the strong impressions of an ardent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, do not open till night; those which require a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> to elevate their juices; in other words, whose juices do not rise but in the morning or evening, do not expand till then; whilst those which need a more lively heat for the same purpose, expand at noon, when the sun is in his meridian strength. Hence it is, that the heat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> being greater between the tropics than elsewhere, plants which are transported from those climates into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> or temperate climates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, expand their flowers much later than in their native <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. Thus, a flower which opens in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> at six o'clock in the morning at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not open at the same season in France and England till eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, nor in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> till ten. Linnaeus distinguishes by the general name of solar (flores solares) all those flowers which observe a determinate time in opening and shutting. These flowers are again divided, from certain circumstances, into three species, or kinds: Equinoctial flowers (flores aquinoctiales) are such as open and shut at all seasons, at a certain fixed or determinate hour. Tropical flowers (flores tropici) are such whose hour of opening is not fixed at all seasons, but accelerated or retarded according as the length of the day is increased or diminished. Meteorous flowers (flores meteorici) are such whose hour of expansion depends upon the dry or humid state of the air, and the greater or less pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. Of this kind is the Siberian fox-thistle, which shuts at night <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ensuing day is to be clear and serene, and opens if it is to be cloudy and rainy. In like manner the African marigold, which in dry serene <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> opens at six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in the morning, and shuts at four o'clock in the afternoon, is a sure indication that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> during the course of the day, when it continues shut after seven.

VIGO
