Pages 188-188

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, with an old castle and a fort. It is seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by the sea-side. It was rendered famous by a sea-fight between the confederate fleet commanded by Sir George Rook, and a squadron of French men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a> with a body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> forces drove the Spaniards from the castles which defended the harbour. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Hopson having with infinite danger broken through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOM">boom</a> made across the mouth of the harbour, the English took four galleons and five <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> men of war, and the Dutch five galleons and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of war. Four galleons, with 14 men of war, were destroyed, with abundance of plate and other rich effects. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 21. N. Lat. 42. 5.

VILLA FRANCA

Pages 188-188

the name of several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; one in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, three miles east of Nice; another of Catalonia, 18 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>; a third, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of St Michael, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZORES">Azores</a>; and a fourth, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, 57 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>.

VILLAGE

Pages 188-188

an assemblage of houses inhabited chiefly by peasants and farmers, and having no market, whereby it is distinguished from a town. The word is French, formed of vil <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vili, "low, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, contemptible;" or rather, from the Latin villa, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>.

VILLAIN

Pages 188-188
or VILLEIN, in our ancient customs, denotes a man of servile or base condition, viz. a bondman or servant.

VILLENAGE

Pages 188-189

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. The folk-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> estates held in villenage, was a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> neither strictly feudal, Norman, or Saxon; but mixed and compounded of them all; and which also, on account of the heriots Villenage, that usually attend it, may seem to have somewhat Danish in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. Under the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> there were, as Sir William Temple speaks, a sort of people in a condition of downright servitude, used and employed in the most servile works, and belonging, both they, their children, and effects, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, like the rest of the cattle or stock upon it. They seem to have been those who held what was called the folk-land, from which they were removable at the lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. On the arrival of the Normans here, it seems not improbable, that they, who were strangers to any other than a feudal state, might give some sparks of enfranchisement to such wretched persons as fell to their share, by admitting them, as well as others, to the oath of fealty; which conferred a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of protection, and raised the tenant to a kind of estate superior to downright <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, but inferior to every other condition. This they called villenage, and the tenants villeins. These villeins, belonging principally to lords of manors, were either villeins regardant, that is, annexed to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> or land; or else they were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a>, or at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, that is, annexed to the person of the lord, and transferable by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> from one owner to another. They could not leave their lord without his permission; but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they ran away, or were purloined from him, might be claimed and recovered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, like beasts or other chattels. They held indeed small portions of land by way of sustaining themselves and families; but it was at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the lord, who might disfranchise them whenever he pleased; and it was upon villain services, that is, to carry out dungs, to hedge and ditch the lord's demesnes, and any other the meanest offices; and their services were not only base, but uncertain both as to their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. A villain could acquire no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> either in lands or goods; if he purchased either, the lord might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> them to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; unless he contrived to disfranchise them again before the lord had seized them, for the lord had then lost his opportunity. In many places also a fine was payable to the lord, if the villain presumed to marry his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to any one with leave from the lord; and, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, the lord might also bring an action against the husband for damages in thus purloining his property. For the children of villeins were also in the same state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> with their parents; whence they were called in Latin nativi, which gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> appellation of a villein, who was called a neife. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> between a freeman and a neife, or a villein and a free-woman, the issue followed the condition of the father, being free if he was free, and a villein if he was villein, contrary to the maxim of the civil law, that partus sequitur ventrem. But no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> could be born a villein, because by another maxim of our law he is nullius filius; and as he can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> nothing by inheritance, it were hard that he should lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> freedom by it. The law, however, protected the persons of villeins against atrocious injuries of the lord: for he might not kill or maim his villein; though he might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> him with impunity. Villeins might be enfranchised by manumission. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time they gained considerable ground on their lords; and in particular strengthened the tenure of their estates to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they came to have in them an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in many places full as good, in others better than Villenage, than their lords. For the good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and benevolence of many lords of manors having, time out of mind, permitted their villeins and their children to enjoy their possessions without interruption, in a regular course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, the common law, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, now gave them <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to prescribe against their lords; and, on performance of the same services, to hold their lands, in spite of any determination of the lord's will. For though in general they are still said to hold their estates at the will of the lord, yet it is such a will as is agreeable to the custom of the manor; which customs are preserved and evidenced by the rolls of the several courts-baron in which they are entered, or kept on foot by the constant immemorial usage of the several manors in which the lands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a>. And as such tenants had nothing to show for their estates but those customs, and admissions in pursuance of them, entered on these rolls, or the copies of such entries witnessed by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, they now began to be called tenants by copy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-roll, and their tenure itself a copyhold. Privileged Villenage, a species of tenure otherwise called villein-seignory. See Tenure. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> demesne consists of those lands or manors which, though now perhaps granted out to private subjects, were actually in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in the time of Edward the Confessor, or William the Conqueror; and so appear to have been, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> survey in the exchequer, called the Domesday-book. The tenants of these lands, under the crown, were not all of the same order or degree. Some of them, as Britton testifies, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time pure and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> villeins, dependent on the will of the lord; and common copyholders in only a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. Others were in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> enfranchised by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> favour; being only bound in respect of their lands to perform some of the better sort of villein-services, but those determinate and certain; as, to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s land for so many days; to supply his court with such a quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; and the like; all of which are now changed into pecuniary rents; and in consideration hereof they had many immunities and privileges granted to them; as, to try the right of their property in a peculiar court of their own, called a court of ancient demesne, by a peculiar process denominated a writ of right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>; not to pay toll or taxes; not to contribute to the expenses of knights of the shire; not to be put on juries, and the like. These tenants therefore, though their tenure be absolutely copyhold, yet have an interest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a freehold: for though their services were of a base and villainous original, yet the tenants were esteemed in all others respects to be highly privileged villeins; and especially for that their services were fixed and determinate, and that they could not be compelled (like pure villeins) to relinquish those tenements at the lord's will, or to hold them against their own: et idem (says Bracton) dieuntur liberi. Lands holding by this tenure are therefore a species of copyhold, and as such preserved and exempted from the operation of the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. Yet they differ from common copyholds, principally in the privileges before mentioned: as also they differ from freeholders by one especial mark and tincture of villenage, noted by Bracton, and remaining to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; viz. that they cannot be conveyed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to man by the general common-law conveyances of seffoment, and the rest; but must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by surrender to the lord or his steward, in the manner of common copyholds: yet with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that, in the surrenders of these lands in ancient demesne, it is not used to say, "to hold at the will of their lord," in their copies; but only, "to hold according to the custom of the manor."

VILLOSE

Pages 189-189
or VILLOUS, something abounding with villi or fibres like short hair; such is one of the coats of the stomack.

VINCA

Pages 189-190

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the clas pentandra; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 30th order, Conortae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. St Vincent, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, which received its name from being discovered on the 22d of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, the feast of that Saint. It is inhabited by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people, of whom Dr Robertson gives this account: "There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distinction in character between the Caribbees and the inhabitants of the larger islands. The former appear manifestly to be a separate race. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is totally different from that of their neighbours in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> islands. They themselves have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> came originally from some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the continent, and having conquered and exterminated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants, took possession of their lands and of their women. Hence they call themselves Banaree, which signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> come from beyond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Accordingly, the Caribbees still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> two distinct languages, one peculiar to the men, and the other to the women. The language of the men has nothing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with that spoken in the large islands. The dialect of the women considerably resembles it. This strongly confirms the tradition which I have mentioned. The Caribbees themselves imagine that they were a colony from the Galibis, a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. But as their fierce manners approach nearer to those of the people in the northern continent, than to those of the natives of South America, and as their language has likewise some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to that spoken in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, their origin should be deduced rather from the former than from the latter. In their wars they still preserve their ancient practice of destroying all the males, and preserving the women either for servitude <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> for breeding." It remained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after it was discovered inhabited by these people, and by another race improperly styled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Caribs, who are in reality <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> descended, as is generally believed, from some who escaped out of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> ship wrecked upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and gradually augmented by such as from time to time fled thither from Barbadoes. These nations were often at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; but when their quarrels were composed, they had a strength sufficient to prevent strangers from settling by force. The French, about half a century ago, at the request of the Caribs, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a>, and attacked the negroes, but were repulsed with loss; and found it their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to conciliate a friendship with both nations by means of presents, and furnishing them with arms and ammunition. St Vincent was long a neutral <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; but, at the peace of 1763, the French agreed that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to it should be vested in the English; who, in the sequel, at the instance of some rapacious planters, engaged in an unjust war against the Caribbees, who inhabited the windward St Vincent, windward side of the island, and who were obliged to content to a peace, by which they ceded a very large tract of valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this was, that in the next war, in 1779, they greatly contributed to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of this island by the French, who, however, restored it by the peace of 1783. Since that time it has <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the possession of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. During the French revolutionary war, the Caribs revolted; and, assisted by the French, spread devastation over the whole island; but by the exertions of the governor and the British forces in the West Indies, the revolt was quelled. St Vincent is in length about 24 miles, and about 18 in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is very warm. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is in generally hilly, in some places mountainous; but interspersed with a variety of pleasant valleys, and some luxuriant plains, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> being everywhere very fertile, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> grounds are at least in general easy of ascent. Few islands are so well watered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. The inhabitants raise all kinds of ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in plenty. The rivers supply them with variety of fish. W. Long, 61° N. Lat. 13°.

VINCI

Pages 190-190

LEONARDO DA, an illustrious Italian painter, descended from a noble Tuscan family, was born in the castle of Vinci, near <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1445. He was placed under Andrea Verrocchio, a celebrated painter in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; but soon surpassed him and all his predecessors so much, as to be reputed the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. But his studies were far from terminating here; no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s genius was more universal: he applied himself to arts, to literature, and to the accomplishments of the body; and he excelled in every thing which he attempted. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Sforza <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> prevailed on him to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the academy for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> established; where Leonardo soon banished all the Gothic fashions, and reduced every thing to the happy simplicity of the Greek and Roman style. By the duke's order he constructed the famous aqueduct that supplies the city of Milan with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>: this canal goes by the name of Morteiana, being above 200 miles in length, and conducts the water of the river Adda quite to the walls of the city. In 1479, he was desired to construct some new device for the entertainment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. of France, who was then to make his entrance into Milan. Leonardo accordingly made a very curious automaton in the form of a lion, which marched out to meet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, reared up on its hinder legs before him, and opening its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, displayed an escutcheon with fleurs de lys quartered on it. The disorders of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, with the misfortunes of his patrons the Sforzi, obliging Leonardo to quit Milan, he retired to Florence, where he flourished under the Medici: here he raised the envy of Michael Angelo, who was his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a>; and Raphael, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of his works, acquired his best manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>. At length, on the invitation of Francis I., he removed to France when above 70 years of age; where the journey and change of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> threw him into his last sickness: he languished for some months at Fontainebleau, where the king came frequently to see him; and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> rising up in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> to acknowledge the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> done him, he fainted, and Francis supporting him, Leonardo died in his arms. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> happened in 1520. Some of his paintings are to be seen in England and other countries, but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them are in Florence and France. He composed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of discourses on various subjects; but none of them have been published but his treatise on the Art of Painting.—For his anatomical knowledge, see ANATOMY (<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of), p. 669.

VINCULUM

Pages 190-190

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, a character in form of a line <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stroke drawn over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a>, divisor, or dividend, when compounded of several letters or quantities to connect them, and shows that they are to be multiplied or divided, &c. together by the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. Thus $d \times a + b - c$ shows that $d$ is to be multiplied into $a + b - c$. VINE. See VITIS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VINEGAR

Pages 190-190

ACETUM, an agreeable acid, prepared from wine, cider, beer, and other liquors; of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, both as a medicine and a sauce. The word is French, vinaigre; formed from vin, "wine," and aigre, "sour." See ACETIC ACID, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Eels in VINEGAR. See ANIMALCULE, n° 9.

VINEYARD

Pages 190-190

a plantation of vines. The best situation of a vineyard is on the declivity of a hill facing the south.

VIOLA

Pages 190-190

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the clasiflyngenicia; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 29th order, Campanaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VIOLATION

Pages 190-190

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of violating, that is, forcing a woman, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> committing a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> upon her.—This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is also used in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> or infringement of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, ordinance, or the like. VIOLET. See VIOLA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. VIOLET-Crab. See CANCER, ENTOMOLOGY Index.

VIOLIN

Pages 190-190
or FIDDLE, a musical instrument mounted with four strings or guts, and struck or played with a bow. The style and sound of the violin is the gayest and most sprightly of all other instruments; and hence it is of all others the fittest for dancing. Yet there are ways of touching it, which render it grave, soft, languishing, and fit for church or chamber music.—It generally makes the treble or highest parts in concerts. Its harmony is from fifth to fifth. Its play is composed of bass, counter-tenor, tenor, and treble; to which may be added, a fifth part: each part has four fifths, which rise to a greater seventeenth.

VIOLONCELLO

Pages 190-190

of the Italians, is properly our fifth violin; which is a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> violin half the size of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> bass violin, and the strings bigger and longer in proportion: consequently its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> lower than our bass violin; which has a noble effect in concerts. VIPER. See OPHIOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VIRAGO

Pages 190-190

a woman of extraordinary stature and courage; who has the mein and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and performs the actions and exercises of men.

VIRGIL

Pages 190-192
or PUBLIUS VIRGILIUS MARO, the most excellent of all the Latin poets, was the son of a potter of Andes, near Mantua, where he was born, 70 years B.C. He studied first at Mantua; then at Cremona, Milan, and Naples; whence going to Rome, he acquired the esteem of the greatest wits and most illustrious persons of his time; and among others of the emperor Augustus, Mecenas, and Pollio. He was well skilled not only in polite literature and poetry, but also in philosophy, Virgil, the mathematics, geography, medicine, and href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history. Though one of the greatest geniuses of his age, and the admiration of the Romans, he always preferred a singular mode, and lived chastely at a time when the manners of the people were extremely corrupt. He carried Latin poetry to such an high perfection, that he was justly esteemed the prince of Latin poets. He first turned himself to pastoral; and being captivated with the beauty and sweetness of Theocritus, was ambitious to introduce this new species of poetry among the Romans. His first performance in this way supposed to have been written U. C. 907, the year before the death of Julius Caesar, when the poet was in his 25th year: it is intitled Alexis. Possibly Palaeemon was his second: it is a close imitation of the fourth and fifth Idylls of Theocritus. Mr Wharton places Silenus next; which is said to have been publicly recited on the stage by Cytheris, a celebrated comedian. Virgil's fifth eclogue is composed in allusion to the death and deification of Caesar. The battle of Philippi in 712 having put an end to the Roman liberty, the veteran soldiers began to murmur for their pay; and Augustus, to reward them, distributed among them the lands of Mantua and Cremona. Virgil was involved in this common calamity; and applied to Varus and Pollio, who warmly recommended him to Augustus, and procured for him his patrimony again. Full of gratitude to Augustus, he composed the Thyrsus, in which he introduces two shepherds; one of them complaining of the distraction of the times, and of the havoc the soldiers made among the Mantuan farmers; the other rejoicing for the recovery of his estate, and promising to honour as a god the person who restored it to him. But our poet's joy was not of long continuance; for we are told, that when he returned to take possession of his farm, he was violently assaulted by the intruder, and would certainly have been killed by him if he had not escaped by swimming hastily over the Mincio. Upon this unexpected disappointment, he returned to Rome to renew his petition; and during his journey seems to have composed his ninth eclogue. The celebrated eclogue, intitled Pollio, was composed U. C. 714, upon the following occasion: The confid Pollio on the part of Antony, and Macenas on the part of Caesar, had made up the differences between them; by agreeing, that Octavia, half-sister to Caesar, should be given in marriage to Antony. This agreement caused an universal joy; and Virgil, in his eclogue, testified his. Octavia was with child by her late husband Marcellus at the time of this marriage; and whereas the Sibylline oracles had foretold, that a child was to be born about this time, who should rule the world, and establish perpetual peace, the poet ingeniously supposes the child in Octavia's womb to be the glorious infant, under whose reign mankind was to be happy, the golden age to return from heaven, and fraud and violence to be no more. In this celebrated poem, the author, with great delicacy at the same time, pays his court to both the chiefs, to his patron Pollio, to Octavia, and to the unborn infant. In 715, Pollio was sent against the Parthians, a people of Illyricum; and during this expedition, Virgil addressed to him a beautiful eclogue, called Pharsacneutria. His tenth and last eclogue was addressed to Gallus. In his 34th year, he retired to Naples, and laid the plan of his Georgics; which he undertook at the intreates of Maecenas, to whom he dedicated them. This wife and able minister resolved, if possible, to revive the decayed spirit of husbandry; to introduce a taste for agriculture, even among the great; and could not think of a better method to effect this, than to recommend it by the infatuating charms of poetry. Virgil fully answered the expectations of his patron by his Georgics. They are divided into four books. Corn and ploughing are the subject of the first, vines of the second, cattle of the third, and bees of the fourth. He is supposed to have been in his 45th year when he began to write the Aeneid; the design of which was to reconcile the Romans to the government of Augustus. Augustus was eager to peruse this poem before it was finished; and intreated him by letters to communicate it. Macrobius has preserved to us part of one of Virgil's answers to the emperor, in which the poet excuses himself: who, however, at length complied, and read himself the sixth book to the emperor; when Octavia, who had just lost her son Marcellus, the darling of Rome, and adopted son of Augustus, made one of the audience. "Virgil had artfully interlaid that beautiful lamentation for the death of young Marcellus, beginning with—O nate, ingentem luculum ne quere tuorum—but suppressed his name till he came to the line—Tu Marcellus eris: upon hearing which, Octavia could bear no more, but fainted away, overcome with surprize and sorrow. When she recovered, she made the poet a present of ten sestertii for every line, which amounted in the whole to above 2000L. The Aeneid being brought to a conclusion, but not to the perfection our author intended to give it, he resolved to travel into Greece, to correct and polish it at leisure. It was probably on this occasion that Horace addressed that affectionate ode to him, Sic te Divo potens Cypri, &c. Augustus returning victorious from the east, met with Virgil at Athens, who thought himself obliged to attend the emperor to Italy; but the poet was suddenly seized with a fatal distemper, which being increased by the agitation of the vessel, put an end to his life as soon as he landed at Brundusium, in his 52d year. He had ordered in his will, that the Aeneid should be burnt as an unfinished poem; but Augustus forbade it, and had it delivered to Varius and Tucca, with the strictest charge to make no additions, but only to publish it correctly. He died with such steadiness and tranquillity, as to be able to dictate his own epitaph in the following words: Mantua me genuit: Calabri rapuere, tenet nunc Parthenope: cecini Pafcua, Rara, Duces. His bones were carried to Naples, according to his earnest request; and a monument was erected at a small distance from the city. Virgil was of a lankish complexion, tall, of a sickly constitution, and afflicted with frequent headaches and spitting of blood. He was so very bashful, that he often ran into the shops to prevent being gazed at in the streets; yet was so honoured by the Roman people, that once coming into the theatre, the whole audience rose up out of respect to him. He was of a thoughtful and melancholy temper; he spoke little, and loved retirement and contemplation. His fortune was affluent; he had a fine house and well furnished library near Maecenas's gardens, on the Esquiline mount at Rome, and al- so a delightful villa in Sicily. He was so benevolent and inoffensive, that most of his contemporary poets, though they envied each other, agreed in loving and esteeming him. He revised his verses with prodigious fervency; and used to compare himself to a she bear, which licked her cubs into shape. The best edition of Virgil's works are those of Mof- vicus, with the notes of Servius, printed at Leiden in 1717, two vols 4to; and that of Burman, at Amsterdam, 1746, in four vols 4to. There are several English translations, which are well known. Virgil, Polydore, an English historian, born at Urbino in Italy, was sent in the beginning of the 16th century, by Pope Alexander VI, as sub-collector of the Papal tax, called Peter-pence, in this kingdom. He had not been long in England before he obtained preferment in the church; for in 1503 he was presented to the rectory of Church-Langton in the archdeaconry of Leicester. In 1507 he was collated to the prebend of Scamlerby in the church of Lincoln; and in the same year was made archdeacon of Wells, and prebendary of Hereford. In 1513, he resigned his prebend of Lincoln, and was collated to that of Osgate in St Paul's, London. We are told, that on his preferment to the archdeaconry of Wells, he resigned the office of sub-collector to the pope, and determined to spend the remainder of his life in England, the History of which kingdom he began in the year 1505, at the command of Henry VII. That work cost him 12 years labour. In 1526, he finished his treatise on Prodigies. Polydore continued in England during the whole reign of Henry VIII, and part of that of Edward VI, whence it is concluded that he was a moderate Papist. In 1550, being now an old man, he requested leave to revisit his native country. He was accordingly dismissed with a present of 300 crowns, together with the privilege of holding his preferments to the end of his life. He died at Urbino in the year 1555. As an historian, he is accused by some as a malignant flatterer of the English nation; yet Jovius remarks, that the French and Scotch accuse him of having flattered that nation too much: (See his Elog. cap. 135. p. 179.) Besides the above, he wrote, 1. De Rerum Inventoribus; of which an English translation was published by Langley in 1663. It was also translated into French and Spanish. 2. De Prodigiis et Soritis. 3. Episcoporum Anglici Catalogus. Manuscript. 4. De Vita Perfectione, Basil, 1546, 1553, 8vo. 5. Epistolae Eruditorum; and some other works.

VIRGINIA

Pages 192-193

one of the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, is bounded on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> and the river Ohio, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, on the south by North Carolina. The boundaries include an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> somewhat triangular of 121,525 miles, whereof 79,650 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> westward of the Alleghany <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and 57,034 westward of the meridian of the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Kanawha. This state is therefore one third larger than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, which are reckoned at 88,357 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in Virginia are, Roanoke, James river, which receives the Rivanna, Appamattox, Chicahominy, Nansemond, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> rivers; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> river, which is formed by the junction of Pamunky and Mattaponi rivers; Rappahannock, and Potomack. The mountains are not solitary and scattered confusedly over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; they commence at about 150 miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and are disposed in ridges one behind another, running nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the coast, though rather approaching it as they advance north-eastwardly. To the south-west, as the tract of country between the sea-coast and the Mississippi becomes narrower, the mountains converge into a single ridge, which, as it approaches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, subsides into plain country, and gives rise to some of the waters of that gulf. From the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of Virginia, it may be expected that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is not the same in all its parts. It is remarkable that, proceeding on the same parallel of latitude westwardly, the climate becomes colder in like manner as when you proceed northwardly. This continues to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> till you attain the summit of the Alleghany, which is the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> between the ocean and the Mississippi. From thence, descending in the same latitude to the Mississippi, the change reverses; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may believe travellers, it becomes warmer there than it is in the same latitude on the sea side. Their testimony is strengthened by the vegetables and animals which subsist and multiply there naturally, and do not on the sea-coast. Thus catalpas grow spontaneously on the Mississippi as far as the latitude of 37°, and reeds as far as 38° degrees. Perroquets even winter on the Soto in the 39th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1779, when the thermometer was at 90 degrees at Monticello, and 96 degrees at Williamsburg, it was 110 degrees at Kalkaska. Perhaps the mountain, which overhangs this village on the north side, may by its reflection have contributed somewhat to produce this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of free inhabitants in this state in 1790 was 454,983, and of slaves 292,627. The whole imports of the state of Virginia amounted in 1796 to 5,268,615 dollars. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of William and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> is the only public seminary of learning in Virginia. It was founded in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Mary, who granted it to 20,000 acres of land, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> duty on certain tobaccos exported from Virginia and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> also gave it by temporary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> a duty on liquors imported, and skins and furs exported. From these resources it received upwards of 3000l. communiens annis. The buildings are of brick, sufficient for an indifferent accommodation of perhaps 100 students. By its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> it was to be under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of 20 visitors, who were to be its legislators; and to have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> and six professorships, which at present stand thus.—A professorship for Law and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">Police</a>; Anatomy and Medicine; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral Philosophy</a>, the Law of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Nations, the Fine Arts; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> Languages; and a fifth, called the professorship of Brafferton, for the instruction of the Indians. In 1787, there were about 30 young gentlemen members of this college, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of which were law students. There are some flourishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> in Virginia; one in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, one at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, one at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, one at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and others in other places. The present denominations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in Virginia are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, who are the most numerous, and in- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> the western parts of the state; Episcopalians, who are the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> settlers, and occupy the eastern and first settled parts of the state. Intermingled with these are great numbers of Baptists and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>. The bulk of these last mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sects are of the poorer sort of people, and many of them are very ignorant (as is indeed the case with the other denominations), but they are generally a virtuous well-meaning set of people. Virginia has produced some of the most distinguished men that have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in effecting the two late important revolutions in America, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> character <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among the first in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The great body of the people do not concern themselves with politics; so that their government, though nominally republican, is in fact oligarchical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> aristocratical. The Virginians who are rich, are in general sensible, polite, and hospitable, and of an independent spirit. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> are ignorant and abject; all are of an inquisitive turn, and in many other respects very much resemble the people in the eastern states. There is a much greater disparity between the rich and the poor in Virginia than in any of the northern states. A spirit for literary inquiries, if not altogether confined to a few, is, among the body of the people, evidently subordinate to a spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> and barbarous sports. At almost every tavern or ordinary on the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> there is a billiard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BACKGAMMON">backgammon</a> table, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, and other implements for various games. To these public houses the gambling gentry in the neighborhood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to kill time which hangs heavily upon them; and at these businesses they are extremely expert, having been accustomed to it from their earliest youth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for cock-fighting, a diversion not only inhumanly barbarous, but infinitely beneath the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is so predominant, that they even advertise their matches in the public newspapers. The executive powers are lodged in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a governor chosen annually, and incapable of acting more than three years in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. He is assisted by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of eight members. The judiciary powers are divided among several courts. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">Legislation</a> is exercised by two houses of assembly; one called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Delegates, composed of two members from each county, chosen annually by the citizens possessing an estate for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in 100 acres of uninhabited land, or 25 acres with a house on it, or in a house or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> in town. The other called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">Senate</a>, consisting of 24 members, chosen quadrennially by the same electors, who for this purpose are distributed into 24 districts. The concurrence of both houses is necessary to the passage of a law. They have the appointment of the governor and council, the judges of the superior courts, auditors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the land office, and delegates to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a>. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, there was exported from this state, communibus annis, to the amount of 850,000l. Virginia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, or 697,142 guineas. The whole country before it was planted was one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> forest interspersed with marshes. No country now produces greater quantities of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and shallow, that after they have cleared a fresh piece of ground out of the woods, it will not bear tobacco after two or three years unless well manured. The forests yield oaks, poplars, pines, cedars, cypresses, sweet myrtles, chestnuts, hickory, live oak, walnut, dogwood, alder, hazel, chinquapins, locust-trees, salalfras, elm, ash, beech, with a great variety of sweet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> and incense, which distill from several trees; pitch, tar, rosin, turpentine, plank <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and yards. Virginia yields also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, plenty of pasture, with coal, quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore.

VIRGO

Pages 193-193

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, one of the signs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>.

VIRTUAL

Pages 193-193
or POTENTIAL; something that has a power or virtue of acting or doing. The term is chiefly understood of something that acts by a secret invisible cause, in opposition to actual and sensible.

VIRTUE

Pages 193-193

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in various significations. In the general it denotes power, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the perfection of anything, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or supernatural, animate, or inanimate, essential or accidental. But, in its more proper or restrained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, virtue signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, which improves and perfects the possessor and his actions. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">MORAL <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">PHILOSOPHY</a>, No. 84.

VIRTUOSO

Pages 193-193

an Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> lately introduced into the English, signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of curiosity and learning, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one who loves and promotes the arts and sciences. But among us the term seems to be appropriated to those who apply themselves to some curious and quaint rather than immediately useful art or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; as antiquaries, collectors of rarities of any kind, microscopical observers, &c.

VIRULENT

Pages 193-193

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to any thing that yields a virus; that is, a contagious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> malignant pus.

VISCERA

Pages 193-193

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying the same with entrails; including the heart, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, lungs, spleen, intestines, and other inward parts of the body.

VISCIDITY

Pages 193-193
or VISCOSITY, the quality of something that is viscid or viscous; that is, glutinous and sticky like bird-lime, which the Latins call by the name of viscus.

VISCOUNT

Pages 193-193

was anciently an officer under an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, to whom, during his attendance at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he acted as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to look after the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. But the name was afterwards made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of as an arbitrary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, without any shadow of office pertaining to it, by Henry VI.; when, in the 18th year of his reign, he created John Beaumont a peer by the name of Viscount Beaumont; which was the first instance of the kind. A viscount is created by patent as an earl is; his title is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a>; his mantle is two doublings and a half of plain fur; and his coronet has only a row of pearls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the circle.

VISCUM

Pages 193-193

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the clas dioecia, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 48th order, aggregate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VISHNOU

Pages 193-193

that person in the triad of the Brahmans who is considered as the preserver of the universe. Brahma is the creator, and Siva the destroyer; and these two, with Vishnu, united in some inexplicable manner, constitute Brahma, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the supreme numen of the Hindoos. See POLYTHEISM, No. 36.

VISIBLE

Pages 193-193

something that is an object of sight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vision; or something whereby the eye is affected so as to produce this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>.

VISIER

Pages 193-194

an officer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> in the Ottoman empire. Vifion pire, whereof there are two kinds; one called by the Turks Vifion-avem, that is, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> vifion," is the prime minister of state in the whole empire. He commands the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, and presides in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVAN">divan</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. Next to him are fix other subordinate vifters, called vifters of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>; who officiate as his counsellors or affeffors in the divan.

VISION

Pages 194-194

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of seeing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perceiving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects by means of the organ of fight, the eye. See ANATOMY, No 142, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>, No 49—54.

VISTULA

Pages 194-194
or WESEL, a large river of Poland, which taking its rise in the mountains south of Silefia, vifts Cracow, Warfaw, &c. and continuing its course northward, falls into the Baltic sea below Dantzig.

VITAL

Pages 194-194

in Physiology, an appellation given to whatever ministers principally to the confifting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> maintaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the bodies of animals: thus the heart, lungs, and brain, are called vital parts; and the operations of these parts by which the life of animals is maintained are called vital functions.

VITIS

Pages 194-194
or VINE, a genus of the clas pentandra, and in the natural fytem arranged under the 46th order, Hederaeae. See BOTANY Index; and for its culture, fee GARDENING. VITREOUS HUMOUR OF THE EYE. See ANATOMY, No 142.

VITRIFICATION

Pages 194-194

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, the conversion of a body into glass by means of fire. See GLASS.

VITRIOL

Pages 194-194

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, formed by the union of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, with sulphuric acid, hence called from the colours <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, blue, and green, according to the metal. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a>.

VITRIOLATED

Pages 194-194

among chemists, something impregnated, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> supposed to be so, with vitriol or its acid. VITRIOLIC ACID. See SULPHURIC Acid and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

VITRUVIUS POLLIO

Pages 194-194

MARCUS, a very celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, was, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, and lived in the reign of Augustus, to whom he dedicated his excellent treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, divided into ten books. William Philander's edition of this celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is esteemed. Claudius Perrault has given an excellent translation of it in French, with learned notes. There are also several English translations of Vitruvius. VITUS'S DANCE. See MEDICINE, No 284.

VIVERRA

Pages 194-194

the WEASEL; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order of fere. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. VIVES. See FARRIERY.

VIVIPAROUS

Pages 194-194

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, an epithet applied to such animals as bring forth their young alive and perfect; in contradiftinction to thofe that lay eggs, which are called oviparous animals.

VOLLEY

Pages 208-208

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> salute, made by discharging a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fire arms at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

VOLONES

Pages 208-208

in Roman antiquity, slaves who in the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> voluntarily offered their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the state, which is the reason of the appellation; upon which they were admitted to citizenship, as none but freemen could be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>.

VOLT

Pages 208-209

in the manage, a round <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circular <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a>; and hence, by the phrase to make volts, is understood a gate of two treads, made by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> going sidewise round a centre, in such a manner that these two treads make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> tracks; one larger, made by the fore feet, and another smaller made by the hind-feet; the croup approaching towards the centre, and the shoulders <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> out. Voltaire, Francis Arquet de, a celebrated French author, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, February 20, 1694. His father, Francis Arquet, was ancien notaire au Chatelet, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the chamber of accounts; his mother, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>-Margaret Draumart. At the birth of this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 85 years and some months, there was little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of his being reared, and for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> remarkably feeble. In his earliest years he displayed a ready <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and a sprightly imagination; and, as he said of himself made verses before he was out of his cradle. He was educated, under Father Poré, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>; and such was his proficiency, that many of his essays are now existing, which, though written when he was between 12 and 14, show no marks of infancy. The famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINON_DE_L_ENCLOS">Ninon de l'Enclos</a>, to whom this ingenious boy was introduced, left him a legacy of 2000 livres to buy him a library. Having been sent to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> on quitting college, he was so disgusted with the dryness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, that he devoted himself entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>. He was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the abbe Cheauleu, the marquis de la Fare, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Sully, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of Vendome, marshal Villars, and the chevalier du Bouillon; and caught from them that easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and delicate humour which distinguished the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Louis XIV. Voltaire had early imbibed a turn for satire; and, for some philippics against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, was imprisoned almost a year in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTILLE">Bastille</a>. He had before this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> produced the tragedy of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OEDIPUS">Oedipus</a>, which was represented in 1718 with great success; and the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> happening to see it performed, was so delighted, that he obtained his release from prison. The poet waiting on the duke to return thanks; "Be wise (said the duke), and I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> take care of you." "I am infinitely obliged (replied the young man); but I intreat your <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> highness not to trouble yourself any farther about my lodging or board." He began his Henriade before he was 18. Having one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> read several cantos of this poem when on a visit to his intimate friend, the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> de Maifons, he was so teased with objections, that he lost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, and threw his manuscript into the fire. The president Henaut with difficulty rescued it. "Remember (said Mr Henaut to him, in one of his letters) it was I that saved the Henriade, and that it cost me a handsome <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of ruffles." Some years after, several copies of this poem having got abroad, while it was only a sketch, an edition of it was published, with many charms, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">League</a>. Instead of fame and friends, the author gained only enemies and mortification, by this first edition. The bigots took fire at it, and the poet was considered as highly criminal for praising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Coligny and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. Endeavours were even used to get the piece suppressed; but this strange <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> proved abortive. His chagrin, on this occasion, first inspired him with the thought of visiting England, in order to finish the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and republish it in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> George I, and more particularly the princess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, afterwards queen of England, raised an immense subscription for him. Their liberality laid the foundation of his fortune; for on his return to France in 1728, he put his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a> established by M. Desfortes, comptroller-general of the finances. The adventurers received a rent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOTEL">Hotel</a>-de-Ville for their tickets; and the prizes were paid in ready money; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> had taken all the tickets, it would have gained a million of livres. He joined with a numerous company of adventurers, and was fortunate. His Lettres Philosophiques, abounding in bold expressions and indecent witticisms against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, having been burnt by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris, and a warrant being issued for apprehending the author in 1733, Voltaire prudently withdrew; and was sheltered by the marchioness du Chatelet, in her castle of Cirey, on the borders of Champagne and Lorraine, who entered with him on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the system of Leibnitz, and the Principia of Newton. A gallery was built, in which Voltaire formed a good collection of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and made an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>. He laboured in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time on his Elements of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, then totally unknown in France, and which the numerous admirers of Descartes were little desirous should be known. In the midst of these philosophic pursuits he produced the tragedy of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALZIRA">Alzira</a>. He was now in the meridian of his age and genius, as was evident from the tragedy of Mahomet, first acted in 1741; but it was represented to the procureur-general as a performance offensive to religion; and the author, by order of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Fleury, withdrew it from the stage. Merope, played two years after, 1743, gave an idea of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of tragedy, of which few models had existed. It was at the representation of this tragedy, that the pit and boxes were clamorous for a sight of the author; yet it was severely criticised when it came from the press. He now became a favourite at court, through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Madame d'Epinay, afterwards marchioness of Pompadour. He was appointed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber in ordinary, and historiographer of France. He had frequently attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> admittance into the Academy of Sciences, but could not obtain his wish till 1746, when he was the first who broke through the absurd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of filling an inaugural speech with the fulsome adulation of Richelieu; an example soon followed by other academicians. From the satires occasioned by this innovation he felt so much uneasiness, that he was glad to retire with the marchioness du Chatelet to Lunville, in the neighbourhood of King Stanislaus. The marchioness dying in 1749, Voltaire returned to Paris, where his stay was but short. The king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> now gave Voltaire an invitation to live with him, which he accepted towards the end of August. Voltaire. gust 1753. On his arrival at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, he was immediately presented with the Order of Merit, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of chamberlain, and a pension of 20,000 livres. From the particular respect that was paid to him, his time was now spent in the most agreeable manner; his apartments were under those of the king, whom he was allowed to visit at stated hours, to read with him the best works of either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors, and to assist his majesty in the literary productions by which he relieved the cares of government. But a dispute which arose between him and Maupeutus soon brought on his disgrace. Maupeutus was at some pains to have it reported at court, that one day while General Maintenue happened to be in the apartments of M. de Voltaire, who was then translating into French the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Russia, composed by that officer, the king, in his usual manner, sent a copy of verses to be examined, when Voltaire said to Maintenue, "Let us leave off for the present, my friend; you see the king has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> me his dirty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> to wash, I will wash yours another time." A single word is sometimes sufficient to ruin a man at court; Maupeutus imputed such a word to Voltaire, and succeeded. It was about this very time that Maupeutus published his very strange Philosophical Letters; and M. de Voltaire did not fail to heighten, with his utmost powers of raillery, everything which he found, or could make, ridiculous, in the projects of M. Maupeutus, who was careful to unite his own cause with that of the king; Voltaire was considered as having failed in respect to his majesty; and therefore, in the most respectful manner, he returned to the king his chamberlain's key, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> of his Order of Merit: accompanied with four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; in which he, with great delicacy, compares his situation to that of a jealous lover, who lends back the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of his mistress. The king returned the key and the ribbon; but they were not followed by an immediate reconciliation. Voltaire set out to pay a visit to her highness the duchess of Gotha, who honoured him with her friendship as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as she lived. While he remained at Gotha, Maupeutus employed all his batteries against him: Voltaire was arrested by the king's orders, but afterwards released. He now settled near <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>; but afterward being obliged to quit that republic, he purchased the castle of Ferney in France, about a league from the lake of Geneva. It was here that he undertook the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the celebrated family of Calas; and it was not long before he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> opportunity of vindicating the innocence of another condemned family of the name of Sirven. It is somewhat remarkable, that in the year 1774, he had the third time a singular opportunity of employing that same zeal which he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to display in the fatal catastrophe of the families of Calas and Sirven. In this retreat M. Voltaire continued long to enjoy the pleasures of a rural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, accompanied with the admiration of a vast number of wits and philosophers throughout all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Wearied at length, however, with his situation, or yielding to the importunities of friends, he came to Paris about the beginning of the year 1778, where he wrote a new tragedy called Irene. By this time his understanding seems to have been impaired, either through the infirmities of age, or continued intoxication by the flattery of others; and he ridiculously suffered himself to be crowned in public with laurel, in testimony of his great poetical merit. He did not long survive this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a>; for having overheated himself with receiving visits, and exhausted his spirits by supplying a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of conversation, he was first seized with a spitting of blood; and at last becoming restless in the night-time, he was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a soporific medicine. Of this he unluckily one night took too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a dose, that he slept 36 hours, and expired a very short time after awakening from it.

VOLUME

Pages 209-209

in matters of literature, a book <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> bulk to be bound by itself. The name is derived from the Latin volvere, "to roll up;" the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manner of making up books being in rolls of bark or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>. See Book.

VOLUNTARY

Pages 209-209

in Music, a piece played by a musician extempore, according to his fancy. This is often used before he begins to let himself to play any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, to try the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the piece he intends to perform.

VOLUNTEERS

Pages 209-209
