persons who, of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state, serve in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> without being enlisted, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and preferment.

VOLUTE

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a kind of spiral scroll used in Ionic and Composite capitals, whereof it makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> characteristic and ornament.

VOLVOX

Pages 209-209

a genus of animals belonging to the vermes infusoriae. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. VOLUSENUS. See Wilson.

VOMICA

Pages 209-209

in Medicine, an abscess of the lungs. See Medicine, No. 186. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUX_VOMICA">Nux VOMICA</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. VOMIT. See Emetic, Materia Medica Index.

VOMITING

Pages 209-209

a retrograde spasmodic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the muscular fibres of the oesophagus, stomach, and intestines, attended with strong convulsions of the muscles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> and diaphragm; which when gentle, create a nausea; when violent, a vomiting.

VOORN

Pages 209-209

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, bounded by the river Maes, which divides it from the continent and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Illemunde, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> called Bies-bocht, on the east; by another branch of the Maes, which divides it from the islands of Gorée and Over-Rackee, on the south; and by the German sea on the west; being about 24 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>.

VORTEX

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a>, a whirlwind, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sudden, rapid, and violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in circles; or that motion of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> called an eddy or whirlpool. Vortex, in the Cartesian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, is a system or collection of particles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> moving the same way, and round the same axis.

VOSSIUS

Pages 209-209

JOHN GERARD, a most learned and laborious writer of the 17th century, was of a considerable family in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>; and was born in 1577, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>, near <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where his father, John Voissius, was minister. He was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>, and afterwards professor of eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, from whence he was called in 1633 to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, to fill the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of professor of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He died in 1649.

VOTE

Pages 209-210

the suffrage <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resolve of each of the members of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, where any affair is to be carried by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOTIVE_MEDALS">Votive Medals</a>, those on which are expressed the vows of the people for the emperors or empresses. See Medal. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">Vow</a>, a solemn and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> or oath. See Oath. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of vows is found in most religions. They make up a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Pagan worship, being made either in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of some deliverance, under some pressing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, or for the success of some enterprise. Among the Jews, all vows were to be voluntary, and made by persons wholly in their own power; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such person made a vow in any thing lawful and possible, he was obliged to fulfil it. If he appointed no particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for accomplishing his vow, he was bound to do it instantly, lest by delay he should prove useless, or be unwilling, to execute his promise. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a person is constituted a religious by taking three vows; that of poverty, chastity, and obedience. Vows, among the Romans, signified sacrifices, offerings, presents, and prayers made for the Caesars, and emperors, particularly for their prosperity and the continuance of their empire. These were at first made every five years, then every fifteen, and afterwards every twenty, and were called quinquennalia, decennalia, and vicesennalia. Vowel, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> which affords a complete <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of itself, or a letter so simple as only to need a bare opening of the mouth to make it heard, and to form a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a> are six in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, viz. A, E, I, O, U, Y. Vowel, John. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOOKER">Hooker</a>. Upholster, Upholsterer, or Upholder, a tradesman that makes beds, and all sorts of furniture thereunto belonging, &c. Upland, denotes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ground, or, as some call it, terra firma, by which it stands opposed to such as is moorish, marshy, or low. Upland, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east by the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the south by the sea of Sudermania, and on the west by Westmania and Gothtricia, from which it is separated by the river Dela. It is about seventy miles in length and forty-five in breadth, and contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UPSALA">Upsala</a>, a rich and considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Sweden, in Upland, with a famous university, and an archbishop's see. The town is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and as straight as a line; but most of the houses are of wood, covered with birch bark, with turf on the top. On an eminence, to the south of the town, is a ruined castle. Those that view the town from hence would take it to be a garden, whose streets represent the alleys; and the houses, which are covered with turf, the grass-plots. It was formerly the residence of the kings, and is now the usual <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they are crowned. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALA">Sala</a>, over which there are two bridges. It is twenty-six miles north-west of Stockholm. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 48'. N. Lat. 59° 52'. Upupa, a genus of birds belonging to the order of Picidae. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Ur, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a citadel of Mesopotamia, situated between the Tigris and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>; taken by force for Ur of the Chaldees, the residence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>. What seems to confirm this is, that from Ur to Haran, the other residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> lies directly for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>. And it is no objection that Ur is said to be in Mesopotamia; because the parts next the Tigris were occupied by the Chaldeans, as seems to be confirmed from Acts vii. 2, 4. It is called Orche, in Strabo; Orchoe, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. Uralian Chain, a range of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which form part of the boundaries of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and anciently known by the name of Riphaei Montes. See Riphæi Montes, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URANIA">Urania</a>, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, was supposed to preside over <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. She is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> represented in an azure robe, crowned with stars, and supporting a large globe with both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URANIUM">Uranium</a>, one of the lately discovered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URANOSCOPUS">Uranoscopus</a>, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of jugularies. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. Raphael d'Urbino. See Raphael. Urchin, or Hedgehog. See Erinaceus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. See Urchin. See Echinus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> Index. Urea. See Chemistry. Ureters. See Anatomy, No. 101. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URETHRA">Urethra</a>. See Anatomy, No. 107. Uric Acid. See Chemistry Index. Urim and Thummim, among the ancient Hebrews, a certain oracular manner of consulting God, which was done by the high-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> dressed in his robes, and having on his pectoral or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>-plate. Various have been the sentiments of commentators concerning the urim and thummim. Josephus, and several others, maintain, that it meant the precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> set in the high-priest's breast-plate, which by extraordinary lustre made known the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of God to those who consulted him. Spencer believes that the urim and thummim were two little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> figures shut up in the pectoral as in a purse, which gave responses with an articulate voice. In short, there are as many opinions concerning the urim and thummim as there are particular authors that wrote about them. The safest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, according to Broughton, seems to be, that the words urim and thummim signify some divine virtue and power annexed to the breast-plate of the high-priest, by which an oracular answer was obtained from God when he was consulted by the high-priest; and that this was called urim and thummim, to express the clearness and perfection which these oracular answers always carried with them; for urim signifies "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>," and thummim "perfection;" these answers not being imperfect and ambiguous, like the heathen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>, but clear and evident. The use made of the urim and thummim was to consult God in difficult <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> relating to the whole state of Israel; and sometimes in cases relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, the sanhedrim, the general of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> personage. Urinal, in Medicine, a vessel fit to receive and hold urine, and used accordingly for the convenience of sick persons. It is usually of glass, but sometimes of metal. Urine, a fluid, separated from the blood, and carried by the emunctory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> to the kidneys, from whence it descends to the bladder by the uterus, and is from time to time emitted thence by the canal of the urethra. See Anatomy, No. 107. For the properties of urine, see Chemistry Index.

VULCAN

Pages 211-212

in Pagan worship, the god of subterraneous fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Juno; and was said to be so remarkably deformed, that his father threw him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEMNOS">Lemnos</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> he broke his leg, and there he set up his forge, and taught men how to soften and polish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Thence he removed to the Liparian isles, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where, by the assistance of the Cyclops, he made Jupiter's thunderbolts, and armour for the other gods. Notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> of his person, he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, and by Jupiter's consent made his addresses to her, but without success. He was, however, more fortunate in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> to Venus; who, after <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, chose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> for her gallant; when Vulcan exposed them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of the other gods, by taking them in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>.

VULGATE

Pages 212-212

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin translation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, and the only one acknowledged by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome to be authentic. See BIBLE.

VULNERARY

Pages 212-212

in Medicine, an epithet formerly given to remedies supposed to possess virtues for the cure of wounds <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ulcers.

VULTUR

Pages 212-212

a genus of birds belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCIPITRES">Accipitres</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. VULVA. See ANATOMY, No 132. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UVULA">UVULA</a>. See ANATOMY, No 102.

WACHENDORFLA

Pages 212-213

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the clas of triandria; and arranged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method under the 6th order, Enfusae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WAFERS

Pages 213-213
or Sealing WAFERS, are made thus: Take very fine flour, mix it with glair of eggs, sugarflats, and a little yeast; mingle the materials; beat them well together; spread the batter, being made thin with gum-water, on even tin plates, and dry them in a stove; then cut them out for use. You may make them of what colour you please, by tinging the paste with brasil or vermilion for red; indigo or verditer, &c., for blue; saffron, turmeric, or gamboge, &c., for yellow. WAGER of LAW. See (Wager of) LAW. WAGER of Battel. See (Wager of) Battel.

WAGGON

Pages 213-213

a wheel-carriage, of which there are various forms accommodated to the different uses they are intended for. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> waggon consists of the shafts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rods, being the two pieces which the hind <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> bears up; the welds; the flotes, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> pieces, which hold the shafts together; the bolster, being that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> on which the fore-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> and the axle-tree turn in wheeling the waggon across the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> or body of the waggon, having the flames or rails fixed thereon; the bales, or hoops which compose the top; the tilt, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> covered with cloth, at the end of the waggon. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, Sec. iv. WAGTAIL. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOTACILLA">Motacilla</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WAIFS

Pages 213-213
BONA WAVIATA, are goods stolen, and waived or thrown away by the thief in his flight, for fear of being apprehended. These are given to the king by the law, as a punishment upon the owner for not himself pursuing the felon, and taking away his goods from him. And therefore if the party robbed do his diligence immediately to follow and apprehend the thief (which is called making fresh suit), or do convict him afterwards, or procure evidence to convict him, he shall have his goods again. Waived goods do also not belong to the king till seized by somebody for his use; for if the party robbed can seize them first, though at the distance of 20 years, the king shall never have them. If the goods are hid by the thief, or left anywhere by him, so that he had them not about him when he fled, and therefore did not throw them away in his flight; these also are not bona waviata, but the owner may have them again when he pleases. The goods of a foreign merchant, though stolen and thrown away in flight, shall never be waifs: the reason whereof may be, not only for the encouragement of trade, but also because there is no willful default in the foreign merchant's not pursuing the thief, he being generally a stranger to our laws, our usages, and our language.

WAIGATS STRAITS

Pages 213-213

situated between <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NOVA_ZEMBLA">Nova Zembla</a> and Russia, through which the Dutch sailed to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as 75°, in order to discover a north-east passage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and the East Indies.

WAINSCOT

Pages 213-213

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> that serves to line the walls of a room, being usually made in panels, and painted, to serve instead of hangings.

WAIVE

Pages 213-213

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a woman that is put out of the protection of the law. She is called waive, as being forsaken of the law; and not outlaw as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is; by reason women cannot be of the decennia, and are not sworn in leets to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, nor to the law, as men are; who are therefore within the law; whereas women are not, and so cannot be outlawed, since they never were within it.

WAKE

Pages 213-215

the print <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> track impressed by the course of a ship on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is formed by the re-union of the body of water which was separated by the ship's bottom whilst moving through it; and may be seen to a considerable distance behind the stern, as smoother than the rest of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Hence it is usually observed by the compass, to discover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-way. A ship is said to be in the wake of another when she follows her on the same track, or a line supposed to be formed on the continuation of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>. Two distant objects observed at sea are called in the wake of each other, when the view of the farther is intercepted by the nearest; so that the observer's eye and the two objects are all placed upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line. WAKE is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>-feast of the dedication of churches, which is kept with feasting and rural diversions. Mr Whitaker, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, has given a particular account of the origin of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAKES">wakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. He observes, that every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at its consecration received the name of some particular saint: this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was practised among the Roman Britons, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> among the Saxons; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Cealchylde, in 816, the name of the denominating saint was expressly required to be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on the altars, and also on the walls of the church, or a tablet within it. The feast of this saint became of course the festival of the church. Thus Christian festivals were substituted in the room of the idolatrous anniversaries of heathenism: accordingly, at the first introduction of Christianity among the Jutes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, Pope Gregory the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> advised, what had been previously done among the Britons, viz. Christian festivals to be instituted in the room of the idolatrous, and the suffering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> whose relics were reposited in the church, or the day on which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> was actually dedicated, to be the established feast of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. Both were appointed and observed; and they were clearly distinguished at first among the Saxons, as appears from the laws of the Confessor, where the dies dedicationis, or dedicatio, is repeatedly discriminated from the propria festivitas sancti, or celebratio sancti. They remained equally distinct to the Reformation; the dedication-day in 1536 being ordered for the future to be kept on the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> in October, and the festival of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> saint to be celebrated no longer. The latter was, by way of pre-eminence, denominated the church's holiday, or its peculiar festival; and while this remains in many parishes at present, the other is so utterly annihilated in all, that Bishop Kennet (says Mr Whitaker) knew nothing of its distinct existence, and has attributed to the day of dedication what is true only concerning the saint's day. Thus instituted at first, the day of the tutelar saint was observed, most probably by the Britons, and certainly by the Saxons, with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. And the evening before every saint's day, in the Saxon Jewish method of reckoning the hours, being an actual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the day, and therefore like that appropriated to the duties of public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, as they reckoned Sunday from the first to commence at the sunset of Saturday; the evening preceding the church's holyday would be observed with all the devotion of the festival. The people actually repaired to the church, and joined in the services of it; and they thus spent the evening of their greater festivities in the monasteries of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, as early as the conclusion of the seventh century. These services were naturally denominated from their late hours wecan or wakes, and vigils or eves. That of the anniversary at Rippon, as early as the commencement of the eighth century, is expressly denominated the vigil. But that of the church's holyday was named cyrie wecan, or church-wake, the church-vigil, or church eve. And it was this commencement of both with a wake, which has now caused the days to be generally preceded with vigils, and the church-holiday particularly to be denominated the church-wake. So religiously was the eve and festival of the patron saint observed for many ages by the Saxons, even as late as the reign of Edgar, the former being spent in the church, and employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. And the wakes, and all the other holidays in the year, were put upon the same footing with the Octaves of Christmas, Easter, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a>. When Gregory recommended the festival of the patron saint, he advised the people to erect booths of branches about the church on the day of the festival, and to fealt and be merry in them with innocence. Accordingly, in every parish, on the returning anniversary of the saint, little pavilions were constructed of boughs, and the people indulged in them to hospitality and mirth. The feasting of the saint's day, however, was soon abused; and even in the body of the church, when the people were assembled for devotion, they began to mind diversions, and to introduce drinking. The growing intemperance gradually stained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the vigil, till the festivity of it was converted, as it now is, into the rigour of a fast. At length they too justly scandalized the Puritans of the last century, and numbers of the wakes were disfused entirely, especially in the east and some western parts of England; but they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> observed in the north, and in the midland counties. This custom of celebrity in the neighbourhood of the church, on the days of particular saints, was introduced into England from the continent, and must have been familiar equally to the Britons and Saxons; being observed among the churches of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> in the fifth century, and by those of the west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> in the seventh. And equally in Asia and Europe, on the continent and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, these celebrities were the causes of those commercial marts which we denominate fairs. The people resorted in crowds to the festival, and a considerable provision would be wanted for their entertainment. The prospect of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> invited the little traders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to come and offer their wares; and thus, among the many pavilions for hospitality in the neighbourhood of the church, various booths were erected for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of different commodities. In larger <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, surrounded with populous districts, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the people to the wakes would be great, and the attendance of traders numerous; and this resort and attendance constitute a fair.—Baili expressly mentions the numerous appearance of traders at these festivals in Asia, and Gregory notes the same custom to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Europe. And as the festival was observed on a feria or holiday, it naturally assumed to itself, and as naturally communicated to the mart, the appellation of feria or fair. Indeed several of our most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fairs appear to have been usually held, and have been continued to our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, on the original church-holidays of the places; besides, it is observable, that fairs were generally kept in church-yards, and even in the churches, and also on Sundays, till the indelicacy and scandal were so great as to need reformation. **Wake-Robin.** See ARUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a>,** a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Europe, bounded on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a> and Transylvania, on the east and south by the river Danube, and on the west by Transylvania. It is 225 miles in length, and 125 in breadth; and was ceded to the Turks by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>, in 1739. It abounds in good horses and cattle; and there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of several kinds. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is so fertile, that it is capable of producing anything; and there are good pastures, with wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and all manner of European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The inhabitants are chiefly of the Greek church. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALCHEREN">Walcheren</a>,** an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Low Countries, and one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of those of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>; separated from Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> by the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>. It is about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles in length, and eight in breadth; and though it lies low, has good arable and pasture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of this island and the whole province is Middleburgh. But the principal sea port is Flushing, which is strongly fortified. Walcheren was taken by the British forces in August 1809; but it soon after was abandoned, the troops having suffered severely by sickness. **Walden,** a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, commonly called Saffron Walden, with a market on Saturdays, and two fairs on Midlent Saturday for horses, and November 1st for cows. It is remarkable for the plenty of saffron that grows about it. This town was incorporated by Edward VI. and is governed by a mayor and 24 aldermen. It is 27 miles north-west-by-north of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHELMSFORD">Chelmsford</a>, and 43 north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 20° N. Lat. 52° 4'. **Waldenses.** See WALDO. **Waldo,** a merchant of Lyons in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the 12th century, who applying himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Scriptures, and finding no warrant there for several of the Romish doctrines, particularly that of transubstantiation, publicly opposed them. His followers, who from him were called Waldenses, being chased from Lyons, spread over Dauphiné and Provence; upon which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. is said to have razed 300 gentlemen's seats, and destroyed several walled towns to stop their growth: but this, instead of suppressing, spread them over a great part of Europe. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, which they drew up and dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, agreed in most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> with those of the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. In the year 1200, those of them who dwelt in the province of Albigeois in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, from whence they were called Albigenesi, stood upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; upon which Philip drove them into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, Savoy, and England. The crusade against them is said to have consisted of 500,000 men, who wore their crosses on their breasts, to distinguish themselves from those who went to the Holy Land, and wore them on their shoulders. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>,** a country situated in the south-west part of of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, into which the ancient Britons retired from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of the Saxons. Anciently it was of greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> than it is at present, and comprehended all the country beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, that is, besides the 12 counties included in it at present, those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, which now are reckoned a part of England, were then inhabited by three different tribes of the Britons, namely, the Silures, the Demetæ, and the Ordovices. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were never able to subdue them, till the reign of Vespasian, when they were reduced by Julius Frontinus, who placed garrisons in their country to keep them in awe. Though the Saxons made themselves masters of all England, they never could get possession of Wales, except the counties of Monmouthshire and Herefordshire, formerly a part of Wales. About the year 870, Roderic king of Wales divided it among his three sons; and the names of these divisions were, Demetia, or South-Wales; Powefa, or Powys-Land; and Venedotia, or North Wales. Another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is mentioned afterwards in the records, viz. North Wales, South Wales, and West Wales; the last comprehending the counties of Monmouth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>. The country derived the name of Wales, and the inhabitants that of Welsh, from the Saxons, who by those terms denote a country and people to which they are strangers; for the Welsh, in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, call their country Cymru, and their language Cymraeg. They continued under their own princes and laws from the above-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and were never entirely subjected to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England till the reign of Edward I., when Llewellyn ap Gryffith, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Wales, lost both his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and dominions. Edward, the better to secure his conquest, and to reconcile the Welsh to a foreign yoke, sent his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERNARVON">Caernarvon</a>, where she was delivered of a prince; to whom the Welsh, on that account, the more readily submitted. Ever since that time, the eldest sons of the kings of England have commonly been created princes of Wales, and as such enjoy certain revenues from that country. As to the character of the Welsh, they are said to be a brave, hospitable people; and though very jealous of affronts, paffionate, and hafty, yet are easily reconciled. The common people look with a suspicious eye on strangers, and bear a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> grudge to the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, by whom their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were expelled from the finest parts of the island. The gentlemen are apt to value themselves upon the antiquity of their families; and with some reason, as they can generally trace them much higher than the inhabitants of most other countries. All the better sort, both in town and country, can speak English, especially in the counties bordering upon England. The common people, in general, only speak their own language, which is the ancient British; and not only differs entirely from the English, but has very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with any of the western tongues, unless we should except the Gaelic, Erse, or Irish. It is said to be a dialect of the ancient Celtic, and in many respects to resemble the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>. Most of the clergy are natives of the country, and understand English so well, that they could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> their functions in any part of Britain. The public worship, however, is as often performed in Welsh as in English, excepting in the towns, where the latter is the prevailing language. The inhabitants are computed at about 300,000. The country, though mountainous, especially in North Wales, is far from being barren or unfruitful; the hills, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> and minerals they contain, feeding vast herds of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, deer, sheep, and goats, and their valleys abounding in corn, as their seas and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> do in fish. Here are also wood, coal, and turf for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, in abundance. Wales is bounded on all sides by the sea and the Severn; except on the east, where it joins to the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, Salop, Hereford, and Monmouth. Its length, from the southernmost part of Glamorganshire to the extremity of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a> north, is computed at about 113 miles; and its greatest breadth, from the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a> east to St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKESHIRE">Pembrokeshire</a> west, is nearly of the same dimensions, being about 90 miles. After the conquest of Wales by Edward I., very material alterations were made in their laws, so as to reduce them nearer to the English standard, especially in the forms of their judicial proceedings; but they still retained very much of their original polity, particularly their rule of inheritance, viz. that their lands were divided equally among all the issue <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a>, and did not descend to the eldest son alone. By other subsequent statutes their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> immunities were still further abridged; but the finishing stroke to their dependency was given by the statute 27 Hen. VIII. c. 26, which at the same time gave the utmost advancement to their civil prosperity, by admitting them to a thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of laws with the subjects of England.—Thus were this brave people gradually conquered into the enjoyment of true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; being infensibly put upon the same footing, and made fellow-citizens, with their conquerors. It is enacted by the 27 Hen. VIII. c. 1. That the dominion of Wales shall be for ever united to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of England. 2. That all Welshmen born shall have the same liberties as other king's subjects. 3. That lands in Wales shall be inheritable according to the English tenures and rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>. 4. That the laws of England, and no other, shall be used in Wales: besides many other regulations of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> of this principality. And the 34 and 35 Hen. VIII. c. 26, confirms the same, adds further regulations, divides it into 12 shires, and, in short, reduces it into the same order in which it stands at this day; differing from the kingdom of England in only a few particulars, and those too of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of privileges (such as having courts within itself, independent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of Westminster-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>), and some other immaterial peculiarities, hardly more than are to be found in many counties of England itself. New WALES. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_BRITAIN">NEW BRITAIN</a>. New South-WALES. See <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">NEW <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">HOLLAND</a>. Prince of WALES. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">ROYAL</a> Family. WALKING <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">Leaf</a>, an insect. See MANTIS Sycophanta. ENTOMOLOGY Index.

WALL

Pages 215-216

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, as serving both to inclose it, and to support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, floors, &c.—Walls are distinguished into various kinds, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> whereof they consist; as <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mud walls, brick walls, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls, flint or boulder walls, and boarded walls. See ARCHITECTURE. Cob or Mud WALL. In those parts of England where stone is scarce, it is usual to make walls and houses of mud, mud, or, as it is called in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, cob; which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and straw, wet up somewhat like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, but well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> and trod together. When a wall is making, after being raised to a certain height, it is allowed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to pitch or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is resumed. Some value themselves on their skill in building with this composition; the price, when materials are found, is generally in Devonshire 3s. per perch of 16½ feet; but a stone foundation costs more. Houses built with this, being covered with thatch, are very dry and warm; a cob wall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in a good situation, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> last 50 or 60 years or more. When pulled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, they are used as manure, and new earth employed to rebuild with.

WALLACE

Pages 216-216

Sir William, a gallant general of the Scots, who endeavoured to rescue his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from the English yoke; but being taken prisoner, he was unjustly tried by the English laws, condemned, and executed as a traitor to Edward I. in 1304. See Scotland, no 103, et seq. WALLACHIA. See Wallachia.

WALLER

Pages 216-216

Edmund, a celebrated English poet, was the son of Robert Waller, Esq. of Agmondesham in Buckinghamshire, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, the sister of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Hamden who distinguished himself so much in the beginning of the civil wars. He was born in 1605; and his father dying when he was very young, the care of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> fell to his mother, who sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> school. He was afterwards sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he must have been very affilious in his studies, since, at fifteen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seventeen years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was chosen into the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of King James I. and served as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> for Agmondesham. He began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> so early as the year 1623; as appears from his verses "upon the danger his majesty (being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>) escaped in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of St Andero;" for there Prince <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, returning from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> that year, had like to have been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away. It was not, however, Mr Waller's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, his fine parts, or his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, that so much occasioned him to be first publicly known, as his carrying off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and sole heiress of a rich citizen, against a rival whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> was espoused by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. It is not known at what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he married his first lady; but he was a widower before he was 25, when he began to have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for Sacharissa, which was a fictitious name for the lady Dorothy Sidney, daughter to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, and afterwards wife to the earl of Sunderland. He was now known at court, cared for by all who had any relish for wit and polite literature; and was one of the famous club of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALKLAND">Falkland</a>, Mr Chillingworth, and other eminent men, were members. He was returned burgess for Agmondesham in the parliament which met in April 1640. An intermission of parliaments having disquieted the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and raised jealousies against the designs of the court, which would be sure to discover themselves whenever the king came to ask for a supply, Mr Waller was one of the first who condemned the preceding <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. He showed himself in opposition to the court, and made a speech in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on this occasion; from which we may gather some notion of his general principles in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; wherein, however, he afterwards proved very variable and inconsistent. He opposed the court also in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> parliament which met in November following, and was chosen to impeach Judge Crawley, which he did in a warm and eloquent speech, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 16th 1641. This speech was so highly applauded, that 20,000 copies of it were sold in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. In 1642, he was one of the commissioners appointed by the parliament to present their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> of peace to the king at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In 1643, he was deeply engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to reduce the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and the tower to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the king; for which he was tried and condemned, together with Mr Tomkins his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and Mr Challoner. The two latter suffered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but Mr Waller obtained a reprieve: he was, however, sentenced to suffer a year's imprisonment, and to pay a fine of 10,000l. After this, he became particularly attached to Oliver Cromwell, upon whom he wrote a very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. He also wrote a noble poem on the death of that great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. At the Restoration, he was treated with great civility by Charles II. who always made him one of the party in his diversions at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>'s and other places. He wrote a panegyric upon his majesty's return; which being thought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> much short of that he had before written on Oliver Cromwell, the king one day asked him in raillery, "How is it, Waller, that you wrote a better encomium on Cromwell than on me?" "May it please your majesty," answered he, "we poets generally succeed best in fiction." He sat in several parliaments after the Restoration, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the full vigour of his genius to the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> vivacity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> him up, and making his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> agreeable to the last. He died of a dropy in 1687, and was interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of Beaconsfield, where a monument is erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Mr Waller has been honoured as the most elegant and harmonious versifier of his time, and a great refiner of the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The best edition of his works, containing poems, speeches, letters, &c. is that published in quarto by Mr Fenton, to 1730.

WALLIS

Pages 216-217

Dr John, a celebrated mathematician, was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; where he became fellow of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to till, by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, he vacated his fellowship. In 1640, he received holy orders, and became chaplain to the lady Vere. While he lived in this family, he cultivated the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECIPHERING">deciphering</a>; and it is said, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, for whom he explained several letters written in ciphers, sent him a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> chain and medal. In 1643 he published, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a> tried; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Animadversions on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Brooke's treatise, called The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> of Truth, &c." The next year he was chosen one of the secretaries or secretaries to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of divines at Westminster. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Turner, Savilian professor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, being ejected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>-visitors in 1649, Mr Wallis was appointed to succeed him in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In 1633 he published at Oxford a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a> of the English Tongue in Latin. In 1655 he entered the lists with Mr Hobbes; and their controversy lasted a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In 1657 the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> published his Mathematical Works. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dr Langbaine, he was chosen custos archivorum of the university. After the Restoration he met with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> himself entertaining a favourable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of him on account of some services he had done both to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> father and himself. He was therefore confirmed in his places, admitted one of the king's chaplains in ordinary, and appointed one of the divines empowered to review the book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. He complied with the terms terms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of uniformity, and continued a steady conformity till his death. He was one of the first members of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, and corresponded with many learned men. In 1697, the curators of the university press at Oxford thought it for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the university to collect the mathematical works of the Doctor, which had been printed separately, some in Latin, some in English, and published them all together in the Latin tongue, in three vols., folio. He died in 1703. He speaks of himself thus: "It hath been my endeavour all along to act by moderate principles, being willing whatever side was uppermost, to promote any good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> for the true <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, of learning, and of the public good." Besides the works above-mentioned, he published many others.

WALLOONS

Pages 217-217

a name for the inhabitants of a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, viz. Artois, Hainault, Naum, Luxemburgh, and part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> and Brabant. WALNUT-TREE. See Juglans, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WALPOLE

Pages 217-218

Sir Robert, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Orford, was born at Houghton in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, September 6th, 1674, and educated on the foundation at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> school. Thence he was elected to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but, succeeding to the family estate by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, he resigned his fellowship. In 1700 he was chosen member of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for King's Lynn, and represented that borough in several succeeding parliaments. In 1705, he was nominated one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> George of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of England; in 1707, appointed secretary at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and, in 1709, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. In 1710, upon the change of the ministry, he was removed from all his posts, and held no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> afterwards during the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s reign. In 1711 he was expelled from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons for what they called notorious corruption in his office as secretary at war. The borough of Lynn, however, re-elected him; and, though the house declared the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> void, yet they persisted in the choice. In the well-known debate relating to Steele for publishing the Crisis, he greatly distinguished himself in behalf of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and added to the popularity he had before acquired. On the death of the queen, a revolution of politics took place, and the Whig party prevailed both at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. Walpole had before recommended himself to the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> by his zeal for its cause, when the commons considered the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> with regard to the Protestant succession; and he had now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to procure the assurance of the house to the new king (which attended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of condolence and congratulation), "That the commons would make good all parliamentary funds." It is therefore not to be wondered at, that his promotion soon took place after the king's arrival; and that in a few days he was appointed receiver and pay-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> general of all the guards and garrisons, and of all other the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> forces in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, paymaster of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at Chelsea, and likewise a privy counsellor. On the opening of a new parliament, a committee of secrecy was chosen to inquire into the conduct of the late ministry, of which Walpole was appointed chairman; and, by his management, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of impeachment were read against the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, Lord Bolingbroke, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, and the earl of Strafford. The eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he was thought to have Walpole done the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, by the vigorous prosecution of those ministers who were deemed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> instruments of the peace, was soon rewarded by the extraordinary promotions to the offices of first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> and under treasurer of the exchequer. In two years <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he resigned all his offices, on account of a misunderstanding which took place between him and the rest of the ministry about certain supplies demanded for the support of his majesty's German dominions. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his resignation he brought in the famous sinking-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, which he presented as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, saying, that he hoped it would not fare the worse for having two fathers; and that his successor Mr Stanhope would bring it to perfection. His calling himself the father of a project, which hath since been so often employed to other purposes than were at first declared, gave his enemies frequent opportunity for satire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; and it hath been sarcastically observed, that the father of this fund appeared in a very bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> when viewed in the capacity of a nurse. In the next session of parliament, Walpole opposed the ministry in every thing; and even Wyndham <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Shippen did not exceed him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a>. Upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in the house for continuing the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, he made a speech of above an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and displayed the danger of a standing army in a free country, with all the powers of eloquence. Early in 1720 the rigour of the patriot began to soften, and the complaisance of the courtier to appear; and he was again appointed paymaster of the forces, and several of his friends were found soon after in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of promotions. No doubt now remained of his entire conversion to court <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>; for, before the end of the year, we find him pleading as strongly for the forces required by the war-office as he had before declaimed against them, even though at this time the same pretences for keeping them on foot did not exist. It was not long before he acquired full ministerial power, being appointed first lord commissioner of the treasury, and chancellor of the exchequer; and, when the king went abroad in 1723, he was nominated one of the lords justices for the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and was sworn sole secretary of state. About this time he received another distinguished mark of the royal favour; his eldest son then on his travels being created a peer, by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron Walpole of Walpole. In 1725 he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the Bath, and the year after knight of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>. The measures of his administration, during the long time he remained prime or rather sole minister, have been often canvassed with all the severity of critical inquiry. It is difficult to discern the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> through the exaggerations and misrepresentations of party. He has indeed been accused of employing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINKING_FUND">sinking fund</a> for the purposes of corruption, of which it was long the fashion to call him the father; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who reflects on the transactions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and his infamous cabal, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> acquit him of the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. He was an enemy to war, and the friend of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; and because he did not resent some petty insults of the court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> so suddenly as the fiery part of the nation thought he should have done, a formidable opposition was formed against him in the house, which had influence enough to to employ in its cause almost all the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> of the nation. Pulteney and Pitt were the great leaders of the party in the house of commons; while Bolingbroke and Pope and Johnson, and almost every man of genius, exerted themselves without doors to enlighten, by pamphlets in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, the minds of the people, and throw the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a Spanish war. This he strenuously opposed, because he knew that the foreign settlements of that power are very remote, and in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> destructive to Englishmen; and that such of them as we might be able to take, we could not possibly retain. The opposition however prevailed. The nation was indulged in a war, of which it surely had no cause to boast of the success; and it is now universally known, that the greater part of those who with honest intentions had, either in parliament or out of it, been engaged to pull <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the minister, lived to repent of their conduct, and do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to the man whom they had so pertinaciously vilified. In order to encourage commerce and improve the revenue, Sir Robert projected a scheme for an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>, as the only means of putting a stop to the frauds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and illicit traders. This was another ground of clamour to the orators within, and the wits without, doors; and while the opposition represented it as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> big with public mischief, Swift and Pope occasionally alluded to it as an oppression calculated to deprive private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of all its comforts. The minister was therefore obliged to abandon the scheme; but in a succeeding administration it was partly carried into execution, at the express solicitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons concerned in that article of trade which it was suggested would be most affected by it; and afterwards the most popular minister that ever directed the councils of this country declared in full senate, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a time should ever arrive which was likely to render the project feasible, he would himself recommend an extension of the excise laws as a measure of the greatest advantage to commerce, to the revenue, and to the general interests of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In 1742 the opposition prevailed; and Sir Robert being no longer able to carry a majority in the house of commons, resigned all his places, and fled for shelter behind the throne. He was soon afterwards created earl of Orford; and the king, in consideration of his long and faithful services, granted him a pension of £4000 per annum. The remainder of his life he spent in tranquillity and retirement, and died, in 1745, in the 71st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He has been severely, and not unjustly, censured for that system of corruption by which he almost avowed that he governed the nation; but the objects which he had in view are now acknowledged to have been in a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> praiseworthy. Johnson, who in the earlier part of his life had joined the other wits in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> against his measures, afterwards honoured his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> for the placability of his temper, and for keeping this country in peace for so many years; and Mr Burke has declared, that his only defect as a minister was the want of sufficient firmness to treat with contempt that popular clamour, which, by his yielding to it, hurried the nation into an expensive and unjust war. But his rancorous prosecution of Atterbury bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> (see Atterbury), by a bill of pains and penalties, may be considered as something worse than a defect: it was a fault for which no apology can be made; because, whether that prelate was innocent or guilty, of his guilt no legal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> ever appeared. In that instance the conduct of the minister was the more extraordinary, that on other occasions he chose to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> over the disaffected by mildness and benevolence, even when he had sufficient proofs of their guilt. Of this the following anecdote, communicated by Lord <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> to Dr Johnson, is a sufficient proof, Sir Robert having got into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> some treasonable papers of his inveterate enemy Shippen, sent for him, and burnt them before his eyes. Some time afterwards, while Shippen was taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to the government in the house of commons, Sir Robert, who stood next to him, and knew his principles to be the same as ever, smiled; upon which Shippen, who had observed him, said "Egad, Robin, that's hardly fair." To whatever objections his ministerial conduct may be liable, in his private character he is universally allowed to have had amiable and benevolent qualities. That he was a tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, a kind master, a benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, a firm friend, an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> that have been seldom disputed; and so calm and equal was his temper, that Pulteney, his great rival and opponent, said, he was sure that Sir Robert Walpole never felt the bitterest invectives against him for half an hour. About the end of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s reign, and the beginning of George I's, he wrote the following pamphlets. 1. The Sovereign's Answer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> Address. The Sovereign meant Charles duke of Somerset, so nicknamed by the Whigs. 2. Answer to the Representation of the House of Lords on the State of the Navy, 1729. 3. The Debts of the Nation stated and considered, in four Papers, 1710. 4. The Thirty-five Millions accounted for, 1710. 5. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> from a foreign Minister in England to Monseigneur Pettecum, 1710. 6. Four Letters to a Friend in Scotland upon Sacheverell's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">Trial</a>; falsely attributed in the General <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> to Mr Maynwaring. 7. A Short <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Parliament. It is an account of the last session of the queen. 8. The South-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Scheme considered. 9. A Pamphlet against the Peerage Bill, 1719. 10. The Report of the Secret Committee, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 9th, 1715. WALRUS. See Trichecus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WALSH

Pages 218-218

WILLIAM, an English critic and poet, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Walsh, Esq. of Abberley in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, was born about the year 1660. He became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of Wadham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, but left the university without taking a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. His writings are printed among the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> Poets, printed in 1749. He was made gentleman of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s reign; and died in 1708. He was the friend of Mr Dryden and of Mr Pope; the former of whom esteemed him the best critic then living; and Mr Pope has celebrated his character in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Criticism.

WALSINGHAM

Pages 219-219

Sir Francis, minister and secretary of state during the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and one of the greatest politicians of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was descended from a noble and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family at Chilhamhurt. After having made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, he was twice sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to France, and at his return to England was employed in the most important affairs, became secretary of state, and was one of the commissioners for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> queen of Scotland. Sir Francis was undoubtedly one of the most refined politicians and most penetrating statesman that any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> ever produced. He had an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, both in discovering and managing the secret recesses of the heart. He had his spies in most courts in Christendom, and allowed them a liberal maintenance; for it was his maxim, That knowledge cannot be bought too dear.
