Now, if \( B \) bears down directly upon \( F \), the latter, by lying to, as in fig. 11, and 11, will present a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROADSIDE">broadside</a> of 40 guns, all bearing for a considerable time on \( B \), while the latter coming down headwise, can only bring the two light guns of her forecastle to bear on \( F \), not to mention that \( F \), by lying broadside to, will have her masts and rigging little exposed to the enemy's shot, while \( B \) standing head on, is exposed to be raked by every shot from \( F \), and in particular her rigging is in the utmost danger. Instead of this objectionable mode of attack, Mr Clerk proposes that \( B \) having the wind, should run down after as in the dotted line at fig. 12, till she gets into the course of \( F \), near her wake, or in such a position as will bring her parallel to \( F \)'s course, and within a proper distance, when she can run up close along side of \( F \), and engage on equal terms; or, that she should shoot ahead, then veer, and run down on the weather bow of \( F \), as in fig. 13, till she can force the chafe to bear. bear away to leeward, keeping close by her, on equal terms, taking care in both cases not to put it in the power of F to bring her broadside to bear on her without retaliation. Fig. 14. is employed by Mr Clerk to illustrate the different procedure of a French and British man of war in firing, the former at the rigging, and the latter at the hull of the enemy, with their effects. Let F represent a large ship desirous of avoiding a close engagement, but lying to, to receive with advantage an enemy's ship B, of equal force. Suppose that F, by firing at the rigging of B, may have carried away some of the principal stays, several of the windward throats, a fore-topmast, or other rigging of less consequence, without having wounded a single man; and suppose a second ship consort to F, receiving an enemy's ship like B, but firing only at her hull, so as to kill 30 or 40 men, without damaging her rigging. Now, when F and her consort wish to avoid a close engagement, it is evident that that ship B, which has lost part of her rigging, is much more disabled from coming to close action than her consort whose rigging is entire, though she may have lost a great number of her men. By the scheme at fig. 15, it is intended to illustrate the impossibility of one ship being exposed to the fire of many ships at one time. Let I, H, F, H, I, represent five ships in line of battle ahead, about a cable's length, or 240 yards astern, and suppose the length of each ship to be 40 yards, so that the whole space between the head of one ship and the head of that next adjacent equals 280 yards. Let the perpendicular line FK, extending from the beam of F six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> lengths or 1440 yards, be divided into six equal parts. It is evident that any ship stationed at E in the line FK, 720 yards distant, cannot long be exposed to the fire of more than the centre ship F of this squadron. For if we suppose that H and K ahead and astern of F, can bring their broadsides to bear on E; by putting themselves in positions for that purpose, they will not only disorder their own line, but one will leave her head and the other her stern exposed to a raking fire from the opposite ships BB in the enemy's line. If B can suffer little from the two ships H, H, at the distance of 720 yards, it is evident that she will suffer still less from these ships as she approaches nearer the enemy's line. Again, if instead of a cable's length astern, we suppose the ships I, F, I, two cables length astern, to bear on the ship B. It is evident from the figure that in this case B will not be more exposed to the fire of I and I at the distance of 1440 yards than she was to that of H and H at half that distance; and so in similar cases. In explaining the principles on which we are to judge of the advantages or defects of different modes of bringing ships to action, Mr Clerk supposes a fleet of 10, 20 or more ships of 80 guns each, drawn up in line of battle to leeward, as at F, fig. 16. And lying to with an intention to avoid an action; while another fleet, as B, of equal number and force, also drawn up in line of battle, three or four miles to windward, wishes to make an attack, and come to close quarters on equal terms. The fleets being thus disposed, should the fleet at B attempt running down to attack the fleet at F, each ship standing head on to the opposite ship in the leeward line, it is to be expected, from what we have already stated, that the attacking ships will be disabled, at least in their rigging, before they can come to close action; but suppose that the commander of the weather fleet, though his ships have been disabled in their rigging during their course a.a.a to leeward, fig. 17, has made them bring to at a great distance, but sufficiently near to injure F. This latter fleet, which has been endeavouring to avoid an action, will now bear away with little injury to a new station, as G, and there remain out of the reach of B's shot, and this fleet must repair its rigging before it can make another attack. Again, suppose that the fleet B, instead of standing head on, were to run down in an angular course, as at fig. 18. It is plain that if any ship in this angular line should be crippled, her defect in failing will occasion a confusion of several of the other ships in that line. It may be said that the stoppage of one ship a-head will not necessarily produce a stoppage of every ship a-stern of her, because they may run to leeward of the disabled ship; but we must observe that by this time the ships a-head in the van A may be engaged, and consequently not having much head way, are nearly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, so that each ship a-stern, in attempting to bear down as at D, D, must be confined to a certain course, and must run the risk of being raked in coming down before the wind, and consequently of being disabled before coming up with the enemy. Thirdly, the van of the fleet B having attained their station at A, a-breadth of the van of F, fig. 19, and having begun the action, the van ships of F, with a view to retreat, may throw in a broadside on the van of B, and then bear away in succession, as at H, followed by the rest of the fleet F, which, after exchanging broadsides with the van of B, may draw up in a new line two or three miles to leeward at I, fig. 20. Suppose again, for further illustration, that B, fig. 1, Plate DLXX., represents a fleet putting before the wind, each ship intending, when brought to at a determined distance at A, to take up her particular antagonists in the line of the enemy F to leeward; and let F be supposed at rest, without any motion a-head. It is easy to conceive that while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> ships of F's line, under cover of the smoke, withdraw from battle to GGG, the intermediate ships left behind them in the line will be sufficient to amuse even the whole of B's fleet, till the ships G shall form a new line HH as a support from the leeward. In such case B, after being disabled, and not having foreseen the manoeuvre, will neither be able to prevent the intermediate ships with which he is engaged from bearing away to join their friends, nor, were he able, would it be advisable to follow them, for the same manoeuvre with equal success can again and again be repeated. To explain the relative motion of these two fleets, let Fig. 2, F, fig. 2, represent a fleet of 12 ships in line of battle, a cable's length astern, and suppose the length of each ship from the end of the jib-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOM">boom</a> to the stern to be 36 fathoms. The whole fleet will occupy a space of two English miles; and if it be supposed to fail in the direction FG, at the rate of four knots an hour, it will in an hour have moved to G, four miles from its former position. Now, let there be an opposite fleet B, also 12 ships, situated four miles to windward, and let the point A be a quarter of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> right to windward of the point G. Then, if B by bearing away in the direction BA, gain the point A at the same time that the leeward fleet F has arrived at G, B will have moved nearly at the rate of 5½ miles an hour, and the angle contained between the direction of its line of bearing and its present course will be nearly four points. Secondly, in fig. 3, if F, by carrying more sail, move at the rate of six miles an hour, from F to G, then B, with a more flanking course, will have more difficulty in keeping the line abreast while coming down to the attack, owing to the additional obstruction which will attend each succeeding ship in such a flanking course. Again, if the leeward fleet shall lie up one point higher, as FG, fig. 4, the rears of the two fleets will be removed to a much greater distance, and the van A must be sooner up with the enemy's van, and of course too much farther from support, while F bringing up his ships in succession, may disable the van of A, and afterwards bear away at pleasure with little injury, as at H. Now B being supposed disabled, and having his rear D disengaged, will be unable to prevent F from escaping. From these considerations it appears that a fleet to windward, by extending its line of battle with a view to stop and attack the whole line of an enemy's fleet to leeward, must labour under considerable disadvantages, and will scarcely succeed in the attempt. On these principles Mr Clerk explains the reason why, before the commencement of the present contest between Britain and France, the French fleets so repeatedly escaped from the British, without any serious defeat or loss, viz. by avoiding a general engagement, and disabling the British van as it bore down to attack them. He therefore recommends a different mode of attack from the windward, which we shall proceed to illustrate by proper diagrams. Let F (fig. 5) represent a fleet in line of battle, under easy sail, willing to avoid an action, but ready to receive an attack in the usual way, from another fleet B, three or four miles to windward, arranged in three columns. How shall B make the attack on F, so as, without aiming at the improbable advantage of taking or destroying the greater part of this fleet, they may secure three or four of the sternmost ships? Mr Clerk advises, that a sufficient strength be detached to secure these ships, while the admiral keeps aloof with the rest of his fleet, disposed as in the figure, ready to make the necessary observations and give the requisite support to the detached ships. If F continues to avoid an action by standing on in line, the detachment, coming into the position BA, will secure the three ships at I; and if the headmost ships of F were to tack, and be followed by the rest in succession as at fig. 6, not only the three ships at I will be left at the mercy of the ships detached from B, but two more, as G, will be exposed to an attack from another squadron of B at C. If all the ships of F tack together, as in fig. 7, the delay, and probably the confusion, consequent on this manoeuvre, will still more endanger the sternmost ships, or will bring on a general and close action. Again, if F attempts to haul off, beginning with his sternmost ship G, and then runs to leeward, as at fig. 8, he will expose his ships to a raking fire from B, and still endanger his sternmost ships by getting too far to leeward for their support; or if the headmost ships at H, fig. 9, veer first, to be followed by the rest aft, the danger would be still greater. Thus it appears that in every assignable case, a fleet to leeward, avoiding an attack from an equal or superior windward, as here advised, by preserving the line, will risk the loss of three or more of their sternmost ships. Now, let us suppose that F, while standing on in fig. 10, 11, line on the larboard tack, when threatened with an attack on his rear from B, veers and passes on opposite tacks to leeward (see fig. 10). The consequence of this will be, that his headmost ships will be forced to leeward by B, and compelled to engage under disadvantageous circumstances, and the disadvantage to F will be much the same, whether he again veers and resumes his former position, as at G, fig. 11, or stands on before the wind, as at P, fig. 12. We have hitherto supposed that the wind has been fixed in one point; but let us suppose it to shift, and let us inquire what will be the effect of such a circumstance on the two lines F and B. While the fleets are in the former position, F in line, and B in four divisions B, B, B, A, steering E, with the wind at N, fig. 13, let the wind shift to the west. The only consequence of this will be, that F will be thrown still farther to leeward, to its greater disadvantage. But let the wind shift to E, so as to be a-head, as in figs. 14, Figs. 14, and 15. Still if the admiral of B manages properly, and carefully watches the motions of F, this change will produce no advantage to the latter. For B has nothing to do but veer as the wind comes round, so as to bring his ships to windward of the three sternmost ships of F, and to leeward of the rest of his line, so as to cut off the three sternmost ships. If the wind should be supposed to veer from point to point all round the compass, so that the fleet F, maintaining the weather-gage of B, shall make a circuit round B to leeward; till if B act cautiously, F will lose the three threatened ships. Lastly, suppose the wind should instantly shift to a Fig. 16, point opposite to what it was at the commencement of the attack, as from N. to S. Before it can be ascertained whether such a change will be to the advantage or disadvantage of F, the relative situations of the two fleets must be considered. Suppose that the van and centre be separated at some distance from his rear, and that in consequence this fleet shall have taken such a position as is shown at fig. 16. Though in this case he Fig. 16, will have got to windward, his three ships can never be regained or preserved from the attack of B. The most favourable situation for F would be when the fleets were in the position denoted by fig. 13, as then he could not only support his three ships with advantage, but even threaten, and cut off a part of B's detachment. In attempting this, however, he incurs the risk of coming to a close engagement, which we have supposed him to be sedulously avoiding. Besides this method of attack from the windward by From the detachments from the main fleet, Mr Clerk shows how leeward, a successful attack may be made by a fleet to leeward, by its breaking the enemy's line, and this either near the rear, near the centre, or not far from the van, of which cases the two former will be most likely to prove successful. The enemy's line can be cut only when the two hostile fleets veer on opposite tacks. The most simple method of effecting this is for the van ship of the attacking squadron, instead of ranging parallel to that of the enemy, and to leeward of him, to pass through the... the first interval that offers, followed by the rest of the line, which is thus led across that of the enemy. In consequence of this manoeuvre, the van of the leeward fleet will be to windward of the enemy's rear, and thus the attacking squadron will have its line entire, while that of its adversary is divided. Again, the ships of the rear division, having their progres obstructed, will probably crowd on each other, get into confusion, and be driven to leeward. We cannot detail the different cases mentioned by Mr Clerk; but for these and many other valuable suggestions on the subject of naval tactics, we must refer to his useful and ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a>. The above is a very faint and meagre outline of Mr Clerk's tactics, but it is all which our limits enable us to give. It will afford general readers some idea of the nature of the proposed improvements, and professional men will naturally consult the original essay. On these or similar principles is founded the method of breaking through the enemy's line, and thus cutting off a part of his fleet, so successfully adopted by the British admirals in the great naval actions that have distinguished the late and present wars with France. We cannot better illustrate the principles above laid down, than by giving a short detail of the last of these memorable engagements, the Battle of Trafalgar. With this we shall conclude our sketch of naval tactics, and our practical observations on the art of War. After having been long blockaded in the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, the combined French and Spanish fleet effected their escape, while the British fleet, under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Nelson, was at a considerable distance. On the 19th of October 1805, the ships which had been left to watch the motions of the enemy, communicated to the commander in chief the agreeable intelligence, that the combined fleet had put to sea, and was sailing with light winds in a westerly direction. Lord Nelson concluding that their destination must be the Mediterranean, immediately made all sail with his ships for the entrance of the straits. Here he was informed by Captain Blackwood, that the enemy had not yet passed the straits. On the 21st of October, at daylight, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Trafalgar bearing east by south about seven leagues distant, the combined fleet was discovered about six or seven miles to the eastward. The wind was about west, and very light. As Lord Nelson had long expected to fall in with the enemy's fleet, he had concerted with his officers the best and most expeditious measures for bringing them to a speedy and decisive action. As soon, therefore, as they hove in sight, he immediately made the signal for the British fleet to bear up in two columns, as they formed in order of sailing. The combined fleet was drawn up in line of battle, with their heads to the northward, and had formed the line with great closeness and correctness. It consisted of 33 ships of the line, 18 French, and 15 Spanish, under Admiral Villeneuve, as commander in chief, who occupied the centre in the Bucentaure, while the Spanish admiral, Gravina, led the rear in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>. The British fleet consisted of 27 ships, including three sixty-fours. Lord Nelson headed the van in the Victory, having under him the Temeraire, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, Conqueror, Leviathan, Ajax, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORION">Orion</a>, Agamemnon, Minotaur, Spartiate, Britannia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, with the Euryalus, Sirius, Phoebe, and Naiad frigates, Pickle <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHOONER">schooner</a>, and Entrepreneure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a>; while the rear, consisting of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Sovereign, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, Belleisle, Tonissant, Belleroophon, Colossus, Achille, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLYPHEMUS">Polyphemus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">Revenge</a>, Swiftsure, Defence, Thunderer, Defiance, Prince, and Dreadnought, was led by Vice-admiral Collingwood in the Royal Sovereign. As the mode of attack adopted by the British was unusual, the combined fleet was obliged to draw up their line in a new manner. It formed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, with its convexity to leeward, so that in leading down to their centre, the rear division of the British had both their van and rear abaft the beam. Before the action commenced, every alternate ship was about a cable's length to windward of her second ahead and aft, thus forming a kind of double line, and appearing, when on their beam, to leave a small interval between them without crowding their ships. The French and Spaniards were not formed in separate divisions, but intermixed without any apparent regard to order of national squadrons. As the British commander had previously communicated to his flag-officers and captains his preconcerted mode of attack, few signals were necessary, and none were made on approaching the enemy, except to direct close order as the lines bore down. The action commenced at noon, by the leading ships of both columns, breaking through the enemy's line, the Victory about the tenth ship from the van, and the Royal Sovereign about the twelfth from the rear; the succeeding ships breaking through in every part after of their leaders, and engaging the enemy at the very muzzles of their guns. By this manoeuvre the van of the enemy was unengaged, and thus the inferiority of the British, in point of number, was of less consequence, while the superior skill and bravery of British seamen soon acquired a decided advantage. The conflict was severe, as the enemy's ships were fought with a gallantry highly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to their commanders. The British attack, however, was irresistible. About three P.M. many of the enemy's ships had struck their colours, and their line had given way. Ten ships of the line, and the frigates, under Admiral Gravina, made their escape, and fled to leeward towards Cadiz. The five headmost ships of their van tacked, and, standing to the southward, to windward of the British line, were brought to action, and the sternmost of them taken. Nineteen ships of the line, with three flag-officers, including the commander in chief, remained in the hands of the British. Never was there a victory more glorious or more decisive; never was the pre-eminence of the British flag more triumphantly conspicuous. The events subsequent to this memorable battle, and the losses sustained on either side, having little connection with the subject of the present article, need not be here detailed. They are fresh in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of our readers, and Britain still laments the loss of her immortal Nelson. * See Nelson. WAR Man-of-WAR <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>. See PELICANUS, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. WAR-Cry was formerly customary in the armies of most nations, when just upon the point of engaging. Sometimes they were only tumultuous shouts, or horrid yells, uttered with an intent to strike terror into their adversaries; such as is now used by the Indians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, called the war whoop.

WARBURTON

Pages 313-316

WILLIAM, a learned English bishop, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in Cheshire, and was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of George Warburton, an attorney at Newark in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, was born at Newark, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 24, 1698. He was first put to school there under a Mr Twells, but had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Okeham in Rutlandshire, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the beginning of the year 1714, and soon after he was put out clerk to an eminent attorney of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Markham in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, where he continued till the year 1719, when he returned to his family at Newark; but whether he practised there <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> elsewhere as an attorney, is not known. He had always expressed a strong inclination to take orders; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of letters, which tended to retard, rather than forward, his progress in the profession chosen for him by his friends, growing every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> stronger in him, it was deemed expedient to give way to that inclination. He therefore devoted himself to the studies necessary to fit him for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and at length in 1723 he was ordained deacon, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in 1727. In 1728 he was presented by Sir Robert Sutton to the rectory of Brand-Broughton, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, where he spent the greater part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and composed all the great works which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> carry his fame <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to posterity. In the same year he was put upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of Masters of Arts, erected on his majesty's visit to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He had already published some juvenile performances, which displayed genius and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, and attracted considerable notice; but it was not till the year 1736 that he may be said to have emerged from the obscurity of a private life into the notice of the world.—The first publication which rendered him afterwards famous now appeared, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">Alliance</a> between Church and State; or, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">Equity</a> of an Established <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> and a Test <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>; demonstrated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> and End of Civil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> Principles of the Law of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Nations." In *Review of this treatise, says Bishop <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSLEY">Horsley</a> *, the author "hath the Cate of shown the general good policy of an establishment, and the necessity of a Test for its security, upon principles which republicans themselves cannot easily deny. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is one of the finest specimens that are to be found perhaps in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, of scientific reasoning applied to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> subject." At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the Alliance was announced the scheme of the Divine Legation of Moses, in which he had then made considerable progress. The first volume of this work was published in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1737-8, under the title of "The Divine Legation of Moses demonstrated on the Principles of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> Deity, from the Ommission of the Doctrine of a future State of Rewards and Punishments in the Jewish Dispensation, in six books, by William Warburton, M. A. author of Vol. XX. Part II. the Alliance between Church and State;" and met Warburton, with a reception which neither the subject, nor the manner in which it was treated, seemed to authorize. It was, as the author afterwards observed, fallen upon in so outrageous and brutal a manner as had been scarcely pardonable, had it been "The Divine Legation of Mahomet."—It produced several answers, and so much abuse from the authors of "The Weekly Miscellany," that in less than two months he was constrained to defend himself, in "A Vindication of the Author of the Divine Legation of Moses, from the Aspersions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">Country</a> Clergyman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> in the Weekly Miscellany of February 24, 1737-8, 8vo." Mr Warburton's extraordinary merit had now attracted the notice of the heir apparent to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, in whose immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> we find him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1738, when he published "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a> working by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a> to Christian Edification, a Sermon, preached at the last episcopal Visitation for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">Confirmation</a> in the Diocese of Lincoln; with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">Preface</a>, showing the Reason of its Publication; and a Postscript, occasioned by some Letters lately published in the Weekly Miscellany; by William Warburton M. A. Chaplain to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Highness the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>." The "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>" had now been published some years; and it is universally supposed, that the author had, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of it, adopted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bolingbroke, whom, on this occasion, he had followed as his guide, without understanding the tendency of his principles. In 1738, M. de Croufaz wrote some remarks on it, accusing the author of Spinozism and Naturalism; which falling into Mr Warburton's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, he published a defence of the first epistle, and soon after of the remaining three, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> letters; of which five were printed in 1739, and the seventh in June 1740, under the title of "A Vindication of Mr Pope's Essay on Man, by the author of the Divine Legation." The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which Mr Pope conceived of these defences, as well as of their author, will be best seen in his letters. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, a firm friendship was established between them, which continued with undiminished fervour until the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mr Pope; who, during the remainder of his life, paid a deference and respect to his friend's judgement and abilities, which will be considered by many as almost bordering on fervency. Towards the end of the year 1739, Mr Warburton published a new and improved edition of the first volume of the Divine Legation; and in 1741, appeared the second part, which completed the argument, though not the entire <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of that work. "A work, says Bishop Hurd *, in all views of the most transcendant Life of merit, whether we consider the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> or the execution. A plain simple argument, yet perfectly new, proving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic law</a>, and laying a sure foundation for the support of Christianity, is there drawn out to a great length by a chain of reasoning so elegantly connected, that the reader is carried along it with ease and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> presented to him is so striking for its own importance, so embellished by a lively fancy, and illustrated from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> by exquisite learning and the most ingenious disquisition, that in the whole compass of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> or ancient <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, there is nothing equal or similar to this extraordinary performance." This is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> of a man reflecting with ten- *Life of Warburton prefixed to his Works. Warburton dernes on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his friend and benefactor; but it approaches much nearer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> than the censures of those cabalistic critics, who, fattening upon some weak part of the Divine Legation, or perhaps never having looked into it, have ridiculously contended that the author was far from being eminent as a scholar, and that his work is inimical to the cause of Christianity! Putting partiality aside, there is in the Divine Legation of Moles abundant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the malignant folly of this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, as no man can read and understand that work without being convinced that its author was a Christian, not only sincere but zealous; that he was, what Johnson calls him*, "a man of vigorous faculties, of a mind fervent and vehement, supplied, by unlimited and incessant inquiry, with a wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and variety of knowledge, which had neither deprived his imagination nor clouded his perspicuity; and that to every work, and this work in particular, he brought a memory full fraught with a fancy fertile of original <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>, exerting at once the powers of the scholar, the reasoner, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>." But we think it must be acknowledged, that his learning was too multifarious to be always exact, and his inquiries too eagerly pushed to be always cautious. We have no hesitation, however, to say, that to the divine this great work, with all its imperfections, is, in our opinion, one of the most valuable that is to be found in any language. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> 1741, Mr Pope and Mr Warburton, in a country ramble, took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in their way. The university was naturally pleased at the arrival of two such strangers, and seemed desirous of enrolling their names among their graduates. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of D.D. was intended for the divine, and that of LL.D. for the poet; but intrigue and envy defeated this scheme; and the university lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of decorating at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the two greatest geniuses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, by the fault of one or two of its members. Pope retired with some indignation to Twickenham, where he confided himself and his friend with this satirical reflection—“We shall take our degree together in fame, whatever we do at the university.” The friendship of this eminent poet was of service to Mr Warburton in more respects than that of increasing his fame. He introduced and warmly recommended him to most of his friends, and among others to Mr Murray, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>, and Ralph Allen, Esq. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>. In consequence of this introduction, we find Mr Warburton at Bath 1742; where he printed a sermon which had been preached at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>-church on the 24th of October, for the benefit of Mr Allen’s favourite Charity, the General <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a> or Infirmary. In this year also he printed a Dissertation on the origin of books of chivalry, at the end of Jarvis’s Preface to a translation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, which Mr Pope tells him, he had not got over two paragraphs of, before he cried out, *Aut Erafimus, aut Diabolus.* In 1742, Mr Warburton published “A Critical and Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on Mr Pope’s Essay on Man,” in which is contained a Vindication of the said Essay from the Mephistophelian M. de Resnial, the French Translator, and of M. de Croufaz, Professor of Philosophy and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a> in the Academy of Laufanne, the Commentator.” It was at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, when Mr Warburton had the entire confidence of Mr Pope, that he advised him to complete the Dunciad, by changing Warburton’s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, and adding to it a fourth book. This was accordingly executed in 1742, and published early in 1743, with notes by our author; who, in consequence of it, received his share of the abuse which Mr Gibber liberally bestowed on both Mr Pope and his annotator. In the latter end of the same year he published complete editions of “The Essay on Man,” and “The Essay on Criticism,” and from the specimen which he there exhibited of his abilities, it may be presumed Mr Pope determined to commit the publication of those works which he should leave to Mr Warburton’s care. At Mr Pope’s desire, he, about this time, revised and corrected the “Essay on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>,” as it now stands in the last edition of that translation. The publication of “The Dunciad” was the last service which our author rendered Mr Pope in his lifetime. After a lingering and tedious illness, the event of which had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> foreseen, this great poet died on the 30th of May 1744; and by his will, dated the 12th of the preceding December, bequeathed to Mr Warburton one half of his library, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of all such of his works already printed as he had not otherwise disposed of or alienated, and all the profits which should arise from any edition to be printed after his death: but at the same time directed that they should be published without any future alterations. “In 1744, Mr Warburton turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the several attacks which had been made on the “Divine Legation,” and defended himself in a manner which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did not prove him to be possessed of much humility or diffidence, at least demonstrated, that he knew how to wield the weapons of controversy with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. His first defence now appeared, under the title of “Remarks on several occasional Reflections, in Answer to the Reverend Dr Middleton, Dr Pococke, the Master of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">Charter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, Dr Richard Grey, and others; serving to explain and justify <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">Passages</a> in the Divine Legation, objected to by those learned Writers. To which is added, A General Review of the Argument of the Divine Legation, as far as it is yet advanced; wherein is considered the Relation the several Parts bear to each other and the whole. Together with an Appendix, in Answer to a late Pamphlet intitled, An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">Examination</a> of Mr W——’s second Proposition.” This was followed next year by “Remarks on several occasional Reflections, in Answer to the Reverend Doctors Siebbing and Sykes; serving to explain and justify the Two Dissertations in the Divine Legation, concerning the Command to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> to offer up his Son, and the Nature of the Jewish Theocracy, objected to by these learned Writers. Part II. and last.” Both these answers are couched in those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> terms of confident superiority, which marked almost every performance that fell from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> during the remainder of his life. On the 5th of September 1745, the friendship between him and Mr Allen was more closely cemented by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Miss Tucker, who survived, and is now, if alive, Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a> Smith of Prior-park. At that important crisis our author preached and published three excellent sermons: 1. “A faithful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">Portrait</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, by which it is seen to be the Reverse of Christianity, as it is the Destruction of Morality, Piety, and Civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a>. Preached at St James’s, Westminster, October <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">WAR</a> Warburton. October 1745." 2. "A Sermon occasioned by the present unnatural Rebellion, &c. Preached in Mr Allen's Chapel at Prior-park, near Bath, November 1745." 3. "The Nature of National Offences truly stated.—Preached on the General Fast-day, Dec. 18. 1745-6." On account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> of these sermons, he was again involved in a controversy with his former antagonist Dr Stebbing, which occasioned "An Apologetical Dedication to the Reverend Dr Henry Stebbing, in Answer to his Censure and Misrepresentations of the Sermon preached on the General Fast, &c." Notwithstanding his great connections, his acknowledged abilities, and his established reputation, a reputation founded on the durable basis of learning, and upheld by the decent and attentive performance of every duty incident to his station; yet we do not find that he received any addition to the preferments given him in 1728 by Sir Robert Sutton (except the chaplainship to the prince of Wales), until April 1746, when he was unanimously called by the Society of Lincoln's Inn to be their preacher. In November he published "A Sermon preached on the Thanksgiving appointed to be observed the 9th of October, for the Suppression of the late unnatural Rebellion." In 1747 appeared his edition of Shakespeare and his Preface to Clarissa; and in the same year he published, 1. "A Letter from an Author to a Member of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> concerning Literary Property." 2. "Preface to Mrs Cockburn's Remarks upon the Principles and Reasonings of Dr Rutherford's Essay on the Nature and Obligations of Virtue, &c." 3. "Preface to a Critical Inquiry into the Opinions and Practice of the ancient Philosophers, concerning the Nature of a Future State, and their Method of teaching by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> Doctrine," (by Mr Towne) 1747, second edition. In 1748, a third edition of "The Alliance between Church and State, corrected and enlarged." "In 1749, a very extraordinary attack was made on the moral character of Mr Pope, from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> where it could be least expected. An insignificant pamphlet, under the name of A Patriotic King, was that year published by Lord Bolingbroke, or by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, with a preface to it, reflecting highly on Mr Pope's honour. The provocation was simply this: The manuscript of that trivial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> had been intrusted to the care of Mr Pope, with the charge (as it was pretended) that only a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of copies should be printed. Mr Pope, in his excessive admiration of his guide, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and friend, took that opportunity, for fear so invaluable a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of patriotic eloquence should be lost to the public, to exceed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, and to run off more copies, which were found, after his death, in the printer's warehouse. This charge, however frivolous, was aggravated beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>; and, notwithstanding the proofs which Lord Bolingbroke had received of Pope's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to him, envenomed with the utmost malignity. Mr Warburton thought it became him to vindicate his deceased friend; and he did it so effectually, as not only to silence his accuser, but to cover him with confusion." About this time the publication of Dr Middleton's Inquiry concerning the miraculous Powers of the Christian Church, gave rise to a controversy, which was managed with great warmth and acrimony on both sides, and not much to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of either party. On this occasion Mr Warburton published an excellent performance, written with a degree of candour and temper, which, it is to be lamented, he did not always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. The title of it was "Julian; or a Discourse concerning the Earthquake and fiery Eruption which defeated the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a>'s attempt to rebuild the Temple at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, 1750." A second edition of this discourse, "with Additions," appeared in 1751, in which year he gave the public his edition of Mr Pope's Works, with Notes, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> volumes 8vo; and in the same year printed "An Answer to a Letter to Dr Middleton, inserted in a Pamphlet intitled, The Argument of the Divine Legation fairly stated," &c.; and "An Account of the Prophecies of Aife Evans, the Welsh Prophet in the last Century," annexed to the first volume of Dr Jortin's Remarks on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, which afterwards subjected him to much trouble. In 1752, Mr Warburton published the first volume of a course of sermons, preached at Lincoln's Inn, intitled, "The Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> and Revealed Religion, occasionally opened and explained;" and this was two years afterwards followed by a second. After the public had been some time promised, it may, from the alarm which was taken, be almost said threatened with, the appearance of Lord Bolingbroke's Works, they were about this time printed. The known abilities and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> of this nobleman had created apprehensions in the minds of many people, of the pernicious effects of his doctrines; and nothing but the appearance of his whole force could have convinced his friends, how little there was to be dreaded from arguments against religion so weakly supported. Many answers were soon published, but none with more acuteness, solidity, and sprightliness, than "A View of Lord Bolingbroke's Philosophy, in two Letters to a Friend, 1754;" the third and fourth letters were published in 1755, with another edition of the two former; and in the same year a smaller edition of the whole; which, though it came into the world without a name, was universally ascribed to Mr Warburton, and afterwards publicly owned by him. To some copies of this is prefixed an excellent complimentary epistle from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> Montesquieu, dated May 26. 1754. At this advanced period of his life, that preferment which his abilities might have claimed, and which had hitherto been withheld, seemed to be approaching towards him. In September 1754, he was appointed one of his majesty's chaplains in ordinary; and in the next year was presented to a prebend in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>. About this time the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Divinity was conferred on him by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">Herring</a>, then archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. A new <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of The Divine Legation being now called for, he printed a fourth edition of the first part of it, corrected and enlarged, divided into two volumes, with a dedication to the earl of Hardwicke. The same year appeared "A Sermon preached before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, President, and the Governors of the Hospital for the Smallpox and for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INOCULATION">Inoculation</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">Parish</a>-church of St Andrew, Holborn, April the 24th, 1755." And in 1756, Natural and Civil Events the Instruments of God's Moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a>; a Sermon, preached on the last public Fast-day, at Lincoln's Inn Chapel." In 1757, Dr Warburton meeting with Mr Hume's tract, WAR Warburton's tract, entitled, The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural History</a> of Religion, filled the margin of the book, as well as some interleaved slips of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, with many severe and shrewd remarks on the infidelity and naturalism of the author. These he put into the hands of his friend Dr Hurd, who, making a few alterations of the style, added a short introduction and conclusion, and published them in a pamphlet, entitled, "Remarks on Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Hume's Natural History of Religion, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a> of Cambridge, in a Letter to the Reverend Dr Warburton." This lively attack upon Mr Hume gave him so much offence, that he thought proper to vent his spleen on the supposed author, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a> discourse which he called his Life; and thus to do greater honour to Dr Hurd than to any other of his numerous antagonists. Towards the end of the year 1757, Dr Warburton was promoted to the deanery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>; and in the beginning of the year 1760, he was, through Mr Allen's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with Mr Pitt, afterwards earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, advanced to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>. That great minister is known to have declared, "that nothing of a private nature, since he had been in office, had given him so much pleasure as bringing our author on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>." There was, however, another minister, who dreaded his promotion, and thought he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a second Atterbury in the new bishop of Gloucester; but Warburton, says Bishop Hurd, had neither talents nor inclination for parliamentary intrigue or parliamentary eloquence: he had other instruments of fame in his hands, and was infinitely above the vanity of being caught "With the fine notion of a busy man." He was consecrated on the 20th of January 1760, and on the 30th of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> preached before the house of lords. In the next year he printed "A Rational Account of the Nature and End of the Sacrament of the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>." In 1762, he published "The Doctrine of Grace; or the Office and Operations of the Holy Spirit vindicated from the Insults of Infidelity and the Abuses of Fanaticism," 2 vols 12mo; and in the succeeding year drew upon himself much illiberal abuse from some writers of the popular party, on occasion of his complaint in the house of lords, on the 15th of November 1763, against Mr Wilkes, for putting his name to certain notes on the infamous "Essay on Woman." In 1765 he published a new edition of the second part of the Divine Legation, in three volumes; and as it had now received its last hand, he presented it to his great friend Lord Mansfield, in a dedication which deserves to be read by every person who esteems the well-being of society as a concern of any importance. It was the appendix to this edition which produced the well-known controversy between him and Dr Lowth, which we have noticed elsewhere (see Lowth), as doing no great honour, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> in which it was conducted, to either party. In the next year he gave a new and much improved edition of the Alliance between the Church and State. This was followed, in 1767, by a third volume of sermons, to which is added, his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIENNIAL">Triennial</a> Charge to the Clergy of the Diocese of Gloucester; which may be safely pronounced one of the most valuable discourses of the kind that is to be found in our own or any other language. With this publication he closed his literary course; except that he made an effort towards publishing, and actually printed, the ninth Warburton and last book of the Divine Legation. This book, with one or two occasional sermons, and some valuable directions for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of theology, have been given to the world in the splendid edition of his works in seven volumes 4to, by his friend and biographer the present bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. That prelate confesses, that the ninth book of the Divine Legation displays little of that vigour of mind and fertility of invention which appear so conspicuous in the former volumes; but he adds, perhaps truly, that under all the disadvantages with which it appears, it is the noblest effort which has hitherto been made to give a rationale of Christianity. While the bishop of Gloucester was thus exerting his last strength in the cause of religion, he projected a method by which he hoped to render it effectual service after his death. He transferred 500l. to Lord Mansfield, Sir Eardley Wilmot, and Mr Charles Yorke, upon trust, to found a lecture, in the form of a course of sermons, to prove the truth of revealed religion in general, and of the Christian in particular, from the completion of the prophecies in the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, which relate to the Christian church, especially to the apostacy of Papal Rome. To this foundation we owe the admirable Introductory Lectures of Hurd, and the well-adapted Continuation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> and Bagot. It is a melancholy reflection, that a life spent in the constant pursuit of knowledge, frequently terminates in the loss of those powers, the cultivation and improvement of which are attended with too strict and unabated a degree of ardour. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with Dr Warburton; and it seems probable that this decline of intellectual vigour was aggravated by the loss of his only son, a promising young man, who died of a consumption but a short time before the bishop, who himself resigned to fate in the year 1779, and in the 81st of his age. A neat marble monument was erected to his memory in the cathedral of Gloucester.

WARD

Pages 316-317

Dr Seth, an English prelate, chiefly distinguished for his knowledge in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUNTINGFORD">Buntingford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, about the year 1617. He was admitted of Sidney <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he applied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> vigour to his studies, particularly to the mathematics, and was chosen fellow of his college. He was much involved in the consequences of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, but soon after the Restoration obtained the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>; in 1667, he was translated to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>; and in 1671 was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>; he was the first Protestant bishop that enjoyed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and he procured it to be annexed to the see of Salisbury. Bishop Ward was one of those unhappy persons who have the misfortune to survive their enemies, which happened in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a fever ill cured; he lived to the Revolution, without knowing anything of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and died in 1690. He was the author of several Latin works in mathematics and astronomy, which were thought excellent in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> has been superseded by later discoveries and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. Ward, is variously used in our old books: a ward in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> is a district <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, committed to the special <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of one of the aldermen; and in London there are 26 wards, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the mayor and aldermen, of which every one has his WAR Ward-hold: his ward for his proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> and jurisdiction. A fol- lowing ret is divided into wards; and a prifon is called a ward. Lastly, the heir of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s tenant, that held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a>, was termed a ward during his nonage; but this ward- ship is taken away by the statute 12 Car. II. c. 24. WARD-Holding, in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. See LAW, No clxv. I. and clxvi. 3. WARD-Hook, or Wadd-hook, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, a rod or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> end turned serpentwise, or like a screw, to draw the wadding out of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> when it is to be unloaded.

WARDEN

Pages 317-317
or GUARDIAN, one who has the charge or keeping of any person, or thing, by office. Such is the warden of the Fleet, the keeper of the Fleet prison; who has the charge of the prisoners there, especially such as are committed from the court of chancery for contempt.

WARDHUYS

Pages 317-317

a port of Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, 120 miles south-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 31. 12. N. Lat. 70. 23. WARDMÔTE, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> so called, which is kept in every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; answering to the curiata <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a> of Rome.

WARDROBE

Pages 317-317

in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, is an apartment wherein his robes, wearing apparel, and other necessaries, are preserved under the care and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of proper officers. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">MAJOR</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Keeper of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>- robe was an officer of great antiquity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> privileges and immunities were conferred on him by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VI, which were confirmed by his successors; and King James I. not only enlarged them, but ordained that this office should be a corporation or body politic for ever. It was the duty of this office to provide robes for the coronations, marriages, and funerals of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family; to furnish the court with hangings, cloths of state, carpets, beds, and other necessaries; to furnish houses for ambassadors at their first arrival; cloths of state, and other furniture, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and all his majesty's ambassadors abroad; to provide all robes for foreign knights of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>, robes for the knights of the garter at home; robes and all other furniture for the officers of the garter; coats for kings, heralds, and pursuivants at arms; robes for the lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer, &c.; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> for the lord chamberlain, grooms of his majesty's privy chamber, officers of his majesty's robes; for the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> justices, for all the barons of the exchequer, and several officers of these courts; all liveries for his majesty's servants, as yeomen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and wardens of the Tower, trumpeters, kettle-drummers, and fifes; the messengers, and all belonging to the stables, as coachmen, footmen, littermen, postilions, and grooms, &c. all the king's coaches, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, harnesses, saddles, bits, bridles, &c. the king's watermen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>-keepers, &c. also furniture for the royal yachts, and all rich embroidered tilts, and other furniture for the barges. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> or keeper of the wardrobe, who had a salary of 200l., there was his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, who had 150l. and a comptroller and a patent clerk, each of whom has a salary of 300l. Besides many other inferior officers and servants, who were all sworn servants to the king. There was likewise a removing wardrobe, who had its own set of officers, and standing wardrobe-keepers at St James's, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> Castle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a> Court, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KENNINGTON">Kennington</a>, and Somerset <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>; but the whole of the wardrobe establishment was abolished by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in 1782, and the duty of it in future to be done by the lord chamberlain.

WARDSHIP

Pages 317-318

in chivalry, one of the incidents of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. See FEODAL System, KNIGHT Service, and TENURE. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a tenant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the heir was under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 21, being a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 14, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> was intitled to the wardship of the heir, and was called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> in chivalry. This wardship consisted in having the custody of the body and lands of such heir, without any account of the profits, till the age of 21 in males, and 16 in females. For the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> supposed the heir-male unable to perform knight-service till 21; but as for the female, she was supposed capable at 14 to marry, and then her husband might perform the service. The lord therefore had no wardship, if at the death of the ancestor the heir-male was of the full age of 21, or the heir-female of 14: yet if she was then under 14, and the lord once had her in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a>, he might keep her so till 16, by virtue of the statute of Westminster, 1. 3 Edw. I. c. 22. the two additional years being given by the legislature for no other reason but merely to benefit the lord. This wardship, so far as it related to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, though it was not nor could be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the law of feuds, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as they were arbitrary, temporary, or for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> only; yet when they became <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, and did consequently often descend upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, who by reason of their age could neither perform nor stipulate for the services of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEUD">feud</a>, does not seem upon feudal principles to have been unreasonable. For the wardship of the land, or custody of the feud, was retained by the lord, that he might out of the profits thereof provide a fit person to supply the infant's services till he should be of age to perform them himself. And if we consider a feud in its original import, as a stipend, fee, or reward for actual service, it could not be thought hard that the lord should withhold the stipend so long as the service was suspended. Though undoubtedly to our English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, where such stipendiary donation was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> supposition or figment, it carried abundance of hardship; and accordingly it was relieved by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of Henry I. which took this custody from the lord, and ordained that the custody, both of the land and the children, should belong to the widow or next of kin. But this noble immunity did not continue many years. The wardship of the body was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the wardship of the land; for he who enjoyed the infant's estate was the properest person to educate and maintain him in his infancy: and also, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> view, the lord was most concerned to give his tenant a suitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, in order to qualify him the better to perform those services which in his maturity he was bound to render. When the male heir arrived at the age of 21, or the heir-female at that of 16, they might sue out their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> or ouster/remain; that is, the delivery of their lands. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">WAR</a> out of their guardian's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. For this they were obliged to pay a fine, namely, half-a-year's profits of the land; though this seems expressly contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>. However, in consideration of their lands having been so long in ward, they were excused all reliefs, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s tenants also all primer seifins. In order to ascertain the profits that arose to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> the heir his livery, the itinerant justices, or justices in eyre, had it formerly in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to make <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> concerning them by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called an inquisitio <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> mortem; which was instituted to inquire (at the death of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of fortune) the value of his estate, the tenure by which it was holden, and who, and of what age, his heir was; thereby to ascertain the relief and value of the primer seifin, or the wardship and livery accruing to the king thereupon. A manner of proceeding that came in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to be greatly abused, and at length an intolerable grievance; it being one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> accusations against Empson and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>, the wicked engines of Henry VII. that by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of false inquisitions they compelled many persons to sue out livery from the crown, who by no means were tenants thereto. And afterwards a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of wards and liveries was erected, for conducting the same inquiries in a more solemn and legal manner. When the heir thus came of full age, provided he held a knight's fee, he was to receive the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, and was compellable to take it upon him, or else pay a fine to the king. For in those heroic times no person was qualified for deeds of arms and chivalry who had not received this order, which was conferred with much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> and solemnity. We may plainly discover the footsteps of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in what Tacitus relates of the Germans, who, in order to qualify their young men to bear arms, presented them in a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> with a shield and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is supposed to have been the original of the feudal knighthood. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, of compelling the vassals to be knighted, or to pay a fine, was expressly recognized in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> by the statute de militibus, 1 Edw. II.; was exerted as an expedient for raising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> by many of our best princes, particularly by Edw. VI. and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; but this was the occasion of heavy murmurs when exerted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.: among whose many misfortunes it was, that neither himself nor his people seemed able to distinguish between the arbitrary stretch and the legal exertion of prerogative. However, among the other concessions made by that unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> before the fatal recourse to arms, he agreed to divest himself of this undoubted flower of the crown; and it was accordingly abolished by statute 16 Car. I. c. 20.

WARP

Pages 318-318

a small rope employed occasionally to remove a ship from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another, in a port, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> river. And hence, To Warp, is to change the situation of a ship, by pulling her from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a harbour, &c. to some other, by means of warps, which are attached to buoys; to anchors sunk in the bottom; or to certain stations upon the shore, as posts, rings, trees, &c. The ship is accordingly drawn forwards to those stations, either by pulling on the warps by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or by the application of some purchase, as a tackle, windlass, or capstern, upon her deck. When this operation is performed by the ship's lesser anchors, these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, together with their warps, are carried out in the boats alternately towards the place where the ship is endeavouring to arrive: so that when she is drawn up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, the other is carried out to a competent distance before her, and being sunk, serves to fix the other warp, by which she is farther advanced. Warping is generally used when the sails are unbent; or when they cannot be successfully employed, which may either arise from the unfavourable state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, the opposition of the tide, or the narrow limits of the channel.

WARRANT

Pages 318-319

is a power and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other officer to apprehend a person accused of any crime. It may be issued in extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, or secretaries of state; but most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> it is issued by justices of the peace. They may do in any cases where they have a jurisdiction over the offence, in order to compel the person accused to appear before them; for it would be absurd to give them power to examine an offender, unless they had also power to compel him to attend and submit to such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>. And this extends to all treasons, felonies, and breaches of the peace; and also to all such offenses as Comment. they have power to punish by statute. Before the granting of the warrant, it is fitting to examine upon oath the party requiring it, as well to ascertain that there is a felony or other crime actually committed, without which no warrant should be granted; as also to prove the cause and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of suspecting the party against whom the warrant is prayed. This warrant ought to be under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; should set forth the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of making, and the cause for which it is made; and should be directed to the constable, or other peace officer, or it may be to any private person by name. A general warrant to apprehend all persons suspected, without naming or particularly describing any person in special, is illegal and void for its uncertainty; for it is the duty of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and ought not to be left to the officer, to judge of the ground of suspicion. Also a warrant to appre- prehend all persons guilty of such a crime, is no legal warrant; for the point upon which its authority rests, is a fact to be decided on a subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>; namely, whether the person apprehended thereupon be guilty or not guilty. When a warrant is received by the officer, he is bound to execute it, so far as the jurisdiction of the magistrate and himself extends.
