A warrant from any of the justices of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> extends over all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and is testified or dated England; but a warrant of a justice of the peace in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, must be backed, that is, signed, by a justice of another county, before it can be executed there. And a warrant for apprehending an English or a Scotch offender, may be indorsed in the opposite kingdom, and the offender carried back to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the united kingdom in which the offence was committed.

WARRANTY

Pages 319-319

Warrantia, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covenant, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, made by the bargainer for himself and his heirs, to warrant and secure the bargainer and his heirs, against all men, for enjoying the thing agreed on or granted between them.

WARREN

Pages 319-319

is a franchise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> privileged by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, for the keeping of beasts and fowls of the warren; which are hares and conies, partridges, pheasants, and some add quails, woodcocks, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-fowl, &c. These being fere <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, every one had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to kill as he could; but upon the introduction of the forest laws at the Norman conquest, these animals being looked upon as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and the sole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> monarchs, this franchise of free-warren was invented to protect them, by giving the grantee a sole and exclusive power of killing such game, so far as his warren extended, on condition of his preventing other persons. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> therefore that has the franchise of warren, is in reality no more than a royal game-keeper; but no man, not even a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, could by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> justify sporting on another's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, or even on his own, unless he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of free-warren. This franchise is almost fallen into disrepute since the new statutes for preserving the game; the name being now chiefly preferred in grounds that are let apart for breeding hares and rabbits. There are many instances of keen sportsmen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, who have sold their estates, and reserved the free-warren, or right of killing game, to themselves; by which means it comes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> that a man and his heirs have sometimes free-warren over another's ground. A warren may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> open; and there is no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of inclosing it as there is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any person offend in a free-warren, he is punishable by the common law, and by statute 21 Edw. III. And if any one enter wrongfully into any warren, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, take, or kill, any conies without the consent of the owner, he shall forfeit treble damages, and suffer three months imprisonment, &c. by 22 and 23 Car. II. c. 25. When conies are on the foil of the party, he hath a property in them by reason of the petition, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> lies for killing them; but if they run out of the warren and eat up a neighbour's corn, the owner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> may kill them, and no action <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> lie.

WARSAW

Pages 319-319

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Masovia. It is built partly in a plain, and partly on a gentle ascent rising from the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>, which is about as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at Westminster, but very shallow in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. This city and its suburbs occupy a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground, and are supposed to contain 70,000 inhabitants, among whom is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of foreigners. The whole has a melancholy appearance, exhibiting the strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> of wealth and poverty, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and distress, which pervades every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this unhappy country. The streets are spacious, but ill paved; the churches and public buildings are large and magnificent; the palaces of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> are numerous and splendid; but the greatest part of the houses, particularly in the suburbs, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and ill-constructed wooden hovels.—Warsaw is 160 miles south-east by south of Dantzig, 130 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>, and 300 north-east by north of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21. 6. N. Lat. 50. 14. WART. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WARWICK

Pages 319-319

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a> in England, and from which this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> derives its name. It is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and supposed by Camden to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Praefidium, where the Dalmatian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> were posted. It stands on a rock of freestone, of which all the public edifices in the town are built. At the Norman invasion it was a considerable place; and had many burgesses, of whom 12 were obliged by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> to accompany the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> in his wars. It is supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> brought in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the town, besides what it derives from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> within it made in the rock; and it is easily kept clean, by being situated upon a declivity. Four streets, from the four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass, meet in the centre of the town. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> public buildings are

WARWICKSHIRE

Pages 319-320

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, 47 miles in length, by 30 in breadth. It is bounded at its northern extremity by a point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>; on the north-east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>; on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>; on the south-west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, and on the south-east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. It is situated partly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Lichfield and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, and partly in that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>; it contains four <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, 12 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 158 parishes; sends six members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is computed at 208,190. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is mild, pleasant, and healthy. The river Avon divides the north <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Woodlands, from the south, called the Feldon; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of both is rich and fertile. Its productions are corn, malt, wood, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, cheese, coal, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of this county are the Avon, Tame, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">Arrow</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> is far superior to it in respect of trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and even to any other town in England. Birmingham, in this county, of which the account given in the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> is very deficient, is one of the most remarkable towns in England, or perhaps in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, variety, elegance, and utility of its manufactures. This town was little distinguished previous to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, but since that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to increase in extent and importance. In the year 1700, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of streets in Birmingham was only 30; they are now nearly 250. In the year 1779 there were only three houses on a particular spot, which in 1791 contained 833. Birmingham owes its prosperity and population to its manufactures, which are in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its vicinity to coal, aided by the spirited and industrious exertions of a few individuals. It has been stated, and no doubt with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, that its prosperity is in no small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> indebted to its exemption from the restrictions of borough and corporate laws. To give some notion of the progress and extent of the manufactures of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it may be mentioned that the late Mr Taylor, who introduced gilt buttons, japanned, gilt, and painted snuff-boxes, with various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of manufacture in enamel, died in 1775, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 64, having amassed a fortune of 200,000l. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> snuff-boxes at so low a rate as one farthing each, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> 3l. 10s. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. The weekly produce of Mr Taylor's manufacture of buttons amounted to 800l. beside many other valuable and curious productions. The manufactory of Messrs Boulton and Watt, which for its extent, variety, and importance, stands unrivalled in Europe, has been already noticed under the word Soho. The new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, which has been often deservedly admired, and the re-stamped dollars, are the productions of the Soho manufactory. The first coining mill was erected at Soho in 1783. It is now so much improved, that eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> driven by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine, are going on at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Each of these machines strikes from 70 to 84 pieces of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> per minute, and hence the whole eight machines <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> off in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> between 30,000 and 40,000 coins. The different processes of the machinery are, 1. Rolling the masses of copper into sheets. 2. Rolling them through cylindrical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> rollers. 3. Clipping the pieces of copper for the dye. 4. Shaking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> in bags. 5. Striking both sides of the coin, and then milling it; after which it is displaced, and another is introduced, to be subjected to the same operation. But the most extraordinary contrivance of this ingenious machinery is, that a precise account of every coin which passes through it is regularly kept, so that it is impossible to practise fraud. Besides the branches of industry already mentioned, there are manufactories of guns, bayonets, and swords, of sporting guns, of whips, of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">japan</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, of numerous works in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and steel, both for ornament and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and at one time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> to a considerable extent. Birmingham contains a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> curiosities, a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, rebuilt since 1791, several churches belonging to the establishment, various dissenting meeting houses, and a number of charitable establishments. In the neighbourhood of Birmingham there are three extensive breweries; and by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> this place has the advantage of easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with almost every part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>.

WASHING

Pages 320-320

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, is when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, drawn with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRAYON">crayon</a>, has some one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> laid over it with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, bitre, or the like, to make it appear more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, by adding the shadow of prominences, apertures, &c., and by imitating the particular matters whereof the thing is supposed to consist. Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> is employed to imitate brick and tile; a pale Indian blue, to imitate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and slate; green, for trees and meadows; saffron or French berries, for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; and several colours for marbles.

WASHING OF ORES

Pages 320-320

the purifying an ore of any metal, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, from earths and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which would otherwise render it difficult of fusion.

WASHINGTON

Pages 320-322

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and now the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the United States. It is situated at the junction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTOMAC">Potomac</a> and the Eastern Branch, extending about four miles up each, including a tract of territory scarcely to be exceeded, in point of convenience, salubrity, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, by any in the world. This territory, which is called Columbia, lies partly in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, and partly in that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>, and was ceded by those two states to the United States of America, and by them established to be the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> after the year 1800. It is divided into squares <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> divisions, by streets running due north and south, and east and west, which form the ground-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. However, from the Capitol, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and some of the important areas in the city, run diagonal streets, from one material object to another, which not only produce a variety of charming prospects, but remove the insipid sameness which renders some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cities unpleasing. The great leading streets are all 160 feet wide, including a pavement of 10 feet, and a gravel walk of 30 feet planted with trees on each side, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> leave 80 feet of paved street for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. The rest of the streets are in general... Washington, general 110 feet wide, with a few only 90 feet, except North, South, and East Capitol Streets, which are 160 feet. The diagonal streets are named after the respective states composing the Union, while those running north and south are, from the Capitol eastward, named East First Street, East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Street, &c., and those west of it are in the same manner called West First Street, West Second Street, &c. Those running east and west are from the Capitol northward named North A Street, North B Street, &c., and those south of it are called South A Street, South B Street, &c. The squares or divisions of the city amount to 1150. The rectangular squares generally contain from three to six acres, and are divided into lots of from 40 to 80 feet in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and their depth from about 110 to 300 feet, according to the size of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> divisions produced by the diagonal streets are some of them small, but generally in valuable situations. Their acute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> are all to be cut off at 40 feet, so that no house in the city will have an acute corner. All the houses must be of brick or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> for the Capitol (or house for the legislative bodies) is situated upon the most beautiful eminence in the city, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the Eastern Branch, and not much more from the Potomac, commanding a full view of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city, as well as a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> around. The president's house will stand upon a rising ground, not far from the banks of the Potomac, presenting a delightful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> prospect, with a commanding view of the Capitol, and some other material parts of the city. The city being situated upon the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, exactly equidistant from the northern and southern extremities of the Union, and nearly so from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> to the river Ohio, upon the best <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and in the midst of the richest commercial territory in America, commanding the most extensive internal resources, is by far the most eligible situation for the residence of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a>; and it is now pressing forward, by the public-spirited enterprise, not only of the people of the United States, but also of foreigners. Washington, George, the celebrated commander of the American <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and the first president of the United States, after their separation from the mother-country, was born in the year 1732, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Washington in Virginia. He was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in Cheshire, of which a branch was established in Virginia about the middle of the 17th century. Little is known concerning his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, or the early years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Before he was 20 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was appointed a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> in the colonial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, and had then an opportunity of displaying those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> talents which have since rendered his name so famous throughout the world. In the disputes which arose between the French and English officers, about settling the limits of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUISIANA">Louisiana</a>, Major Washington was employed by the governor of Virginia as a negociator, and he succeeded in preventing a threatened invasion of the English frontiers by the French and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> allies; but, in the following year, when hostilities seemed inevitable, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>, and soon after to the command of a regiment raised by the colony for its own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. In 1755, Colonel Washington served as a volunteer in the unfortunate expedition of General Braddock, and in that expedition, which was attended with great difficulty, he exhibited so much calmness and intrepidity, that the utmost confidence was reposed in his talents, and perfect obedience paid to his commands by the whole army. After having been employed in a different and more successful expedition to the river Ohio, the state of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> required him, about the year 1758, to resign his military situation; and in the fifteen following years, during which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he married Mrs Custis, a Virginian lady, of amiable character and respectable connections, it would appear that he resided chiefly at his beautiful seat of Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a>, and was occupied in the cultivation of his estate. When the disaffection of the Americans to the British government had become pretty general, and had at last spread to the colony of Virginia, Colonel Washington was appointed a delegate from that state to the congress which met at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a> on the 26th October 1774, and soon after he was appointed to the command of the American army, which had assembled in the provinces of New England. The conduct of Washington during the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, as well as during the period that he presided in the government of the United States, has been fully detailed in another part of this work, that it would be unnecessary repetition, even to give a general outline of it in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. See AMERICA. Washington resigned the presidency in 1796, after having published a farewell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to his countrymen. This address was remarkably distinguished for the simplicity and ingenuousness, moderation and sobriety, the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and honesty, as well as sincere affection for his country and for mankind, which the author of it had always exhibited; it seemed to be a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of his whole life. From the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his resignation till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1798, he lived in retirement at his seat of Mount Vernon. At this period, when the unprincipled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> in the French revolution were carrying on their wicked machinations in every part of the world to which their influence extended, the United States resolved to arm by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in their own defense. General Washington was called from his retirement, and the command of the army was bestowed upon him. This he accepted, because he considered, as he himself expressed it, "every thing we hold dear and sacred was seriously threatened, although he had flattered himself that he had quitted for ever the boundless field of public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, incessant trouble, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> responsibility, in which he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> acted so conspicuous a part." In this situation he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> during the remaining short period of his life. On Thursday the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1799, he was seized with an inflammation in the throat, and was carried off Saturday the 14th of the same month, in the 68th year of his age. In his dying moments he displayed the same calmness, simplicity, and regularity, which had uniformly marked his conduct through life. He <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the approaches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> without fear; and he met them without parade. Even the perfectly well ordered state of the minutest particulars of his private business bear the stamp of that constant authority of prudence and practical reason over his actions which was always the most prominent feature of his character. Washington is the name of many counties, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and villages in the American states; a circumstance which affords a striking <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> in what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of esteem and veneration the name from which they are derived was held by the inhabitants of the new world. WASP. See Vespa, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WATCH

Pages 322-331

is also used for a small portable movement, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> machine, for the measuring of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; having its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> regulated by a spiral <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Watches, strictly taken, are all such movements as show the parts of time; as clocks are such as publish it, by striking on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, &c. But <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the name watch is appropriated to such as are carried in the pocket; and clock to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> movements, whether they strike the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> or not. See CLOCK. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of spring or pocket-watches belongs to the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. It is true, we find mention made of a watch presented to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>: but this, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, was no more than a kind of clock to be set on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, some resemblance whereof we have still remaining in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> pieces made before the year 1670. There was also a story of a watch having been discovered in Scotland belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Robert Bruce; but this we believe has turned out altogether apocryphal. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of this very useful invention lies between Dr Hooke and M. Huyghens; but to which of them it properly belongs, has been greatly disputed; the English ascribing it to the former, and the French, Dutch, &c. to the latter. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>, in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Clockmaker, says roundly, that Dr Hooke was the inventor; and adds, that he contrived various ways of regulation. One way was with a loadstone: another with a tender straight spring, one end whereof played backwards and forwards with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>; so that the balance was to the spring as the bob to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a>, and the spring as the rod thereof: A third method was with two balances, of which there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> forts; some having a spiral spring to the balance for a regulator, and others without. But the way that prevailed, and which continues in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, was with one balance, and one spring running round the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the verge thereof: Though this has a disadvantage, which those with two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, &c. were free from; in that a sudden jerk, or confused shake, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> alter its vibrations, and put it in an unusual hurry. The time of these inventions was about the year 1658; as appears, among other evidences, from an inscription on one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> balance watches presented to King Charles II. viz. Rob. Hooke inven. 1658. T. Tompion fecit, 1675. The invention presently got into reputation, both at home and abroad; and two of them were sent for by the dauphin of France. Soon after this, M. Huygens's watch with a spiral spring got abroad, and made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> noise in England, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> could be found by it. It is certain, however, that his invention was later than the year 1673, when his book de Horol. O'Gillat. was published; wherein he has not one word of this, though he has of several other contrivances in the same way. One of these the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Brouncker sent for out of France, where M. Huygens had got a patent for them. This watch agreed with Dr Hooke's in the application of the spring to the balance; only M. Huygens's had a longer spiral spring, and the pulses and beats were much slower. The balance, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> quite round, as Dr Hooke's, turns several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> every vibration. Mr Derham suggests, that he has reason to doubt M. Huygens's fancy first was set to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> by some intelligence he might have of Dr Hooke's invention from Mr Oldenburgh, or some other of his correspondents in England; and this, notwithstanding Mr Oldenburgh's attempt to vindicate himself in the Philosophical Transactions, appears to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Huygens invented divers other kinds of watches, some of them without any string or chain at all; which he called, particularly, pendulum watches. Striking WATCHES are such as, besides the proper watch-part for measuring of time, have a clock-part for striking the hours, &c. Repeating WATCHES, are such as by pulling a string, &c. repeat the hour, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, or minute, at any time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or night.—This repetition was the invention of Mr Barlow, and first put in practice by him in larger movements or clocks about the year 1676. The contrivance immediately let the other artists to work, who soon contrived divers ways of effecting the same. But its application to pocket-watches was not known before King James II.'s reign; when the ingenious inventor above mentioned, having directed Mr Thompson to make a repeating watch, was soliciting a patent for the same. The talk of a patent engaged Mr Quare to resume the thoughts of a like contrivance, which he had had in view some years before: he now effected it; and being preffed to endeavour to prevent Mr Barlow's patent, a watch of each kind was produced before the king and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of which, the preference was given to Mr Quare's. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them was, that Barlow's was made to repeat by pushing in two pieces on each side the watch-box; one of which repeated the hour, and the other the quarter; whereas Quare's was made to repeat by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> that stuck out near the pendant, which being thrust in (as now Watch. now it is done by thrusting in the pendant itself), repeated both the hour and quarter with the same thrust. Of the Mechanism of a Watch, properly so called. Watches, as well as clocks, are composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> and pinions, and a regulator to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the quickness or slowness of the wheels, and of a spring which communicates motion to the whole machine. But the regulator and spring of a watch are vastly inferior to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and pendulum of a clock, neither of which can be employed in watches. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a pendulum, therefore, we are obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a balance (fig. 1.) to regulate the motion of a watch; and a spring (fig. 2.) which serves in place of a weight, to give motion to the wheels and balance. The wheels of a watch, like those of a clock, are placed in a frame formed of two plates and four pillars. Fig. 3. represents the inside of a watch, after the plate (fig. 4.) is taken off. A is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> which contains the spring (fig. 2.); the chain is rolled about the barrel, with one end of it fixed to the barrel A (fig. 5.), and the other to the fusee B. When a watch is wound up, the chain which was upon the barrel winds about the fusee; and by this means the spring is stretched; for the interior end of the spring is fixed by a hook to the immovable axis, about which the barrel revolves; the exterior end of the spring is fixed to the inside of the barrel, which turns upon an axis. It is therefore easy to perceive how the spring extends itself, and how its elasticity forces the barrel to turn round, and consequently obliges the chain which is upon the fusee to unfold and turn the fusee; the motion of the fusee is communicated to the wheel C (fig. 5.); then, by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> c, which carries the wheel D; then to the pinion d, which carries the wheel E; then to the pinion e, which carries the wheel F; then to the pinion f, upon which is the balance-wheel G, whose pivot runs in the pieces A called the potance, and B called a follower, which are fixed on the plate fig. 4. This plate, of which only a part is represented, is applied to that of fig. 3. in such a manner that the pivots of the wheels enter into holes made in the plate fig. 3. Thus the impressed force of the spring is communicated to the wheels; and the pinion f being then connected to the wheel F, obliges it to turn (fig. 5.). This wheel acts upon the palettes of the verge, 1, 2, (fig. 1.), the axis of which carries the balance HH, (fig. 1.). The pivot I, in the end of the verge, enters into the hole c in the potance A (fig. 4.). In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> the palettes are represented; but the balance is on the other side of the plate, as may be seen in fig. 6. The pivot 3 of the balance enters into a hole of the cock BC (fig. 7.), a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> view of which is represented in fig. 8. Thus the balance turns between the cock and the potance c (fig. 4.), as in a kind of cage. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the balance-wheel upon the palettes 1, 2 (fig. 1.), is the same with what we have described with regard to the same wheel in the clock; i.e., in a watch, the balance-wheel obliges the balance to vibrate backwards and forwards like a pendulum. At each vibration of the balance a palette allows a tooth of the balance-wheel to escape; so that the quickness of the motion of the wheels is entirely determined by the quickness of the vibrations of the balance; and these vibrations of the balance and motion of the wheels are produced by the action of the spring. But the quickness or slowness of the vibrations of the balance depend not solely upon the action of the great Watch. spring, but chiefly upon the action of the spring a, b, c, called the spiral spring (fig. 9.), situated under the ba-Fig. 9. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> H, and represented in perspective (fig. 6.). The exterior end of the spiral is fixed to the pin a, (fig. 9.) This pin is applied near the plate in a, (fig. 6.); the interior end of the spiral is fixed by a peg to the centre of the balance. Hence if the balance is turned upon itself, the plates remaining immovable, the spring will extend itself, and make the balance perform one revolution. Now, after the spiral is thus extended, if the balance be left to itself, the elasticity of the spiral will bring back the balance, and in this manner the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> vibrations of the balance are produced. In fig. 5. all the wheels above described are represented in such a manner, that you may easily perceive at first sight how the motion is communicated from the barrel to the balance. In fig. 10. are represented the wheels under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>-Fig. 10. plate by which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> are moved. The pinion a is adjusted to the force of the prolonged pivot of the wheel D (fig. 5.), and is called a cannon pinion. This wheel revolves in an hour. The end of the axle of the pinion a, upon which the minute-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is fixed, is <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; the pinion (fig. 10.) is indented into the wheel b, which is carried by the pinion a. Fig. 11. is a wheel fixed upon Fig. 11. a barrel, into the cavity of which the pinion a enters, and upon which it turns freely. This wheel revolves in 12 hours, and carries along with it the hour-hand. For a full account of the principles upon which watches and all time-keepers are constructed, we must refer our readers to a short treatise, entitled Thoughts on the Means of improving Watcher, by Thomas Mudge. WATCH-Glass, in a ship, are glasses employed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the watch, or to divide it into any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of equal parts, as hours, half-hours, &c. so that the several stations therein may be regularly kept and relieved, as at the helm, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, look-out, &c. WATCH-Work. There is one part of the movements of clocks and watches of which we have yet given no particular account. This is the method of applying the maintaining power of the wheels to the regulator of the motions, so as not to injure its power of regulation. This part of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> is called SCAPEMENT, and falls to be described under the present article, to which we have referred from SCAPEMENT. The motions of a clock or watch are regulated by a Objects of pendulum or balance, without which check the wheels' escapements impelled by the weight in the clock, or spring in the watch, would run round with a rapidly accelerating motion, till this should be rendered uniform by friction, and the resistance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. If, however, a pendulum or balance be put in the way of this motion, in such a manner that only one tooth of a wheel can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, the revolution of the wheels will depend on the vibration of the pendulum or balance. We cannot here enter on an historical account of the improvements that have been made on the regulating powers of clocks and watches, nor can we detail the principles on which their action depends. It will be sufficient here to notice the most simple construction of escapements, and then to describe two or three of the most improved constructions that have been applied to time-keepers. We know that the motion of a pendulum or balance is alternate, while the pressure of the wheels is constantly exerted in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Hence it is evident that some means must be employed to accommodate these different motions to each other. Now, when a tooth of the wheel has given the pendulum or balance a motion in one direction, it must quit it, that the pendulum or balance may receive an impulsion in the opposite direction. This escape of the tooth has given rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> escapement. The ordinary escapement is extremely simple, and may be thus illustrated. Let \( x y \) fig. 12. Plate DLXXI. represent a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> axis, to which the pendulum \( p \) is attached by a slender rod. This axis has two leaves \( c \) and \( d \), one near each end, and not in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, but so that when the pendulum hangs perpendicularly at rest, \( c \) spreads a few degrees to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and \( d \) as much to the left. These are called the pallets. Let \( a f b \) represent a wheel, turning on a perpendicular axis \( e o \) in the order \( a f e b \). The teeth of this wheel are in the form of those of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, leaning forward in the direction of the rim's motion. This wheel is usually called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-wheel, or in watches the balance-wheel. See CLOCK and WATCH. It generally contains an odd number of teeth. In the figure the pendulum is represented at the extremity of its excursion towards the right, the tooth \( a \) having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> escaped from the pallet \( c \), and \( b \) having just dropped on \( d \). Now it is evident that while the pendulum is moving to the left, in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> \( p g \), the tooth \( b \) still presses on the pallet \( d \); and thus accelerates the pendulum, both in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> along \( p h \), and its ascent up \( h g \), and that when \( d \), by turning round the axis \( x y \), raises its point above the plane of the wheel, the tooth \( b \) escapes from it, and \( i \) drops on \( c \), now nearly perpendicular. Thus \( c \) is pressed to the right, and the motion of the pendulum along \( g p \) is accelerated. Again, while the pendulum hangs perpendicularly in the line \( x h \), the tooth \( b \), by pressing on \( d \), will force the pendulum to the left, in proportion to its lightness, and if it be not too heavy, will force it so far from the perpendicular, that \( b \) will escape, and \( i \) will catch on \( c \), and force the pendulum back to \( p \), when the same motion will be repeated. This effect will be more remarkable, if the rod of the pendulum be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> through \( x y \), and have a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> \( q \) on the other end, to balance \( p \). When \( b \) escapes from \( d \), the balls are moving with a certain velocity and momentum, and in this condition the balance is checked when \( i \) catches on \( c \). It is not, however, instantly stopped, but continues to move a little to the left, and \( i \) is forced a little backward by the pallet \( c \). It cannot make its escape over the top of the tooth \( i \), as all the momentum of the balance was <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the force of \( b \), and \( i \) is of equal power. Besides, when \( i \) catches on \( c \), and the motion of \( c \) to the left continues, the lower point of \( c \) is applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of \( i \), which now acts on the balance by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, soon stops its motion in that direction, and continuing to press on \( c \), urges the balance in the opposite direction. It is easy to see that the motion of the wheel here must be hobbling and unequal, which has given to this escapement the name of the recoiling escapement. In considering the utility of the following improved escapement for clocks, we must keep in mind the following proposition, which, after the above illustration, scarcely requires any direct <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. It is, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> vibrations of a pendulum are isochronous, or are performed in equal times. The great object of the escapement is to preserve this isochronous motion of the pendulum. As the defect of the recoiling escapement was long apparent, several ingenious artists attempted to substitute Cumming's in its place a escapement that should produce a more regular and uniform motion. Of these, the escapement contrived by Mr Cumming appears to be one of the most ingenious in its construction, and most perfect in its operation. The following construction is similar to that of Mr Cumming but rendered rather less complex for the purpose of shortening the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Let \( A B C \), fig. 13, represent a portion of the swing wheel, of which \( O \) is the centre, and \( A \) one of the teeth; \( Z \) is the centre of the crutch, pallets, and pendulum. The crutch is represented of the form of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> \( A \), having in the circular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> piece a slit \( k \), also circular, \( Z \) being the centre. The arm \( Z F \) forms the first detent, and the tooth \( A \) is represented as locked on it at \( F \). \( D \) is the first pallet on the end of the arm \( Z d \), moveable round the same centre with the detents, but independent of them. The arm \( d e \) to which the pallet \( D \) is attached, lies wholly behind the arm \( Z F \) of the detent, being fixed to a round piece of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> \( e f g \), having pivots turning concentric with the axis of the pendulum. To the same piece of brass is fixed the horizontal arm \( e H \), carrying at its extremity the ball \( H \), of such size, that the action of the tooth \( A \) on the pallet \( D \) is just able to raise it up to the position here drawn. \( Z P p \) represents the fork, or pendulum rod, behind both detent and pallet. A pin \( p \) projects forward, coming through the slit \( k \), without touching either margin of it. Attached to the fork is the arm \( m n \), of such length that, when the pendulum rod is perpendicular, the angular distance of \( n g \) from the rod \( e q H \) is just equal to the angular distance of the left side of the pin \( p \) from the left end \( i \) of the slit \( k \). Now, the natural position of the pallet \( D \) is at \( 8 \), represented by the dotted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, resting on the back of the detent \( F \). It is naturally brought into this position by its own weight, and still more by the weight of the ball \( H \). The pallet \( D \), being set on the foreside of the arm at \( Z \), comes into the same plane with the detent \( F \) and the swing-wheel, though here represented in a different position. The tooth \( C \) of the wheel is supposed to have escaped from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> pallet, on which the tooth \( A \) immediately seizes the pallet \( D \), situated at \( 8 \), forces it out, and then rests on the detent \( F \), the pallet \( D \) leaning on the tip of the tooth. After the escape of \( C \), the pendulum, moving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the arch of semivibration, is represented as having attained the vertical position. Proceeding still to the left, the pin \( p \) reaches the extremity \( i \) of the slit \( k \); and, at the same instant, the arm \( n \) touches the rod \( e H \) in \( g \). The pendulum proceeding a hairsbreadth further, withdraws the detent \( F \) from the tooth, which now even pushes off the detent, by acting on the inclining face of it. The wheel being now unlocked, the tooth following \( C \) on the other side acts on its pallet, pushes it off, and rests on its detent, which has been rapidly brought into a proper position by the action of \( A \) on the inclining face of \( F \). By a similar action of \( C \) on its detent at the moment of escape, \( F \) was brought into a position proper for the wheels being locked by the tooth \( A \). As the pendulum still goes on, the ball \( H \), and pallet connected with it, are carried by the arm \( m n \), and before the pin \( p \) again reaches the end... end of the slit, which had been suddenly withdrawn by the action of A on F, the pendulum comes to rest. It now returns towards the right, loaded with the ball H on the left, and thus the motion lost during the last vi- bration is restored. When the pin p, by its motion to the right, reaches the end k of t k, the wheel on the right side is unlocked, and at the same instant the weight H being raised from the pendulum by the action of a tooth like B on the pallet D, ceases to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. In this escapement, both pallets and detents are de- tached from the pendulum, except in the moment of un- locking the wheel, so that, except during this short in- terval, the pendulum may be said to be free during its whole vibration, and of course its motion must be more equable and undisturbed. The constructing of a proper escapement for watches requires peculiar delicacy, owing to the small size of the machine, from which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of \( \frac{1}{360} \) of an inch has as much effect as the error of a whole inch in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> clock. From the necessary lightness of the balance, too, it is extremely difficult to accumulate a sufficient quan- tity of regulating power. This can be done only by giving the balance a great velocity, which is effected by concentrating as much as possible of its weight in the rim, and making its vibrations very wide. The balance rim of a tolerable watch should pass through at least ten inches in every second. In considering the most proper escapements for watches, we may assume the following principle, viz., that the o- scillations of a balance urged by its spring, and undisturbed by extraneous forces, are isochronous. In ordinary pocket watches, the common recoil- ing escapement of clocks is still employed, and answers the common purposes of a watch tolerably well, so that, if properly executed, a good ordinary watch will keep time within a minute in the day. These watches, however, are subject to great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in their rate of going, from any change in the power of the wheels. The following is considered as the best construction of the common watch escapement, and is represented by fig. 14, as it appears when looking straight down on the end of the balance arbor. C marks the centre of the balance and verge; CA represents the upper pallet, or that next the balance, and CB the lower pallet; F and D are two teeth of the crown wheel, moving from left to right; E, G, are two teeth in the lower part, moving from right to left. The tooth D appears as having just escaped from the point of C A, and the tooth E as having just come in contact with CB. In practice, the escapement should not be quite so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, as by a small in- equality of the teeth, D might be kept from escaping at all. The following are thought the best proportions: The distance between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the teeth (that is, of G, F, E, D), and the axis C of the balance, is \( \frac{1}{3} \) of F A, the distance between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the teeth. The length CA, CB of the pallets is \( \frac{1}{3} \) of the same degrees, and the front DH or FK of the teeth makes an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of \( 25^\circ \) with the axis of the crown wheel. The sloping side of the tooth must be of an epicycloidal form, fitted to the relative motion of the tooth and pallet. It appears from these proportions, that by the action of the tooth D, the pallet A can throw out till it reach \( 120^\circ \) from CL, the line of the crown-wheel axis. To this if we add BCA = \( 95^\circ \), we shall have LC = \( 125^\circ \). Again, B will throw out as far on the other side. Now, if from \( 240^\circ \) the sum of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of vibration of both pallets, we take \( 95^\circ \) the angle of the pallets, the remainder \( 145^\circ \) will express the greatest vibration which the balance can make, without striking the front of the teeth. From several causes, however, this mea- sure is too great, and \( 120^\circ \) is reckoned a sufficient vibra- tion in the best ordinary escapement. Of the improvements on the escapements of watches, Graham's one of the most important is that by Mr George Graham, which we shall proceed to describe. DE, fig. 15, represents part of the rim of the balance wheel; A and Fig. 15, and C, two of its teeth with their faces b e formed into planes, inclined to the circumference of the wheel in an angle of about \( 15^\circ \), so that the length b e of the face may be nearly quadruple of its height e m. Let a cir- cular arch ABC be described round the centre of the wheel, and through the middle of the faces of the teeth. The axis of the balance will pass through same point B of this arch, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> circumference of the teeth may be said to pass through the centre of the verge. On this axis is fixed a portion of a thin hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> b c d made of hard tempered <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, or of some hard and tough <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUBY">ruby</a> or sapphire. By this construction the portion of the cylinder occupies \( 210^\circ \) of the circum- ference. The edge b, to which the tooth approaches from without, is rounded off on both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. The other edge d is formed into a plane, inclined to the ra- dius about \( 30^\circ \). Now, suppose the wheel pressed for- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> in the direction AC, the point b of the tooth, touching the rounded edge, will push it outwards, turn- ing round the balance in the direction b c d. The heel e of the tooth will escape from this edge when it is in the position h, and e is in the position f. The point b of the tooth will now be at d, but the edge of the cy- linder will be at i. The tooth therefore rests in the in- side of the cylinder, while the balance continues its vi- bration a little way, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the impulse it has received from the action of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined plane</a>. When this vibration is ended, by the opposition of the balance spring, the balance will return, and the tooth now in the position B, rubbing on the inside of the cy- linder, the balance comes back into its natural posi- tion b c d, with an accelerated motion by the action of its spring, and would of itself vibrate as far as the other side. It is, however, assisted again by the tooth, which precedes on the edge d, pushes it aside till it attain the posi- tion k, when the tooth entirely escapes from the cylin- der. At this instant the other edge of the cylinder, having attained the position l, is in the way of the next tooth, which is now in the position A, while the balance continues its vibration; the tooth resting and rubbing on the outside of the cylinder. When this vibration is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>- ished, the balance, by the action of the spring, resumes its first motion, and as soon as the balance gets into its na- tural position, the tooth begins to act on the edge b, pushes it aside, escapes from it, and drops as before in the inside of the cylinder. In this construction the arch of action or escapement is \( 30^\circ \) = twice the angle which the face of a tooth makes with the circumference. It is necessary to explain how the cylinder is connect- ed with the verge, so as to make such a great revolution round the tooth of the wheel. The triangular tooth e b m is placed on the top of a little pillar fixed into the end of the piece of brass m D formed in the rim of the wheel. Thus the plane of the wedge tooth is pa- rallel. rallied to the plane of the wheel, but at a small distance above it. The verge is represented at fig. 16, and consists of a long hollow cylinder of hard steel, having a great portion of the metal cut out. If spread out flat, this cylinder would assume the form of fig. 17; and if we conceive this flat piece rolled up till the edges GH and G'H' unite, we shall have the exact form. The part acted on by the point of the tooth is denoted by the dotted line b d, and the part D, I, F, E, serves to connect the two ends. This escapement of Mr Graham is called a horizontal escapement, because the balance is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the other wheels. Another escapement of a superior construction was contrived by M. Lepaute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and is of such a singular form as to render it extremely difficult to illustrate it by a figure. The representations at figs. 18 and 19 will, however, give general readers some idea of its mode of action, and a skilful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> will easily see how the several parts may be adapted to each other. ABC fig. 18 represents part of the rim of the balance wheel, having the pins 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, &c., projecting from its faces; the pins 1, 3, 5, being on the side next the eye, and the pins 2 and 4 on the opposite side. D is the centre of the balance and verge, and the small circle round D represents its thickness. But the verge in this place is crooked, that the rim of the wheel may not be intercepted by it. To it is attached a piece of hard tempered steel a b c d, of which the part a b c is a concave arch of a circle, having D for its centre. It wants about 30° of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>. The rest c d is also an arch of a circle, having the same radius with the balance wheel. In the natural position of the balance, a line drawn from D through the middle of the face c d, is a tangent to the circumference of the wheel. But if the balance be turned round, till the point d of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> come to d', and the point e come to 2, in the circumference in which the pins are placed, the pin prefling on the beginning of the horn or pallet, pushes it aside, slides along it, and escapes at d, having generated a certain velocity in the balance. Let another pallet similar to that now described be placed on the other side of the wheel, but in a contrary position, with the acting face of the pallet turned away from the centre of the wheel. Let it be so placed at E, that the moment the pin 1 on the upper side of the wheel escapes from the pallet c d, the pin 4 on the lower side of the wheel falls on the end of the circular arch e f g of the other pallet. Now, if the pallets be connected by equal pulleys G and F on the axis of each, and a thread round both, so that they shall turn one way; the balance on the axis D, having received an impulse from the pin 1, will continue its motion from A towards i, and will carry the other pallet with a similar motion round the centre E from h to k. The pin 4 will therefore rest in the concave arch g f e as the pallet turns round. When the force of the balance is spent, the pallet c d returns towards its first position. The pallet g h turns with it, and when the point of the first has arrived at d, the beginning p of the other arrives at the pin 4; and proceeding farther, this pin escapes from the concave arch e f g, and slides along the pallet g h, pushing it aside, and of course urging the pallet round the centre E, and the balance on the axis D round at the same time, and in the same direction. The pin 4 escapes from the pallet g h, when h arrives at 3; but while the pin 4 is sliding along the yielding pallet g h, the pin 3 is moving in the circumference BDA; and the instant that the pin 4 escapes from h at 3, the pin 3 arrives at 2, where the beginning c of the concave arch c b is ready, to receive it. It therefore rests on this arch, while the balance continues its motion, and this may continue till the point b of the arch comes to 2. The balance now flops, its force being spent, and then returns; and the pin 3 escapes from the circle at c, slides along the yielding pallet c d, and when it escapes at 1, another pin on the lower side of the wheel arrives at 4, and finds the arch g f e ready to receive it. And thus the vibration of the balance will be continued. From the above description we may deduce the proper dimensions of the parts of the pallet. Thus, the length of the pallet c d or g h, must be equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between two succeeding pins, and the distance of the centres D, E, must be double of that interval. The radius D e or E g, may be as small as we choose. The concave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> c b a and g f e, must be continued so far as to allow a pin to rest on them during the whole excursion of the balance. The angle of escapement, in which the balance remains under the influence of the wheels, is obtained by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the lines D c and D d, and we shall find that this angle c D d is here about 30°, though it may be made either greater or less than this. Fig. 19 explains how the two pallets may be combined on one verge. KL is the verge with a pivot at each end. It is bent like a crank MNO, to admit the balance wheel between its branches. BC represents this wheel, seen edgewise, with its pin alternately on different faces. The pallets are also represented by b c d and h g f, fixed to the inside of the branches of the crank, facing each other. The position of their acting faces may be seen in the preceding figure, on the verge D, where the pallet g h is represented by the dotted line 2 i, as situated behind the pallet c d. The remote pallet 2 i is so placed, that when the point d of the near pallet is quitted by a pin 1 on the upper side of the wheel, the angle formed by the face and the arch of rest of the other pallet is just ready to receive the next pin 2, which lies on the lower side of the rim. It is plain that the action here will be the same as if the pallets were on separate axes. The pin 1 escapes from d, and the pin 2 is received on the arch of rest, and locks the wheel, while the balance continues in motion. When the balance returns, 2 gets off the arch of rest, pushes aside the pallet 2 i, escapes from it when i gets to 1, and then the point c is ready to receive the pin 3, &c. The vibrations may be increased by giving a sufficient impulse through the angle of escapement, but they cannot exceed a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, otherwise N, the top of the crank, would strike the rim of the wheel. The vibrations may be easily increased to 180°, by placing the pins at the very edge of the wheel; and by placing them at the points of long teeth, so that the crank may get in between them, the vibrations may be carried to a much greater extent. The construction just described is exceedingly ingenious; and if the machinery be well executed, this escapement will excel the horizontal escapement of Graham, both as it has but two acting faces to form, and as it admits of making the circle of rest extremely small, without lessening the acting face of the pallet. The construction is, however, very delicate and difficult, and must require a very nice workman. An excellent escapement of much more easy construction, is that commonly called Duplaie's escapement, and with this we shall conclude our account of watch-work. Fig. 20 represents the essential parts somewhat magnified. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">AD</a> is a portion of the balance-wheel, having teeth f, h, g, at the circumference. These teeth are for producing the rep of the wheel, while the balance is making excursions beyond the escapement. This is effected by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> cylinder s p g, on the verge. This cylinder has a notch o. When the cylinder turns round in the direction s p g, the notch easily passes the tooth B which is resting on the cylinder surface; but when it returns in the direction q p o, the tooth B gets into the notch, and follows it, pressing on one side of it till the notch comes into the position o. The tooth being then in the position h, escapes from the notch, and another tooth drops on the convex surface of the cylinder at B. The balance-wheel is also furnished with a set of flat-sided pins, standing upright on its rim represented by a D. There is likewise fixed on the verge a larger cylinder G F C above the smaller one o p q, with its lower surface clear of the wheel, and having a pallet C, of sapphire, firmly indented into it, and projecting so far as to keep clear of the pins on the wheel. The position of this cylinder, with respect to the smaller one below it, is such that the tooth b being escaped from the notch, the pallet C has just past the pin a, which was at A while B rested on the small cylinder; but it moved from A to a, while B moved to b. The wheel being now at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, the pin a exerts its pressure on the pallet C in the most direct manner, and gives it a strong impulsion, following and accelerating it till another tooth stops on the little cylinder. The angle of escapement depends partly on the projection of the pallet, and partly on the diameter of the small cylinder, and the advance of the tooth B into the notch. Independent of the action on the small cylinder, the angle of escapement would be the whole arch of the larger cylinder between C and x. But a stops before it be clear of the pallet, and the arch of impulsion is shortened by all the space described by the pin while a tooth moves from B to b. It stops at d. For an account of other escapements we must refer our readers to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy of Sciences at Paris for 1748, Cumming's Elements of Clock and Watchwork, a French work entitled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">Machines</a> approuvées par l'Académie des Sciences, and Young's Lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">Natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, vol. i. p. 193, and Plate 16, vol. ii. p. 193.

WATCHING

Pages 331-331

in Medicine, is when the patient cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. In fevers it is a dangerous symptom, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> ends in a delirium.

WATER

Pages 331-369

a well known fluid, diffused through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and over the surface of the globe, and abounding in a certain proportion in animals, vegetables, and minerals. The uses of water are so universally known, that it would be superfluous to enumerate them in this article. It is essential to animal and vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; it makes easy the intercourse between the most distant regions of the world; and it is one of the most useful powers in the mechanic arts. It is often found combined with various substances, and is then frequently beneficial in curing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> alleviating diseases. Those properties of water which fit it for answering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> purposes are explained in other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">Work</a> (see <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">Hydrodynamics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PNEUMATICS">Pneumatics</a>, No. 3, Water, Resistance, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>); and for the discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of water, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Mineral Waters. For the method of analysing them, see also Chemistry Index. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Mineral Waters, we have given an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of the most remarkable waters in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Holy Water, which is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, as also by the Greeks, and by the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the East of all denominations, is water with a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, blessed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> according to a set form of benediction. It is used in the blessing of persons, things, and places; and is likewise considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> to excite pious thoughts in the minds of the faithful. The priests, in blessing it, first, in the name of God, commands the devils not to hurt the persons who shall be sprinkled with it, nor to abuse the things, nor disturb the places, which shall likewise be so sprinkled. He then prays that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, safety, and the favour of heaven, may be enjoyed by such persons, and by those who shall use such things, or dwell in such places. Veements, vessels, and other such things that are let apart for divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, are sprinkled with it. It is sometimes sprinkled on cattle, with an intention to free or preserve them from diabolical enchantments; and in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> books there are prayers to be said on such occasions, by which the safety of such animals, as being a temporal blessing to the possessors, is begged of God, whose providential care is extended to all his creatures. The hope which Catholics entertain of obtaining such good effects from the devout use of holy water, is grounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> by Christ (St Mark xvi. 17), and on the general efficacy of the prayers of the church; the petition of which prayers God is often pleased to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>; though sometimes, in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, he sees it not expedient to do so. That such effects have been produced by holy water in a remarkable manner, has been asserted by many authors of no small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; as, namely, by St Epiphanius, Haer. 30th; St Hieron., in the Life of St Hilarion; Theodorest Hist. Eccl. lib. v. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 21.; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLADIUS">Palladius</a>, Hist. Lauf.; Bede, lib. v. cap. 4. As a ceremony (says the Catholic), water brings to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>; in which, by water, we were cleansed from original sin. It also puts us in mind of that purity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> which we ought to endeavour always to have, but especially when we are going to worship our God.
