The accidental waves are those occasioned by the wind's reaching upon itself by repercussion from hills and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> shores, and by the washing of the waves themselves, otherwise of the natural kind, against rocks and shoals: all these causes give the waves an elevation, which they can never have in their natural state. For the height of the waves, see Sea.

WAY

Pages 371-372

a passage <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>. The Roman ways are divided into consular, praetorian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, and public; and of these we have four remarkable ones in England: the first, Watling-street, or Watling-street, leading from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUNSTABLE">Dunstable</a>, Towcester, Atterton, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, extending as far as Anglesea in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, called Hikenild or Ikenild street, stretches from Southampton over the river Isis at Newbridge; thence by Camden and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>; then passes the Derwent near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, and ends at Tinmouth. The third, called Fosse-way, because in some places it was never perfected, but lies as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ditch, leads from Cornwall through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, by Tethbury, near Stow in the Wolds; and beside <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, Newark, and so to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>. The fourth, called Ermine or Erminage street, extends from St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, in Wales, to Southampton. WAX <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">Covert</a>, Gang, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCH">Hatch</a>. See COVERT Way, GANG, &c. Way of a Ship, is sometimes the same as her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a>, or run forward or backward: but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> understood of her sailing. WAY-Leaver, in the coal business. See COALERY, No. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">Rights</a> of WAYS, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. This may be grounded on a special permission; as when the owner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> grants to another a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of passing over his grounds, to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, to market, or the like: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the gift or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> is particular, and confined to the grantee alone; it dies with the person; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the grantee leaves the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he cannot assign over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to any other; nor can he justify taking another person in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. A way may be also by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>; as if all the owners and occupiers of such a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> have immemorially used to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> another's ground; for this immemorial usage supposes an original grant, whereby a right of way thus appurtenant to land may clearly be created. A right of way may also arise by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> and operation of law; for if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> grants me a piece of ground in the middle of his field, he at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> tacitly and impliedly gives me a way to come at it; and I may cross his land for that purpose without trespass. For when the law doth give any thing to one, it giveth impliedly whatsoever is necessary for enjoying the same. By the law of the twelve tables at Rome, where a man had the right of way over another's land, and the road was out of repair, he who had the right of way might go over any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the land he pleased; which was the established rule in public as well as private ways. And the law of England, in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, seems to correspond with the Roman. WAYFARING TREE. See Viburnum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WAYGHITES

Pages 372-372
or WAITS, a word which is used only in the plural number, and signifies hautboys. It is now applied to the performers on these and other musical instruments, by a transition from the instruments themselves, and particularly to those performers who parade the streets by night, about the Christmas season of the year.

WAYWODE

Pages 372-372

is properly a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given the governors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> places in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> of Muscovy. The palatines, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governors of provinces in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, also bear the title of waywodes or wawodes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> likewise call the princes of Wallachia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a> waywodes; as esteeming them no other than on the foot of governors; pretending that Wallachia and Moldavia are provinces of Poland. Everywhere else these are called hospodars. Du Cange says, that the name waywode is used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, Croatia, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, for a general of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>: and Leunclavius, in his Pandects of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, tells us, it usually signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> or commander.

WEANING

Pages 372-372

putting a child away from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and bringing it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> food.

WEARING

Pages 372-372
or VEERING, in Seamanship. See Seamanship. WEASEL. See Mustela, Mammalia Index.

WEATHER

Pages 372-372

R denotes the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and other meteors. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a>. Weather, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is used as an adjective, and applied by mariners to every thing lying to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> of a particular situation: thus, a ship is said to have the weather-gage of another, when she is farther to windward. Thus also, when a ship under sail prefers either of her sides to the wind, it is then called the weather-side <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> weather-board; and all the rigging and furniture situated thereon are distinguished by the same epithet, as the weather-sprouts, the weather-lifts, the weather-braces, &c. To WEATHER, in sea-language, is to fail to windward of some ship, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, or head-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>.

WEATHER-COCK

Pages 372-372

a moveable vane, in form of a cock, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other shape, placed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, to be turned round according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and point out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from whence it blows. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">WEATHER</a> GLASS. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">Barometer</a>.

WEATHERING

Pages 372-372

among sailors, signifies the doubling <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> failing by a head-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

WEAVING

Pages 372-372

the art of working a web of cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other stuff, in a loom with a shuttle. For an idea of the manner in which this is performed, see Weaving Cloth.

WEAVING-LOOM

Pages 372-374

a machine for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, &c. by raising the threads of the warp in order to throw in the heddle, and strike it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. Of these there are various kinds, distinguished by the different sorts of cloths, stuffs, silks, &c., in which they are employed, and which are chiefly distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and variety of the threads they raise in order to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> the warp, either plain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in figures, by making more or less of the woof or thread appear through the warp. In order to DLXXXV, give a general idea of weaving, we shall here describe the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> weaver's loom. Fig. 1, in which e, e' are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> posts, and g, g' the back posts of the loom; l, l', m, m' are the lamms in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at O, or, as they are called in some parts of Scotland, the headles, and in others the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. They are composed of strong threads, stretched between two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> bars, an upper and a lower. The threads of one lam are so disposed as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between the upper threads of the warp, while they admit the lower threads to pass through loops or small holes in them, and the disposition of the threads of the other lam is such, that while they pass between the lower threads of the warp, they admit the upper threads to pass through the small holes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned. The lamms are suspended from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> or lam-bearer HH, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> n, n' passing from the upper bars of the lamms over the pulleys at EE, and balanced by weights at the other ends. From the lower bar of each lam or headle a rope passes to the treadles or moveable bars at OO; so that when a foot presses a treadle, the lam fastened to it sinks, while the other rises by means of the balancing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> suspended from the pulley at E. The workman then throws in the woof by means of the shuttle, and closes it by one or two strokes of the lay or batten, of which WB, WB are called the swords, CC the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, or in Scotland the upper shell, DD the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> or under shell, and PP the reed or comb contained between these shells. LL is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> on which the workmen sit; for the loom which our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> represents is constructed for weaving cloth of such a breadth as to require two workmen, who have their quills in a box d on the middle of the bench on which they sit. Between the workmen's bench and the batten or lay is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>-bar I, I, a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> beam, in which there is an opening to let the web through as it is woven. From this opening the web SS passes to the knee roll or web beam GG, round which it is rolled by means of the spokes, visible in the figure, and kept from being unrolled by a wheel with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> and clench, visible likewise in the figure. In some looms the web passes from the knee roll to the wooden frame X, to be dried as it is woven. Opposite to the breast-bar, and on the other side of the batten or lay, is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>-roll or yarn-beam, on which the warp is rolled when put into the loom, and from which it is gradually unrolled as the work proceeds. TT are bobbins filled with yarn of the warp to mend such threads of it as may be broke in the weaving; and Bb, Bb are clues of the same kind of yarn with the borders of the warp, to mend such threads as may there be broken. Fig. 2 represents the common shuttle with the variability in the middle, in which the quill with the woof is placed on a spindle or axis. As this shuttle is thrown with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in at one side of the warp, and received with Weaving, with the other hand at the other side, it is obvious, that when the web is of a breadth too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to reach from one side of it to the other, two workmen must be employed and much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> lost. To remedy this inconvenience, a new shuttle has, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, been lately brought into very general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and called the fig- Fig. 3. ing shuttle, because it flies through the warp with wonderful rapidity on two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> rollers RR (fig. 3.) This shuttle is not thrown with the hand, but moved backwards and forwards by a very simple piece of machinery, of which fig. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> give the reader a sufficiently accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>. To each end of the batten or lay L is fastened a kind of open box B, b, with the bottom or horizontal side exactly on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the threads of the warp of the intended web. In each of these boxes is a vertical piece of wood D, d, of considerable thickness, called a driver. This driver is moved easily on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> spindle or axis from one end of the box to the other by means of a slender rope CCCD, and a handle H is seen in the figure. When the weaver is to begin his work, he lays the shuttle on its rollers in the box B with the iron tip T (fig. 3.) touching, or almost touching, the driver D (fig. 4.). Then moving the handle H, with a sudden jerk, towards the box b, the driver D forces the shuttle with a rapid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> through the warp till it strikes d, which is impelled by the stroke to the further end of the box b. The two drivers D and d have now changed their positions in their respective boxes; so that the driver which was at the front of its box before, is now at the further end of it, and vice versa. Then by a sudden jerk of the hand towards B the shuttle is driven back till it strike D; and thus is the work <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> without the weaver having occasion ever to stretch his arms from one margin of the web to the other. That the shuttle may not, by the unsteadiness of the workman's hand, be driven zig-zag through the warp or out of the place in which it ought to move, the guiding or driving rope CCCD is made to pass through smooth holes or loops C, C, at the ends of the ropes EC, EC, suspended either from the cross bar on the top of the loom or from the treads of the batten. This shuttle, we should think, a great improvement in every kind of weaving loom, though some of the older tradesmen, with whom we have conversed on the subject, contend, that it is valuable only in what they call <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> work, such as cotton or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, or when the web, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> woollen, is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. But as the labour of weaving is pretty severe, Mr Robert Millar, an ingenious calico-printer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>, Scotland, wishing to lessen it, invented, some years ago, a weaving-loom, which may be wrought by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>, horses, or any other power, for which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> he received a patent in 1796. The following is his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of his patent weaving-loom: Fig. 5. represents a side view of the loom, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a>, BB; CC, DD, being the frame. a is an axis (which we shall call the spindle) across the frame. On this axis is a sleeve b, two inches thick, having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> round it, two inches deep, and half an inch wide. The bottom of this groove is circular, except in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> c, where it is filled up to the top; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> d rests on the bottom of this groove, and is lifted up by it when the elevation e comes round to the situation represented in the figure. By this motion, the lever d acts on the ratchet-wheel e, by the catch f, and draws it forward one tooth, each revolution of the sleeve. This ratchet-wheel is in an iron frame gg, which also properly carries the two catches g and h, which are connected with it at v. The catch u holds the ratchet-wheel in its position, while the lever d and the catch f are moved by the groove c in the sleeve. On the arbor of the ratchet is a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> h, working in the wheel f; this wheel is fixed on the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a> e of fig. 7. On the side of the sleeve b is fixed a wiper k, which lifts the treadle l. This treadle turns on its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> in the sleeve E, which is fixed to the side of the frame A and D; it is kept pressing on the bottom of the groove in the sleeve by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> m, fixed to the frame side A, and having a slender rod n from its extremity, joining it with the treadle at l. From the point of the treadle there goes a belt o, which passes over the pulley p, which is seen edgeways in this figure, and is joined to the top of the fly <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> q, of fig. 6. At the end of the frame A is the short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> F; on this rests the yarn-beam j, having a sleeve r, over which passes a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, having a weight s suspended to it. The other end of this cord is fastened to the spring u; the weight causes the yarn-beam to stretch the web from the ratchet-wheel e, with its catch u; and the spring v allows the rope to slide on the sleeve as the ratchet is drawn round during the working. Fig. 6. is a front view of the loom. a a is the spindle which carries the sleeve b, and the wipers d and d', which move the treadles w, w, of fig. 5. These use the treadles of the headles, with which they are connected by cords from the shafts of the headles a, s. From the upper shaft there go two leathern belts f, f, to the roller y, furnished each with a buckle, for tightening them at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The two wipers c, c, on the shaft a, which serve for taking back the lay, have the two treadles x, x, in fig. 7, with a belt from each passing over the roller h 2 of fig. 6, and fixed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of the lay. From the swords of the lay forward is fixed a belt to each end of the roller i; from this roller there goes a cord to the spring j, which serves for taking forward the lay which is hinged on the rocking-tree t. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>-wheel b of fig. 3, and the sleeve b of fig. 1, are fixed to the opposite ends of the spindle a without the frame; and both the wheel and sleeve have a wiper k fixed to them for moving the treadles. In order to drive the shuttle, the belts o, o, go from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the treadles, over the pulleys p, p, to the top of the fly-pin q: This turns on a pin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> in a rail r, which goes across the loom. From its lower end there go two small cords to the shuttle drivers g, g, which slide on the iron rods n, n. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> iron rod v goes across the lay, and is hung on two centres at the ends. In this rod v are fixed two small crooked wires w, w, which are more distinctly marked in the little figure w above, which represents a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the lay. The dot at the lower end of the wire w, in this figure, is the section of the rod v. The shuttle passes between these wires and the lay every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, and lifts them up, causing the rod v to turn round a little. But if the shuttle should not pass these wires, nor lift them, it would be drawn home by the lay, and destroy the web. To prevent this, there is fixed on one end of the rod v a stout crooked wire z, having a broad or flat head, which naturally rests on a plate of iron, marked and fixed to the back of the lay. This plate has a slit in its Weaving, its middle about an inch deep. In this slit rests the rod \(a\) of fig. 7, on which is a short stud, which is caught by the wire \(w\) when the wire \(w\) is not lifted back by the passing shuttle. This will stop the lay from coming home, and will set off the loom. Fig. 7. is another side view of the loom opposite to fig. 5. On the spindle \(a\) is the star wheel \(b\), on the outside of the loom-frame, on the arms of which wheel is fixed the wiper \(k\), as the similar wiper is fixed to the sleeves on the other end of the spindle. The wipers which drive the shuttles are fixed on opposite squares of the spindle, and work alternately. Below the star-wheel is a pinion \(c\), which is on a round spindle, turned by the water-wheel, by means of a wheel on this spindle. In a wheel on this spindle are two studs, on which the pinion \(c\) slides off and on, as the loom is set off and on by the lever \(d\). At the farther end of this lever is the weight \(s\), hanging by a cord which passes over a pulley \(i\), fixed at the outer end of the spring-catch on which the lever \(d\) rests; and thus the loom is drawn in at the upper end of the lever \(d\). But when the shuttle does not lift the wire \(x\), it catches on the stud on the rod \(a\), which is connected with the spring-catch, and the lever \(d\) flies off with the weight \(s\), and the loom stops working. On the head of the post \(F\) is the yarn-beam. The rollers \(e\) and \(f\) are cylinders, pressed together by a screw-lever, and take away the cloth between them at a proper rate. In the roller \(f\) is a groove for a band for driving the roller \(g\), on which the cloth winds itself as it is wrought. Wherever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> are mentioned to be used in the above description, weights may be used in their stead, and to the same effect, and more especially upon the treadle of fig. 5, for driving the shuttle. Fig. 8. is a representation of a ribbon loom. 1. Is the frame of the loom. 2. The castle, containing 48 pulleys. 3. The branches, on which the pulleys turn. 4. The tires, or the riding-cords, which run on the pulleys, and pull up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-lifts. 5. The lift-sticks, to which the high-lifts are tied. 6. The high-lifts, or lifts, are a number of long threads, with platines, or plate-leads at the bottom; and ringlets, or loops, about their middle, through which the cords or crofs-threads of the ground-harness ride. 7. The plate-leads, or platines, are flat pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, of about six inches long, and three or four inches broad at the top, but round at the bottom; some use <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> plates instead of them: their use is to pull <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> those lifts which the workman had raised by the treadle, after his foot is taken off. 8. The branches or cords of the ground harness, which go through the loops in the middle of the high-lifts: on the well ordering of these cords chiefly depends the art of ribbon-weaving, because it is by means of this contrivance that the weaver draws in the thread or silk that makes the flower, and rejects or excludes the rest. 9. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a>: this is the wooden frame that holds the reed or shuttle, and beats or clofs the work: where, observe, that the ribbon-weaver does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> his work; but as soon as the shuttle is passed, and his hand is taken away, the baton is forced, by a spring from the top, to beat the work close. 10. The shuttle, or reed. 11. The spring of the baton, by which it is made to clof the work. 12. The long-harness are the front reeds, by which the figure is raised. 13. The linguas are the long pieces of round or square lead, tied to the end of each thread of the long-harness to keep them tight. Weaving 14. The broad piece of wood, about a foot square, leaning somewhat forward, intended to ease the weaver as he stoops to his shuttle; it is fixed in the middle of the breast-beam. Some weavers, instead of this, have a contrivance of a cord or rope that is fastened to the front-frame, and comes across the breast; this is called a flopfall. 15. The feet-bench; this leans forward very much. 16. The foot-step to the treadles. 17. The breast-beam, being a cross-bar that passes from one of the standards to the other, so as to front the workman's breast: to this breast-bar is fixed a roll, upon which the ribbon passes in its way, to be rolled upon the roller, that turns a little below. 18. The clamps, or pieces of wood, in which the broaches that confine the treadles rest. 19. The treadles are long narrow pieces of wood, to the ends of which the cords that move the lifts are fastened. 20. The treadle-cords are only distinguished from the riding-cords by a board full of holes, which divide them, in order to prevent the plate-leads, which are tied to the high-lifts, from pulling them too high when the workman's foot is off the treadle: which stop is made by a knot in the treadle-cord, too big to be forced through that hole in the board. 21. The lams are two pieces of thin narrow boards, only used in plain works, and then to supply the place of the long-harness. 22. The knee-roll, by which the weaver rolls up his ribbon as he fees proper, or by bit and bit as it is finished. 23. The back-rolls, on which the warp is rolled. It is to be observed, that there is always as many rolls as colours in the work to be woven. 24. The clamps, which support the rollers. 25. The returning-sticks, or, as others call them, the returns, or the tumblers, or pulleys, to which the tiers are tied, to clear the course of cords through the high-lifts. 26. The catch-board for the tumblers. 27. The tire-board. 28. The buttons for the knee-rolls and treadle-board, described in No. 20. It is stated in the proceedings of the National Institute of France, that a report was presented to that body concerning a new machine for weaving ribbed stockings. The advantages which this machine possesses are said to be, that it may be erected at one-half of the expense of the English <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> frame, and that its movements are much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of its operations for two years has confirmed these advantages. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of this machine we have had no opportunity of obtaining any information; but we thought it worth while to insert this short notice, with the view of directing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of such of our readers as may be interested in the improvement of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>.

WEBERA

Pages 374-374

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class and order pentandria monogyinia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WEBSTER

Pages 374-379

ALEXANDER, D.D. was the son of James Webster, minister of the Tolbooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and born in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> about the year 1777. He was only 13 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, and of course could derive little from parental instruction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> example. He studied at the university of Edinburgh the several branches of learning with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> approbation, particularly Webster, particularly those connected with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, for which he discovered an early predilection. He afterwards attended the lectures of the professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and in the year 1733 he was ordained minister of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULROSS">Culross</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1737, he was admitted to be one of the ministers of the Tolbooth church of Edinburgh. His eloquence was noble and manly, his piety conspicuous, and the discharge of his pastoral duties faithful and laborious. To these qualities he added an enlightened zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> interests of the church, a jealousy of corruption, a hatred of false politics and tyrannical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, which sometimes exposed him to calumny from the guilty, but secured him the esteem of all who could value independence of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> and integrity of heart. The prosperity of fortune which placed Mr Webster in the church of his father, and restored him to the polished <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of his native city, was not confined to these favours. Eleven days after his settlement in Edinburgh, he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Erskine, a young lady of considerable fortune, and nearly related to the noble family of Dundonald. The genius of Mr Webster now began to unfold itself. Family connections extended his acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Edinburgh then possessed a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men, both in civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> stations, who have saved or adorned their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. With these he was soon to cooperate in defending the protestant interests from the arms and artifices of rebellion. In the year 1733, five or six ministers seceded from the church, and being anxious to draw away as many as possible from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> which they had renounced, they invited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to Scotland in 1741, Mr George Whitefield, a young preacher of great piety and extraordinary pulpit talents. On his way to Dunfermline, he was met and entertained at Edinburgh by Mr Webster and some of his brethren. From them he learned the state of church parties in Scotland; and though he kept his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of preaching first in Fife, he declined connecting himself with any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. Disappointed of his influence and assistance, the Seceders ascribed the effects of his preaching to sorcery and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, while Mr Webster, in a pamphlet which he published on the occasion, attributed them to the influence of the Holy Spirit, an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> regarded by the Seceders as unfeachable wickedness. In the year 1745, Mr Webster remained in the city when it was taken by the rebels, and employed his universal popularity and vigorous eloquence in retaining the minds of the people in the interests of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>. His exertions in this were not overlooked by most of the spirited gentlemen who acted in quelling the rebellion. He became an intimate friend of Duncan Forbes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULLODEN">Culloden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, and others. He preferred to the latest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> both of mind and body, which distinguished him in the prime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, obtaining at last his frequent with and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, an easy and peaceful death, after a very short indisposition, on the 25th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1784. His remains were deposited in the Greyfriars <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>; and it is not a little remarkable that neither private friendship nor public generosity has yet come forward to testify its regard for two of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the church of Scotland. The ashes of Webster and Blair repose in the same cemetery, undistinguished from the less illustrious dead. No monumental <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> marks the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their dust. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> endowed Dr Webster with strong faculties, which were afterwards improved by a considerable share of erudition. He was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in the knowledge of the world and of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> was engaging; his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> strong as his mind; his convivial powers, as they are called, enchanting. He had a constitutional strength against intoxication, which made it dangerous in most men to attempt bringing him into such a state. His character as a minister was popular in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> was harmonious, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> noble. To the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> he was a father and a friend, a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> to poor students. In his person he was tall, and of a thin and meagre <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. His features were strongly marked, and the conformity of the whole indicated genius and independence. To him the widows of the clergy are indebted for the establishment of the celebrated Scheme, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of which he matured in his mind soon after he was appointed a minister of the Tolbooth church. By it the widows of ministers are entitled to the annual sum of 10, 15, 20, or 25 pounds, according as the clergy pay into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> yearly, 2l. 12s. 6d.—3l. 18s. 9d.—5l. 5s. or 6l. 11s. 3d., or to their children in sums of 100—150—200—or 250l, in favour of which an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> was obtained in terms of a petition (17 Geo. II.) with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to employ the surplus of the annual payments and expenses in loans of 30l. each among the contributors, and to put out the remainder at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, on proper security. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> act was procured in the 22nd year of the same reign (1748) granting liberty to raise the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> to 80,000l, including the sums <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to contributors. The fund is conceived to commence from the 25th <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1744. This was followed by another act in the year 1770, discontinuing the loan granted to contributors, and granting liberty to raise the capital to 100,000l.; and the whole economy of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> was then fixed and determined, a report of the state of the fund being ordered to be made annually to the General <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a>, which was to be afterwards printed. The success of the scheme has been complete.

WEDNESDAY

Pages 379-379

the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, so-called from a Saxon idol named Woden, supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, worshipped on this day. Ash Wednesday, the first day of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, so-called from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, of penitents expressing their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, by appearing in sack-cloth and ashes.

WEEDS

Pages 379-379

also denote a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, worn by the relations of persons deceased, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>.

WEEVIL

Pages 380-380

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of curculio. See Curculio, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and for the method of destroying this troublesome and destructive insect, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">Granary</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">Vermin</a>.

WEIGELIA

Pages 380-380

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clais and order pentandria monogynia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WEIGH

Pages 380-380

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, &c. containing 256 pounds avoirdupois. Of corn, the weigh contains 40 bushels; of barley <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> malt, six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. In some places, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, the weigh of cheese is 300 pounds.

WEIGHING

Pages 380-380

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of examining a body in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> to find its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. WEIGHING <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">Anchor</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> it out of the ground it had been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into, in order to set fail, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quit a port, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, or the like.

WEIGHT

Pages 380-385

in Physics, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bodies, whereby they tend downwards towards the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a>, weight may be defined in a less limited manner, to be a power inherent in all bodies whereby they tend to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> point, called the centre of gravity, or, to speak more accurately, to one another; and that with a greater or less velocity, as they are more or less dense, or as the medium they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through is more or less rare. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>. Weight, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, denotes a body of a known weight appointed to be put in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> against other bodies whose weight is required. The security of commerce depending, in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, on the justness of weights, which are usually of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, most nations have taken care to prevent the falsification thereof, by stamping or marking them by proper officers, after being adjusted by some original standard. Thus, in England, the standard of weights is kept in the exchequer by a particular officer, called the clerk of the market. Weights may be distinguished into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. I. Ancient Weights. 1. Those of the ancient Jews, reduced to the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">troy</a> weight, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> stand as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: | Shekel | lb. oz. dwt. gr. | |--------|-----------------| | | 9 2 4 | | Maneh | 2 3 6 10 7 | |--------|-----------------| | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">Talent</a> | 113 10 1 10 7 | |--------|-----------------| 2. Roman weights, reduced to English troy weight, will stand as is in the following table: | Lentes | oz. dwt. gr. Weight | |--------|---------------------| | 4 Silique | 8 4 3 | | 12 Obolus | 9 1 8 | | 24 Scriptulum | 18 1 4 | | 72 Drachma | 2 6 1 2 | | 96 Sextula | 3 0 7 | | 144 Sicilicus | 4 13 7 | | 192 Duella | 6 1 5 | | 576 Uncia | 18 5 7 | | 6912 Libra | 18 13 4 | The Roman ounce is the English avoirdupois ounce, which they divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> denarii, as well as eight drachmas. 3. Attic Weights. | Drachma | English Troy Weight | |---------|---------------------| | | lb. oz. dwt. gr. | | | 2 16 9 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINA">Mina</a> | 1 1 10 10 | |---------|---------------------| | Talent | 67 7 5 0 | |---------|---------------------| II. Modern Weights. 1. English Weight.—Mr Renardson, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> published in the Philosophical Transactions, has proved, that at first there was but one weight in England, and that this was the avoirdupois. Troy weight was introduced in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Henry VII.: At present, both the troy and avoirdupois weights are used in England. Troy weight seems to have derived its name from <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TROYES">Troyes</a>, a town in France, where a celebrated fair was kept. It is used for weighing <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, jewels, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and all liquors. The avoirdupois is used for weighing other things. TABLE of Troy Weight, as used by the Goldsmiths, &c. | Grains | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">Penny</a>-weights. | |--------|----------------| | 24 | | | 480 | 20 | | 5760 | 240 | TABLE of Troy Weight, as used by the Apothecaries. | Grains | Scruple. | |--------|---------| | 20 | 3 | | 60 | 3 | | 480 | 24 | | 5760 | 288 | The troy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> in Scotland, which by statute is to be the same as the French pound, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed equal Weight equal to 15 ounces and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> troy English weight, or 7560 grains. But by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of the standards kept by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>-of-guild of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, it weighs 7599\(\frac{1}{2}\) or 7600 grains. **Table of Avoirdupois Weight.** | Drams | An ounce. | |-------|-----------| | 16 | | | 256 | A pound. | | 7168 | 448 | | 28672 | 1792 | | 573440| 35840 | The avoirdupois pound is equal to 7004 troy grains, the avoirdupois ounce to 437.75 grains; and it follows of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, that the troy pound is to the avoirdupois pound as 88 to 107 nearly; for as 88 to 107, so is 5760 to 7003.636: that the troy ounce is to the avoirdupois ounce as 80 to 73 nearly; for as 80 to 73, so is 480 to 438. An avoirdupois pound is equal to 1 lb. 2 oz. 11 dwt. 20 gr. troy; a troy ounce is equal to 1 oz. 1.55 dr. avoirdupois; an avoirdupois dram contains 27.34375 grains; 175 troy pounds are equal to 144 avoirdupois pounds. The moneyers have a peculiar subdivision of the grain troy: thus, \[ \begin{align*} \text{Grain} & \quad \text{Mite} \\ \text{Droit} & \quad \text{Periot} \end{align*} \] into \[ \begin{align*} 20 & \quad \text{Mites}, \\ 24 & \quad \text{Droits}, \\ 20 & \quad \text{Periots}, \\ 24 & \quad \text{Blanks}. \end{align*} \] The English weights are used in the United Provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. 2. **French Weights.**—Different weights were formerly used in most of the different provinces of France: These, however, have undergone very material alterations since the revolution in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. See Measure. But as a knowledge of the ancient weights of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is of importance, on account of the books in which they are used, we insert the following tables. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> pound contains 16 ounces, and is divided two ways. | Grains. | Penny-weight. | |---------|---------------| | 24 | | | 72 | 3 | | 576 | 24 | | 4608 | 192 | | 9216 | 384 | The marc is equal, according to M. Tillet, to 4620 French grains. The weights of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> are used to weigh gold, silver, and the richer commodities; and the weights of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> division for commodities of less value. The Paris 2 marc, or pound weight, is equal to 7560 grains troy, and the Paris ounce equal to 472.5 grains troy. lb. oz. dtw. gr. The Paris pound = 1 3 15 0 troy. The Paris ounce = 0 0 19 16.5 troy. A grain troy = 1.2186507 of a Paris grain. But the pound was not the same throughout France. At Lyons, e.g., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> pound was only 14 ounces: so that 100 Lyons pounds, made only 86 Paris pounds. But beside the city pound, they had another at Lyons for silk, containing 15 ounces. At Thoulouse, and throughout the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, the pound was 13 ounces and a half of Paris weight. At Marfelles, and throughout Provence, the pound was 13\(\frac{1}{2}\) ounces of Paris weight. At <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, beside the common Paris pound and marc, they had the weight of the vicomte; which was 16 ounces, a half, and five-sixths of the Paris weight. The weights enumerated under the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of English and French weights are the same that are used throughout the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; only under somewhat different names, divisions, and proportions. French weights were formerly used in all the French American settlements. 3. **Dutch Weights.**—The weight used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> and all over <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> is called Troy weight, and is exactly the same with that used at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>. The Dutch weights are as follows: | Deuskens. | Troyken. | |-----------|----------| | 2 | | | 4 | 2 | | 16 | 8 | | 512 | 256 | | 10240 | 5120 | | 81920 | 40960 | The marc is equal, according to M. Tillet, to 4620 French grains. The Amsterdam pound used in commerce is divided into 16 ounces, 32 loots, or 128 drams. This pound contains 2 marcs troy, and ought therefore to weigh only 10240 as; but it weighs 10280 as, so that it is a little heavier than the Troy pound of Amsterdam: 256 lb. of commerce are equal to 257 lb. troy of Holland. Two different pounds are used by apothecaries; the one containing 2 marcs, the other only 1½. The first is called arseneic pound weight; it contains 16 ounces, the ounce 8 drams, the dram 8 scruples, the scruple 20 grains. The second is called the apothecary's pound; it is divided into 12 ounces, or 24 loots. Three arseneic pounds are equal to 4 apothecary's pounds. The Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> = 8 commercial lb. The Lifpund, or Ll. = 15 The hundred weight = 100 The Schippondt, or Sch. lb. = 300 4. Spanish Weights.—The marc of Castile, used for weighing gold and silver, is divided as follows: | Grains (gold weight). | |-----------------------| | 1½ Grain (silver weight). | | 12 11½ Tomine (gold weight). | | 12½ 12 Tomine (silver weight). | | 37½ 36 3 Adarme | | 75 72 6½ 6 2 Ochava. | | 96 92 8 7½ 2½ 1½ Castellano. | | 600 576 50 48 16 8 Ounce. | | 4800 4608 400 384 128 64 50 Marc. | The marc, according to Tillet, is equal to 7 oz. 4 gros, 8 grains French, which is equal to 4785 as of Holland. One hundred marcs of Castile = about 93½ marcs of Holland; 100 marcs of Holland = 107 marcs of Castile. Medicines are sold by the same marc; but it is divided differently, containing 8 ounces, 64 drachms, 192 scruples, 384 obolos, 1152 caraceras, 4608 grains. The Spanish commercial pound is divided into two marcs, called marcs of Troy, each of which is equal to the marc of Castile. This pound is divided into 16 ounces, 256 adarmes, 9216 grains. 5. Weights of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> marc for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a> silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of 12 deniers, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENIER">denier</a> of 24 grains. The marc of Portugal for weighing gold and silver is equal, according to Tillet, to 7 ounces 3½ gros, and 34 grains French, which makes 4776 as of Holland; so that it is exactly the same with the Lisbon pound. It is divided into 8 ounces, 64 outavas, 192 scruples, 4608 grains. The pound consists of 2 marcs, 16 ounces, or 96 outavas; the arroba of 32 lb.; the quintal of 4 arrobas, or 128 lb. 100 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPORTO">Oporto</a> pounds make 87½ pounds of commerce of Amsterdam. 6. Weights of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.—<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>. Two kinds of weights are used at Genoa, the peso grosso (heavy weight), and the peso fottile (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> weight); the latter is used for weighing gold and silver, the former for other things. The pound of the peso fottile is equal, according to Tillet, to 1 marc, 2 ounces, 2½ gros, 30 grains French. It is divided into 8 ounces, the ounce into 24 deniers, and the denier into 24 grains. The pound of the peso grosso is equal to 1 marc, 2 ounces, 3 gros, 5 grains, French. It is divided into 12 ounces: - The cantaro = 100 lbs. peso grosso. - The rubbo = 25 lbs. - The rotolo = 1½ lb. - 100 lbs. peso grosso = 64½ lb. of commerce of Amsterdam. - 100 lbs. peso fottile = 129 marcs troy of Holland. Rome. The Roman pound consists of 12 ounces, the ounce of 24 deniers, the denier of 24 grains. The Roman pound, according to Tillet, is equal to 1 marc, 3 ounces, ½ gros, 14 grains, French. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. The marc for weighing gold and silver contains 8 ounces, 32 quarti, 1152 carati, or 4608 grani. An hundred marcs of Venice = 97½ marcs troy of Holland, 100 marcs of Holland = 103 of Venice. In Venice they also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a peso grosso and peso fottile. 100 lbs. peso grosso = 94½ commercial lbs. of Amsterdam. 100 lbs. peso fottile = 61½ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>. 7. Swedish Weights.—The marc for weighing gold and silver is equal to 16 lods, 64 quintins, or 4384 as. The pound of 32 lods, used for weighing food, is equal, according to Tillet, to 1 marc, 5 ounces, 7 gros, 8 grains French, which makes 8848 as of Troy of Holland. This answers exactly to the weight of the different pounds, as fixed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, viz. 8848 as = the pound for weighing articles of food; 7821¾ as = marc used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; 7450¾ as = marc used in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and in the country; 7078¾ as = marc used for weighing iron; 7416 as = pound used in medicine. - The skippund = 400 lbs. for weighing food. - The center = 120 lbs. - The waag = 165 lbs. - The sten = 32 lbs. - The Swedith as = 1 as of Holland troy. 8. German Weights.—<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. The marc of Vienna for weighing gold and silver is divided into 16 loths, 64 quintals, or 256 deniers or pfennings; the loth into 4 quintals, or 16 pfennings. This marc, according to Tillet, is equal to 1 marc, 1 ounce, 1 gros, 16 grains, French, = 5831 as troy Holland. The pound of Vienna is divided into 2 marcs, or 4 viertings; the mark into 8 ounces, 16 loths, 64 quintals, or 266 pfennings. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>. The marc for assaying gold is divided into 24 carats; the carat into 12 grains. The marc for silver is divided into 16 loths, and the loth into 18 grains. These marcs consist each of 288 grains, and are therefore equal. This marc, used in Hamburg for gold and silver, is the marc of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, which is equal, according to Tillet, to 7 ounces, 5 gros, 7½ grains, French, = 4866 as troy of Holland. It is divided into 8 ounces, 16 loths, 64 quintins, 256 pfennings, 4352 echtes, or 65536 richt pfennings theile. The apothecary pound used in Hamburg, and almost all Germany, is divided into 12 ounces, 96 drachms, 288 scruples, or 5760 grains; an ounce is equal to 621 as of Holland. The pound of commerce is equal, according to Tillet, to 1083 as of Holland; for half a pound is equal to 7 ounces, 7 gros, 23 grains, French. This pound is divided into 16 ounces, 32 loths, 128 quentins, or 512 pfenings. 9. Russian Weights.—The berckowitz = 400 lbs. The pound = 40 lbs. The pound is divided into 32 loths, or 96 folotnicks. One hundred Ruffian lbs. = 166½ marcs, or 82½ lbs. of Amsterdam. One hundred lbs. of commerce of Amsterdam = 120½ th lbs. of Ruffia. 10. Weights used in the several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, the East Indies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, &c.—In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, &c., they use the batman, or battamant, containing 7½ occos; the occo contains 4 chekys or pounds, each of which, according to Tillet, is equal to 1 marc 2 oz. 3 gros, 28 gr. French. The Turkish weights are divided as follows: | Cantaras. | Batmans. | Occos. | Rotolos. | Chekis. | Mefcals. | Drachms. | |-----------|----------|--------|---------|--------|----------|---------| | 1 = 7½ = 44 = 100 = 176 = 1173 = 17600 | 1 = 6 = 13½ = 24 = 1600 = 2400 | 1 = 2½ = 4 = 266½ = 400 | 1 = 1½ = 10 = 117½ = 176 | 1 = 6½ = 66½ = 100 | At <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> there are three sorts of rottos; the first 720 drachms, making about 7 pounds English, and serving to weigh cottons, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> commodities; the second is 680 drachms, used for all silks but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> ones, which are weighed by the third roto of 700 drachms. At Seyda the roto is 600 drachms. The other ports of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, not named here, use some of these weights; particularly the occa, or ocqua, the rottoli, and roto. The Chinese weights are, the piece for large commodities: it is divided into 100 catis or cattis, though some say into 125; the cati into 16 taels or tales, each tael <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 1½ of an ounce English, or the weight of one rial and ½, and containing 12 mas or marles, and each mas 10 condims. So that the Chinese piece amounts to 137 pounds English avoirdupois, and the cati to 1 pound 8 ounces. The pico for silk containing 66 catis and ½; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAHAR">bahar</a>, bakaire, or barr, containing 300 catis. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TONQUIN">Tonquin</a> has also the same weights, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, &c., as China. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> has only one weight, viz. the cati; which, however, is different from that of China, as containing 20 taels. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, and throughout the states of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, they use the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or maund, whereof they have two kinds; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s maund, or king's weight; and the maund simply; the first used for the weighing of common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, containing 40 feers, or ferres; and each feer a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> Paris pound. The common maund, used in the weighing of merchandise, consists likewise of 40 feers, but each feer is only estimated at 12 Paris ounces, or ¼ of the other feer. The maund may be looked upon as the common weight of the East Indies, though under some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of name, or rather of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>; it being called mao at Cambaya, and in other places mein and maum. The feer is properly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> pound, and of universal use; the like may be said of the bahar, tael, and cati, above mentioned. The weights of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a> are the piece, containing two shans or cattis; but the Siamese cati is only half the Japanese, the latter containing 20 taels and the former only 10; though some make the Chinese cati only 16 taels, and the Siamese 8. The tael contains 4 baats, or ticals, each about a Paris ounce; the baat 4 felings or mayons; the mayon 2 fouangs; the fouang 4 payes; the paye 2 clams; the pompaye half a fouang. It is to be observed, that these are the names of their coins as well as weights; silver and gold being commodities there sold, as other things, by their weights. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, and particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANTAM">Bantam</a>, they use the gantam, which amounts to near 3 Dutch pounds. In Golconda, at Vilapour, and Goa, they have the furatelle, containing 1 pound 14 ounces English; the manganis, or mangelin, for weighing diamonds and precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, weighing at Goa 5 grains, at Golconda, &c. 5½ grains. They have also the rotolo, containing 14½ ounces English; the metrical, containing the sixth part of an ounce; the wall for piastres and ducats, containing the 73rd part of a rial. In Persia they use two kinds of batmans or mans; the one called cali or cheray which is the king's weight, and the other batman of Taurir. The first weighs 13 pounds 10 ounces English; the second 6½ pounds. Its divisions are the ratel, or a 16th; the derhem, or drachm, which is the 50th; the mefchel, which is half the derhem; the dung, which is the sixth part of the mefchel, being equivalent to 6 carat grains; and lastly, the grain, which is the fourth part of the dung. They have also the vakie, which exceeds a little our ounce; the fah-cheray, equal to the 1170th part of the derhem; and the toman, used to weigh out large payments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> without telling; its weight is that of 50 abases. 11. Weights at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>.—Almost every kind of goods has its own weight; these are regulated by the cantaren or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> weight. Rotels. The ordinary cantaren, or hundred weight, weighs 100 The cantaren of quicksilver and tin - 102 coffee, wine, and iron - 105 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> - 100 almonds and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> - 115 woods for dying - 120 arsenic and other drugs - 125 minium and cinnabar - 130 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-arabic, aloes, and other aromatics - 133 The ratel or rotoli is nearly equal to the pound of Marfeilles; 108 lbs. of Marfeilles are equal to 110 rots. The Marfeilles pound consists of 13 ounces of Paris; so that the 100 lbs. of Marfeilles are equal to 81 lbs. Paris, and 100 lbs. Paris = 123 lbs. of Marfeilles. We shall subjoin here Mr Fergulon's table for comparing the English avoirdupois pound with foreign pounds: | <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> pound | <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> | Amsterdam | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBEVILLE">Abbeville</a> | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a> | <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a> | Bordeaux | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> | |--------------|---------|-----------|-----------|--------|---------|----------|--------| | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a> | <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>| <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a> | Dieppe | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANTZIC">Dantzic</a>| <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> | <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> | | 1.0000 | 1.04 | 1.1111 | 1.0089 | 0.78 | 0.8928 | 1.0089 | 0.8 | | Bruges | Calabria| Calais | Dieppe | Dantzic| Ferrara | Flanders | Geneva | | 1.0204 | 0.73 | 0.9345 | 1.0089 | 0.862 | 0.75 | 0.9433 | 1.07 | | Tables and Traits | | | | | | | Genoa | London pound 1.0000 | Bruges 1.0204 | Tables and Traits | Calabria 0.73 | Calais 0.9345 | Dieppe 1.0089 | Dantzic 0.862 | Ferrara 0.75 | Flanders 0.9433 | Geneva 1.07 | Genoa In order to show the proportion of the several weights used throughout Europe, we shall add a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of them to one standard, viz. the London pound. Many attempts have been made to introduce an uniformity of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and measures</a> into the commercial world; but hitherto they have all failed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of such an undertaking would be of infinite advantage to mankind, and certainly claims the most serious <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of those who by their situation can alone bring it about. The undertaking is indeed difficult, but surely not impossible. Something of this kind has been attempted and adopted in France; and, as the method is simple, and exceedingly well adapted for calculation, it surely deserves to be imitated. See Measure. **Weight of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a>.** See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PNEUMATICS">Pneumatics</a>, No. 14—19. Regulation of Weights and Measures, is a branch of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>. See Prerogative and Measure. As weight and measure are things in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> arbitrary and uncertain, it is therefore expedient that they be reduced to some fixed rule or standard: which standard it is impossible to fix by any written <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>; for no man can, by words only, give another an adequate idea of a foot rule, or a pound weight. It is therefore necessary to have recourse to some visible, palpable, material standard; by forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with which all weights and measures may be reduced to one uniform size; and the prerogative of fixing this standard, our ancient law vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, as in Normandy it belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>. This standard was originally kept at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>; and we find in the laws of King Edgar, near a century before the conquest, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> that the one measure, which was kept at Winchester, should be observed throughout the realm. Most nations have regulated the standard of measures of length by comparison with the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body; as the palm, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a>, the foot, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a>, the ell (ulna or arm), the pace, and the fathom. But as these are of different dimensions in men of different proportions, our ancient historians inform us, that a new standard of longitudinal measure was ascertained by King Henry the First; who commanded that the ulna, or ancient ell, which answers to the modern yard, should be made of the exact length of his own arm. And one standard of measure of length being gained, all others are easily derived from thence; those of greater length by multiplying, those of less by dividing, that original standard. Thus, by the statute called compositio ulnorum et peticarum, five yards and a half make a perch; and the yard is subdivided into three feet, and each foot into 12 inches; which inches will be each of the length of three grains of barley. Superficial measures are derived by squaring those of length; and measures of capacity by cubing them. The standard of weights was originally taken from corns of wheat, whence the lowest denomination of weights we have is still called a grain; 32 of which are directed, by the statute called compositio mensurarum, to compose a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNYWEIGHT">pennyweight</a>, whereof 20 make an ounce, 12 ounces a pound, and so upwards. And upon these principles the first standards were made; which, being originally so fixed by the crown, their subsequent regulations have been generally made by the king in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Thus, under King Richard I., in his parliament held at Westminster, A.D. 1197, it was ordained that there should be only one weight and one measure. Weight measure throughout the kingdom, and that the custody of the assize, or standard of weights and measures, should be committed to certain persons in every city and borough; from whence the ancient office of the king's assayer seems to have been derived, whose duty it was, for a certain fee, to measure all cloths made for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, till the office was abolished by the statute 11th and 12th William III. c. 20. In King John's time this ordinance of King Richard was frequently dispensed with for money; which occasioned a provision to be made for enforcing it, in the great charters of King John and his son. These original standards were called pondus regis, and mensura domini regis, and are directed by a variety of subsequent statutes to be kept in the exchequer chamber, by an officer called the clerk of the market, except the wine gallon, which is committed to the city of London, and kept in Guildhall. The Scottish standards are distributed among the oldest boroughs. The eland is kept at Edinburgh, the pint at Stirling, the pound at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANARK">Lanark</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRKIN">firkin</a> at Linlithgow. Various statutes have been enacted for regulating and enforcing an uniformity of weights and measures; and by the articles of union, the English standards are established by law over all Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. But the force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is so strong, that these statutes have been ill observed. The Scottish standards are still universally retained for many purposes; and likewise a variety of local weights and measures are used in particular places of both countries, which differ from the general standards of either.

WEINMANNIA

Pages 385-385

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class oelandia, order monogynia, and arranged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> classification with those plants the order of which is doubtful. The calyx is four-leaved, the corolla has four petals, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> is bilocular and biformated. There are six <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, none of which are natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

WELL

Pages 385-385

an apartment formed in the middle of a ship's hold to inclose the pumps, from the bottom to the lower decks. It is used as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to preserve those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> from being damaged by the friction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> compression of the materials contained in the hold, and particularly to prevent the entrance of ballast, &c. by which the tubes would presently be choked, and the pumps rendered incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. By means of this inclosure, the artificers may likewise more readily descend into the hold, in order to examine the state of the pumps, and repair them as occasion requires. WELL-Room of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">Boat</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the bottom where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> lies between the ceiling and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of the stern-heats, whence it is thrown out into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with a scoop. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a>-WELL. See Burning-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">Spring</a>. WELL of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>-veffel, an apartment in the middle of the hold, which is entirely detached from the raft, being lined with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> on every side, and having the bot- tom thereof penetrated with a competent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small holes palling all through the ship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>; so that the well-water running into the well is always kept as fresh as that in the sea, and yet prevented from communicating itself to the other parts of the hold. WELL-hole, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, is the hole left in a floor for the stairs to come up through.

WELLS

Pages 385-385

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, and see of a bishop; the bishop of Bath being also that of Wells.—It, is supposed to take its name from the many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and wells that are near it. It is not very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; but is adorned with handsome buildings, both public and private. Its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a very beautiful structure, adorned with images and carved <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> joins to the cathedral; and on the other side are the houses for the prebendaries. In the market <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a fine market <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, supported by pillars. It is governed by a mayor, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufacture is knit hose. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 374. N. Lat. 51. 12.

WEREGILD

Pages 385-385

the price of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>; paid partly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> for the loss of a subject, partly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> whose vassal he was, and partly to the next of kin of the person slain.

WERST

Pages 385-386

WURST, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Verft, a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> equal to 3500 English feet. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> contains about 124 wersts and a half. WERTURIAN or URALIAN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, a famous chain of mountains forming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the boundary of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>.
