It begins distinctly (for it may be traced undoubtedly farther south) near the town of Kungur, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Kafan, in latitude 57° 20'; runs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and ends opposite to the Waygatz strait, and rises again in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Nova Zemlya. The Russians also call this range Semennoi Poias, or, the girdle-of-the-world; from a supposition that it encircled the universe. These were the Riphhei montes: Pars mundi damnata a natura rerum, et denfa merfa caligine*; of which only the southern part was known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and that to little as Hip. Nat. to give rise to numberless fables. Beyond these were placed the happy Hyperborei, a fiction most beautifully related by Pomponius Mela. Moderns have not been behind-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in exaggerating several circumstances relative to these noted hills. Ybrand Ides, who crossed them in his embassy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, affirms that they are 5000 toises or fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; others, that they are covered with eternal snow. The last may be true in their more northern parts; but in the usual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> over them, they are free from it three or four months. The heights of part of this chain have been taken by M. l'Abbé d'Auteuche: who, with many assurances of his accuracy, says, that the height of the mountain Kyria near Solikamska, in latitude 60°, does not exceed 471 toises from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, or 286 from the ground on which it stands. But, according to M. Gmelin, the mountain Pauda is much higher, being 752 toises above the sea. From Petersburgh to this chain is a vast plain, mixed with certain elevations or platforms, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the midst of an ocean. The eastern side descends gradually to a great distance into the wooded and morass <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, which forms an im- Wesley, from all the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> taking their rise on that side, some at the amazing distance of latitude 46°; and, after a course of above 27 degrees, falling into the Frozen ocean, in latitude 73° 30′. The Yalik alone, which rises near the southern part of the eastern side, takes a southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and drops into the Caspian sea. The Dvina, the Peczora, and a few other rivers in European Russia, shew the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of that part. All of them run to the northern sea; but their course is comparatively short. Another inclination directs the Dnieper and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> into the Euxine, and the vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a> into the Caspian sea.

WESLEY

Pages 386-388

JOHN, a very extraordinary character, and founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, was the son of the Reverend Samuel Wesley, rector of Epworth in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Axholme in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, and was born in that village in the year 1703. His very infancy was distinguished by an extraordinary incident; for when he was only five years old, the parsonage-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Epworth was burnt to the ground, and the flames had spread with such rapidity, that few things of value could be saved. His mother, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to her son Samuel Wesley, then on the foundation at Westminster school, thanks God that no lives were lost, although for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they gave up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">Poor</a> Jacky, as she expresses herself; for his father had twice attempted to rescue the child, but was beaten back by the flames. Finding all his efforts ineffectual, he resigned him to Divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. But parental tenderness prevailed over <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> fears, and Mr Wesley once more attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his child. By some means equally unexpected and unaccountable, the boy got round to a window in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the house, and was taken out, by one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> on the shoulders of another, and thus getting within his reach. Immediately on his rescue from this very perilous situation, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> fell in. This extraordinary escape explains a certain device, in a print of Mr John Wesley, engraved by Vertue, in the year 1745, from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> by Williams. It represents a house in flames, with this motto from the prophet, "Is he not a brand plucked out of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>?" Many have supposed this device to be merely emblematical of his spiritual deliverance; but from this circumstance it is apparent that it has a primary as well as a secondary meaning; it is real as well as allusive. In the year 1713 he was entered a scholar at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-house in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years under the tuition of the celebrated Dr Walker, and of the Rev. Andrew Tooke author of The Pantheon. Being elected to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, he became a fellow of that college about the year 1725, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Arts in 1726, and was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> with the Rev. Dr Hutchins the rector. He discovered very early an elegant turn for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. Some of his gayer poetical effusions are proofs of a lively fancy and a fine classical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and some translations from the Latin poets, while at college, are allowed to have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> merit. He had early a strong <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, like <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Zinzendorf, of his designation to some extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. This impression received additional force from some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> incidents; all which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> fancy turned to his own account. His wonderful preservation, already noticed, naturally tended to cherish the idea of his being designed by Providence to accomplish some purpose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other, that was out of the ordinary course of human events. The late Rev. Samuel Badcock, in a letter inserted in the Bibliotheca Topographica Britannica, No. XX., says, "There were some strange phenomena perceived at the parsonage at Epworth, and some uncommon noises heard there from time to time, which he was very curious in examining into, and very particular in relating. I have little doubt that he considered himself the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> object of this wonderful visitation. Indeed his father's credulity was in some degree affected by it; since he collected all the evidences that tended to confirm the story, arranged them with scrupulous exactness, in a manuscript consisting of several sheets, and which is still in being. I know not what became of the ghost of Epworth; unless considered as the prelude to the noise of Mr John Wesley made on a more ample stage, it ceased to speak when he began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>." The dawn of Mr Wesley's public mission (continues Mr Badcock) was clouded with mysticism; that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of it which affects silence and solitude; a certain inexplicable introversion of the mind, which abstracts the passions from all sensible objects; and, as the French Quietists express it, perfects itself by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> and intellect, and all the faculties, into the Deity." In this palpable obscurity the excellent Fenelon led himself, when he forsook the shades of Pindus, to wander in quest of pure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with Madam Guyon! Mr Wesley pursued for a while the same ignis fatuus with Mr William <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a> and the Ghost of De Renty. A state, however, so torpid and ignoble, ill-suited the active genius of this singular man. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> mind gained strength by compression; thence bursting glorious, he paused (as he himself somewhere says) "the immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, upborne on an eagle's wings." The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the writings of this Mr William Law, the celebrated author of Christian Perfection, and of A Serious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">Address</a> to the Christian World, contributed moreover, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> Mr John Wesley and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, with a few of their young fellow-students, into a more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> strictness of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. They received the sacrament of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; observed all the fasts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; visited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>; rose at four in the morning; and refrained from all amusements. From the exact method in which they disposed of every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, they acquired the appellation of Methodists; by which their followers have been ever since distinguished. But a more particular account of the origin of this sect, we shall give from a celebrated publication. "The Methodists (says the editor of this work) form a very considerable class, principally of the lower people in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They sprung up about fifty years ago at Oxford, and were soon divided into two parties; the one under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Mr George Whitefield, and the other under that of two brothers, John and Charles Wesley. These leaders, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except Mr William Law, founders of the Methodists, were educated at Oxford, received episcopal ordination, and always professed themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> and liturgy of the established church; though they more <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> practised the dissenting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of worship. But conceiving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of forming separate communities, superior in sanctity and perfection to all other Christian churches, and impressed to a very considerable degree by a zeal of an extravagant and enthusiastic kind, they became itinerant preachers; and, being excluded from most of our churches, exercised their ministry in private houses, fields, Wesley fields, &c., not only in Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, but also in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; thus collecting a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hearers and profelytes, both among the members of the established church and the dissenters. The theological system of Mr Whitefield and his followers is Calvinistic; that of Mr Wesley and his disciples Arminian; and the latter maintains the possibility of attaining <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> perfection in the present state. The subordinate teachers of both these classes of Methodists are generally men of no liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and they pretend to derive their ministerial abilities from special communications of the Spirit. The Methodists of both parties, like other enthusiasts, make true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to consist principally in certain affections and inward feelings which it is impossible to explain; but which, when analyzed, seem to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> in their rising and operation; and they generally maintain, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> will be most likely to succeed in the pursuit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, not by the dictates of reason, or the aids of learning, but by laying their minds open to the direction and influence of divine illumination; and their conduct has been directed by impulses." Our readers will judge for themselves, according to their various modes of education, and to the different lights in which they may respectively view the doctrines of our common Christianity, whether this representation of the origin of the Methodists, and of their distinguishing tenets, be accurate and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>.—Not presuming to sit in judgment on the religious opinions of any man, we shall only observe, that an appellation originally given in reproach, has been glorified in every since by those who have distinguished themselves as the followers either of Mr Whitefield or of Mr Wesley. "After the way called Methodism, to worship them the God of their fathers." But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> and contempt which the singularity of their conduct produced, both John and Charles Wesley were well qualified to bear. They were not to be intimidated by danger, actuated by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, or deterred by disgrace. The boundaries of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> were soon deemed by Mr Wesley too confined for a zeal which displayed the piety of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, and of an intrepidity to which few missionaries had been superior. In 1735 he embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, one of our colonies, which was at that time in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> infancy; and the great object of this voyage was to preach the gospel to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> nations in the vicinity of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. He returned to England in 1737. Of his spiritual labours, both in this country and in America, he himself has given a very copious account, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of Journals printed at different periods. These journals drew upon our laborious preacher and his coadjutors some severe animadversions from two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> reverend prelates; Dr George Lavington bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and Dr William Warburton bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>. The former published, in three parts, The Enthusiasm of the Methodists and Papists compared; the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this performance containing a personal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of immoral conduct. Mr Wesley, in his vindication, published a letter to his lordship, which produced a reply from the latter. Bishop Warburton's attack is contained in his celebrated treatise, entitled The Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>: or, The Office and Operations of the Holy Spirit vindicated from the Insults of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">Infidelity</a>, and the Abuses of Fanaticism: concluding with some thoughts, humbly offered to the consideration of the Established Clergy, Wesley, with regard to the Right Method of defending Religion against the Attacks of either party; 2 vols. small 8vo, 1762. There is much acute reasoning, and much poignant and sprightly <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, in his Doctrine of Grace; but there is too much levity in it for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> bishop, and too much abuse for a candid Christian. On this occasion, Mr Wesley published a letter to the bishop, in which, with great temper and moderation, as well as with great ingenuity and address, he endeavoured to shelter himself from his lordship's attacks; not only under the authority of the Holy Scriptures, but of the church itself, as by law established. On his return from Georgia, Mr Wesley paid a visit to Count Zinzendorf, the celebrated founder of the sect of Moravians, or Herrnhutters, at Herrnhut in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>. In the following year he appeared again in England, and with his brother Charles, at the head of the Methodists. He preached his first field-sermon at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, on the 2d of April 1738; from which time his disciples have continued to increase. In 1741, a serious altercation took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between him and Mr Whitefield. In 1744, attempting to preach at an inn at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a>, he was regularly silenced by the magistrates. Although he chiefly resided for the remainder of his life in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, he occasionally travelled through every part of Great Britain and Ireland, establishing congregations in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In 1750 he married a lady, from whom he was afterwards separated. By this lady, who died in 1781, he had no children. We have already mentioned Mr Wesley as a very various and voluminous writer. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>, both devotional and controversial, biography, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, politics, and poetry, were all, at different times, the subjects of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>: and, whatever <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> may be entertained of his theological sentiments, it is impossible to deny him the merit of having done very extensive good among the lower classes of people. He certainly possessed great abilities, and a fluency which was well accommodated to his hearers, and highly acceptable to them. He had been gradually declining for three years before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; yet he still rose at four in the morning, and preached, and travelled, and wrote as usual. He preached at Leatherhead, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, on the Wednesday before that event. On the Friday following, appeared the first symptoms of his approaching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>. The four succeeding days he spent in praising God; and he left this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, in which his labours had been so extensive and so useful, at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> before ten in the morning of the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1791, in the 88th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His remains, after lying in a kind of state at his chapel in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, draped in the facerdotal robes which he usually wore, and on his head the old clerical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> handkerchief in the other, were, agreeably to his own directions, and after the manner of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> of the late Mr Whitefield, deposited in the cemetery behind his chapel, on the morning of the 9th March, amid an innumerable concourse of his friends and admirers; many of whom appeared in deep <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> on the occasion. One singularity was observable in the funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Instead of, "We give thee hearty thanks, for that it hath pleased thee to deliver this our brother;" it was read "our father." A sermon, previously to the funeral, had been preached by Dr Thomas Whitehead, one of the physicians to the London... Wesley, London <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; and on the 13th the different chapels of his persuasion in London were hung with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. It has been justly observed of Mr Wesley, that his labours were principally devoted to those who had no instructor; to the highways and hedges; to the miners in Cornwall, and the coaliers in Kingwood. These unhappy creatures married and buried among themselves, and often committed murders with impunity, before the Methodists sprung up. By the humane and active endeavours of Mr Wesley and his brother Charles, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of decency, morals, and religion, was introduced into the lowest classes of mankind; the ignorant were instructed, the wretched relieved, and the abandoned reclaimed. His personal influence was greater, perhaps, than that of any other private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in any country. But the limits of this article will not permit us to expatiate further on the character of this extraordinary man.

WEST

Pages 388-388

GILBERT, was the son of Dr West, prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> George I. but at 12 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> lost his father. He studied at Winchester and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and from thence was placed in Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. His studious and fervent turn inclined him to take orders; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cobham, his uncle, diverted him from that pursuit, and gave him a cornetcy in his own regiment. This profession he soon quitted, on account of an opening of another <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which presented him with a flattering prospect of advancement in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of young gentlemen were to be elected from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and, at the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, were to be taught foreign languages; and then sent to the secretaries office, to be initiated into business, and trained there for public services, as envoys, ambassadors, &c. Mr Gilbert West was one of the few pitched upon; and on his first introduction into that office, Lord Townshend, secretary of state, treated him with singular marks of regard, and the strongest inclinations to serve him were testified from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. But his uncle Lord Cobham's strong opposition to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the government, rendered these advantages entirely fruitless; and the ministers honestly told Mr West, that he must not expect them to distinguish his merit, as any favours conferred upon him would be imputed as done to his uncle Lord Cobham. Mr West now left that office, and all his views of making his fortune; and entering into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, retired to Wickham in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, where he lived in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> comfort and tranquil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. He was there visited by his valuable friends, who held the most delightful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, humour, and learning, supported upon the principles of virtue, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> reasoning, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> friendship, which rendered the whole cheerful, animating, and instructive. Mr William Pitt, who was one of those that composed this happy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, becoming paymaster, appointed Mr West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> to Chelsea-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; and he obtained a seat at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-board, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a friendship contracted at the school with one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>'s sons, who procured of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> his being nominated one of the clerks extraordinary of that office. Towards the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mr West's life, he wholly applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Scriptures; being extremely anxious to try his utmost endeavours to reconcile the seeming inconsistencies which gave the enemies to revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> a handle to doubt and discredit their authenticity. His observations on the re- surrection, which, it has been said, were written to confirm the wavering <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of his great friends Pitt and Lyttleton, bear ample testimony to his reasoning powers and the sincerity of his religion; while his translations of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a> show him to have been an eminent Greek scholar, and very considerable poet. He had a mind replete with virtue, and was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but died at 50 years of age.

WESTMINSTER

Pages 388-388

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> which forms the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, but has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> distinct from the rest. This city had its name from the situation of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, anciently called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINSTER">minster</a>, in respect of that of St Paul. That part properly called the city of Westminster, comprehending the parishes of St John and St Margaret, was once an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, called Thorney island, from the thorns with which it was overrun; and the abbey that stood in it, Thorney-abbey. The liberties of Westminster contain the several parishes of St Martin in the Fields, St James's, St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, St Paul, Covent-Garden, St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> le Strand, St Clement Danes, St George, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>, and the precinct of the Savoy. The government, both of the city and liberties, is under the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Westminster, in civil as well as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs; and their authority extends to the precinct of St Martin le <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a>, by Newgate-street, and in some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, which are exempted from the jurisdiction of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>; but the management of the civil part has, ever since the Reformation, been in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of laymen, elected from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and confirmed by the dean and chapter. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of these laymen are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-steward, and the high-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, who hold their offices for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. There are also 16 burgesses and their assistants, out of which are elected two head-burgesses, one for the city, and the other for the liberties. Another officer is the high-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, who has all the other constables under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>.

WESTMORELAND

Pages 388-389

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-west by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>; on the south and south-east by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>; and on the south and south-west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from north-east to south, is 40 miles, and its breadth from the east projection to that in the west, 42. It is generally divided into the baronies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENDAL">Kendal</a> and Westmoreland: the former is very mountainous, but the latter is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> champaign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. These are the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> divisions of this county, which contains eight market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 26 parishes, and 41,617 inhabitants. It lies partly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and partly in that of Carlisle. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Thanet is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the county, which sends only four members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is clear, sharp, and salubrious, the natives being seldom troubled with diseases, and generally living to old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is various; that on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> is very barren, while that in the valleys is fertile, producing good corn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, especially in the meadows near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. In the hilly parts on the western borders it is generally believed there are vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> ore, and veins of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of copper are worked, but most of the ore lies so deep that it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not answer This county yields the finest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and abundance of excellent hams are cured here. The principal rivers are, the Eden, the Lone, and the Ken. It has also several fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, the principal of which is Windermere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">Mere</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Windermere <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. In the forest of Martindale, to the south of Ullswater, the breed of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> deer still exists in a wild state.—<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPLEBY">Appleby</a> is the county town.

WESTPHALIA

Pages 389-389

one of the circles of Germany, anciently the people inhabiting between the Weser and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, were called Wolfphalians; and hence that tract got the name of Wolfphalia: but the circle of that name is of a larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, being surrounded by the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, the United Provinces, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, with the circles of the Upper and Lower Rhine, and comprising a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many different states. The summoning princes and directors of the circle of Westphalia, were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, alternately with the electors of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> and Palatine, as dukes of Cleve and Juliers. The archives belonging to it were before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> (1797) kept at Düsseldorf. Its quota of men and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is somewhat more than the ninth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the whole sum granted by the empire. With respect to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, it is partly Protestant and partly Catholic; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> predominate, and are, at least the greater part of them, Calvinists. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is not reckoned very wholesome, and towards the north is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in winter. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general is marshy and barren; yet there is some good corn and pasture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; but the fruit is chiefly used to feed hogs; and hence it is that their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> and hams are so much valued and admired. Westphalia now forms one of the kingdoms established by Bonaparte.

WESTRINGIA

Pages 389-389

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, formed from eunila fruticosa, which was discovered by Dr Solander in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. Dr Smith describes it as approaching nearer to rosemary, and places it after teucrium in the clas didyma.

WET-COUCH

Pages 389-389

Coming-heaps, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the maltsters for one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of malt-making. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">Brewing</a>, No. 4.

WETSTEIN

Pages 389-389

John James, a learned German divine, was born at Bath in 1693. On his admission to the ministry, he maintained a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> De variis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVI">Novi</a> Testamenti Lectionibus; in which he showed that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of readings of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> afford no argument against the authenticity of the text. He had made these various readings the object of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and travelled into foreign countries to examine all the MSS. he could come at. In 1730, he published Prolegomena <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> Novi Testamenti Graeci editionem accuratissimam, &c. Some divines, dreading his unsettling the present text, procured a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> against his undertaking, and even got him prohibited from officiating in the ministry; on which he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMONSTRANTS">Remonstrants</a> named him to succeed the famous Le Clerc, then superannuated, as professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. At last he published his edition of the New Testament, in 2 vols. folio, 1752; in which he left the text as he found it, placing the various readings, with a critical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, underneath; subjoining two epistles of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CLEMENS_ROMANUS">Clemens Romanus</a>, till then unknown to the learned, but discovered by him in a Syriac MS. of the New Testament. He also published some small works; and is said to have been not only an universal scholar, but to have abounded in good and amiable qualities. He died at Amsterdam in 1754.

WETTERAVIA

Pages 389-389

the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-gravate of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> in Germany, lying along the northern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, and comprehending the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANAU">Hanau</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>.

WEXFORD

Pages 389-389

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. It was once reckoned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Ireland, being the first colony of the English, and is still a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome town, with a very commodious harbour at the mouth of the river Slana, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of St George's channel, 63 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 3. N. Lat. 52. 18. WHALE. See Baleena and Physeter, Cetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WHALE

Pages 389-389

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>. WHALE-Bone. For its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, see Cetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. A patent was granted in October 1806 to Robert Bowman of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a>, in Scotland, for making <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, caps, and bonnets for men and women, of whalebone; harps for harping <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cleansing corn or grain; and also the bottoms of sieves and riddles, and girths for horses; and also a cloth or webbing for making into hats, caps, &c.; and for the backs and seats of chairs and sofas, gigs, coaches, and other similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>; and the bottoms of beds; as also reeds for weavers. WHALE-Fisher. See Cetology.

WHARF

Pages 389-389

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the banks of a haven, creek, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hithe, provided for the convenient loading and unloading of vessels.

WHARTON

Pages 389-391
Philip Duke of, a nobleman of the most brilliant parts, but of the most whimsical, extravagant, and inconsistent turn of mind, was educated by his father's father's express order at home. He very early married a young lady, the daughter of Major-General Holmes, which disappointed his father's views of disposing of him in such a marriage as would have been a considerable addition to the fortune and grandeur of his illustrious family; yet that amiable lady deserved infinitely more felicity than she met with by this alliance. This precipitate marriage is thought to have hastened the death of his father; after which the duke, being free from paternal restraints, plunged into those excesses which rendered him, as Pope expresses it, "A tyrant to the wife his heart approved; "A rebel to the very king he loved." In the beginning of the year 1716, he began his travels; and as he was designed to be instructed in the strictest Whig principles, Geneva was thought a proper place for his residence. He first passed through Holland, and visited several courts of Germany; and being arrived at Geneva, conceived such a disgust against his governor, that he left him, and set out post for Lyons, where he wrote a letter to the chevalier de St George, who then resided at Avignon, and presented him a very fine stout horse; which the chevalier no sooner received than he sent a man of quality to him, who took him privately to his court, where he was entertained with the greatest marks of esteem, and had the title of duke of Northumberland conferred upon him. He, however, remained there but one day, and then returned post to Lyons, whence he set out for Paris. He likewise paid a visit to the court of James II., who then resided at St Germain, to whom he also paid his court. During his stay at Paris, his winning address and abilities gained him the esteem and admiration of all the British subjects of rank of both parties. About the latter end of December 1716, he arrived in England, whence he soon after set out for Ireland, where, though under age, he was allowed the honour to take his seat in the house of peers, and immediately distinguished himself, notwithstanding his former conduct, as a violent partisan for the ministry; in consequence of which zeal the king created him a duke. He no sooner came of age than he was introduced to the house of lords in England with the same blaze of reputation. In a little time he opposed the court, and appeared one of the most vigorous in defence of the bishop of Rochester; and soon after printed his thoughts twice a-week, in a paper called the True Briton, several thousands of which were circulated. The duke's boundless profusion had by this time so burdened his estate, that by a decree of Chancery it was vested in the hands of trustees for the payment of his debts, allowing him a provision of £200 per annum for his subsistence. This being insufficient to support his title with suitable dignity, he went abroad and thence to great advantage, with respect to his personal character, at the imperial court. From thence he made a tour to Spain: the English minister was alarmed at his arrival, fearing that his grace was received in the character of an ambassador: upon which the duke received a summons under the privy-seal to return home; but instead of obeying it, he endeavoured to inflame the Spanish court against that of Great Britain, for exercising an act of power, as he calls it, within the jurisdiction of his Catholic majesty. He then acted openly in the service of the Pretender, and was received at his court with the greatest marks of favour. While his grace was thus employed, his neglected duchess died in England on the 14th of April 1726, without issue. Soon after the duke fell violently in love with M. Oberne, one of the maids of honour to the queen of Spain, the daughter of an Irish colonel, whose fortune chiefly consisted in her personal accomplishments. All his friends, and particularly the queen of Spain, opposed the match; but he falling into a lingering fever, occasioned by his disappointment, the queen gave her consent, and they were soon after married. He then spent some time at Rome, where he accepted of a blue garter, assumed the title of duke of Northumberland, and for a while enjoyed the confidence of the exiled prince. But not always keeping within the bounds of Italian gravity, it became necessary for him to remove from hence; when, going by sea to Barcelona, he wrote a letter to the king of Spain acquainting him that he would assist at the siege of Gibraltar as a volunteer. Soon after he wrote to the chevalier de St George, expressing a desire to visit his court; but the chevalier advised him to draw near to England. The duke seemed resolved to follow his advice; and setting out with his duchess, arrived in Paris in May 1728, whence he soon after proceeded to Rouen, where he took up his residence; and was so far from making any concession to the government of England, that he did not give himself the least trouble about his estate, or any other concern there; though, on his arrival at Rouen, he had only about £520 in his possession, and a bill of indictment was preferred against him in England for high-treason. Soon after the chevalier sent him £2000, which he squandered away in a course of extravagance; when, to save the charges of travelling by land, he went from Orleans to Nantes by water, and laid there till he got a remittance from Paris, which was squandered almost as soon as received. At Nantes he was joined by his ragged servants, and from hence took shipping with them for Bilboa, when the queen of Spain took the duchess to attend her person. About the beginning of the year 1731, the duke, who commanded a regiment, was at Lerida, but declined to fight that he could not move without assistance; yet when free from pain did not lose his gaiety. He, however, received benefit from some mineral waters in Catalonia; but soon after relapsed at a small village, where he was utterly destitute of all the necessaries of life, till some charitable fathers of a Bernardine convent removed him to their house, and gave him all the relief in their power. Under their hospitable roof he languished a week, and then died, without one friend or acquaintance to close his eyes; and his funeral was performed in the same manner in which the fathers inter those of their own fraternity. Thus died Philip duke of Wharton, "who, like Buckingham and Rochester (says Mr Walpole), comforted all the grave and dull, by throwing away the brightest profusion of parts on witty fooleries, debaucheries, and scrapes, which mix graces with a great character, but never can compose one. "With attachment to no party, though with talents to govern any party, this lively man changed the free air of Westminster for the gloom of the Escorial, the prospect of King George's garter for the Pretender's; and Wheat, and with indifference to all religion, the frolic lord who had written the ballad on the archbishop of Canterbury, died in the habit of a capuchin. It is difficult to give an account of the works of a man whose library was a tavern, and women of pleasure his muses. A thousand follies of his imagination may have been lost. There are only two volumes in 8vo, called his Life and Writings. These contain nothing of the latter, but 74 numbers of the True Briton, and his speech in defence of the bishop of Rochester. His other works are the ballads above mentioned; the Drinking Match at Eden-hall, in imitation of the Chevy Chase, printed in a miscellany called Whartoniana; and a parody of a song sung at the opera-house by Mrs Tofts. His lordship also began a play on the story of the queen of Scots. WHEAT. See Triticum, Botany Index; and for the culture of wheat, see Agriculture Index. The three principal kinds of bad wheat are, the blighted, the smutty, and the worm-eaten. Blighted wheat is that of which the stalk is a little twisted and rickety, the blade being of a bluish green and curled up, the grain also is green and tubercled; smutty wheat appears as if great part of the ear had been burnt, some small parts only being free, and, in particular, the stem that rises in the centre of the ear, round which the grain is ranged; worm-eaten or rotten wheat is corrupted without losing much of its natural form, or external appearance; the bulk is filled with a greasy black powder, that is inoffensively feid. It appeared, from the experiments of M. Tillet, that there was a kind of infectious quality in all those kinds of wheat: so that if found wheat was sprinkled with the flour of smutty or rotten wheat, the crop produced would be rotten or smutty. It appeared also, that among the grain which was produced from ground manured with the straw of distempered wheat, there was a much greater proportion of distempered wheat than in that produced from ground manured with the straw of good wheat: the great secret then was to destroy the principle of this contagion in the wheat that was put into the ground; and M. Tillet found, as the result of a great number of experiments, that if the grain, before it is sowed, be well moistened with a solution of sea-salt, or nitre, in common water, none of the ensuing crop will be smutty, or otherwise defective, either in kind or quality; not only supposing the grain that is sowed to be sound, and the soil to be good, but even supposing the grain to be sowed with the flour of smutty wheat, and the ground manured with bad straw. The following receipt for preventing smutty wheat was published in 1769 by order of the Society for the Encouragement of Arts: they received it from Mr John Reynolds of Addington in Kent. A tub is to be procured that has a hole at bottom, in which a staff and tap-hole is to be fixed over a whiff of straw, to prevent any small pieces of lime passing (as in the brewing way); this done, we put 70 gallons of water, then a corn bushel heap-full of stone-lime, unslaked, flinging it well till the whole is dissolved or mixed, letting it stand about 30 hours, and then run it off into another tub as clear as we can (as practised in beer): this generally produces a hoghead of good strong lime-water; then add three pecks of salt, 42 pounds, which, with a little stirring, will soon dissolve; thus we have a proper pickle for the purpose of brining and liming our feed-wheat without any manner of obstacle, which is more than can be said in doing it the common way, and greatly facilitates the drilling. Herein we steep the wheat in a broad-bottomed basket of about 24 inches diameter, and 20 inches deep (for large sowing, made on purpose), running in the grain gradually in small quantities from 10 to 12 gallons up to 16 gallons, stirring the same. What floats, we skim off with a strainer, and is not to be thrown away; then draw up the basket to drain over the pickle, for a few minutes; all which may be performed within half an hour, sufficiently pickled; and so proceed as before. This done, the wheat will be fit for sowing in 24 hours, if required; but if designed for drilling, two hours pickled will be found best; and if prepared four or five days beforehand, in either case it makes no difference at all; but should the feed be clammy, and stick to the notches in the drill-box, more lime must be added to the lime-water; here the master must use his discretion, as the case requires; for some lime has much more drying or astringent qualities in it than others. If lime-water can be obtained conveniently, much less salt will suffice, but some will be found necessary even then, otherwise the light grains will not float, a thing of more consequence than is generally imagined, and it ought to be skimmed off and thrown aside for poultry, &c.

WHEEL

Pages 392-392

Potter's. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">PORCELAIN</a>. Wheel is also the name of a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> criminals are put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> countries. In some, afflains, parricides, and robbers on the highway, are said to be condemned to the wheel, when they are to have their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> first broken with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> on a scaffold, and then to be exposed, and left to expire on the circumference of a wheel. In Germany they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> their bones on the wheel itself.—Of this cruel punishment, it is not certain who was the inventor: it was first used in Germany, and was, indeed, but rarely practised anywhere else, till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Francis I. of France; who, by an edict of the year 1534, appointed it to be inflicted on robbers on the highway.

WHEELER

Pages 392-395

Sir GEORGE, a learned traveller and divine, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Wheeler of Charing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, and was born in 1650 at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>, where his parents as royalists were then in exile. He travelled through various parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and the East, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with Dr James Spon of Lyons; and taking orders on his return, was installed a prebend of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Badingstoke; and afterward rector of Houghton le <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">Spring</a>. He published an account of his travels in 1682 in folio; and in 1689, his Observations on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Edifices of Churches yet remaining in the East, compared Wheelings compared with Eusebius; also the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">Monastery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Christian Oeconomics. He died in 1724.

WHEELINGS

Pages 395-395

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, are different motions made both by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and foot, either to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the right and left about. General Rules for WHEELING—The circle is divided into four equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>: thence, wheeling to the right or left, is only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the circle; wheeling to the right or left about, is one half of the circle. When you wheel to the right, you are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the right, so near as to touch your right-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, but without pressing him; and to look to the left, in order to bring the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> about even. When you wheel to the left, you are to close to the left, and look to the right as above directed. This rule <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve for all the wheeling by ranks; as when a battalion is marching by subdivisions with their ranks open, then each rank <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> distinctly by itself, when it comes to the ground on which the ranks before it wheeled, but not before. In wheeling, the men are to take particular care neither to open nor close their ranks, and to carry their arms well. In wheeling, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of each man is quicker or slower, according to the distance he is from the right or the left: thus, when you wheel to the right, each man moves quicker than his right-hand man; and wheeling to the left, each man moves quicker than his left-hand man; the circle that every man wheels being larger, according to the distance he is from the hand he wheels to; as may be seen by describing several circles within one another, at two feet distance from each, which is nearly the space every man is supposed to take up.

WHELP

Pages 395-395

the young of a dog, fox, lion, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any wild beast.

WHELPS

Pages 395-395

in a ship, the seaman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for those brackets which are set up on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> under the bars; they give the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> to it, and are so contrived that the cable winding about them may not surge so much as it might otherwise do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the body of the captain were quite round and smooth.

WHETSTONE

Pages 395-395

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> so called, because it serves for the whetting of edge tools upon. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WHIDAH

Pages 395-395

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and to the west of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> Coast; extending about 10 miles along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is a populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, well furnished with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> villages; and there are so many small ones, that they are not above a musket-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from each other.—The houses are small, round at the top, and encompassed with mud walls <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hedges, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of all sorts of beautiful and lofty trees, which afford the most beautiful prospect in the world, inasmuch that those that have been here represent it as a perfect paradise. The fields are always green, and they cultivate beans, potatoes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; nor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> here let a foot of ground remain uncultivated. They sow again the very next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after they have reaped. The inhabitants are greatly civilized, very respectful to each other, especially to their superiors, and very industrious. The women brew the beer, dress the victuals, and sell all sorts of commodities at the market. Those that are rich employ their wives and slaves in tilling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and they carry on a considerable trade with the product, as well as in slaves; for some of them are able to deliver 1000 of the latter every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men have generally 40 or 50 wives, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> captains 300 or 400, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> 4000 or 5000. They are extremely jealous, and, on the least suspicion, will sell them to the Europeans for slaves. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any one happen to touch one of the king's wives accidentally, he is doomed to perpetual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. It is no wonder then that the women are not fond of being the king's wives; and some of them will prefer a speedy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to such a miserable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. They have no distinction of hours, days, weeks, months, or years. The rite of circumcision is used here; but they are not able to tell why they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it, nor whence it is derived. They are such great gamesters, that they will stake all they have at play, not excepting their wives and children. They have a vast number of idols; and they deify the most contemptible animal that they see first in a morning, and even stocks and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Their principal regard is for snakes, very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> trees, and the sea. An English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> arrived, found a snake in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>, and killed it without the least scruple; which so incensed the negroes, that they were for revenging the death of the snake, not only upon him that killed it, but upon the whole factory; but by means of presents, and the interposition of the people of the other factories, the affair was made up, and the snake honourably interred. However, to prevent such accidents, they gave them warning not to do the like for the future. They have oxen, cows, goats, sheep, hogs, turkeys, ducks, and hens; which last are extremely plentiful. There are many elephants, buffaloes, tigers, several kinds of deer, and a sort of hares. The fruits are citrons, lemons, oranges, bananas, tamarinds, &c., and they have vast numbers of palm-trees, from which they obtain wine. Whidah was conquered by the king of Dahomy. Their trade consists of slaves, elephants' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, wax, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. The English factory is 200 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Coast Castle, within land. Bows, arrows, beautiful assegais, and clubs, are the principal weapons of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. WHIDAW-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">BIRD</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBERIZA">Emberiza</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WHIRLPOOL

Pages 395-396

an eddy, vortex, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is continually <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round. Those in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, from various accidents, and are usually very trivial, and of little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> they are more rare, but more dangerous. Sibbald has related the effects of a very remarkable marine whirlpool among the Orcades, which would prove very dangerous to strangers, though it is Whirlpool, of no consequence to the people who are used to it. This is not fixed to any particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but appears in various parts of the limits of the sea among these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Wherever it appears, it is very furious; and boats, &c., would inevitably be drawn in and perish with it; but the people who navigate them are prepared for it, and always carry an empty vessel, a log of wood, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bundle of straw, or some such thing, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> with them; as soon as they perceive the whirlpool, they toss this within its vortex, keeping themselves out: this substance, whatever it be, is immediately received into the centre, and carried under water; and as soon as this is done, the surface of the place where the whirlpool was becomes smooth, and they row over it with safety; and in about an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> they see the vortex begin again in some other place, usually at about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>'s distance from the first.

WHIRLWIND

Pages 396-396

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> which moves in a spiral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, as well as horizontally, which is exceedingly rapid and impetuous, but only of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Dr Franklin's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the origin of whirlwinds has been already given in the article <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">WATER</a>-SPOUT. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> be true, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> follow, that no hurricane ever can be so violent as to remove an obstacle of the size of only one cubic inch, provided that was supported by a power <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 15 pounds; for this is the utmost force of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> when rushing into a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>, which never could take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the centre of a whirlwind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> water-sprout. Indeed, notwithstanding the dreadful effects sometimes observed from hurricanes and whirlwinds, we shall easily perceive, that the utmost of their power always falls very far short of this. The diminution of the specific gravity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> by only one-fourth in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, would produce such an afflux of air from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, that an obstacle presenting a surface of one foot <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, would require a force of 504 pounds to prevent it from being carried away; which the strongest walls that can be built by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> art could scarce resist. Nay, even the tenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this, or the diminution of the gravity of the atmosphere by one-fortieth part, would produce a prelude of upwards of 50 pounds on every square foot of surface, which, it is to be doubted, whether any of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> houses could resist. Some philosophers ascribe the vacuum in the atmosphere, to which, according to Dr Franklin's theory, whirlwinds are owing, to a stream of electric <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> rushing with violence into the atmosphere out of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. But they do not inform us how this matter comes to be accumulated in that part of the earth; what induces it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> out of the earth; how it passes invisibly through pure air; or what serves it for a conductor. It seems to be the fashion among certain philosophers to ascribe every phenomenon, with the cause of which we are unacquainted, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>. But this is merely substituting a new name, and serves rather to retard than advance our knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Some kinds of whirlwinds move with a slow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and are injurious only by their vortex; while others seem to do mischief as well by their progressive as their whirling motion. Of this kind are those called typhoons; which, by their frequently following the course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, seem thus also to discover their electrical origin. Of the destructive effects of these, we have an instance in what happened in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARLESTOWN">Charlestown</a> in South Carolina, on the 1st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1761. It was first observed about noon, Whirlwind on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, upwards of 50 miles west by south of Charlestown, and destroyed several houses, &c., as it passed along, in many places making wide avenues through the woods; from whence every tree and shrub was torn up, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> branches of trees were driven about in the column as it passed along. It directed its course to Ashley river, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> which it came with surprising velocity; in its appearance resembling a column of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> or vapour, whose motion was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and tumultuous. Its momentum was so great, that Ashley river was ploughed to the bottom, and the channel laid bare. As it came down this river, it made a constant noise like <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>; its diameter being computed about 300 fathoms. It was met at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Point by another of the same kind which came down <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COOPER">Cooper</a>'s river, but with inferior strength; however, on their meeting together, the agitation of the air was much greater, while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, which were driving in all directions to the place, seemed to be precipitated, and whirled round with incredible velocity. It then fell upon the shipping in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>; entirely destroying some, and damaging others; being scarce three minutes in its passage, though the distance was near two leagues. In that short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it did damage to the amount of 20,000l.; and had not its direction been altered by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> which came down Cooper's river, it must have totally destroyed Charlestown, as no obstacle whatever seemed capable of resisting its fury.

WHISKY

Pages 396-396

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and applied in Scotland and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> to a distilled liquor drawn from barley. WHISPERING-PLACES. See Acoustics, No. 24.

WHIST

Pages 396-399

a well known <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, which requires <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and silence; hence the name. This game is played by four persons, who cut for partners; the two highest and the two lowest are together, and the partners sit opposite to each other: the person who cuts the lowest card is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> first, giving one at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to each person, till he comes to the last card, which is turned up for the trump, and remains on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> till each person has played a card. The person on the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> side of the dealer plays first, and whoever wins the trick is to play again, thus going on till the cards are played out. The ace, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a> of trumps, are called honours; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> any three of these honours have been played between, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by either of the two partners, they reckon for two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> towards the game; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the four honours have been played between, or by either of the two partners, they reckon for four points towards the game, the game consisting of ten points. The honours are reckoned after the tricks; all above six tricks reckoning also towards the game. General Rules for playing the Game of WHIST. 1. He who is to play first should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> from the strongest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>. If he has a sequence of king, queen, and knave, or queen, knave and ten, he may safely lead the highest of the sequence; but if he has five or six in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, he must begin with the lowest. He must always begin with the highest trump, by which he forces out the superior trumps, and can come in again, to make his strong suit. 2. He should never be afraid to play trumps when he has five in his hand, even of the smallest, although he may not have any good cards of any other suit. 3. With 3. With ace and king of any two suits, and only two or three small trumps, the aces and kings should be played out, in order to make as many tricks as possible; and having but two or three small trumps, he should never force his partner to trump, if he finds he cannot follow suit; but endeavour to throw the lead into his partner's hand. 4. He should in general return his partner's lead, unless he has some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> cards of his own. 5. As this game is played with the lurch, that is, to have half the stake, five points must be made before the game is out; he should not venture to play trumps when he is four of the game, unless he is very strong, having at least an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and three trumps, or ace, king, and two small ones. 6. When the game is scored <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, at which stage the honours reckon for nothing, he should be still more cautious how he plays trumps, even if he is strong in hand, and give his partner an opportunity of trumping the adversaries suits, in case he is deficient in them. 7.
