If his adversaries are six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the game, he should play a forward or bold game, that he may have a chance, at the risk of a trick or two, to come up with them. If he has but three trumps and other good cards, he may play trumps, especially if he has a sequence, or queen, knave, and a small one. 8. He should always risk a trick or two when the game is much in his favour; because a new deal is of greater <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the adversary than one or two points are to him. 9. When the player finds there is a likelihood of either saving the game or his lurch, he should risk the odd trick; but if the game is five all, and he can make two tricks in his own hand, he should make them, in order to secure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of two points, which make the game near two to one in his favour. 10. A good player should begin with a small trump, when he has ace, king, and four small ones; for this reason, if his partner has a better trump than the last player, which is an equal wager but he has, he has a chance of fetching out all the trumps, by having three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> of them. 11. The odds are always in his favour that his partner holds an honour; consequently if he has king, queen, and four small ones, he should begin with a small one. 12. When queen, knave, and four small trumps are dealt him, he should play a small one first, the odds being in his favour that his partner holds an honour; if he has knave, ten, and four small trumps, he should also begin with a small one, for the same reason. 13. If he has knave, ten, eight, and three small trumps, the knave should be played first, by which means the nine may be prevented from winning a trick, the odds being in his favour that three honours are played in two rounds. 14. If an honour is turned up against him on his left hand, and he has ten, nine, and eight, with two or three small trumps; when he is to play, he should play through the honours with the ten, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> force the dealer to play his honour to a disadvantage, if the dealer does not choose to leave it to the option of his adversary whether he will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it or not; but if he has six trumps of a lower denomination, and not ten, nine, and eight, and no honour turned up against him, he should begin with a small one. 15. In general, when he has two capital cards in trumps, and two or three small ones, he should begin with a small one, for the reason assigned in No. 12. 16. When he has ace, king, knave, and two small trumps, or even one small trump, by first playing the king, and putting the lead into his partner's hand, who will play a trump; judging him to have ace and knave, from his beginning with the king: in this case the knave should be finessed (A), nothing being against him but the queen. 17. If he has knave, ten, eight, and two small trumps, by playing the knave first, it is odds but in two rounds of trumps the nine falls, or he may finesse the eight when his partner returns trumps. 18. With five trumps of a lower denomination, he should begin with the smallest, unless he has a sequence of ten, nine, and eight; then he should begin with the ten. 19. When he has king, queen, ten, and one small trump, he must begin with the king, and wait for his partner's return of the trumps, in order to finesse the ten, by which means he may win the knave. 20. In order to prevent the ten from winning, when he has queen, knave, nine, and one small trump, he must begin with the queen. And in case he has knave, ten, eight, and one small trump, he should begin with the knave, that the nine may not win. 21. If he has ten, nine, eight, and one small trump, he should begin with the ten; thereby he strengthens his partner's hand, leaving it at his option to take it or not. 22. He should begin with a small one, when he has the ten and three small trumps. 23. If he has a good suit, and ace, king, and four small trumps, he must play three rounds of trumps, in order to secure his strong suit from being trumped. 24. When he has king, queen, ten, and three small trumps, he should begin with the king, because he has a chance of the knave's coming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> round; and to secure his strong suit, he should not wait to finesse the ten. If he should have queen, knave, and three small trumps, and some good suit to make, he must begin with a small one. 25. If he has knave, ten, eight, and two small trumps, with a strong suit, he should begin with the knave, in order to make the nine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the second round; but if he has knave, ten, and three small trumps, with a good suit, he should play a small one first. 26. With ten, nine, eight, and one small trump, provided he has a good suit, he should begin with the ten; by which means he may get the trumps out, and have a chance of making his strong suit. The following observations will enable a player to know that his partner has no more of a suit which either (A) Finesse, is to play a small card which may win, keeping the superior card or cards to lay over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-hand adversary. of them has played. Suppose he leads from queen, ten, nine, and two small cards of any suit, the second hand puts on the knave, his partner plays the eight; in this case, he having queen, ten, and nine, it is a demonstration, if his partner plays well, that he can have no more of that suit. By that discovery, he may play his game accordingly, either by forcing his partner to trump that suit, if he is strong in trumps, or by playing another suit. If he has king, queen, and ten of a suit, and he leads his king, his partner plays the knave; this also demonstrates he has no more of that suit. If he has king, queen, and many more of a suit, and begins with the king, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it is good play in a partner, when he has the ace and one small card in that suit only, to win the king with the ace; for suppose the partner to be very strong in trumps, by taking the king with the ace, he gets the lead and trumps out, and having cleared the board of trumps, his partner returns his lead; and the ace being out, there is room for him to make that whole suit, which could not have been done if the partner had kept the ace. Suppose he has no other good card in his hand besides that suit, he loses nothing by the ace's taking his king; and if it should happen that he has a good card to bring in that suit, he gains all the tricks which he makes to that suit by this method of play: as his partner has taken his king with the ace, and trumps out upon it, he has reason to imagine that his partner has one of that suit to return him; for which reason he should not throw away any of that suit, even to keep a king or queen guarded. Method of playing when an honour is turned up on the right hand.—Suppose the knave is turned up on his right hand, and that he has king, queen, and ten; in order to win the knave, he must begin with the king; by which means, his partner may suppose him to have queen and ten remaining, especially if he has a second lead, and he does not proceed to play the queen. Suppose the knave turned up as before, and he has ace, queen, and ten, by playing his queen, it answers the purpose of the former rule. When the queen is turned up on his right hand, and he has ace, king, and knave, by playing his king, it answers the same purpose of the former rule. In case an honour is turned up on his left hand, supposing he should hold no honour, he should play trumps through the honour as soon as he gets the lead; but if he should hold an honour (except the ace), he must be cautious how he plays trumps, because, in case his partner holds no honour, his adversary will play his own game upon him. Method of playing the sequences.—The highest in sequences of trumps should be played, unless he has ace, king, and queen; and then he should play the lowest, which informs his partner of the state of his game. When he has king, queen, and knave, and two small ones, which are not trumps, he should begin with the knave, whether he is strong in trumps or not, as he makes way for the whole suit by getting the ace out. If he is strong in trumps, and has a sequence of queen, knave, ten, and two small cards of a suit, he should play the highest of his sequence; for if either of the adversaries should trump that suit in the second round, being also strong in trumps, he will make the remainder of that suit, by fetching out the trumps. When he has knave, ten, and nine, and two small cards of a suit, he may play in the like manner. If king, queen, and knave, and one small card of any suit, is the case, whether strong in trumps or not, he should play the king; and when there are only four in number, the same method of play should be observed by inferior sequences. When weak in trumps, he should begin by the lowest of the sequence, provided he has five in number, because if his partner has the ace of that suit he will make it. If he has the ace and four small cards of a suit, and weak in trumps, leading from that suit, he should play the ace. When strong in trumps, the game may be played otherwise. How to make a flam, or win every trick.—Suppose A and B partners against C and D, and C to deal, A to have the king, knave, and nine, and seven of hearts, which are trumps, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> in spades, a tierce-major in diamonds, and the ace and king of clubs. Then suppose B to have nine spades, two clubs, and two diamonds. Also suppose D to have ace, queen, ten, and eight of trumps, with nine clubs, and C to have five trumps and eight diamonds. A leads a trump, which D wins, and D is to play a club, which his partner C is to trump; C leads a trump, which his partner D wins; D then will lead a club, which C will trump; and C will play a trump, which D will win; and D having the best trump will play it; after which D having seven clubs in his hand, makes them, so that he flams A and B. How to play any hand of cards according to the nearest calculations of his partner's holding certain winning cards: 1. That he has not one certain winning card, is 2 to 1 2. That he has not two certain winning cards, is 17 to 2 But it is about 5 to 4 that he has one or both, or 32 to 25 3. That he has one card out of any three certain winning cards, is about 5 to 2 4. That he has not three certain winning cards is about 31 to 1, or 681 to 22 5. That he has not two of them, is about 7 to 2, or 547 to 156. 6. That he has not one of them, is about 7 to 6, or 378 to 325 7. That he holds one or two of them, is in his favour about 13 to 6, or 481 to 222 8. And about 5 to 2 that he holds 1, 2, or all three of them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these calculations is for a whist-player to play his cards to the most advantage. For instance, As the first calculation is two to one that his partner does not hold one certain winning card.—Suppose then a suit is led, of which the second player has the king and a small one only, he should put on the king, because the odds are in his favour, that the third player cannot win it. For the same reason, when he is second player, and to lead, he should play a king in preference to a queen, because it is two to one the ace does not take it; but it is five to four the queen will be taken by either ace or king, which may be in the third hand. According According to the second calculation, of its being five to four that his partner holds one certain winning card out of any two: If he has two honours in any suit, he can play to an advantage, knowing it is five to four in favour of his partner's having one of the two honours; and by the same rule, if he is second player, having a queen and one small card, by playing the queen he plays five to four against himself. It is obvious, from the third calculation, which proves it to be five to two that his partner has one card out of any three certain winning cards, that he who plays the knave second hand, having but the knave and one small card of the same suit, must play five to two against himself, and discovers his game to a great disadvantage; for which reason, he should play the lowest of any sequence which he may hold in his hand, as the knave, if he has king, queen, and knave; the ten, if he has queen, knave, and ten, &c. By so doing, his partner has an opportunity of judging what card to play in that suit, according to the odds for or against him. From the above calculation, if he has ace, king, and two small trumps, he is entitled to win four tricks out of six, provided he has four winning cards of any suit; or five tricks out of seven, if he has five winning cards of any suit: by playing two rounds of trumps, and taking out eight of them, it is five to two but his partner has a third trump; and if it should be so, he makes the tricks intended.

WHISTON

Pages 399-399

WILLIAM, an English divine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> parts, uncommon learning, and of singular character, was born in 1667 at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTON">Norton</a> near Twycroft in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, where his father was rector. He was admitted of Clarehall, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he pursued his studies, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and commenced <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>; which his ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> at length forced him to decline. Having entered into orders, he became chaplain to Dr More bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a> in 1694; and in this station he published his first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled A New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, &c., in which he undertook to prove the Mosaic doctrine of the earth perfectly agreeable to reason and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. This work brought no small reputation to the author. In the beginning of the 18th century he was made Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, and afterwards his successor, in the Lucasian professorship of mathematics; when he resigned a living he had in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, and went to reside at Cambridge. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he published several scientific works, explanatory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian philosophy</a>; and he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be one of the first, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the very first, who rendered these principles popular and intelligible to the generality of readers. About the year 1710, he was known to have adopted Arian principles, and was forming projects to support and propagate them: among other things, he had translated the Apostolical Constitutions into English, which favoured the Arian doctrine, and which he asserted to be genuine. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that he was deprived of his professorship, and banished the university; he nevertheless pursued his scheme, by publishing the next year his Primitive Christianity Revived, 4 vols, 8vo, for which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> fell upon him very vehemently. On his expulsion from Cambridge, Mr Whiston settled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; where, without suffering his zeal to be intimidated, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to write, and propagate his Primitive Christianity, with as much ardour as if he had been in the most flourishing circumstances. In 1721, a subscription was made for the support of his family, which amounted to £70l. For though he drew profits from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> astronomical and philosophical lectures, and also from his publications, which were very numerous, yet these of themselves would have been very insufficient: nor, when joined with the benevolence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> of those who loved and esteemed him for his learning, integrity, and piety, did they prevent his being frequently in great distresses. He continued <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, and regularly frequented its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, though he disapproved of many things in it: but at last he went over to the Baptists, and attended Dr Forster's meeting at Pinner's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, Broadstreet. Among other performances not specified above, he wrote <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and writings, which contain some curious particulars. He was remarkable for speaking the plainest truths on every occasion, and to persons of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. During the year 1725, that he, with Dr Clarke, Dr Berkeley, and others, had the honour to attend <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Caroline on a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, to talk of the progress of science, her majesty one evening took occasion to pay him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> compliment on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and integrity, requesting that he would, with his usual plainness, point out to her any fault that he might have observed in her conduct. At first he begged to be excused, adding, that few persons could bear to have their faults plainly told to them, and least of all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> personages, who, from their elevation, are necessarily surrounded by flatterers, to whose lips truth is a stranger. Her majesty replied, that he was to consider her not as a queen, but as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; and that philosophy is of very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, if it cannot enable its professors to bear without offence truths necessary to their own improvement. Upon this he told her, that the greatest fault which he had observed in her conduct, was her indecent behaviour in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God, which, he assured her, had made very unfavourable impressions on the minds of many persons, who coming to town from distant parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, had gone to the chapel to obtain a sight of her majesty, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and the royal family. The queen made no reply; but in about six weeks afterwards renewed her request, that Mr Whiston would point out the most glaring improprieties in her conduct. To this he answered, that he had laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a maxim, from which he could not deviate, never to point out to any person more than one fault at a time, and never to give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> reproof till he had observed some good consequence to have arisen from the first (A). Much to the queen's honour, she was pleased with this plain-dealing, and continued to think favourably of Mr Whiston. This honest, but whimsical and credulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, died in 1762, at the advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 95.

WHITBY

Pages 399-400

DR DANIEL, a very learned English divine, was born at 1638, and bred at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; where, in 1664, he was elected perpetual fellow of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He afterwards became chaplain to Dr Seth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, bishop (A) Bishop Berkeley was present at these conversations, and from his son we received the account we have given of them. They are likewise mentioned, but not stated so accurately, by Bishop Newton in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>. Whitefield, that he made him a voluntary offer of ordination. Immediately after this regular admission into the ministry, Mr Whitefield applied himself to the most extraordinary, the most indefatigable, duties of his character, preaching daily in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, fields, and open streets, wherever he thought there would be a likelihood of making profelytes. Having at length made himself universally known in England, he embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where the tenets of Methodism began to spread very fast under his friends the Wesleyans; and first determined upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the orphan-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, which he afterwards effected. After a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> course of peregrination, his fortune increased as his fame extended among his followers, and he erected two very extensive buildings for public worship, under the name of Tabernacles; one in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOTTENHAM">Tottenham</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">Road</a>, and another in Moorfields. Here, with the help of some afflantists, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for several years, attended by very crowded congregations, and quitting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> only occasionally. Besides the two tabernacles already mentioned, Mr Whitefield, by being chaplain to the countess dowager of Huntingdon, was connected with two other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> meetings, one at Bath, and the other at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, chiefly erected under that lady's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>. By a lively, fertile, and penetrating genius, by the most unwearying zeal, and by a forcible and persuasive delivery, he never failed of the desired effect upon his ever crowded and admiring audiences. In America, however, which always engaged much of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, he was destined to finish his course; and he died at Newberry, about 40 miles from Bolton in New England, in 1770.

WHITEHAVEN

Pages 400-400

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, with a market on Tuesday, and one fair on August 1st for merchandise and toys. It is seated on a creek of the Irish Sea, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> hill, washed by the tide of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> on the west side, where there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> of hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which gives name to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and which, with the help of a strong stone-wall, secures the harbour, into which small barks may enter. It is lately much improved in its buildings, and noted for its trade in pit-coal and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, there being near it a valuable coal-mine, which runs a considerable way under the sea. They have a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> here; and they carry on a good trade to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and other parts. It is 10 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCKERMOUTH">Cockermouth</a>, and 305 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 34. N. Lat. 54. 36.

WHITES

or FLUOR ALBUS. See MEDICINE, No 250. WHITING. See GADUS, ICHTHYOLOGY Index.

WHITFUNDAY

Pages 400-401
or White-Sunday; because this being one of the stated times for baptism in the ancient church, those who were baptized put on white garments, as types of that spiritual purity they received in baptism. As the descent of the Holy Ghost upon the apostles happened upon the day which the Jews called Pentecost, this festival retained the name of Pentecost among the Christians.

WHITFUNDAY ISLE

Pages 401-401

one of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, which lies about four miles to the south, runs in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and is of the same length, having more sloping exposures than <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>: it appears to be better inhabited, and to contain more plantations. WHORTLEBERRY. See Vaccinium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WHITSUN-FARTHINGS

Pages 400-400

otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">Smoke</a>-farthings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Quadrantes Pentecostales, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> for offerings which were anciently made in Whitfun-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> by every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in England, who occupied a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> with a chimney, to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> in which he lived.

WHITSUNDAY

Pages 400-400

a solemn festival of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, observed on the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after Easter, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the Holy Ghost upon the apostles in the visible appearance of fiery cloven tongues, and of those miraculous powers which were then conferred upon them.

WHYTT

Pages 401-402

Dr Robert, an eminent physician, born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> on the 6th September 1714, was the son of Robert Whytt, Esq. of Bennochy, advocate. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> died six months before the birth of our author, who had also the misfortune to be deprived of his mother before he had attained the seventh year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. After receiving the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of school-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he was sent to the university of St Andrew's; and after the usual course of instruction there, in classical, philosophical, and mathematical learning, he came to Edinburgh, where he entered upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of medicine, under those eminent medical teachers, Monro, Rutherford, Sinclair, Plummer, Alison, and Innes. After learning what was to be acquired at this university, in the prosecution of his studies he visited foreign countries; and after attending the most eminent teachers at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Physic conferred upon him by the university of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> in 1736, being then in the 22nd year of his age. Upon his return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he had the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> also conferred upon him by the university of St Andrew's; where he had before obtained, with applause, the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Arts. Not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> afterwards, in the year 1737, he was admitted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICENTIATE">Licentiate</a> of Medicine by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians of Edinburgh; and the year following he was raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a Fellow of the College. From the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his admission as a licentiate, he entered upon the practice of physic at Edinburgh; and the reputation which he acquired for medical learning, pointed him out as a fit successor for the first vacant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the university. Accordingly, when Dr Sinclair, whose eminent medical abilities, and persuasive powers of oratory, had contributed not a little to the rapid advancement of the medical school of Edinburgh, found that those conspicuous talents which he possessed could no longer be exerted in the manner which they once had been, when he enjoyed bodily vigour unimpaired by age and powers of mind unclouded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, he resigned his academical appointments in favour of Dr Whytt. This admission into the college took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the 20th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1746; and he began his first course of the institutions of medicine at the commencement of the next winter-session. The abilities which he displayed from his academical chair, in no particular disappointed the expectations which had been formed of his lectures. The Latin tongue was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the university of Edinburgh; and he both spoke and wrote in Latin with singular propriety, elegance, and perspicuity. At that time the system and sentiments of Dr Boerhaave, which notwithstanding their errors, must challenge the admiration of later ages, were very generally received by the most intelligent physicians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Dr Whytt had no such idle ardour for novelties as to throw them entirely aside because he could not follow them in every particular. The institutions of Dr Boerhaave, therefore, furnished him with a text for his lectures; and he was no less successful in explaining, illustrating, and establishing the sentiments of the author, when he could freely adopt them, than in refuting them by clear, connected, and decisive arguments, when he had occasion to differ from him. The opinions which he himself propounded, were delivered and enforced with such acuteness of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, such display of facts and force of argument, as could rarely fail to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> universal assent from his numerous auditors; but free from that self-sufficiency which is ever the offspring of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and conceit, he delivered his conclusions with becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and diffidence. From the time that he first entered upon an academical appointment, till the year 1756, his prelections were confined to the institutions of medicine alone. But at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> his learned colleague Dr Rutherford, who then filled the practical chair, who had already taught medicine at Edinburgh with universal applause for more than thirty years, and who had been the first to begin the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of clinical lectures at the Royal Infirmary, found it necessary to retire from the fatiguing duties of an office to which the progress of age rendered him unequal. On this crisis Dr Whytt, Dr Monro, sen. and Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a>, each agreed to take a share in an appointment in which their united exertions promised the highest advantages to the university. By this arrangement students, who had an opportunity of daily witnessing the practice of three such teachers, and of hearing the grounds of that practice explained, could not fail to derive the most <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> advantages. In these two departments, the institutions of medicine in the university, and the clinical lectures in the Royal Infirmary, Dr Whytt's academical labours were attended with the most beneficial consequences both to the students and to the university. But not long after the period we have last mentioned, his lectures on the former of these subjects underwent a considerable change. About this time the illustrious Gaubius, who had succeeded to the chair of Boerhaave, favoured the world with his Institutiones Pathologicae. This branch of medicine had indeed a place in the text which Dr Whytt formerly followed; but, without detracting from the character of Dr Boerhaave, it may justly be said, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> he had bestowed upon it was not equal to its importance. Dr Whytt was sensible of the improved state in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATHOLOGY">pathology</a> now appeared in the writings of Boerhaave's successor; and he made no delay in availing himself of the advantages which were then afforded. In the year 1762, his pathological lectures were entirely new-modelled. Following the publication of Gaubius as a text, he delivered a comment, which was read by every intelligent student with the most unfeigned satisfaction. In these lectures he collected and condensed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of accurate observation and long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Enriched by all the opportunities of information which he had enjoyed, and by all the discernment which he was capable of exerting, they were justly considered as his most finished production. For a period of more than twenty years, during which he was justly held in the highest esteem as a lecturer at Edinburgh, it may readily be supposed that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his practice corresponded to his reputation. In fact, he received both the first emoluments, and the highest honours, which could here be obtained. With extensive practice in Edinburgh, he had numerous consultations from other places. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on medical subjects was daily requested by his most eminent contemporaries in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Britain. Foreigners of the first distinction, and celebrated physicians in the most remote parts of the British empire, courted an intercourse with him by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>. Besides private testimonies of esteem, many public marks of honour were conferred upon him both at home and abroad. In 1752, he was elected a fellow of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of London; in 1761, he was appointed first physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> in Scotland; and in 1764, he was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Royal College of Physicians at Edinburgh. But the fame which Dr Whytt acquired as a practitioner and teacher of medicine, were not a little increased by the information which he communicated to the medical world in different publications. His celebrity as an author was still more extensive than his reputation as a professor. His first publication, An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Vital and other Involuntary Motions of Animals, although it had been begun soon after he had finished his academical course of medical education, did not come from the press till 1753; a period of fifteen years from the time that he had finished his academical course, and obtained a degree in medicine: but the delay of this publication was fully compensated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which it contained, and the improved form under which it appeared. The next subject which employed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of Dr Whytt was one of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> more immediately practical. His Essay on the Virtues of Lime-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">Soap</a> in the Cure of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, first made its appearance in a separate volume in 1752. Part of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> had appeared several years before in the Edinburgh Medical Essays: but it was now presented to the world as a distinct publication with many improvements and additions. His third work, intitled Physiological Essays, was first published in the year 1755. This treatise consisted of two parts; 1st, An Inquiry into the Causes which promote the Circulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a> in the very small Vessels of Animals; and 2ndly, Observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">Sensibility</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRRITABILITY">Irritability</a> of the Parts of Men and other Animals, occasioned by Dr Haller's treatise on that subject. The former of these may be considered as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> and farther illustration of the sentiments which he had already delivered in his Essay on the Vital Motions, while the latter was on a subject of a controversial nature. In both he displayed that acuteness of genius and strength of judgement which appeared in his former writings. From the time at which his Physiological Essays were published, several years were probably employed by our author in preparing for the press a larger and perhaps a more important work than any yet mentioned, his Observations on the Nature, Causes, and Cure of those Disorders which are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called nervous, hypochondriac, and hysterick. This elaborate and useful work was published in the year 1764. The last of Dr Whytt's writings is intitled, Observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">Dropsy</a> in the Brain. This treatise did not appear till two years after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; when all his other works were collected and published in one quarto volume, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of his son and of his intimate friend the late Sir John Pringle. Besides these five works, he wrote many other papers, which appeared in different periodical publications; particularly in the Philosophical Transactions, the Medical Essays, the Medical Observations, and the Physical and Literary Essays. At an early period of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, soon after he had settled as a medical practitioner in Edinburgh, he entered into the married state. His first wife was Miss Robertson, sister to General Robertson governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. By her he had two children; both of whom died in early infancy, and their mother did not long survive them. A few years after the death of his first wife, he married as a second wife Miss Balfour, sister to James Balfour, Esq., of Pilrig. By her he had fourteen children; but in these also he was in some respects unfortunate; for six of them only survived him, three sons and three daughters, and of the former two are since dead. Although the feeling heart of Dr Whytt, amidst the distresses of his family, must have often suffered that uneasiness and anxiety which in such circumstances is the unavoidable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of parental affection and conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>; yet he enjoyed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share of matrimonial felicity. But his course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> was terminated by the death of his wife, which happened in the year 1764; and it is not improbable that this event had some share in hastening his own death; for in the beginning of the year 1765 his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was so far impaired, that he became incapable of his former exertions. A tedious complication of chronic ailments, which chiefly appeared under the form of diabetes, was not to be resisted by all the medical skill which Edinburgh could afford; and at length terminated in death, on the 15th of April 1766, in the 52nd year of his age.

WIBURGH

Pages 402-402

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>, with a bishop's see, remarkable for being the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> assemblies has the archives of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and escaped the terrible fire that happened in the year 1726, and which burned the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Friars, the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; but they have all been rebuilt more magnificent than before. It is seated on the lake <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, 25 miles north-west of Sletwick, and 110 north-by-west of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 50. N. Lat. 56. 20.

WICK

Pages 402-402

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough on the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAITHNESS">Caithness</a>. It is small, and the streets narrow, but a few of its buildings are an ornament to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The present harbour is very inconvenient, but it is proposed to erect a new one, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance to the safety of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> along that coast. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in 1793 amounted to 5000.

WICKET

Pages 402-402

a small door in the gate of a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>,

WICKLIFF

Pages 402-403

JOHN, the first divine in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> who had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to attempt a reformation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was born about the year 1324, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Wycliff, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, first in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s and afterwards in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, of which he was a probationer-fellow. Having acquired the reputation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning and abilities, in 1361 he was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Balliol-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, and in 1365 constituted warden of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> college, by the founder Archbishop Simon de Ilip; but in 1367, he was ejected by the regulars, together with three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> fellows. He thought their proceedings arbitrary, and therefore appealed to the pope; but instead of obtaining redress, the ejectment was confirmed in 1370. This disappointment probably contributed somewhat towards his enmity to the see of Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather to confirm that enmity; for he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before written against the pope's exactions and corruptions of religion. However, his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> in the university <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>; for having taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, he read public lectures with great applause; in which he frequently exposed the impositions of the Mendicant friars. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his sovereign Edward III., against the pope, who had insisted on the homage to which his predecessor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> John had agreed. This defence was the cause of Wickliff's introduction at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and of his being sent one of the ambassadors in 1374 to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, where they met the pope's nuncios, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> several <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> matters relative to the pope's authority. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time Wickliff was presented by the king to the rectory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUTTERWORTH">Lutterworth</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, and in 1375 he obtained a prebend in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WESTBURY">Westbury</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>. Wickliff continued hither-to, without molestation, to oppose the papal authority; but in 1377 a bull was sent over to the archbishop of Canterbury, and to Courtney bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, ordering them to secure this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-heretic, and lay him in irons; at the same time the pope wrote to the king, requesting him to favour the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> in the prosecution; he also sent a bull to Oxford, commanding the university to give him up. Before these bulls reached England Edward III. was dead; and Wickliff, protected by John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, uncle to Richard II. favoured by the queen-mother, and supported by the citizens of London, eluded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of Pope Gregory IX., who died in 1378. In the following year this intrepid reformer presented to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> a severe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> against the tyranny of Rome, wrote against the papal supremacy and infallibility, and published a book On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a> of the Scriptures, intended to prepare the way for an English translation of them, in which he had made considerable progress. In 1381 he published Sixteen Conclusions; in the first of which he ventured to expose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> article of transubstantiation. These conclusions being condemned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of Oxford, Wickliff appealed to the king and parliament; but being deserted by his unsteady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> the duke of Lancaster, he was obliged to make a confession at Oxford; and by an order from the king was expelled the university. He now retired to his living of Lutterworth, where he finished his translation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>. This version, of which there are several manuscript copies in the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, &c., is a very literal translation from the Latin vulgate. In 1383 he was suddenly struck with the palsy; a repetition of which put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1384. He was buried in his own church, where his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were suffered to rest in peace till the year 1428, when, by an order from the pope, they were taken up and burnt.—Besides a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of works that have been printed, he left a prodigious number of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>; an accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of which may be seen in Bishop Tanner's Bib. Brit. Hib. Some of them are in the Bodleian Library, others in the British Museum, &c. Wickliff was doubtless a very extraordinary man, considering the times in which he lived. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sagacity discovered the absurdities and impositions of the church of Rome, and he had the honesty and resolution to promulgate his opinions, which a little more support would probably have enabled him to establish; they were evidently the foundation of the subsequent reformation.

WICKLOW

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; seated on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side, with a narrow harbour, at the mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEITRIM">Leitrim</a>, over which stands a rock, instead of a castle, surrounded by a strong wall, 24 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 7' N. Lat. 52° 55'. WIDGEON. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAS">ANAS</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WIGTON

Pages 404-404

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> to which it gives name. It is of considerable antiquity, and few of its houses have been lately erected. It is supposed to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the ninth century, and that it was made a royal borough in the reign of Robert Bruce. It is governed by a provost, two bailies, and 12 councillors; is extremely healthy, and furnishes many instances of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a>. In 1755, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted to 1032, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in 1793 was 1350.

WIGTONSHIRE

Pages 404-404

sometimes denominated Upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>, is about 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. It is bounded on the south-east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIGTON">Wigton</a>, by which it is separated from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KIRKCUDBRIGHT">Kirkcudbright</a>; on the south and west by the ocean; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a>; and on the east by Kirkcudbright. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is tolerably fertile, but improvements in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> are still in their infancy. The interior and northern parts are hilly and barren, fit only for sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. It contains three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> boroughs, viz. Wigton, Stranraer, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WHITHORN">Whithorn</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of seats belonging to noblemen and gentlemen. It is divided into 17 parishes; and, according to a census taken since the passing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in 1801, the population amounted to 22,918, being an increase of 6452 since the return to Dr Webster in 1755. The valued rent is 67,640l. Scots, while the real rent is computed at 53,890l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. WILDERNESS

Pages 404-405

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trees, in a spacious garden, in which the walks are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made either to intersect each other in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> have the appearance of meanders and labyrinths. Wilderness (says Mr Miller) should always be proportioned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the gardens in which they are made; for it is very ridiculous to see a large wilderness planted with tall trees in a small spot of ground; and, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, nothing can be more absurd than to see little paltry squares, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of wilderness-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in a magnificent large garden. As to the situation of wildernesses, they should never be placed too near the habitation, nor so as to obstruct any distant prospect of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, there being nothing so agreeable as an unconfined prospect; but where, from the situation of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> is confined within the limits of the garden, nothing can so agreeably terminate the prospect as a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of the various kinds of trees judiciously planted; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it is so contrived that the termination is planted circularly, with the concave towards the flight, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have a much better effect than if it end in straight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> or angles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> should always be adapted to the size of the plantation; for it is very absurd for tall trees to be planted in the small squares of a little garden; and in large designs small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> will have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> appearance. It should also be observed never to plant <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a> amongst deciduous trees; but always to place the evergreens in a separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> by themselves, and that chiefly in flight. As to the walks, those that have the appearance of meanders, where the eye cannot discover more than twenty or thirty yards in length, are generally preferable to all others, and these should now and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> into an open circular piece of grass; in the centre of which may be placed either an obelisk, statue, or fountain; and if in the middle of the wilderness there be contrived a large opening, in the centre of which may be erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> or banqueting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, surrounded with a green plot of grass, it will be a considerable addition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the whole. From the sides of the walks and openings, the trees should rise gradually one above another to the middle of the quarters; where should always be planted the largest growing trees, so that the heads of all the trees may appear to view, while their stems will be hid from the sight. Thus, in those parts which are planted with deciduous trees, roses, honeyfuckles, spirea frutex, and other kinds of low flowering shrubs, may be planted next the walks and openings; and at their feet, near the sides of the walks, may be planted primroses, violets, daffodils, &c., not in a straight line, but so as to appear accidental, as in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> wood. Behind these may be placed laurels, hollies, arbutus, and other evergreens of a larger growth. Next to these may be planted alaternus, phyllireas, yews, cypresses, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> cedars, and other trees of the same growth; behind these may be planted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> and silver firs, the true pine, and other sorts of the fir growth; and in the middle should be planted Scotch pines, pinaster, and other sorts of the larger growing evergreens; evergreens; which will afford a most delightful prospect if the different shades of the greens are curiously intermixed. But beside the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> walks and openings (which should always be laid with turf, and kept well mowed), there should be some smaller serpentine walks through the middle of the quarters, where persons may retire for privacy; and by the sides of these private walks may also be scattered some wood-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and plants; which, if artfully planted, will have a very good effect. In the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> these wildernesses, there should not be a studied and stiff correspondence between the several parts; for the greater diversity there is in the distribution of them, the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> they will afford.

WILKIE

Pages 405-405

WILLIAM, D.D., author of a heroic poem called the Epigoniad, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Dalmeny in West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> in Scotland, in October 1721. His father was a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, and was not very fortunate in his worldly affairs. He gave his son, however, a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which he received at the parish school of Dalmeny, and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 13 he was sent to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, where he was soon distinguished as a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius. Among his fellow-students were Dr Robertson the historian, Mr Home the poet, and some other eminent literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. He became acquainted also, in the course of his education, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Hume and Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Ferguson. Before he completed his studies at the university, his father died, leaving him only the stock and unexpired lease of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, with the care of three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, one of whom being afterwards married to an experienced farmer, Wilkie availed himself of his practical knowledge. He formed a system of farming which fully answered his own expectations, and secured to him the approbation of all his neighbours. After becoming a preacher in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland, he still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of living, cultivating his farm, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the classics, and occasionally preaching for the ministers in the neighbourhood. In 1753, he was presented to the church of Ratho by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Lauderdale, who was sensible of his worth, and admired his genius. The duties of his new office he discharged with fidelity, and was celebrated for his impressive mode of preaching, while he did not neglect the amusements of husbandry, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the belles lettres. He published his Epigoniad in the year 1757, the result of fourteen years study, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of it was called for in 1759, in which year he was chosen professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in the university of St Andrews. His whole fortune, when he removed to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, did not exceed £200, which he laid out in the purchase of a few acres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> in the vicinity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He lived in the university in the same studious and retired manner as he had done at Ratho. In the year 1768 he published a volume of fables of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> celebrity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to which the university conferred on him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of D.D. He died, after a lingering illness, on the 10th of October 1772. The manners of Dr Wilkie were in many respects very singular, and in some quite disgusting. For the purpose of promoting perspiration, and thus removing an aguish complaint, with which he had been seized during his residence at Ratho, he generally slept in winter under no fewer than 24 blankets. His aversion to clean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> is altogether unaccountable. It is said that when he slept from home, he not only stipulated for the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of blankets, but requested to be indulged with sheets which had been previously used by some other person. It is scarcely necessary to add, that his dress was slovenly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>. It is somewhat remarkable, that Dr Wilkie never could read aloud the smoothest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in such a manner as to preserve either the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, although his own compositions in verse are greatly distinguished by their smoothness and elegance. It is said that Dr Wilkie, from having studied <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> with great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, was led to project an epic poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet. The subject of it is drawn from the fourth book of the Iliad, where Thetis gives Agamemnon a short account of the taking of Thebes; and as that city was taken by the sons of those who had fallen before it, our author gave to his poem the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Epigoniad, from the Greek word επιγονος, signifying descendants. This title, it is supposed, is not very appropriate, and is not altogether free from quaintness. The subject of the poem has not been selected with much judgement; for the learned reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> prefer studying the manners and actions of ancient heroes in the sublime descriptions of Homer and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, and others will be little interested in scenes and characters so different from those with which they are familiar, and so far removed from their own times. Accordingly, the Epigoniad, with all its merit as an epic poem (and it is not destitute of many of the essential requisites of that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>), is now little known.

WILKINS

Pages 405-405

DR JOHN, a most ingenious and learned English bishop, was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and was born in 1644. He adhered to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> during the civil wars, by whom he was made warden of Wadham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in 1648: he married afterwards the sister of Oliver Cromwell, and procured a dispensation to retain his wardenship notwithstanding. Richard Cromwell made him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Trinity college, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, from which he was ejected on the Restoration. He then became preacher to Gray's-Inn, rector of St Lawrence Jewry, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Rippon, and in 1688 was promoted to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. He died in 1672. Bishop Wilkins thought it prudent to submit to the powers in being; he therefore subscribed to the solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> and covenant while it was enforced, and was equally ready to swear <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> when he was restored: this, with his moderate spirit toward dissenters, rendered him not very agreeable to churchmen. His mathematical and philosophical works, which contain many ingenious and curious pieces, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when they were written, have been collected in one vol. 8vo. He published also some theological tracts. He was the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>.

WILL

Pages 405-407
or Legal WILL, in Law, signifies the declaration of a man's mind and intent relating to the disposition of his lands, goods, or other estate, or of what he would have done after his death. In the common law there is a distinction made between a will and a testament: ment; that is called a will where lands or tenements are given; and when the disposition concerns goods and chattels alone, it is termed a testament. See Testament. Will-with-a-wisp, or Jack-with-a-lantern, two popular names for the meteor called ignis fatuus. See Light, No. 46. William of Malmesbury, an historian of considerable merit in the reign of King Stephen; but of whose life few particulars are known. According to Bale and Pits, he was surnamed Somerestius, from the county in which he was born. From his own preface to his second book De Regibus Anglorum, it appears that he was addicted to learning from his youth; that he applied himself to the study of logic, physic, ethics, and particularly to history. He retired to the Benedictine convent at Malmesbury, became a monk, and was made precentor and librarian; a situation which much favoured his intention of writing the history of this kingdom. In this monastery he spent the remainder of his life, and died in the year 1142. He is one of our most ancient and most faithful historians. His capital work is that intitled De Regibus Anglorum, in five books; with an Appendix, which he styles Historiae Novelle, in two more. It is a judicious collection of whatever he found on record relative to England, from the invasion of the Saxons to his own times. William of Newbury, so called from a monastery in Yorkshire, of which he was a member, wrote a history which begins at the Conquest and ends at the year 1197. His Latin style is preferred to that of Matthew Paris; and he is entitled to particular praise, for his honest regard to truth, in treating the fables of Jeffery of Monmouth with the contempt they deserve; as well as for expressing his approbation of Henry II.'s design of reforming the clergy, by bringing them under the regulation of the secular power. William of Wykeham, bishop of Winchester, was born in the village of Wykeham, in the county of Southampton, in 1324. He was educated at Winchester and Oxford; and having continued near six years in the university, his patron Nicholas Wedal, governor of the province of Southampton, took him into his family, and appointed him his counsellor and secretary. He could not have made choice of a fitter person for that employment, no man in that age writing or speaking more politely than Wykeham. For this reason Edington, bishop of Winchester, lord high-treasurer of the kingdom, appointed him his secretary three years after, and also recommended him to King Edward III., who took him into his service. Being skilled in geometry and architecture, he was appointed surveyor of the royal buildings, and also chief justice in eyre: he superintended the building of Windsor-castle. He was afterward chief secretary of state, a keeper of the privy seal; and in 1367 succeeded Edington in the see of Winchester. A little after he was appointed lord high-chancellor and president of the privy-council. That he might well discharge the several functions of his employments, both ecclesiastical and civil, he endeavoured, on one hand, to regulate his own life according to the strictest maxims, and to promote such parish-priests only as were able to give due instructions to their parishioners, and at the same time led exemplary lives: on the other hand, he did all in his power to cause justice to be impartially administered. In 1371 he resigned his William, chancellorship, and some time after the great seal. Edward returning to England, after having carried on a very successful war in France, found his exchequer in great disorder. The duke of Lancaster, one of his sons, at the head of several lords, having brought complaints against the clergy, who then enjoyed the chief places in the kingdom, the king removed them from their employments. But the laymen, who were raised to them, behaved so ill, that the king was forced to reëlect the ecclesiastics. The duke of Lancaster showed strong animosity to the clergy, and set every engine at work to ruin Wykeham. He impeached him of extortion, and of defrauding things, and obliged him to appear at the King's bench. He got such judges appointed as condemned him; and not satisfied with depriving him of all the temporalities of his bishopric, he advised Edward to banish him: but this prince rejected the proposal, and afterward restored to Wykeham all that he had been divested of. Richard II. was but eleven years old when Edward died; so that the duke of Lancaster had an easy opportunity of reviving the accusations against the bishop of Winchester; nevertheless Wykeham cleared himself. Then he founded two noble colleges, the one in Oxford, the other in Winchester. Whilst he was exerting his utmost endeavours to improve these two fine foundations, he was recalled to court, and in a manner forced to accept of the office of lord high-chancellor in 1389.—Having excellently discharged the duties of that employment for three years, he obtained leave to resign it, foreseeing the disturbances that were going to break out. Being returned to his church, he finished his college, and built there so magnificent a cathedral, that it almost equals that of St Paul's in London. He laid out several sums in things advantageous to the public and to the poor; notwithstanding which, in 1397 he was in great danger; for he and some others were impeached of high-treason in open parliament: however, he was again fully cleared. From that time till his death he kept quiet in his diocese, and there employed himself in all the duties of a good prelate. He died in 1404, in the 81st year of his age. William, the name of several kings of England. See England, No. 87—92, and Britain, No. 302. Fort William, a fortress in the Highlands of Scotland, erected in King William's reign, as was also a small town adjoining, called Maryburgh, in honour of his queen. It is situated in href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness-shire, on a narrow arm of the sea called Loch Eil, which by the completion of the Caledonian canal, will be united to the Western sea. Fort William is of a triangular form; having two bastions, and is capable of admitting a garrison of 800 men; but could not be defended against an attack, as it is commanded by several hills in the neighbourhood. William's Fort, is a factory of Asia belonging to the East-India Company, seated on one of the branches of the river Ganges, in the kingdom of Bengal. The fort was first built in the shape of an irregular tetragon of brick and mortar; and the town has nothing regular in it, because every one built a house as he liked best, and for his own convenience. The governor's house is within the fort, and is the best piece of architecture in these parts. Here there are also convenient lodgings for the factors and writers, with store-houses for the company's company's goods, and magazines for ammunition. About 50 yards from the fort is the church, which was originally built by the merchants. The town of Calcutta is contiguous, containing 50,000 inhabitants. It is governed by a mayor and aldermen, as most of the company's factories in the East Indies now are. In 1737 it was surprized by the nabob of Bengal, who took it, and put most of those that had made resistance into a place called the Black-Hole, where the greater number was suffocated. This nabob was afterwards killed, and another set up in his room, more friendly to the English; and the factory was re-established. E. Long. 86. o. N. Lat. 22. 27. See Calcutta. Sweet-WILLIAM. See Dianthus, Botany Index.

WILLIAMSBURG

Pages 407-407
