a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, and formerly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that state. It is situated between two creeks; one falling into James and the other into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> River. The distance of each landing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the town, which, with the disadvantage of not being able to bring up <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels, and the want of enterprise in the inhabitants, has occasioned its decay. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, designed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the Indians, but which, on account of their aversion to learning, never answered the purpose. It is 60 miles east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76° 30'. N. Lat. 37° 10'.

WILLIAMSTADT

Pages 407-407

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. It is a handsome strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the harbour is well frequented. It was built by William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> in 1585; and in 1732 belonged to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> of Friesland. The river near which it is built is called Butterfield <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Holland Diep; and is one of the bulwarks of the Dutch on the side of Brabant, where they always keep a garrison. This place made a gallant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> in 1793 against the French, who were obliged to raise the siege. It is 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom, and 12 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 30'. N. Lat. 51° 39'.

WILLIS

Pages 407-407

Dr Thomas, a celebrated English physician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Bodwin, in Wiltshire, in 1621, and studied at Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. When that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was garrisoned for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, he, among other scholars, bore arms for his majesty, and devoted his leisure hours to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic. The garrison of Oxford at length surrendering to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he applied himself to the practice of his profession; and soon rendered himself famous by his care and skill. He appropriated a room as an oratory for divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> according to the church of England, whither most of the loyalists in Oxford daily resorted. In 1662, he became Sedleian professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and the same year took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic. In 1664, he discovered the famous medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> at Altropp, near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRACKLEY">Brackley</a>. He was one of the first members of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, and soon made his name illustrious by his excellent writings. In 1666, after the fire of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he removed to Westminster; and his practice became greater than that of any of the physicians his contemporaries. Soon after his settlement in London, his only son Thomas falling into a consumption, he sent him to Montpelier in France for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; and it proved successful. His wife also labouring under the same disorder, he offered to leave the town; but she, not suffering him to neglect the means of providing for his family, died in 1670. He died at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in St Martin's in 1675, and was buried near her in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. Dr Willis was extremely modest and unambitious, and refused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. He was remarkably pious: As he rose early in the morning, that he might be present at divine service, which he constantly frequented before he visited his patients, he procured prayers to be read beyond the accustomed times while he lived; and at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> settled a stipend of 20l. per annum to continue them. He was a liberal benefactor to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> wherever he came, having from his early practice allotted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his profits to charitable uses. He was exact and regular in all his hours: and though his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of most of the great men of London, yet he was remarkable for his plainness, and his being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of little discourse, complaisance, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> society; but he was justly admired for his deep insight into natural and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental philosophy</a>, anatomy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>; for his successful practice; and for the elegance and purity of his Latin style. He wrote, 1. A treatise in English, intitled A plain and easy Method for preserving those that are well from the Infection of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">Plague</a>, and for curing such as are infected. 2. Several Latin works, which were collected and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, in 1682, in 2 vols 4to.

WILLUGHBY

Pages 407-407

Francis, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> historian, was the only son of Sir Francis Willughby, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>. He was fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> from his childhood, and held idleness in abhorrence; he being so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an economist with regard to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as not willingly to lose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> misapply the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, by which means he attained great skill in all branches of learning, and particularly in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. But to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of animals, which was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> neglected by his countrymen, he particularly applied himself; and for this purpose carefully read over what had been written on that subject by others. He then travelled several times over his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and afterwards into France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Germany, and the Low Countries, attended by his ingenious friend Mr John Ray. It is remarkable, that notwithstanding the advantages of birth, fortune, and parts, he was as humble as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the meanest fortune; was sober, temperate, and chaste; scrupulously <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>; so true to his word and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, that a man might venture his estate and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> upon it; so faithful and constant to his friend, as never to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> him when fortune frowned upon him; and remarkably pious, patient, and submissive to the divine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. This is the character given of him by Mr Ray, whose veracity none will doubt. This ingenious and learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> died in 1672, at 37 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; having impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> by his application. He wrote, 1. Ornithologiae libri tres, folio, which was afterwards translated into English, with an Appendix, by Mr Ray, in folio. 2. Historiae Piscium libri quattuor, folio. 3. Letters of Francis Willughby, Esq., added to Philosophical Letters between the learned Mr Ray and several of his correspondents, published, in 8vo, by William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>. 4. Several ingenious papers in the Philosophical Transactions.

WILMOT

Pages 407-408

John, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. the son of Henry earl of Rochester, was born in 1648. He was taught <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> and classical learning at the free-school at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BURFORD">Burford</a>; where he obtained a quick relish of the beauties of the Latin tongue, and afterwards became well versed in the authors of the Augustan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In 1659, he was admitted a nobleman of Wadham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, where he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. He afterwards travelled through France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and at his return was made one of the gentlemen of the bedchamber to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and comptroller of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a>. In 1665, he went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and was in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">Revenge</a>, commanded by Sir Thomas Tiddiman, when an attack was made on the port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>: during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> he showed the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and gained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation for courage; which he supported in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> expedition, but afterwards lost it in a private adventure with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Mulgrave. Before the earl of Rochester travelled, he had indulged in the most disorderly and intemperate way of living; at his return, however, he seemed to have got the better of it entirely. But falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the courtiers, who continually practised these excesses, he became so sunk in debauchery, that he was for five years together so given up to drinking, that during all that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was never cool enough to be master of himself. His violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and his disposition to extravagant mirth, carried him to great excesses. The first involved him in sensuality, and the other led him into many adventures and ridiculous frolics. Once disguising himself so that he could not be known by his nearest friends, he set up in Tower-street for an Italian mountebank, and there dispersed his nostrums for some weeks. He often disguised himself as a porter, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as a beggar, sometimes to follow a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a>; at other times, he would go about merely for diversion, in odd shapes; and acted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> so naturally, that he could not be known even by his friends. In short, by his constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> in wine, women, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> frolics, he entirely wore out an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> before he was 30 years of age. In October 1679, when recovering from a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which ended in a consumption, he was visited by Dr Burnet, upon an intimation that such a visit would be agreeable to him. Dr Burnet published an account of his conferences with Lord Rochester; in which it appears, that though he had lived the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a libertine and atheist, yet he died the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a penitent Christian. His death happened in 1680; since which time his poems have been various times printed, both separately and together; but when once he obtained the character of a lewd and obscene writer, every thing in that strain was ascribed to him; and thus many pieces not of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> have crept into the later editions of his works. The author of the Catalogue of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> and Noble Authors says, he was "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whom the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> were fond to inspire, and ashamed to avow, and who practised without the least reserve that secret which can make verses more read for their defects than their merits." Lord Rochester's Poems have much more obscenity than wit, more wit than <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and more poetry than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>." His writings, besides those already mentioned, are, A Satire against Mankind; Nothing, a poem; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, a tragedy; Fifty-four Letters to Henry Savile, and others; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> more to his Wife and Son; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> on his deathbed to Dr Burnet. He also left behind him several other papers, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Intrigues of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of Charles II.; but his mother, a very devout lady, ordered all his papers to be burned.

WILSON

Pages 408-409

THOMAS, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> bishop of Sodor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, was born in 1663, at Barton in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. He received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the county town, and from thence was removed to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. His allowance at the university was 20l. a-year; a sum, small as it may now appear, which was in those days sufficient for a sober youth in so cheap a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. His first intention was to have applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic; but from this he was diverted by Archdeacon Hewetson, by whose advice he dedicated himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> till the year 1686, when, on the 29th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, he was ordained deacon. The exact <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Mr Wilson's leaving Dublin is not known; but on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> disputes of those days, it was sooner than he intended. On the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, in the same year, he was licensed to the curacy of New Church in Winwick, of which Dr Sherlock, his maternal uncle, was rector. His stipend was no more than 30l. a-year; but being an excellent economist, and having the advantage of living with his uncle, this small income was not only sufficient to supply his own wants, but it enabled him to supply the wants of others; and for this purpose he set apart one-tenth of his income. In 1692 he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain to William <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his son James Lord Strange, with a salary of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILTON">Wilton</a> of £30l. a-year. He was soon after elected <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the alms-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LATHAM">Latham</a>, which brought him in £20l. a-year more. Having now an income far beyond his expectations, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his wishes, except as it increased his ability to do good, he set apart one-fifth of his income for pious uses, and particularly for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. In short, as his income increased, he increased the portion of it which was allotted to the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. At first he set apart a tenth, then a fifth, afterwards a third, and lastly, when he became a bishop, he dedicated the full half of his revenues to pious and charitable uses. He had not been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Lord Derby, before he was offered the valuable living of Buddleworth in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>; which he refused to accept, as being inconsistent with the resolves of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> against non-residence, Lord Derby choosing still to retain him as chaplain and tutor to his son. In 1697 he was promoted, not without some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of compulsion on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, to the bishopric of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Man; a preferment which he held 58 years. In 1698 he married <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Thomas Patten, Esq., of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRINGTON">Warrington</a>. By this lady, who survived her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> about six years, he had four children; none of whom survived him except the late Dr Wilton, prebendary of Wellsminster. "The annual receipts of the bishopric (says the author of his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>) did not exceed £300l. in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Some necessaries in his house, as spices, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, wine, books, &c., must be paid for with money; distrefted or shipwrecked mariners, and some other poor objects, required to be relieved with money; but the poor of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> were fed and clothed, and the house in general supplied from his demesnes, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, without money. The poor, who could weave or spin, found the best market at Bishop's-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, where they bartered the produce of their labour for corn. Tailors and shoemakers were kept in the house constantly employed, to make into garments or shoes that cloth or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> which his corn had purchased; and the aged and infirm were supplied according to their several wants. Mr Moore of Douglas informed the editor, that he was once witness to a pleasing and singular instance of the Bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to some aged poor of the island. As he was distributing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> to some whose eyesight failed them, Mr Moore expressed his surprife, as he well knew not one of them could read a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>. 'No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>,' said the Bishop with a smile, 'they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> enough for them; these spectacles will help them to thread a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, to mend their clothes, or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> need be, to keep themselves free from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>.' So <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> was the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his flock, that no temptation could seduce him from their service. He more than once refused the offer of an English bishopric. There is an anecdote of his lordship and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Fleury, which does great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to them both. The cardinal wanted much to see him, and sent over on purpose to inquire after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of his consecration, as they were the two oldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and he believed the poorest, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; at the same time inviting him to France. The bishop sent the cardinal an answer, which gave him so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of him, that the cardinal obtained an order that no French privateer should ravage the isle of Man. This good prelate lived till the year 1755, dying at the advanced age of 93. His works have lately been published in 2 vols 4to.

WILTON

Pages 409-409

a market town in Wiltshire, three miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>. It was once so considerable as to give <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. It formerly had 12 churches; and Odo, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to William I. was bishop of Wilton. Only one now remains. It sends members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the knights of the shire are chosen. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> manufactory of carpets, which are brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> perfection. Wilton is famous for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>'s seat, so well known through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> for its containing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> assemblage of the productions of the greatest and most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> masters in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>.—Two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are held here annually.

WILTSHIRE

Pages 409-409

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, and on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Hampshire. The length amounts to 30 miles; its breadth to 30; and its circumference to 140. It contains 29 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, 23 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 304 parishes, and about 18,510 souls. Besides two members for the shire, and two for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, each of the following towns sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILTON">Wilton</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWNTON">Downton</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HINDON">Hindon</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEYTESBURY">Heytesbury</a>, Welbury, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALNE">Calne</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol7.html#article-DEVIZES">Devizes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIPPENHAM">Chippenham</a>, Malmesbury, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRICKLADE">Cricklade</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Bedwin, Ludgershall, Old Sarum, Wooton-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASSET">Basset</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this county is very healthy, not only in the more low and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> parts, but also on the hills. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the vales is very rich, and produces corn and grass in great plenty. The beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> in the south yield the finest pasture for sheep, with which they are overspread. The greatest disadvantage the county labours under is want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, as there are no coal-pits, and but little wood. This county is noted for great quantities of very fine cheese, and for its manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cloth, to which it was invited by the great plenty and fineness of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. Besides a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lesser streams, it is watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Ifis, Kennet, Upper and Lower Avon, Willy, Burne, and Nadder, which are well stored with fish.

WINCHELSEA

Pages 409-409

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, which has no market, but has one fair on May 14th for cattle and pedlars <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. It was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, at least the old town, which was swallowed up by the ocean in 1250. It is now dwindled to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> place, though it retains its privileges, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is seated on a rocky cliff, on an inlet of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and had a haven, now choked up. It had 18 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches, now reduced to one. The market-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is in the midst of the town, from whence run four paved streets, at the end of which are four ways, which had formerly buildings on each side for a considerable distance. It is two miles south-west of Rye, and 71 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is governed by a mayor and jurats, though it has but about 70 houses. Three of the gates are still standing, but much decayed. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 44. N. Lat. 50. 58. Winchelsea, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Countess of, a lady of excellent genius, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, was maid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James II. and was afterwards married to Heneage, second son of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Winchelsea. One of the most considerable of the countesses of Winchelsea's poems was that on the Spleen.

WINCHESTER

Pages 409-410

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> in England. It is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, supposed to have been built several centuries before Christ. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called it Venta Belgarum, the Britons Caer Givent, and the Saxons Witanacaster; whence came the present name. It stands upon the river Itchin, in a bottom surrounded with chalky hills; and is generally allowed to have been a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Romans. Some of the first converts to Christianity are supposed to have lived here. In the castle, near the west gate, many of the Saxon kings anciently kept their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> was founded by Kenegulfe, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Mercians; but there were many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and places for their worship here, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pile, and has a venerable look, but is not very elegant. Besides the tombs, there are many curious pieces of workmanship in it; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are, 1. The font, erected in the time of the Saxons. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of James I. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. 3. The bishop's throne. 4. The stalls of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and prebendaries. 5. The screen to the choir and altar. 6. The pavement, inlaid with marble of diverse colours, in various figures. 7. The altar-piece, reckoned the noblest in England. 8. The paintings in the windows, especially the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> east window. At the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a>, every traveller that knocks at the door may claim a manchet of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and a cup of beer; of which a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is provided every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> for that purpose. This hospital was intended for the maintenance of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and 30 pensioners, but only 14 are now maintained in it; and the master enjoys a revenue of 80l. a-year. This city is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in compass, and almost surrounded with a wall of flint; has six gates, large suburbs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> clean streets; but the private houses are in general but ordinary, many of them being very old. The city is interpenetrated with a great many gardens, which contribute to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and healthiness. The corporation consists of a mayor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, recorder, aldermen, two coroners, two bailiffs, 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men, a town clerk, four constables, and four sergeants at mace; and the city gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of marquis to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bolton. A Roman highway leads from hence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTON">Alton</a>; and went formerly, as it is thought, from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The charming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> in the neighbourhood contribute greatly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of the inhabitants. The river Itchin is navigable for barges from hence to Southampton. W. Long. 1. 21. N. Lat. 51. 5.

WINCKLEMAN

Pages 410-411

ABBE JOHN, was born at Stendall, in the old Marche of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, in 1718. His father was a shoemaker. This wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, to all appearance destined by his birth to superintend a little school in an obscure town of Germany, raised himself to the office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of antiquities in the Vatican. After having been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years professor in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Seehaufen near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALZWEDEL">Salzwedel</a>, he went into <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, where he resided seven years more, and was librarian to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Bunau at Nothenitz. When he left this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, 1754, he went to Dresden, where he formed an acquaintance with the ablest artists, and particularly with M. Oester, an excellent painter, and one of the best draughtsmen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In that year he abjured Wincklemanism, and embraced the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. In September 1755, he set out for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and arrived at Rome in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object was to see the Vatican library, and to examine the ruins of Herculaneum. Mr Winckleman carried with him into Italy a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and art, which led him instantly to admire the masterpieces of the Vatican, and with which he began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> them. He soon increased his knowledge; and it was not till after he had thus purified his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and conceived an idea of ideal beauty, which led him into the greatest secrets of art, that he began to think of the explanation of other monuments, in which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning could not fail to distinguish him. His erudition enabled him to fill up his principal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the "<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Art." In 1756 he planned his "Restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">Statues</a>," and a larger <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the Taste of the Greek Artists; and designed an account of the galleries of Rome and Italy, beginning with a volume on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELVEDERE">Belvedere</a> statues, in the manner of Richardson, who, he says, only ran over Rome. He also intended a history of the corruption of taste in art, the restoration of statues, and an illustration of the obscure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. All these different essays led him to his "History of Art," and his "Monumenti Inediti." It must, however, be confessed, that the first of these works has not all the clearness and precision that might be expected in its general plan and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of its parts and objects; but it has enlarged and extended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> both of antiquaries and collectors. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the gems and sulphurs of the Stolz cabinet contributed not a little to extend Mr Winckleman's knowledge. Few persons have opportunities of contemplating such vast collections. The engravings of Lippet and Count Caylus are all that many can arrive at. Mr Winckleman's Monumenti Inediti, of which he had begun the third volume 1767, seem to have secured him the esteem of antiquaries. Had he lived, we should have had a work <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> wished for; a complete collection of the bas-reliefs discovered from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Bartoli to the present, the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which are in the possession of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Albani. When Cardinal Albani succeeded to the place of librarian of the Vatican, he endeavoured to get a place for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> for Winckleman, who refused a canonry, because he would not take the tonsure. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Saxony gave him, 1761, un solicited, the place of Counsellor Richter, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> cabinet of medals and antiquities at Dresden. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the abbé Venuti, 1762, he was appointed president of the antiquities of the apostolic-chamber, with power over all discoveries and exportations of antiquities and pictures. This is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, with an income of 160 feudi per annum. He had a prospect of the place of president of antiquities in the Vatican, going to be created at 16 feudi per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and was named corresponding member of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> offered him, by Col. Quintus Icilius, the place of librarian and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of his cabinet of medals and antiquities, void by the death of M. Gautier de la Croze, with a handsome appointment. He made no scruple of accepting the offer; but when it came to the pope's ears, he added an appointment out of his own purse, and kept him at Rome. In April 1768, he left Rome to go with M. Cava- ceppi over Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. When he came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, he was so pleased with the reception he met with, that he made a longer stay there than he had in- tended. But, being suddenly seized with a secret un- easiness and extraordinary desire to return to Rome, he set out for Italy, putting off his visits to his friends in Germany to a future opportunity. As he passed through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIESTE">Trieste</a>, he was affiliated, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 8, 1768, by a wretch named Arcangeli, a native of Campiglio, a town in the territory of Pioltola, with whom he had made an ac- quaintance on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>. This miscreant had been con- demned for a robbery to work in letters four years, and then to be banished the Austrian territories, on an oath never to return. He had obtained a mitigation of one of his sentences, and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; but, chang- ing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> backwards and forwards, he was so re- duced in circumstances that he at length took up his lodgings at the inn to which the Abbé happened to come. Arcangeli paid such affidavit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to him, that he entirely gained his confidence; and having been fa- voured with a sight of the valuable presents which he had received at Vienna, formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> and rob him. He bought a new sharp <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> on purpose; and as the Abbé (who had in the most friendly manner invited him to Rome) was sitting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>- ly in the morning, he threw a rope over his head, and before he could disengage himself, stabbed him in five different places. The Abbé had still strength to get down to the ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, and call for help; and being laid on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> in the midst of the most violent pain, he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> sufficient to receive the last sacraments, and to make his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, in which he appointed Cardinal Alexander Albani his residuary legatee, and expired in the afternoon. The murderer was soon after appre- hended; and executed on the wheel opposite the inn, June 26. Abbé Winckleman was a middle-sized man; he had a very low forehead, sharp nose, and little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> hollow eyes, which gave him an aspect rather gloomy than otherwise. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he had any thing graceful in his physiog- nomy, it was his mouth. A fiery and impetuous dispo- sition often threw him into extremes. Naturally enthu- siastic, he often indulged an extravagant imagination; but as he possessed a strong and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> judgement, he knew how to give things a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and intrinsic value. In conse- quence of this turn of mind, as well as a neglected educa- tion, a cautious reserve was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> he little knew. If he was bold in his decisions as an author, he was still more so in his conversation, and has often made his friends tremble for his temerity. If ever man knew what friendship was, that man was Mr Winckleman, who regularly practised all his duties; and for this rea- son he could boast of having friends among persons of every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and condition. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">WIND</a> is a sensible agitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, oc- casioned by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> flowing from one place to another. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a>. Hot WINDS. See SAMIEL. WIND-Flower. See ANEMONY, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. WIND-Mill, a kind of mill, the internal parts of which are much the same with those of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mill: from which, however, it differs, in being moved by the impulse of the wind upon its sails <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vanes, which are to be considered as a wheel in axis. See MECHA- NICS Index. WIND-Gage. See Wind-GAGE. WIND-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">Galls</a>. See Farriery Index. WIND-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">Gun</a>. See AIR-GUN, under SCIENCE, Amuse- ments of. Instruments for measuring the strength, velocity, &c. of the WIND. See Wind-GAGE, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANEMOMETER">ANEMOMETER</a> and ANE-

WINDLASS

Pages 411-412

in a ship, is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in small ships, placed upon the deck, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> abaft the foremast. It is made of a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight feet <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, in form WIN form of an axletree, whose length is placed horizontally upon two pieces of wood at the ends thereof, and upon which it is turned about by the help of handspikes put into holes made for that purpose. This instrument serves for weighing anchors, or hoisting of any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in or out of the ship, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> purchase much more than any capstan, and that without any danger to those that heave; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in heaving the windlass about, any of the handspikes should happen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, the windlass would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of itself.

WINDOW

Pages 412-412

an aperture <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> open <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the wall of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to let in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, No. 78. The word is Welch, uyn <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DOR">dor</a>, signifying the passage for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Window is yet principally denominated windor in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>; i.e., wind-door, or the passage for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as that for people was peculiarly called the door. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of glass became general, which was not till towards the end of the 12th century, the windows in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> seem generally to have been composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. Properly prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, this forms no contemptible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against the intrusions of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and makes no incompetent opening for the admission of the light. It is still used by our architects for the temporary windows of unfinished houses, and not unfrequently for the regular ones of our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> shops. But some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings we may reasonably suppose to have been windowed in a superior manner. They could, however, be furnished merely with lattices of wood or sheets of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, as these two remained the only furniture of our cathedrals nearly to the eighth century; and the lattices <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in some of the meaner <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Lancashire to the 18th; and in many districts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and many of the adjoining parts of England, are in use even to the present moment. These seem all to have been fixed in frames that were called coplamenta, and now therefore coplements in Wales and Lancashire.

WINDSOR

Pages 412-412

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, 22 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, most remarkable for the magnificent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> castle situated there on an eminence, which commands the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for many miles, the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> running at the foot of the hill. The knights of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a> are installed in the royal chapel here. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 36. N. Lat. 51. 30.

WINDWARD

Pages 412-412

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, denotes anything towards that point from whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows, in respect of a ship: thus windward-tide, is the tide which runs against the wind.

WINE

Pages 412-417

an agreeable spirituous liquor, produced by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> from those vegetable substances that contain saccharine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. A very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vegetable substances may be made to afford wine, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, currants, mulberries, elders, cherries, apples, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, beans, peas, turnips, radishes, and even grass itself. Hence, under the clasps of wines <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vinous liquors, come not only wines, absolutely so called, but also ale, cyder, &c. Wine, however, is in a more particular manner appropriated to the liquor drawn from the fruit of the vine. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of making wine is as follows: When the grapes are ripe, and the saccharine principle is developed, they are then pressed, and the juice which flows out is received in vessels of a proper capacity, in which the fermentation appears, and proceeds in the following manner: At the end of several days, and frequently after a few hours, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the grapes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the liquid, and temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which the operation is performed, a movement is produced in the liquor, which continually increases; the volume of the fluid increases; it becomes turbid and oily; carbonic acid is discharged, which fills all the unoccupied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the vessel, and the temperature rises to the 72.5th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. At the end of several days these tumultuous motions subside, the mists falls, the liquid becomes clearer, and is found to be less saccharine, more odorant, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> of the ardent spirit upon the colouring matter of pellicle of the grape. The wine is usually taken out of the fermenting vessels at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when all the phenomena of fermentation have subsided. When the mists is settled, the colour of the liquor is well developed, when it has become clear, and its heat has disappeared; it is put into casks, where, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> infensible fermentation, the wine is clarified, its principles combine more perfectly together, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell become more and more developed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this fermentation be stopped or suffocated, the gaseous principles are retained, and the wine is brisker, and more of the nature of must. It appears, from the interesting experiments of the Marquis de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULLION">Bullion</a>, that the vinous fermentation does not take place unless tartar be present. The causes of imperfect fermentation are the following: 1. If the heat be too little, the fermentation imperceptibly languishes, the saccharine and oily matters are not sufficiently elaborated, and the wine is insipid and sweet. 2. If the saccharine body be not sufficiently abundant, as happens in rainy seasons, the wine is weak, and the mucilage, which predominates, causes it to become sour by its decomposition. 3. If the juice be too watery, concentrated and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> must is added. 4. If the saccharine principle be not sufficiently abundant, the defect may be remedied by the addition of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. Macquer has proved that excellent wine may be made of verjuice and sugar; and M. de Bullion has made wine at Bellejames, with the verjuice of his vine rows and moist sugar. There have been many disputes to determine whether grapes should be pressed with the stalks or without. This depends on the nature of the fruit. When they are highly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with saccharine and mucilaginous matter, the stalk corrects the insipidity of the wine by its bitter principle; but when, on the contrary, the juice is not too sweet, the stalk renders it drier, and very rough. The colouring principle of wine is of a resinous nature, and is contained in the pellicle of the grape; and matter of the fluid is not coloured until the wine is formed; for wine, until then there is nothing which can dissolve it: and hence it is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine may be made of red grapes, when the juice of the grape is expressed, and the husk thrown away. If wine be evaporated, the colouring principle remains in the residue, and may be extracted by spirit of wine. Old wines lose their colour; a pellicle being precipitated, which is either deposited on the sides of the bottles, or falls to the bottom. If wine be exposed to the heat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the colouring matter is detached in a pellicle, which falls to the bottom; when the vessel is opened, the discolouring... The vinous fermentation has been examined with great accuracy by M. Lavoisier. According to him, the vegetable juice of which wine is to be made consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a>, hydrogen, and carbone, combined with one another in different proportions, so as to form chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and sugar. The fermentation produces a separation of the elements, and a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of them; a quantity of the oxygen and carbone combine and fly off in the state of carbonic acid; part of the carbone, oxygen, and hydrogen, combine first with each other, and then all together, to form <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>; another part forms acetic acid; the water still remains, and a residuum falls to the bottom composed of the three elements combined in other proportions. The different kinds of wines produced in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and other parts of the world are many; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of them and their qualities are well known: a catalogue of them would serve no purpose here. We shall, however, subjoin a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the quantities of the ingredients of the principal kinds from Neumann's <a class="xref" 6 0 0 4 0 0 2 0 | 9 3 2 0 | | | | Red wine | 2 0 0 0 7 0 0 3 0 | 7 0 0 0 | | | | White | 2 0 0 0 7 0 0 3 0 | 7 0 0 0 | | | The colour of wine is frequently <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>; a deep red is almost always the effect of artificial additions, as of the red woods, elder berries, bilberries, &c. In France no secret is made of these practices, the colouring matters being publicly thrown out after they have been used. It is well known to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice among Adulterators—wine-coopers, innkeepers, and other dealers in wines, to mix adulterate bad wine in order to conceal its defects: if, wine, for instance, the wine be foul, they throw into it a quantity of sugar of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, which entirely takes away the four taste. For similar purposes <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> is often mixed with wine. Such substances, however, are well known to be extremely pernicious to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; it becomes of importance therefore to be able to detect them whenever they happen to be contained in wine. Several chemists who have turned their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to this subject, have furnished us with tests for this purpose. To discover lead dissolved in wine, boil together in a To detect pint of water an ounce of quicklime and half an ounce lead in of flour of brimstone; and when the liquor, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> wine, be of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, pour it into a bottle, and Wotford's cork it up for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. A few drops of this liquor being Chemical dropped into a glass of wine or cider containing lead, will vol. iii. change the whole into a colour more or less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, according to the quantity of lead which it contains. If the wine be wholly free from lead, it will be rendered turbid by the liquor, but the colour will be rather a dirty white than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> brown. By this test, however, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> is also precipitated when dissolved in wine, and is apt to be taken for lead; a mistake which has ruined several honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. The following test is therefore preferable, as not liable to the same inconvenience. Take equal parts of calcined oyster-shells and crude Another fulphur in fine powder, and put them in a crucible, methods which put into a fire, and raise the heat suddenly till it has been exposed to a white heat for 15 minutes. Then take it out, let it cool, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the ingredients to powder, and put them into a well corked bottle. To prepare the test liquor, put 20 grains of this powder together with 120 grains of cream of tartar, and put them into a strong bottle, fill it up with water, boil it for an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and let it cool. Cork the bottle immediately, and shake it from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time. After some hours repose, decant off the clear liquor into an ounce vial, having first put 22 drops of muriatic acid into each vial. Cork these vials accurately with a little wax mixed up with a little turpentine. One part of this liquor, mixed with three parts of suspected wine, will discover the presence of the smallest quantity of lead or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, by a very sensible black precipitate, and of arsenic by an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> precipitate: but will have no effect on iron, if there be any; the presence of which, however, may be ascertained by adding a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, which will turn the liquor black if there be any iron. Pure wine remains limpid after the addition of this liquor. As this subject is of importance, we shall add Mr. State of Fourcroy's observations on the state in which lead exists in wine, and on the methods of discovering its presence: "Of the different principles which compose wine, there was no doubt (says he) but that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> were the only ones which were capable of dissolving oxide (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a>) of lead. But was it the tartarous acid always contained in larger or smaller quantity in wine, or the acetic acid developed in those which have become sharp, and which there is a greater temptation to sweeten?" <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> Wine. Wine had proved to me that the acidulous tartrate of potash, or the cream of tartar, takes oxide of lead from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACETOUS">acetous</a> acid, and a precipitate of tartrate of lead is formed; the pure tartaric acid prepared in Scheele's method produces the same effect. In order to understand how the sharp wine which contains these two acids can hold the oxide of lead in solution, I made the experiments which gave me the following results: 1. The acidulous tartrate (cream tart.) has no sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> upon the oxides of lead. 2. The pure tartaric acid has a slight action upon the oxides, and forms on their surface a little tartrate of lead (tartrated lead), in a white powder. 3. Wine which only contains the tartaric acidule, would not have any action upon the semi-vitrous oxide of lead or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a>. 4. Sharp wine which we attempt to sweeten by this oxide of lead, acts first upon it by the acetous acid it contains. 5. When this acetite of lead is formed, the tartaric acid precipitates it in the form of tartrate of lead: this is proved by the precipitate which the solution of the acetite of lead or sugar of lead forms in the wine. 6. But the acetous acid, if it be in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enough quantity, redissolves the tartrate of lead in the wine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as distilled water would. Bergman has pointed out this solution of tartrate of lead in acetous acid for distinguishing the tartaric <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> from the sulphat of lead (vitriol of lead). 7. As this solution of tartrate of lead in the acetous acid is much quicker, and more easy in sharp wines than in distilled water and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, it is probable that the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> depends upon the citric and malic acids which I have found in wine, and which I shall take notice of again on another occasion. 8. Litharge wine then, or wine sweetened with lead, contains tartrate dissolved in the acetous acid, and perhaps at the same time in the malic and citric acids. "It was necessary afterwards to know the properties of this combination. What experience has taught me is as follows: I particularly examined the tartrate of lead and its solution in acetous acid. The tartrate of lead is scarcely at all soluble in water; it is in the form of powder, or of small white grains which have no sensible taste; when it is dissolved in vinegar, the vinegar is softened, its sharpness is diminished remarkably, and the solution takes a flight twelfth taste, much less strong than that of the pure acetite of lead. This taste proves that the union of the tartrate of lead with vinegar is not only a solution like that of salt in water, by which the properties of the salt are not changed, but a combination which gives occasion to new properties. It is a kind of a triple salt, different from those we have hitherto known, formed of two acids and of one base; whereas the other triple salts described hitherto are composed of one acid and two bases. I name this new triple salt aceto-tartrate of lead. The acetous acid adheres to it more than water in a common solution: what is remarkable in this combination is, that the two acids appear to adhere to the base with an equal force, although they have a different <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> for it: nothing is necessary to produce this equilibrium, but to unite first the oxide of lead with the acid to which it adheres the most strongly, and afterwards to put this first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> in contact with the weaker acid. "It was necessary, in order to discover easy and certain methods of ascertaining the presence of lead in wine, to examine with care the properties and phenomena of the decompositions of the aceto-tartrate of lead. Fixed alkalis and ammoniac (volatile alkali) precipitate from this salt an oxide of lead, which is of a grayish white colour; but as they occasion a precipitate in pure wine, they cannot be of any use. The fulphuric (vitriolic) acid decomposes the aceto-tartrate of lead, and forms with it instantly sulphate of lead; which being very little soluble, and very heavy, is precipitated. The oxalic, or pure saccharine acid, and the acidulous oxalate, or the salt of tartar of the shops, likewise decompose this salt, and take from it the lead. The oxalate of lead is precipitated in great abundance: these two acids, the fulphuric and oxalic acids, not producing any precipitate in pure wine, are very proper to show the presence of lead in wine. The sulphate and oxalate of lead, when they are precipitated from wine, are coloured, whereas they are very white when they are formed in distilled water; but their red or brown colour does not prevent us from discovering them by a very simple method. If the precipitates be collected with care, and are cautiously heated upon a coal with a blow-pipe, they <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, become white, exhale vapours, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> successively through the states of the red and yellow oxides of lead, and at length are reduced into metallic globules at the instant they are perceived to be agitated by a very evident effervescence: if we cease to blow at this instant, we obtain globules upon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>. In order to this, it is necessary, however, that the charcoal be <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and be not cracked, and that we should not have blowed too strongly; otherwise the globules would be absorbed, and would disappear. The sulphate of lead requires a longer time to be reduced than the oxalate of the same metal, and there is a greater hazard of losing the metallic particles, which, beside, are in small quantity. "To these two first processes, already sufficiently certain of themselves, I wished to be able to add one which might be capable of pointing out instantly the presence of lead, by an appearance belonging exclusively to this metal, and which might unite to this advantage that of manifesting very small quantities of it. Distilled water impregnated with fulphurated hydrogenous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, or hepatic gas, extracted from solid alkaline fulphurites (lixivers of sulphur) by acids, presented me with these properties. This solution blackens very deeply that of the aceto-tartrate of lead, and renders \( \frac{1}{10} \) of this salt in water or in wine very sensible. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of this reactive is such, that we may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> litharge wine with a sufficient quantity of water to take away almost entirely the colour of the wine, and this reactive will still produce a very manifest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>. The fulphurated water has, besides the advantage not to occasion any change in the wines which do not contain a metallic substance, and it is not precipitated by the acids of wine, like the solutions of alkaline fulphurites. In order to procure this reactive pure, it is necessary to prepare it at the instant of the experiment, by receiving in a vial full of distilled water, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> upon a shelf of a small hydro-pneumatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, filled with distilled water, the fulphurated hydrogenous gas, separated from the solid fulphurite of potash by the fulphuric or muriatic acid, and first filtered through water in another vial; when the second vial contains the third of its volume of the fulphurated hydrogenous gas, the gas is shaken strongly with the water, which fills the two-thirds of the Wine. the vial; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> is over, the test liquor is prepared. This re-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> changes very quickly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>: it is necessary to make it the moment it is to be employed, and to keep it in a vessel quite full and well corked. If there were any fear that the black colour and the precipitation by the gaseous sulphurated water should not be sufficient to prove the presence of lead in spirituous liquors, I would observe, that this fear would be diminished by employing the three re-actives mentioned in this memoir, and by depending only on the correspondent effects of these three re-actives: but all suspicion would be removed, by reducing the three precipitates by the blow-pipe, and obtaining globules of lead from each of them." Some years ago, the Academy of Lyons proposed the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-question: What is the best method of ascertaining the presence and the quantity of alum dissolved in wine, especially in very deep coloured red wine? The prize was gained by M. J. S. Beraud. From his experiments, it appears that a mixture of lime-water and wine in any proportion whatever, will at the end of 12 or 15 hours furnish a quantity of crystals, which may be separated by filtration, and that these crystals will be easiest discovered when the quantities of wine and lime-water are equal; but that wine containing alum dissolved in it, will not form crystals when mixed with lime-water, but merely deposits a muddy sediment. To know therefore whether any wine contains alum or not, we have only to mix a small quantity of it with lime-water: if crystals are formed, it contains no alum; if not, it does. Again, if wine contains alum, the residue that remains after filtration will, as it dries, split into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRILATERAL">quadrilateral</a> segments, which will detach themselves from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> which contains them; but if the wine contains no alum, the residue, after it is dry, will remain united and attached to the paper. If one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of wine and two-thirds of a measure of lime-water deposit crystals, we are certain that if the wine contains alum, the proportion of that alum to the wine will be less than 1 to 1152; if, when equal parts of wine and lime-water are mixed, no crystals are deposited, we may be sure that more than 1/400th part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of wine consists of alum. A great proportion of the wine consumed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> has always discouraged the importation of French wines by heavy taxes. We are not sure how far such conduct is founded on good policy, as the French wines are confessedly the best, and might be the cheapest; but such is the jealousy and enmity that has always subsisted between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and France, that both nations have been contented to injure themselves, provided they could do a greater injury to their neighbours. Besides, the advantages which Britain derives from the Portugal trade are very great, and it would not be easy perhaps to secure them on any other terms. It may be worth while to insert here a few directions about the treatment of wines after they have been imported into this country.—On landing, the least they are exposed the better; for they are affected by the seasons, and more or less by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and April are the proper times for shipping wines from France, and they will be landed in England and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in the same degree of temperature. The great art in keeping wines is to prevent their fretting, which is done by keeping them in the same degree of heat. In <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, the wines in Bordeaux are subject to changes that may be dangerous, if not prevented by necessary rackings: these changes are solely the effects of the seasons. If wines are chilled, and of course turn foul, from being shipped and landed in cold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, they will soon recover by putting them in a warm vault, well covered with sawdust. As soon as they are in the vault, they ought to be covered up. But if shipped and landed in summer, if the smallest degree of fermentation be found on them, it will be requisite to dip the bung cloths in brandy, and leave the bungs loose for some days, to give it time to cool; and if in a fortnight or three weeks the fermentation do not cease, and the wine become bright, it will be proper to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> it (matching the hogsheads well with brimstone), and force it with the whites of eight eggs. If it then becomes fine, bung it tight, and let it remain so until it is bottled.
