If wines new landed are wanted soon for the bottle, it will be necessary to force them immediately, and let them remain bunged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> for at least a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, to recover from the forcing, or if two months the better; for wines bottled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> order come much sooner into drinking than if bottled when flat, which all wines are after forcing. Wine must never be bottled the least foul, which produces a tendency to fret; and if bottled in this state, will never come in order, but may possibly be lost: for this there is no remedy but repeated rackings; and care must be taken (after rinding the hogsheads well and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> them) to burn a good piece of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> in them. This cools the wine, and there is no danger of hurting the colour, for it recovers it in a little time: but if it did, it is absolutely necessary; for if wine is suffered to continue on the fret, it will wear itself to nothing. Wines bottled in good order may be fit to drink in six months; but they are not in perfection before twelve: from that to two years they may continue so; but it would be improper to keep them longer, for wines in general have not the body they had formerly, from the vines being too much forced. It sometimes happens that wines feckless and stubborn will not fall with one or even two forcings. It will then be proper to give them five or six gallons of good strong wine, and force them with the whites of a dozen eggs, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-spoonful of sand produced from sawing-marble, or a small spoonful of fine salt. Bottled wine in winter should be well covered with sawdust, and if the vaults are cold and damp, strew it deep on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>; if sawdust is thrown upon the hogsheads, and their sides are bedded some inches thick, it will keep them from the fret. The same treatment is to be regarded with white wines, except that they require to be higher matched, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSCAT">Muscat</a> wines; such as Frontignac, Beziers, &c., which being often sweetened with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, are very subject to fret; and these only frequent rackings, with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of brimstone, can cool. Hermitage, from not being sufficiently dried, and possessing more richness than claret, is also very liable to come on the fret, and will require much the same treatment as the Muscat wines. Attention should be had to bottle in fine weather, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; but to avoid cold or frosty weather. The months of April and October are favourable. The best time to bottle port wine is four years. Wine years after the vintage, and to keep them two years in bottle before you begin to use them. When wines are racked, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEES">lees</a> immediately passed through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> bags into close-necked jars, and directly bottled, there will be very little loss by rackings, as the wine when fine may serve for filling up. When wines are destined for warm climates, it may be proper to rinse the hogheads with brandy; and in bottling many rinse the bottles and corks with it. Wines that have remained a certain time (three or four months) in a vault, and made less or more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">lee</a>, ought never to be sent into the country without first racking them, otherwise they may be liable to fret; and if bottled in that state, may risk being lost. Wines which may be ordered for immediate drinking will be forced on the shipping, and in a few weeks after they are landed will be fit for the bottle. The forcings proper for claret are the whites of a dozen eggs, beat up with a tea-spoonful of fine salt, and well worked with a forcing rod. Take care to use no bad <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. This is for one hoghead. The forcing for white wine is isinglass dissolved in wine. One ounce is sufficient for two hogheads. No salt is to be used in forcing the white wines. See Croft on Wines, 8vo, 1788. We shall insert here the following receipt for making raisin wine.—To a 20 gallon vessel take 100 pounds of raisins; pick off the stalks, chop them coarsely, and put them into an open tub more wide than deep. Add two parts in three of the water to them, and let them stand 15 days, stirring them well every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Then strain and press them, putting aside the liquor that runs from them. Add the remainder of the water to the raisins that have thus been pressed, and let it stand upon them one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, frequently stirring them as before. Then press off the liquor, and add it to what you first collected; putting both runnings together into your vessel, together with one quart of brandy. To colour it, burn three-fourths of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of sugar into a small quantity of the liquor, and add this to the wine. When the liquor in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> has done rising, stop the vessel close, and let it stand till fit to be bottled. The greater the quantity which the vessel holds, and the longer it is kept in the wood, the better will it be. As some of the hints for making wines in Champagne may be useful in the manufacture of the wines of this country, we insert the following abridged account of the different processes that are followed in making white and red champagne. Great care is necessary for making white wine. The ripest bunches must be carefully gathered, freed from rotten, dry, and bruised grapes, put into large baskets covered with a cloth to keep them from the sun, carried to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, and kept there till the evening, when they are to be speedily pressed. The grapes being laid on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the press, they are covered with three or four layers of flat <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the press turned. The juice having run for four or five minutes, the press is turned backward, the stones removed, the grapes which have protruded thrust into the heap, the stones replaced, and the press turned again. The juice from three of such presses, which will not require an hour, is put by itself for the best wine into a vat, where it is left all night to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>. The next morning this juice is poured off from the sediment, and put into new well-ringed casks. In these it ferments violently at first, but afterwards imperceptibly, till about the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> it becomes fine, having gone through all the stages of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEPURATION">depuration</a>. It is then racked off in dry weather, on a clear frosty day, and fined with isinglass. About a pound is sufficient for 40 puncheons. The isinglass being dissolved is well beaten, diluted with wine taken from the cask, then poured into it, and the whole well stirred by an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> introduced at the bung-hole. The wine thus left to settle ferments slightly again, till it be stopped by the cold weather, or by time. In a month or six weeks it is racked off again, and has another fining with half the quantity of isinglass. For making red wine, the grapes are gathered with the same precautions as for making white, taking only the black grapes. These are bruised in particular vessels, by men treading on them with strong wooden shoes; part of the stalks are thrown away, and the must is left in covered vessels to ferment sufficiently to extract the colouring matter from the pellicles. In some years, three or four days are sufficient; in others it requires 10, 15, or even 20. When the fermentation begins, the hulls and stalks are forced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> so as to be covered with the must, either by means of strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> pegs, or, which is better, by a couple of strong men going into the vat, and well treading and mixing its contents. When the air above the vat extinguishes a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, the stalks and hulls rise forcibly, whatever pains be taken frequently to sink them, that the must may not acquire a disagreeable taste; the contents of the vat experience a degree of ebullition, and the colouring matter is decomposed. The fermentation must be made to stop here, that the wine may not acquire a hard taste, which even time cannot destroy. About the end of December, when the fermentation has ceased, the wine is racked off from the lees; about the middle of May it is racked off again; the barrels are fresh hooped, and the wine is put into the cellar. When it is to be sent to the consumer, it is racked a third time; the whites of five or six fresh eggs are well beaten up in a pint of water, for every puncheon holding 240 bottles. Good red champagne will keep in bottles from six to twelve years. **Wine-Press**, a machine contrived to squeeze the juice out of grapes, and consisting of several pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, variously disposed, which compose three bodies of timber-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, closely united to the axis, which serves as a swing whereby it may be moved by the vice. Of these there are different sizes as well as different constructions; for an account of which, illustrated by figures, see Miller's Gardener's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, article **Wine-Press**. **Spirit of Wine**, or **Alcohol**, a name given by chemists to every ardent spirit produced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. See **Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>**. **Wing**, that part of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, insect, &c. whereby it is enabled to fly. See **Bird** and **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>**. **Wings**, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, are the two flanks or extremes of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, ranged in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left sides thereof. **Winter**, one of the four seasons or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the year. See **Season**, &c. Winter commences on the day when the sun's distance from the zenith of the place is greatest, and ends on the day day when its distance is at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> between the greatest and least. Under the equator, the winter as well as other seasons returns twice every year; but all other places have only one winter in the year: which in the northern hemisphere begins when the sun is in the tropic of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRICORN">Capricorn</a>, and in the southern hemisphere when in the tropic of Cancer; so that all places in the same hemisphere have their winter at the same time. **WINTER-Berry.** See Physalis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. **WINTERA,** a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the clas of polyandria, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 12th order, Holaraceae. See Botany and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> Index.

WINTON

Pages 417-419

Andrew,** a Scottish poet and historian of the 14th century; but very little is known of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He was a canon regular of St Andrews, and was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Serf in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Loch Leven in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KINROSS_SHIRE">Kinross-shire</a>; for in the chartulary of the priory of St Andrews there are several public instruments of Andrew Winton, as prior of Loch Leven. They are dated between the years 1395 and 1413, so that Winton must have been <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Barbour, whose merits are on several occasions celebrated by him. Winton is best known as the author of the *Orygynale Cronykil of Scotland.* This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was undertaken at the request of Sir John Wemyss, the ancestor of the noble family of that name. It remained neglected for several centuries, but in 1795 a splendid edition of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it relative to Scottish affairs, was published by Mr Macpherson. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Winton's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is unknown; but, as he mentions the death of Robert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>, which happened in 1420, the historian must have been alive at that time. **WIRE,** a piece of metal drawn through the hole of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> into a thread of a fineness answerable to the hole it passed through. Wires are frequently drawn so fine as to be wrought along with other threads of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> drawn into wire are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and iron. Gold-wire is made of cylindrical ingots of silver, covered over with a skin of gold, and thus drawn successively through a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of holes, each smaller and smaller, till at last it is brought to a fineness exceeding that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. That admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a> which makes one of the distinguishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of gold, is nowhere more conspicuous than in this gilt wire. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> of 48 ounces of silver, covered with a coat of gold, only weighing one ounce, as Dr Halley informs us, is usually drawn into a wire, two yards of which weigh no more than one grain; whence 98 yards of the wire weigh no more than 49 grains, and one single grain of gold covers the 98 yards; so that the ten-thousandth part of a grain is above one-eighth of an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. In 1784, Mr Rooswag of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a> presented to the board of trade some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a> made of iron wire, for which he received a reward; and the loom he invented for making it was lodged in the collection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> at Vauxhall. In 1799 Mr Rochon made others, and coated them with a transparent <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>, to be substituted instead of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> for ship lanterns, to be used between decks, and in engagements by night. He has since conceived, that with a thin coating of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> they might be employed to preserve ships from fire, and buildings on shore still more easily; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least that they might render the ravages of fire less frequent, and less terrible. These gauzes might be very useful too for theatrical decorations, which would not be liable to take fire. Their only inconvenience is their being too little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>; but Mr Rochon does not despair of means being found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> to remedy this imperfection, and it was with a view of calling <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to this subject, that he read a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on it to the clas. **Wire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>.** The inhabitants of Lapland have a sort of thinning slender substance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among them on several occasions, which is much of the thickness and appearance of our silver wire, and is therefore called, by those who do not examine its structure or substance, Lapland wire. It is made of the fineness of the rein deer, which being carefully separated in the eating, are, by the women, after soaking in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a>, spun into a sort of thread, of admirable fineness and strength, when wrought to the smallest filaments; but when larger, is very strong, and fit for the purposes of strength and force. Their wire, as it is called, is made of the finest of these threads covered with tin. The women do this business; and the way they take is to melt a piece of tin, and placing at the edge of it a horn, with a hole through it, they draw these finewy threads, covered with the tin, through the hole, which prevents their coming out too thick covered. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> is performed with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; and there is a small piece of bone placed at the top of the hole, where the wire is made flat; so that we always find it rounded on all sides but one, where it is flat. This wire they use in embroidering their clothes, as we do gold and silver; they often sell it to strangers, under the notion of its having certain magical virtues. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a>,** usually denotes a higher and more refined notion of things immediately presented to the mind, as it were, by intuition, without the assistance of ratiocination. Sometimes the word is more immediately used, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, for what we call <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, which consists in the soundness of the judgement, and a conduct answerable thereto. **Wisdom of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>,** one of the books of the Apocrypha. It abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and was probably written after the Cabalistic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> was introduced among the Jews. **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">Wit</a>,** is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of certain thoughts and expressions, much easier perceived than defined. According to Mr Locke, wit lies in the assemblage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, and putting those together with quickness and variety, wherein can be found any resemblance or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRUITY">congruity</a>, thereby to make up pleasant pictures and agreeable visions to the fancy. Mr Addison limited this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> considerably, by observing, that every resemblance of ideas does not constitute wit, but those only which produce delight and surprise. Mr Pope defined wit to be a quick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> and easy delivery; while, according to a late writer, it consists in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSIMILATION">assimilation</a> of distant ideas. The word *wit* originally signified wisdom. A witte was anciently a wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>: the wittenagemot, or Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, an assemblage of wise men. So late as the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, a man of pregnant wit, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wit, was a man of vast judgement. We still say, in his wits, out of his wits, for in or out of found mind. The word, however, is now applied in a more limited sense. Without attempting to expose the inaccuracy of the definitions above mentioned, or hazarding a definition of our own where so many eminent men have failed, we shall endeavour to show in what true wit consists. It is evident that wit excites in the mind an agreeable surprise, and that this is owing entirely to the strange assemblage of related ideas presented to the mind. This end is effected, 1. By debasing things pompous or seemingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>; 2. By aggrandizing things little or frivolous; 3. By setting ordinary objects in a particular and uncommon point of view, by means not only remote but apparently contrary. Of so much <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> are surprise and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, that nothing is more tafteless, and sometimes disgusting, than a joke that has become <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> by frequent repetition. For the same reason, even a pun or happy allusion <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear excellent when thrown out extempore in conversation, which would be deemed execrable in print. In like manner, a witty repartee is infinitely more pleasing than a witty attack: for though, in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the thing may be equally new to the reader or hearer, the effect on him is greatly injured, when there is access to suppose that it may be the slow production of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and premeditation. This, however, holds most with regard to the inferior tribes of witticisms, of which their readiness is the best recommendation. We shall illustrate these observations by subjoining a specimen or two of each of these sorts of wit: Of the first sort, which consists in the debasement of things great and eminent, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a>, amongst a thousand other instances, hath given us those which follow: And now had Phoebus in the lap Of Thetis taken out his nap: And, like a lobster boil'd, the morn From <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> began to turn. _Hudibras_, part ii. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a> 2. Here the low allegorical style of the first couplet, and the simile used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, afford us a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> notion of this lowest <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, which is distinguished by the name of the _ludicrous_. Another specimen from the same author you have in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: Great on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, great in the saddle, That could as well bind o'er as swaddle, Mighty he was at both of these, And fitly'd of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, as well as peace: So some rats of amphibious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, Are either for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or water. _Ibid._ part i. canto 1. In this coarse kind of drollery, those laughable translations or paraphrases of heroic and other serious poems, wherein the authors are said to be travestied, chiefly abound. The second kind, consisting in the aggrandisement of little things, which is by far the most splendid, and displays a soaring imagination, these lines of Pope will serve to illustrate: As Berecynthia, while her offspring vie In homage to the mother of the sky, Surveys around her in the blest abode, An hundred sons, and every son a god: Not with less <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> mighty Dulness <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>'d, Shall take thro' Grubstreet her triumphant round; And her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a> glancing o'er at once, Behold a hundred sons, and each a dunce. This whole multitude is spirited. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of the celestial is contrasted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of night and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>; heaven by Grubstreet; gods by dunces. Besides, the parody it contains on a beautiful passage in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> adds a particular lustre to it. This species we may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> the _thronical_, or the _mock-majestic_. It affects the most pompous language, and florid phraseology, as much as the other affects the reverse, the vilest and most grovelling dialect. To this class also we must refer the application of grave reflections to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> trifles. For that great and serious are naturally associated by the mind, and likewise little and trifling, is sufficiently evinced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> modes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> on these subjects used in every tongue. An apposite instance of such an application we have from Philips: My galligaskins, that have long withstood The winter's fury and encroaching frosts, By time subdued, (What will not time subdue!) An horrid chasm disclose. _Splendid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">Shilling</a>._ Of the third species of wit, which is by far the most multifarious, and which results from what may be called the quirkiness or singularity of the imagery, we shall give a few specimens that will serve to mark some of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> varieties. To illustrate all would be impossible. The first shall be where there is an apparent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> in the things she exhibits as connected. This kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> we have in these lines of Garth: Then Hydrops next appears amongst the throng; Bloated and big he slowly fails along: But like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISER">miser</a> in excess he's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, And pines for thirst amidst her watery store. _Dispensary._ A second sort is, where the things compared are what with dialecticians would come under the denomination of _disparates_, being such as can be ranked under no common genus. Of this we shall subjoin an example from Young: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a> chiefly keeps an Atheist in the dark; A fever argues better than a Clarke: Let but the logic in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> decay, The Grecian he'll renounce, and learn to pray. _Universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">Passion</a>._ A third variety in this species <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> from confounding artfully the proper and the metaphorical sense of an expression. In this way, one will assign as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> what is discovered to be perfectly absurd, when but ever so little attended to; and yet from the ordinary meaning of the words, hath a specious appearance on a single glance. Of this kind we have an instance in the subsequent lines: While thus the lady talk'd, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> Turn'd th' outside of his eyes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, As men of inward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> are wont To turn their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> in upon't. Hudibras, part iii. canto i. For whither can they turn their eyes more properly than to the light? A fourth variety, much resembling the former, is when the argument or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> (for all argument is a kind of comparison) is founded on the supposal of cor- poreal or personal attributes in what is strictly not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUS">sus</a>- ceptible of them; as in this, But Hudibras gave him a twitch As quick as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> in the breech, Just in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>'s lodg'd, As wise philosophers have judg'd: Because a kick in that place more Hurts honour than deep wounds before. Ibid. part ii. canto 3. The fifth, and only other variety which we shall mention, is that which arises from a relation, not in the things signified, but in the signs of all relations, no doubt the slightest. Identity here gives rise to puns and clinches; resemblance to quibbles, cranks, and rhimes: Of these it is quite unnecessary to exhibit speci- mens. Wit, John de, a celebrated pensioner of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and one of the greatest politicians of his time, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> de Wit, burgomaster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>, and was born in 1625. He became well skilled in civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, po- litics, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and other sciences; and wrote a treatise on the Elements of Curved lines, published by Francis Schooten. Having taken his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of law, he travelled into foreign courts, where he be- came esteemed for his genius and prudence. At his re- turn to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in 1650, he became pension- ary of Dort, then counsellor-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENSIONARY">pensionary</a> of Holland and West Friesland, intendant and registrar of the fiefs, and keeper of the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. He was thus at the head of affairs in Holland; but his opposition to the re- establishment of the office of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a>, which he thought a violation of the freedom and independence of the republic, cost him his life, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>'s party prevailed. He and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Corne- lius were assassinated by the populace at The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 1674, aged 47.

WITCHCRAFT

Pages 419-421

a supernatural power which per- sons were formerly supposed to obtain the possession of by entering into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>. They gave themselves up to him body and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; and he engaged, that they should want for nothing, and that he would avenge them upon all their enemies. As soon as the bargain was concluded, the devil delivered to the witch an imp, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> familiar spirit, to be ready at a call, and do whatever it was directed. By the assistance of this imp and the devil together, the witch, who was almost al- ways an old woman, was enabled to transport herself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> on a broomstick or a spit to distant places to at- tend the meetings of the witches. At these meetings the devil always presided. They were enabled also to transform themselves into various shapes, particularly to assume the forms of cats and hares, in which they most delighted; to inflict diseases on whomsoever they thought proper; and to punish their enemies in a variety of ways. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that certain persons were endowed with supernatural power, and that they were afflicted by in- visible spirits, is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. The sagae of the Ro- mans seem rather to have been sorcerers than witches; indeed the idea of a witch, as above described, could not have been prevalent till after the propagation of Christianity, as the heathens had no knowledge of the Christian devil. Witchcraft was universally believed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> till the 16th century, and even maintained its ground with to- lerable firmness till the middle of the 17th. Vast num- bers of reputed witches were convicted and condemned to be burnt every year. The methods of discovering them were various. One was, to weigh the supposed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">Provincial</a> criminal against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she was guilty, would preponderate; another, by making her attempt to say the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a>; this no witch was able to repeat entirely, but would omit some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> thereof. It is remarkable, that all witches did not hesitate at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; some leaving out one part, and some another. Teats, through which the imps sucked, were indubitable marks of a witch: these were always raw, and also inflexible; and, if squeezed, sometimes yielded a drop of blood. A witch could not weep more than three tears, and that only out of the left eye. This want of tears was, by the witch-finders, and even by some judges, considered as a very substan- tial <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of guilt. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">Swimming</a> a witch was another kind of popular ordeal generally practised: for this she was stripped naked, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bound, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> thumb to the left toe, and the left thumb to the right toe. Thus prepared, she was thrown into a pond or river, in which, if guilty, she could not sink; for having, by her compact with the devil, renounced the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, that element, in its turn, renounced her, and refused to receive her into its bosom. Sir Ro- bert Filmer mentions two others by fire: the first, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the thatch of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the suspected witch; the other, burning any animal supposed to be bewitched by her, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a> or ox. These, it was held, would force a witch to confess. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by the stool was another method used for the discovery of witches. It was thus managed: Hav- ing taken the suspected witch, she was placed in the middle of a room upon a stool or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, cross-legged, or in some other uneasy posture; to which if she submitted not, she was then bound with cords: there she was watched, and kept without meat or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> for the space of 24 hours (for, they said, within that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they should see her imp come and suck). A little hole was like- wise made in the door for imps to come in at; and lest it should come in some less discernible shape, they that watched were taught to be ever and anon sweeping the room, and, if they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> any spiders or flies, to kill them: if they could not kill them, then they might be sure they were imps. If witches, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> or tor- ture, would not confess, all their apparel was changed, and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of their body shaven off with a sharp razor, lest they should secrete magical charms to pre- vent their confessing. Witches were most apt to con- fess on Fridays. By such trials as these, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of chil- dren, Witchcraft, dren, old women, and fools, were thousands of unhappy women condemned for witchcraft, and burnt at the stake. In the 18th volume of the Statistical Account of Scotland there is the trial of two witches, William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> and Alfon Dick, in Kirkaldy, in 1636. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> on which they were condemned is absolutely ridiculous: they were, however, burnt for witchcraft. The expenses which the town and kirk-session were put to on this occasion were as follows: In primis.—To Mr James Miller, when he went to Preflowne for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to try them, 47s. Item.—To the man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULROSS">Culross</a>, (the executioner), when he went away the first time, 12s. Item.—For coals for the witches, 24s. Item.—In purchasing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, Item.—For one to go to Finnmouth for the laird to sit upon their affize as judge, Item.—For harden to be jumps to them, Item.—For making of them, Summa for the kirk's part L. 17 10 Scots. The Town's part of expenses defurred extraordinarily upon William Coke and Alfon Dick. In primis.—For 10 loads of coals to burn them, 5 merks, Item.—For a tar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, 14s. Item.—For towes, Item.—To him that brought the executioner, Item.—To the executioner for his pains, Item.—For his expenses here, Item.—For one to go to Finnmouth for the laird Summa town part, L. 17 10 Scots. Both, L. 34 11 Or L. 2 17 7 Ster. For a considerable time after the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> was erected, the trials of witches (as heretics) were confined to that tribunal; but the goods of those who were condemned being confiscated to the holy office, its ministers were so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in discovering sorcerers, that the different governments found it necessary to deprive them of the cognizance of this crime. On the continent, commissioners were then appointed for the discovery and conviction of witches, who, though less active than the inquisitors, were but too zealous in prosecuting their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>. In 1494, Sprenger and Inquisitor, two persons employed in this commission, published a collection of trials, most of which had come before themselves, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Malleus Maleficarum: this served as a kind of institute for their successors. The first writers against witchcraft were stigmatized as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHEISTS">Atheists</a>, though they only endeavoured to prove the imbecility of the persons accused, and the insatiability or the knavery of their accusers. Such were the epithets bestowed by Dr Henry More, and even by Cudworth himself. Wierus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of the celebrated Agrip- pa, gave rise to the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> controversy on this subject. His <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> had taught him <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>; and he endeavoured, but with too feeble a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, to stop the bloody proceedings of the judges. Wierus appears to have been a well-disposed, weak man, with extensive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> on his subject, but too narrow-minded to comprehend it thoroughly. He involved himself in unspeakable difficulties, by admitting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of supernatural powers in certain diseases, and in possessions, while he denied that witches had any concurrence in them. These appearances (said he) are illusions of the devil, who persuades simple and melancholy persons that the mischief he himself performs, is done by them, and at their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He was weak enough to attempt the explanation of every story alleged by his antagonists, without questioning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the facts. Bodinus, a French lawyer of eminence, who had assisted at several trials of witches, wrote against Wierus, in his Demonomania. He urged the concurrent testimonies of sufficient witnesses, and the confessions of the witches themselves, to establish the existence of sorcery. Wierus owned that the unhappy persons believed themselves to be guilty of the crimes alleged against them, but that they were deceived by the devil. But what do you make of the witches meetings, cried Bodinus? The witches (replied his antagonist) are insensible. This explanation was so unsatisfactory that Wierus passed for a magician, whom the devil had furnished with specious arguments to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> others from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. Lerchemer, Godelmann, Ewichius, Ewaldus, and some others, followed him, notwithstanding this stigma; but they were opposed by men of more acuteness and consistency than themselves; by Remigius, who had condemned several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of sorcerers to the flames; Delrio, whose book is a complete Corpus Magiae; Cujas, Erasmus, Scribonius, Camerarius, and a crowd of others. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, while the belief in witchcraft was supported by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> authority (for James I. is universally known to have written on demonology) countenanced by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, and generally adopted among the people, only one writer was hardy enough to oppose it. This was Reginald Scott, who published a collection of impostures detected, under the title of Discoveries of Witchcraft. James ordered the book to be burnt by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> executioner, and the judges <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to burn witches as usual. During the civil wars, upwards of eighty were hanged in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, on the accusations of Hopkins the witch-finder. Webster was the next writer against witchcraft; but he had a different fate from that of Scott, for most of his arguments were refuted by Glanville. This very acute writer was induced to publish his Philosophical Considerations about Witchcraft, by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, that the increasing disbelief of witches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a> tended to affect the evidences of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and even of a Deity. In respect of argument, he was certainly superior to his adversaries; his reasoning is perspicuous, though sometimes fickle, rested on the most precarious foundations of evidence, and arranged with great skill. On the continent, this controversy seemed almost forgotten, till Bekker published his Monde Enchantée, in which he denied the existence of witches on the Cartesian principle, that the Deity is the source of all action, consequently actions opposite to his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and attributes cannot be supposed to exist. He was answered by Frederick Witchcraft Frederick Hoffman, the father of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of medicine, in his dissertation De Diaboli <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIA">Potentia</a> in Corpora. The latest witchcraft frenzy was in New England, about 1692, when the execution of witches became a calamity more dreadful than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> or the pestilence. The accusers became so daring, that neither civil nor <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> authority would have proved a security against their attacks, if all the prosecutions had not been suddenly dropped, and the prisoners set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. So far did those wretches proceed in absurdity, that a dog was accused of throwing persons into fits by looking at them. As soon as the prosecutions were stopped, all reports of witchcraft ceased. It would be ridiculous to attempt a serious refutation of the existence of witches; and at present, luckily, the talk is unnecessary. In this country, at least, the discouragement <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> given to all suspicion of witchcraft, and the repeal of the statutes against that crime, have very much weakened, though perhaps they have not entirely eradicated, the persuasion. On the continent, too, it is evidently in decline; and notwithstanding the exertions of Dr. De Haen, and of the celebrated La-vater, we have little doubt but that in a short time posterity <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> wonder at the credulity of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. That there ever were witches, is an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that cannot for a moment be believed by a thinking man. The actions imputed to them were either absurd or impossible; the witnesses by whose evidence they were condemned, either weak enthusiasts or downright villains; and the confessions ascribed to the witches themselves, effects of a disordered imagination produced by cruel treatment and excessive watchings. As to the nightly meetings, demonologists themselves have been obliged to confess, that they were nothing else but uneasy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, often produced by soporific compositions. The facts which have been brought forward by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for witchcraft bear in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> the most evident marks of trick and imposture; and this has constantly been found out whenever these facts have been properly examined. See Sorcery. WITENA mot, or Witena Gemot, among the Anglo-Saxons, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> which literally signified the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the wise men; and was applied to the great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, of latter days called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. WITHERS of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> of the shoulder-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> at the bottom of the neck and mane, towards the upper part of the shoulder.

WITNESS

Pages 421-421

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a person who gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in any cause, and is sworn to speak the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">Trial</a> by WITNESSES, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of trial without the intervention of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. This is the only method of trial known to the civil law, in which the judge is left to form in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the witnesses examined: but it is very rarely used in the English law, which prefers the trial by jury before it in almost every instance. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">Save</a> only that when a widow brings a writ of dower, and the tenant pleads that the husband is not dead; this being looked upon as a dilatory <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>, is in favour of the widow, and for greater expedition allowed to be tried by witnesses examined before the judges: and so, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> Finch, shall no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in our law. But Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> mentions some others; as, to try whether the tenant in a real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITTENBERG">Wittenberg</a> was duly summoned, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the validity of a challenge to a juror: so that Finch's observation must be confined to the trial of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and not collateral issues. And in every case Sir Edward Coke lays it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, that the affirmative must be proved by two witnesses at the least.

WITTENBERG

Pages 421-421

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, 50 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Dresden. It is under immediate vassalage, and the seat of an aulic judiciary, a general superintendency, an inspection and confirmy. The town is not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; but is well fortified, and contains a famous university, in which Melanchthon was a professor. In this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Martin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> first began to preach against the pope's indulgences; and in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of All Saints he is said to have been buried. In the old citadel of this town the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxon electors used to reside. Besides the university, there is a Latin school in the town, with six masters. The library belonging to the university is said to be very valuable. In 1736 the Polesians being masters of the town, destroyed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its fortifications. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12°. 47'. N. Lat. 51°. 49'. WOAD. See Isatis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; see also <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">Dyeing</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of woad for dyeing, as practised in France, is minutely described by Astruc, in his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. The plant puts forth at first five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six upright leaves, about a foot long and six inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: when these hang downwards, and turn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, they are fit for gathering: five crops are gathered in one year. The leaves are carried directly to a mill, much resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, and ground into a smooth paste. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> was deferred for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they would putrefy, and send forth an insupportable stench. The paste is laid in heaps, pressed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and smooth, and the blackish crust, which forms on the outside, reunited if it happens to crack: if this was neglected, little <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> would be produced in the cracks, and the woad would lose a part of its strength. After lying for fifteen days, the heaps are opened, the crust rubbed and mixed with the inside, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> formed into oval balls, which are pressed close and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> in wooden <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>. These are dried up on hurdles: in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, they turn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> on the outside; in a clofe place, yellowish, especially if the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be rainy. The dealers in this commodity prefer the first, though it is said the workmen find no considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two. The good balls are distinguished by their being weighty, of an agreeable smell, and when rubbed, of a violet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> within. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the dyer, these balls require a farther preparation: they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> with wooden mallets, on a brick or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, into a grofs powder; which is heaped up in the middle of the room to the height of four feet, a space being left for passing round the sides. The powder, moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, ferments, grows hot, and throws out a thick foul fume. It is shovelled backwards and forwards, and moistened every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> for twelve days; after which it is stirred less frequently, without watering, and at length made into a heap for the dyer.

WOAHOO

Pages 421-422

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Morotai, at the distance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues. From the appearance of the north-east and north-west parts, it is the finest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a>. Nothing can exceed the verdure of the hills, the variety of of wood and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, and rich cultivated valleys, which the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> displays. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is formed by the north and west extremities, into which a fine river empties itself, through a deep valley; but as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is brackish for 200 yards from the entrance, wa- tering in it is not convenient. It contains about 60,000 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> Hergest, commander of the Daedalus store-ship, who had been sent from England, in 1791, to New South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and thence to the Southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, with a supply of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> for the Discovery sloop, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Vancouver, then on a voy- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of discovery, was here surprised and murdered by the natives, together with Mr Gooch, the astronomer. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 157. 51. N. Lat. 21. 43. WODEN. See ODIN, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">MYTHOLOGY</a>, No. 40.

WODEVILLE

Pages 422-422

Anthony, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Edward IV. was born in the end of 1442, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the beginning of 1443. Though one of the most accomplished men of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, very little is known of his private <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He was early and con- stantly employed either in the tumults of those turbulent times, or in discharging the duties of some of the highest offices of the state, with which he was invested. Yet he found leisure to cultivate letters, and to be the author of works which, though of little value now, made some noise in that age, when learning was at a low ebb in England. These consisted chiefly of trans- lations from the French; and his lordship and his printer Caxton, were the first English writers who had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to see their works published from the press. This accomplished, brave, and amiable nobleman was treacherously imprisoned by Richard III. in Pomfret castle, where, during his confinement, he composed a short poem, which has been preserved by John Rous of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, and breathes, says Dr Henry, a noble spirit of pious resignation to his approaching fate. He was beheaded on the 23rd of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1483, in the 41st year of his age.

WODROW

Pages 422-426

Robert, a clergyman of the west of Scotland who lived in the beginning of the 18th century; well known as the author of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> during the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the preceding cen- tury. His father, Mr James Wodrow, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of learning and piety. He preached occasionally to the per- secuted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, and taught a little academy of their students of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> at Glasgow, before the Revolution. About that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was ordained one of the ministers of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, continuing his connexion with the academy till he was elected professor of theo- logy by the university in the year 1692. He taught with reputation and success till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1708. His son Robert was born in the year 1679; his mo- ther being then in the 51st year of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Her death (though it did not happen till several years after), was then fully expected; and his father, obnoxious to a ty- rannical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, narrowly escaped imprisonment, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> something worse, by attempting to obtain a last short in- terview with her. As he passed the town <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, he was marked, and soon followed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> into his own house, and even into his wife's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber, where he was concealed. Their officer checked this violence; sent them out of the room, and left the house himself; placing, how- ever, sentinels both within and without, till the birth should be over. In half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after, Mr Wodrow at his wife's suggestion, assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>-coat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the physician then in attendance; and carrying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a> before him, made an easy escape through the midst of the guards. They soon renewed their search with marks of irritation, thrusting their words into the very bed where the lady lay; who pleasantly desired them to desist, "for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> (said she) is now flown." His son Robert went through the usual course of liter- ary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Glasgow, entered the university in 1691; and prosecuted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the languages and the different branches of philosophy, till he became a student of theology under the tuition of his father. He was chosen librarian to the university in the year 1698, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that office four years. There he be- gan his researches into everything connected with the ecclesiastical history of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which he continued to pursue to the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and also imbibed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for medals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, and whatever seemed curi- ous or illustrative of Roman, Celtic, and British anti- quities. He was among the first in Scotland who attended to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history. From a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of letters in his own handwriting, begun about this time, it appears that he was in habits of the utmost intimacy with a select number of literary gentlemen, animated with the same ardour of research; that they corresponded regularly with one another, made collections of finger- <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, of fossils, petrified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, fishes, &c., and ex- changed what they could spare from their respective stores. Among his correspondents were Mr William Nicolson, archdeacon, afterwards bishop of Carlisle, and at last of Derry, author of the Historical <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">Libraries</a>; Mr Edward Lhwyd keeper of the Ashmolean cloister at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; Sir Robert Sibbald, physician in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, author of a natural history of Scotland, and another of Fife; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Pitmedden; Messrs James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a>, Laughlan Campbell minister of Campbellton, and others. In a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Mr Lhwyd dated August 1709, Mr Wodrow tells him his name was but at a little distance from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they had been litho-copying together, during a visit of Mr Lhwyd to Scotland. "My <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARO">paro</a>- chial <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> (he continues) does not allow me the same time I had then for those subterranean studies; but my inclination is equally strong, perhaps stronger. I take it to be one of the best diversions from serious study, and in itself a great duty, to admire my Maker's works. I have got some store of fossils here from our marle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, &c., and heartily with I had the knowing Mr Lhwyd here to pick out what he wants, and help me to class a great many <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> which I know not what to make of." He informs him, in the end of the letter, that he had 500 or 600 species of one thing or another relative to natural history. Mr Wodrow, when he left Glasgow, resided a short time in the neighbourhood, in the house of a very distant relation, Sir ——— Maxwell of Nether Pollock, then one of the Scots judges. It being within the bounds of the presbytery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAISLEY">Paisley</a>, he offered himself to them for probationary trials, and obtained their licence to preach the gospel in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1703. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> fol- lowing, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Eastwood, where Lord Pollock lived, becoming vacant, by the death of Mr Matthew Crawford (another Scots historian), a petition, with an unanimous call or invitation from the parish to Mr Wodrow to be their minister, was presented to the presbytery; presbytery; and they, wavering part of the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> trials, in order to expedite the business, ordained Mr Wodrow to be minister of Eastwood on the 28th of October 1734. In this charge he continued to the end of his life. Notwithstanding his ministerial duty, he still found some time to gratify the early bent of his mind towards natural history, and his curiosity to learn everything in his power, not only at home, but concerning the natural productions of other countries, and the opinions, customs, manners, and way of living of their inhabitants. In his farewell letters to his friends, about to fail to the Scottish settlement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a> or to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, &c., he directed their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and enquiries to these subjects; and something similar he frequently wrote to other friends going to reside in remote places of the Highlands, or even on the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The collection of his MS. letters bound up in five or six thick 8vo volumes, though reaching nearly to the end of his life, seems to consist only of the first draught of his own letters to his friends, not a single scrap is now to be found of their answers to him. After his ordination, however, this worthy man, considering the duties of his office as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and only proper business, rose into distinguished reputation and usefulness as a preacher, and was looked upon as one of the first clergymen in the west of Scotland. Humble and unambitious of public notice, he was well entitled to it, by his conscientious and exemplary piety, his learning, not only in professional, but in other branches of knowledge, his natural good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> judgement, his benevolent obliging spirit to all, his warm <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his friends, who formed a wide circle around him, and especially his deep concern for the best interests of his people, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> exertions for their instruction and improvement. His weekly sermons were all distinctly written out in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and even his lectures in shorthand. Accustomed to regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, he had acquired an uncommon facility in it. His countenance and appearance in the pulpit was manly and dignified; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> clear and commanding; his manner serious and animated; these things, joined with the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> in his favour, added to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the plain edifying discourses he delivered, without papers, to his hearers; and living in the near neighbourhood of Glasgow his little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was often crowded, especially when he dispensed the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>, conferred in Scotland as the principal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> solemnity. Yet these talents, and this merited popularity which followed them, made little impression on his own modest conscientious mind; for he chose to continue in the obscure country parish with which he was first connected, resisting all the attempts made by his friends or by strangers to get him translated into several other more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and opulent parishes, who were desirous of the benefit of his ministry, however convenient the change might have proved for the education of his family. In the year 1712, the magistrates of Glasgow invited him to be one of the ministers of that city; and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1717, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> from the town of Stirling did the same. On the other hand, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, heirs, and elders of his own parish, strenuously opposed the translation. The presbytery, who had it in their power to have appointed it, found great difficulties in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> bonum ecclesiae; referred the decision in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>, and in the last to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of the General <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a>, and Wodrow, the courts thought proper to put no restraint on the minister's judgement or inclination, as he himself was certainly the best judge of his comparative usefulness in two different situations. Mr Wodrow was equally conscientious and assiduous in the business of the ecclesiastical courts, as in his parochial duty. Notwithstanding his studious turn, he punctually attended the meetings of Presbytery, Synod, and General Assembly, when elected, as he often was, a member of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and also the commissions in November and March, which regularly met during that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the church. His connexion with Lord Pollock made his journeys to Edinburgh easy; and after he began to collect materials for his voluminous history, his personal inspection of the public records and of the various MSS. accumulated in the Edinburgh libraries, made his visits to that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> frequent and necessary. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the great body of the Presbyterians, he had strongly imbibed what are called Whig principles; in other words, he was warmly attached to the constitutional liberties of the people, as established by the revolution settlement. No wonder! The dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> and oppression they had suffered during the two preceding reigns were still fresh and galling to their minds: they considered the elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William to the throne and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> succession, as the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> bulwarks raised up by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, for the security both of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. They trembled at every dark appearance threatening to this security, such as the death of King William. That cloud, however, was soon dissipated by the perseverance of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s ministers in his views and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and the splendid victories of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> and his allies over the armies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. But the elevation of the Tory ministry in the latter part of the queen's reign was a severe <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> to the Scottish Presbyterians, and involved the conscientious part of their clergy in very serious difficulties and dangers. The oath of abjuration required at that time from clergymen, and enforced by civil penalties, and even the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> for a national thanksgiving, after the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, pressed hard upon the scrupulous consciences of many of the clergy. The very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the oath seemed to them dubious and jejune, hostile to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Hanover's newly acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, conferred on him by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> and the people; and as to the other point, they had not freedom to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> their people, in a solemn thanksgiving to Heaven for a peace, termed safe and honourable, which they and the generality of their hearers considered as dangerous and disgraceful. Mr Wodrow, as might be expected, was one of the recusants of the oath; for nothing could move him to flatter with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. At the same time the liberality and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> of his mind led him to judge candidly of the consciences of others. Accordingly, he made every effort in his power to reconcile his clerical brethren, and his own people, to such of the clergy as had the freedom to take it, and by so doing, had rendered themselves obnoxious to popular prejudice and odium. With such, this good man still continued to live, not only in Christian, but ministerial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>; endeavouring to soften and remove the prejudices against them, and, in as far as his influence reached, to revive and cherish a spirit of mutual forbearance. Many proposals he made, and private meetings... meetings and conferences he held with his brethren, to prevent their differences from rising, as they threatened to do, into a schism; to prevent them especially from entering at all into the church courts; justly afraid of the sparks of animosity too apt to be kindled there. His endeavours and those of his friends were seconded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> of the superior courts, especially the commission of the General Assembly. Whatever passed there in the way of admonition to the rest of the church, breathed the spirit of mutual forbearance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>.
