How he managed the other difficult and delicate point, the Thanksgiving, in a consistency with his duty, does not appear in his letters; nor is it now worth while to investigate this as a trait of his character, which might be done, perhaps, from his MS. sermons preached at the time. Only it is pleasing to remark from the letters, that the same spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and mild forbearance which animated the majority of the clergy in the west, seems also to have pervaded the officers of the crown, justices of the peace, and other civil magistrates in Scotland at the time. The oath was not pressed on the recusants, and the execution of the legal penalties incurred by the neglect of it avoided; for their general loyalty was undoubted. A more severe stroke was inflicted on their adversaries by the Tory ministry in the year 1710 by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the British parliament which restored <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> to its former full force. An act of the Scotch parliament passed after the Revolution had extracted the chief sting of that grievance, by placing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of the minister of every parish in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the landed proprietors, called heritors, in conjunction with the elders, or members of the kirk-session. A majority of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> body, at a meeting appointed for the purpose, drew up a call or written invitation, which they subscribed to a particular candidate to be their minister. This was presented to the presbytery of the bounds, the proper judges of his learning and moral character; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> these were found unexceptionable, he was ordained, or solemnly consecrated and installed into the office. This Scotch act having continued in force for twenty years, and being conceived to have become perpetual by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the Union, was now repealed; and the choice of a minister to every parish was in effect placed in the power of a single person, a patron, because he had in fact the sole power of nominating the only candidate who could enjoy the benefice. Mr Wodrow was exceedingly averse from the revival of the power of patronage; and in this he was influenced both by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and religious principles. In his letters, he seems to have looked upon a patron of a parish, as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a>; or at least like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who had no restraints laid on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, to prevent or check the abuse of it. The paramount power or trust committed to a patron, this conscientious minister could not reconcile with the apostolic counsels, to commit the keeping of religious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> to faithful men, able also to instruct others. He thought it very improper to leave the choice of a religious instructor, in the first instance, to any single person whatever, especially to one generally a stranger to the circumstances of the parishioners; one who had little knowledge, and therefore little sympathy with them in their religious sentiments and feelings. He was persuaded that the purposes of edification, and the peace of the country, circumstanced as Scotland then was, were Wodrow much better secured by the restraints laid on a patron in the act 1690, that is, by admitting the two principal bodies of the parish to a participation with him in his choice, than by trusting it wholly to himself; and he threw out many judicious hints in his letters, and even schemes or proposals to his brethren, on this difficult and important subject. On the other hand, he wished nothing to be attempted but in a constitutional way, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> with the civil power. Few men were so sensible as he was of the abuses incident to popular government, either in church or state, and of the danger of resisting, even unjust and oppressive laws, in a tumultuous or disorderly manner. The Presbyterian church, in the outward order or form of it, he viewed as a well regulated republic. He did not consider the people in their individual capacity, as qualified to vote even on the choice of their own minister. The elders of the parish he looked upon as the representatives of the people in the ecclesiastical courts; and their number, in his own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, he restricted to a very few, four or five at most, fit to assist him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of church <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> within the parish. The rest of his fellows were deacons, whose jurisdiction was confined to the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, visiting the sick, and distributing the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and wine at the communion, but could not, like the former, be chosen to represent the parish in the presbytery and superior courts. In this sense of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of order and subordination, he persevered to the end of his life. When, contrary to his judgement or vote, an unpopular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> was to be ordained in a parish within twelve or fifteen miles distant from Eastwood, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of the General Assembly, to be executed, perhaps with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> assistance; this aged minister thought it his duty, regardless of personal danger or odium, to countenance the young brother, by joining with the rest of the clergy in laying their hands on him, inviting him afterwards to his pulpit, and exerting any influence he had to conciliate the irritated minds of that parish. The only publication for which the world is indebted to Mr Wodrow, is The History of the Singular Sufferings of the Church of Scotland during the twenty-eight years immediately preceding the Revolution. It was written at a proper distance of time from the events it records; and printed at Edinburgh in the year 1721, in two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> folio volumes, with two appendixes consisting of copies of the public records, and of many private, family, and personal papers, letters, &c., inserted as vouchers of the historical facts. In collecting this great body of information, the author was assisted by his friends, who cheerfully seconded his own almost incredible industry and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> of research. In consequence of this, the book has more the appearance of a biographical, than of a historical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. It has, however, the form, and all the essentials of a regular history, divided into books, chapters, and sections, with proper margins and indexes; written in a plain, rather too familiar style, unavoidably interfered with Scotticism, yet these sufficiently intelligible to an English reader. It exhibits a distinct sketch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> both of the principal sufferers, and of their persecutors; of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the persecution, in the unjustifiable plans and measures of an arbitrary government; with the motives of the advisers and executors of them. The unfortunate and innocent Wodrow. innocent sufferers, our author viewed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, not of a set of wild fanatics, as they were called by their contemporaries, and frequently too by later historians; many of them were most respectable for their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in their country, as well as for their talents and virtues; but even those in the lower ranks of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, as confessors and martyrs in the noble cause which they had espoused, the support of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of conscience, and of national liberty. The subject of the history is the most melancholy that could be chosen; a long and severe persecution of a people, who had been guilty of nothing undutiful to their civil or ecclesiastical rulers; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of open acts of injustice and tyranny, perpetrated under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and this with such an increasing and merciless violence, as to sink the usual spirit of a free people, and easily quell one or two feeble ill-timed attempts to resist their oppressors. No wonder that the continued view of such a wretched and melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, without anything joyful to interrupt it, should give a melancholy tinge to the mind of the writer, easily communicated to his readers. On the other hand some things have happily an opposite tendency. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of biographical intelligence, though it must be confessed it is much too voluminous, and too minute for the management of any historian whatsoever, yet furnishes a variety of anecdotes, which give some needful relaxation or relief to the sympathy of the reader. These indeed are in part the simple annals of the poor, without the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> or easy elegance of polished life; but even in this shape they are not destitute, both of entertainment and instruction; and then the minuteness in the detail of names, of persons, places, and other particular circumstances, adds to the impressiveness of the facts, by placing their certainty beyond all reasonable doubt. If faithfully to record past facts, and transmit the knowledge of them to posterity, be the principal duty of a historian, this Wodrow has certainly aimed at; and also to repel any feelings hostile to his fidelity and impartiality; in short, to come as near as he was able to the motto prefixed to his volumes, Nec studio, nec odio. Doubtless, like all other men, he had some political, and many theological prejudices, the last chiefly imbued from education, and confirmed by too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> a veneration for the characters of our first reformers—prejudices which warped his personal opinions and feelings on both subjects. But he seems to have made a considerable effort to prevent his party prejudices from warping or perverting his judgement of the truth or falsehood of stubborn historical facts. Nothing almost oratorical enters into his narratives, though there is room for admiration, and much scope for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> indignation; no exaggerated encomiums on his friends, or strong opprobrious language in speaking of his and their enemies, the unprovoked persecutors of his church. He allows the facts which he has recorded to speak for both, and transmit to posterity a memorial to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> or their infamy. The chief fault of this historical collection already hinted at, is its minuteness, and excessive copiousness. The prodigious multitude of facts it embraces, though different from one another in their circumstances, are in other respects somewhat similar. This must necessarily occasion some repetition and lateness, especially to a fatigued reader, who has it, however, in his power to gratify his taste by selecting what is most agreeable to it. Nevertheless a candid and patient reader can be at no loss to form a proper judgement of the principal transactions of the period, from the authentic accounts of them before him, to appreciate the true characters of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>, or of the motives and views from which they acted. And an inquisitive and penetrating reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be gratified by seeing not a little of the peculiar principles, opinions, sentiments, habits, and manners of that age, as distinguished from the present; and may thus estimate the gradual progress towards much noble and useful improvement; and on the other hand, the progress towards a very hurtful corruption and degeneracy of manners, which have both taken place during the last hundred and twenty years. At the time of its first publication, the book met with less general attention than might have been expected in Scotland, and scarcely any attention in England, except from professed readers. As it came to be more studied, it was the more valued, except where there was an evident bias on the opposite side. Few can be at a loss to see why such historians as Hume, Macpherson, and Dalrymple should neglect or undervalue such a book. Our later Scotch historians, Somerville and Laing, have done it more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. In truth, there is a very near coincidence in their estimates of the characters they draw, and their accounts of the facts they relate, in common with Wodrow. But especially our late illustrious patriot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Fox, whose high abilities, uncommon candour, and sweetness of disposition, almost remove the suspected bias of his party spirit—Mr Fox has, in the historical fragment published since his death, given a very honourable testimony to the fidelity and accuracy of our historian. After mentioning the execution of three females, he adds, page 131, "To relate all the instances of cruelty which occurred would be endless. But it may be necessary to remark, that no historical facts are better ascertained, than the accounts of them which are to be found in Wodrow. In every instance, where there has been an opportunity of comparing these accounts with the records, and other authentic monuments, they appear to be quite correct." The collection of the materials for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the church history from the public records, and many other authentic sources, must have cost the author a prodigious labour and time. The pecuniary expense incurred was considerable, and scarcely refunded from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the book. The only <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> profit, he has been heard to say, which accrued from it, was one or two hundred pounds that he received from the king, to whom it was dedicated. The last twelve years of Mr Wodrow's life were chiefly occupied in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up a biography of the principal persons concerned in introducing the reformation of religion into Scotland, and settling the different forms or modes of ecclesiastical government attempted to be established there from the beginning to the end of that period, namely from about the year 1560 to 1660, when the printed history of the sufferings commences. Had it pleased God to continue his useful life till this larger work was finished, public curiosity would have been much gratified; for it contains the lives, not only of John Knox, George Buchanan, and others already well known, but the lives of a great number more, very learned. Wodrow, learned, ingenious, respectable, and worthy men, scarcely at all known to the literary world; besides a variety of anecdotes naturally entering into such a work, illustrative of the history and the living manners of that age. Happily these manuscript lives are still preserved, all written with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, and some of the longest of them copied, probably during his last long illness, in a more legible hand. Whatever important or curious information they may contain, they are not fit for the press in their present state. They are now deposited in the library of the university of Glasgow. Besides writing the history and the biography, both extended by himself for publication, and two days every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> regularly appropriated to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for the pulpit, much of his time must have been occasionally spent in writing letters, some of them like dissertations, on theological and other literary subjects; for he corresponded with a very wide circle of acquaintances and friends in Scotland, England, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and with a few on the continent and in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> in the first part of life was robust and strong, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> in general good; but his studious habits or constant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, and especially incessant writing, it is supposed, may have brought on the bodily complaint which occasioned his death. In the latter end of the year 1731, a swelling about the size of a small chestnut appeared on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, near the collar bone. It was on the same place where a spark of fire had fallen when he was a child, and had then left a little lump and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> like a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>. About a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after the swelling began, it had increased to the size of a plum, and in April 1732 was as large as a man's fist. It was attempted to be removed by cautery; the attempt failed. His body became greatly emaciated, and he gradually declined till his death, which happened on the 21st of March 1734. Supported by the testimony of a good conscience, joined with the strong consolation and well-founded hope of the gospel, he bore this long-continued severe distress with admirable fortitude, unabated piety and resignation; never uttering a murmur, but behaving to his friends who came to see him, and to all about him, with much ease and affection; thus leaving, both in the active exertions of a useful life, and in his patient sufferings at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of it, a very edifying example to his family and his flock. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> before his death, he gathered his children around his bed, gave each of them his dying blessing, with counsels suitable to their ages and circumstances; last of all two boys, neither of them four years old, too young to understand and feel these marks of his affection, yet, after the example of the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, Gen. xlviii. 15, even them he drew to him, laid his hands upon their heads, and devoutly prayed, that the God of his fathers, the angel who had redeemed him from all evil, would bless the lads. Mr Wodrow was married in the end of 1708, to Margaret Warner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the reverend Mr William Guthrie of Penwick, well known in Scotland by his writings, and daughter of the reverend Patrick Warner, then living on his estate of Ardeer in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a>. Mr Warner, in the early part of his life, had been chaplain to the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a>. After his return home, he was driven from his ministry and from the kingdom, by the persecution of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; but returned in consequence of King James's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, and became minister of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRVINE">Irvine</a>. He had a personal interview on his last return with the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, a short time before the history, an account of which appears in the history, vol. ii. p. 604. Mr Wodrow had a family of 16 children, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of whom, with his widow, survived him in decent circumstances, without any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> among them for above 25 years. The only remaining survivor is the reverend Dr James Wodrow of Stevenston in Ayrshire. Besides his collection of foths, and a few Roman and British medals, Mr Wodrow left a valuable library of books, many volumes of pamphlets and also of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> written by others; sent to him in presents, or copied by his orders. The most valuable part of them is now in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> library, and in the repositories of the church at Edinburgh. His own manuscript biography, as has been already said, is in the library of the university of Glasgow.

WOLAW

Pages 426-426

a town in Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name. It is surrounded with strong walls and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the houses are built with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The castle is also encompassed with deep ditches, and the greatest part of the inhabitants are employed in a woollen manufacture. In 1709 a Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was allowed to be built here. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, 20 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, and 32 south-east of Glogau. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 54'. N. Lat. 51° 18'.

WOLFE

Pages 426-427
Major-General James, was born at Wellesham in the county of Kent, about the beginning of the year 1726. His father was Lieutenant-general Edward Wolfe. He went into the army when very young; and applying himself with unrewarded assiduity to the study of his profession, soon became remarkable for his knowledge and his genius. He distinguished himself at the battle of Laffert when little more than 20, and received the highest encomiums from the commander-in-chief. After the peace he still continued to cultivate the art of war. He contrived to introduce the greatest regularity and the exactest discipline into his corps, and at the same time to preserve the affection of every soldier. In 1758 he was present as a brigadier-general at the siege of Louisbourg. He landed first on the island at the head of division; and in spite of the violence of the surf, and the force and well directed fire of the enemy, drove them from their post with great precipitation. The surrender of the town, which happened soon after, was in a great measure owing to his activity, bravery, and skill. The fame which he acquired during this siege pointed him out to Mr Pitt, who was then minister, as the properest person to command the army destined to attack Quebec. This was the most difficult and the most arduous undertaking of the whole war. Quebec was the capital of the French dominions in North America; it was well fortified, situated in the midst of a hostile country, and defended by an army of 20,000 men, regulars and militia, besides a considerable number of Indian allies. The troops destined for this expedition consisted of ten battalions, making up altogether about 7000 men. Such was the army army destined to oppose three times their own number, defended by fortifications, in a country altogether unknown, and in a late season in that climate for military operations. But this little army, says an officer who was present at that expedition, and who has been so obliging as to communicate all the information we desired, was always languishing of success; for they were commanded by General Wolfe, who, by a very uncommon magnanimity and nobleness of behaviour, had attached the troops so much to his person, and inspired them with such resolution and steadiness in the execution of their duty, that nothing seemed too difficult for them to accomplish. The admirable skill with which his measures were planned, and the prudence and vigour with which they were executed, are well known. He landed his army on the northern shore of the river St Lawrence in spite of the enemy, and forced them to a battle, in which they were completely defeated. The consequence of this battle was the reduction of Quebec, and the conquest of Canada. In the beginning of the battle General Wolfe was wounded in the wrist by a musket-ball; he wrapped his handkerchief round it, continued to give his orders with his usual calmness and perspicuity, and informed the soldiers that the advanced parties on the front had his orders to retire, and that they needed not be surprised when it happened. Towards the end of the battle he received a new wound in the breast; he immediately retired behind the rear-rank supported by a grenadier, and laid himself down on the ground. Soon after a shout was heard; and one of the officers who stood by him exclaimed, "See how they run!" The dying hero asked with some emotion, "Who run?" "The enemy (replied the officer); they give way everywhere." The general then said, "Pray, do one of you run to Colonel Burton, and tell him to march Webb's regiment with all speed down to Charles river, to cut off the retreat of the fugitives from the bridge." Now, God be praised, I shall die happy!" He then turned on his side, closed his eyes, and expired. The death of General Wolfe was a national loss universally lamented. He inherited from nature an animating fervour of sentiment, an intuitive perception, an extensive capacity, and a passion for glory, which stimulated him to acquire every species of military knowledge that study could comprehend, that actual service could illustrate and confirm. This noble warmth of disposition seldom fails to call forth and unfold all the liberal virtues of the soul. Brave above all estimation of danger; generous, gentle, complacent, and humane; the pattern of the officer, the darling of the soldier. There was a sublimity in his genius which soared above the pitch of ordinary minds; and had his faculties been exercised to their full extent by opportunity and action, had his judgement been fully matured by age and experience, he would, without doubt, have rivalled in reputation the most celebrated captains of antiquity. His body was brought to England, and buried with military honours in Westminster abbey, where a magnificent monument is erected to his memory. Wolfe, Christian, a celebrated German philosopher, was born at Breitau in 1679. After having been well instructed in the rudiments of learning and science in his own country, Wolfe prosecuted his studies successively in the universities of Jena, Hamburgh, and Leipzig. At the age of 26 he had acquired so much distinction, that he was appointed professor of mathematics, and soon afterwards of philosophy in general, in the university of Hall. After Leibnitz had published his Thodicea, Wolfe struck with the novelty of the edifice which that philosopher had raised, assiduously laboured in the investigation of new metaphysical truths. He also digested the Elements of Mathematics in a new method, and attempted an improvement of the art of reasoning, in a treatise On the Powers of the Human Understanding. Upon the foundation of Leibnitz's doctrine of Monads, he formed a new system of Cosmology and Pneumatology, digested and demonstrated in a mathematical method. This work, entitled Thoughts on God, the World, and the Human Soul, was published in the year 1710; to which were added, in a subsequent edition, Heads of Ethics and Policy. Wolfe was now rising towards the summit of philosophical reputation, when the opinion which he entertained on the doctrine of necessity being deemed by his colleagues inimical to religion, and an oration which he delivered in praise of the morality of the Chinese having given much offence, an accusation of heresy was publicly brought against him; and, though he attempted to justify himself in a treatise which he wrote on the subject of fatality, a royal mandate was issued in November 1723, requiring him to leave the Prussian dominions. Having been formerly invited by the landgrave of Hesse-Cassel to fill a professor's chair in the university of Cassel, Wolfe now put himself under the patronage of that prince, who had the liberality to afford him a secure asylum, and appointed him professor of mathematics and philosophy. The question concerning the grounds of the censure which had been passed upon Wolfe was now everywhere freely canvassed; almost every German university was inflamed with disputes on the subject of liberty and necessity; and the names of Wolfians and Anti-Wolfians were everywhere heard. After an interval of nine years, the king of Prussia reversed his sentence of exile, and appointed him vice-chancellor of the university of Hall, where his return was welcomed with every expression of triumph. From this time he was employed in completing his Institutes of Philosophy, which he lived to accomplish in every branch except poetry. In 1745 he was created a baron by the elector of Bavaria, and succeeded Ludovig in the office of chancellor of the university. He continued to enjoy these honours till the year 1754, when he expired. He possessed a clear and methodical understanding; which, by long exercise in mathematical investigations, was particularly fitted for the employment of digesting the several branches of knowledge into regular systems; and his fertile powers of invention enabled him to enrich almost every field of science in which he laboured, with some valuable additions. The lucid order which appears in all his writings enables his reader to follow his conceptions with ease and certainty, through the longest trains of reasoning. Wolfenbuttle, a considerable town of Germany, in the circle of Lower Saxony, and duchy of Brunswick, with a castle where the duke of Brunswick Wolfenbuttle resides. It is one of the strongest places in Germany, though the fortifications want repairing in several places. There is an excellent library, kept in a building lately erected for that purpose, consisting of 116,000 printed books, and 2000 uncommon books, with

WOLFSBERG

Pages 428-428

a town of Germany, in Lower Carinthia, with a castle, on which the district about it depends, which is 20 miles in length, and 10 in breadth. It is seated on the river Lavand, at the foot of a mountain covered with wood, and full of wolves, from whence the town took its name. It is 36 miles east of Clagenfurt. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15°. N. Lat. 46°. 56'.

WOLGAST

Pages 428-428

a considerable town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and in Pomerania, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name, with a castle, and one of the best and largest harbours on the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is a well-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and seated on the river Pfin. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14°. 4°. N. Lat. 54°. 1'.

WOLLASTON

Pages 428-428

William, descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, was born in 1659. He was in 1674 admitted a pensioner in Sidney <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where, notwithstanding several disadvantages, he acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of reputation. In 1682, seeing no prospect of preferment, he became assistant to the head <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> school. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he got a small lecture about two miles distant, but did the duty the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>; which, together with the business of a great free-school for about four years, began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. During this space he likewise underwent a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of trouble and uneasiness, in order to extricate two of his brothers from some inconveniences, to which their own imprudence had subjected them. In 1688 affairs took a new turn. He found himself by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> entitled to a very ample estate; and came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> that same year, where he settled; choosing a private, retired, and studious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he published his treatise, entitled The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> Delineated; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> for which so great a demand was made, that more than 10,000 were sold in a very few years. He had scarcely completed the publication of it, when he unfortunately broke an arm; and this adding strength to distempers that had been growing upon him for some time, accelerated his death; which happened upon the 29th of October 1724. He was a tender, humane, and in all respects worthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; but is represented to have had something of the irascible in his constitution and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>. His Religion of Nature Delineated exposed him to some censure, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had put a slight upon Christianity, by laying so much stress, as he does in this work, upon the obligations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, reason, and virtue; and by making no mention of revealed religion. But this censure must have been the offspring of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> envy, since it appears from the introduction to his work, that he intended to treat of revealed religion in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, which he lived not to finish.

WOLSEY

Pages 428-428

Thomas, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> and archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, is said to have been the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a>. He studied at Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he became acquainted with the learned Erasmus; and in the year 1500 became rector of Lymington in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>: he was afterwards made chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. and obtained several preferments. Having gradually acquired an entire ascendancy over the mind of Henry VIII. he successively obtained several bishoprics, and at length was made archbishop of York, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England, and prime minister; and was for several years the arbiter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Pope Leo X. created him cardinal in 1513, and made him legate a latere; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. and the French king Francis I. loaded him with favours, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> him over to their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; but after having first sided with the emperor, he deserted him to espouse the interest of France. As his revenues were immense, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and ostentation were carried to the greatest height. He had 500 servants; among whom were 9 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 10 lords, 15 knights, and 40 esquires. His ambition to be pope, his pride, his exactions, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> delay of Henry's divorce, occasioned his disgrace. In the earlier <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he seems to have been licentious in his manners; it was reported, that soon after his preferment to the living of Lymington in Somersetshire, he was put into the stocks by Sir Amias Paulet, a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, for getting drunk and making a riot at a fair. This treatment Wolsey did not forget when he arrived at the high station of lord-chancellor of England; but summoned his corrector up to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and, after a severe reprimand, enjoined him five years <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> confinement in the Temple. Whatever may have been his faults, there can be no doubt of their having been aggravated both by the zealous reformers and by the creatures of Henry VIII. who was himself neither Papist nor Protestant; for there is every reason to believe that the cardinal was sincere in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and sincerity, or at least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, was then a crime. Wolsey was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learned men; a judge and munificent encourager of the polite arts; and ought to be considered as the founder of Christchurch college, Oxford; where, as well as in other places, many remains of his magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> still exist. He died in 1530. WOLVERENE. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URSUS">Ursus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WOMBAT

Pages 428-428

an animal lately discovered in New South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. See Dasysurus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WOOD

Pages 432-433

Rotten, Illumination of. This is a subject which has often been discussed by naturalists. Spallan- zani maintained, that there is a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between the illumination of rotten wood, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> phos- phorus; and he imagines, that in the putrid fermenta- tion, the hydrogen and the carbure of the wood come more easily in contact with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> of the atmos- phere, by which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> a slow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a>, and the illumination of the wood, is produced; and he thinks that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> cannot proceed in the irrespire- ble kinds of gases. Rotten wood also, in which the ne- cessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of hydrogen and carbure is not at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> disengaged, does not obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of illuminating. Mr Corrado, however, objects to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, that the slow combustion does not take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> ac- cording to the above theory, as the wood, at the time when it begins to illuminate, is mostly deprived of its resinous particles, and consequently contains but very little hydrogen and carbure; and it appears to him more probable, that the more it loses of combustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, the more it obtains the property of illuminating. There is, he thinks, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and the artificial phosphorus. Mr Hum- boldt concludes, from his experiments, that the illumi- <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of rotten wood takes place only when it gets into contact with oxygen; and when it has lost the property of emitting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in irrespirable gases, it recovers it again by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> it to oxygen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a>. Dr Gartner, how- ever, is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that, according to his experiments, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of humidity is always requisite, and he thinks that oxygen gas is not quite necessary though the illumination be increased by it. This phenomenon, however, being so very different from all known pro- cesses of combustion, where light is disengaged, Dr Gartner asks, whether it be not more agreeing with the animal process of respiration, than with a true combus- tion, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> whether the illumination of the wood be produced by phosphorus and carbure in a proportion hitherto un- known. Dr Gartner is, on the whole, inclined to think, that it is at present impossible to give a satisfac- tory explanation of all the phenomena that occur in this process. Beckmann has made numerous experiments on the illumination of rotten wood, in different gases and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, in order to throw some light on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the above naturalists. The results of these experiments dif- fer in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> from what the experiments of those gentlemen have shown, which, however, Beckmann attributes to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of rotten wood, as a substance that is not always of the same kind, and has not always an equal degree of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> and humidity. It seems also to differ materially from the artificial phosphorus in the following particulars. 1. It shines in oxygen gas at a very low temperature. 2. It emits light in all irre- spirable gases, at least for a short time. 3. In muriatic acid gas its light is suddenly extinguished. 4. It shines in a less degree in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> rarefied by the air-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>. 5. Ac- cording to Mr Corrado, it even shines in the torricellian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>. 6. Its illumination is extinguished in oxy- gen gas, as well as in other kinds of gases, when they are heated. 7. By its illumination in oxygen gas, car- bonic acid gas is produced. 8. One may suffer the rotten wood to be extinguished several times, one after an- other, in irrespirable gases, without depriving them of the property of making new pieces of rotten wood shine again. 9. Humidity greatly promotes the illumination, and even seems to be necessary in producing it. 10. The rotten wood continues to shine under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and other fluids, and in some of them its light is even in- creased. All this seems to show, that the extinction of rotten wood, in different media, does not immediately depend on a want of oxygen, but rather on a particular change, to which the wood itself has been exposed. WOOD-Cock. See Scolopax, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. WOOD-Goat. See Capra, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. WOOD-Louse. See Oniscus, Entomology Index. (A) The parts of the print intended to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> are not even touched by the wood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>. WOOD-PECKER. See PICUS, ORNITHOLOGY Index. WOODMOTTE. See FOREST <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">COURT</a>.

WOODSTOCK

Pages 433-433

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, in England, pleasantly seated on a rising ground, and on a rivulet; a well compacted borough-town, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; but is chiefly noted for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLENHEIM">Blenheim</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, built in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the victory obtained by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> over the French and Bavarians in August 1704. It was erected at the public expense, and is one of the noblest seats in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. One of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> to it is over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> with one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, 190 feet in diameter, resembling the Rialto at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. The gardens take up 100 acres of ground; and the offices, which are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>, have room enough to accommodate 300 people. The apartments of the palace are magnificently furnished; and the staircases, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, paintings, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, surprisingly fine. The town is about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the palace, having several good inns; and a manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> chains for watches, and excellent gloves. A steel chain has been made at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which sold for £100. — The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is estimated at 1300 persons. It is eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and 60 west-north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. i. 15. N. Lut. 57. 52.

WOODWARD

Pages 433-433

Dr John, was born in 1665, and educated at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> school, where he learned the Latin and Greek languages, and was afterwards sent to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he is said to have been put apprentice to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>-draper. He was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in that station, till he became acquainted with Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Barwick, an eminent physician, who took him under his tuition and into his family. Here he prosecuted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> vigour and success the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, anatomy, and physic. In 1692, Dr Skillingsfleet quitting the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of professor of physic in Graham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, our author was chosen to succeed him, and the year following was elected F.R.S. In 1695 he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.D. by patent from Archbishop Tenison; and the same year he published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> towards a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>. He afterwards wrote many other pieces, which have been well received by the learned world. He founded a lecture in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, to be read there upon his Essay, &c. and handsomely endowed it. He died in 1728.

WOOL

Pages 433-435

the covering of sheep. See OVIS and SHEEP. Wool resembles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many particulars; but besides its fineness, which constitutes an obvious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, there are other particulars which may serve also to distinguish them from one another. Wool, like the hair of horses, cattle, and most other animals, completes its growth in a year, and then falls off as hair does, and is succeeded by a fresh crop. It differs from hair, however, in the uniformity of its growth, and the regularity of its shedding. Every filament of wool seems to keep exact pace with another in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body of the animal; the whole crop <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> up at once; the whole advances uniformly together; the whole loosens from the skin nearly at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and thus falls off, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not previously shorn, leaving the animal covered with a short coat of young wool, which in its turn undergoes the same regular mutations. Hairs are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of the same thickness in every part; but wool constantly varies in thickness in different parts, being generally thicker at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> than at the roots. That part of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a> of sheep which grows during the winter is finer than what grows in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. This was first observed by Dr Anderson, the editor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">Bee</a>, and published in his Observations on the Means of exciting a Spirit of National Industry. While the wool remains in the state it was first shorn off the sheep's back, and not sorted into its different kinds, it is called fleece. Each fleece consists of wool of diverse qualities and degrees of fineness, which the dealers therein take care to separate. The French and English usually separate each fleece into three sorts, viz. 1. Mother-wool, which is that of the back and neck. 2. The wool of the tails and legs. 3. That of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and under the belly. The Spaniards make the like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> into three sorts, which they call prime, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third; and for the greater ease, mark each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">bale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pack with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, denoting the sort. If the triage or separation be well made, in 15 bales there <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 12 marked R, that is, refine, or prime; two marked F, for fine, or second; and one S, for thirds. The wools most esteemed are the English, chiefly those about Leominster, Cotswold, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight; the Spanish, principally those about Segovia; and the French, about Berry: which last are said to have this peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, that they will knot or bind with any other sort; whereas the rest will only knot with their own kind. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the wools of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, Laodicea, Apulia, and especially those of Tarentum, Parma, and Altino, were the most valued. Varro assures us, that the people there used to clothe their sheep with skins, to secure the wool from being damaged. Of late a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> has been paid to wool in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as well as several others. Several very spirited attempts have been made to improve it, by introducing superior breeds of sheep, and better methods of managing them. For this purpose has been formed the British Wool <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> formed for the purpose of obtaining the best breeds of fine-wooled sheep, with a view of ascertaining, by actual experiments, how far each <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> or variety is calculated for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; the qualities of their wool respectively; the uses to which each kind of wool could be most profitably employed in different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; and the comparative value of each species of sheep, so far as the same can be determined. Attention had for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> been paid by the Highland Society to a famous breed of fine-wooled sheep in Shetland; but it occurred to Sir John Sinclair of Ulbster, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a>, and to Dr James Anderson, well known as the author of many useful publications, that the improvement of British wool was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of too much importance to be entrusted to a society which is obliged to devote its attention to such a variety of objects as the general improvement of the Highlands of Scotland. The latter of these gentlemen, therefore, in an Appendix to the Report of the Committee of the Highland Society... Society of Scotland, for the year 1792, proposed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a patriotic association for the improvement of British wool; and the former, who was convenor of the committee to whom the subject of Shetland wool had been referred, wrote circular letters, recommending the plan. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which was, that on the 31st of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1791, several noblemen and gentlemen of the highest respectability met in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and constituted themselves into a Society for the Improvement of British Wool. Of this society Sir John Sinclair was elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>; after which, in an excellent speech, he pointed out to the members the objects of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, the means by which those objects could be attained, and the advantages which would result from their united labours. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> was afterwards printed by order of the society. The particular breeds of sheep to which the society proposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> its attention, were sheep for the hilly parts of Scotland; sheep for the plains, or the Lowland breed; and sheep for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. They were to try experiments also with sheep from foreign countries, distinguished by any particular property. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects which the members had in view, during the first year of their association, were, 1. To collect specimens of the best breeds which Great Britain at that period afforded, in order to ascertain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection to which sheep had already been brought in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. 2. To procure from every country, distinguished for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of its sheep and wool, specimens of the different breeds it possessed, in order to ascertain how far the original breed, or a mixed breed from it and the native sheep of the country, could thrive in Scotland. 3. To distribute as much as possible all these breeds, both foreign and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>, over the whole kingdom, wherever proper persons could be found to take <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of them, in order to try experiments on a more extensive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> than the society itself could do; to spread information, and to excite a spirit for the improvement of sheep and wool in every part of the country. Sir John Sinclair had previously collected a flock, consisting of sheep of the Spanish, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, Southdown, Cheviot, Lomond hills, and Shetland breeds, and of a mixed breed from these different sheep. This flock amounted to 110 rams, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>. M. d'Aubenton, in consequence of a correspondence with Sir John Sinclair, sent over to the society ten rams and five ewes, of real Spanish breed, which had been originally entrusted to his care by the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France: these, after encountering a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of obstacles, and after being shipped and threatened to be slaughtered at the customhouse of Brighthelmstone for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, arrived safe at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>, at the same time, sent to the society four rams and six ewes of the Southdown and Spanish breeds. Mr Bilton of Killall, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, presented them with three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a> rams, reckoned by many the best breed in England; the society at the same time ordered 150 ewes of the same breed, and two ewes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> Mountain breed, reckoned the best in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, to be sent along with them. They purchased 57 rams and 173 ewes of the Cheviot breed, reckoned the best in Scotland, for the hilly parts of the country. Lord Dacre sent them 20 ewes of an excellent breed, which existed at Mochrum in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>. The late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> sent them in a present three rams of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> crossed by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope breed. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">Grant</a> junior of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, in conjunction with Mr Sibbald, merchant at Leith, presented them an Apulian ram and ewe; the ram arrived in safety, but the ewe unfortunately died on the passage. Mr Baron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SETON">Seton</a> of Preston, in Linlithgowshire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> them a ram and two ewes of a Spanish breed, which had been for some time kept in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> unmixed with any other. They purchased 100 ewes of a small breed existing in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Leuchars in Fife, much resembling the Shetland. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> William Conyngham of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> sent them 11 Spanish rams, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> Spanish ewes, 15 three-fourth breed and 16 one-half breed Spanish and Irish ewes. Lord Sheffield sent them eight rams and 18 ewes; and his Majesty made them a present of two rams. Thus, in the course of one year, the society acquired by donation or purchase about 800 sheep of different sorts and ages, and many of them from foreign countries: about 500 of these were distributed over different parts of Scotland, the greater number of which were sold to gentlemen anxious to promote the views of the society, and well qualified to make experiments on the different breeds which they had obtained. The greatest part of the remainder were taken by different gentlemen who kept them for the society, and according to their directions, without any expense. It is impossible to produce an influence of so much having been accomplished by a society of private individuals in so short a time. Nor was this all; the same year Mr Andrew Kerr, a very intelligent sheep-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> on the borders of England, was sent, at the expense of the society, to examine the state of sheep-farming along the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Scotland and the interior parts of the Highlands. His tour was printed by order of the society, and contains the first intimation of the possibility of the Cheviot breed thriving in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Scotland. In the year 1792, Messrs Redhead, Laing, and Marshall, were sent by the society, to make a survey of the state of sheep-farming through some of the principal counties of England; the result of which was also published by the society, and contains more information on the subject of the different breeds of England than any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> hitherto published; and in 1794, Mr John Naifmyth was sent on a tour through the southern districts of Scotland, which completed the circuit of almost the whole kingdom. Thus a few private individuals, unaided by the public purse, had boldness enough to undertake ascertaining the comparative value of the different kinds of sheep in their own country, and to introduce some of the most celebrated breeds of other countries, and succeeded in the spirited attempt. It is impossible in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to state more minutely the various other transactions of the society; to enter into any detail of the premiums given by this respectable institution for the improvement of the celebrated Shetland breed; or to explain how, as if it were by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, in a country where the manufacture of wool was little known, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> manufactured of that material were made, rivaling, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> surpassing, the most celebrated fabrics of other countries. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> having unfortunately arisen, it became impossible to pay the same attention, or to carry on with the same success, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> enterprises; even old old establishments often <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> a sacrifice amidst the horrors of war. The utmost that the British Wool Society could expect to do, was to preserve the institution in such a state, that when peace shall be happily restored it may revive with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> energy and spirit. It is a curious fact that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, during their residence in Britain, established a manufactory of woollen cloth at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, which was so extensive as to supply their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and there is reason to believe that the trade which they introduced into Britain, was not neglected by the native inhabitants, for the first 920 years of the Christian era. The long Spanish wool was imported into this country so early as the 12th century, and we find that since the days of Edward III. British fleeces were admirably adapted to the kind of cloth which was in greatest request, though now they are generally unequal to the production of that which is sought after. WOOL-Combing, a well known operation, which, when performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is laborious, tedious, and expensive. The expense of it through all England has been calculated at no less a sum than £80,000; and to lessen this expense, the Rev. Edmund Cartwright of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DONCASTER">Doncaster</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> betook himself, some years ago, to carding wool by machinery. After repeated attempts and improvements, for which he took out three patents, he found that wool can be combed in perfection by machinery, of which he gives the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Fig. 1. is the crank lather. A is a tube through which the material, being formed into a sliver, and slightly twisted, is drawn forward by the delivering rollers; B, a wheel fast upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of the crank; C, a wheel, on the opposite end of whose axis is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> working in a wheel upon the axis of one of the delivering rollers. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>. When two or more slivers are required, the cans or baskets, in which they are contained, are placed upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> under the lather (as represented at D), which, by having a slow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, twists them together as they go up. Fig. 2. is the circular clearing comb, for giving work in the head, carried in a frame by two cranks. Fig. 3. the comb-table, having the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> pointing towards the centre, moved by cogs upon the rim, and carried round upon trucks like the head of a windmill. a, b, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> rollers. c, d, Callendar, or conducting rollers. Note. Underneath the table is another <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of rollers, for drawing out the backings. In the above specification, we have omitted the frame in which the machine stands, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, shafts, &c. Had these been introduced, the drawing would have been crowded and confused; besides, as matters of information, they would have been unnecessary, every mechanic, when he knows the principles of a machine, being competent to apply the movements to it. The wool, if for particularly nice work, goes through three operations, otherwise two are sufficient: the first operation opens the wool, and makes it connect together into a rough sliver, but does not clear it. The clearing is performed by the second, and, if necessary, a third operation. A set of machinery, consisting of three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, will require the attendance of an overseer and ten children, and will comb a pack, or 240 lb., in twelve hours. As neither fire nor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is necessary for machine-combing, the saving of those articles, even the fire alone, will, in general, pay the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> of the overseer and children; so that the actual saving to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a> is the whole of what the combing costs, by the old imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of hand-combing. Machine-combed wool is better, especially for machine-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>, by at least 12 per cent. being all equally mixed, and the slivers uniform, and of any required length.

WOOLSTON

Pages 435-435

Thomas, an English divine, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a> in 1669, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. His first appearance in the learned world was in 1705, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled, The Old Apology for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, against the Jews and Gentiles, revived. He afterwards wrote many pieces; but what made the most noise, were his six Discourses on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a> of Christ; which occasioned a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books and pamphlets upon the subject, and raised a prosecution against him. At his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in Guildhall, before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> Raymond, he spoke several times himself; and urged, that "he thought it very hard that he should be tried by a set of men who, though otherwise very learned and worthy persons, were no more judges of the subjects on which he wrote, than himself was a judge of the most crabbed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>." He was sentenced to a year's imprisonment, and to pay a fine of £100. He purchased the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the year, being unable to pay the fine. The greatest obstruction to his deliverance from confinement was, the obligation of giving security not to offend by any future writings, he being refused to write again as freely as before. Whilst some supposed that this author wrote with the settled intention of subverting Christianity under the pretence of defending it, others believed him disordered in his mind; and many circumstances concurred which gave countenance to this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. He died, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 27, 1732-3, after an illness of four days; and, a few minutes before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, uttered these words: "This is a struggle which all men must go through, and which I bear not only patiently, but with willingness." His body was interred in St George's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard, Southwark.

WOOLWICH

Pages 435-435

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, with a market on Fridays, but no fair. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> for its fine docks and yards, where men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> are built; as also for its vast magazines of great guns, mortars, bombs, cannon-balls, powder, and other warlike stores. It has likewise an academy, where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> are taught, and young officers instructed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art. It is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 10. N. Lat. 51. 30.

WORCESTER

Pages 435-437

in Latin Wigornia, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England of the same name, stands on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, but so low that it can hardly be seen till one is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> upon it. It is supposed to be the Brannium of Antoninus, the Branogenium of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, and to have been built by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to awe the Britons on the other side of the Severn. It was made an episcopal see about the year 680 by Sexulphus bishop of the Mercians; but the present <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> was begun by Wulfston in the year 1084. The town hath been several times burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; first, in 1041, by Hardicanute, who also massacred the citizens; secondly, not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after William Rufus's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and a third time, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Stephen besieged and took it. Here, in latter times, Worcester was fought that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. with his Scots <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, was defeated by Cromwell. In a garden near the south gate of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was hottest, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the slain are often dug up. It had formerly strong walls and a castle; but these have been demolished long ago. It is now a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> city, the streets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and well paved, and some of them very regular and well built, particularly Foregate-street; so that in general it is a very agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The cathedral is a stately edifice, and among other monuments in it are those of King John, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>, elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to Henry VIII., and of the counts of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, who gave occasion to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> in and about the city; of which that built and endowed by Robert Berkeley of Spechley, Esq., is a very noble one. There is a school founded by Henry VIII., three other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-schools. The guildhall and the workhouse are stately structures. The churches, St Nicholas and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALL_SAINTS">All-Saints</a>, have been lately rebuilt, and are very handsome edifices.
