The city carries on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade; for which it is chiefly indebted to its situation upon the Severn. A prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people are employed in and about it in the manufacture of broad-cloth and gloves. The Welch inhabit a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, and speak their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Its market is well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, corn, and cattle, and its quay is much frequented by ships. By a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from James I. it is governed by a mayor, six aldermen, who are justices of the peace, and chosen out of 24 capital citizens; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, the city being a county of itself; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, consisting of 48 other citizens, out of which two chamberlains are yearly chosen; a recorder, town-clerk, two coroners, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-bearer, 13 constables, and four sergeants at mace. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of this see, there have been, it is said, one pope, four saints, seven <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-chancellors, 11 archbishops, two lord treasurers, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, one lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and one vice-president. The city at present gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> and marquis to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a>. W. Long. i. 55. N. Lat. 52. 10. Worcester, Edward Somerset, Marquis of, was a distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> character in the time of Charles I., by whom he was created earl of Glamorgan, while heir-apparent to the marquis of Worcester. This nobleman flourished chiefly in the reign of Charles I., and seems to have been a most zealous adherent to the cause of that unfortunate monarch, on whose account it is said that he and his father wasted an immense sum. Of this the king was so sensible, that he granted to the earl a most extraordinary patent, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> powers of which were, to make him <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a> of three armies, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> with nomination of his officers; to enable him to raise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> by selling his majesty's woods, wardships, customs, and prerogatives; and to create by blank patents, to be filled up at Glamorgan's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of marquis to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any thing, says Lord Orford, could justify the delegation of such authority, besides his majesty having lost all authority, when he conferred it, it was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> with which the king concluded of bestowing the princess <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> on Glamorgan's son. This patent was given up by the marquis to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> after the restoration. He died not long after that era, in 1667, after he had published what Lord Orford calls the following amazing piece of folly. "A century of the names and scantlings of such inventions, as at present I can call to mind to have tried and perfected, which (my former notes being lost) I have, at the instance of a powerful friend, endeavoured now in the year 1655, to let these down in such a way as may sufficiently instruct me to put any of them in practice." Some of the inventions referred to in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> are the following. A ship-destroying engine, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a>-topping engine, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-work, a bucket fountain, an ebbing and flowing cattle clock, a tinder-box pistol, a pocket <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a>, a most admirable way to raise weights, a stupendous water-work. For the last contrivance the marquis procured an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in 1663, for the sole benefit arising from it, one-tenth of it being appropriated to Charles II. and his successors. In a manuscript addition to a copy of the Century of Inventions, the stupendous or water-commanding engine is described as boundless for height or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, requiring no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a>, or even additional help or force to be set or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, but what intrinsically is afforded from its own operation, nor yet the twentieth part thereof, and the engine consisteth of the following particulars. 1. A perfect counterpoise for what quantitysoever of water. 2. A perfect countervail for what heightsoever it is to be brought unto. 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMUM_MOBILE">primum <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOBILE">mobile</a>, commanding both height and quantity, regulator-wife. 4. A vicegerent or countervail, supplying the place, and performing the full force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, beast, or mill. 5. A helm or stern, with bit and reins, wherewith any child may guide, order, and control the whole operation. 6. A particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for water, according to the intended quantity or height of water. 7. A place for the original fountain, or even river to run into, and naturally of its own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> incorporate itself with the rising water, and at the very bottom of the same aqueduct, though never so big or high. Various and very opposite opinions have been held with regard to the title of this nobleman to be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> genius. Lord Orford has pronounced his work an amazing piece of folly; and Mr Hume, speaking of his political conduct, says, "that the king judged aright of this nobleman's character, appears from his Century of Arts, or Scantling of Inventions, which is a ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of lies, chimeras, and impossibilities, and shows what might be expected from such a man." Hist. of England. It may be fairly presumed from the quotations now made, that neither Lord Orford nor Mr Hume was qualified to judge of the marquis's work, otherwise a more temperate or a more modified <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> would have been given. By others, the author of the inventions has been regarded as one of the greatest mechanical geniuses, and is to be considered as the inventor of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine, which he denominates a stupendous water-work. There seems to be no reason to suppose that any steam-engine was erected by the marquis himself; but it is said that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Savary, after <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the marquis's books, tried many experiments upon the power and force of steam, and at last fell upon a method of applying it to raise water; and having bought up and destroyed all the marquis's books that could be got, claimed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> to himself, and obtained a patent for it. The marquis of Worcester is sometimes confounded with John Tiptoft, earl of Worcester, a very accomplished literary character, who lived in the times of Henry VI. and Edward IV. Being attached to Edward, he absconded during the short restoration of Henry, and being taken concealed in a tree in Waybridge forest in Huntingdonshire, he was brought to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, accused of cruelty in his administration of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and condemned and beheaded at the Tower in the year 1476. This nobleman translated Cicero de Amicitia, some parts of Caesar's Commentaries, and was the author of several other works.

WORCESTERSHIRE

Pages 437-437

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a> on the east, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> on the south, by the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a> and Salop on the west, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>. According to Templeman, it is 36 miles in length, 28 in breadth, and about 130 in circumference, within which it contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of two others, 11 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, of which three are boroughs, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, namely <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, 152 parishes, about 540,000 acres, and 139,518 inhabitants. This being an inland county, well cultivated, and free from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, marshes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stagnant waters, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very sweet and wholesome all over it. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general is very rich, producing corn, fruit, especially pears, of which they make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of perry; hops and pasture. The hills are covered with sheep, and the meadows with cattle. Hence they have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and cheese in abundance. They are also well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, either wood or coal, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRINE">brine</a> pits and salt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. Of the last they have not only enough for themselves, but export <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>; which noble river, to the great convenience and emolument of the inhabitants, runs from north to south through the very middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, enriching the soil, and yielding it plenty of fish, and an easy expeditious conveyance of goods to and from it. The other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> by which it is watered are the Stour, Avon, Teme, &c. It sends <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. two for the county, two for the city of Worcester, two for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROITWICH">Droitwich</a>, two for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVESHAM">Evesham</a>, and one for Bewdley; and lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Worcester, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> circuit.

WORD

Pages 437-437

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, an articulate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> designed to represent some idea <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> notion. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">GRAMMAR</a> and LANGUAGE. See also LOGIC, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. chap. i. Word, or Watch-word, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, is some peculiar word or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> know and distinguish one another in the night, &c. and by which spies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> persons are discovered. It is used also to prevent surprizes. The word is given out in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> every night to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, who gives it to the majors of the brigades, and they to the adjutants; who give it first to the field-officers, and afterwards to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, who carry it to the subalterns. In garrisons it is given after the gate is shut to the town-major, who gives it to the adjutants, and they to the sergeants. Words of Command. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">EXERCISE</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">MANUAL</a>. Signals by the Drum, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in exercising of the Army, instead of the WORD of Command, viz. Signals by the drum. A short roll, A flam, To arms, The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, The quiet march, The point of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, The retreat, Drum ceasing, Two short rolls, The dragoon march, The grenadier march, The troop, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> roll, The grenadier march, The preparative, The general, Two long rolls, Operations. To caution. To perform any distinct thing. To form the line or battalion. To advance, except when intended for a salute. To advance quick. To march and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. To retreat. To halt. To perform the flank firing. To open the battalion. To form the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> divisions. To form the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. To reduce the square to the column. To make ready and fire. To cease firing. To bring or lodge the colours.

WORK

Pages 437-439

Carpenters, Clock, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a>, Field, Fire, Fret, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROTESQUE">Grotesque</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, Mosaic. See the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, together with FORTIFICATION and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYROTECHNY">PYROTECHNY</a>. WORK-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where indigent, vagrant, and idle people, are set to work, and supplied with food and clothing. Work-houses are of two kinds, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least are employed for two different purposes. Some are used as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> for vagrants or sturdy beggars, who are there confined and compelled to labour for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> which maintains them; whilst others, sometimes called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-house, are charitable asylums for such indigent persons as through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> or infirmity are unable to support themselves by their own labour. The former kind of work-house, when under proper management, may be made to serve the best of purposes; of the latter we are acquainted with none which entirely commands our approbation. To make confinement in a work-house operate to the correction of vagrants and disorderly persons (and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it produce not this effect it can hardly be considered as a beneficial <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>), the prisoners should be shut up in separate cells, and compelled to labour for their own subsistence. A crew of thieves and vagabonds associating with each other is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in which every individual is hardened in his crimes by the countenance and conversation of his companions; and wretches who, when at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, choose to beg or steal rather than to earn a comfortable livelihood by honest industry, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> submit to any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> which a humane overseer can inflict rather than work for the benefit of others. No punishment indeed will compel a vagrant to labour. He may assume the appearance of it, but he will make no progress; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of fickleness or weakness is ever at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> for an excuse. Hence it is that thieves and trumpets... strumpets are too often dismissed from work-houses and bridewells ten times more the children of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> than when they entered them. To remedy these evils, we can think of no better method than to confine each prisoner in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> by himself, and to furnish him daily with such an allowance of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> as may preserve him from immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; for the only compulsion to make such men work seriously is the fear of want, and the only way to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> them is to leave them to their own meditations on the consequences of their past conduct. There are surely very few persons, if any, whose aversion from labour would not be conquered by the pinching of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and the certain prospect of perishing by famine; and it is to be hoped that there are not many so totally divested of every latent principle of virtue as not to be brought by such solitude to a due <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of their former wickedness. Should one or two, however, be occasionally found to be very obdurate as to suffer themselves to perish rather than work, their deaths would prove a salutary beacon to others, and their blood would be on their own heads; for we have the express command of St Paul himself, that "if any will not work, neither should he eat." No doubt it would be proper that the meditations of vagabonds confined in a work-house should be directed by the private admonitions of a pious and intelligent clergyman; but it is not every clergyman who is qualified to discharge such a duty. If he be actuated by a zeal not according to knowledge, or if he have not with equal care studied <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and the word of God, his admonitions will be more likely to provoke the profane <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of his auditor, and harden him in his wickedness, than to excite in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> such sorrow for his sins as shall "bring forth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> meet for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>." To render the instruction of thieves and vagrants of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, it must be accurately adapted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of each individual; and however excellent it may be in itself, it will not be listened to unless offered at seasons of uncommon severity, which the instructor should therefore carefully observe. That such wholesome severity as this would often reform the inhabitants of work-houses, appears extremely probable from the effects of a similar treatment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> prostitutes mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames in his Sketches of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>: "A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those wretches were in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> confined in a house of correction, on a daily allowance of threepence, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> was embezzled by the servants of the house. Pinching hunger did not reform their manners; for being absolutely idle, they encouraged each other in vice, waiting impatiently for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of deliverance. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a> the superintendent, with the consent of the magistrates, removed them to a clean house; and, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, appointed for each a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of oatmeal daily, with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, water, and fire for cooking. Relieved now from distress, they longed for comfort. What would they not give for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> or ale? Work (says he) will procure you plenty. To some who offered to spin, he gave <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, engaging to pay them half the price of their yarn, retaining the other half for the materials furnished. The spinners earned about ninepence weekly; a comfortable addition to what they had before. The rest undertook to spin, one after another; and before the end of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> they were all of them intent upon work. It was a branch of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> to let free such as merited that favour; and some of them appeared to be so thoroughly reformed as to be in no danger of a relapse." Work-houses erected as charitable asylums appear to us, in every view that we can take of them, as institutions which can serve no good purpose. Economy is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> which inclines people to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of providing for the poor. There is comparatively but a very small number of mankind in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> so aged and infirm as not to be able to contribute, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, to their subsistence by their own labour; and in such houses it is thought that proper work may be provided for them, so that the public shall have nothing to give in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> but what the poor are absolutely unable to procure for themselves. It is imagined likewise, that numbers collected at a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, can be maintained at less expense than in separate houses; and feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> are given for an example, who could not live on their pay if they did not meet together. But the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>. "Soldiers having the management of their pay, can club for a bit of meat; but as the inhabitants of a poor-house are maintained by the public, the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> must be allotted to each. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is what might be expected: the bulk of them reserve part of their victuals for purchasing ale or spirits. It is vain to expect work from them: poor wretches void of shame will never work seriously, where the profit accrues to the public, not to themselves. Hunger is the only effectual means for compelling such persons to work." The poor, therefore, should be supported in their own houses; and to support them properly, the first thing to be done is, to estimate what each can earn by his own labour; for as far only as that falls short of maintenance, is there room for charity. In repairing those evils which society did not or could not prevent, it ought to be careful not to counteract the wise purposes of nature, nor to do more than to give the poor a fair chance to work for themselves. The present distress must be relieved, the sick and the aged provided for; but the children must be instructed; and labour, not alms, offered to those who have some ability to work, however small that ability may be. They will be as industrious as possible, because they work for themselves; and a weekly sum of charity under their own management will turn to better account than in a poor-house under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of mercenaries. Not a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> of it will be laid out on fermented liquors, unless perhaps as a medicine in sickness. Nor does such low fair call for pity to those who can afford no better. Ale makes no part of the maintenance of those who, in many parts of Scotland, live by the sweat of their brows; and yet the person who should banish ale from a charity work-house, would be exclaimed against as hard-hearted, and even void of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. That such a mode of supporting the poor in their own houses is practicable, will hardly admit of a dispute; for it has been actually put in practice in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> ever since the year 1788. At that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> such revenues as had till then been expended in alms by the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-wardens, and those of which the administration had been connected with the workhouse, were united under one administration with such sums as were collected from private benevolence. The city was divided into sixty districts, containing each an equal equal number of poor; and over these 180 overseers were appointed. Actual relief was the first object; but at the very moment that this provision was secured, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> were taken to prevent any man from receiving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> which he could have been able to earn for himself. By these methods, which our limits will not permit us to state, the overseers were able to make a calculation tolerably exact of what each pauper wanted for bare subsistence, in addition to the fruits of his own labour. A flax-yarn-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> manufacture was established, in which the yarn is paid for, not by its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, but by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. The clean flax is sold to the poor at a low price, and a certain measure of yarn again bought from them at 30 per cent. above the usual price; so that the overseers are sure that all the yarn spun by the poor will be brought into their office. Every pauper brings with him a book in which the quantity delivered is carefully noted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, which furnishes the overseers with a continual <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> of the state of industry among their poor. As soon as this institution was established, the overseers went through their difficulties, and asked, in all such mansions as could be supposed to harbour want, if the inhabitants stood in need of support? The question to all such poor as wished for relief, and were able to spin, was, Whether they did earn by their work 1s. 6d. a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>? For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> had taught the inhabitants of Hamburgh, that many poor live upon that sum; and they knew enough of their poor to suppose, that 1s. 6d. avowed earning was equal to something more. If the answer was affirmative, the pauper stood not in need of weekly assistance. If it was <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, work was given him, which, by being paid 30 per cent. above its value, afforded him 1s. 6d. a-week easily, if he was even an indifferent hand. The far more frequent cases were partial inability by age, or weakness, or want of skill. For poor of the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> a school was opened, and in three months <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the buffaloes was easily learnt. During that time, the pauper got first 2s. a-week, and every week afterwards 2d. less, till in the twelfth week he got nothing at all but his earnings, and was dismissed, with a wheel and a pound of flax gratis. The quantity of work which disabled poor were capable of doing in a week was easily and accurately ascertained by a week's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in the spinning-school. The result was produced weekly before appointed members of the committee, and the sum which the poor could earn was noted down in their small books. The overseer was directed to pay them weekly what their earnings fell short of 1s. 6d. in every such week, when it appeared from their books that they had earned to the known <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their abilities. From that moment applications became less frequent; and the committee had an infallible standard for distinguishing real want: for whenever the pauper, if in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> (if not, he was peculiarly provided for), had not earned what he could, then he had either been lazy, or had found more lucrative work; in either case, he was not entitled to a relief for that week, whatever he might be for the following. This mode of providing for the poor, which attracted the notice and obtained the eulogium of the minister and the British house of commons, has for six years been in Hamburgh attended with the happiest consequences. In the streets of that city a beggar is rarely to be seen, whilst those who stand in need of the charitable contributions of the rich, are much more comfortably, as well as at much less expense, maintained at home, with their children about them, than they could be in work-houses, under the management of mercenary overseers. For a fuller account of this judicious institution, we must refer the readers to Voght's Account of the Management of the Poor in Hamburgh, since the year 1788, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to some Friends of the Poor in Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

WORLD

Pages 439-439

the assemblage of parts which compose the globe of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">GEOGRAPHY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>.

WORM

Pages 439-440

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, a screw of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, to be fixed on the end of a rammer, to pull out the wad of a firelock, carbine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pistol, being the same with the wad-hook, only the one is more proper for small arms, and the other for cannon. Worm, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> winding pipe, placed in a tub of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to cool and condense the vapours in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of spirits. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">Blind</a>-Worm, or Slow-Worm. See Anguis, Reptology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>-Worm. See Lumbricus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> Index. Glow-Worm. See Lampyris, Entomology Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">Silk</a>-Worm. See Silk, No. 5. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, Vermes. See Helminthology and <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a>. Worms, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. See Medicine, No. 497. Worms, in horses. See Farriery. Worms, in dogs. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>. Worms for bait. See Fishing. Worms, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, with a bishop's see, whose bishop is a sovereign and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire. It is a free and imperial city, and the inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 1689 it was taken by the French, who almost reduced it to ashes.—The bishop afterwards built a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> in it; and it is famous for a diet held here in 1521, at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> assisted in person. The Protestants have lately built a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, where Luther is represented as appearing at the diet. It is noted for the excellent wine that grows in the neighbourhood, which they call our Lady's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of 1743, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Geo. II. took up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> in this city, and lodged at the bishop's palace after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Dettingen. It is seated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Rhine, 14 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>, 20 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, and 32 south-west of Franckfort. E. Long. 8° 29'. N. Lat. 49° 32'. Worming of dogs. All dogs have certain strings under their tongues, by most called a worm; this must be taken out when they are about two months old, with the help of a sharp <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> to slit it, and a shoemaker's awl to raise it up; you must be careful to take all out, or else your pains is to little purpose; for till then he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be hardly ever fat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, in regard the worm or string will grow foul and troublesome, and hinder his rest and eating. This cruel operation is generally recommended as a preventive of madness in dogs, or at least disabling them, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> mad, from biting in that condition. In this operation, of which the vulgar account is given, Worming ven above, which we have justly denominated a cruel one, it is not a string that is removed, but the duct by which the saliva is conveyed from the gland in which it is secreted to the mouth for the purpose of mixing with the food and promoting its deglutition and digestion. Now this operation by no means prevents the animal from biting, nor can it, in our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, obstruct the flow of the saliva by which the dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> hydrophobia is communicated.

WORMIUS

Pages 440-440

OLAUS, a learned Danish physician, born in 1688 at Arhusen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>. After beginning his studies at home, he studied at several foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and travelled to various parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> for improvement. He returned to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in 1613, and was made professor of the belles lettres in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. In 1615, he was translated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of the Greek professor; and in 1624, to the professorship of physic, which he held to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. These occupations did not hinder him from practising in his profession, and from being the fashionable physician; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> always employed him; and Christian IV. as a recompense for his services, conferred on him a canonry of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUND">Lund</a>. He published some pieces on subjects relating to his profession, several works in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARISTOTLE_S_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" href="</a>vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and several concerning the antiquities of Denmark and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>; for which latter he is principally regarded, as they are very learned, and contain many curious particulars. He died in 1614. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">WORMWOOD</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">ARTEMISIA</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WORSHIP OF GOD

Pages 440-441

amounts to the same with what we otherwise call <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. This worship consists in paying a due respect, veneration, and homage to the Deity, under a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of reward. And this internal respect, &c. is to be shown and testified by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> acts; as prayers, sacrifices, thanksgivings, &c. The Quietists, and some other mystic divines, set aside not only all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of external worship, but even the consideration of rewards and punishments. Yet even the heathens had a notion that God did not require us to serve him for nought: "Dii quamobrem colendi sint (says Cicero), non intelligo, nullo nee accepto <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> illis nec sacerato bono." The school-divines divide worship into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds, viz. latria, that rendered to God; and idolatria, that rendered to idols <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> images. To which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> add, dulia, that rendered to saints; and hyperdulia, that to the Virgin. Some theological writers have observed, that the Greek word, προσκύνησις, to worship, is not descriptive only of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which is appropriated to God, but is indifferently used to signify the honour and respect which are paid to superiors of all kinds in heaven or on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Accordingly, they have distinguished between civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship. That it is the duty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to worship his Maker, has been sufficiently proved under other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">PRAYER</a>; and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">THEOLOGY</a>, No 40—45). It is not indeed easy to be conceived how any one who has tolerably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> notions of the attributes and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> of God, can possibly neglect the duty of private worship; and though we have admitted in the last of the two articles referred to, that public worship does not seem to be enjoined in that system which is called the religion of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, yet it is most expressly commanded by the religion of Christ, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be regularly performed by every one who reflects on its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> utility. As the illiterate vulgar cannot form to themselves correct notions of the divine providence and attributes, it is obvious, that without the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of public worship, they would never think of worshipping God at all, unless perhaps occasionally, when under the pressure of some severe calamity; but occasional worship, the offspring of compulsion, could have little of the reigned spirit of true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. Ignorant, however, as the lowest of the vulgar are, and necessarily must be, it cannot be denied, that in most Christian countries, perhaps in all, they are more accurately acquainted with the first principles of religion, and the laws of morality, than even the leaders of barbarous nations. This superiority is doubtless owing in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to their access to the Sacred Scriptures, but much more, we are persuaded, to the instruction which they receive in the assemblies which they frequent for public worship. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this be admitted, public worship may be easily proved to be the duty of every individual of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>: For were those, who may be supposed to stand in no need either of the contagion of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> to kindle their own devotion, or of the preaching of a clergyman to instruct them in the doctrines and precepts of the gospel, to "forbear, on these accounts, the assembling themselves together, as the manner of some is," religious assemblies and public worship would very quickly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into universal disuse. Man is an animal prone to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>; and every order in society is ambitious of treading in the footsteps of the order immediately above it. Were the wife and the good, therefore, permitted to absent themselves from the assemblies instituted for the public worship of the Creator and Redeemer of the world, others would quickly follow their example; impelled to it not only by this universal propensity, but by the additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of wishing to appear both to the world and to themselves as wife and as good as their privileged neighbours. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is obvious: one man would stay from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with the serious intention perhaps of employing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in private devotion and religious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; another, following his example, would absent himself upon the same pretence, but would in reality waste the day in dozing indolence or in secret sensuality. For these and other reasons which might be easily assigned, no sincere Christian will think himself at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to dispute a practice enjoined by the inspired preachers of his religion, coeval with the institution, and retained by every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> into which it has since been unhappily divided. As Christian worship consists of prayers and praises, it has been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of some debate whether it is most properly performed by preconcerted forms or liturgies, or by extemporaneous addresses to the Almighty. Both these modes have their advantages and disadvantages; and by the sacred writers neither of them is preferred in opposition to the other. The advantages of a liturgy are, that it prevents absurd, extravagant, or impious addresses to God, which the folly or enthusiasm of individuals must always be in danger of producing; it gives the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> an opportunity of joining in the prayers which are put up for them, which they cannot possibly do in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of extemporaneous petitions, since before they can attend to Worship, any one of these and make it their own, their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is necessarily called away to that which succeeds it; and it relieves the clergyman from the labour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, which seems incompatible with that fervour which constitutes the spirit of devotion. The disadvantages of a fixed liturgy, which are the recommendations of extemporary prayer, are principally two. The forms composed in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> must, by the unavoidable change of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, circumstances, and opinions, become in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> unfit for another; and the perpetual repetition of the same form of words is very apt to produce inattentive laxitude in the congregation. Would the clergy of the church of England take that liberty which is allowed them in the bidding prayer before sermon, perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of that church would unite in itself all the advantages both of liturgical and extemporary worship. We have only to add on this subject, that public prayers, whether precomposed or not, ought to be compendious; that they ought to express just conceptions of the Divine attributes; recite such wants as the congregation are likely to feel, and no other; that they ought to contain as few controverted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> as possible; and that, if it can be done without offence, the pompous style of the state should be laid aside in our prayers for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and all that are in authority; because in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> which carries the mind to God, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> greatness must be annihilated.

WORT

Pages 441-441

the infusion of malt, of which beer is made. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">Brewing</a>. The uses of this infusion in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> affairs are well known. By Dr M'Brice it has lately been found to have a strong antiseptic virtue, and to be useful in preventing the scurvy and other diseases to which sailors are liable; this was confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook in his voyages. See Means of Preserving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a> of Seamen. It is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a> to be able to ascertain with facility and precision the real strength of worts, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of saccharine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> contained in the infusion. This is accomplished by determining the specific gravity by means of instruments, which, from the purpose to which they are applied, have obtained the name of saccharimeters. But as these instruments, from the very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the material of which they are constructed, are liable to considerable change, the results which they afford cannot always be depended on. With the view of obviating these inconveniences, the patent areometrical beads have been invented by Mrs Lovi of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. We have already noticed these beads, on account of their accuracy, simplicity, and facility of application for ascertaining the specific gravity, or the real strength and value, of spirituous liquors. See vol. xix. p. 599.; and we now recommend them with greater confidence, from having had opportunities of knowing that they are capable of a more extended application, as in the manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and salts of different kinds; to ascertain the strength of acids, or that of saline solutions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>; to determine the strength of liquids employed in the different processes of calico <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, and not only for the purpose of examining the strength of the acids employed, but also particularly to ascertain the density or specific gravity of the colouring matters which are used in these arts, so that the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> required may be always obtained. It has been suggested, that these beads might be conveniently employed in determining the strength of mineral waters, which, it is well known, vary considerably at different seasons of the year. As the patent beads are constructed on the same principle from 800, the specific gravity of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>, to 2000, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the specific gravity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and as they are divided into different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, each of which includes a range of specific gravities applicable to the particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, the density or strength of which is required, we have no hesitation in asserting that they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found extremely convenient and useful to all manufacturers and dealers, who wish to ascertain with accuracy the real strength and value of liquids. It has been objected to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these beads, that they require a longer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> than other instruments in using them. The same objection has been made to the introduction of other new instruments, the application of which frequent use has afterwards rendered familiar and easy. We have had opportunities of knowing that this objection is completely obviated, by those who have been accustomed to use the beads. They find that they can determine the specific gravity of a liquid by means of the beads with the same facility, and in as short a time, as with any other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>.

WOTTON

Pages 441-442

Sir Henry, an eminent writer, was the son of Thomas Wotton, Esq. and was born in 1568. He studied for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at New-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, whence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s college, where he made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in logic and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; wrote a tragedy for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of that college, called Tancredo; and afterwards received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. After this, leaving the university, he travelled into France, Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and having spent about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years abroad, he returned to England, and became secretary to Robert <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, with whom he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till that earl was apprehended for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. He then retired to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, where he became known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, who sent him privately with letters to James VI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Scotland, under the name of Octavio Baldi, to inform that king of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Some months after he went back to Florence; but King James coming to the possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England, Mr Wotton returned home, was knighted by his majesty, and sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; and afterwards was employed in many other embassies to that and other courts; but the only reward he obtained for these services was his having the provostship of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> conferred upon him about the year 1623, which he kept till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1639. After his decease some of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> and printed tracts were published together in a volume, intitled, Reliquiae Wottonianae. Wotton, Dr William, a learned divine and writer, was the son of Mr Henry Wotton, B.D. rector of Wrentham, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, where he was born in 1666. He was educated by his father, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> well skilled in the learned languages; under whom he made such amazing proficiency, that at five years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> it is said he could render several chapters in the gospels out of Latin and Greek, and many psalms in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, into his mother tongue. When he was very young, he remembered the whole of almost every discourse he had heard, and often surprised a preacher by repeating his sermon to him. He was admitted into Catharine-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> some months before he was ten years old; when the progress he made in learning in that university engaged gaged Dr Duport, then master of Magdalen college, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Peterborough, to write an elegant copy of Latin verses in his praise. In 1670 he took the degree of bachelor of arts when he was but twelve years and five months old; and the winter following he was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by Dr Gilbert Burnet, then preacher at the Rolls, who introduced him to most of the learned men in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and particularly to Dr William Lloyd, bishop of St Asaph; to whom he recommended himself by repeating to him one of his sermons, as Dr Burnet had engaged he should. In 1691 he commenced bachelor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. The same year Bishop Lloyd gave him the sinecure of Llandrillo, in Denbighshire. He was afterwards made chaplain to the earl of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, then secretary of state, who presented him to the rectory of Middleton Keynes, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>, and to whom he dedicated his Reflections upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> Learning. In 1705, Bishop Burnet gave him a prebend in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>; and in 1707, Archbishop Tenison presented him with the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of divinity: but in 1714, the difficulties he laboured under with respect to his private fortune, obliged him to retire into South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, where he was treated with great kindness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> by the gentlemen of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and wrote there the "<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">Cathedral</a> Churches of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s and Landaff;" and his "Miscellaneous Discourses relating to the Traditions and Usages of the Scribes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>," which were afterwards printed. He died in 1726. This great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was remarkable for his humanity and friendliness of temper; the narrowness of a party spirit never broke in upon any of his friendships; and his time and abilities were at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of any person who was making advances in real learning. He wrote, besides the above works, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Rome. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of his Reflections upon Ancient and Modern Learning. 3. A Discourse concerning the Languages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>. 4. Advice to a young Student, with a Method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">Study</a> for the first four Years; and other learned pieces.

WOUNDS

Pages 442-454

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, have been divided into simple, contused <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lacerated, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. Of Simple Wounds.—The first thing to be considered in the inspection of a wound is, whether it be likely to prove mortal or not. This knowledge can only be had from anatomy, by which the surgeon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be able to determine what parts are injured; and, from the offices which these parts are calculated to perform, whether the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frame can subsist under such injuries. It is not, however, easy for the most expert anatomist always to prognosticate the event with certainty; but this rule he ought always to lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to himself, to draw the most favourable prognosis the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> will bear, or even more than the rules of his art will allow. This is particularly incumbent on him in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-engagements, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is executed as soon as pronounced, and the miserable patient is thrown alive into the sea, upon the surgeon's declaring his wound to be mortal. There are, besides, many instances on record, where wounds have healed, which the most skilful surgeons have deemed mortal. The following wounds may be reckoned mortal. 1. Those which penetrate the cavities of the heart, and all those wounds of the viscera where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> blood-vessels are opened; because their situation will not admit of proper applications to restrain the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of Wounds' blood. 2. Those which entirely cut off the passage of the nervous influence through the body. Such are wounds of the brain, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, and spinal marrow. Wounds likewise of the small blood-vessels within the brain are attended with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> danger, from the effused <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> pressing upon the brain. Nor is there less danger where the nerves which tend to the heart are wounded, or entirely divided; for, after this, it is impossible for the heart to continue its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. 3. All wounds which entirely deprive the animal of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of breathing. 4. Those wounds which interrupt the course of the chyle to the heart; such are wounds of the receptacle of the chyle, thoracic duct, and larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACTEALS">lacteals</a>, &c. 5. There are other wounds which prove fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> neglected and left to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: such are wounds of the larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> blood-vessels, which might be remedied by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a>. Wounds of such parts generally prove fatal; and though a few instances may have occurred where people have recovered after them, yet they are always to be considered as extremely dangerous. Portions of the brain have been destroyed, and wounds have been made into it, and the patients have lived. It is possible, too, that the thoracic duct might be wounded and the patient live; Mr A. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COOPER">Cooper</a> having shown, in a very ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in the Medical Records and Researches, that it may become obstructed, and the chyle conveyed into the system by anastomosing lymphatics. In examining wounds, the next consideration is, whether the parts injured are such as may be supposed to induce dangerous symptoms, either immediately or at some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> during the course of the cure. In order to proceed with any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of certainty, it is necessary to be well acquainted with those symptoms which attend injuries of the different parts of the body. If the skin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cellular substance are only divided, the first effects are an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood; the lips of the wound retract, become tumefied, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and inflamed, leaving a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">gap</a> of considerable wideness according to the length and deepness of the wound. If a very considerable portion of skin and cellular substance is divided, a slight fever seizes the patient; the effusion of blood in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> stops, and the wound is partly filled up, with a cake of coagulated blood. Below this cake, the small vessels pour forth a clear liquor, which in a short time is converted into pus (see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Pus and Mucus). Below this pus granulations of new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> arise, the cake of coagulated blood looses, a new skin covers the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the wound was, and the whole is healed up; and there only remains a mark, called a cicatrix or scar, showing where the injury had been received. All wounds are accompanied with a considerable degree of pain, especially when the inflammation comes on, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> reaches no farther than the skin and cellular substance. If the muscular fibres are divided, the pain is much greater, because the found part of the muscle is stretched by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the divided part and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the antagonist muscle, which it is now less fitted to bear. The wound also gaps much more than where the cellular substance is alone. Wounds, alone divided, inasmuch that, if left to itself, the skin will cover the muscular fibres, without any intervention of cellular substance; and not only a very unsightly cicatrix remains, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the muscle is in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> lost.—If the muscle happens to be totally divided, its fibres retract to a very considerable distance; and unless proper methods be taken to bring them into contact, the use of it is ever afterwards lost. If by a wound any considerable artery happens to be divided, the blood flows out with great velocity, and by starts; the patient soon becomes faint with loss of blood; nor does the hemorrhage stop until he faints away altogether; and if as much vis viva still remains as is sufficient to renew the operations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he recovers after some time, and the wound heals up as usual. The part of the artery which is below the wound in the meantime becomes useless, so that all the inferior part of the limb would be deprived of blood, were it not that the small branches sent off from the artery above the wounded place become enlarged, and capable of carrying on the circulation. Nature, also, after a wonderful manner, often produces new vessels from the superior extremity of the divided artery, by which the circulation is carried on as formerly. The consequences of such a profuse hemorrhage may be, however, very dangerous to the patient, by inducing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> debility, or an universal dropy. This great hemorrhage happens especially where the artery is partially divided; because then the vessel cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> in such a manner as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the orifice: however, if the wound is but small, the blood gets into the cellular substance, swelling up the member to an extreme degree, forming what is called a diffused aneurysm. Thus the hemorrhage soon flows externally, but great mischief is apt to flow from the confinement of the extravasated blood, from bringing on exterior suppuration among the muscles and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; and thus not only the use of the limb is entirely lost, but the patient is brought into great danger of his life. Wounds of the ligaments, nerves, and tendons, are likewise attended with bad consequences. When a nerve is entirely divided, the pain is but trifling, though the consequences are often dangerous. If the nerve is large, all the parts to which it is distributed below the wound immediately lose the power of motion and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. This, however, takes place only when all or the greatest part of the nerves belonging to a particular part are divided. If the spinal marrow, for instance, be divided near the head, the parts below soon lose their sensation irrecoverably; or if the bundle of nerves passing out of the axilla be divided or tied, fenation in the greatest part of the arm below will be lost. But though a nerve should be divided, and a temporary palsy be produced, it may reunite, and perform its former functions. If a nerve be wounded only, instead of being divided, the worst symptoms frequently ensue. Wounds which penetrate the cavities of the thorax are always exceedingly dangerous, because there is a fear of possibility of all the viscera escaping unhurt. A wound is known to have penetrated the cavity of the thorax principally by the discharge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> from it at each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, by an extreme difficulty of breathing, and by coughing up blood. Such wounds, however, are not always mortal; the lungs have frequently been wounded, and yet the patient has recovered.—Wounds of the diaphragm are almost always mortal, either by inducing fatal convulsions immediately, or by the ascent of the stomach, which the pressure of the abdominal muscles forces up through the wound into the cavity of the thorax; of this Van Swieten gives several instances.—Even though the wound do not penetrate into the cavity of the thorax, the very worst symptoms may follow. For if the wound descends deeply among the external muscles, and its orifice lies higher, the extravasated blood will be therein collected, stagnate, and form various sinuses; which after having eroded the pleura, may at length <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the cavity of the thorax. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> having once found a vent into this cavity, will be continually augmenting from the discharge of the sinus ulcer, and the lungs will at last suffer by the surrounding matter. If, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of wounds in the thorax, the ribs or sternum happen to become carious, the cure will be extremely tedious and difficult. Galen relates the case of a lad who received a blow upon his sternum in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>: it was first neglected, and afterwards badly healed; but, four months afterwards, matter appeared at the place which had received the blow. A physician made an incision into the part, and it was soon after cicatrized: but in a short time a new collection made its appearance, and upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> incision the wound refused to heal. Galen found the sternum carious; and having cut off the diseased part, the pericardium itself was observed to be corroded, so that the heart could be seen quite naked; notwithstanding which, the wound was cured in no very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time. There is sometimes difficulty in determining whether the wound has really penetrated into the thorax or into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>; for the former defends much farther towards the sides than at the middle. But as the lungs are almost always wounded when the cavity of the thorax is penetrated, the symptoms arising from thence can scarcely be mistaken.—Another symptom which frequently, though not always, attends wounds of the thorax, is an emphysema. This is occasioned by the air escaping from the wounded lungs, and infusing itself into the cellular substance; which being pervious to it over the whole body, the tumor passes from one part to another, till at last every part is inflated to a surprising degree. An instance is given in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy, of a tumour of this kind, which on the thorax was eleven inches thick, on the abdomen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, on the neck six, and on the rest of the body four; the eyes were in a great measure thrust out of their orbits by the inflation of the cellular substance; and the patient died the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. This was occasioned by a stab with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. Wounds of the abdomen are not less dangerous than those of the thorax, on account of the importance of the organs and its viscera which it contains. When the wound does not penetrate the cavity, there is some danger of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a> being formed by the protrusion of the peritoneum through the weakened integuments, and the danger is greater the larger the wound is. Those wounds which run obliquely between the interstices of the muscles often produce sinus ulcers of a bad kind. For as there is a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fat interposed everywhere between the muscles of the abdomen, if a wound happens to run between them, the matter there collected, not meeting with free egress through the mouth of the wound, often makes its way in a surprising manner through the cellu- Wounds, lar substance, and forms deep sinuosities between the muscles; in which case the cure is always difficult, and sometimes impossible. If a large wound penetrate the cavity of the abdomen, some of the viscera will certainly be protruded through it; or if the wound is but small, and closed up with fat so that none of the intestines can be protruded, we may know that the cavity of the abdomen is pierced, and probably some of the viscera wounded, by the acute pain and fever, paleness, anxiety, faintings, hiccup, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> sweats, and weakened <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, all of which accompany injuries of the internal parts. The mischief which attend wounds of this kind proceed not only from the injury done to the viscera themselves, but from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRAVASATION">extravasation</a> of blood and the discharge of the contents of the intestines into the cavity of the abdomen; which, being of a very putrefactive nature, soon bring on the most violent disorders. Hence wounds of the abdominal viscera are very often mortal. This, however, is not always the case, for the small intestines have been totally divided, and yet the patient has recovered. Wounds both of the small and large intestines have healed spontaneously, even when they were of such magnitude that the contents of the intestine were freely discharged through the wound into the abdomen, and after part of the intestine itself has been protruded through the wound of the integuments. When the mesentery is injured, the danger is extreme, on account of its numerous vessels and nerves. Wounds of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, spleen, and pancreas, are also exceedingly dangerous, although there are some instances of the spleen being cut out of living animals without any considerable injury. From the preceding account of the symptoms attending wounds in the different parts of the body, the surgeon may be enabled to judge in some measure of the event; though it must always be remembered, that wounds, even those which seem at first to be of the slightest nature, have, contrary to all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, proved mortal, chiefly by inducing convulsions, or a locked jaw; so that no certain prognostic can be drawn on sight of recent wounds. We shall now, however, proceed to consider their treatment. For the cure of wounds, it has been already observed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> imagined balms, the juice of herbs, &c., to be <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIFICS">specifics</a>.
