The statute further ordains, that the sheriff of the county shall be bound to keep the goods a year and a day (as in France for one year, agreeable to the maritime laws of Oleron, and in Holland for a year and a half), that if any man can prove a property in them, either in his own right or by right of representa- tion, they shall be restored to him without delay; but if no such property be proved within that time, they then shall be the king's. If the goods are of a perish- able nature, the sheriff may sell them, and the money shall be liable in their stead. This revenue of wrecks is frequently granted out to lords of manors as a royal franchise; and if any one be thus intitled to wrecks in his own land, and the king's goods are wrecked there- on, the king may claim them at any time, even after the year and day. It is to be observed, that, in order to constitute a le- gal wreck, the goods must come to land. If they con- tinue at sea, the law distinguishes them by the barbarous and uncouth appellations of jettam, flotsam, and lagan. Jettam is where goods are cast into the sea, and there sink and remain under water: flotsam is where they continue swimming on the surface of the waves: lagan is where they are sunk in the sea, but tied to a cork or buoy, in order to be found again. These are also the king's, if no owner appears to claim them; but if any owner appears, he is intitled to recover the possession. Vol. XX. Part II. (A) In like manner Constantine the Great, finding that by the imperial law the revenue of wrecks was given to the prince's treasury or fiscus, restrained it by an edict (Cod. ii. 5. i.) and ordered them to remain to the owners; adding this humane expostulation: "Quod enim jus habet fiscus in aliena calamitate, ut de re tam iucuosa com- pendium seceatur." WRECK is punished by the statute 8 Eliz. c. 13, with a forfeiture of 100l. or outlawry. Moreover, by the statute of Geo. II. pilfering any goods cast adrift is declared to be petty larceny; and many other salutary regulations are made, for the more effectually preserving ships of any nation in distress. By the civil law, to destroy persons shipwrecked, or prevent their saving the ship, is capital. And to steal even a plank from a vessel in distress or wrecked, makes the party liable to answer for the whole ship and cargo. The laws also of the Visigoths, and the most early Neapolitan constitutions, punished with the utmost severity all those who neglected to assist any ship in distress, or plundered any goods cast on shore. WREN. See Motacilla, Ornithology Index.

WREN

Pages 456-456

Sir Christopher, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and one of the most learned and most eminent architects of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was the son of Christopher Wren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Windor, and was born in 1632. He studied at Wadham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in 1653, and was chosen fellow of All Souls college. When very young he discovered a surprising genius for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; in which science he made great advances before he was sixteen years old. In 1657, he was made professor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> at Gresham college, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; which he resigned in 1662, on his being chosen to the Savilian professorship of astronomy in Oxford: he was next year created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws, and in 1663 was elected fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. He was one of the commissioners for the reparation of St Paul's; and in 1665 travelled into France, to examine the most beautiful edifices there, when he made many curious observations. At his return to England, he drew a noble <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for rebuilding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London after the fire, which he presented to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and upon the decease of Sir John Denham in 1668, was made surveyor-general of his majesty's works; and from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of public edifices, by which he acquired the highest reputation. He built the magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> at Oxford, St Paul's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, the churches of St Stephen Walbrook, and St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>-le-Bow, the Monument, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, Chelsea college, one of the wings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and many other beautiful edifices. He was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Royal Society, one of the commissioners of Chelsea college, and twice member of parliament; first for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and then for Melcombe Regis in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; but in 1718 was removed from his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of surveyor-general. He died in 1723, and was interred in the vault under St Paul's. This great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> also distinguished himself by many curious inventions and discoveries in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and, among many others, contrived an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for measuring the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> that falls on any space of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> for a year; he invented many ways of making astronomical observations more accurate and easy; and was the first author of the anatomical experiment of injecting liquors into the veins of animals, &c. He translated into Latin Mr Oughtred's Horologiorographica Geometrica; and wrote a Survey of the cathedral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, and other pieces. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> his posthumous works and draughts were published by his son.

WRESTLING

Pages 456-456

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> engagement between two persons unarmed, body to body, to prove their strength and dexterity, and try which can throw his opponent to the ground. Wrestling is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity and fame. It was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the heroic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; witness <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, who wrestled with Antaeus. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the highest repute, and had considerable rewards and honours assigned to it at the Olympic games. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> to anoint their bodies with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, to give the lefs hold to their antagonists. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a> ordered the Spartan maids to wrestle in public quite naked, in order, as it is observed, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them of their too much delicacy and niceness, to make them appear more robust, and to familiarize the people, &c., to such audacities.

WRIT

Pages 456-457

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies, in general, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s precept in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, issuing out of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other officer, and commanding something to be done in relation to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, or giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to have the same done. And, according to Fitzherbert, a writ is said to be a formal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the king in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, sealed with his seal, and directed to some judge, officer, or minister, &c., at the suit of a subject, for the cause briefly expressed, which is to be determined in the proper court according to law. Writs, in civil actions, are either original or judicial: original, are such as are issued out of the court of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> for the summoning of a defendant to appear, and are granted before the suit is commenced, in order to begin the same; and judicial writs issue out of the court where the original is returned, after the suit is begun. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">Process</a>. The original writ is the foundation of the suit. See Suit. When a person hath received an injury, and thinks it worth his while to demand a satisfaction for it, he is to consider with himself, or take advice, what redress the law has given for that injury; and thereupon is to make application or suit to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, the fountain of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, for that particular specific remedy which he is determined or advised to pursue. As for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> due on bond, an action of debt; for goods detained without force, an action of detenue or trover; or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> taken with force, an action of trepans vi et armis; or, to try the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of lands, a writ of entry or action of trespass in ejectment; or for any consequential injury received, a special action on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. To this end he is to sue out, or purchase by paying the stated fees, an original or original writ, from the court of chancery, which is the officina justitiae, the shop or mint of justice, wherein all the king's writs are framed. It is a mandatory letter from the king in parchment, sealed with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> seal, and directed to the sheriff of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> wherein the injury is committed, or supposed to be, requiring him to command the wrong-doer or party accused, either to do justice to the complainant, or else to appear in court, and answer the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> against him. Whatever the sheriff does in pursuance of this writ, he must return or certify to the court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-pleas, together with the writ itself: which is the foundation of the jurisdiction of that court, being the king's warrant for the judges to proceed to the determination of the cause. For it was a maxim introduced by the Normans, that there should be be no proceedings in common-pleas before the king's justices without his original writ; because they held it unfit that those justices, being only the substitutes of the crown, should take cognizance of any thing but what was thus expressly referred to their judgement. However, in small actions, below the value of forty shillings, which are brought in the court-baron or county-court, no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> writ is necessary; but the foundation of such suits continue to be (as in the times of the Saxons), not by original writ, but by plaint; that is, by a private memorial tendered in open court to the judge, wherein the party injured sets forth his cause of action: and the judge is bound of common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to administer justice therein, without any special mandate from the king. Now indeed even the royal writs are held to be demandable of common right, on paying the usual fees: for any delay in the granting them, or setting an unusual or exorbitant price upon them, would be a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>, c. 29. "nulli vend.mus, nulli negabimus, aut differemus iustitiam vel rectum." Original writs are either optional or peremptory; or, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of our law, they are either a praecipe or a fit te feceritis securum. The praecipe is in the alternative, commanding the defendant to do the thing required, or show the reason wherefore he hath not done it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this writ is where something certain is demanded by the plaintiff, which is in the power of the defendant himself to perform; as, to restore the possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, to pay a certain liquidated debt, to perform a specific covenant, to render an account, and the like; in all which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the writ is drawn up in the form of a praecipe or command, to do thus, or show cause to the contrary; giving the defendant his choice to redress the injury or stand the suit. The other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of original writs is called a fit feceritis securum, from the words of the writ; which directs the sheriff to cause the defendant to appear in court, without any option given him, provided the plaintiff gives the sheriff security effectually to prosecute his claim. This writ is in use where nothing is specifically demanded, but only a satisfaction in general; to obtain which, and minister complete redress, the intervention of some judicature is necessary. Such are writs of trespass, or on the case, wherein no debt or other specific thing is sued for in certain, but only damages to be assessed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. For this end the defendant is immediately called upon to appear in court, provided the plaintiff gives good security of prosecuting his claim. Both species of writs are tested, or witnessed, in the king's own name; "witnessest ourself at Westminster," or wherever the chancery may be held. The security here spoken of, to be given by the plaintiff for prosecuting his claim, is common to both writs, though it gives denomination only to the latter. The whole of it is at present become a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of form; and John Doe and Richard Roe are always returned as the standing pledges for this purpose.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> use of them was to answer for the plaintiff, who in case he brought an action without cause, or failed in the prosecution of it when brought, was liable to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERCEMENT">amercement</a> from the crown for raising a false accusation; and so the form of the judgement fell is. In like manner, as by the Gothic constitutions no person was permitted to lay a complaint against another nisi sub scriptura aut specificatione trium testium, quod allium vellet perseguiri: and, as by the laws of Sancho I. king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, damages were given against a plaintiff who prosecuted a groundless action. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which the defendant is ordered to appear in court, and on which the sheriff is to bring in the writ, and report how far he has obeyed it, is called the return of the writ; it being then returned by him to the king's justices at Westminster. And it is always made returnable at the distance of at least 15 days from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> or test, that the defendant may have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to come up to Westminster, even from the most remote parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and upon some day in one of the four terms, in which the court sits for the dispatch of business.

WRITING

Pages 457-458

the art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of signifying and conveying our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> to others, by letters or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> visible to the eye. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">COMPOSITION</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">GRAMMAR</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">LANGUAGE</a>. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> remains of writing, which have been transmitted to us, are upon hard substances, such as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, which were used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> for edicts and matters of public notoriety; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECALOGUE">decalogue</a> was written on two tables of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; but this practice was not peculiar to the Jews, for it was used by most of the eastern nations, as well as by the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> which Voltaire attempts to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the book of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, where the people are commanded to write the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> on stones, is absurd; for what is there said by no means implies, that other materials might not be used on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> occasions. The laws penal, civil, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>, among the Greeks, were engraven on tables of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> which were called cyrbes. We find that wood was also used for writing on in different countries. In the Sloanian library (No. 4852) are fix specimens of Kufic writing, on boards about two feet in length, and six inches in depth. The Chinese, before the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, wrote or engraved with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> tool upon thin boards or on bamboo. Pliny says, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> books of wood were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. These table books were called by the Romans pupillares. The wood was cut into thin slices, and finely planed and polished. The writing was at first upon the bare wood, with an iron <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called a stylus. In later times these tables were usually waxed over, and written upon with that instrument. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> written upon the tables which were thus waxed over was easily effaced, and by smoothing the wax new matter might be substituted in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of what had been written before. The Greeks and Romans <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the use of waxed table-books <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPYRUS">papyrus</a>, leaves, and skins, became common, because they were so convenient for correcting extemporary compositions. Table books of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> are still used for memorandums, but they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> written upon with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> pencils. The practice of writing on table-books covered with wax was not entirely laid aside till the commencement of the 14th century. The bark of trees was also used for writing by the ancients, and is still used in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. The same thing may be said of the leaves of trees. It is needless to observe the use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, papyrus and paper, for writing; it is too well known. The method of fabricating these substances has been already described as they occurred in the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. It is obvious, that when men wrote, or rather engraved, on hard substances, instruments of metal were necessary, such as the chisel and the fly-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>; but the latter was chiefly used for writing upon boards, waxed tablets, or on bark. When the ancients wrote on softer materials than wood or metal, other instruments were used for writing with, of which reeds and canes seem to have been the first. Reeds and canes are still used as instruments for writing by the Tartars, the Indians, the Persians, the Turks, and the Greeks. Pencils made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> are used by the Chinese for their writing: they first liquefy their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and dip their pencils into it. Hair-pencils have likewise been used for writing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">Large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> letters were made with them from the time of the Roman emperors till the 16th century. After the invention of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> they were drawn by the illuminators. Quills of geese, swans, peacocks, crows, and other birds, have been used in these western parts for writing with, but how long is not easy to ascertain. St Isidore of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, who lived about the middle of the 7th century, describes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> made of a quill as used in his time. Method of restoring decayed Writings. In the 77th volume of the Phil. Trans., there is a paper on this subject by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Blagden. One of the best methods he found upon experiment to be, covering the letters with phlogisticated or prussic alkali, with the addition of a diluted mineral acid; upon the application of which, the letters changed very speedily to a deep blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and intensity. To prevent the spreading of the colour, which, by blotting the parchment, detracts greatly from the legibility, the alkali should be put on first, and the diluted acid added upon it. The method found to answer best has been, to spread the alkali thin with a feather over the traces of the letters, and then to touch it gently, as nearly upon or over the letters as can be done with the diluted acid, by means of a feather or a bit of stick cut to a blunt point. Though the alkali should occasion no sensible change of colour, yet the moment the acid comes upon it, every trace of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> turns at once to a fine blue, which soon acquires its full intensity, and is beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> stronger than the colour of the original trace had been. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, then, the corner of a bit of blotting paper be carefully and dexterously applied near the letters, so as to imbibe the superfluous liquor, the staining of the parchment may be in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> avoided; for it is this superfluous liquor which, absorbing part of the colouring matter from the letters, becomes a dye to whatever it touches. Care must be taken not to bring the blotting paper in contact with the letters, because the colouring matter is soft whilst wet, and may easily be rubbed off. The acid chiefly employed was the marine; but both the vitriolic and nitrous succeed very well. They should be so far diluted as not to be in danger of corroding the parchment, after which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of strength does not seem to be a matter of much nicety. Method of Copying Writings. The ingenious Mr Watt, some years ago, invented a method of copying writings very speedily, and without the possibility of committing mistakes. A piece of thin unfixed paper is to be taken exactly of the size of the paper to be copied; it is to be moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or, what is better, with the following liquid: Take of distilled <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> two pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, dissolve it in one ounce of boric acid; then take four ounces of oyster-shells calcined to whiteness, and carefully freed from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> crust; put them into the vinegar, shake the mixture frequently for 24 hours, then let it stand until it deposits its sediment; filter the clear part through unfixed paper into a glass vessel; then add two ounces of the best blue <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a> bruised, and place the liquor in a warm place, shaking it frequently for 24 hours; then filter the liquor again through unfixed paper, and add to it after filtration one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a>, ale measure, of pure water. It must then stand 24 hours, and be filtered again if it shows a disposition to deposit any sediment, which it generally does. When the paper has been wet with this liquid, put it between two thick unfixed papers to absorb the superfluous moisture; then lay it over the writing to be copied, and put a piece of clean writing paper above it. Put the whole on the board of a rolling-press, and press them through the rolls, as is done in printing copperplates, and a copy of the writing shall appear on both sides of the thin moistened paper; on one side in a reversed order and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, but on the other side in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order and direction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. WRITTEN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">MOUNTAINS</a>. See MOUNTAINS. WRY-NECK. See JYX, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

WURTEMBERG

Pages 458-458
or WIRTEMBERG, a sovereign duchy of Germany, in Swabia; bounded on the north by Franconia, the archbishopric of Mentz, and the palatinate of the Rhine; on the east by the county of Oetting, the marquisate of Burgau, and the territory of Ulm; on the south by the principality of Hoen-Zollern, Furlenburg, and the marquisate of Hohenburg; and on the west by the palatinate of the Rhine, the marquisate of Baden, and the Black Forest. It is 65 miles in length, and as much in breadth, and the river Neckar runs almost through the middle of it from south to north. Though there are many mountains and woods, yet it is one of the most populous and fertile countries in Germany, producing plenty of grapes, corn, fruits, and a great deal of wine towards the confines of the palatinate. There are also mines, and salt springs, with plenty of game and fish. It contains 645 villages, 88 towns, and 26 cities, of which Stuttgart is the capital.

WURTSBURG

Pages 458-458

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bishopric in Germany, comprehending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Franconia. It is bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Henneburg, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Coburg, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FULDA">Fulda</a>, the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, the marquisate of Anspach, the bishopric of Bamberg, and the county of Wertheim; being about 65 miles in length, and 30 in breadth, and divided into 50 bailiwicks. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fertile, and produces more corn and wine than the inhabitants consume. The territories of the bishop comprehend above 400 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, of which he is sovereign, being one of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> princes of the empire.

WURTZBURG

Pages 458-459

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, and one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> in the circle of Franconia. It is defended with good fortifications, and has a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. There is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, in which... Wartburg, which are generally 400 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> men and women. The Wycherley castle is at a small distance from the city, and commands it, as it stands upon an eminence. It communicates with the city by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, on which are 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, representing as many saints. The arsenal and the cellars of the bishop deserve the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the curious. There is also an university, founded in 1493. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 2. N. Lat. 49. 40.

WYCHERLEY

Pages 459-459

WILLIAM, an eminent English comic poet, was born about 1640. A little before the restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, he became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he was reconciled by Dr Barlow to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, which he had a little before abandoned in his travels. He afterwards entered himself in the Middle-temple, but soon quitted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> for pursuits more agreeable to his own genius, as well as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> his first play, entitled, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> in a Wood, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St James's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, which was acted in 1672, he became acquainted with several of the celebrated wits both of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> and town, and likewise with the duchess of Cleveland. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after appeared his comedies, called The Gentleman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">Dancing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>, the Plain Dealer, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">Country</a> Wife; all which were acted with applause. George <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> had a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem for him, and bestowed on him several advantageous posts. King Charles also showed him signal marks of favour; and once gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his esteem, which perhaps never any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> before had given to a private gentleman. Mr Wycherley being ill of a fever, at his lodgings in Bow-street, the king did him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a visit. Finding him extremely weakened, he commanded him to take a journey to the south of France, and assured him, at the same time, that he would order him £500 to defray the charges of the journey. Mr Wycherley accordingly went into France; and having spent the winter there, returned to England entirely restored to his former vigour. The king, shortly after his arrival, told him, that he had a son, who he was resolved should be educated like the son of a king, and that he could not choose a more proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> for his governor than Mr Wycherley; for which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> £500 per annum should be settled upon him. Immediately after this offer he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, where walking one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> upon the Well's walk with his friend Mr Fairbeard, of Gray's Inn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as he came up to the bookseller's shop, the countess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROGHEDA">Drogheda</a>, a young widow, rich, noble, and beautiful, came there to inquire for the Plain Dealer; "Madam," says Mr Fairbeard, "since you are for the Plain Dealer, there he is for you;" pushing Mr Wycherley towards her. "Yes," says Mr Wycherley, "this lady can bear plain dealing; for she appears to be so accomplished, that what would be a compliment to others, would be plain dealing to her." "No, truly, Sir," said the countess, "I am not without my faults, any more than the rest of my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and yet notwithstanding, I love plain dealing, and am never more fond of it than when it tells me of them." "Then, madam," says Mr Fairbeard, "you and the Plain Dealer seem designed by Heaven for each other." In short, Mr Wycherley walked a turn or two with the countess, waited upon her home, visited her daily while she staid at Tunbridge, and married her soon after without acquainting the king. By this step, which was looked upon as a contempt of his majesty's orders, he forfeited the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> favour. The countess of Drogheda settled her whole fortune upon him; but his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> being disputed after her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he was so reduced by the expenses of the law and other incumbrances, as to be unable to satisfy the impatience of his creditors, who threw him into prison; and the bookseller who printed his Plain Dealer, by which he got almost as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> as the other gained reputation, was so ungrateful as to refuse to lend him £200, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. In that confinement he languished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years; but at length King James going to see the above play, was so charmed with it, that he gave immediate orders for the payment of his debts, and even granted him a pension of £500 per annum. But the prince's bountiful intentions were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> defeated merely through Mr Wycherley's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>; he being ashamed to tell the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Mulgrave, whom the king had sent to demand it, a true state of his debts. He laboured under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of these difficulties till his father died, who left him £600 a-year. But this estate was under limitations, he being only a tenant for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and not being allowed to raise any money for the payment of his debts. However, he took a method of doing it which few suspected to be his choice; and this was making a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINTURE">jointure</a>. He had often declared, that he was resolved to die married, though he could not bear the thoughts of living in that state again: accordingly, just at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> of his death, he married a young gentlewoman with £5000 fortune, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which he applied to the uses he wanted it for. Eleven days after the celebration of these nuptials, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1715, he died, and was interred in the vault of Covent-garden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Besides his plays above mentioned, he published a volume of poems in folio. In 1728 his posthumous works in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> were published by Mr Theobald.

WYE

Pages 459-460

a river of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, which issuing out of Plinlymon Hill, very near the source of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, crosses the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east corner of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>, giving name to the town of Rhaydergowy (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">Fall</a> of the Wye), where it is precipitated in a cataract: then flowing between this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> and Brecknockshire, it crosses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, and dividing the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, falls into the mouth of the Severn, below <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEPSTOW">Chepstow</a>. The romantic beauties of the Wye, which flows in a deep Wye, deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, between lofty rocks clothed with hanging woods, and here and there crowned by ruined castles, have employed the descriptive powers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>. Wye is also the name of a river in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, which rises in the north-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, above <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUXTON">Buxton</a>; and, flowing south-east, falls into the Derwent, below <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKEWELL">Bakewell</a>. Wye, the name of a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, with a market on Thursday, seated on the Stour, 10 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, and 59 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 4. N. Lat. 51. 10. Wye, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in a territory of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Gallen, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. It is built on an eminence 16 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>. E. Long. 9. 4. N. Lat. 47. 34. Xanthium X, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> x, is the 22d <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> consonant. It was not used by the Hebrews or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks; for, as it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> letter, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who used <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> simplicity in their writings, expressed this letter by its component letters e.g. Neither have the Italians this letter, but express it by /f/. X begins no word in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> but such as are of Greek original; and is in few others but what are of Latin derivation; as perplex, reflection, defluxion, &c. We often express this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> by single letters, as cks, in backs, necks; by ks, in books, breaks; by cc, in access, accident; by ct, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, union, &c. The English and French pronounce it like ce or ke; the Spaniards like c before a, viz. Alexandro, as it were Alejandro. In numerals it expresses 10, whence in old Roman <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> it is used for denarius; and as such seems to be made of two V's placed one over the other. When a dash is added over it, thus X̄, it signifies 10,000.

WYNDHAM

Pages 459-459

SIR WILLIAM, descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, was born about the year 1687, and succeeded young to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and estate of his father. On his return from his travels, he was chosen member for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Somerset; in which station he served in the three last parliaments of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, and as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived: after the change of the ministry in 1710, he was appointed secretary at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and in 1713 was raised to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bolingbroke, he adhered to the interests of the latter. He was removed from his employment on the accession of George I, and falling under suspicion on the breaking out of the rebellion in 1715, was apprehended. He made his escape; a reward was published for apprehending him; he surrendered, was committed to the Tower, but never brought to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. After he regained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in opposition to the several administrations under which he lived; and died in 1740.

XANTHUM

Pages 460-460

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class monocotyledons, and arranged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> classification under the 49th order, composite. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. XANTHOXYLUM. See ZANTHOXYLUM.

XEBEC

Pages 460-460
or ZEBEC, a small three-masted vessel, navigated in the Mediterranean sea, and on the coasts of Spain, Portugal, and Barbary. See Plate fig. 10. The sails of the xebec are in general similar to those of the palaacre, but the hull is extremely different from that and almost every other vessel. It is furnished with a strong prow: and the extremity of the stern, which is nothing more than a sort of railed platform or gallery, projects farther behind the counter and buttock than that of any European ship. Being generally equipped as a corsair, the xebec is constructed with a narrow floor, to be more swift in pursuit of the enemy; and of a great breadth, to enable her to carry a greater force of sail for this purpose without danger of overturning. As these vessels are usually very low built, their decks are formed with a great convexity from the middle of their breadth towards the sides, in order to carry off the water which falls aboard more readily by their scuppers. But as this extreme convexity would render it very difficult to walk thereon at sea, particularly when the vessel rocks by the agitation of the waves, there is a platform of grating extending along the deck from the sides of the vessel towards the middle, whereon the crew may walk dry-footed whilst the water is conveyed through the grating to the scuppers. The xebecs, which are generally armed as vessels of war by the Algerines, mount from 16 to 24 cannon, and carry from 300 to 450 men, two-thirds of whom are generally soldiers. By the very complicated and inconvenient method of working these vessels, what one of their captains of Algiers told Mr Falconer will be readily believed, viz. that every xebec requires at least the labour of three square-rigged ships, wherein the standing sails are calculated to answer every situation of the wind.

XENOCRATES

Pages 460-461

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Chalcodon in the 95th Olympiad. At first he attached himself to Alcinus, but afterwards became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, who took much pains in cultivating his genius, which was naturally heavy. His temper was gloomy, his aspect severe, and his manners little inclined with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. These material defects his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to correct; frequently advising him to sacrifice to the Graces: and the pupil was patient of instruction, and knew how to value the kindness of his preceptor. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as Plato lived, Xenocrates was one of his most esteemed disciples; after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he closely adhered to his doctrine; and, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year of the 110th Olympiad, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the academy, as the successor of Speusippus. Xenocrates was celebrated among the Athenians, not only for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, but for his virtues. So eminent was his reputation for integrity, that when he was called upon to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in a judicial transaction, in which an oath was usually required, the judges unanimously agreed, that his simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> should be taken, as a public testimony to his merit. Even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon found it impossible to corrupt him. So abstemious was he with respect to food, that his provision was frequently spoiled before it was consumed. His chastity was invincible. Phryne, a celebrated Athenian courtezan, attempted without success to seduce him. Of his humanity the following pathetic incident is a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>: A sparrow, which was pursued by a hawk, flew into his bosom; he afforded it protection till its enemy was out of sight, and then let it go, saying, that he would never betray a suppliant. He was fond of retirement, and was seldom seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He was discreet in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and carefully allotted a certain portion of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. Xenocrates day to its proper business. One of these he employed in silent meditation. He was an admirer of the mathematical sciences; and was so fully convinced of their utility, that when a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who was unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, desired admission into the academy, he refused his request, saying, that he was not yet possessed of the handles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In fine, Xenocrates was eminent both for the purity of his morals and for his acquaintance with science, and supported the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> school, by his lectures, his writings, and his conduct. He lived to the first year of the 116th Olympiad, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the 82 of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when he lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by accidentally falling, in the dark, into a reservoir of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.

XENOPHANES

Pages 461-461

the founder of the Eleatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> among the Greeks, was born at Colophon probably about the 65th Olympiad. From some cause <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other he left his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> early, and took refuge in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where he supported himself by reciting, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Hiero, elegiac and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IAMBIC">iambic</a> verses, which he had written in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the theogonies of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. From Sicily he passed over into Magna Graecia, where he took up the profession of philosophy, and became a celebrated preceptor in the Pythagorean school. Indulging, however, a greater freedom of thought than was usual among the disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, he ventured to introduce new opinions of his own, and in many particulars to oppose the doctrines of Epimenides, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THALES">Thales</a>, and Pythagoras. Xenophanes possessed the Pythagorean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of philosophy about seventy years, and lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of a hundred years, that is, according to Eudoxus, till the 81st Olympiad. The doctrine of Xenophanes concerning <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is so imperfectly preserved, and obscurely expressed, that it is no wonder that it has been differently represented by different writers. Perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, that he held the universe to be one in nature and substance, but distinguished in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of which all things consist, and that latent divine force which, though not a distinct substance but an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a>, is necessarily inherent in the universe, and is the cause of all its perfection.

XENOPHON

Pages 461-461

an illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, general, and historian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in the 3d year of the 82d Olympiad. When he was a youth, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, struck with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance, determined to admit him into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his pupils. Meeting him by accident in a narrow passage, the philosopher put his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> across the path, and stopping him, asked, where those things were to be purchased which are necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>? Xenophon appearing at a loss for a reply to this unexpected salutation, Socrates proceeded to ask him, where honest and good men were to be found? Xenophon still hesitating, Socrates said to him, "Follow me, and learn." From that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Xenophon became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Socrates, and made a rapid progress in that moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> for which his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was so eminent. Xenophon accompanied Socrates in the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and fought courageously in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He afterwards entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> as a private volunteer in his expedition against his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. This enterprise proving unfortunate, Xenophon, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cyrus, advised his fellow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to attempt a retreat into their own country. They listened to his advice; and having had many proofs of his wisdom as well as courage, they gave him the command of the army, in the room of Proxenus who had fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. In this command he acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and firmness with which he conducted them back, through the midst of innumerable dangers, into their own country. The particulars of this memorable adventure are related by Xenophon himself in his Retreat of the Ten Thousand. After his return into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, he joined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGESILAUS">Agesilaus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, and fought with him against the Thebans in the celebrated battle of Charonea. The Athenians, displeased at this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, brought a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> against him for his former conduct in engaging in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Cyrus, and condemned him to exile. The Spartans, upon this, took Xenophon, as an injured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, under their protection, and provided him a comfortable retreat at Scilluntes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEA">Elea</a>. Here, with his wife and two children, he remained several years, and passed his time in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of his friends, and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> those historical works which have rendered his name immortal. A war at length arose between the Spartans and Eleans; and Xenophon was obliged to retire to Lepreus, where his eldest son had settled. He afterwards removed, with his whole family, to Corinth, where, in the first year of the hundred and fifth Olympiad, he finished his days. XENOPHON the Younger, a Greek writer, so called to distinguish him from the celebrated Xenophon, was born at Ephesus, and lived, according to some authors, before Heliodorus, that is, about the beginning of the 4th century. He is only known by his Ephesian, a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> in five books, which is esteemed, and contains the amours <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> adventures of Abracomes and Anthia. This romance was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in Greek and Latin, in 1724, 4to. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">XERXES</a> I, the fifth king of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, memorable for the vast army he is said to have carried into the field against Leonidas king of Sparta; consisting, according to some historians, of 800,000 men, while others make it amount to 3,000,000, exclusive of attendants. The fleet that attended this prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> force is likewise made to consist of 2000 sail; and all the succours they met with was the taking and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Athens; for the army was shamefully repulsed near the straits of Thermopylae by Leonidas, and the fleet was dispersed and partly destroyed by Themistocles at the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, who had only 380 sail under his command. Xerxes was assassinated by Artabanes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of his guards, and his distinguished favourite. See SPARTA.

XIMENES

Pages 461-463

FRANCIS, a justly celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, and prime minister of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, was born at Torrelaguna, in Old Castile, in 1437, and studied at Alcala and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>. He then went to Rome; and being robbed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, brought nothing back but a bull for obtaining the first vacant prebend: but the archbishop of Toledo refused it him, and threw him into prison. Being at length restored to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he obtained a benefice in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Siguenza, where Cardinal Gonzales de Mendoza, who was the bishop, made him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>. Ximenes some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after entered among the Franciscans of Toledo; but being there troubled with visits, he retired to a solitude named Cañuelo, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and the oriental tongues. At his return to Toledo, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Isabella of Castile chose him for her confessor, and afterwards nominated him archbishop of Toledo; which, next to the papacy, is the richest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome. "This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> (says Dr Robertson) he declined with a firmness..." firmness which nothing but the authoritative <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> of the pope was able to overcome. Nor did this height of promotion change his manners. Though obliged to display in public that magnificence which became his station, he himself retained his monastic severity. Under his pontifical robes he constantly wore the coarse frock of St Francis, the rents of which he used to patch with his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. He at no time used <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, but was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> clad in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-cloth. He slept always in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; most frequently on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> on boards, and rarely in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. He did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> any of the delicacies which appeared at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, but satisfied himself with that simple diet which the rule of his order prescribed. Notwithstanding these peculiarities, so opposite to the manners of the world, he possessed a thorough knowledge of its affairs, and discovered talents for business which rendered the fame of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> equal to that of his sanctity." His first care was to provide for the necessities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; to visit the churches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>; to purge his diocese of usurers and places of debauchery; to degrade corrupt judges, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in their rooms persons whom he knew to be distinguished by their probity and disinterestedness. He erected a famous university at Alcalá; and in 1499 founded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ILDEFONSO">Ildefonso</a>. Three years after he undertook the Polyglot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>; and for that purpose sent for many learned men to come to him at Toledo, purchased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> copies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> for 4000 crowns, and gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> price for Latin and Greek <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>. At this Bible they laboured above 12 years. It contains the Hebrew text of the Bible; the version of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, with a literal translation; that of St Jerome, and the Chaldee paraphrases of Onkelos; and Ximenes added to it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of the Hebrew and Chaldee words contained in the Bible. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is called Ximenes's Polyglot. In 1507 Pope Julius II. gave him the cardinal's hat, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Ferdinand the Catholic entrusted him with the administration of affairs. Cardinal Ximenes was from this moment the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of every thing that passed in Spain. He distinguished himself at the beginning of his ministry by discharging the people from the burdensome tax called acavado, which had been <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>; and laboured with such zeal and success in the conversion of the Mahometans, that he made 3000 converts, among whom was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the blood of the kings of Granada. In 1509 Cardinal Ximenes extended the dominions of Ferdinand, by taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Algiers. He undertook this conquest at his own expense, and marched in person at the head of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> clothed in his pontifical ornaments, and accompanied by a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> and monks. Some time after, foreseeing an extraordinary scarcity, he erected public granaries at Toledo, Alcalá, and Torrelaguna, and had them filled with corn at his own expense; which gained the people's hearts to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> they had an eulogium upon it cut on marble, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Toledo, and in the marketplace. King Ferdinand dying in 1516, left Cardinal Ximenes regent of his dominions; and the archduke <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, who was afterwards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Charles V., confirmed that nomination. The cardinal immediately made a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> of the officers of the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and put a stop to the oppression of the grandees. He vindicated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the people against the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; and as by the feudal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> power was lodged in the hands of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, and men of inferior condition were called into the field only as their vassals, a king with scanty revenues depended on them in all his operations. From this state Ximenes resolved to deliver the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and issued a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, commanding every city in Castile to enrol a certain number of its burgesses, and teach them military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; he himself engaging to provide officers to command them at the public expense. This was vigorously opposed by the nobles; but by his intrepidity and superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> he carried his point. He then endeavoured to diminish the possessions of the nobility, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECLAIMING">reclaiming</a> all the crown-lands, and putting a stop to the pensions granted by the late king Ferdinand. This addition made to the revenues enabled him to discharge all the debts of Ferdinand, and to establish magazines of warlike stores. The nobles, alarmed at these repeated attacks, uttered loud complaints; but before they proceeded to extremities, appointed some grandees of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> to examine the powers in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he exercised acts of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> authority. Ximenes received them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> civility; produced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a> of Ferdinand, by which he was appointed regent, together with the ratification of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> by Charles. To both these they objected; and he endeavoured to establish their validity. As the conversation grew warm, he led them insensibly to a balcony, from which they had a view of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of troops under arms, and of a formidable train of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. "Behold (says he, pointing to these, and raising his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>) the powers which I have received from his Catholic majesty! With these I govern Castile; and with these I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> govern it, till the king, your <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and mine, takes possession of his kingdom!" A <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> so bold and haughty silenced them, and affronted their associates. They <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that he was prepared for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and laid aside all thoughts of a general confederacy against his administration. At length, from the repeated intreates of Ximenes, and the impatient murmurs of the Spanish ministry, Charles V. embarked, and landed in Spain, accompanied by his favourites. Ximenes was advancing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> to meet him, but at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a> Léquillo was seized with a violent disorder, which his followers considered as the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>. This accident obliging Ximenes to stop, he wrote to the king, and with his usual boldness advised him to dismiss all the strangers in his train, whose number and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> already gave offence to the Spaniards, and earnestly desired to have an interview with him, that he might inform him of the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and the temper of his subjects. To prevent this, not only the Flemings, but the Spanish grandees, employed all their addresses to keep Charles at a distance from Aranda, the place to which the cardinal had removed. His advice was now flouted and despised. Ximenes, conscious of his own integrity and merit, expected a more grateful return from a prince to whom he delivered a kingdom more flourishing than it had been in any former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and a more extensive authority than the most illustrious of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had ever possessed; and lamented the fate of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, about to be ruined by the rapaciousness and insolence of foreign favourites. While his mind was agitated by these passions, he received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the king; in which, after a few Ximenes cold and formal expressions of regard, he was allowed to retire to his diocese; and he expired a few hours after <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> it in 1517, in the 81st year of his age. This famous cardinal ought not to be confounded with Roderic Ximenes, archbishop of Toledo, in the 13th century, who wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Spain in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> books; nor with several other Spanish writers of the name of Ximenes. Xiphias, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">Sword</a>-Fish; a genus of fishes belonging to the order of apodæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This fish is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, especially in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which separates <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and which has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> celebrated for it: the promontory Pelorus, now Capo di <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, was a place noted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the xiphias, or possibly the station of the speculators, or the persons who watched and gave notice of the approach of the fish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> method of taking them is particularly described by Strabo, and agrees exactly with that practised by the moderns. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> ascends one of the cliffs that overhangs the sea; as soon as he spies the fish, he gives notice, either by his voice or by signs, of the course it takes. Another that is stationed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, climbs up the mast, and on seeing the sword-fish, directs the rowers towards it. As soon as they think they are got within reach, he descends, and taking a spear in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, strikes it into the fish; which, after wearing itself with its agitation, is seized and drawn into the boat. It is much esteemed by the Sicilians, who buy it up eagerly, and at its first coming into season give it about sixpence English per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. The season lasts from May till August. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used to cut this fish into pieces and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> it; whence it was called Tomus Thurianus, from Thurii, a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Tarentum, where it was taken and cured. The sword-fish is said to be very voracious, and that it is a great enemy to the tunny, which (according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELON">Belon</a>) are as much terrified at it as sheep are at the sight of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>. It is a great enemy to whales, and frequently destroys them.

XYLO-ALOES

Pages 463-464
or Aloe wood, in the Materia Medica, is the product of a tree growing in China and some of the Indian islands. See Exocaria. This drug is distinguished into three sorts; the calambac or tambac, the common lignum aloes, and calambour. The calambac, or finest aloes wood, called by authors lignum aloes praeflantissimum, and by the Chinese fak-hiang, is the most resinous of all the woods we are acquainted with: it is of a light spongy texture, very porous, and its pores so filled up with a soft and fragrant resin, that the whole may be pressed and dented by the fingers like wax, or moulded about by chewing in the mouth, in the manner of mastic. This kind, laid on the fire, melts in great parts like resin, and burns away in a few moments with a bright flame and perfumed smell. Its scent, while in the mass, is very fragrant and agreeable; and its taste acid and bitterish, but very aromatic and agreeable. It is so variable in its colour, that some have divided it into three kinds; the one variegated with black and purple; the second, with the same black, but with yellowish instead of purple; and the third, yellow alone like the yolk of an egg: this last is the least scented of the three. The variation, however, is owing to the trunk of the tree being itself of three different colours; and the heart of it is the valuable part first described.
