The two following are supposed to be the other parts of the trunk; though this seems doubtful, especially in regard to the last sort, from the circumstance mentioned of its being found in large logs entire, and sometimes only the heart, which, as above noticed, constitutes the calambac. The lignum aloes vulgare is the second in value. This is of a more dense and compact texture, and consequently less resinous than the other; there is some of it, however, that is spongy, and has the holes filled up with the right resinous matter; and all of it, when good, has veins of the same resin in it. We meet with it in small fragments, which have been cut and split from larger: these are of a tolerably dense texture in the more solid pieces, and of a dusky brown colour, variegated with resinous black veins. It is in this state very heavy, and less fragrant than those pieces which show a multitude of little holes, filled up with the same blackish matter that forms the veins in others. The woody part of these last pieces is somewhat darker than the other, and is not unfrequently purplish, or even blackish. The smell of the common aloe wood is very agreeable, but not so strongly perfumed as the former. Its taste is somewhat bitter and acrid, but very aromatic. The calambour, called also agallochum sylvestre, and lignum aloes mexicanum, is light and friable, of a dusky and often mottled colour, between a dusky green black and a deep brown. Its smell is fragrant and agreeable, but much less sweet than that of either of the others; and its taste bitterish, but not so much acid or aromatic as either of the two former. This is said to be met with very frequently, and in large logs; and these sometimes entire, sometimes only the heart of the tree. This is the aloe wood used by the cabinet-makers and inlayers. This drug is esteemed a cordial taken inwardly; and is sometimes given in disorders of the stomach and bowels, and to destroy the worms. A very fragrant oil may be procured from it by distillation; which is recommended in paralytic cases from five to fifteen drops. It is at present, however, but little used; and would scarce be met with anywhere in the shops, but that it is an ingredient in some of the old compositions. Xynoecia, in Grecian antiquity, an anniversary feast observed by the Athenians in honour of Minerva, upon the sixteenth of Hecatombaion, to commemorate their leaving, by the persuasion of Theseus, their country seats, in which they lay dispersed here and there in Attica, and uniting together in one body. Xystarcha, in antiquity, the master or director of the xystus. In the Greek gymnasion the xystarcha was the second officer, and the gymnasiarcha the first; the former was his lieutenant, and presided over the two xysti, and all exercises of the athlete therein. Xystus, among the Greeks, was a long portico, open or covered at the top, where the athlete practised wrestling and running: the gladiators, who practised therein, were called xystici. Among the Romans, the xystus was only an alley, or double row of trees, meeting like an arbour, and forming a shade to walk under. Y, or y, the 23rd letter of our alphabet: its sound is formed by expelling the breath with a sudden expansion of the lips from that configuration by which we express the vowel u. It is one of the ambigential letters, being a consonant in the beginning of words, and placed before all vowels, as in yard, yield, young, &c., but before no consonant. At the end of words it is a vowel, and is substituted for the sound of i, as in try, defery, &c. In the middle of words it is not used so frequently as i is, unless in words derived from the Greek, as in chyle, empyreal, &c., though it is admitted into the middle of some pure English words, as in dying, flying, &c. The Romans had no capital of this letter, but used the small one in the middle and last syllables of words, as in corvambus, onyx, martyr. Y is also a numeral, signifying 150, or, according to Baronius, 159; and with a dash a-top, as Y, it signified 150,000.

YACHT

Pages 464-464
or YATCH, a vessel of state, usually employed to convey princes, ambassadors, or other great personages, from one kingdom to another. As the principal design of a yacht is to accommodate the passengers, it is usually fitted with a variety of convenient apartments, with suitable furniture, according to the quality or number of the persons contained therein. The royal yachts are commonly rigged as ketches, except the principal one reserved for the sovereign, which is equipped with three masts like a ship. They are in general elegantly furnished, and richly ornamented with sculpture; and always commanded by captains in his majesty's navy. Besides these, there are many other yachts of a smaller kind, employed by the commissioners of the excise, navy, and customs; or used as pleasure-boats by private gentlemen. YAMS. See DIOSCOREA. YAMBOO. See EUGENIA. YARD of a Ship, a long piece of timber suspended upon the masts of a ship, to extend the sails to the wind. See MAST and SAIL. All yards are either square or lateen; the former of which are suspended across the masts at right angles, and the latter obliquely. The square yards are nearly of a cylindrical surface. They taper from the middle, which is called the flings, towards the extremities, which are termed the yard-arms; and the distance between the flings and the yard-arms on each side is by the artificers divided into quarters, which are distinguished into the first, second, third quarters, and yard-arms. The middle quarters are formed into eight squares, and each of the end parts is figured like the frustum of a cone. All the yards of a ship are square except that of the mizen. The proportions for the length of yards, according to the different classes of ships in the British navy, are as follows: | Yard | Guns | Yard | |------|-----|-----| | 560 : main-yard, fig. I. | 100 | | 559 : Pl. CCCCLXVIII. | 90 80 | | 570 : Note, the figure represents the yard and sails of a ship of 74 guns. | 60 | | 575 : | 50 | | 561 : | 44 | | 1000 : main-yard | 100 90 80 | | 880 : fore-yard | all the rest | To apply this rule to practice, suppose the gun-deck 144 feet. The proportion for this length is, as 1000 is to 575, so is 144 to 83; which will be the length of the main-yard in feet, and so of all the rest. | Yard | Guns | |------|-----| | 520 : main-yard | 100 90 80 60 44 | | 547 : mizen-yard | 70 | | 540 : | 24 | | 1000 : main yard | all the rest. | | 724 : main topail-yard | 70 | | 719 : fore topail-yard | 34 | | 1000 : fore-yard | all the rest. | | 666 : main top gallant-yard all the rates. | 70 | | 690 : fore top gallant-yard | all the rest. | | 763 : mizen topail-yard | 70 | Crofs-jack and sprit-fail yards equal to the fore topail-yard. Sprit-topail-yard equal to the fore top-gallant-yard. The diameters of yards are in the following proportions to their length. The main and fore yards five-sevenths of an inch to one yard. The topail, crofs-jack, and sprit-fail yards, nine-fourteenths of an inch to one yard. The top-gallant, mizen topail, and sprit-fail topail yards, eight-thirteenths of an inch to one yard. The mizen-yard five-ninths of an inch to one yard. All fudding-fail booms and yards half an inch to one yard in length. The lifts of the main-yard are exhibited in the above figure by g g; the hores and their flirups by h h; the reef-tackles and their pendents by k l; and the braces and brace-pendents by m n. The lateen-yards evidently derive their names from having been peculiar to the ancient Romans. They are usually composed of several pieces fastened together by wooldings, which also serve as steps whereby the sailors climb to the peak or upper extremity, in order to furl or cast loose the sail. The mizen-yard of a ship, and the main-yard of a bilander, are hung obliquely on the mast, almost in the same manner as the lateen-yard of a xebec, fettee, or polacre.

YARDS ALSO

Pages 465-465

s also denotes places belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, where the ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, &c., are laid up in harbour.—There are belonging to his majesty's navy five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> yards, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOLWICH">Woolwich</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>; these yards are fitted with several docks, wharfs, launches, and graving places, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, repairing, and cleaning of his majesty's ships; and therein are lodged great quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, planks, anchors, and other materials: there are also convenient store-houses in each yard, in which are laid up vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, rigging, sails, blocks, and all other sorts of stores needful for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> navy.

YARE

Pages 465-465

among sailors, implies ready <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quick: as, be yare at the helm; that is, be quick, ready, and expeditious at the helm. It is sometimes also used for bright by seamen: as, to keep his arms yare; that is, to keep them clean and bright. Yare, a river of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, which runs from west to east through that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, passing by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, and falling into the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a>.

YARMOUTH

Pages 465-465

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, with a market on Wednesdays and Saturdays, and a fair on Friday and Saturday in Easter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> for petty chapmen. It is seated on the river Yare, where it falls into the sea; and is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength, both by art and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, being almost surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and there is a drawbridge over the river. It is esteemed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and is a clean handsome place, whose houses are well built, it being a considerable town for trade. It has one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and a neat chapel, and the steeple of St Nicholas is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> that it serves for a sea-mark. It is governed by a mayor. The harbour is a very fine one, though it is very dangerous for strangers in windy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and it has for its security a pretty strong fort. It is 27 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, and 112 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 55'. N. Lat. 52° 45'. Yarmouth, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Wight, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, with a market on Fridays, and one fair on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 26th for toys. It is seated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, on the sea-shore, and is encompassed with water; for, not many years ago a channel was cut through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, over which there is a drawbridge, and it is defended by a strong castle on the quay. It is a handsome place, whose houses are chiefly built with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and covered with slate; and it sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The market is now disused. W. Long. 1° 28'. N. Lat. 50° 40'.

YARN

Pages 465-465
wool or flax spun into thread, of which they weave cloth. See CLOTH. YARROW. See Achillæa, Botany Index. Yawning, an involuntary opening of the mouth, generally produced by weariness or an inclination to sleep. Yawning, according to Boerhaave, is performed by expanding at once and the same time all the muscles capable of spontaneous motion; by greatly extending the lungs; by drawing in gradually and slowly a large quantity of air; and gradually and slowly breathing it out, after it has been retained for some time and rarefied; and then restoring the muscles to their natural state. Hence the effect of yawning is to move, accelerate, and equally distribute all the humours through all the vessels of the body, and consequently to qualify Yawning, the muscles and organs of sensation for their various functions. Sanctorius observes, that a great deal is insensibly discharged, when nature endeavours to get rid of the retained perspirable matter, by yawning and stretching of the limbs. To these a person is most inclined just after sleep, because a greater quantity going off by the pores of the skin than at other times, whenever a person wakes, the increasing contraction that then happens closes a great deal of the perspirable matter in the cutaneous passages, which will continually give such irritations as excite yawning and stretching; and such motions, by shaking the membranes of the whole body, and shifting the contacts of their fibres, and the inclosed matter, by degrees throw it off. Hence we see the reason why healthful strong people are most inclined to such motions, because they perspire most in time of sleep, and therefore have more of the perspirable matter to lodge in the pores, and greater irritations thereunto. The advantages of some little exercise just after waking in a morning are considerable, as it throws off all the perspirable matter that is ready for its exit out of the body. When yawning is troublesome, Hippocrates says that long deep respiration or drawing in the air at long intervals cures it.

YEAR

Pages 465-466

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>. See Astronomy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDAR">Kalendar</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman year was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> year, which, as first settled by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, consisted of only 10 months; viz. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, containing 31 days. 2. April, 30. 3. May, 31. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, 30. 5. Quintilis, 31. 6. Sextilis, 30. 7. September, 30. 8. October, 31. 9. November, 30. 10. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, 30.—In all 304 days; which came short of the true lunar year by 50 days, and of the solar, by 61 days. Numa Pompilius corrected this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the year, and composed two new months, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> and February, of the days that were used to be added to the former year. The ancient Egyptian year, called also the year of Nabonassar, on account of the epoch of Nabonassar, is the solar year of 365 days, divided into 12 months, of 30 days each, besides five intercalary days added at the end. The names, &c., of the months are as follows: 1. Thoth. 2. Paophi. 3. Athyr. 4. Choiac. 5. Tybi. 6. Mecheir. 7. Phamenoth. 8. Pharmuthi. 9. Pachon. 10. Pauni. 11. Epiphi. 12. Mefori; beside the ἑπτά ἐπιστροφαί. The ancient Greek year was lunar; consisting of 12 months, which at first had 30 days apiece, then alternately 30 and 29 days, computed from the first appearance of the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; with the addition of an embolismic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of 30 days, every 3d, 5th, 8th, 11th, 14th, 16th, and 19th year of a cycle of 19 years; in order to keep the new and full moons to the same terms <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seasons of the year. Their year commenced with that new moon, the full moon of which comes next after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice. The order, &c., of their months was thus: 1. Ἐκανονικός, containing 29 days. 2. Μητροπολιτικός, 30. 3. Βασιλεύς, 29. 4. Μαγιστροπολιτικός, 30. 5. Πυραμίδας, 29. 6. Περιστέρας, 30. 7. Γενελάως, 29. 8. Αἰγυπτιακός, 30. 9. Ελευθερίας, 30. 10. Μεγάλου, 30. 11. Θεοχάλκιος, 29. 12. Σειραφεστών, 30. The ancient Jewish year is a lunar year, consisting <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> commonly of 11 months, which alternately contain 30 and 29 days. It was made to agree with the solar year, either by the adding of 11, and sometimes 12 days, at the end of the year, or by an embolismic month. The names and quantities of the months stand thus: 1. Nilan, or Abib, 30 days. 2. Jiar, or Zius, 29. 3. Siban, or Siwan, 30. 4. Thammuz, or Tamuz, 29. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">Ab</a>, 30. 6. Elul, 29. 7. Tifri, or Ethanim, 30. 8. Marchelvam, or Bul, 29. 9. Cilleu, 30. 10. Tebeth, 29. 11. Sabat, or Schebeth, 30. 12. Adar, in the embolismic year, 30. Adar, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> year, was but 29. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, in the defective year, Cilleu was only 29 days; and in the redundant year, Marchelvam was 30. The Perian year is a solar year of about 365 days; consisting of 12 months of 30 days each, with five intercalary days added at the end. The Arabic, Mahometan, and Turkish years, called also the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, is a lunar year, equal to 354 days eight hours and 48 minutes, and consists of 12 months, which contain alternately 30 and 29 days. The Hindoo year differs from all these, and is indeed different in different provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The best account that we have of it is by Mr Cavendish, in the Phil. Trans. of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> for the year 1792. "Before I speak of the civil year of the Hindoos (says this eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>), it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be proper to say a few words of the astronomical year, by which it is regulated. "The astronomical year begins at the instant when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> comes to the first point of the Hindoo <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>. In the year 1792, it began on April 9th, at 22h. 14' after midnight of their first meridian, which is about 41' of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>; but, according to Mr Gentil's account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> astronomy, it began 3h. 24' earlier. As this year, however, is longer than ours, its commencement falls continually later, in respect of the Julian year, by 50' 26" in four years. This year is divided into 12 months, each of which corresponds to the time of the sun's stay in some sign; so that they are of different lengths, and seldom begin at the beginning of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. "The civil day in all parts of India begins at sunrise, and is divided into 60 parts called dandas, which are again divided into 60 palas. In those parts of India in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a> almanac, or as it is there called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRAS">patras</a>, is used, the civil year is lunifolar, consisting of 12 lunar months, with an intercalary month inserted between them occasionally. It begins at the day after the new moon next before the beginning of the solar year. The lunar month is divided into 30 parts called teethee; these are not strictly of the same length, but are equal to the time in which the moon's true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> from the sun is 12°. From the new moon till the moon arrives at 12° distance from the sun is called the first teethee; from thence till it comes to 24°, is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> teethee; and so on till the full moon, after which the teethees return in the same order as before. "The civil day is constantly called by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of that teethee which expires during the course of the day; and as the teethee is sometimes longer than one day, a day sometimes occurs in which no teethee ends. When this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the day is called by the same number as the following day; so that two successive days go by the same name. It oftener happens, however, that two teethees end on the same day; in which case the number of the first of them gives name to the day, and there is no day called by the number of the last, so that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">gap</a> is made in the order of the days. In the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the month the days are counted from the full moon, in the same manner as in the former part they are counted from the new moon; only the last day, or that on which the new moon happens, is called the 30th, instead of the 1st. It appears, therefore, that each half of the month constantly begins on the day after that on which the new or full moon falls; only sometimes the half month begins with the second day, the first being wanting. "This manner of counting the days is sufficiently intricate; but that of counting the months is still more so. "The civil year, as was before said, begins at the day after the new moon; and, moreover, in the years which have an intercalary month, this month begins at the day after the new moon; but notwithstanding this, the ordinary civil month begins at the day after the full moon. To make their method more intelligible, we will call the time from new moon to new moon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> month. The civil month Vilaika, the first in the Hindoo kalender, which extends from the 9th of our April to the 10th of May, begins at the day after that full moon which is nearest to the instant at which the sun enters Melha, the first in order of the Indian signs, whether before or after; however, it is not always accurately the nearest. "A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this way of counting the months is, that the first half of Chitra, the last month in the Indian kalender, extending from March the 10th to April the 9th, falls in one year, and the latter half in the following year; and whenever the sun enters no sign during a natural month, this month is intercalary. The number of days in the month varies from 29 to 32. Indeed the Hindoo months, both solar and lunar, consist neither of a determinate number of days, nor are regulated by any cycle, but depend solely on the motions of the sun and moon; so that a Hindoo has no way of knowing what day of the month it is but by consulting his almanac; and what is more, the month ought sometimes to begin on different days, in different places, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in latitude and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, not to mention the difference which may arise from errors in computation. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of computing time must be attended with many inconveniences; but in the transactions of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the Hindoos do not much regard it. A disagreement, however, in the computation of the teethee, which sometimes also happens, occasions no small perplexity; because by the teethees or lunar days are regulated most of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> festivals. Every Brahmin in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of a temple, or whose duty it is to announce the times for the observance of religious ceremonies, is therefore furnished with one of their almanacs; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he be an astronomer, he makes such corrections in it as the difference of latitude and longitude renders necessary." New Year's Gift. See Gift.

YEAST

Pages 466-467
or YEST, a head or scum rising upon beer or ale while working or fermenting in the vat. See Brewing. It is used for a leaven or ferment in the baking of bread, as serving to swell or puff it up very considerably. Yeast in a little time, and to make it much lighter, softer, and more delicate. See Baking, Barn, and Bread. Mr Henry has published a method of preparing artificial yeast, by which good bread may be made without the affluence of any other ferment. The method is this: Boil flour and water together to the consistence of treacle, and when the mixture is cold saturate it with fixed air. Pour the mixture thus saturated into one or more large bottles or narrow-mouthed jars; cover it over loofely with paper, and upon that lay a plate or board with a weight to keep it steady. Place the vessel in a situation where the thermometer will stand from 70° to 80°, and stir up the mixture two or three times in 24 hours. In about two days such a degree of fermentation will have taken place, as to give the mixture the appearance of yeast. With the yeast in this state, and before it has acquired a thoroughly vinous smell, mix the quantity of flour intended for bread, in the proportion of five pounds of flour to a quart of the yeast, and a sufficient portion of warm water. Knead them well together in a proper vessel, and covering it with a cloth, let the dough stand for 12 hours, or till it appears to be sufficiently fermented in the fore-mentioned degree of warmth. It is then to be formed into loaves and baked. Mr Henry adds, that perhaps the yeast would be more perfect, if a decoction of malt were used instead of simple water. It has lately been discovered, that a decoction of malt alone, without any addition, will produce a yeast proper enough for the purpose of brewing. This discovery was made by Joseph Senyor, servant of the reverend Mr Malon of Alton near Rotherham; and he received for it a reward of £20. from the Society for promoting Arts, Manufactures, and Commerce. The process is as follows: Procure three earthen or wooden vessels of different sizes and apertures, one capable of holding two quarts, the other three or four, and the third five or six: boil a quarter of a peck of malt for about eight or ten minutes in three pints of water; and when a quart is poured off from the grains, let it stand in the first or smaller vessel in a cool place till not quite cold, but retaining that degree of heat which the brewers usually find to be proper when they begin to work their liquor. Then remove the vessel into some warm situation near a fire, where the thermometer stands between 70° and 80° degrees Fahrenheit, and there let it remain till the fermentation begins, which will be plainly perceived within 30 hours: add then two quarts more of a like decoction of malt, when cool, as the first was; and mix the whole in the second or larger vessel, and stir it well in, which must be repeated in the usual way, as it rises in a common vat: then add a still greater quantity of the same decoction, to be worked in the largest vessel, which will produce yeast enough for a brewing of 40 gallons. Common ale yeast may be kept fresh and fit for use several months by the following method: Put a quantity of it into a close canvas bag, and gently squeeze out the moisture in a screw-press till the remaining matter be as firm and stiff as clay. In this state it may be closely packed up in a tight cask for securing it from the air; and will keep fresh, sound, and fit for use, for a long time. This is a secret that might be of great use to the brewers and distillers, who, though they employ very large quantities of yeast, seem to know no method of preserving it, or raising nurseries of it; for want of which they sustain a very considerable loss; whereas the brewers in Flanders make a very great advantage of supplying the malt distillers of Holland with yeast, which is rendered lasting and fit for carriage by this easy expedient.

YELL

Pages 467-467

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Shetland, lying northeast from the Mainland, and divided from it by an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, called Yell-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>. By some it is thought to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THULE">Thule</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. In the old descriptions it is said to be 20 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 8 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. It is very mountainous and full of moss; but there are pretty considerable pastures in which they feed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many sheep; and it also affords plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>. It has eight <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> harbours, which would not be thought defpicable in other countries. Anciently it seems to have been pretty populous, since there are in it three churches, twenty chapels, and many burgs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pictish forts.

YELLOW

Pages 467-467

one of the original colours of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. YELLOW-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. See COLOUR-Making. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> YELLOW, a beautiful colour much used by painters, formerly thought to be prepared from arsenic, but now discovered to have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> for its basis. YELLOW-Hammer. See FRINGILLA, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. YELLOW-Fever. See MEDICINE, No 168.

YEMEN

Pages 467-467

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, stretching along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, and forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> once known by the name of Arabia Felix.

YEOMAN

Pages 467-467

the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> among the plebeians of England, next in order to the gentry. The yeomen are properly freeholders, who having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of their own, live on good husbandry. YEOMAN of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">Guard</a> were anciently 250 men of the best <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> under gentry, and of larger stature than ordinary, each being required to be six feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. At present there are but 100 yeomen in constant duty, and 70 more not in duty; and as any of the 100 dies, his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is supplied out of the 70. They go dressed after the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They formerly had diet as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> when in waiting; but this was taken off in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>.

YEST

Pages 467-468
or YEAST. See YEAST. YEW. See TAXUS, BOTANY Index. Yew trees are remarkable for their duration. There are now growing within 300 yards of the old Gothic ruins of Fountain's abbey, near Rippon, in Yorkshire, seven very large yew trees, commonly called the Seven Sisters, whose exact ages cannot be accurately ascertained, though tradition says that they were standing in the year 1088. It is said also, that when the great Fountain's abbey was building, which is 700 feet long, and was finished in 1283, the masons used to work their stones, during the hot summers, under the shade of these trees. The circumference of the Seven Sisters, when measured by a curious traveller, were of the following sizes:—the smallest tree, round its body, 5 yards 1 foot; four others are from 5½ to 7½ yards; the fifth is 9½ yards; and the seventh is 11 yards 1 foot 7 inches in circumference, being 2 yards 10 inches larger than the greatest. great yew tree now growing in the churchyard at Gref- ford, in North Wales, which is 9 yards 9 inches. These trees are the largest and oldest in the British dominions.

YOLK

Pages 468-468

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the middle of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> (see Egg). It contains a lymphatic substance mixed with a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of mild <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which, on account of this mixture, is soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. When exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, it assumes a consistence not so hard as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of the egg; and when bruised gives out the oil which it contains. This oil has been used externally as a liniment.

YONNE

Pages 468-468

a river in France, which rising in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and running <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> through Nivernois and Champagne, falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> at Montereau sur Yonne.

YORK

Pages 468-468

in Latin Eboracum, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in England. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> that the origin of it is uncertain. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> a legion was stationed here, it being then the capital of the Brigantes; and here died the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus, and Flavius Valerius Constantius Chlorus, father of Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. There was then also a temple of Bellona here, and no less than three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> ways went from hence. In the time of the Saxons it was erected into an archbishopric by Pope Honorius, to which are now subject the bishoprics of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, Carlisle, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>; though anciently 12 bishoprics in England, and all Scotland, were. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> is still kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINSTER">minster</a>, by which Ulphius, one of the Saxon princes, bestowed all his lands and revenues upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. This city suffered very much during the ravages of the Danes; but, after the Conquest, it began to flourish again. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which cost a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time and a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, is a most stately Gothic pile. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is particularly admired for its painted glass, its fine marble stalls, its pillars of alabaster, and curious contrivance. In it is the following line in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> letters: Ut Roja, flore florum, fic est <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">Domus</a> ista Domorum. The choir is remarkable for its fine carvings, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of all the English monarchs; and the windows are exquisitely painted with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. The lantorn steeple is 70 feet <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and 188 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the windows are 45. At the south end is a circular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, called the marigold window from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of its glass; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end is a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> represents <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>. This city is generally reckoned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> city in England; but though it stands upon more ground, it is inferior in trade, wealth, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>. The inhabitants are reckoned at 16,145. It is situated in a fine plain, in the middle of the shire, on both sides the Ouse, walled and divided into four wards, containing 28 parishes. It enjoys large privileges and immunities, conferred upon it by a succession of kings from Henry II. and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor, which is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> peculiar to it and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Richard II. made it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself. The conservancy of most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of the county, within certain limits, belongs to the lord mayor and aldermen. The middle <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> here over the Ouse is thought to equal the Rialto at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, height, and breadth, the diameter being 81 feet, and the height 31. Though this city is 60 miles distant from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, yet ships of 70 tons burden come up the river to it. The town-house <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> guild-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> stands upon the bridge, and is superior in all respects to that of London. In the Popish times there were <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> abbeys here, and a vast number of churches; but of the latter there are only 17 now. The steeple of that of Allhallows is reckoned the finest in England. The archbishop has a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>-room, designed by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a>, is very noble. Here are plays, assemblies, concerts, and the like entertainments, at some house or other, almost every night in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. In the old castle, built originally by William the Conqueror, and repaired in 1701, the assizes are kept. It serves also for the county-gaol, which is the neatest and pleasantest in England, with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> larger than that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, and it has a handsome chapel in it, with a good allowance for a preacher. This city has long given the title of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to some branch of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. The plenty and cheapness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> induces many persons of small fortune, or that would live frugally, to take up their abode here; and the venerable remains of Roman antiquities, and those of a later <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>, as abbeys, churches, and castles, procure this city a visit from every curious traveller. Many Roman altars, urns, coins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, &c., have been found; and Saxon coins are still extant that have been struck here. The members, being two in number, for this city, have precedence of all others, except those of London, in the house of commons. An infirmary, after the manner of those of Bath, Bristol, &c., hath been erected in it; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COTTON_MANUFACTURE">cotton manufacture</a> established and brought to great perfection. Besides four weekly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, it has a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>; one, in particular, every other Thursday for cattle and sheep. W. Long. i. i. N. Lat. 53. 59.

YORKSHIRE

Pages 468-470

the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>; on the east by the German ocean; and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Cheshire.—It is upwards of 80 miles in length from east to west, nearly as much in breadth, and about 360 in circumference, containing, in the whole, 26 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wapentakes, 49 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 563 parishes, 242 vicarages, with many chapels of ease, and 2330 villages. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is computed by some at 4684 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, by others at 3,770,000 acres, and its inhabitants at 878,892. It is divided into three parts or ridings, viz. the West, East, and North; so denominated from their situation, in respect of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. Each of these is as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not larger, than any ordinary county. There are other divisions, as Richmondshire, Allertonshire, Howdenshire, Hallamshire, Craven, Cleveland, Marshland, Holderness, &c. As the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> vary greatly, so does the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. In the hilly parts the air is good, but the soil very indifferent; of the lower form are marshy, others drier, and the soil of both rich; but the air of the former York. former is more foggy and unhealthy than that of the latter. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this county are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a> and hard-wares; particularly knives, bits, and spurs; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are stockings and woollen cloth, with which it supplies in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> Germany and the North. As to the produce, it abounds in corn, cattle, horses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, coal, wood, lime, liquorice, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, jet, &c. It lies wholly in the northern circuit, and much the greater part of it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of York; that only which is called Richmondshire belonging to the diocese of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. The members it sends to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> are 30; of which two are for the shire and 28 for the towns. New-York, one of the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, is bounded towards the south-east by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>; east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONNECTICUT">Connecticut</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSACHUSETTS">Massachusetts</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERMONT">Vermont</a>; north by the 45th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>; north-westwardly by the river Iroquois or St Lawrence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a> and Erie; south-west and south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>. The whole state contains about 44,000 square miles, equal to 28,163,000 acres. The settlements already made in this state are chiefly upon two narrow oblongs, extending from the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New York</a> east and north. The one east is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which is 140 miles long, and narrow, and surrounded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The one extending north is about 40 miles in breadth, and bisected by Hudson's river. And such is the intersection of the whole state by the branches of the Hudson, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a>, the Susquehannah, and other large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, that there are few places throughout its whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> which are more than 15 or 20 miles from some navigable stream. There are few fish in the rivers, but in the brooks are plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>; and in the lakes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> perch, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-fish, salmon-trout, cat-fish, and a variety of others. The State, to speak generally, abounds with lakes, some of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and others of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is intersected by ridges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> running in a north-east and south-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Beyond the Alleghany mountains, however, the country is a dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, of a fine rich soil, covered, in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, with maple, beech, birch, cherry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-walnut, locust, hickory, and some mulberry trees. On the banks of lake Erie are a few chestnut and oak ridges. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">Hemlock</a> swamps are interspersed thinly through the country. All the creeks that empty into lake Erie have falls, which afford many excellent mill seats. East of the Alleghany mountains, the country is broken into hills with rich intervening valleys. The hills are clothed thick with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and when cleared afford fine pasture; the valleys, when cultivated, produce wheat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, peas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, oats, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn. Of the commodities produced from culture, wheat is the staple; of which immense quantities are raised and exported. Indian corn and peas are likewise raised for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>; and rye, oats, barley, &c., for home consumption. In some parts of the State excellent dairies are kept, which furnish for the market <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> and cheese. The situation of New-York, with respect to foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, has decidedly the preference to any other of the United States. It has at all seasons of the year a short and easy access to the ocean. Its exports to the West Indies are, biscuit, peas, Indian corn apples, onions, boards, flaxes, horses, sheep, butter, cheese, pickled oysters, beef, and pork. But wheat is the staple commodity of the State, of which no less than 677,700 bushels were exported in the year 1775, besides 255 tons of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and 2828 tons of flour. Inspectors of flour are appointed to prevent imposition, and to see that none is exported but that which is deemed by them merchantable. Besides the above-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, are exported flax-seed, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, sarsaparilla, coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, pig-iron, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>-iron, pot-ash, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PEARL_ASH"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-ash, furs, deer-skins, logwood, futick, mahogany, bees wax, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a> wine, rum, tar, pitch, turpentine, whale-fins, fish, sugars, molasses, salt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, &c., but most of these articles are imported for re-exportation. In the year 1774, there were employed, in the trade of this State, 1075 vessels, whose tonnage amounted to 40,812. Since the revolution, the literature of the State has engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the legislature. In one of their earliest sessions an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> passed, constituting 21 gentlemen (of whom the governor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> being are members ex officio) a body corporate and politic, by the name and style of "The regents of the university of the State of New-York." They are intrusted with the care of literature in general in the State, and have power to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> charters of incorporation for erecting colleges and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> throughout the state—are to visit these institutions as often as they shall think proper, and report their state to the legislature once a-year. All degrees above that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts are to be conferred by the regents. A universal toleration is granted in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The supreme legislative powers of the State are vested in two branches, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. The members of the senate are elected by the freeholders of the State, who possess freehold estates to the value of 100l. clear of debts. For the purpose of electing senators, the State is divided into four great districts, each of which chooses a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The assembly of the State is composed of representatives from the several counties, chosen annually in May. Every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> inhabitant of full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, who has resided in the state six months preceding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, and possessing a freehold to the value of 20l. in the county where he is to give his vote; or has rented a tenement therein of the yearly value of forty shillings, and has been rated and actually paid taxes—is entitled to vote for representatives in assembly. The number of representatives is limited to 300. The supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a> of the State is vested in a governor chosen once in three years by the freemen of the state. The lieutenant-governor is, by his office, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the senate; and, upon an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of voices, has a casting vote; but has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> on other occasions. The governor has not a seat in the legislature; but as a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of revision and council of appointment, he has a vast influence in the state. The council of revision is composed of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, the judges of the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, or any of them, and the governor. In the year 1790 the number of inhabitants in this state was 340,120, of whom 21,324 were <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>; but in 1795 the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the state amounted to 530,177, making an increase of 190,057 in five years. New-York, a city of North America, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the state of the same name. It is situated at the south-west point. point of an island, at the confluence of Hudson and East rivers, and is about four miles in circumference. The situation is both healthy and pleasant. Surrounded on all sides by water, it is refreshed by cool breezes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and the air in winter is more temperate than in other places under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>. York island is 15 miles in length, and hardly one in breadth. It is joined to the main by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s bridge. The channels between Long and Staten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and between Long and York islands, are so narrow as to occasion an unusual rapidity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, which is increased by the confluence of the waters of Hudson and East rivers. This rapidity, in general, prevents the obstruction of the channel by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. There is no harbor or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> for the reception of ships; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> where they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in East river is defended from the violence of the sea by the islands which interlock with each other; so that, except that of Rhode island, the harbour of New-York, which admits ships of any burden, is the best of the United States. The number of the inhabitants in 1786 was 23,614. The most magnificent edifice in this city is Federal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, at the head of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">Broad</a>-street; in a gallery in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of which General <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WASHINGTON">Washington</a>, attended by the senate and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of representatives, took his oath of office at the commencement of the operation of the federal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, 30th April, 1789. The other public buildings in the city are, three houses for public worship for the Dutch Reformed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, four for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, three for Episcopalians, two for German Lutherans and Calvinists, two for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, two for Baptists, two for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, one for Moravians, one for Catholics, one for French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and a Jewish synagogue. King's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> was chiefly founded by the voluntary contributions of the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, assisted by the general assembly, and the corporation of Trinity Church; in the year 1754, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> (and grant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>) being then obtained, incorporating a number of gentlemen therein mentioned, by the name of "The Governors of the College of the Province of New-York, in the city of New-York, in America;" granting to them the power of conferring all such degrees as are usually conferred by either of the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> consists of an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> edifice, three stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, with four staircases, 12 apartments in each, a chapel, hall, library, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and a school for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. It is situated on a dry gravelly soil, about 150 yards from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of Hudson's river, commanding a beautiful and extensive prospect. Since the revolution, the legislature passed an act constituting 21 gentlemen (of whom the governor and lieutenant-governor for the time being, are members ex officio) a body corporate and politic by the name of "The Regents of the University of the State of New-York." They are entrusted with the care of literature in general, and have power to grant charters for erecting colleges and academies through the state. It is now denominated Columbia college. The annual revenue arising from the estate belonging to the college amounts to £335l. currency, exclusive of some bonds which are not as yet productive. It consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of arts, and one of physic, the first having a president and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> professors, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, and the same number of professors. The library and museum were destroyed during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, after which upwards of £800l. were expended on books to enlarge the library. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of this city is at present in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a mayor, aldermen, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> council, and the city is divided into seven wards, in each of which an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a> and assistant are annually chosen by the people. A court of session is held for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of criminal causes. It is esteemed the most eligible situation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in the United States; but the want of good water is a great inconvenience, there being few <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> in the city, and most of the people are supplied with fresh water conveyed to their doors in casks from the head of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> street. The number of inhabitants in 1796 is stated at more than 33,000; and according to some it is supposed that they amount at this time to nearly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>. The entries from foreign ports in 1795, were 178 ships, 309 brigs, 9 barges, 7 snows, 268 schooners, and 170 sloops. Works of defense have been erected to a considerable extent, and when completed on the original <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> afford great security to the city. New-York is 95 miles N. E. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, 197 N. E. of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALTIMORE">Baltimore</a>, and 913 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLESTON">Charleston</a>. W. Long. 74° 9' 45". N. Lat. 40° 42' 8".

YOUNG

Pages 470-471

Dr Edward, was the son of a clergyman of the same name, and was born about the year 1679. When sufficiently qualified, he was matriculated into All-Souls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and desirous to follow the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in that profession. In this situation he wrote his poem called The Last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, published in 1704; which coming from a layman gave universal satisfaction: this was soon after followed by another, entitled The Force of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Vanquished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>. These productions gained him a respectable acquaintance; he was intimate with Addison, and thus became one of the writers of the Spectator; but the turn of his mind leading him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he took orders, was made one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s chaplains, and obtained the living of Welwyn in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, worth about £500 per annum, but he never rose to higher preferment. For some years before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, Dr Young attended his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> pretty constantly; but upon his decease all his hopes of church preferment vanished; however, upon the death of Dr Hales, he was taken into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the princess-dowager of Wales, and succeeded him as her privy chaplain. When pretty far advanced in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he married the lady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>. This lady was a widow, and had an amiable son and daughter, who both died young. What he felt for their loss, as well as for that of his wife, is finely expressed in his Night Thoughts, in which the young lady is characterized under the name of Narcissa; her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> by that of Philander; and his wife, though nameless, is frequently mentioned; and he thus, in an apostrophe to death, deplores the loss of all the three. Infatiate archer, could not once suffice! Thy shaft flew thrice, and thrice my peace was slain, And thrice ere thrice yon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> renew'd her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. He wrote three tragedies, The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">Revenge</a>, Bufonis, and The Brothers. His satires, called Love of Fame the universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">Passion</a>, are by many esteemed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> performance; though Swift said the poet should have been... Young, been either more angry or more merry: they have been characterized as a string of epigrams written on one subject, that tire the reader before he gets through them. His Complaint, or Night Thoughts, exhibit him as a moral and melancholy poet, and are esteemed his masterpiece. They form a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> peculiarly his own, and in which he has been unrivalled by all those who attempted to write in this manner. They were written under the recent pressure of his sorrow for the loss of his wife, daughter, and son-in-law; they are addressed to Lorenzo, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and the world, and who, as it is intimated by some, is his own son, but then labouring under his father's displeasure. As a prose-writer, he arraigned the prevailing manners of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> called The Centaur not Fabulous; and when he was above 80 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, published Conjectures on Original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">Composition</a>. He published some pieces; and the whole of his works are collected in 4 and 5 vols 12mo. Dr Young's turn of mind was naturally solemn; and he usually, when at home in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, spent many hours of the day walking in his own church-yard among the tombs. His conversation, his writings, had all a reference to the life after this; and this turn of disposition mixed itself even with his improvements in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>. He had, for instance, an alcove with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, so painted, near his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, that at a distance it looked as a real one which the spectator was then approaching. Upon coming up near it, however, the deception was perceived, and this motto appeared, *Invisibilis non decipiant*, "The things unseen do not deceive us." Yet, notwithstanding this gloominess of temper, he was fond of innocent sports and amusement: he instituted an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a>-green in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of which he was rector, and often promoted the gaiety of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in person. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> was generally poignant, and ever levelled at those who testified any contempt for decency and religion. His epigram, spoken extempore on Voltaire, is well known; who happening in his company to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, and the allegorical personages of Death and Sin, Young thus addressed him: Thou art so witty, profligate, and thin, You seem a Milton with his Death and Sin. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, preaching in office at St James's, he found, that though he strove to make his audience attentive, he could not prevail. Upon which his pity for their folly got the better of all decorums, and he sat back in the pulpit and burst into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> of tears. Towards the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of life he knew his own infirmities, and suffered himself to be in pupillage to his house-keeper; for he considered that, at a certain time of life, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> childhood of age demanded its wonted protection. His son, whose boyish follies were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> obnoxious to paternal severity, was at last forgiven in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>; and our poet died regretted by all, having performed all that man could do to fill his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. His death happened in 1765.

YOUTH

Pages 471-471

that state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in which he approaches towards his greatest perfection of body.

YPRES

Pages 471-471

a handsome, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and populous town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, with a bishop's see. It has a considerable manufactory in cloth and ferges, and every year in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> there is a considerable fair. It is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, but was besieged and taken by the French in 1744, and also in 1794. It is seated in a fertile plain on the river Ypre, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 48'. N. Lat. 50. 51'.

YTTRIA

Pages 471-471

one of the lately discovered earths. For an account of its properties and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No. 1457. YTTRIO-Tantalite, a mineral substance containing the new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> yttria, and the new metal tantalum, which latter is found by Dr Wollaston to be identical with columbium.

YUCCA

Pages 471-471
Adam's Needle, a genus of plants of the class hexandra. The species of this plant are all exceedingly curious in their growth, and are therefore much cultivated in gardens. The Indians make a kind of bread from the roots of this plant.

YUNX

Pages 471-471

a genus of birds of the order Picce. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Z. Z, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> z, the 24th and last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and the 19th consonant of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of which is formed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the tongue from the palate downwards and upwards to it again, with a fluttering and opening of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. This letter has been reputed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> consonant, having the sound ds; but some think with very little reason: and, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we thought otherwise, we often double it, as in puzzle, muzzle, &c. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, Z was a numeral letter, signifying 2000; and with a dash added atop, Z signified 2000 times 2000, or 4,000,000. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a> this letter formerly stood as a mark for several sorts of weights; sometimes it signified an ounce and a half; and very frequently it stood for half an ounce; sometimes for the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an ounce, or a dram <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">troy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and it has in earlier times been used to express the third part of an ounce or eight scruples. ZZ were used by some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physicians to express <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, and at present they are often used to signify zinzibier or ginger.

ZAARA

Pages 471-472

Zapara, Sahara, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">Desert</a>, a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Barbary, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZZAN">Fezzan</a> and Calima, on the south by Tomboctoo, and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. Zaara contains a variety of wandering nations, all proceeding from Arabs, Moors, and fugitive Portuguese, who took refuge there when the family of the Sherifs made themselves masters of the three kingdoms of Barbary. ZAF All these people bear indiscriminately the names of Nars, Moors, or Arabs. They are subdivided into various nations, of which the most considerable are the Mongearts, Trafars, and Brannars. The Mongearts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a wandering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and live chiefly on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of their flocks, with a little barley-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and some dates. The poorer sort go naked, except the females, who <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> wrap a clout about their middle, and wear a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> on their head; but the wealthier sort have a kind of loose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, made of blue calico, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sleeves, that is brought them from Negroland. When they move from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another for fresh pasture, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or prey, most of them ride on camels, which have generally a sort of saddle between the bunch and the neck, with a string or strap run through their nostrils, which serves for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>; and instead of spurs they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BODKIN">bodkin</a>. Their tents or huts are covered with a coarse stuff, made of camel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> or moss that grows on the palm trees.
