These Arabs live here under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of their sheiks or cheyeks; as in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and other places. The other two tribes are rather more civilized. They are all Mahometans.

ZABULON

Pages 472-472

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a very strong town in the tribe of that name, on the Mediterranean, named of men, near <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a>: its vicinity to which makes it probable that it was also Chabulon, unless either name is a faulty <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> in Josephus; distant about 60 stadia from Ptolemais.

ZACYNTHUS

Pages 472-472

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> to the south of Cephalenia 60 stadia, but nearer to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, in the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, formerly subject to Ulysses, in compass above 160 stadia, woody and fruitful, with a considerable cognominal town and a port. The island lies over against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, having a colony of Achaeans from Peloponnesus, over against the Corinthian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>. Both island and town are now called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZANTE">Zante</a>.

ZAECUCUS

Pages 472-472

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of the Locrians, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, flourished 500 years B.C. He made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by which he punished adulterers with the loss of both their eyes; and his son offending, was not absolved from this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>: yet, to show the father as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> lawgiver, he put out his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and his son's left eye. This example of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and severity made so strong an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the minds of his subjects, that no instance was found of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of that vice during the reign of that legislator. It is added, that Zaleucus forbade any wine being given to the sick on pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, unless it was prescribed by the physicians; and that he was so jealous of his laws, that he ordered, that whoever was desirous of changing them, should be obliged, when he made the proposal, to have a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> about his neck, in order that he might be immediately strangled, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> those alterations were esteemed no better than the laws already established. Diodorus Siculus attributes the same thing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARONDAS">Charondas</a> legislator of the Sybarites.

ZAFFRE

Pages 472-472

is the oxide of cobalt, employed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> of a blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The method of preparing it is as follows: The cobalt taken out of the mine is broken with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a> into pieces about the size of a hen's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; and the flinty involucrum, with such other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matters as are distinguishable by the eye, are separated as much as possible. The chosen mineral is then pounded in stamping <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, and sifted through <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> wire sieves. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> parts are washed off by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and it is afterwards put into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flat-bottomed arched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a> oven, where the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of the wood reverberates upon the ore; which is occasionally stirred and turned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> handled <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> hooks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rakes; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till it ceases to emit any fumes. The oven or furnace is terminated by a long <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> gallery, which serves for a chimney; in which the arsenic, naturally mixed with the ore, sublimes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the ore contains a little bitumen, as this semifluid is very fusible, it is collected at the bottom of the furnace. The cobalt remains in the state of a dark gray oxide, and is called zaffre. One hundred pounds of the cobalt ore lose 20 and even 30 per cent. during this operation, which is continued 4 or even 9 hours, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the ore. The roasted ore being taken out from the furnace, such parts as are concreted into lumps are pounded and sifted afresh. Zaffre, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, is never pure, being mixed with two or rather three parts of powdered flints. A proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the best sort of thefe, after being ignited in a furnace, is thrown into water to render it friable, and more easily reduced to powder; which, being sifted, is mixed with the zaffre, according to the before-mentioned dose; and the mixture is put into casks, after being mitten with water. This oxide, fused with three parts of sand and one of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, forms a blue glass; which, when pounded, sifted, and afterwards ground in mills, included in large casks, forms faults. The blue of zaffre is the most <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and fixed of all the colours that can be employed in vitrification. It suffers no change from the most violent fire. It is successfully employed to give shades of blue to enamels, and to the crystal-glass made in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of some opaque and transparent precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli, the turquois, the sapphire, and others of this kind.

ZAMA

Pages 472-474

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Chamane, a district of Cappadocia, of unknown situation.—Another Zama, of Mesoopotamia, the Saorcas, to the south of Nitibis.—A third, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, distant five days' journey to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>: it was the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of the kings of Numidia, hence called Zama Regia. It stood in a plain; was stronger by art than <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; richly supplied with every necessary; and abounding in men, and every weapon both of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> and annoyance. The last of these is remarkable for the decisive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the two greatest commanders in the world, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> the Carthaginian and Scipio Africanus. Of this engagement, the most important perhaps that ever was fought, Mr Hooke gives the following account. "Scipio drew up his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> after the Roman manner, except that he placed the cohorts of the Principes directly behind those of the Hastati, so as to leave sufficient space for the enemy's elephants to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through..." from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> to rear. C. Laelius was posted on the left wing with the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and Massinissa with his Numidians on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. The intervals of the first line Scipio filled up with his Velites, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-armed troops, ordering them, upon a signal given, to begin the battle; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they were repulsed, or broke by the elephants, to run back through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> before mentioned, and continue on their flight till they were got behind the Triarii. Those that were wounded, or in danger of being overtaken, were to turn off to the right and left through the spaces between the lines, and that way escape to the rear. "The army thus drawn up, Scipio went from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> to rank, urging his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to consider the consequences of a defeat and the rewards of victory: on the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> (for they had no town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> strong enough to protect them); on the other, not only a lasting superiority over Carthage, but the empire of the rest of the world. "Hannibal ranged all his elephants, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of above 82, in one front. Behind these he placed his mercenaries, consisting of 12,000 men, Ligurians, Gauls, Baleares, and Mauritians. "The new levies of Carthaginians and other Africans, together with 4000 Macedonians, under a general named Sopater, composed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> line. And in the rear of all, at the distance of about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURLONG">furlong</a>, he posted his Italian troops, in whom he chiefly confided. The Carthaginian horse formed his right wing, the Numidians his left. "He ordered their several leaders to exhort their troops not to be discouraged by their own weakness, but to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the hope of victory in him and his Italian army; and particularly directed the captains of the Carthaginians to represent to them what would be the fate of their wives and children <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the event of this battle should not prove successful. The general himself, walking through the ranks of his Italian troops, called upon them to be mindful of the 17 campaigns in which they had been fellow-soldiers with him; and of that constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of victories by which they had extinguished in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> all hope of ever being conquerors. He urged them to remember, above all, the battles of Trebia, Thrasymenus, and Cannae; with any of which the approaching battle was in no wise to be compared, either with respect to the bravery or the number of the enemy. "The Romans were yet unfoiled, and in the height of their strength, when you first met them in the field; nevertheless you vanquished them. The soldiers now before us are either the children of the vanquished, or the remains of those whom you have often put to flight in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Maintain therefore your general's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and your own, and establish to yourselves the name of invincible, by which you are become famous throughout the world." "When the Numidians of the two armies had skirmished a while, Hannibal ordered the managers of the elephants to drive them upon the enemy. Some of the beasts, frightened at the noise of the trumpets and other instruments of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> which founded on all sides, immediately ran back amongst the Numidians of the Carthaginian left wing, and put them into confusion; which Massinissa taking advantage of, entirely routed them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> destruction was made of the Velites by the rest of the elephants, till these also being terrified, some of them ran through the void spaces of the Roman army which Scipio had left for that purpose; others falling in among the cavalry of the enemy's right wing, gave Laelius the same opportunity against the Carthaginian horse as had been given to Massinissa against the Numidian, and of which the Roman did not fail to make the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. After this the infantry of the foremost lines joined battle. Hannibal's mercenaries had the advantage in the beginning of the conflict; but the Roman Hastati, followed and encouraged by the Principes, who exhorted them to fight manfully, and showed themselves ready to assist them, bravely frustrated the attack, and at length gained ground upon the enemy. The mercenaries not being feebly supported by their second line, and therefore thinking themselves betrayed, they in their retreat fell furiously upon the Africans; so that these, the Hastati coming up, were obliged to fight for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> both against their own mercenaries and the enemy. When the two Carthaginian lines had ceased their mutual rage, they joined their strength; and though now but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> throng of men, broke the Hastati: but then the Principes advancing to the assistance of the latter, restored the battle; and most of the Africans and mercenaries were here cut off. Hannibal did not advance to their relief, the Roman Triarii not having yet engaged, and the Principes being still in good order; and left the routed Africans and mercenaries should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the ranks of his Italian soldiers, he commanded these to present their spears at those who fled to them for protection, which obliged the runaways to move off to the right and left. "The ground over which the Romans must <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> before they could attack Hannibal being strewed with heaps of dead bodies and weapons, and being slippery with blood, Scipio feared that the order of his battalions would be broke, should he pass it hastily. To avoid this mischief, he commanded the Hastati to give over the pursuit, and halt where they were, opposite to the enemy's centre: after which, having sent all his wounded to the rear, he advanced leisurely with the Principes and Triarii, and placed them on the wings of the Hastati. Then followed a sharp engagement, in which victory was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and eagerly disputed. It would seem that the Romans, though superior in number, were once upon the point of losing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; for Polybius tells us, that Massinissa and Laelius came very feebly, and as if sent from heaven, to their assistance. These generals being returned from the pursuit of the cavalry, fell suddenly upon the rear of Hannibal's men, most of whom were cut off in their ranks; and of those that fled, very few escaped the horse, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> all around being a plain. "There died of the Carthaginians in the fight above 20,000, and almost the like number were taken prisoners. The loss on the side of the Romans amounted to about 2000 men. Hannibal escaped with a few horse to Adrumetum, having performed every thing in the engagement which could be expected from a great general. His army (says Polybius) could not have been more skilfully drawn up. For as the order of the Roman battalions makes it extremely difficult to break them, the Carthaginian wisely placed his elephants in the front, that they might put the enemy in confusion before the armies should engage. In his first line he placed the mercenaries; men bold and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, but not well well disciplined, that by their impetuosity he might give a check to the ardour of the Romans. The Africans and Carthaginians, whose courage he doubted, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>- ed in the middle between the mercenaries and his Ita- lian soldiers, that they might be forced to fight, or at least that the Romans, by slaughtering them, might fa- tigue themselves and blunt their weapons. Last of all, he drew up the troops he had disciplined himself, and in whom he chiefly confided, at a good distance from the second line, that they might not be broken by the route of the Africans and mercenaries, and kept them in reserve for a vigorous attack upon a tired and weak- ened enemy."

ZANGUEBAR

Pages 474-474

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, between three degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and 18 south. It includes several petty kingdoms, in which the Portuguese have various settlements. The inhabitants, except those converted by the Portuguese, are all Mahometans <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> idolaters; and the latter much the more numerous. The names of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> terri- tories are Mombaza, Lamon, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELINDA">Melinda</a>, Quioia, and Mo- sambique. The Portuguese have built several forts in Mombaza and Mosambique, and have settled several colonies there. They trade with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> for slaves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, ostrich-feathers, wax, and drugs. The productions are much the same as in other parts of Afri- ca between the tropics.

ZANONIA

Pages 474-474

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class pentan- dria. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZANTE

Pages 474-474

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Mediterranean, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Morea, 19 miles south-east of the island of Cephalonia, belonging to the Venetians. It is about 24 miles in length and 12 in breadth, and very pleasant and fertile; but its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> consist in currants, with which it greatly abounds. They are cultivated in a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain, under the shelter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> on the shore of this island; for which reason the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> has greater power to bring them to perfect maturity. The town called Zante may contain near 20,000 inhabitants; the whole island contains about 40,000. The houses are low, on account of the frequent earthquakes, for scarce a year passes without one; however, they do no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> damage. The natives speak both Greek and Ita- lian. There are very few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> among them; but they have a bishop as well as the Greeks. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has no fortifications, but there is a fortress upon an eminence planted with cannon. In one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this island is a place which thakes when trod upon like a quagmire; and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> which throws out a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of bitumen, especially at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of an earthquake. It serves instead of pitch to pay the bottoms of the ships, and about 100 barrels in a year are used for this pur- pose. There are about 50 villages in the island; but no other large town beside Zante. It is seated on the eastern side of the island, and has a good harbour. The English and Dutch have each a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> here. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21. 3. N. Lat. 37° 53'.

ZANTHOXYLUM

Pages 474-474

the Toothache-tree, a ge- nus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class of dioecia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 46th order, Hederaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZAPATA

Pages 474-474

a kind of feast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> held in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the courts of certain princes, on St Nicholas's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; wherein people hide presents in the shoes or slip- pers of those they would do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to, in such a manner as may surprise them on the morrow when they come to dress; being done in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the practice of St Nicholas, who used in the night-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to throw purses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in at the windows to marry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> maids withal.

ZEA

Pages 474-475
INDIAN CORN; a genus of plants of the clas- monocotyledon. See Botany Index.—There is only one spe- cies, the Maya, maize. The Indians in New England, and many other parts of America, had no other vege- table but maize or Indian corn for making their bread. They call it weachin; and in the United States of A- merica there is much of the bread of the country made of this grain, not of the European corn. In Italy and Germany also there is a species of maize which is the food of the poor inhabitants. The ear of the maize yields a much greater quan- tity of grain than any of our corn ears. There are com- monly about eight rows of grain in the ear, often more, if the ground be good. Each of these rows contains at least 30 grains, and each of these gives much more flour than a grain of any of our corn. The grains are usually either white or yellowish; but sometimes they are red, bluish, greenish, or olive-coloured, and some- times striped and variegated. This sort of grain, though so essentially necessary to the natives of the place, is yet liable to many accidents. It does not ripen till the end of September; so that the rains often fall heavy upon it while on the stalk, and the birds in general peck it when it is soft and unripe. Nature has, to defend it from these accidents, covered it with a thick hull, which keeps off slight rains very well; but the birds, if not frightened away, often eat through it, and devour a great quantity of the grain. There are three or four varieties of maize in different parts of America. That of Virginia is very tall and robust, growing to seven or eight feet high; that of New England is shorter and lower. And the Indians farther up in the country have a yet smaller kind in common use. The stalk of the maize is jointed like the sugar-cane; it is very soft and juicy, and the juice is so sweet and saccharine, that a syrup, as sweet as that of sugar, has been often made of it; and things sweetened with it have been found not distinguishable from those done with sugar. It has not been tried yet whether it will crystallize into sugar; but in all probability it will. The Americans plant this corn any time from the be- ginning of March to the beginning of June; but the best season is the middle of April. The savage Indians, who knew nothing of our account of months, used to guide themselves in the seed-time of this useful plant by the budding of some particular trees of that country, and by the coming up of a sort of fish into their rivers which they call the aloofe. These things were both so regular, that they were in no danger of mistaking the time. The manner of planting maize is in rows, at equal di- stances, every way about five or six feet. They open the earth with a hoe, taking away the surface to three or four inches deep, and of the breadth of the hoe; then they throw in a little of the finer earth, so as to leave the hoe four inches deep or thereabouts, and in each of these holes they place four or five grains at a little distance from one another. If two or three of these grow up, it is very well; some of them are usual- ly destroyed either by the birds or other animals. When the young plants appear, they hoe up the weeds from time to time; and when the stalk gathers some strength, they raise the earth a little about it, and continue this at every hoeing till it begins to put forth the ears; then they enlarge the hill of earth, round the root, to the size of a hop-hill, and after this they leave it till the time of harvest, without any farther care. When they gather the ears, they either immediately strip off the corn, or else hang up the ears, tied in traces at distances from one another; for if they are laid near together, they will heat and rot or else sprout and grow; but kept cool and separate, they will remain good all the winter. The best method is to thrust out the corn as soon as the harvest is over, to dry it well on mats in the sun, and then lay it up in holes of the ground, well lined with mats, grass, or the like, and afterwards covered at top with more earth. The most careful among the Indians use this method, and this sort of subterranean granary always proves good. The uses of this plant among the Indians are very many. The great article is the making their bread of it; but besides this, the stalks, when cut up before they are too much dried, are an excellent winter food for cattle; but they usually leave them on the ground for the cattle to feed on. The husks about the ear are usually separated from the rest, and make a particular sort of fodder, not inferior to our hay. The Indian women have a way of splitting them into narrow parts, and then they weave them artificially into baskets and many other toys. The original way of eating the grain among the Indians was this: they boiled it whole in water till it swelled and became tender, and then they fed on it either alone or ate it with their fish and venison instead of bread. After this, they found the way of boiling it into a sort of pudding, after bruising it in a mortar; but the way of reducing it to flour is the best of all. They do this by parching it carefully in the fire, without burning, and then beating it in mortars and setting it. This flour they lay up in bags as their constant provision, and take it out with them when they go to war, eating it either dry or with water. The English have contrived, by mixing it into a stiff paste, either by itself or with rye or wheat-meal, fermenting it with leaven or yeast, and baking it in a hot oven, to make good bread of it. They have likewise found out a method of making good beer, either of the bread or by malting the grain.

ZEAL

Pages 475-475

passionate ardour for any person <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cause. It is most frequently used to denote a strong and warm <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the distinguishing doctrines or worship of some particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Thus we say, a zealous Calvinist, Arminian, or Papist; though we may likewise with the greatest propriety say of an upright and benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, that he is zealous of good works.

ZEALAND

Pages 475-475

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the United <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, consisting of eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>, bounded by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, from which they are separated by a narrow channel on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; by Brabant on the east; by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, from which they are separated by one of the branches of the Scheldt, on the south; and by the German ocean on the west. [Merged from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">NEW ZEALAND</a>, p.475] a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, first discovered by Tasman, the Dutch navigator, in the year 1642, who gave it the name of Staten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, though it has been generally distinguished in our maps and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> by the name of New Zealand, and supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a southern continent: but it is now known, from the late discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook who sailed round it, to consist of two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> islands, divided from each other by a strait four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. They are situated between the latitudes of 34 and 48 degrees south, and between the longitudes of 166 and 180 degrees east from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. One of these islands is for the most part mountainous, rather barren, and but thinly inhabited; but the other is much more fertile, and of a better appearance. In the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks and Dr Solander, every kind of European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, grain, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, would flourish here in the utmost luxuriance. From the vegetables found here, it is supposed that the winters are milder than those in England, and the summers not hotter, though more equally warm; so that it is imagined, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this country were settled by people from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, they would, with moderate industry, be soon supplied, not only with the necessaries, but the luxuries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance. Here are forests of vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, filled with very large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> trees; and near 400 plants were found here that had not been described by the naturalists. The inhabitants of New Zealand are stout and robust, and equal in stature to the largest Europeans. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> in general is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, but in few deeper than that of the Spaniard who has been exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and in many not so deep; and both sexes have good features. Their dress is very uncouth, and they mark their bodies in a manner similar to the inhabitants of Tahiti, and which is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TATTOOING">tattooing</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> weapons are lances, darts, and a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-axes; and they have generally shown themselves very hostile to the Europeans who have visited them.

ZEALOTS

Pages 475-475

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Jews, so called from their pretended zeal for God's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. ZEBRA. See Equus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZECHARIAH

Pages 475-475

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. See Scripture, No 80.

ZEMBLA

Pages 475-475

Nova, a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, lying in the Northern ocean, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Russia, from which it is separated by the strait of Waigate. It has no inhabitants except wild beasts, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> foxes and bears. In 1595 a Dutch vessel was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and the ship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> were obliged to winter here.

ZEMINDAR

Pages 475-476

in its original meaning, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> landholder of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>; but it is now more strictly applicable to those who have their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> constituted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> confirmed by a patent or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, by which they hold their lands or zemindaries upon certain conditions. It appears from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that, in times <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the irruption of the Mahomedans, the rajas who held their residence at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, and possessed the sovereignty of Hindostan, deputed officers to collect their revenues. The word zemindar is Persian, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> can have had no currency in the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, until it was introduced by the people of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. When the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Shehab-ul-Dien Ghory conquered the empire of Hindostan at the end of the 12th century, he left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Cutub-ul-Dien to be his viceroy at Delhi, and administer the government of Hindostan. From that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the customs and practices of the Mahomedans began gradually to be established in India: their armies were sent into the countries of the reduced rajas, under the command of omrahs, in order to preserve the conquest; and lands were allotted to them to defray the expense. From hence arose the system of Jaghireddary in Hindostan. But when these Omrah Jaghireddars had established their own strength, several of them rebelled against the imperial authority, and aspired at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Thus circumstanced, the emperors, in order to obviate these mischiefs, thought it would be more politic to commit the management of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the native Hindoos, who had most distinguished themselves by the readiness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of their obedience to the sovereign power. In pursuance of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, districts were allotted to numbers of them under a reasonable revenue (Jummah Monalib), which they were required to pay in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the governors of the provinces, deputed from the emperor. And in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> any one of the omrahs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> governors should swerve from his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZEMINDARS">zemindars</a> of that country were to exert themselves in such a manner as should check rebellion, and restore good government. For this purpose, grants of zemindary were frequently conferred upon such of the Hindoos as were obedient; describing their apportionment of the country; and every person who had received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> under the authority of the crown was thereby fully invested with the functions of zemindar. The functions of a zemindar are, 1st, The preservation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of their respective boundaries from traitors and insurgents. 2dly, The tranquillity of the subjects, the abundance of cultivators, and increase of his revenue. 3dly, The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of thieves and robbers, the prevention of crimes, and the destruction of highwaymen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of these objects is considered in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> grant as the discharge of office to the sovereign; and on that account the word office (khidmat) is employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEWANNY">Dewanny</a> Sunnud for a zemindary. It was a rule in the times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> emperors, that when any of the zemindars died, their effects and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> were sequestrated by the government. After which, in consideration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, which is incumbent on sovereigns, and elevates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the employer, funnuds for the office of zemindar were granted to the children of the deceased zemindar; and no other person was accepted, because the inhabitants could never feel for any stranger the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> and affection which they naturally entertain for the family of their zemindar, and would have been afflicted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any other had been put over them. For this reason, the emperors, considering it as a means of conciliating the minds of the people, graciously fixed and confirmed the children of the deceased zemindar in the office of their fathers and grandfathers, by issuing new funnuds to transfer the possession to them. By degrees zemindaries became truly heritable property, which, however, could be transferred by gift or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> from one family to another. They could likewise be forfeited to the sovereign, by the zemindar's deviating from his allegiance, neglecting to pay his tribute, or to discharge the duties of his station. It is universally known, says Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Routh Boughton, that, when the three provinces of Bengal, Bihar, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORISSA">Orissa</a>, were ceded to the British East India <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, the country was distributed among the zemindars and talookdars or holders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, who paid a stipulated revenue, by twelve instalments, to the sovereign power or its delegates. They assembled at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> in the beginning of every Bengal year (commencing in April), in order to complete their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> payments, and make up their annual accounts; to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a> to be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> upon their several remittances in various coins for the purpose of reducing them to one standard, or adjust their concerns with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>; to petition for remissions on account of storms, drought, inundation, disturbances, and such like; to make their representations of the state and occurrences of their districts: after all which they entered upon the collections of the new year; of which, however, they were not permitted to begin receiving the rents from their own farmers, till they had completely closed the accounts of the preceding year, so that they might not encroach upon the new rents, to make up the deficiency of the past. Our author proves, we think completely, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the zemindars to transfer their possessions, either by inheritance to their children, or, with the consent of the sovereign, to other families; and he argues strenuously and successfully against the bad policy, as well as injustice, of interfering with these rights, as long as the zemindars discharge the duties of their several stations.

ZEND

Pages 476-477
or ZENDAVESTA, a book ascribed to Zoroaster, and containing his pretended revelations; which the ancient Magicians and modern Persees, called also Gours, observe reverence in the same manner as the Christians do the Bible, and the Mahometans the Koran, making it the sole rule both of their faith and manners. The word, it is said, originally signifies any instrument for kindling fire, and is applied to this book to denote its aptitude for kindling the flame of religion in the hearts of those who read it. The Zend contains a reformed system of Magianism, teaching that there is a Supreme Being, eternal, self-existent, and independent, who created both light and darkness, out of which he made all other things; that these are in a state of conflict, which will continue till the end of the world; that then there shall be a general resurrection and judgement; and that just retribution shall shall be rendered unto men according to their works; that the angel of darkness with his followers shall be configned to a place of everlasting darkness and punishment, and the angel of light with his disciples introduced into a state of everlasting light and happiness; after which light and darkness shall no more interfere with each other. The Zend also enjoins the constant maintenance of sacred fires and fire temples for religious worship; the distinction of clean and unclean beasts; the payment of tithes to priests, which are to be of one family or tribe; a multitude of washings and purifications, resembling those of the Jewish law; and a variety of rules and exhortations for the exercise of benevolence and charity. In this book there are many passages evidently taken out of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, particularly out of the Psalms of David: The author represents Adam and Eve as the first parents of all mankind, gives in substance the same account of the creation and deluge with Moses, differing indeed with regard to the former, by converting the six days of the Mosaic account into five times, comprehending in the whole 365 days; and speaks also of Abraham, Joseph, Moses, and Solomon. Moreover, Dr Baumgarten affirms, that this work contains doctrines, opinions, and facts, actually borrowed from the Jews, Christians, and Mahometans; whence, and from other circumstances, he concludes that both the history and writings of this prophet were probably invented in the later ages, when the fire-worshippers under the Mahometan government thought fit to vindicate their religion from the suspicion of idolatry. At whatever period the Zend may have been written, we are assured by Dr Hyde, that it is in the pure old Persian language, and in the character called Pahlavi. Some parts of it contain the original next, and others Zoroaster's second thoughts subjoined, for explaining more fully his doctrine. These were occasioned by the opposition of adversaries, and unforeseen circumstances which occurred during the fabrication of the imposture. About 300 years ago, when the old Persian language had become antiquated and little understood, one of the deacons or high-priests among the Persians composed the Sadda, which is a compendium in the vulgar or modern Persian tongue, of those parts of the Zend that relate to religion, or a kind of code of canons and precepts, drawn from the theological writings of Zoroaster, serving as an authoritative rule of faith and practice for his followers. This Sadda is written in a low kind of Persian verse, and as Dr Hyde informs us, it is bonorum et malorum farra, having many good and pious things, and others very superstitious and trifling. See Perseus and Zoroaster.

ZENITH

Pages 477-478

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the vertical point, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a point in the heavens directly over our heads. ZENO Eleates, an eminent Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEA">Elea</a> about 504 years before Christ. He was a zealous friend of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and is celebrated for his courageous and successful opposition to tyrants; but the inconclusiveness of the stories related by different writers concerning him in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> destroys their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. He chose to reside in his small native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Elea rather than at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, because it afforded freer scope to his independent and generous spirit, which could not easily submit to the restraints of authority. It is related, that he vindicated the warmth with which he received reproach, by saying, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> I were indifferent to censure, I should also be indifferent to praise." The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the dialectic art has been improperly ascribed to Zeno; but there can be no doubt that this philosopher, and other metaphysical disputants in the Eleatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, employed much ingenuity and subtlety in exhibiting examples of most of the logical arts, which were afterwards reduced to rule by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and others. According to Aristotle, he taught, that nothing can be produced either from that which is similar or dissimilar; that there is only one being, God; who is eternal, homogeneous, and spherical, neither finite nor infinite, neither quiescent nor moveable; that there are many worlds; that there is in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>; that all bodies are composed of four elements, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and moisture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and dryness; and that the body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> an equal mixture of these four elements. He argued with great subtlety against the possibility of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. If Seneca's account of this philosopher deserves credit, he reached the highest point of skepticism, and denied the real existence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, that after all that has been advanced by different writers, it is impossible to determine whether Zeno understood the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> one, metaphysically, logically, or physically; or whether he admitted or denied a nature properly divine. Zeno, the founder of the sect of the Stoics, was born about 300 years before Christ at Citium, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> having been originally peopled by a colony of Phoenicians, Zeno is sometimes called a Phoenician. His father was by profession a merchant, but discovering in the youth a strong propensity towards learning, he early devoted him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In his mercantile capacity he had frequent occasion to visit Athens, where he purchased for his son several of the writings of the most eminent Socratic philosophers. These he read with great avidity; and when he was about 30 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he determined to take a voyage to a city which was so celebrated both as a mart of trade and of science. If it be true, as some writers relate, that he brought with him a valuable cargo of Phoenician purple, which was lost by shipwreck upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Piraeus, this circumstance <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> account for the facility with which he at first attached himself to a sect whose leading principle was the contempt of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. Upon his first arrival in Athens, going accidentally into the shop of a bookseller, he took up a volume of the Commentaries of Xenophon; and after <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> a few <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, was so much delighted with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and formed so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> an idea of the author, that he asked the bookseller where he might meet with such men. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATES">Crates</a> the Cynic philosopher happening at that instant to be passing by, the bookseller pointed to him, and said, "Follow that man." Zeno attended upon the instructions of Crates, and was so well pleased with his doctrine that he became one of his disciples. But though he admired the general principles of the Cynic school, he could not easily reconcile himself to their peculiar manners. Besides, his inquisitive turn of mind would not allow him to adopt that indifference to every scientific inquiry which was one of the characteristic distinctions of the sect. He therefore attended upon other matters, who professed to instruct their disciples in the nature and causes of things. When Crates, displeased at his following other philosophers, attempted to drag him by force out of the school of Stilpo, Zeno said to him, "You may take my body, but Stilpo has laid hold of my mind." After continuing to attend upon the lectures of Stilpo several years, he passed over to other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, particularly to those of Xenocrates and Diodorus Cronus. By the latter he was instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALECTICS">dialectics</a>. He was so much delighted with this branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, that he presented to his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pecuniary gratuity, in return for his free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of some of his ingenious subtleties. At last, after attending almost every other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, he offered himself as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMO">Polemo</a>. This philosopher appears to have been aware, that Zeno's intention in thus removing from one school to another, was to collect materials from various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> for a new system of his own; for, when he came into Polemo's school, he said to him, "I am no stranger, Zeno, to your Phoenician arts; I perceive that your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is to creep flyly into my garden, and steal away my fruit." Polemo was not mistaken in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. Having made himself master of the tenets of others, Zeno determined to become the founder of a new sect. The place which he made choice of for his school was a public portico, adorned with the pictures of Polygnotus, and other eminent painters. It was the most famous portico in Athens, and called, by way of eminence, Στοά, "the Porch." It was from this circumstance that the followers of Zeno were called Stoics. In his person Zeno was tall and slender; his aspect was severe, and his brow contracted. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was feeble, but he preserved his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> by great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>. The supplies of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> consisted of figs, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; notwithstanding which, he was frequently honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of great men. In public company, to avoid every appearance of an assuming temper, he <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> took the lowest place. Indeed so great was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, that he seldom chose to mingle with a crowd, or wished for the company of more than two or three friends at once. He paid more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to neatness and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a> in external appearance than the Cynic philosophers. In his dress indeed he was plain, and in all his expenses frugal; but this is not to be imputed to avarice, but a contempt of external magnificence. He showed as much respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> as to the rich; and conversed freely with persons of the meanest occupations. He had only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, or, according to Seneca, none. Zeno lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> age of 98; and at last, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an accident, voluntarily put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. As he was walking out of his school he fell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> broke one of his fingers; upon which he was so affected with a consciousness of infirmity, that, striking the earth, he said, "Why am I thus importuned? I obey thy summons;" and immediately went home and strangled himself. He died in the first year of the 120th Olympiad. The Athenians, at the request of Antigonus, erected a monument to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> in the Ceramicum. We ought not to confound the two Zenos already mentioned with

ZEPHANIAH

Pages 478-478

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. See SCRIPTURE, no. 79.

ZEPHYR

Pages 478-478

the WEST <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which blows from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> point of the horizon opposite to the east.

ZEPHYRUS

Pages 478-478

one of the Pagan deities, was represented as the son of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>, and the lover of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Chloris, according to the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of Flora according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and as presiding over the growth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. He is described as giving a refreshing coolness to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> by his soft and agreeable breath, and as moderating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> by fanning the air with his silken wings. He is depicted under the form of a youth, with a very tender air, with wings resembling those of the butterfly, and with his head crowned with a variety of flowers. As the poets of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome lived in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, they are lavish in their praise of this beneficent deity, and under his name describe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and advantage they received from the western breezes. ZERDA. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">CANIS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZERTA

Pages 478-478

the ZERTE, a fish caught in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and some other places, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the chub, and called by authors capito anodromus, and the alike. It seldom grows to more than two pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and at times lives in rivers, at times in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and is esteemed a very well tailed fish, especially a little before the season of its spawning. The zerta is that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cyprinus described by Gellner and others under the name of capito anodromus.

ZEST

Pages 478-478

the woody thick skin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERING">quartering</a> the kernel of a walnut; prescribed by some physicians, when dried and taken with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine, as a remedy against the gravel. ZEST is also used for a chip of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lemon peel; such as is usually squeezed into ale, wine, &c., to give it a flavour; or the fine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> which spurts out of that peel on squeezing it.

ZEUXIS

Pages 478-479

a celebrated painter of antiquity, flourished about 400 years before Christ. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERACLEA">Heraclea</a>; but as there have been many cities of that name, it cannot be certainly determined which of them had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his birth. Some learned men, however, conjecture, that it was the Heraclea near Crotona in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> to a much higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a> had left it; discovered the art of properly disposing of lights and shades, and particularly excelled in colouring. He amassed immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>; and then resolved to sell no more of his pictures, but gave them away; saying very frankly, "That he could not set a price on them equal to their value." Before this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he made people pay for seeing them; and nobody was admitted to see his Helena without ready <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which occasioned the wags calling his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> Helen the Courtezan. It is not known whether this Helen of Zeuxis was the same with that which was at Rome in Pliny's time, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which he painted for the inhabitants Zeuxis inhabitants of Crotona to be hung up in the temple of Juno: this last he painted from five beautiful girls of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, copying from each her greatest excellencies. Pliny observes, that this admirable painter, disputing for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of painting with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARRHASIUS">Parrhasius</a>, painted some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> so naturally, that the birds flew <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to peck them. Parrhasius, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, painted a curtain so very artfully, that Zeuxis mistaking it for a real one that hid his rival's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, ordered the curtain to be drawn aside, to show what Parrhasius had done; but having found his mistake, he ingeniously confessed himself vanquished, since he had only imposed upon birds, while Parrhasius had deceived even a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the art. Another time he painted a boy loaded with grapes; when the birds also flew to this picture, at which he was vexed; and confessed, that this work was not sufficiently finished, since had he painted the boy as perfectly as the grapes, the birds would have been afraid of him. Archelaus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of Zeuxis's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> for the embellishment of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. One of this painter's finest pieces was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> strangling some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> in his cradle, in the presence of his affrighted mother: but he himself chiefly effeemed his Athleta, or Champion, under which he placed a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> that afterwards became very famous, and in which he says, "That it was easier to criticise than to imitate the picture." He made a present of his Alcmena to the Argigarettes. Zeuxis did not value himself on speedily finishing his pictures; but knowing that Agatharchus gloried in his being able to paint with ease and in a little time, he said, "That for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> he, on the contrary, gloried in his slowness; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in painting, it was because he painted for eternity." Verrius Flaccus says, that Zeuxis having painted an old woman, he laughed so very heartily at the sight of this picture, that he died: but as no other of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> has mentioned this particular, there is the greatest reason to believe it fabulous. Carlo Dati has composed in Italian the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Zeuxis, with those of Parrhasius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APELLES">Apelles</a>, and Protogenes. This work was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1667.

ZICLAG

Pages 479-479
or ZIKLAG, in Ancient Geography, a town of the tribe of Simeon, on the borders of the Philistines (Joshua xv. and xix.), but in the hands of the Philistines till David's time (1 Sam. xxvii. and xxx.)

ZIMENT-WATER

Pages 479-479
Copper-water, the name by which some have called water found in places where there are copper-mines, which is impregnated with particles of that metal. The most famous spring of this kind is about a mile distant from Newohl in Hungary, in the great copper-mine called by the Germans herrngrundt. The water in this mine is found at different depths, and is received into basins, for the purpose of separating the copper from it: in some of these it is much more fated with this metal than in others, and will make the supposed change of iron into that metal much sooner. The most common pieces of iron used in the experiments are horseshoes, nails, and the like; and they are found very little altered in shape, after the operation, except that their surfaces are more raised. The water appears greenish in the basin, where it stands; but if a glass of it be taken up, it looks clear as crystal: it has no smell, but a strong vitriolic astringent taste, insomuch that the lips and tongue are blistered and scorched upon tasting it.

ZINC

Pages 479-481

a metallic substance, formerly considered as one of the brittle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to the distinction of the older chemists, a semi-metal or an imperfect metal, because it was found to be destitute of some of the properties of other metals which were considered as perfect. For an account of the properties and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of zinc, as they were then known, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of its ores, see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index. But in the progress of chemical discovery it has been found that zinc is not a less perfect metal than others; for in the year 1805, it was announced that a patent was granted to Mr. Hobson and Sylvester of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a> for a method of manufacturing zinc. From their discovery it appears, that zinc raised to a temperature of between 210° and 300° of Fahrenheit, is not only very malleable, but may be passed through rollers, or drawn into wire. After the metal has been treated in this manner, it does not return to its former brittleness, but continues soft, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, and extensible, and may be applied to many uses for which this metal was before thought unfit. We must, however, notice, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> claim to the discovery of rendering zinc ductile and malleable, has been made by Mr. Lowry, in favour of a Mr. Sheffield of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERTON">Somerton</a>. Twenty years before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Mr. Hobson and Sylvester's patent being announced, Mr. Sheffield, in making an alloy of some blende, was impatient to examine the metal, struck an ingot for the purpose of breaking it while it was yet hot, but was much surprised to find instead of being brittle, and breaking with the usual fracture of zinc, it was extremely tough, and when he succeeded in breaking it, after many bendings backward and forward, it exhibited a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>-grained <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> texture. At first he doubted of the metal being zinc, but he repeated the experiment on what he knew to be pure metal, and obtained the same result; and from this he concluded that zinc at a certain temperature is equally malleable and ductile with other metals. This he found to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> it into wire, and laminating it between rollers, by which he produced plates not exceeding the 1/30 of an inch, and possessing the strength and tenacity of silver. Since the time that our article Chemistry was printed, the decomposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, soda, the alkaline earths, and some other bodies which were formerly considered as simple, or were only conjectured from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, has been effected by Mr. Davy; and as we were disposed to entertain hopes that something new might be added to the unexpected and brilliant discoveries of that celebrated chemist, we have deferred, till near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, giving any account of them. This is the reason that the fact was merely announced under the words Potash and Soda, and a reference made to Galvanic Trough, under which it was intended to give a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> employed in the experiments which led to the discoveries alluded to. For the same reason we were induced to make a farther reference to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, because zinc is one of the metallic substances usually employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of galvanic apparatus. We shall therefore here employ a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, 1st, In a description of the improvements which have been made in the construction of galvanic apparatus; and, 2d, We shall lay before our readers a view of the discoveries in galvanic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> since the treatises on Chemistry and <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol9.html#article-GALVANISM">Galvanism</a> in this work were printed. Galvanic Apparatus.—A very considerable improvement has been made on the construction of galvanic batteries, by which they are rendered, not only more convenient and manageable, but far more powerful. Under the article Galvanism, we have described particularly the construction of the galvanic trough, and we have noticed that the soldering of the plates of zinc and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> employed for this purpose was attended with considerable difficulty. In the new method of construction the plates are not soldered together, but are merely connected by means of a metallic arc. In this way each <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of plates can be removed from the trough at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, for the purpose of examining and cleaning them. The new apparatus is constructed precisely on the same principle as the couronne de Taffes, proposed by Volta, and described at p. 333 of Galvanism. The trough employed in this apparatus is prepared in the same way as when the plates of zinc and copper soldered together were fixed in it by means of cement; but in place of the metallic plates, plates of glass, or some other non-conducting substance, are introduced and secured by cement, so that there shall be no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the different cells into which the liquid is introduced. The plates of zinc and copper connected by means of the metallic arc, at the distance of about half an inch, are placed in different cells, having a plate of glass between each pair of plates. Each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> then contains a plate of each of the metals, which are unconnected, excepting through the medium of the liquid which is to be the conductor of the electricity. It is scarcely necessary to mention, that the proper order of arrangement shall be observed, so that throughout the whole trough or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> there shall be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of zinc, copper, and liquid. Beside the convenience and simplicity of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of constructing galvanic troughs, it possesses this farther advantage of being more powerful, because instead of one surface of the plates, as in the former construction of this apparatus, both surfaces are exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of electricity, and therefore the power is greatly increased. A farther improvement, it is said, has been made in constructing batteries of this kind, which consists in employing troughs of Wedgwood's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, with partitions of the same material, instead of wooden troughs with partitions of glass. This improvement was first suggested by Dr Babington. The following is the account of the construction of galvanic apparatus, with the view of ascertaining in what way the greatest effect might be produced, with the least waste of power and expense. The experiments which we are now to mention were made by Mr Children*. For this purpose a battery was constructed on the new method, with plates of copper and zinc, connected by leaden strips, soldered on the top of each pair of plates. Twenty pairs of plates were employed, and each plate was four feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> by two feet wide. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of surface exposed amounted to 92,160 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inches; the trough was made of wood, with wooden partitions, covered with cement, to resist the action of the acid employed. The battery was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with a mixture of three parts of fuming nitrous, and one of sulphuric acid, diluted with thirty of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> employed was 120 gallons. With this apparatus the following experiments were made. Exper. 1. Eighteen inches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">platina</a> wire, of one-thirtieth of an inch diameter were completely fused in about twenty seconds. Exper. 2. Three feet of the same wire were heated to a bright <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, visible by strong daylight. Exper. 3. Four feet of the same wire were rendered very hot, but not perceptibly red by daylight. Exper. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">Charcoal</a> burnt with intense brilliancy. Exper. 5. Ten inches of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-wire of 1/4th of an inch diameter, were barely fused; three feet of the same wire were not ignited. Exper. 6. No effect was produced on imperfect conductors. Exper. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> leaves of the electrometer were not affected. Exper. 8. When the cuticle was dry, no shock was given by the battery, and it was scarcely perceptible when the skin was wet. To <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> the effects of this apparatus with another differing in the size and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of plates, the author employed 200 pairs of plates, each about two inches square, placed in half pint pots of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s ware. The same liquid was employed, with the addition of a fresh portion of sulphuric acid, in the proportion of about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a pint to a gallon. The experiments with this apparatus gave the following results. Exper. 1. Potash and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARYTES">barytes</a> were readily decomposed. Exper. 2. The metallization of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">ammonia</a> was produced with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> facility. Exper. 3. Charcoal was vividly ignited. Exper. 4. The gold leaves of the electrometer diverged considerably. Exper. 5. After the battery was in action three hours, it gave a vivid spark; at the end of 24 hours it metallized ammonia; at the end of 41 hours it was nearly exhausted.
