From the results of these experiments, Mr Children concludes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the mode of action of the voltaic battery proposed by Mr Davy is confirmed, namely, that the intensity increases with the number, and the quantity with the extent of the series. This is proved by the effects produced on the platina and iron wires, in the 1st and 5th experiments with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> battery, as well as by the experiments on imperfect conductors in the small apparatus; for as the platina wire is a perfect conductor, and not liable to oxidation, it allows the electricities to be freely transmitted, and from the immense quantity given out from a surface of such extent, they evolve, on their mutual annihilation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> sufficient to raise the temperature of the platina to the point of fusion. But a very small portion of the electricity passes through the iron wire, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its easy oxidation, and the thin coat of oxide formed on its surface. This arises from the low state of the intensity of the electricity, as appears also from its want of power on the gold leaves of the electrometer. From the same deficient intensity, the decomposition of barytes could not be effected by the large battery, and the same battery exhibited a very weak action on imperfect conductors; but the small battery exerted great power on that class of bodies, and decomposed them readily, although its surface was 30 times less than the surface of the great battery; but the number... Zinc. ber of plates was nearly ten times greater. Another circumstance, of considerable importance in conducting experiments by means of the galvanic battery, is here noticed by the author; that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> action of the small battery was owing to the large capacity of the cells containing a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> quantity of liquor. And beside this advantage he adds, that with very large combinations, a certain distance between each pair of plates is absolutely necessary to prevent spontaneous discharges, which are accompanied with vivid flashes of electric <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. This happened to the author with a battery of 1250 four-inch plates, constructed according to the new method. From the experiments and observations, some of which we have detailed, and for others we refer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> itself, the author concludes with the following remarks: "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> effect of a voltaic apparatus seems to be in the compound ratio of the number and size of the plates. The intensity of the electricity being as the former, the quantity given out as the latter, consequently regard must be had, in its construction, to the purpose for which it is designed. For experiments on imperfect conductors, very large plates are to be preferred, a small number of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably be sufficient; but where the resistance of imperfect conductors is to be overcome, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> must be great, but the size of the plates may be small: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> quantity and intensity be both required, then a large number of large plates will be necessary. For general purposes, four inches square will be found to be the most convenient size." * Ibid. 37. Discoveries in Galvanism.—At the close of the article Galvanism, we noticed some experiments which were made about the beginning of the year 1805, which seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the conclusion, that muriatic acid and soda were formed by means of galvanic electricity. In experiments on the decomposition of water, which was supposed to be in a state of the utmost purity, the appearance of muriatic acid and soda was adduced in support of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. The accuracy of this conclusion, which seemed to be at variance with known facts, excited doubt, and probably led to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> which was undertaken by Mr Davy, and carried on with great ingenuity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> by the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, till it terminated in the brilliant discoveries, an account of which we are now to detail. Mr Davy's researches in galvanism, an account of which he laid before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in a memoir entitled, On Some Chemical Agencies of Electricity, may be considered as the first step in this train of investigation.

ZINNIA

Pages 497-497

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class Syngenesia, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZINZENDORFF

Pages 497-498

NICHOLAS <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">LEWIS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">COUNT</a>, was the noted founder of the German <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> called Moravians, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Herrnhuters, or, as they pretend, the reformer of that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. From his own narrative it appears, that when he came of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in 1721, his thoughts were wholly bent on gathering together a little society of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>, among whom he might live, and who should entirely employ themselves in exercises of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> under him. He accordingly purchased an estate at Bertholdorff in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>, where, being joined by some followers, he gave the curacy of the village to a person of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>; and Bertholdorff soon became talked of for a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of piety. One Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, a carpenter, brought a few profylites from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>: they began a new town about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from the village, where Count Zinzendorff fixed his residence among them, and whither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of Moravians flocked and established themselves under his protection; so that in 1732 their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> amounted to 600. An adjacent hill, called the Huthberg, gave occasion to these colonists to call their new settlement Huth des Herrn, and afterwards Herrnhuth; which may be interpreted "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> or protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>:" and from this the whole sect have taken their name. The count spared neither pains nor art to propagate his opinions; he went himself all over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and at least twice to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; and sent missionaries throughout the world. Count Zinzendorff died in 1760. Those who wish to know more of the Moravian tenets may consult Rimius's account. account of them, translated in 1753. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UNITED_BRETHREN">UNITED BRETHREN</a>.

ZION

Pages 498-498
or Sion, in Ancient Geography, a very famous mountain, standing on the north side of the city of Jerusalem, (Pfal. xlvii. 2;) containing the upper city, built by King David; and where stood the royal palace, (Josephus.) A part of Zion, situated at its extremity, was called Millo, or in the city of David, (2 Chron. xxii. 5.) Modern travellers, who have been upon the spot, say, that Zion is the whole of the mountain, on which Jerusalem stands at this day, though not to the extent in which it anciently stood on the same mountain, as appears Phil. ix. 12, 15. lxv. i. lxxxv. 2, 3. If. lxii. 1. It is swelled into several eminences or tops; as Moriah, Acra Bezetha, and Zion, a particular eminence or mount, and Zion Proper, &c. encompassed on three sides, east, west, and south, with one continued very deep and steep valley; by means of which it was impregnable on these three sides, and always attacked and taken, according to Josephus, by the enemy on the north side, where Mount Zion became level, and the vales of Gihon and Jehoshaphat gradually lose themselves. This deep and steep valley incontestably constitutes the compass of the old Jerusalem on those three sides, as plainly appears to any person who has been upon the spot. On that particular top of the mount called Zion stood the fortress of the Jebusites; which being afterwards taken by David, came to be called the City of David, where he had his royal residence and kept his court. That part of the valley which lay to the east was called Jehoshaphat's, having Mount Olivet lying beyond it; that to the south Gelinnou; and that to the west, Gihon, from cognominal mountains lying beyond it. At the west end of Gihon, without the city, stood Golgotha or Calvary. The pretended Golgotha, shown at this day within the walls, is the spurious brat of interested and fraudulent monks, (Korte.) There is another Zion, the same with Hermon.

ZIPH

Pages 498-498
or Siph, in Ancient Geography, the name of a wilderness or desert in the tribe of Judah, where David was fugitive; lying to the south-east of Hebron; so called from Ziph or Siph, a twofold town in this tribe; the one more to the south towards Idumea, on the confines of Eleutheropolis, (Jerome;) the other eight miles to the east of Hebron, towards the Dead Sea, inclining southwards, because near Mount Carmel. Here was a mountain, mentioned 1 Sam. xxiii. 14, in which David abode, said by Jerome to be rugged, dismal, and always overcast. Ziphim, Zipheri, or Ziphenes, the inhabitants of Ziph, ver. 19.

ZIRCHNITZER-SEE

Pages 498-498

otherwise called the Lake of Czirnitz, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>, is about one German <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four English miles in length, and half as much in breadth; contains three beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and is encompassed at some distance with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and forests. But what is most remarkable is, that it disappears generally once a year, about St John's or St James's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, running off through holes or pits in the bottom; sometimes it disappears twice or thrice a-year, and sometimes even in winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be dry. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it has been known to continue two or three years without running off. Of the holes or pits, there are five much larger than the rest, each of which successively, when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> runs off, stands empty five days; so that the whole lake becomes dry in 25. As soon as the beginning of the ebb is observed, the filling in the pits begins, which belongs to five seignories. The fish, which are carp, tench, pike, eels, and two other sorts called Schleien and Ruten, are caught by laying nets over the holes. Mr Keyfeler tells us, that upon the ringing of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> at Zirknitz, when the waters begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, the peasants, both men and women, run to the pools quite naked.

ZIRCON

Pages 498-498

a mineral substance containing a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZISCA

Pages 498-498

JOHN, a famous general of the forces of the Hulites, in the 15th century, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> educated at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, in the reign of Wenceslaus. He entered very young into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and after distinguishing himself on several occasions, lost an eye in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, whence he was called Zisca, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> One-eyed. At length the Reformation, begun by John Hus, spreading through almost all Bohemia, Zisca placed himself at the head of the Hulites, and had soon under his command a body of 40,000 men. With this army he gained several victories over those of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, who carried on a kind of crusade against them, and built a town in an advantageous situation, to which he gave the name of Tabor; whence the Hulites were afterwards called Taborites. Zisca lost his other eye by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> at the siege of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rubi; but this did not prevent his continuing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, his fighting battles, and gaining several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> victories, among which was that of Ausig on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, in which 9000 of the enemy were left dead on the field. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Sigismund, alarmed at his progress, caused very advantageous proposals to be offered to him; which he readily accepted, and set out to meet Sigismund, but died on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>. He ordered that his body should be left a prey to the birds and wild beasts; and that a drum should be made of his skin, being persuaded that the enemy would fly as soon as they heard the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. It is added, that the Hulites executed his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>; and that the news of this order made such an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the disturbed imaginations of the German Papists, that in many battles they actually fled at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> of the drum with the utmost precipitation, leaving their baggage and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> behind them.

ZIZANIA

Pages 498-498

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the clas monoccia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 4th order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZODIAC

Pages 498-499

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> circle, whose middle is the ecliptic, and its extremes two circles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> thereto, at such a distance from it as to bound <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> comprehend the excursions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, (see <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>.) It is a curious enough fact, that the solar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> zodiac is the same in substance with that of the Greeks, and yet that it has not been borrowed either from the Greeks or the Arabians. The identity, or at least striking similarity, of the division, is universally known; and M. Montuela has endeavoured to prove, that the Brahmins received it from the Arabs. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, we believe, has been very generally admitted; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of the Asiatic Researches, the accomplished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> Sir William Jones has proved unanswerably, that neither of those nations borrowed that division from the other; that it has been known among the the Hindoos from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial; and that it was probably invented by the first progenitors of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, whom he considers as the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of mankind, before their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>. The question is not of importance sufficiently general, frustrated as we are by the limits prescribed us, for our entering into the dispute; but we think it our duty to mention it, that our astronomical readers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they think it worth their while, may have recourse to the original writers for further information.

ZOEGEA

Pages 499-499

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class syngenesia, S:z <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZONE

Pages 499-499

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the teraqueous globe with respect to the different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> found in the different parts thereof. The zones are denominated torrid, frigid, and temperate. The torrid zone is a band, surrounding the teraqueous globe, and terminated by the two tropics. Its breadth is 46° 58'. The equator, running through the middle of it, divides it into two equal parts, each containing 23° 29'. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> imagined the torrid zone uninhabitable. The temperate zones are contained between the tropics and the polar circles. The breadth of each is 43° 2'. The frigid zones are segments of the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, terminated, one by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTARCTIC">antarctic</a>, and the other by the arctic circle. The breadth of each is 46° 58'.

ZOOLOGY

Pages 499-500

is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> which relates to animals. See Natural History. ZOOPHYTES. The name Zoophytes, Zoophyta (i.e., animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, from ζωος, animal, and φυτα, plant), has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> appropriated to a numerous assemblage of marine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> aqueous productions, which have puzzled the ingenuity of naturalists to ascertain their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the chain of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>'s works, and which have been alternately ranked among vegetable and animal, and sometimes even among mineral substances. At length, however, they seem, by general consent, to have been configned over to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and, with the addition of several tribes from the Linnaean orders of Intestina, Molusca, and Infusoria, have, by Cuvier and his colleagues of the French school, been elevated to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a separate class. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a>, No. II. In the Linnaean system, the zoophytes of earlier <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> naturalists constitute the 4th order of the class Vermes, and as such have been enumerated under Helminthology; but, as the circumscribed limits of that article did not admit of our describing or figuring many <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, we shall now so far as possible supply that deficiency by selecting a few of the most curious or interesting species of the Linnaean zoophytes; and we shall take this opportunity of making a few observations on some of the genera to which they belong. Figs. 1. and 2. represent the Tubipora musica, crimson tubipore, or organ coral; one of the most elegant of these singular productions. This species is distinguished from its congeners by having the tubes connected into fascicules or bundles, and separated from each other by transverse membranous partitions. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> consists of upright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> tubes, rising over each other by stages, something like the cells of a honeycomb. These tubes vary in height from half an inch to an inch; and are from one-tenth to one-eighth of an inch in diameter. Examined internally, they appear to contain a smaller tube divided at certain distances by radiated partitions (see fig. 2.), by means of which the transverse septa sometimes communicate with each other. These trans- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> septa are of unequal heights. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the mass Zoophyte is a deep purple, or a rich crimson. The size of the mass varies considerably; but specimens have been obtained of from a foot to three feet in diameter. It is found abundantly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, and on the shores of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In its recent state it is covered with a mucous or gelatinous substance, which pervades the whole mass and enters within each tube. The inhabiting animal is not certainly ascertained, but seems to be allied to the nereis tribe. Figs. 3. and 4. exhibit two views of the Madrepora fungites, or mushroom madreporite. This body fungites exactly resembles a mushroom, that it has very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Fig. 3. & 4. ly been regarded as that vegetable in a state of petrifaction; but recent observations seem to prove that it is formed by small animals like medusae. The convex side of this madreporite is conical, sometimes obtusely pointed, and exhibits on its surface those stellate pores which form the distinguishing character of the genus, while the concave surface is divided into numerous radiated furrows so as to represent the gills of a mushroom. When first obtained, it is of a delicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> colour, especially on the concave part, but it soon acquires a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or yellowish tinge. It is found of various sizes, from an inch to five inches in diameter. It is met with chiefly in the Indian ocean and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> sea. At fig. 5. is represented that elegant coral called by Isis hippocampus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and white jointed coral of Ellis. The specific character of this coral is that it is composed of white striated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> united by black junctures; but this structure is not visible till after the coral has been freed from a whitish soft fleshy part, with which the branches are covered in their natural state. See fig. 6. It is found chiefly in the Indian seas, and varies in height from a few inches to nearly two feet. Fig. 7. represents the Antipathes myrophylla, var. Antipathes row antipathor, or sea-garrow, of its natural size; while myophy- Plate DLXXXIX. This is one of those zoophytes which in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and appearance almost exactly resemble some of the vegetable tribes, and hence have received the names of sea-fern, sea-cypress, sea-fennel, &c. From their colour they are usually denominated black coral. This species, though one of the smallest, is not the least elegant of the tribe. It consists of numerous branches, composed of very slender pinnae arranged in no certain order. The whole coral is seldom above a foot in height, and rough on its outer surface. This also is a native of the Indian ocean, being found more especially on the coasts of the Molucca islands, and is sometimes met with in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> South sea. Fig. 9. exhibits a specimen of red coral, the Isis nobilis, Gorgonia lis of Linné, and Gorgonia nobilis of later naturalists. This substance, though now nearly exploded from our cabinets for its intrinsic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and elegant appearance; but when examined on its native beds, or soon after being fished up, it shews a very different surface from that under which we usually see it. Fig. 9. represents it as prepared for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> by being deprived of its fleety animal bark or coating, but retaining the striated appearance which marks its specific character; but fig. 10. exhibits a piece of it in its natural state, with polypes extruded from the fleety coat, and shewing still more distinctly at the extremities the streaks below. Red coral is found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> beds or reefs in several parts of the Mediterranean sea, and coral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> are established on the coasts and near the islands. A fishery of this kind in the straits of Messina is minutely described by Spallanzani in his *Travels in the two Sicilies*, vol. iv. To tear the coral from the rocks they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a machine composed of two beams tied across each other, and furnished with a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> to sink them, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of loose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and several strong nets to entangle the branches of the coral. To this machine is attached a strong rope, which is held by the fishers, and serves both to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> and to draw it up when the coral is entangled. Several boats go in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, each containing eight men, and the fishery lasts from April to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. The quantity collected every year amounts on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> to twelve Sicilian quintals, each equal to 250 pounds <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, and each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> usually sells for about four shillings and sixpence. They do not fish on the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> oftener than once in ten years, as this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is deemed necessary for the coral to acquire its full size and vigour. Another beautiful species of gorgonia, the *Gorgonia ceratophyta*, is figured at fig. 11. This is distinguished by its dichotomous flat-tipped stem, and ascending branches. The outer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is of a purplish colour, and the branches are furnished with two rows of scattered pores from which the polypi appear. It is found in the Mediterranean, and sometimes on the eastern coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Nearly allied to the gorgonias is the species of alcyonium represented at fig. 12. This is the *Alcyonium gorgonoides* of Gmelin. It is of a cinereous colour, of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> flecky consistence, having radiated warty cellules. It is found on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of South America, especially near the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Curaçoa. The zoophytes which naturalists distinguish by the generic name alcyonium, sometimes form independent bodies of a rounded form, such as those called the *sea-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>*, *sea-fish*, &c.; or cover the surface of shells and other marine bodies like a kind of bark. Their internal part or base is friable, and, when dried, appears to be composed of fine fibres, which are either longitudinal, as in the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, diverging, or circular. This base is covered with a soft crust, that in drying assumes a leathery consistence, and is pierced with numerous little cells inhabited by polypi. In some species these cells are dispersed over the whole surface of the coral, while in others they are confined to particular spots or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>. They are all inhabitants of the ocean, where they are usually fixed to rocks or other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies. In the article *Helminthology* we have sufficiently treated of the nature and properties of the sponges, and have there mentioned particularly the common or *official sponge*. At fig. 13, is represented a more curious species, the *Sp. tubulosa* or *filifera*, the tubular or pipey sponge. This consists of simple upright, attenuated, rigid tubes, tuberculated on the outer surface, which is of a black colour. It is found in the seas that wash the coasts of America. The *filiferae* are a tribe of insignificant zoophytes, which seem scarcely entitled to the rank which they hold in the animal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. They are formed of a congeries of superficial cells, placed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, like those of a honeycomb, but generally occupying only a single surface. Sometimes this substance forms a coating to some other marine body, at others it is unattached and forms a floating foliaceous mass or mat. The species represented at fig. 14, is one of the most curious, and is described by Ellis under the name of *English sea-mat*, called in the *Linnaean Transactions*, vol. v. *Flustra arenosa*. It is composed of sandy particles agglutinated together with slime, and in shape resembles the fore part of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s hoof. It is very friable, and so thin as to be easily broken. These *filiferae* are found abundantly on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, and about Holy-head on the Welsh coast. Fig. 15 represents a specimen of *Sertularia fetacea*, *Sertularia* the small sea-bristle coralline of Ellis, of its natural size; *fetacea*, and fig. 16 shows the same specimen considerably magnified. This species is distinguished by being simply pinnated, with bent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> pinnae, furnished with very remote processes growing only on one side, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> axillary ovaries. It is one of the smallest and most delicate of the tribe, seldom exceeding an inch and a half in height. It is very common, and is found on the British coasts. None of the zoophytes bear a nearer resemblance to vegetables than the *fertulariae*. Their creeping roots, their branched stem, and tufts of feeming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> (the polypine processes) give them all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of plants. Hence they were long considered as *sea-mats*, and described by botanists under that name. See Ray's *Synopsis*, p. 38, and 39. When attentively examined, however, their animal nature <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarcely be disputed. Externally they are composed of a horny substance, perfectly transparent, and through this may be distinguished the animal substance traversing the centre of the stem and branches like the pith of a plant, and appearing externally as little knots or protuberances in the form of tentaculated polypes. These extraneous polypes are considered by Cuvier, (*Tableau Elementaire*, p. 768.) not as distinct animals, but only as parts of the same animal which constitutes the sole inhabitant of the *fertulariae*. These zoophytes adhere to rocks, shells, &c., by creeping roots, and appear to propagate by means of eggs. They are among the most common of this class of animated beings. The *Pennatulæ* or *Sea-pens* constitute a very curious tribe of zoophytes, which are completely locomotive, and swim in the manner of fishes. They consist of Fig. 17, an internal bone or rather horny substance, covered with a sensitive flecky coat. Their lower extremity is simple like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of a quill, while the upper extremity is expanded into a flattened part, that is generally composed of pinnae like the barbs of a quill, though it is sometimes merely a simple expanded mass furnished with polypine processes. Fig. 17 represents one of the most common *sea-pens* properly so called, the *Pennatula phosphorea*, phosphorescent pennatula, of its natural size. It has a flecky stem, a rough middle part, and imbricated pinnae. The pinnae are furnished on one side with lesser pinnae, at the extremities of which appear the polypes. See fig. 18, which shows one of the separate pinnae, a little magnified. This species is of a fine red or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> scarlet colour, and when alive exhibits a strong phosphorescent light, so as to render distinctly visible objects that are near it. It is pretty common on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and is sometimes taken in the fisherman's nets, or adhering to the baits. For figures of two other Linnaean zoophytes, the *Tubularia magnifica*, and *<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">Hydra</a> viridis*, see Plate CCLIII.

ZOOTOMY

Pages 500-507

the art of defining animals <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> living creatures, being the same with anatomy. See ANATOMY.

ZORILLE

Pages 507-507

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of weasel which inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and other parts of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; and is said to be remarkable for its feil odour.

ZOROASTER

Pages 507-507
or ZERDUSHT, a celebrated ancient philosopher, said to have been the reformer or the founder of the religion of the magi. It is wholly uncertain how many eminent men the name of Zoroaster belonged. Some have maintained that there was but one Zoroaster, and that he was a Persian; others have said that there were six eminent founders of philosophy of this name. Ham the son of Noah, Moses, Osiris, Mithras, and others, both gods and men, have by different writers been asserted to have been the same with Zoroaster. Many different opinions have also been advanced concerning the time in which he flourished. Aristotle and Pliny fix his date at so remote a period as 6000 years before the death of Plato. According to Laertius, he flourished 600 years before the Trojan war; according to Suidas, 500. If, in the midst of so much uncertainty, anything can be advanced with the appearance of probability, it seems to be this; that there was a Zoroaster, a Perseus-Median, who flourished about the time of Darius Hystaspes; and that besides him there was another Zoroaster, who lived in a much more remote period among the Babylonians, and taught them astronomy. The Greek and Arabian writers are agreed concerning the existence of the Persian Zoroaster; and the ancients unanimously ascribe to a philosopher, whom they call Zoroaster, the origin of the Chaldean astronomy, which is certainly of much earlier date than the time of Hystaspes: it seems, therefore, necessary to suppose a Chaldean Zoroaster distinct from the Persian. Concerning this Zoroaster, however, nothing more is known, than that he flourished towards the beginning of the Babylonian empire, and was the father of the Chaldean astrology and magic. All the writings that have been ascribed to Zoroaster are unquestionably spurious.

ZOSIMUS

Pages 507-507

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historian who lived at the end of the fourth and beginning of the fifth century. There are five books of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> extant; in the first of which he runs over the Roman affairs in a very succinct manner from Augustus to Diocletian; the other five are written more distinctly. Zosimus was a zealous Pagan; whence we find him frequently inveighing with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bitterness against the Christian princes, particularly against Constantine the Great, and the elder Theodosius. His history has been published with the Latin version of Leunclavius at Frankfort, 1590, with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> historians of Rome, in folio; and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 8vo, 1679.

ZOSTERA

Pages 507-507

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class gynandra, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> order, Piperite. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZUG

Pages 507-507

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, bounded on the east and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, on the south by Schweiz and Lucern, and on the west by the canton of Lucern and the Freye-Amt <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Free Provinces. It is not above 12 miles either way; but very populous and fruitful, yielding wine, wheat, chestnuts, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, in its vales, and excellent pasture on its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The inhabitants of this canton are staunch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. It lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is democratical. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in it abounding in fish, particularly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> carps, pikes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of trouts called roelts; as well as several woods full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>. Zug, which gives name to it, and is its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, stands on the east side of a lake of the same name, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and is a strong neat town, containing a priory and two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>.

ZUGMA

Pages 478-478

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, whereby an adjective <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> verb which agrees with a nearer word, is also, by way of supplement, referred to another more remote.

ZUILA

Pages 507-507

a town in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZZAN">Fezzan</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, which stands on a space of about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in circuit, but was formerly of much greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. The environs are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and fertile, planted with groves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> trees, and the inhabitants pay much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. N. Lat. 27. 29. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 39.

ZUINGLIUS

Pages 507-507

ULRICUS, an able and zealous reformer, who laid the foundation of a separation from Rome in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> did like in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, was born at Wildehausen in 1487. While he officiated as preacher at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, a Franciscan fent by Leo X. came to publish indulgences there; against which Zuinglius, after the example of Luther, declaimed powerfully. In the course of this opposition he started a new doctrine, which he called Evangelical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a>; and from the beginning of 1519 to 1523, he preached not only against indulgences, but against other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. But though Zuinglius made no less progress than Luther, he conducted himself with more moderation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>; and wishing to have the concurrence of the civil powers, procured two assemblies to be called at Zurich: by the first, he was authorized to proceed as he had begun; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the outward worship and ceremonies of the church of Rome were abolished. During these transactions, Zuinglius published several books in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his doctrines; but treating of the eucharist, and prescribing a form of celebrating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a> different from Luther, he was involved in violent disputes with the rest of his reforming brethren. Respecting the divine decrees, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Zuinglius and his followers differed very little from that of the Pelagians: and instead of declaring with Calvin, that the church is a separate independent body, vested with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a> for itself, Zuinglius ascribed to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and unbounded power in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> matters, allowing at the same time a certain subordination among the ministers of the church. This was abundantly agreeable to the magistrates of Zurich; but the rest of the Swiss cantons disallowing of their proceedings, other assemblies were called, and things tending to tumult, both sides had recourse to arms; when Zuinglius, who began as a preacher, died in arms as a soldier, in 1531. His works are in four volumes folio.

ZURICH

Pages 508-508

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of the same name in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, stands in a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, near where the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a> flows from the lake that takes its name from the town, 23 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHAFFHAUSEN">Schaffhausen</a>, and 114 from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. After having been ruined by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTILA">Attila</a> the Hun, it is said to have been restored by Thurius, son of Theodoric <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, from whom it took the name of Thuricum, corrupted afterwards into that of Zurich. It is fortified in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> way, and has wide ditches, faced with free-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. There are five arsenals in it, well stored with arms and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>; an academy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, having 15 professors; a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, or chamber of rarities; a stately town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the pillars in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of which are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, streaked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; and a town library. The sovereignty and administration of all affairs are lodged in the greater and lesser <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, out of which are chosen the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>-officers, as the councils are out of the 13 companies of burgheers. There are several other councils or colleges, each of which has its particular department. Here are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cotton, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; this being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the greatest trade in all Switzerland. The town is well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> by and from its lake. The streets are neat, and houses well built, but not magnificent. In the town-library are several letters to Bullinger from Lady Jane Gray, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>. In one of the arsenals is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of William Tell, dressed and armed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Swiss manner, with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow whence he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> that struck the apple off his child's head. Both men and women are so fond of music, that there are few of them that cannot play on some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a burgher goes out of town, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> enters it, without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, they are liable to be fined. No persons, whatever their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or office may be, are exempted from the fumitory laws. The burgomasters, who are the same as the advoyers at Bern, have the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of excellence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> here are neat and well endowed. The environs are pleasant and fruitful; for which it is not a little indebted to the lake. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it which is next Zurich is called the Lower Lake, and the other end the Upper. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, or great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> here, is collegiate. The present city is said to owe its origin to a nunnery, founded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> I., near where the ancient Tigurum stood. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 30. N. Lat. 47. 20.

ZUTPHEN

Pages 508-508

a strong and considerable town of the United Provinces in Guelderland, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. It has a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and is surrounded with walls. It was taken by the French in 1674, who in 1674 delivered it up to the States-General. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Berkel and Yssel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVENTER">Deventer</a>, and 55 east by south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 0. N. Lat. 52. 10.

ZUYDER-ZEE

Pages 508-508

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the German ocean, which extends from south to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> in the United Provinces, between Friesland, Over-Yssel, Guelderland, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. It is so called from its situation towards the south. It is said that the Zuyder-zee was formerly a lake, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is swallowed up which united North-Holland with Friesland.

ZYGOMA

Pages 508-508

a bone of the head, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather an union or assemblage of two protuberances or eminences of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. See Bones of the Head, under Anatomy.

ZYGOMATICUS

Pages 508-508

a muscle of the head, arising from the Os Zygoma, whence its name, and terminating at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the lips.

ZYGOPHYLLUM

Pages 508-508

BEAN-CATER, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the class of decandria, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 14th order, Cruciferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ZYMOSIMETER

Pages 508-508

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> proposed by Swammerdam, in his book De Respiratione, with which to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> occasioned by the mixture of different matters, and the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> which those matters acquire in fermenting; the same instrument is employed to ascertain the heat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a> of the blood of animals.
